entries.title: SQL Injection
entries.summary: User input reaches a database query without being separated from the query's own syntax, so it can change what the query does.
entries.description:
The application builds SQL queries by combining fixed query text with values supplied by the user, without separating the two. A value containing SQL syntax, such as a quotation mark followed by further clauses, is therefore read by the database as part of the query rather than as data.

SQL injection can be confirmed directly, where the database's own error messages or the results of an altered query are returned in the response, or indirectly, where the application behaves differently when a condition injected into the query is true or false, or responds more slowly when a delay is injected. The indirect forms, often called blind SQL injection, are as exploitable as the direct one, though extracting data takes more requests.

Automated tools such as sqlmap can identify and exploit every form of the weakness with little effort, so the risk does not depend on an attacker's skill.
entries.impact: An attacker can read any data the application's database account can reach, including other users' records, password hashes and secrets kept in the database. Depending on that account's privileges and the database platform, they may also be able to change or delete data, bypass authentication, read or write files on the database server, or run operating system commands on it, which would give them a foothold in the hosting environment.
entries.remediation:
Keep data apart from query syntax everywhere the application talks to its database:

  • Use parameterised queries (prepared statements) for every query that includes a value from outside the application, including values from cookies, headers and other systems. The query text is fixed, and each value is bound to a placeholder, so it can never change the query's structure.
  • Where an ORM or query builder is used, use its parameter binding rather than its raw query methods, and review any place where query text is built by concatenation.
  • Where a value cannot be a parameter, such as a column name or sort direction, choose it from a fixed allowlist in the code rather than passing the user's value through.
  • Run the application's database account with the least privilege it needs, without administrative rights, file access or the ability to run system commands.

As an interim measure, a web application firewall rule can block known injection payloads on the affected parameters, but it can be bypassed and is not a fix. Confirm the fix by repeating the original test against every affected parameter and confirming that the injected syntax is treated as a literal value.

patterns: \bSQL[- ]?injection\b|\bSQLi\b|sql-injection|\b(database|SQL) query built from user-controlled sources\b|\btainted SQL\b|\bformatted SQL query\b

entries.title: NoSQL Injection
entries.summary: User input reaches a NoSQL database query as query structure, such as an operator or server-side JavaScript, so it can change which records the query selects.
entries.description:
The application builds queries for a NoSQL database, typically MongoDB or a similar document store, from values supplied by the user without making sure each value is treated as plain data. Where the request parser turns input such as username[$ne]=x, or a JSON body in which a field holds an object rather than a string, into an object, that object is passed into the query and its keys are read as query operators. A condition meant to match one value can then match every record, or stop restricting the query at all. Some NoSQL databases also accept query text, and building that text by concatenation causes the same problem as SQL injection.

NoSQL injection typically shows itself on a test when an operator supplied in place of a value changes the result: a login that succeeds with $ne in the password field, a search that returns every record, or a response that differs when a $regex condition is true or false, which allows values to be extracted one character at a time. Where input reaches an operator that runs JavaScript on the database server, such as $where, injected code is evaluated as well. Scanners detect only some forms, so the weakness is usually confirmed manually by replaying requests with operator objects, arrays and changed data types.
entries.impact: An attacker can typically bypass authentication checks that depend on a database lookup and read records beyond those the query was meant to return, including other users' data and stored credentials or tokens. Depending on the operation affected, they may also be able to change records. Where server-side JavaScript is enabled and reachable, injected code runs in the database's restricted scripting environment, which can be used to extract data or exhaust the server's resources. No authentication is needed when the affected query sits behind a login form or a public search.
entries.remediation:
Make sure every value from outside the application reaches the database as a value of the expected type, never as query structure:

  • Validate the type of each input before it is used in a query. Where a string or number is expected, reject objects and arrays and convert the value explicitly, so that operator syntax cannot be supplied.
  • Reject or remove keys that begin with $ or contain . in any object built from user input, and validate request bodies against a strict schema that rejects unexpected properties.
  • Use the driver's or object mapper's query builder with fixed field names and operators, and never build query documents or query text by concatenating user input.
  • Avoid operators that evaluate JavaScript, such as $where, $function and $accumulator, and disable server-side JavaScript execution in the database configuration where it is not needed.
  • Run the application with a database account limited to the collections and operations it needs.

As an interim measure, a web application firewall rule that blocks parameter names and JSON keys beginning with $ reduces exposure, but it can be bypassed. Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with operator objects, arrays and type changes in each affected parameter, and checking that they are rejected or treated as literal values.

entries.title: OS Command Injection
entries.summary: User input is placed into an operating system command that the application runs through a shell, so it can add to or change the commands that are executed.
entries.description:
The application runs operating system commands to carry out some of its functions, such as network diagnostics, file conversion or image processing, and includes values supplied by the user in the command line. When the command is passed to a shell, characters such as ;, |, &, backticks, $() and line breaks let the input end the intended command and start another, which the server then runs with the application's privileges.

The weakness can be confirmed directly, where the output of an injected command appears in the response, or blind, where the response does not change but an injected delay (such as sleep or a repeated ping) slows it down, or an injected DNS lookup or HTTP request reaches a server under the tester's control. Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP and other scanners report OS command injection using these techniques, and tools such as Commix automate its exploitation.

A related form, argument injection, occurs when the application avoids the shell but lets input that begins with a hyphen be read as an option of the program it runs, which for some programs allows files to be written or further commands to be run.
entries.impact: An attacker can run arbitrary commands on the server with the privileges of the account that runs the application. This typically allows them to read and change application data and configuration, including credentials for databases and other services, to install persistent access such as a web shell, and to use the server to reach other systems on the internal network. Where the application runs as a highly privileged account, the whole host is compromised. No user interaction is needed, and the weakness is commonly found and exploited by automated tools.
entries.remediation:
Remove the shell from the path between user input and the operating system:

  • Where possible, perform the task with a library or built-in API instead of an external program, for example a DNS or file-handling library rather than calling nslookup or cp.
  • Where running an external program cannot be avoided, call it directly with an argument array and without a shell, for example execFile() or spawn() without the shell option in Node.js, subprocess.run() with a list of arguments and shell=False in Python, or ProcessBuilder in Java. Never build a single command string from user input.
  • Validate each value against a strict allowlist of expected formats, such as a hostname or IP address, and place -- before user-supplied arguments where the program supports it, so that they cannot be read as options.
  • Run the application with the least privilege it needs, and restrict what its account can execute and reach on the network.

As an interim measure, a web application firewall rule can block shell metacharacters on the affected parameters, but it can be bypassed and is not a fix. Confirm the fix by repeating the time-based and out-of-band tests against every affected parameter.

entries.title: Server-Side Code Injection
entries.summary: User input is evaluated as program code by the server-side language, for example through eval(), so an attacker can run their own code on the server.
entries.description:
The application passes values supplied by the user to a function that compiles or evaluates code in its own language at run time, such as eval() in PHP, Python, JavaScript or Ruby, exec() in Python, the Function constructor in JavaScript, or a scripting engine that evaluates expressions held in strings. Developers often do this to evaluate a calculation, to read a data structure written in the language's own syntax, or to call a function chosen by name. Any input that reaches such a function can contain code of the attacker's choosing.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when an expression supplied in a parameter is evaluated, for example an arithmetic expression whose result appears in the response, a language function that produces a measurable delay, or an error message showing that the input was parsed as code. Scanners such as Burp Suite report it under language-specific names, such as PHP code injection or server-side JavaScript code injection, and blind cases are confirmed with time delays or out-of-band DNS lookups.

It differs from OS command injection in that the input is run by the application's own interpreter rather than by a shell, although the interpreter can usually be used to run operating system commands as well.
entries.impact: An attacker can run arbitrary code inside the application process, with the privileges of the account that runs it. From there they can read and modify all data the application can reach, read secrets from its configuration and environment, run operating system commands and use the server as a foothold for attacking internal systems. No user interaction is needed, and the impact is usually equivalent to a full compromise of the application server.
entries.remediation:
Do not evaluate user input as code:

  • Remove calls that evaluate strings as code, such as eval(), exec(), new Function() and string arguments to setTimeout(), wherever any part of the string can come from outside the application.
  • Replace them with alternatives that treat input as data: a JSON parser instead of evaluating object literals, a purpose-built expression parser or arithmetic library for user-defined formulas, and an allowlist that maps permitted names to functions instead of resolving a function or class from a user-supplied name.
  • Do not rely on blocklists or on language-level sandboxes, such as the Node.js vm module, to make evaluation safe. They are routinely bypassed and are not security boundaries.
  • Run the application with the least privilege it needs and with restricted outbound network access, so that successful exploitation gives as little as possible.

As an interim measure, disable the affected feature or block the affected parameters at a web application firewall until the code is changed. Confirm the fix by repeating the original test with expressions that would produce a measurable result or delay if evaluated, and checking that they are treated as literal text.

entries.title: Server-Side Template Injection
entries.summary: User input is placed into a server-side template's source rather than passed to it as data, so the template engine evaluates the attacker's template syntax.
entries.description:
The application uses a server-side template engine, such as Jinja2, Twig, FreeMarker, Velocity, Thymeleaf, Smarty or ERB, and builds part of a template's source from values supplied by the user, for example by concatenating a name into a greeting template or by letting users edit email or page templates. The engine then evaluates any template syntax in that input. Because template languages can call methods on the objects passed to them, an attacker can often move from those objects to the language's runtime and execute code.

Server-side template injection typically shows itself on a test when a template expression in a parameter is evaluated, for example ${7*7} or its double curly-brace equivalent returning 49 in the response, or when a malformed expression produces an error naming the engine. Further expressions identify the engine, after which known payloads for that engine confirm the impact. Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP report the weakness as server-side template injection, and tools such as SSTImap automate its detection and exploitation.

It should be distinguished from cross-site scripting: the input is evaluated on the server, so a payload that appears as harmless text in the browser may still be running code on the host.
entries.impact: In most template engines an attacker can run arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the application, giving them its data, configuration secrets and access to the underlying host. Where the engine runs in a sandbox or is logic-less, the impact may be limited to reading the objects and variables passed to the template, which can still include sensitive data, and sandbox escapes are published regularly. No user interaction is needed, although some affected features, such as those that let users customise templates, require an account.
entries.remediation:
Keep user input out of template source:

  • Load templates only from fixed files or strings defined by the application, and pass user input to them as context variables. Never concatenate or format user input into a template before it is rendered.
  • Where users must be able to customise content, offer a limited set of placeholders that the application substitutes itself, or use a logic-less template language that cannot call methods or reach application objects.
  • If a full template engine must process templates written by users, enable its sandbox (for example Jinja2's sandboxed environment or Twig's sandbox extension) with a strict allowlist, pass only simple data objects into the context, and render in an isolated, low-privilege process or container.
  • Keep the template engine and framework up to date, as sandbox escapes are fixed in new releases.

As an interim measure, disable any feature that lets users edit templates. Confirm the fix by repeating the original expressions and checking that they appear in the response as literal text.

entries.title: Expression Language Injection
entries.summary: User input is evaluated by an expression language such as Java EL, SpEL or OGNL, letting an attacker run expressions that reach the server's runtime and execute code.
entries.description:
Java web frameworks use expression languages to bind data and evaluate logic: the Jakarta Expression Language in JSP and JSF pages, the Spring Expression Language (SpEL), OGNL in Apache Struts, and MVEL in some rule and workflow engines. Expression language injection occurs when a value supplied by the user is evaluated as an expression, for example when it is passed to an expression parser, placed into a validation or error message that the framework interpolates, or processed twice by a tag that evaluates its attribute. These languages can create objects and call methods, so an injected expression can usually reach the Java runtime and start operating system processes.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when an expression such as ${7*7} or #{7*7} in a parameter or header is returned as 49, or when it causes an error from the expression parser. Burp Suite reports it as expression language injection. Several widely exploited vulnerabilities in Struts and Spring products were of this type, so it is found in outdated frameworks as well as in custom code.
entries.impact: An attacker can usually run arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the Java process, giving them the application's data, its configuration secrets and access to the host. Where the expression is evaluated in a restricted context, the impact may be limited to reading or changing application objects, which can still expose sensitive data or bypass security checks. No user interaction is needed, and public exploits exist for many framework-level instances.
entries.remediation:
Do not evaluate user input as an expression:

  • Remove code that passes user input to an expression parser, such as SpEL's parseExpression(), OGNL evaluation or an EL processor, and pass input to fixed expressions as variables or plain values instead.
  • Do not include user input in messages that the framework interpolates, such as custom Bean Validation constraint messages; supply it as a message parameter instead.
  • Where SpEL must evaluate an expression involving untrusted data, use SimpleEvaluationContext, which excludes type references, constructors and bean references, rather than StandardEvaluationContext.
  • Keep the framework and its libraries up to date, as many expression language injection flaws have been in framework code rather than in the application itself.

As an interim measure, a web application firewall rule can block expression delimiters such as ${ and #{ on the affected parameters, but it can be bypassed. Confirm the fix by repeating the original expressions and checking that they are returned as literal text and cause no parser errors.

entries.title: LDAP Injection
entries.summary: User input is placed into an LDAP search filter or distinguished name without escaping, so it can change which directory entries a query matches.
entries.description:
The application queries an LDAP directory, such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP, and builds the search filter or distinguished name by inserting values supplied by the user. Characters with special meaning in a filter, such as *, (, ), \ and the NUL character, or in a distinguished name, such as ,, +, = and ;, are not escaped, so input can add conditions, wildcards or extra clauses to the query.

LDAP injection typically shows itself on a test when a * in a search or login field returns every entry or succeeds where it should not, when an unbalanced parenthesis causes a directory error, or when injected conditions that are always true or always false give consistently different responses. The last form allows attribute values to be inferred one character at a time even when results are not displayed. Common places are login forms that look the user up with a filter, staff directories, and address book or group membership searches.
entries.impact: An attacker can read directory entries and attributes beyond those the query was meant to return, such as other users' details, group memberships and descriptive attributes that sometimes hold sensitive information, and may be able to bypass authentication where the application decides whether a login succeeded from the result of a search. The data exposed is limited by the permissions of the account the application uses to query the directory, which are often broader than necessary.
entries.remediation:
Treat every value placed in an LDAP query as data:

  • Escape user input with the encoding for the context it is used in, filter encoding for values in search filters and distinguished name encoding for values in DNs, using the directory library's own functions, for example ldap_escape() in PHP or escape_filter_chars() in the Python ldap3 library.
  • Where the library offers a filter builder that encodes values, use it rather than building filter strings by concatenation.
  • Validate input against the expected format before use, such as a username pattern, and reject wildcards where searching by pattern is not a feature.
  • Authenticate users by binding to the directory with their own credentials, rejecting empty passwords before the bind, rather than deciding the outcome from a search result.
  • Give the account the application uses for directory queries read-only access to only the entries and attributes it needs.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original tests with wildcards, parentheses and always-true conditions, and checking that they are treated as literal characters.

entries.title: XPath Injection
entries.summary: User input is inserted into an XPath expression that queries XML data, so it can change the expression and return or test data it was not meant to reach.
entries.description:
The application stores data such as user accounts, configuration or catalogue records in XML documents and queries them with XPath expressions built by concatenating values supplied by the user. A quotation mark in the input ends the intended string literal, after which the rest of the input is read as XPath syntax, so a condition such as ' or '1'='1 changes which nodes the expression selects.

XPath injection typically shows itself on a test when a quotation mark causes an XPath error, when an always-true condition bypasses a login or returns all records, or when always-true and always-false conditions give consistently different responses. XPath has no access control within a document, and functions such as count(), string-length() and substring() allow a whole document to be extracted one character at a time even when results are not shown. Scanners, including Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP, report XPath injection from error messages and response differences.
entries.impact: An attacker can read any data in the XML document that the expression queries, which can include credentials or personal data where the document is used as a user store, and may be able to bypass authentication or other checks that depend on the expression's result. XPath 1.0 cannot change a document, so the impact is normally limited to the confidentiality of that document and to decisions based on it.
entries.remediation:
Keep XPath expressions fixed and pass user input as values:

  • Use an XPath API that supports variables: write each expression in the application code with variables in place of values, and bind the user's input to them, for example with an XPathVariableResolver in Java or keyword variables to the xpath() method of Python's lxml.
  • Where the user chooses between kinds of query, map each choice to a complete, fixed expression and reject unknown choices, rather than building paths or predicates from input.
  • Validate input against the expected type and format before use, as a second layer of defence.
  • Keep XPath errors, expressions and document contents out of responses.
  • Where the document holds credentials, store them as salted password hashes rather than in a form that would be useful if extracted.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original tests with quotation marks and always-true conditions, and checking that they are treated as literal values.

entries.title: Server-Side Includes (SSI) Injection
entries.summary: User input is written into a page that the web server parses for Server-Side Include directives, so an attacker can inject directives that read files or run commands.
entries.description:
Server-Side Includes (SSI) are directives written as HTML comments, such as <!--#include virtual="..." -->, that a web server processes before it sends a page. SSI injection occurs when the application places user input into content that the server then parses for these directives: a file written from user input into a directory where SSI processing is enabled, or dynamic output passed through the server's SSI filter. Because the input is not HTML-encoded, a directive within it is carried out by the server.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a directive such as <!--#echo var="DATE_LOCAL" --> submitted in a parameter is replaced in the response by the server's date, or when an include directive returns the content of another file. Whether the #exec directive, which runs operating system commands, is available depends on the server: Apache permits it under Options Includes but not under IncludesNOEXEC, and the nginx SSI module does not support it at all. Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP both test for SSI injection.
entries.impact: Where the exec directive is available, an attacker can run operating system commands with the privileges of the web server, which amounts to a full compromise of the application host. Otherwise they can typically disclose server environment variables and the content of files and scripts reachable through include directives, and alter pages served to other users. No user interaction is needed, although exploitation depends on user input reaching content that the server parses for directives.
entries.remediation:
Stop user input from reaching content that is parsed for directives, and remove the ability to run commands:

  • Disable SSI processing wherever it is not needed, by removing the Includes option and any SSI handlers or filters in Apache, or by leaving ssi off in nginx.
  • Where SSI is required, use IncludesNOEXEC in Apache so that commands cannot be run, and limit SSI processing to static files that contain no user input.
  • HTML-encode user input before it is written into any page, so that it cannot form a directive, and never write user input into files stored where SSI is processed.
  • Do not pass dynamic application output through the server's SSI filter.
# Apache: no SSI by default <Directory "/var/www/html"> Options -Includes </Directory> # only where SSI is required, without exec <Directory "/var/www/html/ssi"> Options IncludesNOEXEC </Directory>

As an interim measure, a web application firewall rule can block <!--# in request parameters. Confirm the fix by repeating the original directives and checking that they are returned as encoded text and are not processed.

entries.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
entries.summary: The application's XML parser resolves external entities declared in user-supplied XML, letting an attacker read local files or make the server send requests.
entries.description:
The application parses XML received from users, such as SOAP or REST request bodies, uploaded files (SVG images, Office documents, which are zipped XML, and XML imports) or SAML messages, with a parser that processes document type definitions (DTDs) and resolves external entities. An attacker can declare an entity whose value is loaded from a URI, such as file:///etc/passwd or an internal web address, and reference it in the document, so that the parser reads the resource and places its content in the parsed data.

XML external entity injection typically shows itself on a test when the content of a local file appears in the response or, in blind cases, when the parser makes a DNS or HTTP request to a server under the tester's control, which can also carry file content out through parameter entities and an external DTD. Error messages that include the resolved value are another channel. Burp Suite and other scanners test for XXE with out-of-band interactions. Several common parsers, particularly in Java, resolve external entities unless configured otherwise, and endpoints that normally accept JSON sometimes also accept XML when the content type is changed.

A related weakness, entity expansion (the billion laughs attack), uses nested internal entities to exhaust the server's memory.
entries.impact: An attacker can read files that the application's account can access, such as configuration files containing credentials, source code and private keys, and can make the server send requests to internal systems, which turns the weakness into server-side request forgery against services that are not reachable from the internet. Depending on the platform, the same techniques can cause denial of service and, in rare configurations, code execution. No authentication is needed where the affected endpoint is public.
entries.remediation:
Configure every XML parser that handles untrusted input to refuse DTDs, or at least external entities:

  • Disable DTD processing entirely where it is not needed, which prevents external entities and entity expansion together. In Java, set the disallow-doctype-decl feature on DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory; in .NET, set DtdProcessing to Prohibit and XmlResolver to null; in Python, use the defusedxml package; in PHP, do not enable LIBXML_NOENT or LIBXML_DTDLOAD for untrusted input.
  • Where DTDs are required, disable external general entities, external parameter entities and external DTD loading, and leave XInclude disabled.
  • Keep XML libraries up to date, and apply the same settings to components that parse XML indirectly, such as those that process SVG images, Office documents and SAML messages.
  • Prefer simpler formats such as JSON where the interface allows, and reject XML on endpoints that are not meant to accept it.
// Java DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(); dbf.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); dbf.setXIncludeAware(false); // .NET var settings = new XmlReaderSettings(); settings.DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit; settings.XmlResolver = null;

Confirm the fix by repeating the original tests, including out-of-band payloads, and checking that the document is rejected or the entities are not resolved.

entries.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
entries.summary: The server fetches a URL or contacts a host chosen by the user, so an attacker can make it send requests to internal systems or cloud services it can reach.
entries.description:
The application makes HTTP or other network requests to an address that the user supplies or influences, for example when importing a file or image from a URL, generating a link preview, calling a webhook, rendering a page to PDF, or passing a host name or path to a back-end service. The request comes from the server, so it can reach systems that the attacker cannot: services bound to the loopback interface, hosts on the internal network, and the cloud instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254.

SSRF typically shows itself on a test when a URL pointing to a server under the tester's control receives a request from the application, which Burp Suite reports as an external service interaction, and is then confirmed by targeting internal addresses and comparing responses, error messages and timings. In blind cases the response is never returned, and only timing or out-of-band interactions show that requests are made. Filters that block internal addresses are often incomplete and can be bypassed with alternative IP notations, DNS names that resolve to internal addresses, redirects from an allowed host, or differences between URL parsers.
entries.impact: An attacker can use the server to reach systems behind the perimeter: reading data from internal web services and administration interfaces that trust requests from the internal network, scanning internal hosts and ports, and, on cloud platforms, querying the instance metadata service to obtain temporary credentials for the server's cloud identity. The impact depends on what the server can reach and whether responses are returned to the attacker. Full responses, a metadata service that accepts simple requests and internal services without authentication raise it considerably.
entries.remediation:
Control where the server's outbound requests can go:

  • Where the destinations are known in advance, allow only those: map user choices to fixed URLs, or check the scheme, host and port of each request against an exact allowlist.
  • Where arbitrary URLs must be fetched, allow only http and https, resolve the host name, refuse the request if any resolved address is in a loopback, private, link-local or other internal range, and connect to the address that was checked, so that a DNS change between the check and the request cannot redirect it. Disable automatic following of redirects, or repeat the check for each one.
  • Do not return raw responses or detailed connection errors from fetched resources to the user.
  • Send outbound requests through an egress proxy or network segment that cannot reach internal ranges or the metadata service.
  • On cloud platforms, require the token-based version of the metadata service where available (IMDSv2 on AWS), and give the server's cloud identity only the permissions it needs.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests against internal addresses, alternative IP notations and redirecting URLs, and checking that each is refused.

entries.title: CRLF Injection and HTTP Response Splitting
entries.summary: User input containing carriage return and line feed characters is written into an HTTP response header, letting an attacker add headers or split the response.
entries.description:
The application places values supplied by the user into HTTP response headers, most often the Location header of a redirect, a Set-Cookie header or a custom header, without removing carriage return and line feed characters (CR and LF, URL-encoded as %0d and %0a). HTTP/1.1 separates headers with CRLF, so an encoded line break in the input ends the intended header and starts a new one of the attacker's choosing. Two line breaks end the headers altogether, and the rest of the input becomes the response body, which is known as HTTP response splitting.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a payload such as %0d%0aSet-Cookie:test=1 in a parameter produces a separate header in the raw response. Burp Suite reports it as HTTP response header injection and OWASP ZAP as CRLF injection. Most current frameworks reject line breaks in header values, so it is now found mainly in older platforms, custom servers, and web server or load balancer rules that copy a decoded part of the URL into a header, such as a redirect built from a normalised path.
entries.impact: An attacker who persuades a user to follow a crafted link can set or overwrite cookies in the user's browser, which can enable session fixation, add or override security headers, and, where the body can be injected, run script in the user's session as with cross-site scripting. Where a shared cache stores the manipulated response, the effect can reach other users without any further interaction.
entries.remediation:
Keep line breaks out of response headers:

  • Remove or reject carriage return, line feed and NUL characters, after decoding, in any value written to a response header. HTTP itself treats these characters in header values as invalid.
  • Set headers only through the framework's header API rather than writing raw responses, and keep the framework and web server up to date so that their own checks apply.
  • For redirects, validate the destination against an allowlist and encode it as a URL, rather than copying input into the Location header.
  • Review web server and proxy rules that build headers from request data. In nginx, use $request_uri, which keeps the original encoding, rather than the decoded $uri in return and rewrite targets and in add_header values.
# nginx: vulnerable, $uri is decoded return 302 https://$server_name$uri; # safer return 302 https://$server_name$request_uri;

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with encoded CR and LF characters, including double-encoded forms, and checking that the raw response contains no injected header.

entries.title: Host Header Injection
entries.summary: The application trusts the client-supplied Host header, or a forwarding header that overrides it, when it builds links, redirects or routing decisions.
entries.description:
The application, or the web server or proxy in front of it, treats the Host request header as a trusted statement of its own name, although the client sets it. Override headers such as X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host and Forwarded are often trusted in the same way when the application sits behind a proxy. The value is then used to build absolute URLs in pages, redirects and emails, such as password reset links, to choose a site or tenant, or to decide whether a request is internal.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a modified Host header, or an added override header, is reflected in links, redirect locations or generated emails, or when changing it reaches a different virtual host. Ambiguous requests, such as duplicate Host headers or an absolute URL in the request line, can bypass validation that checks only one of the values. Where a reverse proxy routes requests by host name, setting the header to an internal address can reach internal systems. Scanners commonly flag the issue when an injected host value appears in a response.
entries.impact: The most common consequence is password reset poisoning: an attacker requests a reset for a victim with a host value pointing to their own server, and receives the token when the victim, or a mail security product that opens links, follows the link in the genuine email. The same weakness can let an attacker poison shared caches with links to their server, reach internal virtual hosts or administration interfaces, or use a routing proxy for server-side request forgery. Reflection alone, without a cache or an email, is of limited use, because a victim's browser always sends the correct host.
entries.remediation:
Stop using the request as the source of the application's own name:

  • Configure the canonical host name, or names, in the application and build absolute URLs, especially those in emails, from that configuration rather than from the request.
  • Validate the Host header against an allowlist of expected names and reject other values. Most frameworks provide a setting for this, such as ALLOWED_HOSTS in Django and AllowedHosts in ASP.NET Core.
  • Give the web server or load balancer a default virtual host that rejects requests for unknown names, so that only expected names reach the application.
  • Trust X-Forwarded-Host and Forwarded only when they are set by the organisation's own proxy, which should overwrite any value sent by the client, and ignore them otherwise.
  • Make reverse proxies route only to an explicit list of back ends rather than to the host named in the request.
# nginx: refuse requests for unknown host names server { listen 80 default_server; server_name _; return 444; }

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with modified, duplicated and override host headers, and checking that they are rejected or ignored.

entries.title: Email Header Injection
entries.summary: User input containing line breaks reaches the headers of an email the application sends, so an attacker can add recipients or headers, or replace the message body.
entries.description:
The application sends email using values supplied by the user, such as the sender's name, reply-to address or subject in a contact, feedback or share form, and builds the message headers as text without removing carriage return and line feed characters. Email headers are separated by line breaks, so input containing an encoded CRLF sequence ends the intended header and adds new ones, such as Bcc: or Cc: with further recipients, or a blank line followed by content that replaces the message body. Where the application talks to a mail server directly, the same characters can sometimes inject SMTP commands.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a field containing %0d%0aBcc: followed by an address under the tester's control causes a copy of the message to arrive at that address, or when the received message shows the injected headers. Some scanners report it as SMTP or email header injection. In some mail libraries the sender address is also passed to the local mail program as a command-line argument, which has led to more serious argument injection flaws.
entries.impact: An attacker can use the application to send email with content they control to any recipients, through the organisation's own mail infrastructure. The messages pass the domain's sender authentication checks and carry its reputation, which makes them effective for spam and phishing, and abuse of this kind can get the domain or its mail servers placed on block lists. The weakness does not usually expose data held by the application unless the messages it sends contain such data.
entries.remediation:
Build email headers in a way that input cannot alter:

  • Use a maintained mail library that sets headers through structured fields and rejects line breaks, rather than assembling header text in application code.
  • Reject carriage return, line feed and NUL characters in every value placed in a header, including names and subjects, and validate email addresses as a single address in the expected format.
  • Fix the recipients of contact and feedback forms on the server, and never take a recipient address from the request.
  • Do not pass user-supplied addresses to the mail program's command line, for example through the additional parameters of PHP's mail() function, unless they have been strictly validated.
  • Apply rate limits and bot protection to forms that send email, so that any remaining abuse is limited.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original submissions with encoded line breaks in each field, and checking that no additional recipients or headers appear in the delivered message.

entries.title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
entries.summary: Input from a request is returned straight away in the page without encoding for its context, so a crafted link can run an attacker's script in the victim's browser.
entries.description:
The application takes a value from the request, such as a search term, error message or URL parameter, and includes it in the HTML response without encoding it for the context in which it appears. A value containing markup or script, such as a <script> element, an event handler attribute or a javascript: URL, is therefore interpreted by the browser as part of the page. Because the script runs on the application's own origin, the browser gives it the same access as the application's legitimate code.

The attack is delivered by persuading a victim to open a crafted link, or to visit a page that submits the request, usually while logged in. The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a unique string with special characters is returned unencoded and a payload is then confirmed to execute in a browser. The context matters: element content, attribute values, JavaScript strings and URLs each need different encoding, and filters that remove particular tags or words are commonly bypassed. Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, Acunetix and Nuclei templates all detect common forms.
entries.impact: Script injected through the link runs in the victim's session, so the attacker can do anything the victim can do in the application: read data shown to them, perform actions on their behalf, capture what they type, display a convincing fake login form, or read session tokens that are not protected by the HttpOnly attribute. Each victim must be persuaded to follow a link, which limits the scale. The impact is greater where victims include administrators, and lower where a strict Content Security Policy blocks injected script.
entries.remediation:
Encode output for its context, and limit what injected script could do:

  • Encode all untrusted data for the context where it is placed in the page: HTML entity encoding for element content, attribute encoding for quoted attribute values, JavaScript string encoding for values in scripts, and URL encoding for URL parameters. Use a template engine that encodes automatically, and avoid helpers that bypass it, such as raw output functions.
  • Do not place untrusted data directly in script blocks, event handlers or style elements. Pass it in a data attribute or a safely encoded JSON object, and read it from there.
  • Where a URL from the user is placed in a link or redirect, allow only the http and https schemes.
  • Validate input against the expected format as an extra layer of defence.
  • Deploy a Content Security Policy that allows scripts only by nonce or hash, without unsafe-inline, and set the HttpOnly attribute on session cookies.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original payloads, and variants for the same context, and checking that they are displayed as text and do not execute.

entries.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
entries.summary: Input that the application stores is later shown to other users without encoding for its context, so script saved by an attacker runs in their browsers.
entries.description:
The application saves values supplied by users, such as profile fields, comments, messages, support tickets, file names or log entries, and later includes them in pages viewed by other users without encoding them for the context in which they appear. Script or markup saved by an attacker is therefore interpreted as part of the page by every browser that displays it, with the same access as the application's own code.

Unlike the reflected form, no crafted link is needed: the payload runs whenever the affected page is viewed in the normal course of use, often in back-office or administrative views that the attacker cannot see, which is known as blind cross-site scripting. The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a unique string with special characters, submitted through one function, appears unencoded wherever the stored value is displayed, including views used by other roles. Rich-text fields that accept HTML, and uploaded HTML or SVG files served from the application's own origin, are common sources. Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP detect common forms, and out-of-band payloads are used to find blind cases.
entries.impact: An attacker with an ordinary account can run script in the session of every user who views the affected content, which often includes staff and administrators. The script can read anything those users can see and perform any action they can perform, such as changing account details, creating users or altering configuration, and can read session tokens not protected by the HttpOnly attribute. The effect persists until the stored value is removed. Where the content is shown only to the user who supplied it, or a strict Content Security Policy blocks the script, the impact is much lower.
entries.remediation:
Encode stored data whenever it is displayed, and limit what injected script could do:

  • Encode stored data for the context where it is displayed, every time it is displayed, using a template engine that encodes automatically: HTML entity encoding for element content, attribute encoding for quoted attributes, and JavaScript or URL encoding where those contexts cannot be avoided. Avoid raw output helpers.
  • Where users must be able to submit formatted text, sanitise it with a maintained HTML sanitiser that uses an allowlist of elements and attributes, or offer a restricted markup language such as Markdown rendered by a safe library.
  • Serve user-uploaded files with a Content-Disposition: attachment header and an explicit, safe Content-Type, preferably from a separate domain.
  • Deploy a Content Security Policy that allows scripts only by nonce or hash, and set HttpOnly on session cookies.
  • Validate input against the expected format when it is stored, as an extra layer.

After fixing the code, find and remove any malicious content already stored. Confirm the fix by repeating the original payloads in every affected field and checking that they display as text in every view.

entries.title: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
entries.summary: The page's own JavaScript passes attacker-controllable data, such as part of the URL, to a function that treats it as markup or code, so a crafted link can run script.
entries.description:
Client-side JavaScript in the application reads data from a source that an attacker can control, such as location.hash, location.search, document.referrer, window.name, web storage or messages received through postMessage, and passes it to a sink that interprets it as markup or code, such as innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML(), document.write(), eval(), setTimeout() with a string argument, or an element's href or src set to a javascript: URL. Library functions that parse HTML, such as jQuery's html(), act as sinks too.

Because the payload is handled entirely in the browser, it may never appear in a server response, and anything after the # in a URL is not sent to the server at all, so server-side validation and logging do not see it. The weakness typically shows itself on a test through review of the page's JavaScript for flows from sources to sinks, helped by tools such as Burp Suite's DOM Invader, and is confirmed by executing a payload through a crafted URL. Burp Suite reports it as DOM-based cross-site scripting, and scanners that run a browser engine detect common cases.
entries.impact: As with reflected cross-site scripting, the attacker's script runs in the victim's session when they open a crafted link, so it can read data shown to the victim, act on their behalf, capture what they type and read session tokens that are not protected by the HttpOnly attribute. Each victim must be persuaded to follow a link. The impact is greater where victims include administrators, and lower where a Content Security Policy or Trusted Types block the affected sink.
entries.remediation:
Keep untrusted data away from sinks that interpret markup or code:

  • Use sinks that treat data as text: set textContent rather than innerHTML, create elements and set attributes with DOM methods, and never pass strings derived from input to eval(), Function() or setTimeout().
  • Where HTML built from input must be inserted, sanitise it first with a maintained client-side sanitiser such as DOMPurify.
  • Before assigning a URL from input to href, src or location, parse it and allow only the http and https schemes.
  • In frameworks, rely on their automatic encoding and avoid the functions that bypass it, such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React, v-html in Vue and bypassSecurityTrustHtml() in Angular, unless the value has been sanitised.
  • Enforce Trusted Types with the Content Security Policy directive require-trusted-types-for 'script' in browsers that support it, so that dangerous sinks accept only values that have passed through an approved policy.
  • Keep third-party JavaScript libraries up to date, as several have contained DOM-based XSS flaws.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original crafted URLs and reviewing the code path from each source to its sink.

entries.title: HTML Injection
entries.summary: Input is returned in a page without HTML encoding, so an attacker can inject markup such as forms and links, although script execution is prevented.
entries.description:
The application includes values from the request in its HTML responses without encoding them, so markup in the input is rendered by the browser. Unlike cross-site scripting, script execution is prevented, typically because a filter removes script elements and event handlers or because a Content Security Policy blocks inline script. The root cause is the same missing output encoding, and a weak filter often means the finding can be developed into full cross-site scripting.

Even without script, injected markup can change what the victim sees and does. It can add a convincing login form that submits to the attacker's server, insert links and images, add a <meta> refresh that redirects the page, or add a <base> element that changes where relative links point. An unclosed attribute or tag can also capture the rest of the page, including any tokens in it, and send it to the attacker's server, a technique known as dangling markup injection, although some browsers block its common forms. The weakness typically shows itself on a test when harmless markup, such as a heading or a link, submitted in a parameter is rendered rather than displayed as text.
entries.impact: An attacker who persuades a victim to follow a crafted link can present content on the application's own domain, which makes credential phishing through an injected login form considerably more convincing, and may be able to capture tokens or other page content through dangling markup. The attacker cannot run script, so they cannot act within the victim's session directly. The impact rises to that of cross-site scripting if the filter that prevents script can be bypassed.
entries.remediation:
Fix the missing encoding rather than the symptoms:

  • Encode all untrusted data for the context in which it appears, as for cross-site scripting: HTML entity encoding for element content and attribute encoding for quoted attribute values, using a template engine that encodes automatically. Do not rely on filters that remove particular tags.
  • Where formatted text must be accepted, sanitise it with a maintained HTML sanitiser using a strict allowlist that excludes forms, inputs, meta and base elements.
  • Strengthen the Content Security Policy with form-action 'self', so that injected forms cannot submit to other sites, and base-uri 'none' or 'self', so that injected base elements are ignored.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original markup in each affected parameter and checking that it is displayed as text.

entries.title: Content Spoofing (Text Injection)
entries.summary: The application displays text taken from the request as part of its own page, so an attacker can make the site show misleading messages to users who follow a crafted link.
entries.description:
The application takes text from the request, typically from a URL parameter or the path, and displays it in a page as though it were the site's own content, for example as an error, status or welcome message. The text is correctly encoded, so no markup or script can be injected, but its wording is entirely under the control of whoever built the link. An attacker can therefore write a message that appears on the genuine site, under its address and certificate, such as a warning that an account has been suspended together with a telephone number or web address to contact.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a parameter such as message or error is changed to arbitrary text and the page displays it where the site's own messages appear. Pages that echo the requested path, such as custom error pages, are a common variant. It differs from HTML injection in that only plain text can be injected, and some scanners report it as text injection.
entries.impact: An attacker can use links to the genuine site to support phishing and other social engineering, for example directing users to call a fraudulent support line or to visit a look-alike site, with the credibility of the organisation's own domain. The attacker cannot change data, run script or read anything from the application, and each victim must open the crafted link and act on the message, so the impact depends on how convincingly the text fits the page.
entries.remediation:
Keep the wording of the site's messages under the application's control:

  • Do not take the text of user-facing messages from the request. Pass a short message code instead, look up the text in a fixed set held by the application, and reject unknown codes.
  • Where user input must be shown, such as a search term, present it clearly as the user's own input, for example quoted after a fixed label, and limit its length.
  • Avoid echoing the requested path in error pages, or truncate it and label it as the address requested.
  • Validate parameters against their expected format and length, as for any other input.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with arbitrary text and checking that it is no longer displayed as a message from the site.

entries.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
entries.summary: State-changing requests are accepted on the strength of the browser's cookies alone, so another site can make a logged-in user's browser perform actions without their knowledge.
entries.description:
The application relies only on credentials that the browser sends automatically, usually the session cookie, to authenticate requests that change state, such as updating account details, changing settings, making payments or performing administrative actions. It does not require a value that another site cannot know, such as an anti-CSRF token, and does not check where the request came from. A page on any other site can therefore make a logged-in user's browser submit such a request, through an automatically submitted form, an image or a link, and the application processes it as the user's own action.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a state-changing request still succeeds after its token is removed, emptied or replaced with one from another session, when its method can be changed from POST to GET, or when a JSON endpoint accepts a cross-site form submission. Burp Suite can generate a proof-of-concept page, and OWASP ZAP reports forms without anti-CSRF tokens. Browser defaults now reduce the exposure: cookies marked SameSite=Lax or Strict are not sent with cross-site form submissions, and some browsers apply Lax when no attribute is set. Requests that change state through GET, cookies set with SameSite=None, browsers without that default, and attacks from a sibling subdomain, which counts as the same site, remain exploitable.
entries.impact: An attacker can make victims perform any unprotected state-changing action, with the victim's privileges, by luring them to a page while they are logged in. Typical results include changing the account's email address or password, which can lead to account takeover, changing settings, making purchases or transfers and, where the victim is an administrator, creating accounts or changing configuration. The attacker cannot read the responses, and the impact depends on which functions are affected.
entries.remediation:
Require proof that each state-changing request was made by the application's own pages:

  • Protect every state-changing request with the framework's built-in CSRF protection, which uses a token tied to the session and checked on the server, or a signed double-submit cookie where the application is stateless.
  • Alternatively, or as well, reject state-changing requests whose Sec-Fetch-Site header is cross-site, falling back to checking the Origin header against the application's own origins for browsers that do not send it.
  • Never change state in response to GET requests.
  • Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies as an extra layer, not as the only defence.
  • For APIs, require a custom request header or a JSON content type, which a cross-site form cannot send without a CORS preflight, and keep the CORS policy strict.
  • Require re-authentication for the most sensitive changes, such as a new email address or password.

Confirm the fix by replaying each affected request from a page on another origin, and with the token removed or altered, and checking that it is rejected.

entries.title: Clickjacking (Missing Frame Protection)
entries.summary: The application's pages can be loaded in a frame on another site, so an attacker can disguise them and trick users into clicking on them.
entries.description:
The application does not tell browsers to refuse to display its pages inside a frame on another site, which is done with the Content Security Policy frame-ancestors directive or the older X-Frame-Options header. An attacker can therefore load a page from the application in an invisible or disguised frame on a site they control, positioned so that a victim who clicks an apparently harmless element is actually clicking a button in the application. The technique is known as clickjacking or UI redressing.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when HTML responses lack both headers and a page loads in a frame on a test page. Burp Suite reports it as a frameable response and OWASP ZAP as a missing anti-clickjacking header. Exploitation needs an action that can be completed with a few clicks and, for actions that need a login, a browser that sends the session cookie to the framed page. Cookies marked SameSite=Lax or Strict are withheld from cross-site frames, and current browsers restrict cookies without the attribute in that situation, so on most applications exploitation now needs a session cookie set with SameSite=None, a page on a sibling subdomain, or an action that works without logging in.
entries.impact: Where those conditions are met, an attacker can trick users into performing actions in the application with their own privileges, such as changing settings, granting permissions, deleting data or confirming a transaction. Each attack needs the victim to visit the attacker's page and click as directed, and actions that need several steps or typed input are hard to achieve. The risk rises where a sensitive action is completed in a single click.
entries.remediation:
Tell browsers which sites may frame the application:

  • Send the Content Security Policy directive frame-ancestors 'none' on all HTML responses, or 'self' or a list of specific trusted origins where the application must be framed. Add it to the existing policy where one is already set.
  • Also send X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN for older browsers. The ALLOW-FROM value is obsolete and ignored by current browsers.
  • Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies.
  • Require a confirmation that cannot be completed with a single click, such as re-entering a password, for the most sensitive actions.
# nginx add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'" always; add_header X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN" always; # Apache (mod_headers) Header always set Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'self'" Header always set X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN" <!-- IIS web.config, inside system.webServer --> <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <add name="Content-Security-Policy" value="frame-ancestors 'self'" /> <add name="X-Frame-Options" value="SAMEORIGIN" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol>

Confirm the fix by checking the headers on all HTML responses and attempting to load the pages in a frame on another origin.

entries.title: Insecure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Policy
entries.summary: The application's CORS policy lets untrusted origins read its responses with the user's credentials, so a malicious site can read a logged-in user's data.
entries.description:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) lets a server relax the browser's same-origin policy for chosen origins through response headers. The application's policy trusts origins it should not: it reflects any value of the request's Origin header in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, accepts the null origin, or validates origins with a pattern that matches unintended domains, such as a check that the origin merely ends with or contains the organisation's domain, or a regular expression with an unescaped dot. Where it also returns Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, script on a trusted origin can make requests that carry the user's cookies and read the responses.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a request with an arbitrary or crafted Origin header receives a response that echoes it with credentials allowed. Burp Suite reports trust of arbitrary origins, unencrypted origins and all subdomains as separate CORS issues. A wildcard on its own is not usually exploitable for authenticated data, because browsers refuse to combine it with credentials, but it matters where a response is protected only by network location. Exploitation also needs the browser to send the session cookie with the cross-site request, which current defaults restrict unless the cookie is set with SameSite=None or the attacker controls a page on a trusted or same-site origin.
entries.impact: When a logged-in user visits a page controlled by the attacker, the page can read any response that the affected endpoints return to that user, such as personal data, account details, API keys and anti-CSRF tokens, and can use those tokens to perform further actions in the user's name. Where only a trusted subdomain can exploit the policy, the attacker first needs a cross-site scripting flaw on, or takeover of, that subdomain.
entries.remediation:
Grant cross-origin access only to origins that are trusted, and only where it is needed:

  • Compare the Origin header with an exact list of trusted origins, including scheme, host and port, and return it in Access-Control-Allow-Origin only on a match. Never reflect arbitrary values, trust null, or match origins by prefix, suffix or loose pattern.
  • Return Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true only on endpoints that genuinely need credentialed cross-origin access, and only to trusted origins.
  • Do not trust http origins for an application served over HTTPS.
  • Add Vary: Origin to responses whose CORS headers depend on the request's origin, so that caches do not serve one origin's response to another.
  • Apply CORS headers only to the routes that need them rather than to the whole application, and set SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies.

Confirm the fix by sending requests with arbitrary, null, look-alike and subdomain origins and checking that none is reflected with credentials allowed.

entries.title: Open Redirect
entries.summary: The application redirects users to an address taken from the request without validating it, so a link to the genuine site can send users on to any other site.
entries.description:
The application takes the destination of a redirect from a value in the request, commonly a parameter named something like returnUrl, next, redirect or url that is used after login or logout, and sends the browser there without checking that it belongs to the application. A link that starts on the genuine domain can therefore end on any site the attacker chooses. The redirect may be issued by the server, through a Location header or a meta refresh, or by client-side script that assigns the value to window.location, which is the DOM-based form.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when an external address placed in such a parameter is followed by the browser. Checks that only look for the application's domain somewhere in the value, or that block values starting with http, are commonly bypassed with addresses beginning // or /\, embedded credentials or alternative encodings. Burp Suite reports open redirection in reflected and DOM-based forms, and OWASP ZAP reports it as an external redirect.
entries.impact: An attacker can make phishing links more convincing, because they begin with the organisation's genuine domain, and can use the redirect to get past filters that allow links to that domain. In some designs the redirect also helps to steal tokens: where an OAuth or single sign-on flow accepts any address on the trusted domain, a redirect from there can pass the user's token on to the attacker. Client-side redirects that accept javascript: URLs can lead to cross-site scripting. Each victim must follow the link.
entries.remediation:
Decide redirect destinations on the server:

  • Avoid taking redirect destinations from the request. Where the destination varies, pass an identifier and map it to a fixed list of destinations on the server.
  • Where a return address is needed, accept only relative paths within the application: require a single leading /, reject values beginning // or /\, and check the value after decoding.
  • Where external destinations are genuinely required, parse the URL with a standard parser and compare its scheme and host exactly with an allowlist, rather than searching the string.
  • For client-side redirects, apply the same checks before assigning to window.location, and allow only the http and https schemes.
  • Where users must be sent to arbitrary external sites, show an intermediate page that names the destination and asks the user to continue.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with external, protocol-relative and encoded destinations and checking that none redirects away from the application.

entries.title: Path Traversal
entries.summary: A file path built from user input is not confined to its intended directory, so sequences such as ../ let an attacker read, or sometimes write, other files on the server.
entries.description:
The application uses a value supplied by the user, such as a file name in a download, image, template or language parameter, to build a path that it then opens with a file-system call. It does not make sure that the resulting path stays inside the intended directory, so sequences such as ../ (or ..\ on Windows), or an absolute path, let the input step out of that directory and reach any file that the application's account can read. Where the path is used to save a file, such as an upload or an entry extracted from an archive, the same flaw lets files be written elsewhere.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a request for a known system file, such as /etc/passwd on Linux or win.ini on Windows, returns its content, often after filters are bypassed with URL encoding, double encoding, nested sequences such as ....// that survive a single removal of ../, or an absolute path. Burp Suite reports it as file path traversal and OWASP ZAP as path traversal, and Nuclei includes templates for known cases. The file is read or written as data. When the path is instead passed to the language's include mechanism, so that the file is run as code, the issue is local file inclusion.
entries.impact: An attacker can read any file the application's account can access, typically including application source code, configuration files holding database passwords, API keys and other secrets, private keys and system files, and those secrets often give access to further systems. Where the flaw allows writing, the attacker may be able to overwrite application or configuration files, or place a script in the web root, which can lead to code execution. No authentication is needed where the affected function is public.
entries.remediation:
Make sure file paths can only resolve inside the intended directory:

  • Avoid using user input in file paths. Refer to files by an identifier, such as a database key, and look up the stored path on the server.
  • Where a file name must come from the user, validate it against a strict allowlist, such as letters, digits and a single permitted extension, and reject path separators and ...
  • Then resolve the full path, including any symbolic links, and check that it still lies inside the intended base directory before opening it.
  • When extracting archives, apply the same check to the path of every entry.
  • Run the application with an account that can read only the files it needs, and make its own code and configuration read-only to it.
// Java Path base = Paths.get("/srv/app/files").toRealPath(); Path target = base.resolve(name).toRealPath(); if (!target.startsWith(base)) { throw new SecurityException("Invalid path"); }

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests, including encoded and nested sequences and absolute paths, and checking that each is refused.

entries.title: Local File Inclusion
entries.summary: User input selects the file that the server-side language includes and runs, so an attacker can include unintended local files, disclosing them or running code they contain.
entries.description:
The application passes a value supplied by the user to the language's file inclusion mechanism, most often PHP's include or require statements, to choose a page, template or language file, for example ?page=about. The included file is not simply read: the interpreter runs any code it contains and outputs the rest. Without a strict allowlist, traversal sequences or absolute paths let the input select any local file the application can read. This is what distinguishes local file inclusion from path traversal, where a file is only returned as data.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a system file such as /etc/passwd appears in the page, when an error message reveals the include path, or when a PHP stream wrapper such as php://filter with a Base64 conversion returns the encoded source of the application's own scripts. A fixed prefix or suffix added by the code, such as a directory name or .php, limits which files can be reached but rarely removes the issue. Code execution follows where the attacker can get PHP code into any file the include can reach, such as a log file containing a crafted User-Agent header, a session file or an uploaded file, and in some configurations through chains of PHP filters without writing a file at all. Scanners report it as local file inclusion or as path traversal.
entries.impact: An attacker can read local files that the application's account can access, including the application's source code and configuration secrets, and can often go on to run arbitrary code on the server with the web server's privileges by including a file they have been able to put code into. Code execution depends on conditions such as writable log or session files and the form of the vulnerable path, so it is not always achieved, but where it is, the application host is fully compromised.
entries.remediation:
Keep user input away from the include mechanism:

  • Never pass user input to include, require or equivalent functions. Map each permitted value to a fixed file name in the code, and fall back to a default for anything else.
  • Where file names must be dynamic, validate them against an allowlist of known files rather than filtering traversal sequences.
  • Set open_basedir to limit the directories PHP can open, keep allow_url_include off, and keep uploads, logs and session files outside any directory the application includes from.
  • Run the web server with an account that cannot write to the application's code directories, and restrict read access to log and session files.
// PHP: choose from a fixed map, never from the raw value $pages = ['home' => 'home.php', 'about' => 'about.php']; $file = $pages[$_GET['page'] ?? 'home'] ?? 'home.php'; include __DIR__ . '/pages/' . $file;

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with traversal sequences, absolute paths and PHP wrappers, and checking that only the permitted pages can be loaded.

entries.title: Remote File Inclusion
entries.summary: User input controls the file that the server-side language includes and a remote address is accepted, so the server fetches and runs code from an attacker's server.
entries.description:
The application passes a value supplied by the user to the language's file inclusion mechanism, typically PHP's include or require statements, and the platform allows that value to be a remote address. Supplying the URL of a file on a server the attacker controls makes the application fetch the file and run it as part of the page, so the attacker's code executes on the server directly, without any need to place a file there first. In PHP this requires the allow_url_include setting, which is off by default, so remote file inclusion is now found mainly on legacy or deliberately reconfigured systems. On Windows servers, a UNC path to an attacker's file share can have the same effect where outbound SMB connections are allowed, because it is treated as a local path.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a URL pointing to a server under the tester's control, placed in an include parameter, causes the application to request it, and a harmless test script served from there is executed, for example printing a marker string. Scanners, including OWASP ZAP and Nuclei, test for remote file inclusion by referencing external resources.
entries.impact: An attacker can run arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the web server process, typically installing a web shell for persistent access, reading application data and configuration secrets, and using the host as a foothold to attack internal systems. No user interaction or authentication is needed where the affected page is public, and exploitation is simple and reliable.
entries.remediation:
Remove the ability to include code from outside the application:

  • Never pass user input to include, require or equivalent functions. Map each permitted value to a fixed local file in the code.
  • Turn allow_url_include off, and allow_url_fopen off as well unless the application needs it for other purposes.
  • Restrict outbound connections from web servers, including HTTP, HTTPS and SMB, to the destinations they genuinely need.
  • Set open_basedir to limit the directories PHP can open, and run the web server with an account that cannot write to the application's code directories.
  • Check the server for signs of earlier exploitation, such as unfamiliar scripts in the web root, before relying on the fix.
; php.ini allow_url_include = Off allow_url_fopen = Off open_basedir = /var/www/app/ ; add upload_tmp_dir and session.save_path to open_basedir if they lie outside it

Confirm the fix by repeating the original request with an external URL and checking that no request reaches the external server and no remote code runs.

entries.title: Unrestricted File Upload
entries.summary: The application accepts uploaded files without properly restricting their type, content and storage, so dangerous files can be run by the server or served to users.
entries.description:
The application lets users upload files but does not adequately control what is accepted and how it is stored and served. Typical gaps are relying on the file extension or the Content-Type header sent by the client, checking extensions against a blocklist that misses alternatives such as .phtml, .phar or other script extensions the server will run, keeping the user's file name, and storing files inside the web root where the server executes scripts. Files that change server behaviour, such as .htaccess or web.config, and HTML or SVG files served from the application's own origin, are dangerous even where scripts cannot run.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a file with an executable extension, or one that passes the checks through a double extension, a change of case, an altered content type or an image header placed in front of script code, is accepted and its stored address can be requested. Running a harmless marker script confirms code execution, and an uploaded HTML or SVG file that runs script in the browser confirms stored cross-site scripting.
