Missing size limits, unsafe processing of archives and documents, and file names containing traversal sequences are related findings in the same function. The issue is largely found manually, with scanner support for common bypasses.
entries.impact: Where an uploaded script can be executed, an attacker can run arbitrary code on the server with the web server's privileges, typically through a web shell, giving them the application's data, its secrets and a foothold in the network. Where execution is not possible, uploaded HTML or SVG files can deliver stored cross-site scripting to other users, and the application can be used to host malware or phishing content under the organisation's domain. Most upload functions require an account, which reduces the exposure but not the impact.
entries.remediation:
Control what is accepted, what it is called, where it is kept and how it is served:

  • Allow only the file types the function needs, using an allowlist of extensions, and check that each file's content matches its type. Re-encode images where practical, which removes embedded content.
  • Ignore the user's file name: generate a random name on the server and add the extension from the allowlist.
  • Store uploads outside the web root, or in separate object storage, and serve them through a handler that sets an explicit Content-Type, Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Serve user content from a separate domain where it must be displayed in the browser.
  • Where files must stay under the web root, disable script execution and configuration overrides for the upload directory, for example by removing script handler mappings and setting AllowOverride None in Apache.
  • Enforce size limits, scan uploads for malware, and process documents and archives with up-to-date libraries.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original uploads, including bypass variants, and checking that they are rejected or stored in a way that cannot be executed or rendered.

entries.title: Insecure Deserialisation
entries.summary: The application rebuilds objects from serialised data that users can supply, so a crafted object graph can run code or change the application's behaviour when it is deserialised.
entries.description:
The application accepts data in a native serialisation format, which can describe objects of arbitrary types, and deserialises it without restricting the types it creates. Examples include Java's ObjectInputStream and libraries such as XStream, .NET's BinaryFormatter or Json.NET with type name handling enabled, PHP's unserialize(), Python's pickle and unsafe YAML loaders, and Ruby's Marshal. Creating an object can run code in its class, such as methods that are called automatically during deserialisation, so an attacker who chains such methods from libraries the application already loads, known as gadget chains, can make deserialisation itself run commands.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when serialised data is found in cookies, hidden fields, view state, API parameters or message queues, recognisable by markers such as rO0 (the Base64 form of a Java serialisation header) or PHP's O: object notation. It is then confirmed by sending payloads generated with tools such as ysoserial, ysoserial.net or PHPGGC that trigger a DNS lookup or a delay. Burp Suite reports serialised objects in HTTP messages, and extensions add active checks for known gadget chains.
entries.impact: Where a usable gadget chain exists, which is common in Java and .NET applications with typical libraries, an attacker can run arbitrary code on the server with the application's privileges, usually without authentication. Even without one, deserialisation can be abused to change object properties that the application trusts, such as roles or prices, or to exhaust memory and processor time. The weakness is often exploitable before any application-level checks run.
entries.remediation:
Stop deserialising untrusted data into arbitrary types:

  • Do not deserialise untrusted data with native formats. Use a data-only format such as JSON, mapped to simple types defined by the application, and validate it against a schema.
  • Disable polymorphic type handling in data formats: keep Json.NET's TypeNameHandling at None, and avoid default typing in Jackson or restrict it to an allowlist of types.
  • Stop using BinaryFormatter, which Microsoft states cannot be made secure. In PHP, use json_decode() rather than unserialize(); in Python, never unpickle untrusted data, and load YAML with yaml.safe_load().
  • Where native deserialisation cannot yet be removed, sign the data with an HMAC and verify the signature before deserialising, and in Java apply a serialisation filter (ObjectInputFilter) that allows only the expected classes.
  • Keep libraries up to date, remove unused libraries that provide gadgets, and run the application with the least privilege it needs.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original out-of-band payloads and checking that no interaction or deserialisation error results.

entries.title: Server-Side Prototype Pollution
entries.summary: Server-side JavaScript merges user-supplied keys such as __proto__ into objects, so an attacker can add properties to every object in the application process.
entries.description:
The application, typically built on Node.js, copies values from user-supplied JSON or query parameters into objects with a recursive merge, clone or path-assignment function that does not exclude the special keys __proto__, constructor and prototype. A request containing such a key then adds or changes properties on Object.prototype, which almost every object in the process inherits, so the injected value appears wherever the code reads a property that an object does not set itself. The vulnerable function may be in the application or in a dependency, as several popular merge and query-parsing libraries have had this flaw.

The impact depends on gadgets: code that reads an inherited property and uses it in a security decision, a configuration option or a dangerous function, such as the options passed to child_process functions. The weakness typically shows itself on a test through non-destructive changes, such as polluting a property that alters the formatting or status code of JSON responses, followed by a search for gadgets. Burp Suite includes checks for server-side prototype pollution. Testing needs care, because a polluted prototype persists for the life of the process and affects every user until the application restarts.
entries.impact: Depending on the gadgets available, an attacker can escalate privileges by injecting properties such as role flags, change application behaviour for all users, cause a denial of service that lasts until the process restarts, or run arbitrary code on the server, for example through options that control how child processes are started. No authentication is needed where an affected endpoint is public, and code execution, where achievable, compromises the application host.
entries.remediation:
Stop untrusted keys from reaching object prototypes:

  • Do not merge, clone or assign user-supplied objects into application objects with generic recursive functions. Copy only expected properties, or validate request bodies against a strict schema that rejects unknown properties.
  • Where recursive merging is needed, use library versions that are patched against prototype pollution, and reject the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype at every level.
  • Use Map objects, or objects created with Object.create(null), for dictionaries built from user input, so that they have no prototype to pollute.
  • Consider freezing Object.prototype at start-up with Object.freeze(), after testing that dependencies still work, and running Node.js with --disable-proto=delete as defence in depth.
  • Keep dependencies up to date, and use software composition analysis to find vulnerable merge and parsing libraries.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with prototype keys and checking that no property is added to unrelated objects, then restart the application to clear any pollution left by testing.

entries.title: Client-Side Prototype Pollution
entries.summary: Client-side JavaScript copies attacker-controllable keys from the URL or other input into objects, polluting the page's prototype and often enabling DOM-based XSS through gadgets.
entries.description:
Client-side JavaScript in the application parses data that an attacker can control, most often the query string or fragment of the URL, into nested objects, or merges such data into existing objects, with code that does not exclude the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype. A crafted link containing, for example, ?__proto__[test]=value then adds a property to Object.prototype in the victim's browser, so that every object on the page appears to have it. The vulnerable code is frequently in a third-party library, such as an older URL parameter parser or deep-merge function.

Pollution alone changes little. The impact comes from gadgets: code in the page or its libraries that reads a property which is normally undefined and uses it in a dangerous way, for example as the address of a script or as HTML written into the page, which turns the pollution into DOM-based cross-site scripting. The weakness typically shows itself on a test when a prototype key in the URL makes the property appear on new objects in the browser console. Burp Suite's DOM Invader finds both pollution sources and known gadgets, and Burp Suite's scanner reports client-side prototype pollution.
entries.impact: Where a usable gadget exists, an attacker who persuades a victim to follow a crafted link can run script in the victim's session, with the same consequences as DOM-based cross-site scripting: reading data shown to the victim and acting on their behalf. Without a gadget, the effect is usually limited to changing the page's behaviour. Each victim must follow a link, and the outcome depends on the libraries the page loads.
entries.remediation:
Remove the pollution source and reduce what gadgets can do:

  • Update or replace third-party libraries with known prototype pollution flaws, and keep client-side dependencies under regular review.
  • Do not parse URL parameters or other untrusted input into nested objects with generic code. Read individual parameters with URLSearchParams, and copy only expected properties.
  • Reject the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype in any merge or assignment code, and use Map or Object.create(null) for dictionaries built from input.
  • Consider freezing Object.prototype early in page load, after testing that the page still works.
  • Limit the effect of gadgets with a Content Security Policy that restricts script sources and, in supporting browsers, Trusted Types.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original crafted URLs and checking that no property is added to Object.prototype and no gadget fires.

entries.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
entries.summary: A front-end server and the back end behind it disagree about where each HTTP request ends, so an attacker can hide a request inside another and interfere with other users' requests.
entries.description:
Most web applications sit behind a front-end server, such as a load balancer, reverse proxy or content delivery network, that forwards requests to back-end servers over shared, reused connections. HTTP/1.1 offers two ways to mark the end of a request body, the Content-Length header and chunked Transfer-Encoding. When the front end and back end interpret an ambiguous request differently, for example one honouring Content-Length and the other Transfer-Encoding (the CL.TE and TE.CL variants), or one accepting an obfuscated header that the other ignores, part of the attacker's request is left on the back-end connection and treated as the start of the next request, which may belong to another user. The same problem arises when a front end that speaks HTTP/2 to clients rewrites requests into HTTP/1.1 for the back end.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test through timing differences and through responses to a follow-up request that change, found with tools such as Burp Suite's scanner and its HTTP Request Smuggler extension. Testing needs care, because a successful probe can alter the responses that real users receive.
entries.impact: An attacker can bypass access controls that are enforced only by the front end, such as restrictions on administrative paths; capture other users' requests, including their session cookies and submitted data; deliver reflected cross-site scripting or redirects to other users without any interaction; and poison caches. Exploitation does not need authentication, but success against other users depends on timing and traffic beyond the attacker's control, and attempts can disrupt the service for legitimate users.
entries.remediation:
Make every server in the chain interpret requests the same way, and reject those that are ambiguous:

  • Use HTTP/2 end to end where possible, so that requests are not rewritten into HTTP/1.1 between the front end and the back end.
  • Configure the front end to normalise ambiguous requests and to reject requests that contain both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, multiple or invalid Content-Length values, or malformed or obfuscated Transfer-Encoding headers.
  • Make the back end reject the same ambiguous requests, or process them by Transfer-Encoding alone and close the connection afterwards, as HTTP/1.1 requires.
  • Keep load balancers, proxies, content delivery configuration and web servers up to date, as many smuggling flaws are in their request parsing.
  • Where a full fix will take time, disable reuse of back-end connections, at some cost to performance.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original tests and checking that ambiguous requests are rejected and follow-up requests are unaffected.

entries.title: Web Cache Poisoning
entries.summary: A shared cache stores a response that was shaped by a request input it does not include in its cache key, so an attacker's harmful response is served to other users.
entries.description:
The application sits behind a shared cache, such as a content delivery network, reverse proxy or framework cache, which decides whether two requests are the same by a cache key, usually the method, host, path and query string. The application's responses, however, are also influenced by inputs outside that key, known as unkeyed inputs: headers such as X-Forwarded-Host or X-Forwarded-Scheme, query parameters excluded from the key, cookies or a request body. An attacker sends a request in which an unkeyed input makes the response harmful, for example by pointing a script import at their own server or by reflecting a cross-site scripting payload, and the cache stores that response and serves it to everyone who requests the same key.

The weakness typically shows itself on a test when an added header or parameter changes the response while cache headers such as Age or X-Cache show that it is being stored. Tools such as the Param Miner extension for Burp Suite find unkeyed inputs by guessing them. Tests should include a unique cache-busting parameter so that real users are not served a test response. Burp Suite reports confirmed cases as web cache poisoning.
entries.impact: An attacker can make the cache serve content of their choosing to every user who requests the affected page while the entry remains cached, without those users following any link. Depending on the input involved, this can run script in the browsers of all visitors, redirect them to another site, or make a page unusable by caching an error, which is a form of denial of service. The attacker can repeat the request to keep the entry poisoned. Success depends on the cache's timing and key behaviour, which the attacker must study first.
entries.remediation:
Make sure the cache key covers everything that can change a cacheable response:

  • Do not let any request input outside the cache key change a cacheable response. Remove or overwrite forwarding headers such as X-Forwarded-Host at the edge unless they are set by the organisation's own proxy, and build absolute URLs from configuration.
  • Include every input that legitimately changes a response in the cache key, using the Vary header for request headers, or reject that input on cacheable routes.
  • Cache only responses that are meant to be shared, and set Cache-Control: no-store or private on dynamic and personalised responses. Avoid caching error responses, or cache them only briefly.
  • Apply the same URL normalisation and parameter handling at the cache and at the origin, and reject request bodies on GET routes.
  • After fixing, purge every affected cache layer.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests with a cache buster and checking that the unkeyed inputs no longer change the response.

entries.title: Web Cache Deception
entries.summary: A caching layer stores a personalised page as if it were a static file, so another person can retrieve a signed-in user's private content from the cache.
entries.description:
Web cache deception arises when a cache in front of the application, such as a content delivery network, reverse proxy or load balancer, decides what to store from the shape of the address, for example a static file extension or a static directory, while the application maps the same address to a dynamic, personalised page. A request for an address such as /account/settings/logo.css is answered by the application with the user's account page, because it ignores or tolerates the extra path segment, and the cache stores that response as if it were a public stylesheet.

An attacker sends a signed-in user a link to such an address. When the user follows it, their page is cached, and the attacker then requests the same address and receives the cached copy without any session.

The weakness can be confirmed by requesting a personalised page with a static-looking suffix while signed in, checking that the personalised content is returned and that cache headers such as Age, X-Cache or a provider-specific cache status show it was stored, then requesting the same address with no session. Variants rely on other differences in how the cache and the application read an address: delimiters such as ; or an encoded ? or #, encoded path separators, dot segments that one side normalises and the other does not, and cache rules keyed on static directories or well-known file names.
entries.impact: An attacker can read the cached copy of any page a victim is lured into requesting: personal details, account and order information, and any tokens embedded in the page, such as anti-CSRF tokens or API keys, which may allow further actions as the victim. Each victim exposes only their own pages, the victim must be signed in and follow a crafted link, and the copy is only available until the cache entry expires. A shared cache at a content delivery network makes collecting victims' pages straightforward, and the issue is worse where personalised pages carry long-lived secrets.
entries.remediation:
Make the cache decide what to store from the application's own response rather than from the address, and make the application refuse addresses it does not recognise:

  • Send Cache-Control: no-store (or at least private) on every authenticated or personalised response, and configure the cache to respect the origin's caching headers rather than overriding them with rules based on file extension.
  • Configure the application's routing to return 404 for paths that do not exactly match a defined route, rather than serving the nearest dynamic page for extra path segments, delimiters or encoded characters.
  • Limit caching to dedicated static paths that only ever serve static files and, where the cache supports it, only cache a response when its Content-Type matches the file extension requested.
  • Make the cache and the application decode and normalise paths in the same way, including encoded characters and dot segments.

As an interim measure, add cache rules that bypass caching for the affected routes and purge cached copies of personalised pages. Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests: each should either return 404 or come back uncached, and an unauthenticated request should never return personalised content.

entries.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
entries.summary: The application uses an identifier supplied by the user to find a record or file without checking that the user may access that particular object.
entries.description:
The application locates records or files using an identifier supplied in the request, such as a number in the path (/invoices/10452), a query parameter, a form field or a value in a JSON body, and returns or changes the object without checking that the signed-in user is entitled to that particular object. Changing the identifier to another valid value therefore gives access to another user's data. Authentication is in place, but authorisation at the level of the individual object is missing.

The weakness is identified by testing with at least two accounts, ideally in different roles and, for multi-tenant services, in different tenants: identifiers belonging to one account are substituted into the requests of the other, for reads, updates, deletions and file downloads, including identifiers in nested objects and secondary parameters. Burp Suite extensions such as Autorize help to replay requests across sessions. Automated scanners rarely find the issue, because they cannot tell which user should own which object.

Sequential or predictable identifiers make enumeration trivial. Random identifiers such as UUIDs make objects harder to find but do not fix the missing check, since identifiers also appear in links, shared documents, logs and other responses.
entries.impact: An attacker holding any valid account can read other users' records, such as personal details, invoices, messages or documents and, where the same pattern applies to update and delete operations, change or remove them, which can extend to taking over accounts by changing another user's email address. With predictable identifiers the whole data set can be harvested with a simple script. The impact is greatest where the flaw crosses tenant boundaries or covers sensitive personal or financial data, and an exposure of personal data at that scale may also create regulatory obligations for the organisation.
entries.remediation:
Check, on the server, that the signed-in user may access the specific object in every request that references one:

  • Scope every data access by the identity held in the server-side session, not by an identifier the client sends. For example, look up an invoice by its identifier and the current user's customer identifier together, and return 404 when no row matches.
  • Implement the check once, in a shared data access layer, policy or middleware that every endpoint uses, and deny access by default when no rule grants it.
  • Where users only ever need their own records, take the owner from the session (/account/invoices) rather than from the address (/users/123/invoices).
  • Apply the same check to file downloads, exports and every HTTP method on the resource.
  • Use random, non-sequential identifiers as defence in depth, never as the control.
  • Add automated tests that attempt cross-user and cross-tenant access for each endpoint, so regressions are caught.
-- Unsafe: trusts the identifier alone SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ? -- Safe: scoped to the customer in the session SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND customer_id = ?

Confirm the fix by repeating the tests with two accounts: requests for another user's objects should be refused, and the refusals should be logged.

entries.title: Missing Function-Level Access Control
entries.summary: Privileged functions check that a user is signed in but not that their role permits the action, so lower-privileged users can call them directly.
entries.description:
The application exposes functions intended for particular roles, such as administration pages, user management, configuration changes, data exports or approval steps, without checking on the server that the caller's role permits them. The user interface often hides the relevant menu items or buttons from lower-privileged users, but the underlying page or API endpoint still responds to anyone who requests it, and sometimes to unauthenticated requests as well.

Common variants include administrative endpoints reachable by standard users, checks applied to one HTTP method but not another on the same route (for example GET protected but PUT or DELETE not), checks enforced on a page but not on the API that page calls, and decisions based on a role or flag sent by the client.

The weakness is identified by recording the requests available to the most privileged role, then replaying them with sessions for lower-privileged roles and with no session at all, and by reviewing client-side code, which often lists administrative API routes that the interface never shows. Burp Suite extensions such as Autorize make this replay systematic. Automated scanners rarely find the issue, because they do not know which roles should reach which functions.
entries.impact: A user with a low-privileged account, or an attacker who registers or compromises one, can perform actions reserved for more privileged roles. Depending on the functions exposed, this can include creating accounts, granting themselves administrative rights, changing configuration, reading or exporting all users' data and approving transactions. The impact is greatest where user and role management is exposed, since that gives full control of the application, and where the functions can be reached without authentication.
entries.remediation:
Enforce authorisation on the server for every function, based on the role and permissions held in the user's session:

  • Deny by default: every route and API operation should require an explicit permission, and any route without one should be refused.
  • Implement the checks centrally rather than in each handler, using the framework's own mechanisms, for example Spring Security's @PreAuthorize or URL authorisation rules, ASP.NET Core authorisation policies applied with [Authorize(Policy = "...")], or shared middleware in Express and similar frameworks.
  • Apply the check to every HTTP method on a route and to every API that a page calls, not only to the page itself.
  • Never base decisions on hidden interface elements or on role values sent by the client.
  • Keep administrative functions under a separate route prefix or host with its own policy, so they can also be restricted at the network edge.
  • Maintain a matrix of roles and permitted functions, and turn it into automated tests that run on every release.

Confirm the fix by replaying each privileged request with lower-privileged sessions and with no session, and checking that every one is refused.

entries.title: Mass Assignment
entries.summary: The application binds request properties straight onto its data objects, so a user can set fields they should not control, such as their role or account status.
entries.description:
Many frameworks can copy the properties of a request directly onto a model or data object, which saves code when handling forms and API calls. If the application binds the whole request in this way without limiting which properties may be set, a user can add properties that the form or client never shows, such as role, isAdmin, verified, credit, ownerId or tenantId, and the application saves them. The weakness is known as mass assignment in Ruby on Rails, Laravel and Node.js, and as autobinding or over-posting in Spring MVC and ASP.NET.

It is identified by comparing the properties an object exposes, for example in the response to a request that reads it, with those accepted when it is created or updated, then adding protected properties to those requests and checking whether the stored object changes. Client-side code, API documentation and error messages often reveal property names, and parameter discovery tools can guess others.
entries.impact: An attacker with an ordinary account can change properties that the application relies on for security or business rules. Typical results are granting themselves an administrative role, marking an account as verified or paid, adding credit, extending a subscription, or moving a record into another user's or tenant's ownership. The severity depends on which properties the bound object holds: it is greatest where roles, permissions, ownership or financial values sit on the same object as user-editable fields.
entries.remediation:
Bind requests only to the properties a user is allowed to set:

  • Accept input through dedicated input objects (data transfer objects or view models) that contain only the user-editable properties, and map them explicitly onto the stored entity.
  • Where the framework binds directly to models, use an allowlist of permitted properties rather than a denylist, so that new properties are protected by default: strong parameters in Ruby on Rails, $fillable rather than $guarded in Laravel, [Bind] with named properties or input models in ASP.NET, setAllowedFields in a Spring @InitBinder method, and explicit fields on Django forms and serialisers.
  • Mark sensitive properties as read-only in API serialisers, for example with read_only_fields in Django REST Framework.
  • Change roles, ownership and financial values only through dedicated functions that carry their own authorisation checks.
# Ruby on Rails: strong parameters params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email) // Laravel: allowlist on the model protected $fillable = ['name', 'email']; // Spring MVC: allowlist on the binder binder.setAllowedFields("name", "email");

Confirm the fix by resending create and update requests with added protected properties, and checking that they are ignored or rejected and that the stored object is unchanged.

entries.title: Files Accessible Without Authentication
entries.summary: Private files such as uploads, reports or exports can be downloaded by anyone who has their address, because file requests are not checked for a valid session.
entries.description:
Files that should only be available to particular signed-in users, such as uploaded documents, generated reports, invoices, data exports and attachments, are stored where the web server or a storage service delivers them directly. The application checks the user before showing a link to the file, but the request for the file itself is not checked, so anyone who has the address can download it without a session.

The weakness is identified by taking the address of a private file and requesting it again with no session cookie or token, for example from a private browser window, and with a different user's session. File names and paths are then examined: sequential numbers, dates, user identifiers or original file names make other files easy to guess, whereas long random names mean an attacker needs the address itself. Signed links that do not expire, or that stay valid for long periods, show the same weakness in a different form.

Addresses of private files leak more widely than is often assumed: through browser history, shared emails and chat messages, proxy and server logs, Referer headers sent to third parties, and search engine indexing of any page that links to them.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains or guesses a file's address can read it without an account, and the access is not tied to any user. Where names are predictable, every file of that kind can be downloaded by script. The impact depends on the content: personal data, identity documents, financial records and commercially sensitive reports are common, and their exposure may also create regulatory obligations for the organisation. Long random names reduce the risk to files whose addresses have leaked, but do not remove it.
entries.remediation:
Check authentication and authorisation every time a private file is requested:

  • Store private files outside the web root, or in a private storage container, so that they cannot be fetched directly.
  • Serve them through an application endpoint that checks, on every request, that the signed-in user may access that specific file, then streams it. To keep the web server doing the transfer, the application can respond with an internal redirect, such as nginx's X-Accel-Redirect header pointing to a location marked internal.
  • Where files must be delivered directly by a storage service or content delivery network, issue short-lived signed links only after the authorisation check.
  • Use long random file identifiers as defence in depth, and send Cache-Control: no-store with private files so that shared caches do not keep copies.
# nginx: files reachable only through the application location /protected-files/ { internal; alias /srv/app/private-files/; }

As an interim measure, deny direct requests to the storage path at the web server. Confirm the fix by requesting private files with no session and with another user's session: both should be refused.

entries.title: Business Logic Flaw
entries.summary: The application does not enforce the rules of its own processes, so steps can be skipped, repeated or combined in ways that give a user an unintended advantage.
entries.description:
Business logic flaws arise when the application accepts each request as valid on its own terms but does not enforce the rules that should govern the process as a whole: the order of steps, the state an object must be in, the limits on a value, or who may act on what. The application assumes that users will follow the path its interface presents, and an attacker who sends requests directly can depart from it.

Typical examples include skipping a step in a multi-stage process, such as going straight to confirmation without completing payment, verification or approval; repeating an action meant to happen once, such as applying a single-use voucher or submitting a refund twice; combining offers that should be exclusive; approving one's own request; acting on an object after it has been locked, cancelled or completed; and supplying values the process never anticipated, such as negative amounts.

These flaws are identified by manual testing: understanding the intended process and its rules, then reordering, skipping, repeating and altering requests with an intercepting proxy and observing whether the application notices. Automated scanners rarely find them, because they have no model of what the application is supposed to allow, and the requests involved look legitimate to a web application firewall.
entries.impact: The impact depends entirely on the process affected. Common outcomes are financial loss through unpaid orders, repeated discounts or refunds, the bypass of verification or approval controls that the organisation relies on, and records left in states that undermine the integrity of later processing or reporting. Exploitation usually needs only an ordinary account and produces activity that looks like normal use, so it can continue unnoticed until reconciliation or audit.
entries.remediation:
Enforce the business rules on the server, at the point each action takes effect:

  • Model multi-step processes as a server-side state machine: record the state of each order, application or request on the server, and have each step check that the object is in the state it requires before acting, rejecting anything out of sequence.
  • Keep process state on the server, tied to the session and the object, rather than in hidden fields, cookies or client-side storage.
  • Validate each value against the business rules where it is used, not only at an earlier step: signs, ranges, totals, eligibility, ownership and single-use conditions.
  • Make once-only actions atomic, recording that a voucher or refund has been used in the same transaction that applies it.
  • Enforce separation of duties, so that users cannot approve their own requests.
  • Include abuse cases in design reviews and threat modelling, and turn each one into an automated test.

Monitoring for anomalies, such as unusual discounts, refunds or state changes, provides an interim safeguard while fixes are made. Confirm the fix by repeating the specific sequence that exposed the flaw and checking that the application refuses it.

entries.title: Race Condition (Limit Overrun)
entries.summary: A limit is checked and then updated in separate steps, so requests sent at the same moment can all pass the check and exceed the limit.
entries.description:
The application enforces a limit by first checking it and then recording the action in a separate step, without making the two steps a single atomic operation. When several identical requests arrive at the same moment, each one passes the check before any of them records its effect, so the limit is exceeded. This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition, often called limit overrun.

Typical targets are single-use vouchers and gift cards redeemed several times, a balance spent or withdrawn twice, one-per-user actions such as votes, trials, referral bonuses or reviews repeated, and counters that protect against brute force, such as limits on sign-in or one-time code attempts, bypassed. The window between check and update is often only milliseconds, but sending requests in parallel makes it practical to hit: techniques such as the single-packet attack over HTTP/2 make many requests arrive together, and tools such as Burp Suite's Repeater, sending a group of requests in parallel, and Turbo Intruder automate this.

The weakness is identified by sending the same limited request many times at once and checking whether more than one succeeds, by comparing balances, counts or records before and after. Automated scanners rarely find it.
entries.impact: An attacker can obtain more than the application intends to allow: repeated discounts, duplicated credit or withdrawals, extra votes or bonuses, or many more guesses at a password or one-time code than the lockout permits. The financial or integrity impact depends on the limit involved and on how many requests win the race, which is often several per attempt. Exploitation usually requires an account, and the duplicated actions can be hard to distinguish from genuine ones afterwards.
entries.remediation:
Make the check and the update a single atomic operation, so that only one request can ever succeed:

  • Put the condition into the update itself and act only if it changed a row, for example a conditional UPDATE that marks a voucher used only where it is still unused, or deducts from a balance only where the balance is sufficient.
  • Otherwise, read and update within one database transaction that locks the row, for example with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  • Use database constraints for one-per-user rules, such as a unique index on the user and the offer, so that duplicate inserts fail.
  • Use atomic counters, such as Redis INCR, for attempt limits, incrementing before the attempt is processed rather than after it fails.
  • Accept an idempotency key on operations that must happen once per request, and reject repeats.
-- Check and update in one statement; proceed only if one row changed UPDATE vouchers SET redeemed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, redeemed_by = ? WHERE code = ? AND redeemed_at IS NULL;

Confirm the fix by repeating the parallel requests and checking that exactly one succeeds and the others are refused.
keywords: time of check time of use

entries.title: Price or Quantity Manipulation
entries.summary: The application trusts prices, totals or quantities sent by the browser, so a buyer can change what they are charged or order negative or fractional quantities.
entries.description:
The application takes the price, discount, total, currency or quantity of an order from values the client sends, such as hidden form fields, JSON properties, cookies or a basket held in the browser, and uses them to work out the amount charged, instead of looking up prices and recalculating totals on the server. Values that the interface never lets a user choose, such as a negative, zero, fractional or extremely large quantity, are also accepted.

The weakness is identified by intercepting the requests that add items to a basket, apply discounts, choose delivery options, check out and start payment, changing the price, quantity, currency and discount values, and checking the resulting order total, the amount passed to the payment provider and the confirmation. A related form appears in payment integrations where the amount travels through the user's browser to the payment provider and the application does not check, when payment is confirmed, that the amount and currency paid match the order total.

Negative quantities can reduce the total charged for other items in a basket or create credit, and very large values can overflow the numeric types used in calculations.
entries.impact: An attacker can buy goods or services for less than their price or for nothing, generate credit or refunds, or combine discounts beyond the intended limits. The result is direct financial loss and possible fraud, which often goes unnoticed until orders are reconciled. Where guest checkout is offered no account is needed, and the attack can be repeated as often as the attacker likes.
entries.remediation:
Treat every price, total and quantity from the client as untrusted, and calculate charges on the server:

  • Accept only product identifiers and quantities from the client, and take prices from the server's catalogue. Recalculate discounts, tax, delivery and the order total on the server whenever the basket changes and again at the point of order.
  • Validate quantities as whole numbers within sensible minimum and maximum values and available stock, and reject zero, negative and fractional values. Use decimal types for money rather than floating point.
  • Check discount codes on the server for eligibility, expiry, single use and combination rules, and never allow a line or order total below zero.
  • Send the amount to the payment provider from the server, or in a request the provider can verify, and when payment is confirmed, verify the notification's authenticity and that the amount and currency paid match the order total before fulfilling the order.

As an interim measure, reconcile orders against catalogue prices and hold any whose totals do not match for review. Confirm the fix by repeating the tampered requests and checking that the server ignores client-supplied prices and rejects invalid quantities.

entries.title: Reliance on Client-Side Security Controls
entries.summary: Security checks are carried out only in the browser, so anyone who sends requests directly to the server can bypass them.
entries.description:
The application relies on controls that run in the user's browser to enforce rules that matter for security: JavaScript validation of input, length limits set in the page, drop-down lists or radio buttons that restrict the values offered, fields that are disabled, hidden or marked read-only, buttons hidden for some roles, and decisions based on flags held in JavaScript variables, cookies or browser storage. The server accepts whatever it receives, on the assumption that the browser has already applied these rules.

Because every request can be intercepted, changed or written from scratch with an intercepting proxy, a command-line tool or a script, none of these controls binds an attacker. The weakness is identified by sending requests with values the interface prevents, such as out-of-range or over-length input, options that are not in a list, changed values in disabled or hidden fields and altered client-side flags, then checking whether the server accepts and acts on them.

Specific forms of this weakness, such as trusting prices sent by the browser or binding unexpected properties onto data objects, are often reported separately where they have their own impact.
entries.impact: An attacker can submit data that the application never expected, bypass business rules and reach functions that the interface hides. Depending on what the server trusts, this can lead to invalid or malicious data being stored and later processed by other components, which may enable injection attacks there, to actions performed beyond a user's permitted limits, and to features or records being reached that the user should not see. The attacker usually needs only an ordinary account.
entries.remediation:
Enforce every security-relevant rule on the server, and treat client-side checks as a convenience for users only:

  • Validate all input on the server for type, length, format and range, and check selections against an allowlist of the values that user may choose.
  • Make authorisation and feature decisions on the server for every request, using the identity and permissions in the server-side session, never flags supplied by the client.
  • Keep state that affects security on the server. Where a value must make a round trip through the client, protect it with a server-side signature, such as an HMAC, and verify it on return.
  • Where the same rules are needed in the browser and on the server, define them once, for example as a shared schema, and always enforce them on the server.
  • Ensure that features which are disabled or hidden in the interface are also disabled on the server.

Confirm the fix by sending requests directly with the values the interface prevents, and checking that the server rejects each one.

entries.title: CSV (Formula) Injection
entries.summary: User-supplied values are written into CSV or spreadsheet exports without neutralisation, so a spreadsheet program can run them as formulas when the export is opened.
entries.description:
The application writes values entered by users, such as names, addresses, comments or ticket subjects, into CSV or spreadsheet exports without neutralising them. Spreadsheet programs such as Microsoft Excel and LibreOffice Calc treat a cell that begins with =, +, - or @, and in some cases a tab or carriage return character, as a formula when the file is opened. An attacker who can place text in a field that is later exported can therefore embed a formula that is evaluated on the computer of whoever opens the file, typically a member of staff or an administrator.

Common payloads use HYPERLINK formulas that send the contents of other cells to an external server when the cell is clicked, formulas that fetch external data, and legacy Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) formulas that can start other programs on Windows. Current versions of Microsoft Excel do not start other programs through DDE unless a setting that is off by default has been turned on, and the common spreadsheet programs usually warn the user before fetching external content, so the more serious outcomes depend on older software, changed settings or the user accepting warnings.

The weakness is identified by entering harmless formulas, such as =1+1, into fields that appear in exports, exporting the data and opening it in a spreadsheet program to see whether the formula is evaluated. Exports built without quoting each field correctly can also allow a separator character in the input to start a new cell that begins with a formula.
entries.impact: When a victim opens the export, a formula can send data from the spreadsheet to a server the attacker controls once a link is clicked, show misleading values or, where older software or changed settings allow it and the victim accepts any warnings, run commands on their computer and give the attacker a foothold on a staff workstation. The attack needs the victim to open the file and usually to interact with it, and its success depends on the spreadsheet program's settings. The risk is higher where exports are routinely opened by privileged staff.
entries.remediation:
Neutralise formula characters in every exported cell that can contain user-supplied text:

  • When a cell begins with =, +, -, @, a tab or a carriage return, prefix it with a single quotation mark ('), so that spreadsheet programs treat it as text. Fields that are validated as numbers can be left unchanged.
  • Generate CSV with a library that encloses every field in double quotation marks and doubles any quotation marks within it, so that input cannot break out of its cell.
  • Where users need a spreadsheet rather than CSV, generate the file with a library that writes user-supplied values as text cells rather than formulas.
  • Validate input on entry where formula characters are not expected, such as in names, as defence in depth.
  • Advise staff not to enable content or accept warnings in exported files.
import csv def neutralise(value): text = str(value) if text.startswith(('=', '+', '-', '@', '\t', '\r')): return "'" + text return text writer = csv.writer(output, quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL)

Confirm the fix by exporting records that contain test formulas and opening the file: each should be displayed as text.

entries.title: Reverse Tabnabbing
entries.summary: A page opened from the application in a new tab keeps a reference to the original tab, so a malicious page can silently replace it with a phishing page.
entries.description:
When a page opens another page in a new tab or window, the browser can give the new page a reference to the original through window.opener. If the new page is cross-origin it cannot read the original, but it can still change its location. A page under an attacker's control, reached from a link that users can post or from a compromised third-party site, can use this to navigate the original tab to a convincing copy of the application's sign-in page while the user is looking at the new tab. When the user returns, they may sign in again on the fake page.

The opener reference is created by links with target="_blank" in older browsers, by links that also carry rel="opener", and by window.open() calls that do not pass noopener. Current versions of the major browsers treat target="_blank" links as if rel="noopener" were set, so the issue now arises mainly from window.open(), from explicit rel="opener", and from users on older browsers.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the page source and scripts for links and calls that open external or user-supplied addresses in a new tab without noopener, and can be confirmed with a test page that changes window.opener.location. Scanners often report the pattern as a low or informational issue.
entries.impact: An attacker can redirect a user's original tab to a page of their choosing, most usefully a fake sign-in page, and collect any credentials the user enters there. The attack requires the user to follow a link to a page the attacker controls, then return to the original tab without noticing that its address has changed. It does not give the attacker access to the original page's content or session.
entries.remediation:
Remove the opener reference wherever the application opens another page:

  • Add rel="noopener" to every link that opens in a new tab, or rel="noopener noreferrer" where the destination should not receive the Referer header, and remove rel="opener" unless an integration genuinely needs it. Apply this automatically to user-supplied links when they are rendered.
  • Pass noopener in the features argument of window.open(), or set the new window's opener property to null before navigating it.
  • Send the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin header, which places cross-origin pages opened from the application in a separate browsing context group with no reference back to it. Test it first, as it also breaks pop-up flows that depend on the opener, such as some payment and sign-in integrations.
<a href="https://www.example.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">...</a> window.open(url, "_blank", "noopener"); Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin

Confirm the fix by repeating the test with the test page: window.opener should be null in every page opened from the application.

entries.title: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking
entries.summary: The WebSocket handshake is authenticated by cookies alone and its Origin is not checked, so a malicious site can open a connection as a signed-in visitor.
entries.description:
A WebSocket connection starts with an HTTP handshake request, to which the browser attaches the site's cookies. Neither the same-origin policy nor CORS stops a page on another site from opening a WebSocket connection to any server. If the server authenticates the connection only by the session cookie, or by other credentials the browser sends automatically, and does not check the Origin header of the handshake, a malicious page visited by a signed-in user can open a connection as that user. Unlike cross-site request forgery, the attacker's page can both send messages and read every response, so it has two-way, interactive access with the user's privileges.

The weakness is identified by examining the handshake for authentication that relies only on cookies, with no token in the request or the first message, then replaying it with an Origin header for another site and checking whether the server still accepts it (101 Switching Protocols) and answers messages. A proof of concept page hosted elsewhere confirms it.

The SameSite cookie attribute affects the result: cookies marked Lax or Strict, or treated as Lax by browsers that apply it by default, are not sent with a cross-site handshake. However, cookies marked None are sent, as are cookies without the attribute in browsers that do not apply the default, unless the browser blocks third-party cookies, as some now do by default. Pages on sibling subdomains count as the same site, so the attribute does not stop a handshake started from one of them.
entries.impact: An attacker's page can act as the victim over the WebSocket for as long as it stays open, reading data the application streams to the user, such as messages, notifications or account information, and sending messages that perform actions, such as posting content, changing settings or placing orders. The victim must be signed in and visit the attacker's page in a browser that sends the session cookie with the handshake. The impact depends on what the WebSocket carries, and is greatest where it handles sensitive data or privileged operations.
entries.remediation:
Authenticate WebSocket connections in a way that a third-party page cannot reproduce:

  • Check the Origin header of every handshake against an exact allowlist of the application's own origins, and refuse any other value. Avoid prefix, suffix or loose pattern matches.
  • Do not rely on cookies alone. Require a token that a cross-site page cannot obtain, such as an anti-CSRF token or a short-lived, single-use ticket issued by an authenticated request, in the handshake or the first message, and accept no other messages until it is validated. Prefer the first message to the address, which may be logged.
  • Set session cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict as defence in depth.
  • Authorise each message on the server, as for any other request.
// ASP.NET Core var options = new WebSocketOptions(); options.AllowedOrigins.Add("https://app.example.com"); app.UseWebSockets(options); // Spring registry.addHandler(handler, "/ws").setAllowedOrigins("https://app.example.com");

Confirm the fix by repeating the handshake with a foreign Origin header and from a test page on another site: both should be refused.

entries.title: Insecure postMessage Handling
entries.summary: The page exchanges window.postMessage messages without checking the origin of the sender or recipient, so another website can send it commands or receive its data.
entries.description:
The application uses the browser's window.postMessage() API to pass messages between windows or frames from different origins, for example between a page and an embedded widget, a payment frame or a single sign-on popup. The API exists to allow cross-origin communication, so each side must check who it is talking to. The receiving page's message event handler does not compare event.origin with the origins it expects, or checks it loosely, for example by looking for the expected domain name anywhere in the origin string, which a domain registered by an attacker can also satisfy. It then acts on event.data.

The weakness also appears on the sending side, where a page posts sensitive data, such as tokens or personal details, with a target origin of *, so whichever document is loaded in the target window receives it.

The issue is identified by reviewing client-side JavaScript for message event listeners and postMessage() calls, then confirming from a page on another origin that opens or frames the application and sends crafted messages. It is most serious when message data reaches a dangerous sink such as innerHTML, eval() or location, which turns it into DOM-based cross-site scripting.
entries.impact: An attacker who persuades a logged-in user to visit a page under their control can open or frame the vulnerable page and send it messages that it treats as trusted. Depending on what the handler does, this can run script in the application's origin, and so act as the user and read their data, change settings, trigger actions or redirect the user. Where sensitive data is posted with a wildcard target origin, the attacker's page can receive it directly. Exploitation requires the user to visit the attacker's page.
entries.remediation:
Treat every message as untrusted input from another website:

  • In each message handler, compare event.origin exactly with an allowlist of expected origins (scheme, host and port) and ignore messages from anything else. Do not use substring, prefix or unanchored pattern checks.
  • Where the sender is a known window, also check that event.source is that window.
  • Validate the structure and type of event.data before use, treat it as data only, and never pass it to eval(), innerHTML, document.write() or a URL that is navigated to; use textContent and safe DOM methods instead.
  • When sending, always give the exact target origin as the second argument of postMessage(), never * for anything that is not public.
  • Remove message handlers that are no longer needed, including those added by third-party scripts that are no longer used.
const allowedOrigins = new Set(["https://app.example.com"]); window.addEventListener("message", (event) => { if (!allowedOrigins.has(event.origin)) return; const msg = event.data; if (typeof msg !== "object" || msg === null || msg.type !== "resize") return; // act on the validated message; write text with textContent, not innerHTML });

A Content Security Policy that blocks inline script and eval() limits the effect of an injection through a message handler while the code is corrected. Confirm the fix by sending crafted messages from a page on another origin and checking that they are ignored.

entries.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution
entries.summary: The application handles a parameter supplied more than once inconsistently, so one component can validate one value while another acts on a different one.
entries.description:
HTTP does not define what should happen when the same parameter name appears more than once in a query string or request body, and platforms differ: PHP keeps the last occurrence, the getParameter() method of Java servlets returns the first, classic ASP.NET joins the values with commas, and Node.js frameworks such as Express typically return an array. HTTP parameter pollution (HPP) exploits these differences.

The weakness arises when two components see different values for the same request. A web application firewall or validation layer may check one occurrence while the code that acts on the request uses another. Where the application inserts a user-supplied value into a request it makes to an internal service or API (server-side parameter pollution), an extra &name=value pair, sometimes URL-encoded as %26, can add or override a parameter in that request. Client-side variants occur where a value is reflected into links or form actions without encoding, so an injected parameter is carried into the user's next request.

The issue is identified by repeating parameters, injecting encoded separators into parameter values and observing which value each part of the application acts on. Its impact depends entirely on what the overridden parameter controls.
entries.impact: An attacker may be able to bypass input validation or a web application firewall rule, override a value that the application sets itself in a back-end request, such as an account identifier, role or price, or alter links and forms presented to other users. In most cases the effect is limited to changing the behaviour of a single function, and exploitation requires knowledge of how each component handles duplicate parameters. Where the overridden parameter controls authorisation or a financial value, the issue should be rated on that effect.
entries.remediation:
• Define how each endpoint treats repeated parameters and enforce it: reject requests that contain a duplicate of a parameter that should appear once, rather than silently picking one occurrence.
  • Make sure validation and use read the same occurrence through the same framework call, and that any front-end filter, web application firewall and back end agree on the behaviour.
  • When building requests to other services, never concatenate user input into a query string or body. Use the HTTP client's parameter encoding or a URL builder, so that characters such as &, = and # in a value are encoded, and set server-controlled parameters independently of user input.
  • Encode user-supplied values when reflecting them into URLs, links and form actions.
  • In Node.js, where parameters can arrive as arrays, check the type of each value before use; middleware such as hpp can enforce a single value.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original tests with duplicated and encoded parameters and checking that the request is rejected or handled consistently.

entries.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS)
entries.summary: A regular expression applied to user input can take exponential time on crafted input, letting a few requests tie up the server's processing capacity.
entries.description:
The application validates or parses user-supplied input with a regular expression whose matching time can grow exponentially, or polynomially to a high degree, with the length of the input. Most regular expression engines in common use, including those in JavaScript, Java, .NET, Python and PCRE, work by backtracking. When part of a pattern can match the same characters in many different ways, for example through nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ or overlapping alternatives such as (a|aa)*, a string that almost matches but then fails forces the engine to try every combination before giving up.

A short input of a few dozen characters can therefore keep a processor core busy for seconds, minutes or longer. The effect is most severe on single-threaded runtimes such as Node.js, where one slow match blocks the event loop and every other request waits, but on any platform a handful of concurrent requests can occupy all worker threads.

The issue is identified by reviewing patterns applied to untrusted input, in validation code, routing, parsers and third-party libraries, by static analysis tools that flag catastrophic backtracking, and by sending crafted near-matching strings of increasing length while measuring response times. Testing is normally limited to demonstrating a measurable slowdown rather than an outage.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can degrade or deny service to all users by sending a small number of crafted requests, with little bandwidth and no special tooling. The effect usually lasts only while the attack continues, but on single-threaded platforms a single request can make the whole application unresponsive, and platforms that scale automatically may add capacity and cost. The weakness does not expose or change data. Where the vulnerable pattern is reachable only after authentication, or input length is already tightly limited, the practical impact is lower.
entries.remediation:
• Rewrite vulnerable patterns so that each part of the input can be matched in only one way: remove nested quantifiers and overlapping alternatives, anchor the pattern, and use possessive quantifiers or atomic groups where the engine supports them.
  • Where available, use a linear-time engine for untrusted input, such as RE2 and its bindings, the Go regexp package, the Rust regex crate or RegexOptions.NonBacktracking in .NET 7 and later.
  • Enforce a maximum input length before any pattern is applied.
  • Set a match timeout where the platform supports one, such as the matchTimeout argument of the .NET Regex constructor, and treat a timeout as a validation failure.
  • Prefer well-tested library validators for common formats such as email addresses and URLs over hand-written patterns, and keep third-party libraries up to date, as many ReDoS flaws are fixed in library releases.
  • Add a regular expression linter or static analysis rule to the build to catch new vulnerable patterns.

Rate limiting reduces the effect while patterns are corrected but does not remove it. Confirm the fix by repeating the crafted inputs and checking that response times stay flat as input length grows.

entries.title: Insecure JSONP Endpoint
entries.summary: An endpoint returns data as JSONP, a script any website can load, so other sites may read data meant for the logged-in user or inject script through the callback name.
entries.description:
JSONP (JSON with padding) is a legacy technique for sharing data across origins that predates CORS. The endpoint wraps its JSON response in a call to a function named by a request parameter, commonly callback or jsonp, and returns it as JavaScript. Because browsers let a page load and run a script from any origin, any website can include the endpoint with a <script> element and receive the data in its own function, and the same-origin policy, which normally stops one site reading another's responses, does not apply.

Two problems follow. Where the endpoint returns data specific to the user and identifies them by cookie, a site the user visits may be able to read that data, a form of cross-site script inclusion. Current browsers limit this: Chromium-based browsers do not send cookies that lack a SameSite attribute, or are marked Lax or Strict, with such requests, and other browsers block or partition third-party cookies, so the exposure mainly arises where session cookies are marked SameSite=None or the endpoint trusts network location rather than a login. Separately, where the callback name is not restricted, an attacker controls the start of a script served from the application's origin, which can be used to bypass a Content Security Policy that trusts that origin, and can lead to cross-site scripting if the response is served as HTML.

The issue is identified by adding a callback parameter to JSON endpoints, observing whether the response is wrapped, and checking which characters the callback accepts.
entries.impact: Where the conditions above are met, an attacker who lures a logged-in user to their website can read whatever the endpoint returns for that user, such as personal details, account data or anti-CSRF tokens, without the user noticing. An unrestricted callback also lets an attacker use the endpoint to defeat a Content Security Policy that would otherwise contain an injection flaw elsewhere. The impact depends on the sensitivity of the returned data and on the session cookie's SameSite setting; with current browser defaults, theft of authenticated data through JSONP is often blocked.
entries.remediation:
• Retire JSONP. Serve data as JSON with the application/json content type and, where another origin genuinely needs it, allow that origin explicitly with CORS rather than allowing every site.
  • Until the endpoint can be removed, do not return user-specific or sensitive data through it, and disable the callback parameter on every endpoint that does not need it, including framework defaults.
  • Restrict the callback name to a short allowlist of known function names, or at minimum to letters, digits, underscores and dots, and reject anything else.
  • Serve JSONP responses with a JavaScript content type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, never as HTML.
  • Reject cross-site requests for authenticated data by checking the Sec-Fetch-Site request header (a resource isolation policy), and set session cookies to SameSite=Lax or Strict unless cross-site use is required.

Confirm the fix by requesting the endpoint with a callback parameter and checking that a JSON response, not a script, is returned.

entries.title: Overly Permissive Cross-Domain Policy File
entries.summary: A crossdomain.xml or clientaccesspolicy.xml file allows content from any domain to read the site's responses through browser plug-ins that are now obsolete.
entries.description:
Adobe Flash Player and Microsoft Silverlight enforced their own cross-origin rules. Before content from one domain could read responses from another, the plug-in fetched a policy file from the target site: /crossdomain.xml for Flash, a format some other clients also adopted, and /clientaccesspolicy.xml for Silverlight. The site's policy file allows any domain, through an entry such as <allow-access-from domain="*" /> in crossdomain.xml or <domain uri="*" /> in clientaccesspolicy.xml, or it trusts a broad wildcard of domains. Content hosted anywhere could then make requests to the site carrying the user's cookies and read the responses.

Both plug-ins have reached end of life and are not supported by current browsers, so the file has little practical effect for most users today. It remains worth reporting because it shows legacy configuration that has not been reviewed, because some older or specialised clients may still honour it, and because the same trust decisions are often repeated in other cross-origin settings.

The issue is identified by requesting the two files from the site root and other directories and reviewing the domains they allow. Scanners report it from the presence of a wildcard entry.
entries.impact: For a user still running a client that honours the policy, a malicious site could read any content the user can access on the affected site, including personal data and anti-CSRF tokens, and so perform actions as the user. With Flash and Silverlight no longer supported by mainstream browsers, the realistic likelihood is low, and the finding is mainly a sign of outdated configuration. The impact is higher where specialised clients that honour the file are in use.
entries.remediation:
• Delete crossdomain.xml and clientaccesspolicy.xml unless a supported client still needs them. Check the whole site, not just the root, and remove copies from other directories and from deployment templates.
  • Where a policy file must remain, list only specific trusted domains, never * or a broad wildcard, and do not allow request headers with a wildcard.
  • Send X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: none to tell clients that honour policy files not to use any on the site, or master-only where a single root policy is still needed.
  • Use CORS, with an explicit list of allowed origins, for any cross-origin access that current browsers need.
nginx: add_header X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies "none" always; Apache httpd: Header always set X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies "none" IIS (web.config, inside system.webServer): <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <add name="X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies" value="none" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol>

Confirm the fix by requesting both files and checking that they are no longer served.

entries.title: Verbose Error Messages
entries.summary: Error responses reveal internal details such as stack traces, file paths, software versions or database queries that help an attacker plan further attacks.
entries.description:
When the application meets an unexpected condition, such as malformed input, a missing parameter or a failed database call, it returns detailed diagnostic information to the user instead of a generic message. Typical examples are full stack traces from Java, .NET, Python or PHP code; framework error pages; database error messages that include fragments of the failing SQL query; and messages that disclose server-side file paths, internal host names, configuration values or the exact versions of components in use.

The behaviour usually stems from development settings left in place, error handling that passes exception text straight to the response, or web server and framework default error pages shown in production. It is identified by sending unexpected input (wrong data types, very long values, special characters, unexpected HTTP methods or malformed requests) to each function and reviewing the responses; automated scanners flag recognisable stack trace and database error patterns.

A database error that reflects injected syntax is a strong indicator of SQL injection and should be investigated, and reported, as that issue. This finding covers the disclosure itself.
entries.impact: The disclosed details do not compromise the application by themselves, but they reduce the effort needed to attack it: software versions can be matched to known vulnerabilities, paths and queries reveal how the application is built, and error behaviour can confirm whether an injection attempt is reaching the back end. Occasionally error output includes more sensitive values, such as connection strings, credentials or other users' data, in which case the impact is higher and should be rated on what was exposed.
entries.remediation:
• Configure a global exception handler that logs full details on the server with a correlation identifier and returns a generic message and an appropriate status code to the user. Include the identifier in the response so that support staff can find the log entry.
  • Disable development error output in production. For example, set customErrors to On or RemoteOnly in ASP.NET, use the developer exception page only in the Development environment in ASP.NET Core, set display_errors = Off in PHP, set DEBUG = False in Django and set APP_DEBUG=false in Laravel.
  • Replace the default error pages of the web server and application server with custom pages for common status codes such as 400, 403, 404 and 500.
  • Return consistent, generic error responses from APIs, for example in a problem details format without exception text.
  • Check what is logged, so that secrets are not written to the logs instead.

Confirm the fix by repeating the inputs that produced detailed errors and checking that only generic messages are returned.

patterns: \b(verbose|detailed|application|debug) error (message|messages|disclosure|page)|\bstack trace\b|\berror message(s)? (containing|disclos)|\bapplication error disclosure\b|\bdebug error messages\b

entries.title: Server Software Version Disclosure
entries.summary: HTTP response headers or default pages name the web server, framework or language and their versions, which helps an attacker select known exploits.
entries.description:
The server identifies the software that handles requests, and often its exact version, in HTTP response headers and default content. Common sources are the Server header, for example naming Apache httpd, nginx or IIS with a version number and operating system; X-Powered-By, for example naming PHP or ASP.NET; X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version; generator meta tags added by content management systems; and the signature line on default error pages.

The information is collected passively from ordinary responses and is reported by almost every scanner. It is useful to an attacker because a precise version can be compared with published vulnerabilities, but it is not proof that the software is vulnerable: operating system vendors often backport security fixes without changing the version string, so a version that appears outdated should be confirmed against the vendor's patch information before a missing patch is reported. Removing the banner also does not prevent fingerprinting, as software can usually be identified from its behaviour, default pages and response formats.

Where the disclosed version is confirmed to be outdated or unsupported, that should be reported as a separate finding.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. The disclosure saves an attacker some reconnaissance effort and lets automated tools target the server with exploits for the identified version, so it matters more if the software is not kept up to date. Removing it is a hardening measure that reduces the information freely available, not a substitute for patching.
entries.remediation:
Remove or minimise identifying headers and banners on every server and proxy in the request path:

  • nginx: set server_tokens off; to remove the version from the Server header and error pages, and use proxy_hide_header or fastcgi_hide_header to drop X-Powered-By from upstream responses.
  • Apache httpd: set ServerTokens Prod and ServerSignature Off in the main server configuration.
  • IIS and ASP.NET: remove X-Powered-By under customHeaders, set enableVersionHeader="false" on httpRuntime, set MvcHandler.DisableMvcResponseHeader = true for ASP.NET MVC and, on IIS versions that support it, set removeServerHeader="true" on requestFiltering.
  • PHP: set expose_php = Off in php.ini.
  • Remove generator meta tags and version strings from page templates, and replace default error pages with custom ones.
nginx (http block): server_tokens off; fastcgi_hide_header X-Powered-By; Apache httpd (main server configuration): ServerTokens Prod ServerSignature Off IIS (web.config): <system.web> <httpRuntime enableVersionHeader="false" /> </system.web> <system.webServer> <security> <requestFiltering removeServerHeader="true" /> </security> <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <remove name="X-Powered-By" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol> </system.webServer>

The nginx and Apache settings still name the product, without its version. Confirm the change by inspecting the headers of normal pages, error pages and static files.

patterns.re: \bserver leaks (version )?information\b|\bserver (version|banner) disclosure\b|\bX-Powered-By\b|\bweb server version\b|\bHTTP Server Type and Version\b|\bversion (disclosure|information) (in|via)\b.*\b(header|server)\b|\bbanner_(server|application)\b

entries.title: Directory Listing Enabled
entries.summary: The web server lists the contents of directories that have no index page, revealing files that were never meant to be linked or downloaded.
entries.description:
When a request is made for a directory that has no default document, such as index.html, the web server generates and returns a list of every file and subdirectory in it. Automatic indexing is a feature of most web servers, including mod_autoindex in Apache httpd, the autoindex module in nginx, directory browsing in IIS and the default servlets of Java application servers, and it is enabled either in the global configuration or for particular directories.

The weakness lies in what the listings expose. Files that are not linked from the application can normally be found only by guessing their names; a listing removes that obstacle and reveals backup copies, archives, uploaded documents, logs, configuration and include files, temporary files and old versions of scripts, as well as the structure of the application.
