The issue is identified by requesting directory paths, including those found in page source, scripts and other responses, and looking for the server's characteristic "Index of" pages or their equivalent. Scanners report it wherever a listing is returned. Its severity depends on what the listed directories contain: a listing of public images is of little consequence, whereas one of an uploads or backup directory can expose sensitive data.
entries.impact: An attacker can browse the listed directories and download any file the web server will serve from them, including content never intended to be public, such as other users' uploaded documents, backups that contain source code or credentials, and log files. Even where nothing sensitive is listed, the structure and file names help an attacker map the application and plan further attacks. The impact is limited to what the listed directories contain.
entries.remediation:
• Disable automatic directory listings globally, and enable them only for directories that are deliberately meant to be browsed.
  • Review the directories that were listed and remove anything that should not be on the web server, such as backups, archives, logs and old files. Move uploaded files and other data outside the web root or behind an access-controlled download handler.
  • Rotate any credentials or keys found in files that were exposed.
Apache httpd (server configuration, virtual host, directory or .htaccess): Options -Indexes nginx (http, server or location block; off is the default): autoindex off; IIS (web.config, inside system.webServer): <directoryBrowse enabled="false" />

For Java application servers, make sure the default servlet's listings parameter is false, as it is by default in Apache Tomcat. An empty index file in each directory hides the listing but is not a substitute for disabling the feature. Confirm the fix by requesting the previously listed directories and checking that a 403 or 404 response is returned.

entries.title: Backup or Temporary Files Exposed
entries.summary: Backup, temporary or archive copies of files are left in web-accessible locations, where they can be downloaded and may reveal source code, credentials or data.
entries.description:
Copies of files have been left in directories that the web server serves: editor backups and swap files (index.php~, .index.php.swp), copies made by hand before a change (config.php.bak, web.config.old, login.aspx.orig), archives of the site or its database (backup.zip, site.tar.gz, dump.sql), and temporary or log files. Because the server does not recognise these extensions as code to run, it returns their raw contents: a request for config.php runs the script and returns nothing of interest, whereas config.php.bak returns its source, including any credentials it holds.

Such files are found with content discovery tools such as ffuf, Gobuster and dirsearch, using wordlists and permutations of known file names with backup extensions, and through directory listings and references in pages. Web server scanners such as Nikto report common names. The files usually arise from editing directly on the server, from manual backups taken before an update, and from archives created during migrations and never removed.
entries.impact: Anyone can download the files without authentication once their names are found. Source code reveals the application's logic, hidden functions and further weaknesses; configuration copies often contain database passwords, API keys and other secrets; and database dumps can expose personal data and password hashes. The impact depends on the content: copies of static files matter little, while a configuration file or database backup can lead directly to a wider compromise.
entries.remediation:
Remove the files, then stop new ones reaching web-accessible locations:

  • Delete backup, temporary and archive files from the web root, and keep backups on separate storage outside it, with its own access control.
  • Deploy from a clean build artefact through an automated process that replaces the whole application directory, rather than editing files on the server, so that stray files are not carried forward.
  • Block requests for backup and temporary file patterns at the web server as defence in depth, adjusting the list to what the site legitimately serves. On IIS, request filtering can deny the same file name extensions.
  • Rotate any credentials or keys found in the exposed files, and review access logs for earlier downloads of them.
# nginx location ~* (\.(bak|old|orig|save|swp|tmp|sql)|~)$ { return 404; } # Apache <FilesMatch "(\.(bak|old|orig|save|swp|tmp|sql)|~)$"> Require all denied </FilesMatch>

Confirm the fix by repeating content discovery against the site and requesting the files previously found: each should return 404 or 403.

entries.title: Source Code Repository Exposed
entries.summary: A version control directory such as .git is served by the web server, letting anyone rebuild the application's source code and full change history.
entries.description:
The application has been deployed as a working copy of its version control repository, and the repository's metadata directory, most often .git but also .svn, .hg or .bzr, is inside the web root and served. For Git, files such as HEAD, config, index and the object store can be downloaded and, because object names can be worked out from the references and the index, the whole repository can be rebuilt even when directory listing is disabled. Tools such as git-dumper and GitTools automate this. For Subversion, the wc.db database lists every file, and pristine copies of their contents are kept alongside it.

The weakness is identified by requesting files such as /.git/HEAD, which returns a reference line beginning ref:, /.git/config and /.svn/wc.db. A 403 response for the directory itself does not mean that the files inside are protected, so individual files are requested directly. Content discovery tools and many web scanners check these paths.
entries.impact: An attacker can obtain the application's complete source code and history without authentication. The code allows a detailed search for further vulnerabilities, and repositories commonly hold secrets such as database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys and private keys in configuration files, including secrets deleted in later commits, which remain in the history. Commit metadata also reveals developers' names and email addresses and internal host names. The weakness frequently leads to a compromise that extends beyond the application itself.
entries.remediation:
Remove the repository metadata from the web server and treat everything in it as disclosed:

  • Deploy build artefacts produced by a pipeline or by git archive, rather than cloning or pulling a working copy into the web root.
  • Delete version control directories from the deployed site.
  • Block requests for version control directories at the web server as defence in depth, as below. On IIS, add .git and the other directory names as hidden segments in request filtering.
  • Rotate every credential and key that appears anywhere in the repository or its history, and move secrets out of the code into a secrets manager or the deployment environment.
  • Review the code for vulnerabilities on the assumption that it is public, and check logs for earlier downloads of repository files.
# nginx: refuse hidden files and directories, but keep ACME challenges working location ~ /\.(?!well-known/) { deny all; } # Apache RedirectMatch 404 /\.(git|svn|hg|bzr)(/|$)

Confirm the fix by requesting /.git/HEAD, /.git/config and the equivalent files for other systems: each should return 404 or 403, and dumping tools should recover nothing.

entries.title: Configuration Files Exposed
entries.summary: Configuration files containing settings and secrets, such as .env files, can be downloaded from the web server without authentication.
entries.description:
Configuration files are reachable through the web server and returned as plain text. Common examples are the .env files used by many frameworks and container deployments, appsettings.json, application.properties and application.yml, config.json, docker-compose.yml, .npmrc, and copies of files such as wp-config.php. They typically hold database connection strings, cloud access keys, API tokens for payment, email and other services, and the secret keys an application uses to sign or encrypt sessions and cookies.

The usual cause is a web server whose document root is the project directory rather than the framework's public directory, so that files beside the code become downloadable. Files with extensions the server does not run as code, such as .env, .yml, .json and .ini, are then returned as they are. Other causes are configuration files copied into static content folders and storage buckets used to host the site.

The weakness is identified by requesting common configuration file names at the site root and in likely subdirectories with content discovery tools and wordlists, which most web scanners also include.
entries.impact: An attacker obtains secrets without authentication, and their reach often extends well beyond the application: database credentials can give direct access to stored data, cloud keys to the hosting account, and service tokens to email, payment or storage platforms. Application signing and encryption keys can allow session tokens or cookies to be forged, and in some frameworks this can lead to code execution. The impact depends on the secrets present, but a single exposed file commonly leads to a significant compromise.
entries.remediation:
Move configuration out of reach of the web server, and treat its secrets as compromised:

  • Set the web server's document root to the framework's public directory only, such as public in Laravel and Symfony projects, so that configuration and code sit outside it.
  • Keep secrets out of files deployed with the code: supply them at run time from environment variables set by the platform, or from a secrets manager.
  • Block requests for hidden files and common configuration file names at the web server as defence in depth, as below.
  • Rotate every credential, token and key in the exposed files, invalidate sessions signed with exposed keys, and review the logs of the affected services for misuse.
# nginx: refuse hidden files such as .env, but keep ACME challenges working location ~ /\.(?!well-known/) { deny all; } # Apache: refuse files whose names begin with a dot <FilesMatch "^\."> Require all denied </FilesMatch>

Confirm the fix by requesting the exposed files and common configuration names again: each should return 404 or 403, and the rotated credentials should no longer work.

entries.title: phpinfo() Page Exposed
entries.summary: A page that calls phpinfo() is publicly accessible, revealing detailed PHP, server and environment information, including values that may be secret.
entries.description:
A script that calls the PHP function phpinfo(), often named phpinfo.php, info.php or test.php, has been left on the server and can be requested by anyone. The function prints a detailed report of the PHP installation: its version and build options, every loaded extension and its version, the effective settings from php.ini (such as disable_functions, open_basedir, allow_url_include and the session and upload settings), file system paths including the document root, the operating system and host name, environment variables, and the request itself, including all headers and cookies received.

Environment variables shown in the report can include database passwords and API keys, particularly where the application is configured through its environment, as is common with containers. Because the page also displays the cookies the server received, including those marked HttpOnly, a cross-site scripting flaw elsewhere on the same site can read a user's session cookie by fetching the page.

The page is found through content discovery with common file names, and most web scanners report it.
entries.impact: The report gives an attacker an accurate picture for targeting further attacks: exact versions to match against known vulnerabilities, settings that show which exploitation techniques will work, and absolute paths that help with file inclusion and path traversal attacks. Where secrets are present in the environment variables, the disclosure leads directly to wider access, and the display of cookies removes the protection that HttpOnly gives session cookies against cross-site scripting. No authentication is needed.
entries.remediation:
Remove the page, and prevent similar diagnostic output in production:

  • Delete scripts that call phpinfo() from all production servers, searching the web root for the function name, and keep diagnostic scripts out of deployment packages.
  • Disable the function in production by adding it to disable_functions in php.ini, keeping any functions already listed.
  • Where diagnostic information is needed, collect it from the command line or restrict it to authenticated administrators.
  • Set expose_php = Off to stop PHP announcing its version in response headers.
  • Rotate any secrets that appeared in the page's environment variables.
; php.ini disable_functions = phpinfo expose_php = Off

Confirm the fix by requesting the page, and common alternative names for it, again: each should return 404.

entries.title: Server Status Page Exposed
entries.summary: A web server status page, such as Apache's /server-status, is publicly reachable and shows live details of the server and the requests it is handling.
entries.description:
Web servers can publish a status page for administrators, and this page is reachable from untrusted networks. The most common is the Apache HTTP Server status page provided by mod_status, usually at /server-status. With extended status enabled it lists every worker's current request, showing the client's IP address, the virtual host and the full request line, including any query string, as well as the server version, uptime, load and traffic figures. The related /server-info page from mod_info shows the server's loaded configuration. Other servers offer simpler equivalents, such as the nginx stub_status page, which shows only connection counts and is of little value to an attacker.

A frequent cause is an access rule such as Require local on a server that sits behind a reverse proxy on the same host: every request then arrives from the local address and passes the rule.

The page is found by requesting common paths such as /server-status, /server-status?auto, /server-info and /nginx_status, and most web scanners report it.
entries.impact: An attacker can watch the requests other users are making: their IP addresses, which are personal data, and the addresses they request, which can include session identifiers, password reset tokens or other secrets passed in query strings. The page also reveals hidden paths, virtual host names and software versions that help with targeting. What it discloses depends on the traffic at the moment it is viewed, though repeated polling gathers more. No authentication is needed.
entries.remediation:
Disable status pages where they are not needed, and restrict them where they are:

  • On Apache, disable mod_status and mod_info if they are not used, for example with a2dismod status info on Debian and Ubuntu, or by commenting out their LoadModule lines.
  • Where the status page is needed, restrict it to a management network or to authenticated administrators, and do not rely on Require local when a proxy runs on the same host.
  • Set ExtendedStatus Off unless the per-request detail is needed, so that client addresses and requested addresses are not shown.
  • Block the status paths at any reverse proxy or load balancer in front of the server.
  • Avoid passing tokens or other secrets in query strings, so that they cannot appear in status pages or logs.
# Apache: management network only (documentation range shown) <Location "/server-status"> SetHandler server-status Require ip 192.0.2.0/24 </Location> # nginx location = /nginx_status { stub_status; allow 127.0.0.1; deny all; }

Confirm the fix by requesting the status paths from an untrusted network: each should return 403 or 404.

entries.title: Spring Boot Actuator Endpoints Exposed
entries.summary: Spring Boot Actuator management endpoints are reachable without authentication, exposing configuration, memory contents and administrative functions.
entries.description:
Spring Boot Actuator adds management endpoints to an application, usually under /actuator or, in old versions, at the root (for example /env and /heapdump), and these endpoints are reachable over HTTP without authentication. Endpoints commonly found exposed include env and configprops (configuration properties and their sources), heapdump (a full dump of the Java heap), threaddump, mappings (every route in the application), beans, loggers (which accepts changes to log levels), httpexchanges or the older httptrace and trace (recent requests with their headers) and, where enabled, shutdown, as well as endpoints added by other libraries, such as gateway and jolokia.

Current versions expose only the health endpoint over HTTP by default and mask the values shown by env and configprops, so exposure usually comes from configuration such as management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* without matching security rules, or from older versions. The masking does not apply to the heap dump, which holds the real values of everything in memory.

The weakness is identified by requesting /actuator, which lists the exposed endpoints, and the individual endpoint paths, including under alternative base paths and on a separate management port. A downloaded heap dump can be searched with Java heap analysis tools.
entries.impact: Without authentication, an attacker can obtain whatever the exposed endpoints reveal. A heap dump typically contains database and service credentials, API keys, encryption keys, the session identifiers of signed-in users and fragments of recent requests, which can lead to account takeover and access to connected systems. Other endpoints disclose the application's full route map and configuration, allow log levels to be changed or, where enabled, the application to be shut down, and in some versions and configurations endpoints such as gateway and jolokia have allowed code execution. The impact depends on which endpoints are exposed, and is high whenever heapdump or an unmasked env is among them.
entries.remediation:
Expose only the endpoints that are needed, and require authentication for every other one:

  • Limit web exposure to what monitoring needs, usually health, with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health, and never use * in production.
  • Protect any further endpoints with Spring Security, requiring an administrative role for actuator requests, as below.
  • Serve management endpoints on a separate port bound to a loopback or internal address, with management.server.port and management.server.address, and block /actuator at the reverse proxy or load balancer.
  • Disable endpoints that are not needed, particularly heapdump, env, shutdown and jolokia, and keep the masking of values in env and configprops.
  • If heapdump or an unmasked env was exposed, rotate every secret the application holds and invalidate active sessions.
# application.properties management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health management.server.port=8081 management.server.address=127.0.0.1 // Spring Security: require a role for actuator endpoints http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()) .authorizeHttpRequests((requests) -> requests.anyRequest().hasRole("ENDPOINT_ADMIN"));

Confirm the fix by requesting /actuator and each previously exposed endpoint from an untrusted network: each should be refused or not found.

entries.title: IIS Short Filename Disclosure
entries.summary: IIS responds differently to requests that match a file's short 8.3 name, letting an attacker work out the start of file and folder names in the web root.
entries.description:
Windows NTFS volumes can give each file and folder with a long name an additional short name in the old 8.3 format, made up of the first characters of the name, a tilde and a number, and a three-character extension (for example BACKUP~1.ZIP). Microsoft IIS responds differently to requests that contain a tilde and wildcard characters depending on whether a matching short name exists, so an attacker can work out, one character at a time, the first six characters of the names of files and folders under the web root and the first three characters of their extensions. This works whether or not directory listing is enabled, and reveals files that nothing links to.

The behaviour depends on short name creation having been enabled on the volume when the files were created: switching it off later does not remove short names that already exist. The HTTP methods and response codes involved vary between IIS versions and configurations.

The issue is reported by many web scanners, and is confirmed with tools such as the IIS Short Name Scanner, or by comparing the responses to crafted requests for a name that exists and one that does not.
entries.impact: An attacker can discover the beginnings of the names of unlinked files and folders, which points them to content worth guessing in full, such as backups, archives, old versions of pages, administrative scripts and configuration copies. The issue does not reveal the content of any file and the full names must still be guessed, so its value depends on what the web root contains. It is most useful to an attacker where sensitive files have been left in web-accessible directories.
entries.remediation:
Remove the short names from the web content and stop new ones being created:

  • Disable 8.3 name creation with fsutil 8dot3name set: the value 1 on its own disables it for all volumes (it sets the registry value NtfsDisable8dot3NameCreation under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem), while a volume followed by 1 disables it for that volume when the system-wide setting allows per-volume control. fsutil 8dot3name query shows the current state.
  • Remove existing short names from the web content with fsutil 8dot3name strip, running it first with /t, which only reports what would change, because some software relies on short names. Alternatively, recreate the content by copying it to a new folder once creation is disabled.
  • Keep backups, archives and other non-public files out of web-accessible directories, so that discovering a name gains nothing.
  • As an interim measure, use IIS request filtering to reject URLs that contain a tilde, after checking that the application does not use tildes in legitimate addresses.
fsutil 8dot3name query D: fsutil 8dot3name set D: 1 fsutil 8dot3name strip /t /s /v D:\inetpub\wwwroot <system.webServer> <security> <requestFiltering> <denyUrlSequences> <add sequence="~" /> </denyUrlSequences> </requestFiltering> </security> </system.webServer>

Confirm the fix by repeating the scan, which should no longer recover any names.

entries.title: Debug Mode Enabled in Production
entries.summary: The application or its framework runs with debug settings in production, exposing detailed errors, internal data and sometimes interactive debugging tools.
entries.description:
The application, or the framework it is built on, is running in production with settings intended for development. The signs vary by platform: Django with DEBUG = True, which shows detailed error pages and, for unknown addresses, a list of the application's URL patterns; Flask run with the Werkzeug debugger enabled; Laravel with APP_DEBUG=true; Symfony in its development environment, with the web profiler at /_profiler; Ruby on Rails in development mode; ASP.NET with customErrors set to Off or with debug="true" on the compilation element; ASP.NET Core in the Development environment with the developer exception page; and Express applications run without NODE_ENV=production.

Debug output typically includes stack traces, fragments of source code, framework and library versions, file paths, database queries, request data and, on some platforms, configuration values and environment variables. Some debug tools go further: the Werkzeug debugger offers an interactive Python console in the browser, protected by a PIN that can sometimes be derived from information disclosed elsewhere.

Debug mode is identified by causing errors, for example by requesting addresses that do not exist or sending malformed input, and by recognising framework debug pages, profiler toolbars, debug headers such as Symfony's X-Debug-Token, and known debug paths. Web scanners recognise the debug pages of the common frameworks.
entries.impact: An attacker learns how the application is built and configured, which makes finding and exploiting other weaknesses considerably easier. Where the debug output includes configuration values or environment variables, it can disclose credentials and secret keys directly. Where an interactive debugger or console is reachable, an attacker who can use it can run code on the server with the application's privileges. Anyone who can reach the application can usually trigger the debug output, without authentication.
entries.remediation:
Run production with production settings, and make that hard to get wrong:

  • Turn debug settings off in the production configuration of each platform in use, as below, and run Python applications under a production server rather than the framework's development server.
  • Leave development-only packages, such as profilers and debug toolbars, out of production builds, for example by using composer install --no-dev for PHP applications.
  • Show users a generic error page with a reference number, and record the details in server-side logs.
  • Add a check to the deployment pipeline that fails the release if a debug setting is enabled.
  • If an interactive debugger was reachable, review the server for signs of misuse and rotate the secrets the application holds.
# Django (settings.py) DEBUG = False # Laravel (.env) APP_ENV=production APP_DEBUG=false # Symfony (environment) APP_ENV=prod # ASP.NET (web.config) <system.web> <customErrors mode="RemoteOnly" /> <compilation debug="false" /> </system.web> # ASP.NET Core and Node.js (environment) ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production NODE_ENV=production

Confirm the fix by repeating the requests that produced debug output: each should return a generic error page.

entries.title: Administrative Interface Publicly Accessible
entries.summary: An administrative interface can be reached from the internet, so anyone can attempt to sign in to it or attack weaknesses in it.
entries.description:
An administrative interface is reachable from the internet rather than only from a management network. Examples include content management system back ends such as /wp-admin and /administrator, the application's own administration area, application server consoles such as the Apache Tomcat Manager, database tools such as phpMyAdmin and Adminer, hosting control panels, and monitoring or build tools such as Grafana, Kibana and Jenkins.

The interface may require authentication, but its exposure still allows anyone to attempt to sign in, to try passwords at scale and to exploit any vulnerability in the administrative software, which is often complex, highly privileged and less hardened than the public application. Where no authentication is required at all, or default credentials are accepted, that is a more serious issue reported in its own right.

Exposed interfaces are found by content discovery against common administrative paths, by enumerating subdomains and alternative ports, and through search engines and certificate transparency logs, which attackers use in the same way.
entries.impact: An attacker can run password guessing, password spraying and credential stuffing attacks against the interface, and can exploit any published or undiscovered vulnerability in it without first gaining a foothold elsewhere. Access to an administrative interface usually gives control of the application and its data, and often code execution on the server, for example by deploying a web application archive through the Tomcat Manager or by editing plugins in a content management system. The risk is lower where multi-factor authentication, strong passwords, rate limiting and prompt patching are in place, and higher where any of them is missing.
entries.remediation:
Make the administrative interface reachable only from trusted networks, and protect the accounts that use it:

  • Restrict access at the firewall, reverse proxy or web server to a management network, a VPN or a zero trust access service, and refuse it from everywhere else.
  • Where possible, host administrative functions on a separate host name or port that is not published to the internet, so that network controls can apply to them as a whole.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for every administrative account.
  • Enforce strong, unique passwords, limit the rate of sign-in attempts, and alert on repeated failures.
  • Keep the administrative software patched, and remove administrative components that are not used.
# nginx: management network only (documentation range shown) location /admin/ { allow 192.0.2.0/24; deny all; } # Apache <Location "/admin/"> Require ip 192.0.2.0/24 </Location>

As an interim measure while network restrictions are arranged, enable multi-factor authentication and rate limiting. Confirm the fix by requesting the interface from an untrusted network: it should be refused or unreachable.

entries.title: Default or Sample Content Present
entries.summary: Default pages, sample applications or documentation installed with the server or framework remain accessible on the production site.
entries.description:
Content installed by default with a web server, application server, framework or content management system has been left on the production server. Examples include web server welcome and test pages, such as the default pages of Apache, IIS and nginx, the Apache HTTP Server manual, the Apache Tomcat examples and docs applications, sample scripts shipped with frameworks and products, installation and upgrade scripts, and readme, changelog and licence files.

Such content identifies the product and often its version, and suggests that the server has not been fully hardened. Sample applications are written to demonstrate features rather than to be secure: some display request, session and server details, and some let visitors change data, such as the Tomcat examples that allow session attributes to be set. Installation scripts left in place may let a visitor run setup steps again. A default page served for an unrecognised host name can also reveal a forgotten or unmanaged virtual host.

Default content is found by content discovery, and is recognised by web scanners such as Nikto, which hold lists of known default files.
entries.impact: The content helps an attacker identify the software in use and target known vulnerabilities in it, and sample applications can themselves contain exploitable flaws, such as cross-site scripting or the disclosure of request and session details. The direct impact is usually limited, but it rises where sample code or installation scripts allow changes to data or configuration. The presence of such content can also indicate wider gaps in the server's hardening.
entries.remediation:
Remove everything from production that the application does not need:

  • Delete default and sample content: web server welcome pages, the Apache manual and its configuration alias, the Tomcat examples and docs applications (and manager and host-manager where they are not used), framework samples, installation and upgrade scripts, and readme and changelog files.
  • Configure the default virtual host to return a neutral response, such as 404, for unrecognised host names, rather than a default page.
  • Build servers from a hardened baseline or image that excludes sample content, and include a check for known default files in the deployment process.

Confirm the fix by repeating content discovery and requesting the files previously found: each should return 404.

entries.title: Unnecessary HTTP Methods Enabled
entries.summary: The server accepts HTTP methods the application does not need, such as PUT, DELETE or WebDAV methods, widening what an attacker can attempt.
entries.description:
The web server or application accepts HTTP methods beyond those the application needs, which for most web applications are GET, HEAD and POST, with PUT, PATCH and DELETE added only where an API is designed to use them. Commonly found are PUT and DELETE, which can create, replace or remove files where a handler or WebDAV module processes them; the WebDAV methods, such as PROPFIND, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE and LOCK, which can list and change content; and arbitrary or unknown methods that the server treats as GET.

Access rules written for particular methods can also be bypassed this way: rules in Apache <Limit GET POST> blocks, or Java EE security constraints that list specific methods, leave every other method unrestricted, so the same request sent with another method may reach the protected resource without authentication.

The methods are identified by sending an OPTIONS request and reading the Allow header but, because that header is not always accurate, each method is also tested directly, for example with curl or the Nmap http-methods script. A method that is shown to change or reveal content, such as a successful PUT upload, is normally reported as a more serious finding in its own right.
entries.impact: Where an unnecessary method is honoured, an attacker may be able to upload files, including web shells that run code on the server, alter or delete content, list directory contents, or bypass access rules that cover only some methods. In the typical case the methods are accepted but no damaging effect can be shown, because file permissions or handlers prevent it, and the finding represents unnecessary attack surface that a later configuration change could make exploitable.
entries.remediation:
Accept only the methods each part of the application needs, and refuse the rest, ideally with 405 Method Not Allowed:

  • Disable WebDAV where it is not used, for example by removing the WebDAV Publishing feature on IIS, or by disabling mod_dav and mod_dav_fs on Apache.
  • Restrict methods at the web server, as below, and in API frameworks, where each route should accept only the methods it implements. Allow OPTIONS only where cross-origin preflight requests need it.
  • Write access rules that apply to every method and deny by default: use <LimitExcept> rather than <Limit> in Apache, and <deny-uncovered-http-methods/> in Java web.xml files.
# nginx location / { limit_except GET POST { deny all; } } # Apache <Location "/"> <LimitExcept GET POST> Require all denied </LimitExcept> </Location> <!-- IIS (web.config) --> <system.webServer> <security> <requestFiltering> <verbs allowUnlisted="false"> <add verb="GET" allowed="true" /> <add verb="HEAD" allowed="true" /> <add verb="POST" allowed="true" /> </verbs> </requestFiltering> </security> </system.webServer>

In nginx and Apache, allowing GET also allows HEAD. Confirm the fix by sending each unneeded method to the application's paths: each should be refused.

patterns: \b(insecure|unnecessary|dangerous|risky|potentially risky) HTTP methods?\b|\bHTTP methods? allowed\b|\bHTTP (PUT|DELETE) method\b|\bWebDAV\b.*(enabled|methods)

entries.title: HTTP TRACE Method Enabled
entries.summary: The server answers HTTP TRACE requests by echoing back the request it received, which can reveal headers added by proxies and other intermediaries.
entries.description:
The web server, or a proxy or load balancer in front of it, responds to TRACE requests by returning the request it received, including every header, in the body of the response. The method exists for diagnosing how requests change on their way to the server and is rarely needed in production. Microsoft IIS has historically supported a similar TRACK method.

The method was the basis of cross-site tracing (XST), in which script running in a victim's browser sent a TRACE request and read cookies or Authorization headers from the echoed response, bypassing the HttpOnly cookie attribute. Current browsers do not allow script to send TRACE requests, so this attack no longer works on its own. The remaining concern is that the echoed request shows headers added by intermediaries, which can include internal IP addresses and host names, routing or authentication headers, and identifying details of the infrastructure.

The method is identified by sending a TRACE request, for example with curl or the Nmap http-methods script, and checking for a successful response with the message/http content type that repeats the request. Requests for different host names and paths can reach different servers behind a proxy, each of which may respond differently.
entries.impact: On its own the method gives an attacker little. They can see headers that proxies, load balancers or web application firewalls add to requests, which can reveal internal addresses and software and, occasionally, credentials or tokens that those systems add. Theft of a user's cookies through cross-site tracing would need another weakness or an outdated client. The finding mainly reflects a configuration that has not been hardened.
entries.remediation:
Disable the TRACE and TRACK methods on every server, proxy and load balancer that handles the application's traffic:

  • Apache HTTP Server: set TraceEnable Off in the server configuration.
  • IIS: deny the TRACE and TRACK verbs with request filtering, as below.
  • Apache Tomcat: leave the connector's allowTrace attribute at its default of false.
  • nginx rejects TRACE requests itself, but servers behind it, and any other route to them, should still be checked.
  • Check that load balancers, content delivery networks and web application firewalls neither answer nor forward TRACE, and block it with a rule where they do.
# Apache (httpd.conf) TraceEnable Off <!-- IIS (web.config) --> <system.webServer> <security> <requestFiltering> <verbs> <add verb="TRACE" allowed="false" /> <add verb="TRACK" allowed="false" /> </verbs> </requestFiltering> </security> </system.webServer>

Confirm the fix by sending a TRACE request to each host name that serves the application: each should be refused, typically with 405 or 403 (IIS request filtering answers 404), and should not repeat the request.

entries.title: WordPress XML-RPC Enabled
entries.summary: The WordPress XML-RPC interface (xmlrpc.php) is reachable, giving attackers another login route for password guessing and a pingback function that makes the server fetch addresses they choose.
entries.description:
The WordPress XML-RPC interface, served at /xmlrpc.php, is enabled and reachable from the internet. XML-RPC lets remote clients, such as publishing apps and plugins including Jetpack, call WordPress functions over HTTP. It is enabled by default and the administration interface offers no setting to turn it off, so it is often left exposed on sites that never use it.

The interface interests an attacker for two reasons. Many of its methods take a user name and password with each call, so it is a second login route, which may not be covered by the lockout, CAPTCHA or multi-factor controls applied to the normal login page, depending on the plugins in use. Older WordPress releases also accepted hundreds of password attempts in a single request through system.multicall; current releases stop checking passwords within a request once one attempt has failed. Separately, the pingback.ping method makes the server fetch an address supplied by the caller in order to verify a link, which can be abused to direct traffic at other sites or to learn the server's real IP address when it sits behind a content delivery network or web application firewall.

The interface is confirmed by sending a system.listMethods call in a POST request to /xmlrpc.php, which returns the methods available; a GET request returns a short message saying that the server accepts POST requests only. WordPress scanners such as WPScan report the interface as enabled.
entries.impact: An attacker can guess, spray or stuff passwords against user accounts through XML-RPC, possibly outside the rate limiting and multi-factor controls that protect the login page. A recovered administrator password gives full control of the site and usually of the code it runs, since administrators can install plugins. Through pingbacks, an attacker can make the server send requests to third parties, enlisting the site in attacks on others, and can often learn its real IP address, allowing them to bypass a content delivery network or web application firewall placed in front of it. The risk is lower where every account has a strong, unique password and multi-factor authentication that also covers XML-RPC, and where no published content accepts pingbacks.
entries.remediation:
Disable XML-RPC unless something the organisation relies on needs it:

  • Where nothing uses it, block requests to xmlrpc.php at the web server, reverse proxy or web application firewall, so that WordPress never processes them. Check first whether Jetpack, a mobile publishing app or another remote client depends on it, because blocking the file stops these working.
  • Where XML-RPC must stay available, remove the pingback methods with the xmlrpc_methods filter, restrict access to the addresses of the services that need it where these are known, and make sure login rate limiting and multi-factor authentication apply to XML-RPC as well as to the login page. The xmlrpc_enabled filter only disables methods that require authentication; it does not stop pingbacks.
  • Enforce strong, unique passwords for every account with publishing or administrative rights.
nginx: location = /xmlrpc.php { deny all; } Apache 2.4 (virtual host or .htaccess): <Files xmlrpc.php> Require all denied </Files> WordPress (a small plugin), keeping XML-RPC but removing pingbacks: add_filter( 'xmlrpc_methods', function ( $methods ) { unset( $methods['pingback.ping'], $methods['pingback.extensions.getPingbacks'] ); return $methods; } );

Confirm the fix by sending a system.listMethods request to /xmlrpc.php and checking that it is refused or, where XML-RPC is kept, that the pingback methods are no longer listed.

entries.title: Unencrypted HTTP Service
entries.summary: The web service is offered over plain HTTP, so anyone on the network path can read and alter its traffic, including credentials and session cookies.
entries.description:
The web service accepts connections over plain HTTP and serves its content without Transport Layer Security (TLS). Everything exchanged between a user's browser and the server, including credentials, session cookies, form data and the pages themselves, crosses the network unencrypted and without any check that it has not been altered on the way.

The weakness takes two main forms. In the first, the service is only available over HTTP. In the second, HTTPS is available but the same content is also served over HTTP rather than the HTTP listener redirecting every request to HTTPS, so users who type the address without a scheme, follow an old link or use a bookmark carry on in cleartext. A partial form is an HTTP listener that redirects some paths but still serves others, such as API endpoints, static files or legacy pages.

The issue is confirmed by requesting the service with an http:// address and observing that content is returned rather than a redirect to HTTPS, and by capturing traffic to show that it is readable. Browsers label such pages as not secure, and scanners report the service as unencrypted or, where a login form is involved, as sending credentials in cleartext.
entries.impact: An attacker with a position on the network path between users and the server, such as on a shared or public wireless network, a compromised router or an intermediate provider, can read everything exchanged, including user names, passwords and session cookies, and use them to take over accounts. They can also change content in transit, for example injecting script into pages, altering downloads, or rewriting links and form destinations, and users have no way to notice. The impact is greatest where the service handles logins, personal data or administrative functions; a service that only publishes public information without a login is affected mainly through the alteration of its content.
entries.remediation:
Serve the service only over HTTPS:

  • Obtain a certificate from a publicly trusted certificate authority, using automated issuance and renewal (for example through the ACME protocol) where possible, and configure the service to accept TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 only.
  • Configure the HTTP listener to answer every request with a permanent redirect (301 or 308) to the same path over HTTPS and to serve no content itself, or close the HTTP port where nothing needs it.
  • Once the whole site works over HTTPS, send the Strict-Transport-Security header so that browsers stop making HTTP requests to it, and mark cookies with the Secure attribute.
  • Update links, redirects, API clients and integrations so that they use https:// addresses directly.
nginx: server { listen 80; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } Apache (virtual host on port 80, mod_rewrite): RewriteEngine On RewriteRule ^ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]

On IIS, use a URL Rewrite rule to redirect HTTP requests to HTTPS. Confirm the fix by requesting several paths over http:// and checking that each returns a redirect to the same path over HTTPS and that no content is served in cleartext.

patterns: \b(unencrypted|cleartext|plain[- ]?text|non-ssl|insecure) HTTP\b|\bHTTP service\b.*(unencrypted|without (TLS|SSL|HTTPS))|\bno HTTPS\b|\bHTTP to HTTPS redirect\b.*(missing|not)|\bsensitive (data|information|form) (transmitted|sent|submitted) (over|via) (HTTP|an unencrypted)

entries.title: Mixed Content
entries.summary: Pages served over HTTPS load some resources over plain HTTP, which an attacker on the network path can observe or replace, depending on the browser.
entries.description:
Pages delivered over HTTPS load some of their resources, such as images, scripts, stylesheets, fonts, frames or data fetched by script, from http:// addresses. Those requests travel without encryption, so the protection the page appears to have does not extend to everything it loads.

Browsers handle mixed content according to its type. Current browsers block scripts, stylesheets, frames, fonts and requests made from script, and most now upgrade images, audio and video to HTTPS automatically, dropping them if the upgrade fails. Older browsers may still load images and media over HTTP, sometimes with only a warning. On current browsers the visible effect is therefore often broken functionality rather than exposure, but the protection users receive depends on the browser they use.

The issue is identified by reviewing page source and the browser's developer console, which reports blocked and upgraded requests, or by scanners that list the http:// resources referenced from HTTPS pages. Related forms are a form on an HTTPS page that submits to an http:// address, which browsers generally warn about before sending, and download links that use HTTP.
entries.impact: In browsers that still load passive content over HTTP, an attacker on the network path, such as on a shared wireless network, can replace images or media with content of their choosing, for example to mislead users or deface the page, and can see which of those resources a user requests. The impact rises in three cases: where a browser loads an active resource such as a script over HTTP, which current browsers refuse to do, the attacker could run code in the page and take over the user's session; where a session cookie lacks the Secure attribute, it is sent in cleartext with any HTTP request to the same host; and where a form submits to an HTTP address, whatever the user enters is exposed.
entries.remediation:
Load every resource over HTTPS:

  • Change each http:// reference in pages, templates, stylesheets, scripts and stored content to https://, or to a relative path for resources on the same site. Content management systems often keep absolute http:// addresses in content held in the database, so search there as well as in the code.
  • Where a third-party resource is not available over HTTPS, host a copy on the site or replace it.
  • Make every form's action an HTTPS address, and serve downloads over HTTPS.
  • As a safety net, send the Content Security Policy directive upgrade-insecure-requests, which tells browsers to request the page's HTTP resources over HTTPS instead. It relies on each resource being available over HTTPS and does not change links that lead to other sites.
Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests

Confirm the fix by loading each affected page with the browser's developer console open and checking that no mixed content warnings or blocked requests are reported.

entries.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Not Enforced
entries.summary: The site does not send an effective Strict-Transport-Security header, so browsers may still make HTTP requests to it that an attacker can intercept and downgrade.
entries.description:
The application is available over HTTPS but does not instruct browsers, through the Strict-Transport-Security response header, to use HTTPS for every future request to the domain. Without that instruction, a browser makes a plain HTTP request whenever a user types the address without a scheme or follows an http:// link or bookmark, and relies on the server's redirect to reach HTTPS. That first request and the redirect can be intercepted.

The weakness takes several forms: the header is absent; it is sent with a short max-age, so protection lapses soon after each visit; it omits includeSubDomains where subdomains also serve the application or receive its cookies; or it is sent only over HTTP, where browsers ignore it. Even a correct header cannot protect a user's first visit, which is why a domain can also be added to the preload list built into browsers.

The issue is confirmed by inspecting HTTPS responses for the header and its directives. Scanners commonly report it as a missing security header.
entries.impact: An attacker on the network path, such as on a shared or public wireless network, can intercept a user's initial HTTP request and keep the user on an unencrypted connection to the attacker while relaying to the real site over HTTPS, an attack known as SSL stripping. The attacker can then read credentials, session cookies that lack the Secure attribute and other data the user enters, and can alter pages. The attack needs the user to start from an HTTP address while the attacker is on the path, and an attentive user may notice that the connection is not secure. Without HSTS, browsers also let users click through certificate warnings for the site, which helps an attacker presenting a forged certificate.
entries.remediation:
Send the Strict-Transport-Security header on every HTTPS response from the domain:

  • Use a max-age of at least one year (31536000 seconds). Where subdomains have not been checked, start with a short value and raise it once nothing has broken.
  • Add includeSubDomains once every subdomain is confirmed to work over HTTPS, since it applies the policy to all of them.
  • Keep any HTTP listener as a permanent redirect to HTTPS; browsers ignore the header when it arrives over HTTP.
  • To protect first visits, consider submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list once the policy has run without problems. This needs includeSubDomains, a max-age of at least one year and the preload directive, and is slow to reverse.
nginx: add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always; Apache (mod_headers): Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" IIS (web.config, within system.webServer): <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <add name="Strict-Transport-Security" value="max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol>

In nginx, an add_header directive in a location block replaces those inherited from the server block, so check each location; recent IIS versions also offer a native HSTS setting for each site. Confirm the fix by checking that HTTPS responses, including redirects and error pages, carry the header with the intended directives.

entries.title: Content Security Policy Missing or Weak
entries.summary: The application sends no Content Security Policy, or one too permissive to stop injected script running, so the browser places no effective limit on what its pages may load or execute.
entries.description:
Content Security Policy (CSP) is delivered in the Content-Security-Policy response header and tells the browser which sources of script, styles, frames and other content a page may use, whether inline script may run, and which sites may frame the page. A well-built policy means that script injected through a cross-site scripting flaw does not run, because it neither comes from an allowed source nor carries the expected nonce or hash.

The finding covers two cases. In the first, no policy is sent, or one is sent only as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, which reports violations but enforces nothing. In the second, a policy is enforced but does not restrict script effectively, for example because script-src, or default-src where that is absent, allows 'unsafe-inline' without a nonce or hash, 'unsafe-eval', wildcards, whole schemes such as https: or data:, or domains that host user content or libraries known to allow bypasses; or because object-src and base-uri are left unrestricted. A policy set in a meta element cannot use frame-ancestors or reporting.

The policy is reviewed in the responses, and tools such as CSP Evaluator point out common weaknesses and bypasses.
entries.impact: A missing or weak policy has no direct impact of its own. It matters when the application has, or later gains, a flaw that lets an attacker inject content, chiefly cross-site scripting: without an effective policy, injected script runs with the user's session and can read data, act as the user or capture what they type. A strong policy would often stop such script running at all, turning a serious flaw into a much lesser one. The absence of a policy is therefore most significant in applications that handle sensitive data or display content supplied by users.
entries.remediation:
Deploy an enforced policy that restricts script, built for the application rather than copied from elsewhere:

  • Prefer a strict policy based on nonces or hashes: a new random nonce generated for every response and added to each legitimate script element, with 'strict-dynamic' so that scripts loaded by trusted scripts are trusted too. Move inline event handlers and javascript: links into script files or nonced scripts, since such a policy blocks them.
  • Set object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' (or 'self'), and use frame-ancestors to control framing.
  • Avoid 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', wildcards and whole schemes in script-src, and do not allow domains that serve arbitrary or user-uploaded content.
  • Introduce the policy as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with a reporting endpoint, fix what it reports, then switch to the enforcing header.
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-{RANDOM}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'

Here {RANDOM} stands for the nonce generated for that response. Where script cannot yet be restricted, a policy limited to object-src, base-uri and frame-ancestors still removes some attack routes in the meantime. Confirm the fix by checking that the enforcing header is present on all HTML responses, that legitimate pages report no violations, and that an evaluation tool finds no remaining bypass.

entries.title: X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
entries.summary: Responses do not carry the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header, so browsers may guess a response's content type instead of relying on the declared one.
entries.description:
The application does not send the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff response header. Without it, browsers may examine a response's content to decide how to handle it, known as MIME sniffing, where the Content-Type header is missing, generic or inconsistent with the content, and may then treat the response as a different type from the one the server intended, for example rendering an uploaded text file that contains markup as HTML.

With nosniff, the browser uses the declared type without examining the content, refuses to run a response as script or apply it as a stylesheet unless it has a JavaScript or CSS media type, and does not treat a non-HTML response as a page. Current browsers sniff in fewer circumstances than older ones did, so the header mainly closes remaining edge cases and protects users of older browsers.

The issue is identified by inspecting response headers, and scanners report it as a missing security header. It is most relevant where the application serves files uploaded by users or returns user-controlled data with an imprecise content type.
entries.impact: The missing header has no direct impact. It can contribute to an attack where the application serves content an attacker controls with a missing or imprecise content type: a browser that sniffs that content as HTML or script could run the attacker's script in the application's origin, resulting in cross-site scripting. Where every response carries an accurate Content-Type and uploaded files are served from a separate domain or as downloads, the header adds little.
entries.remediation:
Send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on every response, and make sure each response declares the correct Content-Type, with a charset for text types, because once sniffing is disabled a wrongly labelled resource will stop working.

nginx: add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always; Apache (mod_headers): Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" IIS (web.config, within system.webServer): <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <add name="X-Content-Type-Options" value="nosniff" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol>

Serve files uploaded by users with an explicit, safe content type and, where they need not be displayed in the browser, with Content-Disposition: attachment, ideally from a separate domain. Confirm the fix by checking that the header is present on HTML, script, stylesheet and file download responses.

entries.title: Referrer-Policy Header Missing
entries.summary: No Referrer-Policy header is set, so how much of a page's address is sent to other sites in the Referer header depends on each browser's default.
entries.description:
When a user follows a link or a page loads a resource, the browser sends the address of the current page in the Referer request header. The Referrer-Policy response header controls how much of that address is sent, and to which destinations. The application does not set it, so each browser's default applies.

Current versions of the major browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin: the full address is sent only with same-origin requests, other sites receive only the origin (scheme, host and port), and nothing is sent from an HTTPS page to an HTTP address. Older browsers defaulted to no-referrer-when-downgrade, which sends the full address, including its path and query string, to any HTTPS destination. A missing header therefore mainly affects users of older browsers, and pages whose addresses carry sensitive values such as tokens, identifiers or search terms.

The issue is identified by inspecting response headers, together with any meta elements and referrerpolicy attributes in the pages, which can also set or weaken the policy.
entries.impact: The missing header has no direct impact in current browsers. In older browsers, and wherever a page or element sets a more permissive policy such as unsafe-url, the full address of a page is sent to third-party sites it links to or loads resources from, such as analytics, advertising or content delivery providers. Where those addresses contain tokens, personal data or internal paths, the values are disclosed to the third party and kept in its logs.
entries.remediation:
Set an explicit policy on every response so that behaviour does not depend on the browser. strict-origin-when-cross-origin suits most sites, while no-referrer or same-origin suits applications whose addresses carry sensitive values.

nginx: add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always; Apache (mod_headers): Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" IIS (web.config, within system.webServer): <httpProtocol> <customHeaders> <add name="Referrer-Policy" value="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" /> </customHeaders> </httpProtocol>

Review the pages for meta elements and referrerpolicy attributes that set unsafe-url or no-referrer-when-downgrade, and keep sensitive values out of addresses altogether rather than relying on the policy alone. Confirm the fix by checking that the header is present on HTML responses and, in the browser's developer tools, that requests to other sites carry only the origin.

entries.title: Permissions-Policy Header Missing
entries.summary: No Permissions-Policy header restricts which powerful browser features, such as the camera, microphone or geolocation, the application's pages and embedded frames may use.
entries.description:
The Permissions-Policy response header lets a site declare which browser features its pages, and the frames they embed, may use: for example the camera, microphone, geolocation, payment requests, fullscreen display and USB devices. A feature disabled in the policy cannot be used by the page or its frames, whatever script runs there. The application does not send the header, so each feature falls back to the browser's default, which typically allows the page itself and same-origin frames to request it and requires a cross-origin frame to be granted it through the frame's allow attribute.

Features that need the user's consent still prompt the user before use. The header is therefore a hardening measure that limits what injected or third-party script could ask for, rather than a fix for a vulnerability. Support varies between browsers, and the older Feature-Policy header that it replaced used a different syntax.

The issue is identified by inspecting response headers; scanners report it as a missing security header.
entries.impact: The missing header has no direct impact. If an attacker were able to run script in the application, through cross-site scripting or a compromised third-party script, or if an embedded frame were malicious, an explicit policy would stop that script requesting features the application never uses, such as the camera, microphone or location; the user would still have to grant any such request. The header is of most value in applications that embed third-party content.
entries.remediation:
Send a Permissions-Policy header that disables every feature the application does not use and limits those it does use to its own origin, and grant features to embedded frames only through their allow attribute where needed.

Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=() nginx: add_header Permissions-Policy "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=()" always; Apache (mod_headers): Header always set Permissions-Policy "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=()"

On IIS, add the same header under customHeaders in web.config. Where a feature is needed, allow it for the application's own origin only, for example geolocation=(self). Confirm the fix by checking that the header is present on HTML responses with the intended directives.

entries.title: Sensitive Content Cacheable
entries.summary: Pages or API responses containing sensitive data are sent without directives that stop browsers and intermediate caches storing them, so copies may be recovered later.
entries.description:
Responses that contain sensitive information, such as account details, personal or financial data or authenticated API output, are sent without caching directives that prevent them being stored, or with directives that allow it, such as Cache-Control: public or a long max-age. Browsers may then keep copies in their disk cache, and shared caches, such as corporate proxies or content delivery networks that can see the traffic, may store them too.

Copies in a browser's cache remain after the user logs out and can be viewed by the next person using the same computer and profile, for example on a shared, public or kiosk machine, or recovered from the cache files on disk. A shared cache that stores an authenticated response may serve it to other users.

The issue is identified by reviewing the Cache-Control, Expires and Pragma headers on authenticated responses, and by logging out and then inspecting the browser's cache or using the back button to see whether sensitive pages are shown again. Scanners report it as cacheable HTTPS responses.
entries.impact: A person who later uses the same computer and browser profile, or who obtains its cache files, can read sensitive pages that a previous user viewed, even after that user has logged out. Where a shared cache stores authenticated responses, other users of that cache may receive one user's data. The impact depends on what the cached responses contain and where the application is used: it is greatest for applications used on shared or public computers and low where users have their own managed devices.
entries.remediation:
Mark every response that contains sensitive or user-specific data so that caches do not store it:

  • Send Cache-Control: no-store on authenticated pages, API responses containing personal or sensitive data, and downloads of such data. Where old HTTP/1.0 caches must be allowed for, also send Pragma: no-cache and Expires: 0.
  • Where a response may be kept by the browser but never by a shared cache, use Cache-Control: private. Use no-cache only where revalidation before each use is the intention, since it still allows storage.
  • Set caching headers for authenticated routes as a whole in the application or framework, rather than page by page, while leaving static public assets cacheable.
  • Configure any content delivery network or reverse proxy not to cache responses to authenticated requests.
  • Consider sending Clear-Site-Data: "cache" when a user logs out.
Cache-Control: no-store

Confirm the fix by checking the headers on authenticated responses and that, after logging out, sensitive pages are not shown from the browser's cache.

entries.title: Cookie Without the Secure Attribute
entries.summary: A sensitive cookie, often the session cookie, is set without the Secure attribute, so the browser will also send it over unencrypted HTTP connections to the same host.
entries.description:
The application sets one or more sensitive cookies, such as session identifiers or authentication tokens, without the Secure attribute. The attribute tells the browser to send the cookie only over HTTPS. Without it, the browser includes the cookie in any plain HTTP request to the same host, even if the application itself is only ever used over HTTPS.

An attacker on the network path does not need the user to visit an HTTP page of the application deliberately. Any HTTP navigation to the host sends the cookie, and an attacker who can tamper with the user's other unencrypted traffic can cause one, for example by redirecting an HTTP page the user visits to the host's http:// address; the attacker can answer that request on the network even if the server does not listen on port 80. An HTTP Strict Transport Security policy covering the host stops the browser making such requests, but only once the browser has received it.

The issue is identified by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers or the browser's cookie storage. Cookies holding only non-sensitive values, such as display preferences, do not need the attribute for security, though setting it on every cookie is simpler.
entries.impact: An attacker able to observe and tamper with the user's network traffic, such as on a shared wireless network, can cause the browser to send the cookie over HTTP and read it. Where the cookie is a session identifier, the attacker can then use the session as the user, with the user's privileges, until it expires or is ended. The attacker needs a position on the network path while the user's session is active, which limits the opportunity, and an HSTS policy covering the host removes most of it. An attacker in that position can also set or overwrite cookies that lack the attribute through a forged HTTP response.
entries.remediation:
Set the Secure attribute on every cookie that carries a session identifier, authentication token or other sensitive value, and preferably on all cookies, since the application is served over HTTPS:

  • Enable the framework or server setting that marks session cookies as secure, for example session.cookie_secure in PHP, requireSSL on httpCookies and on forms authentication in ASP.NET, CookieSecurePolicy.Always in ASP.NET Core, cookie.secure in express-session, or <secure>true</secure> under session-config and cookie-config in a Java web.xml.
  • Where a load balancer or proxy terminates TLS, make sure the application knows the original request used HTTPS, for example through a trusted X-Forwarded-Proto header, since some frameworks only set the attribute on requests they believe are secure.
  • Use the __Host- name prefix for session cookies where possible: browsers only accept such a cookie when it has Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute.
  • Enable HSTS on the host so that browsers do not make HTTP requests to it at all.
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=38afes7a8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

Confirm the fix by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers after login and checking that the cookie is not sent with an HTTP request to the host.

entries.title: Cookie Without the HttpOnly Attribute
entries.summary: A sensitive cookie is set without the HttpOnly attribute, so script running in the page, including script injected through cross-site scripting, can read its value.
entries.description:
The application sets one or more sensitive cookies, such as session identifiers or authentication tokens, without the HttpOnly attribute. The attribute stops script in the page reading or changing the cookie through document.cookie, while the browser still sends it with requests as normal. Without it, any script running in the application's origin can read the cookie's value.

The attribute is a defence-in-depth measure against cross-site scripting. It does not prevent cross-site scripting, and injected script can still send requests that carry the cookie and act as the user while it runs, but it stops the session identifier itself being copied out and reused elsewhere. Some cookies, such as anti-forgery tokens using the double-submit pattern or settings read by client-side code, must be readable by script and so cannot carry the attribute.

The issue is identified by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers or the browser's cookie storage, and confirmed for a given cookie by reading document.cookie in the browser's console.
entries.impact: The missing attribute has no direct impact. If the application has a cross-site scripting flaw, an attacker exploiting it can read the cookie, send it to a server they control and then use the session from their own browser until it expires or is ended, without depending on the victim's page staying open. With the attribute set, the same attacker is limited to acting through the victim's browser while the injected script runs.
entries.remediation:
Set the HttpOnly attribute on every cookie that carries a session identifier, authentication token or other value that client-side code does not need to read:

  • Use the framework or server setting for session cookies, for example session.cookie_httponly in PHP, httpOnlyCookies on httpCookies in ASP.NET, Cookie.HttpOnly in ASP.NET Core cookie options, cookie.httpOnly in express-session, or <http-only>true</http-only> under session-config and cookie-config in a Java web.xml.
  • Where client-side code reads a sensitive cookie, change the design so that script does not need the value.
  • Set Secure and an appropriate SameSite value on the same cookies.
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=38afes7a8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

Treat the attribute as a complement to preventing cross-site scripting, not a substitute for it. Confirm the fix by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers after login and checking that the session cookie no longer appears in document.cookie.

entries.title: Cookie Without a SameSite Attribute
entries.summary: A sensitive cookie is set without a SameSite attribute, so whether browsers attach it to requests started by other sites depends on each browser's default.
entries.description:
The SameSite cookie attribute controls whether the browser sends a cookie with requests that another site causes. Strict withholds it from all of them; Lax sends it with them only when they are top-level navigations using a safe method such as GET; and None sends it with all of them and requires Secure. The application sets one or more sensitive cookies without the attribute, so each browser's default applies.

The defaults differ. Chromium-based browsers, such as Chrome and Edge, treat a cookie without the attribute as Lax, but still send it with cross-site top-level POST requests made within two minutes of the cookie being set. Firefox and Safari do not apply Lax by default: they restrict cookies in embedded third-party contexts, but send them with cross-site top-level navigations, including form submissions using POST. The protection users receive therefore depends on their browser. The attribute also treats every subdomain of the same registrable domain as the same site, so it offers no protection against requests from those.

The issue is identified by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers. A cookie explicitly set to SameSite=None without a need for cross-site use is a related, weaker configuration.
entries.impact: The missing attribute has no direct impact. It removes a layer of defence against cross-site request forgery, cross-site WebSocket hijacking and some cross-site information leaks: for users of browsers that do not default to Lax, a page on another site can make requests that carry the session cookie, so any state-changing function without its own anti-forgery protection can be triggered as the logged-in user. Where the application uses anti-forgery tokens throughout, the absence of the attribute adds little.
entries.remediation:
Set an explicit SameSite value on every cookie:

  • Use SameSite=Lax for session cookies in most applications. Users still arrive logged in when following links from other sites, while the cookie is withheld from cross-site POST requests and embedded requests.
  • Use SameSite=Strict for cookies that authorise sensitive actions where users never need to arrive from another site already logged in, or pair a Strict cookie for sensitive actions with a Lax cookie for general browsing.
  • Use SameSite=None; Secure only for cookies that must be sent in cross-site contexts, such as an application embedded in another site's frame or some single sign-on flows, and protect those requests in other ways.
  • Set the value through the framework where possible, for example session.cookie_samesite in PHP, Cookie.SameSite in ASP.NET Core cookie options or cookie.sameSite in express-session.
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=38afes7a8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

Keep anti-forgery tokens on state-changing requests as well, since the attribute does not cover requests from other subdomains of the same site or browsers that ignore it. Confirm the fix by inspecting the Set-Cookie headers after login.

entries.title: Overly Broad Cookie Scope
entries.summary: A sensitive cookie is scoped to a parent domain or an over-broad path, so the browser also sends it to other hosts or applications that should not receive it.
entries.description:
The application sets a sensitive cookie, such as a session identifier, with a Domain attribute naming a parent domain, for example the organisation's main domain rather than the application's own host name. A cookie with a Domain attribute is sent to that domain and to every subdomain of it, so every other host under the domain receives the cookie with each request, and script on any of them can read it unless it is HttpOnly. A cookie set without a Domain attribute is sent only to the host that set it.

A related form is a Path attribute broader than the application needs where several applications share one host name under different paths. The path is not a security boundary between pages of the same origin, because script on one path can read cookies for another through a frame, so applications that need to be isolated from each other need separate host names.

The issue is identified by inspecting the Domain and Path attributes in the Set-Cookie headers and by reviewing which other hosts exist under the domain, for example from DNS records and certificate transparency logs.
entries.impact: Every host under the cookie's domain receives the cookie. An attacker who controls any one of them, whether through cross-site scripting or another flaw on a less well protected site, a subdomain takeover of a name still pointing at a decommissioned service, or because a third party operates that host, can capture the cookie and hijack the user's session in the application. The risk grows with the number and variety of hosts under the domain, particularly where some are run by other teams or suppliers, and is low where the domain holds a few well-maintained hosts.
entries.remediation:
Scope sensitive cookies as narrowly as the application allows:

  • Omit the Domain attribute on session and authentication cookies, so that they are sent only to the host that set them. Where a cookie genuinely must be shared between hosts, name the narrowest common domain and hold every host under it to the same standard.
  • Use the __Host- name prefix for session cookies: browsers only accept such a cookie when it has Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute, so its scope cannot be widened by mistake and other hosts cannot set a cookie of that name for it.
  • Run applications that must be isolated from each other on separate host names rather than separate paths of one host.
  • Review the hosts under the domain, remove DNS records that point at decommissioned services, and move sites operated by third parties to a separate domain where practical.
  • Where users need single sign-on across hosts, use a federation protocol such as OpenID Connect or SAML rather than a session cookie shared across the domain.
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=38afes7a8; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

Confirm the fix by checking that session cookies are set without a Domain attribute and are not sent to other hosts under the domain.

patterns: \bloosely scoped cookie\b|\bcookie scoped to (parent|the parent) domain\b|\bcookie\b.*\b(domain|path) (attribute|scope)

entries.title: Password Field Autocomplete Enabled
