entries.summary: A password field does not disable browser autocompletion, so browsers may offer to save the credentials, although current browsers ignore that setting for login fields.
entries.description:
The application's login or password forms do not set autocomplete="off" on the password field or on the form, so browsers may offer to save the credentials entered and fill them in later. Scanners commonly report this as a password field with autocomplete enabled.

Current browsers do not honour autocomplete="off" on login fields: their built-in password managers offer to save credentials whatever the attribute says, because saved, unique passwords are considered better for users than reused, memorable ones. The attribute still stops browsers saving entries for other form fields, and browsers use autocomplete="new-password" to avoid filling in a saved password where a new one is being set.

The finding is therefore largely informational. It remains relevant to applications used on shared or kiosk computers, where a password saved on one user's behalf is available to the next person using the same browser profile.
entries.impact: The finding has no direct impact in current browsers, which offer to save passwords regardless. Where a browser does save a password, anyone who can use the same computer and browser profile can log in as that user or recover the password from the browser's store, and malware running as the user can extract saved passwords. The concern is greatest for applications used on shared, public or kiosk computers.
entries.remediation:
Do not rely on autocomplete="off" to protect credentials: current browsers ignore it for login fields, and blocking password managers tends to push users towards weaker, reused passwords. Instead:

  • Use accurate autocomplete values so that password managers behave predictably: username and current-password on login forms, and new-password where a password is set or changed.
  • Protect accounts with multi-factor authentication, so that a password recovered from a browser is not enough to log in.
  • Where the application is used on shared or kiosk computers, manage those browsers centrally to turn off password saving, for example with the PasswordManagerEnabled policy in Chrome and Edge, and clear profiles between users.
  • Advise users not to save passwords on shared computers, and apply short session timeouts there.

Confirm any change by reviewing the form markup and, on managed computers, checking that the browser no longer offers to save the password.

entries.title: Third-Party Scripts Without Subresource Integrity
entries.summary: Scripts or stylesheets are loaded from third-party servers without an integrity hash, so a malicious change to those files would run in the application's pages unchecked.
entries.description:
The application's pages load scripts or stylesheets from servers outside the organisation's control, such as public content delivery networks or a supplier's servers, without the integrity attribute. Subresource Integrity (SRI) lets a page state the cryptographic hash of the file it expects, and the browser refuses to use a file whose content does not match. Without it, the page runs whatever the third-party server delivers.

The weakness only matters if the third-party file is changed maliciously, for example because the provider or its account is compromised, the domain serving it changes hands, or a storage bucket hosting it can be written by others. Such incidents have affected widely used script providers, and one change reaches every site that loads the file.

SRI suits files fixed at a specific version. It cannot be used for resources that the provider changes deliberately, such as analytics or advertising tags or addresses that always serve the latest release, and a cross-origin resource loaded with it must be requested with the crossorigin attribute and served with suitable CORS headers. The issue is identified by reviewing the script and link elements that reference other origins.
entries.impact: If an attacker alters a third-party file that the pages load, their code runs in the application's pages with the same access as the application's own script: it can read what users see and type, including credentials and payment details, act as logged-in users and change what the pages show. Exploitation depends on first compromising the third party, which is outside the attacker's direct reach and outside the organisation's control, but one success affects every user of every site that loads the file. The impact is greatest on pages that handle logins, payments or personal data.
entries.remediation:
Remove the application's dependence on the integrity of third-party servers:

  • Add an integrity attribute holding a SHA-384 or SHA-512 hash of the exact file, together with crossorigin="anonymous", to every script and stylesheet link element that loads a fixed version of a file from another origin.
  • Reference specific versions rather than addresses that always serve the latest release, and update the hash deliberately when upgrading.
  • Prefer to serve copies of third-party libraries from the application's own servers, bundled through the build process, where they are covered by the same controls as the rest of the code.
  • For scripts that cannot use SRI, such as supplier tags, review whether they are needed on sensitive pages, and use a Content Security Policy to limit which origins may supply script.
<script src="https://cdn.example.net/library/1.2.3/library.min.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous"></script> Generating the hash of a file: openssl dgst -sha384 -binary library.min.js | openssl base64 -A

Confirm the fix by checking that third-party script and link elements carry integrity attributes and that the pages load without integrity errors in the browser's console.

patterns: \bsubresource integrity\b|\bSRI\b|\bcross-domain javascript source file inclusion\b|\bscript (included|loaded) from (an )?external\b

entries.title: Vulnerable JavaScript Library
entries.summary: The application serves a client-side JavaScript library version with publicly known vulnerabilities, such as cross-site scripting or prototype pollution flaws.
entries.description:
The application loads a version of a client-side JavaScript library, such as a DOM manipulation library, front-end framework, rich text editor or plugin, for which security flaws have been published. Typical flaws in such libraries are cross-site scripting through functions that turn strings into HTML, prototype pollution in functions that merge objects, and regular expression denial of service.

A published flaw in a library does not by itself make the application exploitable. Most require the application to pass attacker-controlled input to a particular function or option, so the finding is established in two steps: identifying the library and version and matching them against published advisories, which is what tools such as Retire.js and dependency scanners do, and, where time allows, showing that a vulnerable function is reachable with input an attacker controls. Version detection can be wrong where a supplier has patched or modified a bundled copy, so the reported version should be checked against the file itself.

Several outdated libraries are often found together, which usually indicates that client-side dependencies are not managed or patched.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the flaw and on how the application uses the library. Where a cross-site scripting flaw is reachable, an attacker can run script in a victim's browser in the application's origin, typically by persuading the victim to follow a link or view crafted content, and can then read data, act as the victim or capture what they type. Prototype pollution can lead to the same result or to bypasses of client-side logic, and regular expression flaws can freeze the user's browser tab. Where no vulnerable function is used with untrusted input, the practical risk is low, though later changes to the application can make a flaw reachable.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade each affected library to a current, supported version that fixes the published flaws, and test the application with it, since major upgrades can change behaviour:

  • Manage client-side libraries through a package manager and lock file rather than copied files, so that their versions are recorded and can be checked automatically, for example with npm audit or a software composition analysis tool in the build pipeline.
  • Remove libraries the application no longer uses, including those pulled in only by old plugins or templates.
  • Replace libraries that are no longer maintained, since their flaws will not be fixed.
  • Where an upgrade cannot be made at once, check whether the application passes untrusted input to the vulnerable functions, stop doing so or sanitise that input, and apply any workaround the advisory describes.
  • Follow security advisories for the libraries in use and include client-side dependencies in the regular patching process.

A Content Security Policy that restricts script sources reduces the impact of any cross-site scripting flaw in the meantime. Confirm the fix by rescanning the pages and checking the version in each library file.

entries.title: Outdated Content Management System or Plugins
entries.summary: The content management system, or plugins, themes or modules installed in it, is an outdated release with publicly known vulnerabilities, some exploitable without logging in.
entries.description:
The site runs an outdated release of a content management system (CMS), such as WordPress, Drupal or Joomla, or outdated plugins, themes, extensions or modules installed in it, for which security fixes have been published. CMS add-ons are written by many independent developers and are a frequent source of serious flaws, such as SQL injection, arbitrary file upload, privilege escalation and authentication bypass, and exploit code for popular ones is often published soon after a fix.

Versions can be identified from generator meta tags, readme and changelog files, version parameters added to script and stylesheet addresses, and characteristic files, using tools such as WPScan, droopescan or JoomScan, and then matched against vendors' advisories and vulnerability databases. Each identified flaw should be checked for its preconditions, since many need a particular configuration or an authenticated account with a given role. Some add-ons have been abandoned by their authors and will never receive a fix.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the flaws present. Flaws that need no authentication, such as SQL injection, arbitrary file upload or remote code execution in the core or a plugin, can give an attacker control of the site and the server it runs on, access to its database, including user accounts and personal data, and a platform for defacement, malware distribution or attacks on visitors. Flaws that need an account are a lesser but real risk, particularly where the site allows public registration. Automated campaigns scan the internet for vulnerable CMS installations and exploit them, often soon after an exploit becomes public, so exposure does not depend on the site being chosen as a target.
entries.remediation:
Bring the CMS and every add-on up to date, and keep them there:

  • Update the CMS core to the latest supported release, then each plugin, theme, extension and module, testing on a staging copy first where the site is complex. Move off any major version that is no longer supported.
  • Remove add-ons that are not in use, including deactivated ones, whose files remain on the server and may still be reachable, and replace any that are abandoned or have unfixed flaws.
  • Turn on automatic updates for security releases where the platform supports them, and follow the security advisories for the CMS and its add-ons.
  • Keep an inventory of the add-ons and versions in each installation and include them in regular vulnerability scanning.
  • Limit the damage of a future flaw: restrict access to the administration interface, require strong passwords and multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts, disable file editing from the administration interface, and set file permissions so that the web server cannot write to the site's code.

Where an update must wait, a web application firewall with rules for the specific flaws can reduce the risk in the meantime, but it is not a substitute for updating. Confirm the fix by rescanning the site and checking the reported versions of the core and each add-on against the current releases.

patterns: \b(WordPress|Drupal|Joomla!?|Magento|TYPO3|Umbraco|Sitecore|DNN|DotNetNuke|Craft CMS|Ghost CMS|Concrete ?CMS|PrestaShop|Moodle)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Sensitive Information in URLs
entries.summary: Sensitive values such as passwords, API keys, tokens or personal data are placed in URLs, where browsers, servers, proxies and third parties record them.
entries.description:
The application places sensitive values in URLs, usually in the query string of GET requests. Typical examples are credentials or API keys passed as parameters, login or search forms submitted with GET, access or reset tokens that remain valid after use, and personal data such as email addresses, names or account numbers used as identifiers.

Unlike request bodies and most headers, URLs are recorded in many places outside the application's control: browser history and address bar suggestions, bookmarks, web server and application logs, the logs of proxies, load balancers and content delivery networks, analytics and monitoring tools, and, depending on the referrer policy, the Referer header sent to other sites that a page links to or loads resources from. HTTPS does not prevent this, because the URL is visible at both ends of the connection.

The issue is identified by reviewing the requests the application makes, for example through an intercepting proxy, for parameters that carry such values. Session identifiers in URLs are a closely related and more serious case.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read one of the places where URLs are recorded, such as another person using the same computer, an administrator or attacker with access to server or proxy logs, or a third party receiving the Referer header, can obtain the values. Depending on what they are, this can disclose personal data or give access to accounts or services: a password or API key in a URL remains usable until it is changed. The exposure lasts as long as the logs and history are kept, and the access needed to reach them limits who can exploit it.
entries.remediation:
Keep sensitive values out of URLs:

  • Send credentials, tokens and personal data in the body of POST requests or in request headers, such as the Authorization header for API keys and bearer tokens, never as query parameters.
  • Submit login, registration and other forms that carry sensitive fields with the POST method.
  • Use opaque, random identifiers in place of email addresses or account numbers where a record must be referenced in a URL.
  • Where a token must appear in a URL, as in a password reset or email verification link, make it single-use and short-lived, and once it has been used, send the user on to an address without it.
  • Set Referrer-Policy: no-referrer or same-origin on pages whose addresses may carry such values, and exclude or mask sensitive parameters in logs.
  • Change any credential or key found in URLs, since it should be treated as exposed, and purge it from logs where possible.

Confirm the fix by repeating the affected actions through an intercepting proxy and checking that no sensitive value appears in any request URL.

entries.title: Credentials or API Keys in Client-Side Code
entries.summary: Secret credentials, such as private API keys, cloud access keys or service passwords, are embedded in JavaScript or other files sent to the browser, where anyone can read them.
entries.description:
The application includes secret credentials in code delivered to the browser, such as JavaScript bundles, inline scripts, source maps, configuration files fetched by the front end, or HTML. Anything sent to the browser can be read by any user, and by anyone at all where the files are public, so a secret placed there is disclosed whatever is done to hide it, including minification and obfuscation.

Typical findings include private API keys for payment, email, messaging or other third-party services, cloud storage or access keys, credentials for internal APIs or databases, and tokens for source control or build services. They are found by searching the delivered files, including source maps and older bundles still on the server, for known key formats and words such as secret, token and password, using browser developer tools or secret scanning tools.

Not every key in client-side code is a finding. Some are designed to be public and are restricted by other means, such as publishable payment keys, Firebase web configuration and browser keys for mapping services restricted to the site's own pages. Each key found should be identified and, where safe and within the agreed scope, tested to establish what it grants.
entries.impact: An attacker who extracts a secret can use it directly against the service it belongs to, with whatever rights it grants and usually without any further control. Depending on the key, this can mean reading or changing data held in the organisation's account with a provider, sending email or messages in the organisation's name, reaching cloud storage or internal APIs, or running up charges. Because the code is public, the secret should be assumed to have been collected already, and its misuse is often hard to distinguish from the application's own use in the provider's logs.
entries.remediation:
Remove secrets from client-side code and treat every exposed one as compromised:

  • Revoke or rotate each exposed credential at once, and review the provider's logs for misuse since it was first exposed.
  • Move calls that need a secret to the server: the browser calls the application's own back end, which authenticates the user, applies authorisation and rate limits, and then calls the third-party service with a secret held only on the server, ideally in a secrets manager.
  • Where the browser must call a service directly, use credentials designed for that purpose: publishable or browser keys restricted to the site and to the minimum scope, or short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens issued by the back end for each user.
  • Remove secrets from source maps, configuration files and old bundles, stop publishing source maps to production unless they are needed, and add secret scanning to the build pipeline and source repository so that new secrets are caught before release.
  • Remove exposed secrets from source control history too, in case the repository is ever exposed.

Confirm the fix by searching the delivered files again and checking that the old credentials no longer work.

entries.title: Sensitive Information in Source Code Comments
entries.summary: HTML, JavaScript or CSS comments sent to the browser contain information useful to an attacker, such as internal host names, file paths, developer notes or credentials.
entries.description:
Comments left in HTML, JavaScript or CSS that the server sends to the browser contain information not meant for users. Anyone can read them by viewing the page source or the delivered files. Typical content includes developer notes about known problems or unfinished security controls, commented-out links to administrative, test or unreleased functions, internal host names, IP addresses and file paths, names and email addresses of developers, details of the software in use and, occasionally, credentials, keys or test accounts.

Comments in server-side code are removed before the response is sent and are not exposed in this way; the finding concerns comments that reach the client, including those kept in unminified scripts and in source maps.

The issue is identified by reviewing the source of the application's pages and scripts, manually or with tools that extract comments from responses, such as the comment-finding features of intercepting proxies.
entries.impact: The disclosed details rarely compromise the application by themselves, but they reduce an attacker's effort: hidden functions and parameters become targets, internal names and paths help plan further attacks, and notes about weaknesses show where to look. Where comments contain credentials, keys or test accounts, the impact is higher and should be rated on what those give access to.
entries.remediation:
Keep comments meant for developers out of what is sent to the browser:

  • Strip comments from scripts and stylesheets in the build process, for example through minification, and in templates use the template language's own comments, which the server does not send, such as @* *@ in Razor or {# #} in Jinja and Twig, in place of HTML comments.
  • Review the comments that remain, and remove any that describe internal systems, unfinished work or security controls.
  • Remove commented-out code, particularly links or forms for functions that are not meant to be available, and make sure those functions are themselves removed or protected on the server.
  • Do not publish source maps to production unless they are needed, or restrict who can fetch them.
  • Change any credential or key found in a comment, since it should be treated as exposed.

Confirm the fix by reviewing the source of the affected pages and files again.

entries.title: Internal IP Address Disclosure
entries.summary: Responses reveal private IP addresses or internal host names of the servers behind the application, giving an attacker details of the internal network.
entries.description:
The application or its supporting infrastructure discloses private (RFC 1918) IP addresses, or internal host names, of the servers behind it. Common sources are the Location and Content-Location headers in responses to requests sent without a Host header or as HTTP/1.0, headers added by load balancers and proxies, such as Via or custom headers naming the back-end server, persistence cookies set by load balancers that encode the back-end address, error messages, page content and comments, and the challenge in NTLM authentication, which reveals internal domain and host names.

The issue is identified by inspecting responses for private address ranges and internal names, including responses to deliberately unusual requests. Scanners commonly report it from the Location header of a redirect.
entries.impact: An internal address or host name gives an attacker no access by itself. It helps them map the internal network and its addressing, aim server-side request forgery or other flaws that reach internal systems, and recognise which systems they have reached if they later gain a foothold. It can also show how many back-end servers there are and how they are named.
entries.remediation:
Stop the application and its infrastructure from including internal addresses and names in responses:

  • Configure web servers to build redirects and other self-referencing headers from the public host name rather than the server's own address: on IIS, set the alternateHostName attribute of the serverRuntime section to the public host name; on Apache, set ServerName and, where appropriate, UseCanonicalName On; on nginx, review server_name_in_redirect and absolute_redirect.
  • Remove or rewrite headers added by load balancers and reverse proxies that name back-end servers, and configure load balancer persistence cookies to be encrypted or to carry an opaque value.
  • Replace detailed error messages with generic ones, and remove internal addresses from comments and page content.
  • Where NTLM authentication is offered to the internet, consider whether it is needed there.

Confirm the fix by repeating the requests that produced the disclosure, including HTTP/1.0 requests without a Host header, and checking that no private address or internal name is returned.

entries.title: Sensitive Paths Disclosed in robots.txt
entries.summary: The robots.txt file lists paths the organisation would rather keep hidden, such as administrative or internal areas, pointing anyone who reads it straight to them.
entries.description:
The site's robots.txt file, which tells search engine crawlers which paths not to visit, lists paths that reveal sensitive or unadvertised areas, such as administrative interfaces, staging or test areas, backups, internal tools or APIs. The file is public by design and is one of the first resources an attacker or tester requests, so a Disallow entry draws attention to a path rather than hiding it.

The file is a request to well-behaved crawlers, not an access control: it does not stop anyone, or any crawler that chooses to ignore it, from requesting the listed paths, and a disallowed page that is linked from elsewhere may still appear in search results by its address. Each listed path should be requested to establish whether it is reachable and whether it requires authentication; a listed path that exposes content without authentication is a separate and more serious finding.
entries.impact: The file gives an attacker no access by itself. It saves them effort in finding administrative, test and other unadvertised areas of the site, which they can then target for weak authentication, default credentials or unpatched software. The impact therefore depends on whether the listed paths are properly protected.
entries.remediation:
Do not use robots.txt to hide sensitive areas:

  • Remove entries that name administrative, internal, test or backup paths, keeping only those needed to manage how search engines crawl public content.
  • Protect sensitive areas with authentication and authorisation, and restrict administrative interfaces to trusted networks where possible, so that it does not matter whether their paths are known.
  • Remove test, staging and backup content from production servers altogether.
  • To keep public pages out of search results, use a noindex directive in a meta element or in the X-Robots-Tag response header; crawlers only see it if the page is not disallowed in robots.txt.

Confirm the fix by reviewing the published robots.txt and requesting each previously listed path to check that it has been removed or is protected.

entries.title: security.txt Not Published
entries.summary: The site does not publish a security.txt file, so people who find a vulnerability have no clear, standard way to report it to the organisation.
entries.description:
The site does not publish a security.txt file at /.well-known/security.txt. Defined in RFC 9116, the file is a short, machine-readable text document that tells security researchers and others how to report a vulnerability to the organisation. It must contain at least one Contact field, such as an email address or web form, and an Expires field, and can also link to the organisation's vulnerability disclosure policy and encryption key, state preferred languages and name its own canonical address.

Without it, or an equivalent, clearly published disclosure policy, someone who finds a security issue may not know whom to tell, may send the report to a general address where it is overlooked, or may give up or disclose it publicly instead. A file that has passed its Expires date, names an unmonitored address or is not served over HTTPS is a weaker variant of the same finding.

The issue is identified by requesting /.well-known/security.txt over HTTPS, and the older location /security.txt, on the organisation's main domains.
entries.impact: A missing security.txt file is not a vulnerability and gives an attacker nothing. Its absence makes it more likely that vulnerabilities found by others reach the organisation late, through the wrong channel or not at all, which lengthens the period in which they could be exploited. The value of publishing one is greatest for organisations with a large internet-facing presence.
entries.remediation:
Publish a security.txt file at /.well-known/security.txt on each main web domain, served over HTTPS as plain text:

  • Include at least one Contact field pointing to a monitored address or form, and an Expires field less than a year ahead, with a process to renew it before it lapses.
  • Add a Policy field linking to a vulnerability disclosure policy that sets out what may be tested, how reports are handled and how researchers acting in good faith will be treated, and optionally Encryption, Preferred-Languages and Canonical fields.
  • Consider signing the file with OpenPGP, as the standard recommends, and redirecting /security.txt to the well-known location for older tools.
  • Make sure reports sent to the contact are triaged and acknowledged within a defined time.
Contact: mailto:security@example.com Expires: 2027-10-31T23:00:00.000Z Policy: https://example.com/vulnerability-disclosure-policy Preferred-Languages: en Canonical: https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt

Confirm the fix by requesting the file over HTTPS and checking that the required fields are present and the expiry date is in the future.

entries.title: Default or Well-Known Credentials
entries.summary: A system still accepts a vendor default or widely published username and password, so anyone who knows the product can sign in with it.
entries.description:
The application, device or service accepts a username and password that are set by the vendor at installation, printed in its documentation or otherwise widely known, such as admin with the password admin, a blank password or a product-specific default. Default credentials for most products are collected in public lists and built into attack tools, so they are among the first values any attacker tries.

The weakness is most often found on administrative interfaces: application server managers, network, storage and virtualisation appliances, printers, CCTV and building management systems, database consoles, continuous integration and monitoring tools, and sample or setup accounts left behind by an installation. It is confirmed by signing in with the documented default for the identified product. Vulnerability scanners, Nmap scripts, Metasploit modules and dedicated default-credential checkers test common defaults automatically, and usually report the product, the account and the credential that worked.

Related variants include a password set during a standard build and reused on every system of the same type, and passwords derived from the product, device or organisation name, which attackers try just as readily.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the login interface can sign in with the privileges of the default account, which on administrative interfaces usually means full control of the system. Depending on the product, this can allow the attacker to read and change its configuration and data, create further accounts, deploy code (for example a web application archive through an application server's manager), intercept or redirect traffic passing through a network device, or use the system as a foothold to attack the rest of the network. The attack needs no skill or prior access beyond network reachability, and is routinely automated by botnets and opportunistic attackers scanning the internet.
entries.remediation:
• Change the password of every default account to a unique, randomly generated value held in a password manager or privileged access management system, or disable or remove the account where the product allows it.
  • Make changing default credentials part of the build and commissioning process for every new system and device, and check it before the system goes live. Prefer products that require a unique password to be set at first use.
  • Remove sample applications, setup accounts and test users left behind by installation.
  • Restrict administrative interfaces to a management network or VPN, and require multi-factor authentication for them where the product supports it.
  • Test systems regularly for default credentials, for example with authenticated vulnerability scans, so that newly deployed or factory-reset devices are caught.

Where a device's credentials cannot be changed immediately, restrict access to its management interface to named administrative hosts as an interim measure. Confirm the fix by repeating the login attempts with the published defaults and confirming that each is rejected.

entries.title: Weak or Guessable Passwords in Use
entries.summary: Accounts use passwords that are common, short or follow predictable patterns, so an attacker can sign in by trying a few likely values.
entries.description:
Accounts on the application or service were found to use passwords that are easily guessed: common passwords such as Password1 or Welcome123, a season or month followed by the year, the company or product name with a number, the username repeated, short numeric values, or passwords that appear in public breach collections. Such passwords fall within the first few attempts of a dictionary or password spraying attack. Complexity rules do not prevent them, because predictable patterns satisfy most composition requirements.

The finding is usually confirmed by trying a small number of likely passwords against each account at the login interface while staying below any lockout threshold (password spraying), by cracking password hashes recovered elsewhere in the test, or by reviewing credentials found in configuration files and scripts. Tools such as Hydra, Burp Suite Intruder and dedicated spraying tools are commonly used. Service, shared and administrative accounts are frequent offenders, because their passwords are set by hand, rarely changed and often exempt from the policy applied to ordinary users.
entries.impact: An attacker who guesses a password can sign in as that user and act with all of the user's access: reading and changing their data, using any function available to them and, where the account is privileged or its password is reused on other systems, extending access further. Spraying a few common passwords across many accounts makes success likely wherever weak passwords are in use, and leaves little trace when each account receives only one or two attempts. The impact is greatest for administrative, service and remote access accounts, and is much reduced where multi-factor authentication is enforced, because the password alone is then not enough to sign in.
entries.remediation:
• Require the affected users to change their passwords at once, starting with privileged, service and remote access accounts, and review the accounts' recent activity for signs of misuse.
  • Screen every new password against a blocklist of common, expected and breached values, including the organisation's own name, product names and keyboard and seasonal patterns. NIST SP 800-63B requires this check, and services such as the Pwned Passwords range API allow it without sending the password or its full hash.
  • Enforce a minimum length rather than composition rules: NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets 15 characters for passwords used as the only factor and 8 characters for passwords used with a second factor, and recommends allowing at least 64 characters so that passphrases can be used.
  • Enforce multi-factor authentication, which removes most of the value of a guessed password.
  • Replace passwords on service accounts with long random values held in a secrets manager, or with managed identities or keys where the platform supports them.
  • Rate limit login attempts and monitor for password spraying, where many accounts each receive a few attempts.

Confirm the fix by repeating the guessing attempts against the affected accounts, and by attempting to set a known weak password through the normal password change function.

entries.title: Username Enumeration
entries.summary: The application responds differently to valid and invalid usernames, letting an attacker build a list of real accounts to target.
entries.description:
The application reveals whether a username or email address belongs to an existing account through a difference in its behaviour. The difference may be explicit, such as a login error that says the user does not exist for one value and that the password is wrong for another, or a registration form that reports an address is already in use. It may also be subtle: a different HTTP status code, redirect, response length, page element or cookie, or a measurably longer response time for valid users, typically because the application only computes a password hash when the account exists.

Login, registration, forgotten password, account recovery and invitation functions, and API endpoints that look up users, are all common sources. Enumeration is identified by submitting known valid and invalid usernames to each function and comparing the full responses, including headers and timing, for example with Burp Suite Intruder and Comparer. It matters most where usernames are not already public, such as the email addresses of customers or staff, and where no rate limiting stops large lists from being tested.
entries.impact: An attacker can confirm which usernames or email addresses hold accounts, which turns password spraying, credential stuffing and targeted phishing from guesswork into focused attacks against real users. Where the accounts belong to members of the public, confirming that a person has an account may itself be a privacy concern, for example on a service whose membership is sensitive. The weakness does not grant access on its own; its impact rises where login rate limiting is weak and multi-factor authentication is absent.
entries.remediation:
• Return the same response for valid and invalid usernames in every authentication-related function: the same message, status code, redirect, headers, cookies and page structure, for example "Invalid username or password" at login and "If an account exists for this address, an email has been sent" for password recovery.
  • Make response times uniform, for example by verifying the submitted password against a dummy hash when the account does not exist, and by sending recovery emails asynchronously.
  • At registration, send a message to the address instead of reporting on screen that it is already registered, where the user experience allows.
  • Apply rate limiting, CAPTCHA or other anti-automation controls to login, registration, recovery and user lookup endpoints so that enumeration cannot be carried out at scale.
  • Avoid user lookup functions in public APIs, and require authentication and authorisation for any that are needed.

Confirm the fix by repeating the comparison of responses and timings for valid and invalid usernames in each affected function.

entries.title: No Account Lockout or Login Rate Limiting
entries.summary: The login function allows unlimited password attempts, so an attacker can guess passwords at speed without being slowed or blocked.
entries.description:
The authentication function places no effective limit on failed login attempts. Incorrect passwords for the same account are processed without the account being locked, the responses being delayed, a CAPTCHA being presented or the source being blocked, so an attacker can try large password lists against one account (brute force), a few common passwords against many accounts (password spraying), or username and password pairs leaked from other services (credential stuffing).

The finding is confirmed by sending a series of failed attempts well beyond any reasonable threshold, observing that each continues to be processed, and showing that the correct password is still accepted at the end of the sequence. Partial controls are common variants: limits enforced only per source IP address, which are evaded by rotating addresses or by a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header that the application trusts; counters that reset when the attacker signs in successfully to their own account; CAPTCHAs that are only checked by the client; and limits on the web login that do not apply to API, mobile, legacy or single sign-on endpoints checking the same password. Unlimited attempts at one-time codes, PINs and password reset codes are a closely related variant.
entries.impact: An attacker can guess passwords as fast as the server allows, which makes the compromise of any account with a weak or reused password likely. A successful guess gives the attacker the user's access to the application and its data. Large volumes of attempts can also degrade the login service for other users. The risk is lower where multi-factor authentication is enforced or passwords are long and screened against breached lists, and higher for internet-facing services and administrative accounts.
entries.remediation:
• Count failed attempts per account, not only per source address, and slow or block further attempts once a threshold is reached. Progressive delays or short temporary lockouts limit guessing while reducing the risk of attackers deliberately locking users out. NIST SP 800-63B requires verifiers to limit consecutive failed attempts on a single account to no more than 100.
  • Add defences against distributed attacks: detect many accounts failing from one source and one account failing from many sources, and present a CAPTCHA or other challenge when the pattern suggests automation.
  • Apply the same limits to every interface that checks the password, including APIs, mobile endpoints, legacy protocols and one-time code verification.
  • Do not trust client-supplied headers such as X-Forwarded-For for rate limiting unless they are set by a trusted proxy.
  • Enforce multi-factor authentication and screen passwords against breached lists, so that a guessed password is both less likely and less useful.
  • Log failed logins and lockouts, and alert on unusual volumes.

A rate limit at a web application firewall or API gateway can be applied as an interim measure. Confirm the fix by repeating the sequence of failed attempts and confirming that further attempts are delayed or refused.

entries.title: Weak Password Policy
entries.summary: The application lets users choose short, common or breached passwords, which makes accounts easier to guess online or crack offline.
entries.description:
The password policy enforced by the application allows passwords that are too short or too predictable to resist guessing. Common examples are a minimum of six or eight characters for passwords that are the only authentication factor, no check against lists of common or breached passwords, and acceptance of the username, the application's name or simple sequences as the password. Some policies rely instead on composition rules (an upper-case letter, a digit and a symbol), which users satisfy with predictable patterns such as a capitalised word followed by a year and an exclamation mark, and which do little to stop guessing.

The policy is identified by attempting to register or change a password to a range of weak values, such as a short password, a dictionary word, a well-known breached password and the username, and recording which are accepted. Related weaknesses include a low maximum length that rules out passphrases, silent truncation of long passwords, blocking paste into password fields, which discourages password managers, and forced periodic changes, which tend to produce predictable sequences. The policy may also differ between interfaces, for example between the web sign-up form and an API or administrative function that creates accounts.
entries.impact: Weak passwords permitted by the policy can be guessed online, particularly where login rate limiting is weak, and recovered quickly by offline cracking if password hashes are ever obtained. An attacker who guesses or cracks a password gains the user's access to the application and its data, and may reuse the password against other services. The policy is a root cause rather than proof that weak passwords are in use, so the practical risk depends on how many accounts actually have weak passwords and on whether multi-factor authentication is enforced.
entries.remediation:
Align the policy with NIST SP 800-63B-4 and the OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet:

  • Require at least 15 characters for passwords used as the only authentication factor, and at least 8 characters where the password is always combined with a second factor.
  • Allow at least 64 characters, all printable characters, spaces and Unicode, so that passphrases can be used, and never truncate passwords silently.
  • Check every new password against a blocklist of common, expected and breached values, including context-specific words such as the product and organisation names, and tell the user why a password was rejected.
  • Remove composition rules and periodic expiry, and require a change only when there is evidence that a password has been compromised.
  • Allow paste and password managers, and show a strength indicator to guide users.
  • Apply the same policy in every function that sets a password, including registration, password change, reset, administrative account creation and APIs.

Existing passwords can be checked against the new policy when users next sign in, and users asked to change any that fail. Confirm the fix by attempting to set the weak passwords used in testing through each function and confirming that they are rejected.

patterns: \bweak password policy\b|\bpassword policy\b.*(weak|insufficient|not enforced)|\binsufficient password (complexity|length) requirements\b

entries.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Not Enforced
entries.summary: Users can sign in with a password alone, so a stolen, guessed or reused password is enough to take over an account.
entries.description:
The application, or one of the routes into it, authenticates users with a password alone. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) may be unavailable, available but optional and largely unused, or enforced on the main web login while other routes that accept the same password, such as an API, a mobile application endpoint, a legacy protocol or an administrative interface, do not require it.

The finding is confirmed by signing in with valid credentials and observing that no second factor is requested, and by reviewing which account types and access routes MFA covers. It is useful to record whether MFA is absent for everyone, optional for users, or missing for privileged accounts and remote access, since these carry different levels of risk. Where MFA relies on codes sent by SMS or voice call, it is weaker against SIM swap and interception than authenticator applications or phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys and FIDO2 security keys, though still far stronger than a password alone.
entries.impact: Any attacker who obtains a user's password, through phishing, malware, reuse of a password leaked from another service, password spraying or guessing, can sign in as that user with nothing further to overcome. Credential stuffing and password spraying are widely automated, so without MFA every account is protected only by the strength and secrecy of its password. The impact equals the access of the compromised account and is greatest for administrators, remote access and accounts holding sensitive or financial data.
entries.remediation:
• Enforce MFA for all users, and as a priority for administrative, privileged and remote access accounts and for any account with access to sensitive data.
  • Prefer phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or FIDO2 security keys, or authenticator applications using time-based codes or push approval with number matching; treat SMS and voice codes as a fallback rather than the default.
  • Apply MFA to every route that accepts the password, including APIs, mobile and legacy endpoints, and retire protocols that cannot support it.
  • Require a second factor or re-authentication before sensitive actions such as changing the password, email address or MFA settings.
  • Provide secure enrolment and recovery, such as single-use recovery codes, so that the recovery process does not become a way around MFA.
  • Where the application supports single sign-on, delegate authentication to an identity provider that enforces MFA.

Until MFA is enforced, strengthen login rate limiting and breached-password screening, and monitor for password spraying. Confirm the fix by signing in with valid credentials through each route and confirming that a second factor is required.

entries.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Bypass
entries.summary: The second authentication factor can be skipped, guessed or defeated, so an attacker who knows a user's password can sign in without it.
entries.description:
The application asks for a second factor but does not enforce it reliably, so an attacker who knows a user's password can complete sign-in without a valid second factor. The flaw lies in how the application implements the step, not in the factor itself.

Common variants met on tests include: the session issued after the password step already grants access to authenticated pages or API endpoints, so the MFA page can simply be skipped; the outcome of the check is decided by something the client controls, such as a response value that can be changed from false to true; one-time codes that can be brute-forced because attempts are not limited, or that stay valid for long periods or can be reused; codes that are not bound to the account, so a valid code from the attacker's own account is accepted; codes returned in a response or written to logs; other sign-in routes, such as an API, mobile endpoint or remember-device token, that skip the factor; and recovery or reset functions that remove MFA after weak checks. Each is confirmed by signing in to a test account with its password and attempting the bypass, recording the requests that grant access without a valid second factor.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains a user's password, by phishing, reuse from another breach or guessing, can sign in as that user despite MFA, so the account is in practice protected by the password alone. Because MFA is usually applied to the accounts and systems the organisation considers most valuable, such as administrators, remote access and financial functions, the accounts exposed are often high-value. The organisation may also be relying on MFA as a compensating control elsewhere, so the bypass can undermine defences it believes are in place.
entries.remediation:
• Track authentication state on the server: after the password step, issue a session marked as partially authenticated that allows nothing but the MFA step, and grant access only once the server has verified the second factor. Issue a new session identifier when MFA succeeds.
  • Make the MFA decision entirely on the server, never from a client-supplied flag or response value.
  • Limit attempts at each one-time code, invalidating the challenge after a small number of failures, make codes single use and short-lived, and bind each code to the account and sign-in attempt it was issued for.
  • Enforce the same MFA requirement on every route that accepts the password, including APIs, mobile and legacy endpoints and single sign-on callbacks.
  • Protect remember-device features with signed, expiring tokens bound to the device, and require re-authentication with an existing factor before MFA can be disabled, reset or changed, notifying the user when it is.

Confirm the fix by repeating each bypass used in testing and confirming that access is granted only after a valid, unused second factor for the correct account has been presented.

entries.title: Insecure Password Reset Mechanism
entries.summary: The password reset process can be abused to take over other users' accounts, for example through guessable, reusable or misdirected reset tokens.
entries.description:
The forgotten password or account recovery process does not reliably prove that the person resetting a password controls the account's registered email address or phone number. Because a reset replaces the password without knowledge of the old one, a weakness here gives an alternative way into accounts that bypasses the password entirely.

Variants met on tests include: reset tokens or codes that are short, sequential, time-based or otherwise predictable; tokens that do not expire, remain valid after use, or remain valid after a newer token has been issued; tokens that are not bound to the account, so a token issued for the attacker's account resets another user's password when the username or user identifier in the request is changed; reset requests that accept an extra or altered email address parameter and send the token there; tokens or codes returned in the application's response; numeric codes that can be guessed because attempts are not limited; reliance on security questions whose answers can be researched; and reset links sent over unencrypted HTTP or leaked to third parties in the Referer header. Each is identified by requesting resets for test accounts, analysing the tokens issued, and replaying or modifying the reset requests.
entries.impact: An attacker can reset the password of another user's account and sign in as that user, without knowing the original password and often without any action by the victim. Where the weakness affects any account, it can be used against administrators to take full control of the application. A successful reset also locks the legitimate user out, which may delay detection. The impact is reduced where the account also requires multi-factor authentication that the reset process does not remove.
entries.remediation:
• Generate reset tokens with a cryptographically secure random number generator, long enough to make guessing impractical (for example 128 bits or more of randomness), and store only a hash of each token.
  • Bind each token to a single account on the server, ignore any username, user identifier or email address supplied alongside the token, and send reset links only to the address already registered on the account.
  • Make tokens single use and short-lived, invalidate outstanding tokens when a new one is issued or the password is changed, and end existing sessions after a reset.
  • Limit attempts to submit numeric reset codes, and rate limit reset requests per account.
  • Never return tokens or codes in responses, and serve the reset page over HTTPS with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer so that the token is not sent to third parties.
  • Do not use security questions as the sole means of recovery, and require the existing second factor or a recovery code where the account has MFA.
  • Notify the user when a reset is requested and when it is completed.

Confirm the fix by repeating the reset tests, including replaying used and expired tokens and changing the account identifiers in reset requests.

entries.title: Password Reset Link Poisoning
entries.summary: Password reset emails build their link from the request's Host header, so an attacker can make a victim's genuine reset email point to a server they control.
entries.description:
The application builds the absolute URL in password reset emails from information in the reset request itself, usually the HTTP Host header or a forwarding header such as X-Forwarded-Host, instead of from a fixed, configured address. An attacker can request a password reset for a victim's account while supplying their own domain in that header. The application then sends the victim a genuine reset email, from its own mail system, whose link points to the attacker's server and carries the victim's valid reset token.

The weakness is confirmed by requesting a reset for a test account with a modified Host, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host or Forwarded header, or with a duplicated Host header or an absolute URL in the request line, and inspecting the link in the email received. An external interaction server, such as Burp Collaborator, shows whether the token is delivered when the link is followed. The usual cause is a framework or reverse proxy that passes client-supplied host values to the application unchecked, or an application that trusts forwarding headers from any source. The same poisoning can affect other emails that contain links, such as account verification and invitation messages.
entries.impact: When the victim clicks the link in what is a genuine email from the application, or when an email security product follows the link automatically to scan it, the reset token is sent to the attacker's server. The attacker can then use it to set a new password and take over the account. The attack can target any user whose email address or username is known, including administrators. It relies on the link being followed before the token expires, so short token lifetimes limit the exposure.
entries.remediation:
• Build links in emails from a fixed base URL held in the application's configuration, never from the Host header or any forwarding header in the request.
  • Configure the framework's list of allowed host names so that requests with unexpected Host values are rejected, for example ALLOWED_HOSTS in Django or AllowedHosts in ASP.NET Core, and in nginx make the default server block, which receives requests for unknown host names, refuse them rather than passing them to the application.
  • Accept X-Forwarded-Host and similar headers only from trusted reverse proxies, and have the proxy overwrite them rather than pass on values supplied by the client.
  • Keep reset tokens single use and short-lived, so that any token that does leak is useful for as little time as possible.

Confirm the fix by repeating the reset request with each modified host header and confirming that the emailed link always points to the application's own domain.

entries.title: Credentials Transmitted Over an Unencrypted Channel
entries.summary: Usernames, passwords or authentication tokens are sent without encryption, so anyone able to observe the traffic can capture them.
entries.description:
The application sends authentication credentials across the network without transport encryption. Typical cases are a login form served or submitted over plain HTTP; HTTP Basic authentication over HTTP; an API that accepts passwords, API keys or bearer tokens over HTTP; and a login page delivered over HTTP that posts to an HTTPS address, which still lets an attacker who can modify the page send the submission elsewhere. Thick clients, mobile applications and integrations that send credentials over unencrypted protocols have the same weakness.

The finding is confirmed by intercepting the authentication exchange, with an intercepting proxy or a packet capture, and showing the credentials or token in readable form, or by showing that an HTTPS login endpoint also accepts submissions over HTTP. HTTP Basic authentication only encodes the username and password with base64, which offers no protection. Scanners commonly report the issue as cleartext submission of a password, or as a password field served or submitted over HTTP.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe the network path between users and the application, for example on shared or public Wi-Fi, through a compromised network device or from within an internal network, can capture credentials and session tokens as users sign in, and reuse them to access their accounts. Captured passwords may also work on other systems where users have reused them. An attacker able to modify traffic can also alter the login page to send credentials elsewhere. The attack requires a position on the network path, which limits it to attackers on the same network or with access to intermediate infrastructure.
entries.remediation:
• Serve the login page, the credential submission and all authenticated pages and API endpoints over HTTPS only, using TLS 1.2 or 1.3.
  • Redirect plain HTTP requests to HTTPS before any credentials are entered, and stop accepting credentials or tokens on HTTP endpoints altogether, so that a mistaken HTTP request fails rather than succeeding in clear text.
  • Send the Strict-Transport-Security header so that browsers use HTTPS for every later request, and consider HSTS preloading for public sites.
  • Set the Secure attribute on session cookies so that they are never sent over HTTP.
  • Replace unencrypted protocols used by clients and integrations with their encrypted equivalents, and enforce encryption on the server rather than leaving it optional.
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

Users whose credentials may have been exposed should be asked to change their passwords. Confirm the fix by attempting to sign in and to call authenticated endpoints over plain HTTP, and confirming that no credentials are accepted or sent unencrypted.

patterns: \b(credentials|password|passwords|login|authentication) (sent|transmitted|submitted|sent in clear|over) (over |via |in )?(HTTP|an unencrypted|clear ?text|plain ?text|unencrypted)|\bcleartext (submission|transmission) of (password|credentials)|\bbasic authentication over (HTTP|an unencrypted)|\bunencrypted (login|authentication) (form|page)

entries.title: Authentication Bypass
entries.summary: Protected functions or data can be reached without valid credentials, because the authentication check can be skipped or deceived.
entries.description:
The application requires users to sign in, but an attacker can reach authenticated functions or data without valid credentials because the authentication check can be avoided or deceived. Unlike content that was simply left unprotected, the application does implement authentication; the flaw is that it is not enforced on every path, or that its decision can be influenced by the client.

Variants met on tests include: pages or routes protected only by a redirect to the login page, where the protected content is still returned in the body of the redirect response; access checks applied to some forms of a path but not others, bypassed with altered case, a trailing slash, path parameters such as ;, encoded characters or an alternative route to the same handler; sign-in logic that trusts a client-controlled value, such as a cookie or parameter named loggedIn, role or admin; client-side authentication, where a browser or mobile application decides whether sign-in succeeded and the server does not check again; comparisons that succeed without the correct password through type juggling or empty or null values; and headers such as X-Original-URL or X-Forwarded-For trusted to rewrite the path that is checked or to grant access to apparently internal addresses. Each is confirmed by obtaining authenticated content, or performing an authenticated action, from a session that never presented valid credentials.
entries.impact: An attacker can use protected functions and read or change data without an account, often with the privileges of an authenticated user or administrator. Depending on what lies behind the authentication, this can expose all of the application's data, allow changes to its configuration and users, and provide a starting point for further attacks on the hosting environment. No credentials, user interaction or prior access are needed, and once found the bypass is usually simple to automate.
entries.remediation:
• Enforce authentication on the server for every request to protected content and functions, in one central mechanism such as framework middleware, filters or an API gateway policy, denying by default so that new routes are protected unless explicitly made public.
  • When a request is not authenticated, stop processing and return an error or redirect without the protected content; do not rely on the browser following a redirect.
  • Base authentication decisions only on a server-side session or a properly verified token, never on cookies, parameters or headers whose values the client controls.
  • Normalise the request path once, before both routing and access checks, and make sure that any proxy or gateway and the application interpret paths in the same way.
  • Ignore headers such as X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL and X-Forwarded-For unless they are set by a trusted proxy, and do not grant access based on source address alone.
  • Use strict comparisons in authentication code and reject empty or missing credentials explicitly.

Add automated tests that request each protected route without a session and expect it to be refused. Confirm the fix by repeating each bypass technique used in testing.

entries.title: Session Fixation
entries.summary: The application keeps the same session identifier after login, so an attacker who plants an identifier in a victim's browser can use the session once they sign in.
entries.description:
The application does not issue a new session identifier when a user authenticates. The identifier the browser held before sign-in, which may have been chosen or obtained by an attacker, becomes an authenticated session once the user signs in. An attacker who can place a known identifier in the victim's browser can then use the same identifier to act as the victim.

Fixation is confirmed by noting the session identifier before sign-in, signing in, and observing that the same identifier remains valid and is now authenticated. Exploitation also needs a way to set the identifier in the victim's browser. Common routes are applications that accept a session identifier from a URL parameter or path, through URL rewriting; applications that accept any identifier the client presents and create a session for it (permissive session management); cookie injection from a vulnerable or attacker-controlled subdomain sharing the parent domain; and script injection or response splitting elsewhere in the application. The same weakness applies when the identifier is not renewed on other privilege changes, such as completing a second authentication factor or switching to an administrative role.
entries.impact: An attacker who succeeds in fixing a victim's session identifier gains the victim's authenticated session, with all of the victim's privileges, as soon as the victim signs in, without needing their password. The attack requires the victim to sign in after the identifier has been planted, and requires a separate means of planting it, which limits how widely it can be used; where the application accepts session identifiers in URLs, a crafted link is enough.
entries.remediation:
• Generate a new session identifier immediately after successful authentication and destroy the pre-authentication session on the server, for example with session_regenerate_id(true) in PHP, HttpServletRequest.changeSessionId() in Java servlets, or the session fixation protection built into frameworks such as Spring Security.
  • Renew the identifier on every other privilege change, including completion of multi-factor authentication and elevation to an administrative role.
  • Accept session identifiers only from cookies, never from URL parameters or the request path, and disable URL rewriting in the application server.
  • Accept only identifiers that the application itself has issued (strict session management), and reject unknown values.
  • Set session cookies with the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes and without a broad Domain attribute, or use the __Host- name prefix so that subdomains cannot set them.

Confirm the fix by recording the session identifier before sign-in and confirming that it is replaced, and the old value rejected, after authentication.

entries.title: Session Not Invalidated on Logout
entries.summary: Logging out does not end the session on the server, so a session token captured earlier keeps working after the user has logged out.
entries.description:
When a user logs out, the application clears or replaces the session cookie in the browser but does not invalidate the session on the server. The old session identifier or token therefore stays valid until it expires naturally, and any copy of it can still be used to access the account. The same pattern is common with stateless tokens such as JSON Web Tokens, where logging out only deletes the token from browser storage and the server has no way to reject it before its expiry time.

The finding is confirmed by capturing an authenticated request, logging out through the application, and replaying the request with the original session cookie or token; if authenticated content is still returned, the session was not invalidated. Related variants include sessions that survive a password change or the disabling of the account, refresh tokens that remain usable after logout, and single sign-on logouts that end the identity provider's session but leave the application's own session active, or the reverse.
entries.impact: A session token obtained by other means, for example from a shared or public computer, browser history, proxy or server logs, or through script injection, remains usable after the user has logged out believing their session is closed, and the attacker can continue to access the account through it until it expires. The weakness does not expose tokens itself; it extends the window in which a token captured through another weakness or through physical access remains useful, so its impact depends heavily on how long sessions last.
entries.remediation:
• Invalidate the session on the server when the user logs out, for example with HttpSession.invalidate() in Java, session_destroy() in PHP or the framework's equivalent, so that the old identifier is rejected on any later request.
  • Clear the session cookie in the logout response by setting an empty value with an expiry date in the past, and consider sending Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "cookies", "storage" to remove other data held by the browser.
  • For token-based authentication, keep access tokens short-lived and revoke the refresh token at logout; where immediate revocation is needed, check tokens against a server-side denylist or use opaque tokens that can be deleted.
  • End all of a user's sessions when their password is changed or reset or their account is disabled, and give users a way to log out of their other sessions.
  • Where single sign-on is used, implement the logout protocol of the identity provider so that logging out ends both the application and identity provider sessions as intended.

Confirm the fix by replaying a request with a session token captured before logout and confirming that it is rejected.

entries.title: Excessive Session Timeout
entries.summary: Sessions stay valid through long periods of inactivity or without any overall limit, extending the time a stolen or unattended session can be used.
entries.description:
The application keeps authenticated sessions alive for longer than its risk justifies. Two limits are usually assessed: the idle timeout, after which a session with no activity should end, and the absolute timeout, after which a session should end regardless of activity. Findings range from idle timeouts of many hours or days, through sessions that never expire on the server, to persistent cookies or tokens that keep the user signed in indefinitely without any deliberate choice to stay signed in.

The timeouts are measured by leaving an authenticated session idle for a set period and then making a request, and by keeping a session active over a long period. Server-side behaviour matters more than the cookie's own expiry date, since a server that never expires the session will accept a replayed cookie. As a guide, the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet gives common idle timeouts of 2 to 5 minutes for high-value applications and 15 to 30 minutes for lower-risk ones, and an absolute timeout of 4 to 8 hours for an application used through a working day. Client-side timers that only hide the page, while the server-side session remains valid, are a common variant.
entries.impact: A long-lived session increases the time during which an unattended, signed-in device can be used by someone else, and during which a session token captured through another weakness, such as script injection, a leaked log or a shared computer, remains usable. The weakness does not expose sessions itself, so its impact depends on the sensitivity of the application and how likely sessions are to be exposed; it matters most for administrative and financial functions and for use on shared devices.
entries.remediation:
• Enforce an idle timeout and an absolute timeout on the server, set according to the sensitivity of the application, and invalidate the session when either is reached.
  • Configure the timeouts in the platform's session settings, for example <session-timeout> in a Java web.xml (in minutes), ExpireTimeSpan and SlidingExpiration in ASP.NET Core cookie authentication options, or SESSION_COOKIE_AGE in Django (in seconds), and add an absolute limit in application code where the platform does not provide one.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived, and limit the lifetime of refresh tokens, rotating them on use.
  • Offer persistent sign-in only as a deliberate choice by the user, backed by a separate revocable token, and not for administrative accounts.
  • Warn users before the session expires, so that a shorter timeout does not cause lost work, and require re-authentication for sensitive actions whatever the age of the session.

Confirm the fix by leaving a session idle beyond the configured limit, and by keeping a session active beyond the absolute limit, and confirming that the server rejects each.

entries.title: Concurrent Sessions Permitted
entries.summary: The same account can hold several active sessions at once without the user being told, which can hide an attacker using a compromised account.
entries.description:
The application allows an account to be signed in from several browsers, devices or locations at the same time without limiting the number of sessions, notifying the user of new sign-ins, or giving the user a way to see and end their other sessions. Many applications allow concurrent sessions by design, and doing so is not a vulnerability in itself; the weakness lies in the lack of visibility and control over them.

The behaviour is confirmed by signing in to the same account from two separate browsers, confirming that both sessions remain usable, and checking that neither the interface nor any notification tells the user that another session exists. Related observations include new sign-ins that do not end older sessions where the application intends to allow only one, and password changes that leave other sessions active.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. Where an account has been compromised by other means, an attacker can use it in parallel with the legitimate user without either session being ended, and the user has no way to notice or end the attacker's session. Visibility and control of active sessions is a hardening measure that helps users and administrators detect and respond to account compromise.
entries.remediation:
• Decide, as a design choice based on the application's risk, whether multiple sessions per account are allowed; where they are not, end the previous session or ask the user which session to keep when a new sign-in occurs.
  • Show users their active sessions with useful details (device, browser, approximate location and sign-in time), and let them end any or all of them.
  • Notify users of sign-ins from new devices or locations, by email or within the application.
  • End all other sessions when a user changes or resets their password, enables multi-factor authentication or reports suspicious activity.
  • Log session creation and termination so that concurrent use from unusual locations can be detected and investigated.

Confirm the change by signing in from two browsers and checking that the chosen policy is enforced and that the user can see and end the other session.

entries.title: Session Token in URL
entries.summary: Session identifiers or authentication tokens are placed in URLs, where they leak into logs, browser history and Referer headers.
entries.description:
The application passes the session identifier or another authentication token in the URL: as a query string parameter, as a path parameter such as ;jsessionid= added by URL rewriting, or within links generated for the user. URLs are not treated as secret. They are recorded in browser history and bookmarks, and in web server, proxy, load balancer and analytics logs, and are sent to other sites in the Referer header when a page loads external resources or the user follows a link. Users also share URLs by copying them into emails and chat messages.

The finding is identified by reviewing authenticated traffic for tokens in request URLs and in links within responses, and by checking whether a session identifier supplied in the URL is accepted in place of the cookie. Scanners commonly report it as a session token in the URL or as cross-domain Referer leakage. Variants include single sign-on and emailed sign-in links that leave a long-lived token in the address bar, access tokens added to WebSocket or file download URLs, and applications that fall back to URL-based sessions when cookies are disabled.
entries.impact: Anyone with access to a place where the URL has been recorded, such as a proxy or server log, an analytics platform, a third-party site that receives the Referer header, or a shared computer's history, can obtain a valid token and take over the user's session while it remains active. Tokens in URLs also make session fixation easier, because a crafted link can carry an identifier chosen by the attacker. The risk depends on how long tokens stay valid and how widely URLs are logged or shared.
entries.remediation:
• Carry session identifiers only in cookies with the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes, or for APIs in the Authorization header, and never in URLs.
  • Disable URL rewriting in the application server, for example by setting <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode> in the session configuration of a Java web.xml, and reject session identifiers supplied in URLs.
  • Where a token must appear in a URL, such as a one-time sign-in link or a download link, make it single use and short-lived, exchange it immediately for a session cookie, and redirect to a URL without it.
  • Set a Referrer-Policy of no-referrer or strict-origin-when-cross-origin to limit what is sent to other sites.
  • Invalidate sessions whose tokens may already have been logged, and remove tokens from existing logs where practical.

Confirm the fix by reviewing authenticated traffic and generated links for tokens, and by confirming that a session identifier supplied in the URL is not accepted.

entries.title: Predictable Session Identifiers
entries.summary: Session identifiers are generated in a way that lets an attacker predict or guess values issued to other users, and so take over their sessions.
entries.description:
The application issues session identifiers that are not generated from a cryptographically secure source of randomness, so values issued to other users can be predicted, or narrowed down to a small set that can be tried in turn. Common causes are identifiers built from a counter, a timestamp, the username or user ID, or a hash of such values, and identifiers produced by a general-purpose random number generator (such as java.util.Random in Java, Math.random() in JavaScript or mt_rand() in PHP) whose output can be predicted from values already seen.
