Identifiers that are too short are a related form: even when random, the range of possible values is small enough to search.

The weakness is usually found in custom session or token schemes rather than in the session management built into mature frameworks. It can be identified by collecting a large sample of identifiers, for example with the Sequencer tool in Burp Suite, and analysing them for low entropy, shared prefixes, sequences or a relationship to the time of issue. Decoding identifiers that look encoded (Base64 or hexadecimal) often reveals the values they were built from. Logging in repeatedly in quick succession, and as different users, and comparing the identifiers issued is a quick manual check.
entries.impact: An attacker who can predict a valid identifier can take over another user's session without knowing their password or interacting with them, and act with that user's privileges for as long as the session remains valid. Where identifiers follow a simple sequence or are derived from known values, every active session can be hijacked, including those of administrators. Where only part of the identifier is predictable, the attacker must make many guesses, which is slower and more likely to be noticed, but remains practical where requests are not rate limited. Short session lifetimes narrow the window but do not remove the risk.
entries.remediation:
Replace the identifier generation with a cryptographically secure source:

  • Use the session management built into the application framework or platform (for example the servlet container's sessions in Java, ASP.NET Core's authentication cookies, or express-session in Node.js) rather than a custom scheme, and keep it up to date.
  • Where a custom identifier or token is unavoidable, generate at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure random number generator, such as SecureRandom in Java, the secrets module in Python, crypto.randomBytes() in Node.js, random_bytes() in PHP or RandomNumberGenerator in .NET, and encode it as hexadecimal or Base64url.
  • Do not derive identifiers from usernames, user IDs, timestamps, counters or hashes of them, and do not give the value any meaning.
  • Issue a new identifier at login and at any change of privilege, and invalidate identifiers at logout and after a period of inactivity.

As an interim measure, rate limiting and alerting on requests that present invalid session identifiers make guessing slower and more visible. Confirm the fix by repeating the statistical analysis on a fresh sample of identifiers and checking that no pattern, and no relationship to the user or the time of issue, remains.

entries.title: Insecure Persistent Login Token
entries.summary: The 'remember me' cookie that keeps users signed in is built from guessable or recoverable values, lasts too long or is never revoked, so a stolen or forged token gives lasting access.
entries.description:
The application offers a 'remember me' or 'keep me signed in' option that sets a long-lived cookie, which signs the user back in without a password once the normal session has ended. While it is valid, the cookie is as powerful as the password, so it needs the same care. It is insecure when one or more of the following applies:

  • it contains the username and password, or a hash of the password, in encoded or reversibly encrypted form, so it can be decoded or cracked offline to recover the password;
  • it is built from values an attacker can know or guess, such as the username, user ID or a timestamp, or a hash of them, so a valid token can be forged for another user;
  • it remains valid for months or indefinitely, is not invalidated at logout or password change, and can be used again and again;
  • it is stored on the server in plain text, so anyone who can read the database can sign in as any user who chose the option.

The weakness can be identified by decoding the cookie and comparing tokens issued to different accounts and at different times, by checking whether the same token can be used repeatedly, and by testing whether it still signs the user in after logout and after a password change.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains a user's persistent token, for example through cross-site scripting, malware, a shared or unattended computer or a copy of the server's database, can sign in as that user and keep doing so long after the original session has ended, even after the user logs out or changes their password. Where the token contains the password or its hash, the attacker can also recover the password, which may be reused on other services. Where the token can be forged from known values, the attacker can sign in as any user, including administrators, without stealing anything first, which would make the issue high or critical.
entries.remediation:
Rebuild the persistent login mechanism so that the token is random, stored safely and revocable:

  • Generate the token from at least 128 bits of a cryptographically secure random number generator. A common design issues two random values, a selector used to look up the record and a validator that is compared with a hash stored on the server, so a copy of the database does not yield usable tokens.
  • Never place the password, a password hash or other user data in the cookie.
  • Give each token a fixed expiry, replace it with a new token each time it is used, and delete all of a user's tokens when they log out of all devices, change or reset their password, or the account is disabled.
  • Set the cookie with the Secure and HttpOnly attributes and a suitable SameSite value.
  • Ask for the password again before sensitive actions, such as changing the email address, password or multi-factor settings, in a session restored from the token.
  • Let users see and revoke the devices on which they are remembered.

As an interim measure, shorten the token lifetime and invalidate all existing persistent tokens so that users sign in again. Confirm the fix by checking that tokens are random and unrelated across accounts, that a token is rejected once it has been used and replaced, and that tokens stop working after logout and password change.

entries.title: JWT Signature Not Verified
entries.summary: The application accepts JSON Web Tokens without checking their signature, so anyone can change the claims in a token, such as the user ID or role, and the change is trusted.
entries.description:
A JSON Web Token (JWT) carries claims, such as the user's identity, their role and the token's expiry, in a payload that is only Base64url encoded. Its integrity depends entirely on the signature, which the server must check against a trusted key before any claim is used. The application decodes and trusts the token's claims without verifying that signature, so a token whose payload has been altered is still accepted.

The usual cause is code that calls a library's decode function rather than its verify function (for example jwt.decode() in the Node.js jsonwebtoken package, which does not check the signature, or PyJWT's decode() with signature verification switched off), a verification step that is skipped for some routes or token types, or a check that runs only when a signature is present. API gateways and internal services that assume another component has already verified the token are a frequent source.

The weakness can be confirmed by changing a claim in a valid token, such as the subject or role, while leaving the original signature in place, or by removing the signature altogether, and observing that the modified token is accepted. Tools such as jwt_tool and the JWT Editor extension for Burp Suite automate these checks. Acceptance of tokens whose header names the none algorithm is a closely related fault, described in the separate finding on JWT algorithm confusion.
entries.impact: An attacker can create or modify tokens to claim any identity or privilege the application recognises, for example by changing the user identifier to impersonate another user, or by setting a role claim to administrator. No credentials are needed beyond, at most, one token from which to copy the format. This normally gives access to every account and function protected by the token, including administrative functions, and in a microservice architecture it may extend to every service that relies on the same unverified token.
entries.remediation:
Verify every token's signature before using any of its claims:

  • Use the library's verification function, never a decode-only function, wherever a token is received, and treat any verification failure as an authentication failure.
  • Configure verification explicitly: the expected key, the list of accepted algorithms, and the expected issuer (iss) and audience (aud). Check the expiry (exp) and not-before (nbf) times.
  • Reject tokens with no signature, tokens using the none algorithm, and tokens signed with any algorithm or key other than the one configured.
  • Verify in shared middleware or at the API gateway, and also in each service that makes decisions on the claims, rather than relying on another component having done it.
// Node.js (jsonwebtoken) const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer: expectedIssuer, audience: expectedAudience }); # Python (PyJWT) claims = jwt.decode(token, public_key, algorithms=['RS256'], issuer=expected_issuer, audience=expected_audience)

If forged tokens may already have been used, rotate the signing keys and review logs for tokens with unexpected claims. Confirm the fix by repeating the tests with modified, unsigned and re-signed tokens and checking that each is rejected.

entries.title: JWT Signed With a Weak Secret
entries.summary: JSON Web Tokens are signed with an HMAC secret that is short or guessable, so it can be recovered offline from any valid token and used to forge new ones.
entries.description:
Tokens signed with the HMAC algorithms (HS256, HS384 or HS512) are protected by a shared secret: anyone who knows it can create tokens the application will accept. The application uses a secret that is short, a dictionary word, a value copied from documentation or sample code, or a default shipped with a framework or product, rather than a long random key.

Because every token contains both the signed data and its signature, the secret can be attacked offline. An attacker with a single valid token can try candidate secrets at very high speed without sending any request to the application, so lockout and monitoring do not come into play. Tools such as hashcat and jwt_tool, used with wordlists of common and published JWT secrets, recover weak secrets quickly.

The weakness is identified by taking a token issued to a test account, confirming from its header that an HMAC algorithm is used, and running such a cracking attempt against it. Recovery of the secret proves the issue, and it can be demonstrated by signing a modified token with the recovered secret and observing that the application accepts it. The same secret is sometimes also found in source code, configuration files or container images, which is a separate exposure with the same result.
entries.impact: An attacker who recovers the secret can sign tokens with any claims, so they can impersonate any user, raise their own role to administrator and extend token lifetimes at will, with the same effect as having no signature check at all. Forged tokens are indistinguishable from genuine ones, which makes the abuse hard to detect. Where the same secret is shared by several applications or environments, all of them are affected. The attacker needs one valid token, which normally means holding an ordinary account or seeing a token issued to someone else.
entries.remediation:
Replace the secret and manage it as a cryptographic key:

  • Generate a new secret with a cryptographically secure random number generator, at least as long as the hash output of the algorithm (256 bits for HS256, as RFC 7518 requires), for example with openssl rand -base64 32 or longer.
  • Keep the secret out of source code and images: load it from a secrets manager or key vault, use a different secret for each environment and application, and restrict who can read it.
  • Where tokens are verified by more than one service, or by parties that should not be able to issue tokens, move to an asymmetric algorithm such as RS256, PS256 or ES256, so that verifiers hold only the public key.
  • Plan for rotation by supporting more than one active key, identified by the kid header, so the key can be changed without disruption.

Replacing the secret invalidates every existing token, so plan for users to sign in again, and do not keep accepting the old secret. If forged tokens may already have been used, review logs for unexpected claims or privilege changes. Confirm the fix by repeating the cracking attempt against a newly issued token with the same wordlists and checking that the secret is not recovered.

entries.title: JWT Algorithm Confusion
entries.summary: The application lets a token's own header choose how it is verified, so an attacker can sign tokens using the public key as an HMAC secret, or send them with no signature.
entries.description:
Each JSON Web Token names its signing algorithm in the alg field of its header. The application, or the library it uses, takes that field at face value when verifying the token instead of enforcing the algorithm its key is meant for. Two forms are common:

  • Key confusion: the application expects tokens signed with an asymmetric algorithm such as RS256 and verifies them with its public key. If an attacker changes the header to HS256, a vulnerable verifier uses that public key as an HMAC secret. The public key is often published at a JWKS endpoint, and can otherwise be recovered from two signed tokens, so the attacker can sign tokens that pass the check.
  • Unsigned tokens: the verifier accepts the none algorithm, which is defined for unsecured tokens, and so accepts a token with an empty signature. Some filters block only the lower-case value, so variants such as None or NONE succeed.

The same root cause, trusting the token to say how it should be verified, appears in the header parameters that select the key: a jwk header carrying the attacker's own public key, a jku or x5u address pointing to a key set the attacker hosts, or a kid value used unsafely in a file path or database query. The weakness is confirmed by forging a token by each of these routes and observing that it is accepted. Tools such as jwt_tool and the JWT Editor extension for Burp Suite support these tests.
entries.impact: An attacker can forge tokens with any claims and have them accepted, so they can impersonate any user, including administrators, without credentials. Key confusion needs only the public key, which is usually available to anyone, and the unsigned and injected key forms need nothing at all. The result is normally a complete bypass of the authentication the tokens provide, across every service that shares the vulnerable verification. Where kid is used in a file path or query, the attacker may also be able to read files or inject into the database.
entries.remediation:
Decide the algorithm and key on the server, never from the token:

  • Configure each verifier with an explicit allowlist containing only the expected algorithm, for example algorithms: ['RS256'] in the Node.js jsonwebtoken package or algorithms=['RS256'] in PyJWT, and bind each key to a single algorithm.
  • Reject none in any capitalisation, and any token whose algorithm does not match the key it is checked with.
  • Ignore the jwk, jku, x5u and x5c header parameters unless they are needed; where they are, accept only keys from a trusted, preconfigured key set or allowlisted addresses.
  • Use kid only to look up a key in a fixed set held by the server, never as a file path or in a query.
  • Keep the JWT library up to date, as several libraries have corrected defects in algorithm handling, and follow the JSON Web Token Best Current Practices (RFC 8725).

If forged tokens may already have been accepted, rotate the signing keys and review logs for tokens with unexpected headers or claims. Confirm the fix by repeating the key confusion, unsigned token and header injection tests and checking that every forged token is rejected.

entries.title: JWT Without Expiry or With an Excessive Lifetime
entries.summary: JSON Web Tokens have no expiry or stay valid for a long time and cannot be revoked, so a stolen token remains usable for days, months or indefinitely.
entries.description:
A JSON Web Token is normally accepted on the strength of its signature and claims alone, without a lookup on the server, so it remains valid until the time in its exp (expiry) claim. The application issues tokens with no exp claim, or with an expiry days, months or years after issue, or verifies tokens without enforcing the expiry. Because most implementations keep no record of the tokens they have issued, logging out, changing the password or disabling the account does not stop an issued token from working.

The weakness is identified by decoding a token and reading its iat (issued at) and exp claims, and by testing whether the token is still accepted after its stated expiry, after the user logs out and after the password is changed. Long lifetimes are often chosen to avoid building a refresh mechanism, and are common in mobile applications and in single-page applications that keep the token in browser storage.
entries.impact: The weakness does not expose tokens by itself, but it greatly lengthens the time for which a stolen token can be used. A token taken through cross-site scripting, from browser storage on a shared or compromised device, from logs or from a leaked request remains usable long after the theft, and the user cannot end the attacker's access by logging out or changing their password. The impact therefore depends on how easily tokens could be obtained and what the account can do, and is greater for administrative accounts and for tokens accepted by several services.
entries.remediation:
Keep access tokens short-lived and provide a way to end sessions:

  • Include an exp claim in every token, keep access token lifetimes short (minutes rather than hours or days), and require and enforce exp on verification, rejecting tokens without one. Allow only a small clock skew.
  • Keep users signed in with refresh tokens rather than long-lived access tokens. Hold refresh tokens on the server or in an HttpOnly cookie, replace them each time they are used, and give them an absolute maximum lifetime.
  • Provide revocation: invalidate refresh tokens at logout, password change, account disablement and on request, and where access tokens must stop working at once, check a denylist of revoked token identifiers (jti) or a per-user token version on each request.
  • Where the application needs server-side control over every request, consider opaque session identifiers or reference tokens instead of self-contained JWTs.

Confirm the fix by checking that new tokens carry a short expiry, that expired and revoked tokens are rejected, and that logging out and changing the password end access through existing refresh tokens.

entries.title: Sensitive Data in JWT Payload
entries.summary: JSON Web Tokens carry personal data, internal details or secrets in their payload, which is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone who sees a token can read them.
entries.description:
The payload of a signed JSON Web Token (a JWS, the usual form) is Base64url encoded, not encrypted. The signature protects it from being changed, but anyone who holds or sees the token can decode and read it without any key. The application places information in the payload that should not be readable by everyone who may see the token, such as personal data (full name, date of birth, address, telephone number or national identifiers), internal identifiers, database or infrastructure details, permissions beyond what the client needs to know, or secrets such as passwords, password hashes and API keys.

Tokens travel further than their owner: they are kept in browser storage, sent to every service that accepts them, and can appear in logs, monitoring tools and error reports, and, where they are placed in URLs, in browser history and Referer headers. The weakness is identified by decoding tokens issued to test accounts, with any Base64url decoder or a tool such as jwt_tool, and reviewing every claim for information that would be sensitive if read by a third party.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains a token, including through logs, intermediaries or a compromised client device, can read the information in it without breaking any protection. Personal data exposed in this way may need to be handled as a data protection matter, and internal details help an attacker plan further attacks. A user reading their own token mostly sees their own data, so the impact depends on what the claims contain and how widely tokens are copied and logged. Secrets such as API keys or passwords in a token give direct access to other systems and would raise the severity.
entries.remediation:
Keep tokens to the minimum their recipients need:

  • Limit claims to what the receiving services need to make their decisions, typically an opaque user identifier, the issuer, audience and expiry, and the scopes or roles required. Retrieve personal and other sensitive details from the server when they are needed instead of carrying them in the token.
  • Never place passwords, password hashes, API keys, connection strings or other secrets in a token.
  • Where sensitive claims must travel with the token, encrypt it as a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) token, or give the client an opaque reference token that the API exchanges internally for the full token.
  • Avoid placing tokens in URLs, and keep them out of logs by masking the Authorization header and token parameters in application, proxy and monitoring logs.

Rotate any secret that has appeared in a token, and treat tokens already issued as exposed until they expire. Confirm the fix by decoding newly issued tokens and checking that only the intended claims are present.

entries.title: OAuth Redirect URI Not Validated
entries.summary: The OAuth or OpenID Connect authorisation server does not strictly check the redirect URI, so a crafted link can send a user's authorisation code or token to an attacker.
entries.description:
In OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, the authorisation server returns the user to the client application with an authorisation code or token at the address given in the redirect_uri parameter. The server must compare that address with the values registered for the client and refuse anything else. The authorisation server accepts addresses that were not registered, or checks them loosely, so an attacker can craft an authorisation link that delivers the result of the user's sign-in to a location the attacker controls or can read.

Common forms are: no validation at all; matching only the start of the address, so extra path segments, path traversal sequences or a different port are accepted; matching only the domain or a wildcard subdomain, so any page or subdomain qualifies, including one with an open redirect or content an attacker can place; and parsing differences, where the server and the browser interpret an unusual address (with embedded credentials, encoded characters or a second redirect_uri parameter) differently.

The weakness is identified by changing redirect_uri in an authorisation request to each of these variants, including an external domain, and observing whether the server redirects to it with a code or token. The same test applies to a custom-built authorisation server and to an identity platform configured with wildcard or overly broad redirect addresses.
entries.impact: A user who follows the attacker's link while signed in to the authorisation server, or who signs in when prompted, has their code or token sent to the attacker. Where an access token is returned directly, as in the implicit flow, the attacker can use it at once to reach the user's data within the granted scopes. Where an authorisation code is leaked, the attacker can often use it to sign in to the client application as the user, particularly where the token endpoint does not check that the redirect URI matches the one in the original request. The usual result is takeover of the user's account in the client application, and users who have already consented to the client may see nothing unusual.
entries.remediation:
Enforce exact matching of redirect addresses at the authorisation server:

  • Register the complete redirect URI for each client and compare the value in each request with the registered values by exact string comparison, as the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice requires. Do not use prefix, domain, wildcard or pattern matching. The only accepted exception is the port number of a loopback address used by native applications.
  • Reject a request with a missing, unregistered or repeated redirect_uri parameter by showing an error at the authorisation server, without redirecting.
  • At the token endpoint, check that the redirect URI sent with the code is identical to the one used in the authorisation request.
  • In identity platforms such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0 or Keycloak, review each application's registered redirect URIs, remove wildcards, unused entries and development addresses such as localhost from production clients, and register only HTTPS addresses for web clients.
  • Use the authorisation code flow with PKCE, and remove open redirects from the client's domains, so that a leaked code or a redirect chain is of less use.

Confirm the fix by repeating the modified redirect_uri tests and checking that every variant is refused without a redirect.

entries.title: OAuth Flow Without a State Parameter
entries.summary: The OAuth client does not bind the sign-in response to the user's browser with a state value, so an attacker can make a victim complete a sign-in or account link of the attacker's choosing.
entries.description:
When a client application sends a user to an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect authorisation server, it should include a state parameter holding an unguessable value tied to the user's session, and check on the user's return that the same value comes back before it accepts the authorisation code. This binds the response to the browser that started the flow. The client omits the parameter, uses a fixed or predictable value, or does not check it on return, and no other protection takes its place (PKCE, or in OpenID Connect a checked nonce, also prevents the attack when properly enforced).

Without that binding, the client's redirect endpoint is open to cross-site request forgery. An attacker starts a sign-in with their own account at the identity provider, stops before their authorisation code is used, and then makes the victim's browser load the client's redirect address with the attacker's code, for example through a link or a hidden image on a page the victim visits. The victim is then signed in to the client as the attacker or, where the flow links an external identity to an existing account, the attacker's external identity is linked to the victim's account.

The weakness is identified by checking authorisation requests for a state value, and by replaying a redirect with the parameter removed, altered or taken from another session to see whether the client still accepts the code.
entries.impact: Where the flow is used for sign-in, the victim is silently logged in to the attacker's account, and anything they then enter, such as personal details, payment information or documents, is stored in an account the attacker controls. Where the same redirect endpoint is used to connect a social or enterprise identity to an existing account, the attacker can link their own external identity to the victim's account and then sign in as the victim at will, which is an account takeover and would raise the severity. That form needs the victim to be signed in to the client when they visit the attacker's page; no other interaction is needed.
entries.remediation:
Bind every authorisation response to the session that started it:

  • Generate a new unguessable state value (at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure generator) for each authorisation request, store it in the user's session or a short-lived HttpOnly cookie, and send it with the request.
  • On the redirect back, reject the response unless state is present and exactly matches the stored value, then discard the stored value so it cannot be used again.
  • Use PKCE for every client and, in OpenID Connect, send a nonce and check it in the ID token. Both also bind the response to the browser that started the flow.
  • Where the client links external identities to existing accounts, ask the user to confirm the link, and notify the account owner whenever a new identity is linked.
  • Prefer a maintained OAuth or OpenID Connect client library, which handles state, nonce and PKCE correctly when configured to.

Confirm the fix by replaying the redirect with a missing, altered and reused state value, and with a code obtained in another session, and checking that each is rejected.

entries.title: OAuth Implicit Flow in Use
entries.summary: The application obtains OAuth access tokens through the implicit flow, which returns them in the browser's address bar, where they are easier to leak, steal or inject.
entries.description:
In the OAuth 2.0 implicit grant, requested with response_type=token (or id_token token in OpenID Connect), the authorisation server returns the access token directly in the fragment of the redirect address, instead of issuing a code that the client exchanges for a token. The flow was designed for browser-based applications at a time when browsers could not make cross-origin requests to a token endpoint, and older single-page application libraries and identity platform configurations still use it.

Placing the token in the address exposes it in more places: browser history, scripts running on the redirect page (including third-party scripts), open redirects that carry the fragment on to another site, and malicious browser extensions. The client also cannot tell whether a token it receives was issued to it, so a token obtained elsewhere can be injected into the flow, and the token cannot be bound to the client that requested it. The IETF's OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice therefore advises that clients should not use the implicit grant, or any other response type that returns access tokens from the authorisation endpoint.

The weakness is identified by observing response_type=token or id_token token in authorisation requests and an access_token value in the fragment of the redirect address, and by checking in the identity platform whether the implicit grant is enabled for the client.
entries.impact: The flow does not expose tokens by itself, but it makes it more likely that a token is leaked or stolen through another weakness, such as cross-site scripting on the client, an open redirect or a compromised script, and offers no way to stop a stolen token being used elsewhere. An attacker who obtains a token can use it within its scopes until it expires. Exploitation depends on such a further weakness and on the user signing in, and the tokens involved are usually short-lived, which keeps the typical risk low.
entries.remediation:
Move the client to the authorisation code flow with PKCE:

  • Request response_type=code, send a PKCE code_challenge with code_challenge_method=S256, and exchange the code for tokens at the token endpoint with the matching code_verifier. Current OAuth and OpenID Connect libraries for single-page and mobile applications support this.
  • Where possible, use a backend-for-frontend design, in which a server-side component completes the flow and holds the tokens, and the browser receives only an HttpOnly, Secure session cookie.
  • Once the change is made, disable the implicit grant for the client at the authorisation server, for example by clearing the implicit grant options in the app registration in Microsoft Entra ID, or removing the implicit grant type from the client's settings on other platforms, so it cannot be used even if requested.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived and limited to the scopes the client needs.

Confirm the fix by checking that authorisation requests use response_type=code with a code challenge, that no token appears in the redirect address, and that the authorisation server refuses an implicit request for the client.

entries.title: OAuth Authorisation Code Flow Without PKCE
entries.summary: The OAuth authorisation code flow is used without Proof Key for Code Exchange, so an intercepted or leaked authorisation code can be redeemed or injected by someone else.
entries.description:
Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE, RFC 7636) binds an authorisation code to the client instance that requested it. The client creates a random secret, the code verifier, and sends a hash of it, the code challenge, with the authorisation request; when it redeems the code, it must present the verifier, which only it knows. The client application uses the authorisation code flow without PKCE, or the authorisation server accepts code redemptions without checking a verifier, or accepts the weaker plain method, in which the challenge is the verifier itself.

Without PKCE, the code alone is enough to obtain tokens, or to complete the sign-in in a browser. This matters most for public clients, which cannot keep a client secret: single-page applications, and mobile and desktop applications, where another application on the device registered for the same custom URL scheme can receive the redirect. For confidential clients that authenticate to the token endpoint, a stolen code cannot be redeemed directly, but it can be injected into the attacker's own session with the client to sign in as the victim. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for confidential ones.

The weakness is identified by checking authorisation requests for the code_challenge and code_challenge_method parameters, and by redeeming a code without a verifier, or with a wrong one, to see whether the authorisation server enforces PKCE.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains an authorisation code, for example through a malicious application on the same mobile device, a code leaked into logs or Referer headers, or an open redirect combined with weak redirect URI checks, can exchange it for the victim's tokens or use it to sign in to the client as the victim. Exploitation depends on such a way of intercepting codes and on the victim signing in, so the risk is typically low for confidential web applications and higher for mobile, desktop and single-page applications. Any resulting access is limited to the user's account, the granted scopes and the token lifetime.
entries.remediation:
Use PKCE in every authorisation code flow and enforce it at the authorisation server:

  • For each authorisation request, have the client generate a new code verifier (a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters), send its SHA-256 hash as code_challenge with code_challenge_method=S256, and send the verifier as code_verifier when redeeming the code. Current OAuth and OpenID Connect client libraries do this when PKCE is enabled.
  • Configure the authorisation server to require PKCE for every client, or at least every public client, to reject the plain method, and to reject a token request that carries a verifier when no challenge was sent with the authorisation request.
  • For mobile applications, prefer claimed HTTPS redirects (Android App Links or iOS Universal Links) to custom URL schemes, and use the system browser rather than an embedded web view.
  • Keep authorisation codes single-use and short-lived, and revoke tokens already issued from a code that is presented a second time.

Confirm the fix by checking that authorisation requests carry an S256 code challenge and that a code cannot be redeemed without the correct verifier.

entries.title: SAML Response Signature Not Validated
entries.summary: The service provider accepts SAML responses or assertions without properly validating their signature, so an attacker can forge or alter an assertion and sign in as any user.
entries.description:
In SAML single sign-on, the identity provider signs the response, or the assertion inside it, and the service provider (the application) must verify that signature against the identity provider's known certificate before trusting the identity and attributes in the assertion. The application's validation is missing or incomplete, so an assertion that has been altered or created by an attacker is accepted. The forms a tester meets include:

  • No signature required: an assertion modified, for example, to change the NameID is accepted once its Signature element is removed.
  • Wrong key: the signature is verified with the certificate carried in the message's KeyInfo rather than the identity provider's configured certificate, so an assertion signed with the attacker's own certificate is accepted.
  • Signature wrapping: the signature is valid but covers a different element from the one the application reads, so a forged assertion placed alongside the signed one is used.
  • Comment injection: a comment inserted into the NameID leaves the signature valid but truncates the value the application reads, changing the identity.

The weakness is identified by capturing a SAML response for a test account and replaying it with altered attributes, with the signature removed, re-signed with a self-generated certificate, and restructured with the wrapping variants, for example with the SAML Raider extension for Burp Suite, and checking which versions grant access.
entries.impact: An attacker can sign in to the application as any user, including administrators, by presenting a forged or altered assertion, and can set any attribute the application trusts, such as group membership or role. The forms that need no valid assertion can be exploited without any account, while signature wrapping and comment injection need one valid response, which any user of the identity provider can obtain. Because the application trusts single sign-on for every user, the weakness typically gives control of all accounts and data in the application, and the forged sign-ins do not appear in the identity provider's logs.
entries.remediation:
Validate every SAML response strictly, using a maintained library rather than custom XML handling:

  • Require a valid signature on the assertion, or on the response that contains it where the library supports that, and reject any response or assertion that is unsigned.
  • Verify the signature only with the identity provider's certificate taken from trusted, preconfigured metadata, never with a key or certificate supplied in the message.
  • Use only the assertion that the library returns as verified, rather than querying the original XML document again, and reject responses that contain more than one assertion.
  • Check the Issuer, Audience, Recipient and Destination values, the NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter times, and InResponseTo for sign-ins started by the service provider, and reject assertion identifiers that have already been used.
  • Keep the SAML and XML security libraries up to date, as signature wrapping and comment handling flaws have been fixed in several of them, and disable DTD processing in the XML parser.

If the fix cannot be deployed at once, consider disabling SAML sign-in for the application, or restricting access to it, until it is. Confirm the fix by repeating the unsigned, self-signed, wrapped and comment-injected tests and checking that each response is rejected.

entries.title: Weak Password Hashing
entries.summary: User passwords are stored with a fast or unsalted hash such as MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256, so they can be recovered quickly by offline cracking from a copy of the database.
entries.description:
Passwords should be stored with a deliberately slow, salted password hashing function, so that recovering them from a stolen copy of the database is costly. The application stores them with a general-purpose hash function such as MD5, SHA-1 or the SHA-2 family, without a salt, with one salt shared by all accounts or with too few iterations, or it uses a suitable function such as bcrypt or PBKDF2 with a work factor far below current guidance. General-purpose hashes are designed to be fast, and current graphics hardware can test billions of MD5 or SHA-1 candidates per second, so a large proportion of real passwords can be recovered with dictionary and rule-based attacks. Without a unique salt per password, identical passwords produce identical hashes and precomputed tables can be used.

The weakness is usually identified when password hashes become visible during testing: through database access gained by another finding, backups or exports, API responses, the configuration of the identity store, or source code review. Hash formats are recognisable by length and prefix: 32 hexadecimal characters for MD5, 40 for SHA-1 and 64 for SHA-256, compared with self-describing formats such as $2b$ for bcrypt or $argon2id$ for Argon2id. Cracking a sample with a tool such as hashcat or John the Ripper shows the practical risk.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains the password hashes, through SQL injection, a backup, a compromised server or an insider, can recover a large share of the passwords offline, with no interaction with the application that could be detected or rate limited. Recovered passwords give access to the corresponding accounts, including administrative ones, and, because passwords are widely reused, often to the same users' accounts on other services and on the organisation's other systems. The weakness needs a separate compromise of the stored hashes first, but it decides how much damage such a breach does.
entries.remediation:
Move to a password hashing function designed for the purpose, with a unique salt per password and a work factor set from current guidance:

  • Use Argon2id where it is available; otherwise scrypt, bcrypt (which uses only the first 72 bytes of a password), or PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 where a FIPS-approved algorithm is required. Use the parameters recommended in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet, and raise them over time as hardware improves.
  • Use the platform's maintained implementation, such as password_hash() in PHP, the ASP.NET Core Identity password hasher, Spring Security's password encoders or a maintained Argon2 or bcrypt library, rather than building a scheme from hash primitives.
  • Protect existing hashes without waiting for users: wrap each legacy hash in the new function (for example, store the Argon2id hash of the existing MD5 hash), then replace it with a direct hash of the password the next time the user signs in.
  • Optionally add a pepper, a secret key held outside the database, for example in a hardware security module or key vault.

If the existing hashes may have been exposed, require password resets and treat the passwords as compromised. Confirm the fix by checking that newly stored hashes use the chosen algorithm, a unique salt and the intended work factor, and that no unwrapped legacy hashes remain.

entries.title: Passwords Stored in Plain Text or Reversible Form
entries.summary: User passwords are stored as plain text, in an encoding, or encrypted with a key the application holds, so anyone who reads the store and key can recover every password.
entries.description:
The application stores user passwords in a form from which the original value can be recovered: as plain text, in an encoding such as Base64 or hexadecimal, or encrypted with a key that the application itself holds and uses to decrypt them. Encryption does not change the outcome much, because the key is normally kept on the same servers, in configuration or in the code, and anyone with the access needed to read the passwords is likely to be able to read the key as well.

The weakness can be identified directly, by inspecting the user table or an export where testing gives database access, or indirectly from the application's behaviour: a password reminder that emails the current password, a profile or administration page that displays it, support staff who can tell a user their password, or a response that returns it. Source code and configuration review show it plainly, for example a password column written without any hashing step, or a call to an encryption routine where a password hashing function is expected.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the password store, or the store and its key, obtains every user's password at once, with no cracking needed. That includes attackers exploiting another weakness such as SQL injection, anyone holding a backup or database export, and administrators and support staff, who should never be able to see passwords. The passwords give access to every account in the application, including administrative ones, and, because passwords are widely reused, often to the same users' accounts on other services and on the organisation's own systems.
entries.remediation:
Store only a one-way password hash, and remove every recoverable copy:

  • Hash passwords with a dedicated password hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 where FIPS compliance is required), with a unique salt per password and the work factors recommended in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet, using the platform's maintained implementation.
  • Convert all existing passwords in one operation: because the plain text or decryptable values are available, each can be hashed immediately, without waiting for users to sign in.
  • Then delete the plain text or encrypted column, destroy the encryption key that protected it, and remove old copies from exports, logs and test environments, and from backups as they are rotated.
  • Replace any feature that reveals the password, such as a reminder email or a display to support staff, with a secure reset link that lets the user set a new password.

Because the existing passwords may already have been seen by anyone with database, backup or key access, consider requiring all users to change their password after the migration, and notify them if a compromise is suspected. Confirm the fix by inspecting newly stored values and the migrated records, and by checking that no feature or response can return a user's password.

entries.title: Password Returned in Application Responses
entries.summary: The application sends a user's current password, or its hash, back in pages or API responses, where it can be read from the browser, caches, logs or intercepting tools.
entries.description:
The application includes a stored password, or the password hash, in data it returns to the browser or API client. Typical examples are a profile or settings page that pre-fills a password field with the user's current password (visible in the page source even though the field is masked), an API that serialises the whole user record including the password or hash field, an administration page or user listing that shows other users' passwords, and registration or account responses that echo the password back.

Returning the password in readable form also shows that it is stored in plain text or a reversible form, which is a separate and more serious finding. A returned hash is less directly useful, but it can be cracked offline.

The weakness is identified by reviewing responses in an intercepting proxy for password or hash values, including in hidden fields, JavaScript variables and JSON properties that the user interface does not display, and in the responses to other users' and administrators' views of an account.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the response can obtain the password: an attacker exploiting cross-site scripting, someone using a shared computer where the page is cached or kept in history, a proxy, monitoring tool or log that records response bodies, or a person reading the page source over the user's shoulder. The password gives full access to the account and, because passwords are often reused, possibly to the user's accounts elsewhere. Where responses expose other users' passwords or hashes, for example in an administration view or a user API, the impact is much greater.
entries.remediation:
Never send stored passwords or password hashes to a client:

  • Remove password and hash fields from every response. Build responses from explicit allowlists of fields, using response models, data transfer objects or serialiser settings that exclude credential fields, rather than serialising whole database records.
  • Render password fields empty. A page for changing the password should ask for the current and new passwords, never display the existing one.
  • Do not echo submitted passwords in confirmation pages, responses or emails.
  • Store passwords only as salted hashes from a dedicated password hashing function, so that no feature is able to return the original value.
  • Send Cache-Control: no-store on authentication and account pages, and make sure logging and monitoring tools do not record request or response bodies that carry credentials.

If passwords have appeared in responses that may have been cached or logged, ask the affected users to change them. Confirm the fix by reviewing the affected pages and API responses again and checking that no password or hash value appears.

entries.title: Sensitive Account Changes Without Re-Authentication
entries.summary: A signed-in session can change the password, email address or multi-factor settings without the current password, so anyone holding the session can take the account over for good.
entries.description:
Some account changes amount to control of the account: changing the password, the email address or telephone number used for recovery, multi-factor authentication settings and recovery codes and, depending on the application, linked identities, API keys, or payout and payment details. The application allows these changes on the strength of the current session alone, without asking for the current password or a fresh multi-factor check.

A session is weaker evidence of identity than the password: it may have been stolen through cross-site scripting, a leaked token or malware, or simply used by someone else on an unattended or shared device. Without a re-authentication step, anyone holding it can turn temporary access into permanent control. Where cross-site request forgery affects these functions, the same gap makes it more damaging.

The weakness is identified by making each sensitive change in an authenticated session and observing whether the current password or a second factor is requested, and whether the change can be made by replaying the request without that value. Checks that appear in the user interface but are not enforced by the server are common, so the request should also be replayed with the field removed. A change of email address that takes effect without confirmation is a closely related weakness.
entries.impact: An attacker with temporary access to a user's session can change the password and recovery details, or turn off multi-factor authentication, and so lock the legitimate user out and keep control of the account after the session ends. Recovery then depends on the organisation's support process. The attacker first needs a session, through another weakness such as cross-site scripting or by using an unattended device, but this weakness decides whether that brief access becomes a lasting account takeover. The impact is greatest for administrative and other high-value accounts.
entries.remediation:
Require fresh proof of identity before any change that affects control of the account:

  • Ask for the current password, or a multi-factor confirmation for users who have set it up, before changing the password, email address, telephone number, multi-factor settings or recovery codes, and before other sensitive actions such as creating API keys or changing payment details. Enforce the check on the server, as part of the same request as the change.
  • Alternatively, require a recent authentication: record the time of the last full sign-in and ask the user to sign in again if it is older than a short limit. With federated sign-in, the OpenID Connect max_age and prompt=login parameters and the auth_time claim support this.
  • For email address changes, confirm the new address with a link before the change takes effect, and notify the old address with a way to reverse it.
  • Notify the user of every sensitive change through an existing channel, and end other sessions after a password change.
  • Rate limit the current password check, as it could otherwise be used to guess the password.

Confirm the fix by repeating each sensitive change with the current password missing or wrong, and checking that the server refuses it.

entries.title: Broken Object-Level Authorisation (BOLA)
entries.summary: API endpoints act on the object identifier supplied in the request without checking that the caller may access that object, so users can read or change other users' records.
entries.description:
APIs identify the objects they act on through values in the request: path segments, query parameters, fields in a JSON body, headers, or node identifiers in GraphQL. The API checks that the caller is authenticated, but not that the specific object requested belongs to the caller or is one they are permitted to reach, so changing the identifier gives access to another user's or another tenant's object. This is the first item in the OWASP API Security Top 10, and it is the API form of what is often reported in web applications as an insecure direct object reference.

The weakness is frequent in APIs because each endpoint, method and version needs its own check, and because mobile and single-page clients make every identifier visible to the user. Variants include endpoints that check ownership on read but not on update or delete, nested resources where the parent is checked but the child is not, bulk and export endpoints that accept lists of identifiers, and multi-tenant APIs that trust a tenant or organisation identifier sent by the client. Unpredictable identifiers such as UUIDs make objects harder to find, but do not prevent access once an identifier is known or leaked.

The weakness is identified by repeating each request that carries an identifier with two accounts of the same role, and across tenants, substituting the other account's identifiers and comparing the responses. Tools such as the Autorize extension for Burp Suite automate the comparison.
entries.impact: An attacker with an ordinary account can read and, depending on the methods affected, change or delete the records of other users or tenants by iterating through or harvesting identifiers. Typical consequences are exposure of personal data, documents, orders, messages or financial details at scale, and unauthorised changes to other users' data. Where identifiers are sequential, the whole data set can be enumerated with a simple script. The impact depends on the sensitivity of the objects and on whether write and delete operations are affected.
entries.remediation:
Check authorisation for the specific object on every request, on the server:

  • For every endpoint and method that takes an object identifier, verify that the authenticated caller may perform that action on that object before acting on it. Derive the caller's identity and tenant from the validated session or token, never from a field supplied by the client.
  • Enforce the check where data is retrieved, for example by scoping queries to the caller (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?, or a tenant filter applied to every query by the data access layer), so that an object the caller may not see is never loaded. Return the same not found response for objects that do not exist and for objects the caller may not access.
  • Centralise the rules in a policy or authorisation layer used by every endpoint, version and method, including bulk and export endpoints and GraphQL resolvers, and deny by default.
  • Where the design allows, prefer endpoints that act on the caller's own resources without taking an identifier, such as /me/orders.
  • Add automated tests that call each endpoint as a second user and as another tenant, and fail the build if access succeeds.

Random identifiers add some defence in depth but are not a fix. Confirm the fix by repeating the cross-account and cross-tenant requests for every affected endpoint and method and checking that each is refused.

entries.title: Broken Function-Level Authorisation (BFLA)
entries.summary: API functions meant for administrators or other privileged roles do not check the caller's role, so an ordinary user can call them directly.
entries.description:
APIs expose functions with different privilege requirements: ordinary user operations, operations for managers or support staff, and administrative functions such as managing users, roles, configuration or other tenants. The API checks that the caller is authenticated but not that their role permits the function, or the check exists only in the client, which hides the corresponding buttons and menus. Any authenticated user who sends the request directly can therefore use the function.

Common forms are administrative endpoints under a predictable path (for example an /admin/ or /internal/ segment, or a different API version) that rely on not being linked; endpoints where reading is restricted but another method on the same path, such as PUT, PATCH or DELETE, is not; role checks present in one service or gateway route but missing from another that reaches the same function; and checks that trust a role or permission value sent by the client.

The weakness is identified by mapping the API's functions from documentation, client code and traffic captured as a privileged user, then replaying each privileged request with an ordinary user's session or token and comparing the results. Changing the HTTP method and trying administrative paths alongside known ones finds functions the client never calls. The Autorize extension for Burp Suite automates much of the comparison.
entries.impact: An ordinary user, or anyone who can register an account, can perform actions reserved for more privileged roles. Depending on the functions exposed, this can mean creating or promoting accounts, changing other users' permissions, reading or exporting all data, changing configuration or deleting records, which often amounts to full administrative control of the application. Where the API serves several tenants, administrative functions may also reach other tenants' data. The impact is lower where the exposed functions are limited, such as read-only reporting.
entries.remediation:
Enforce role and permission checks on the server for every function:

  • Deny by default: require every endpoint and method to declare the roles or permissions it needs, and reject requests that do not meet them. Use the framework's authorisation features, for example authorisation policies or [Authorize(Roles = ...)] in ASP.NET Core, method security with @PreAuthorize in Spring Security, or shared middleware in Node.js, rather than ad hoc checks in each handler.
  • Take the caller's roles from the validated session or token, or from the server's own records, never from a value supplied by the client.
  • Check each HTTP method separately, so that permission to read a resource does not imply permission to change or delete it.
  • Where practical, separate administrative functions from the public API: a separate service, host or gateway route that is reachable only from trusted networks and requires stronger authentication.
  • Keep a matrix of functions against roles and test it automatically, calling each privileged function as each lower role and failing the build if access succeeds.

Confirm the fix by repeating every privileged request as each lower-privileged role and checking that the server refuses it.

entries.title: Excessive Data Exposure in API Responses
entries.summary: API responses return more properties than the client needs, including sensitive ones, and rely on the client to hide them, so anyone reading the raw response sees them.
entries.description:
The API returns whole objects, or more of their properties than the client application uses, and relies on the client to display only what each user should see. The additional properties are visible to anyone who reads the raw response in a browser's developer tools or an intercepting proxy. Typical examples are user objects that include email addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, password hashes, multi-factor secrets, internal flags or roles; search, listing and mention endpoints that return full records of other users when the interface shows only their names; and objects carrying internal notes, cost prices or other fields meant for staff.

The weakness often comes from serialising database entities or ORM models directly to JSON, from generic endpoints shared by the public client and internal tools, and, in GraphQL, from types whose sensitive fields are not protected by field-level authorisation. It is part of what the OWASP API Security Top 10 calls broken object property level authorisation, the read-side counterpart of mass assignment.

The weakness is identified by comparing each API response with what the user interface displays, for each role, and reviewing every property for data the caller should not receive, with particular attention to responses that describe other users.
entries.impact: Any authenticated user, and on public endpoints anyone, can collect the extra data by reading responses directly or by scripting requests to the affected endpoints. Depending on the fields, this can expose other users' personal data, credentials or secrets that enable further attacks, or commercially sensitive information. Where a listing or search endpoint is affected, data about many users can be harvested quickly. The impact rises with the sensitivity of the exposed properties and the number of records that can be reached.
entries.remediation:
Decide on the server which properties each caller may receive:

  • Return explicit response models (data transfer objects or view models) that list the properties each endpoint needs, instead of serialising database entities or ORM objects directly. Where a framework serialiser is used, configure it with an allowlist of fields rather than a list of exclusions.
  • Where different roles need different views of the same object, build a separate response model for each role, or apply property-level authorisation in the serialiser.
  • Never include secrets such as password hashes, tokens, API keys or multi-factor seeds in any response.
  • In GraphQL, apply authorisation in the resolvers of sensitive fields, not only at the type or query level.
  • Define response schemas in the API specification and validate responses against them in testing, so that new properties cannot appear unnoticed.

Confirm the fix by repeating the affected requests for each role and checking that responses contain only the documented, necessary properties.

entries.title: No Rate Limiting on API Endpoints
entries.summary: API endpoints accept an unlimited number, rate or size of requests from a single client, which allows resource exhaustion, guessing attacks, data harvesting and runaway costs.
entries.description:
The API does not limit how many requests a client, user, API key or source address can make in a period, or how much work a single request can cause, so every request is processed in full regardless of volume. The weakness shows itself in several ways:

  • no request rate limit, so a script can send thousands of requests a minute without receiving 429 Too Many Requests or being slowed down;
  • no limit on the work per request, such as page size parameters that accept very large values, unbounded exports and searches, bulk operations with no cap on the number of items, or uploads with no size limit;
  • no limit on operations that cost money, such as sending SMS messages or emails, calling paid third-party services or generating reports.

The weakness is identified by sending bursts of requests to representative endpoints, including verification code, search, export and other resource-intensive operations, and observing whether any are rejected, delayed or blocked, and by testing parameters that control the amount of work, such as page size, with large values. Testing is normally kept to modest volumes that show the absence of limits without degrading the service. Limits on password guessing at sign-in are covered by a separate finding.
entries.impact: An attacker can degrade or interrupt the service for other users by sending large volumes of requests or a few very expensive ones, harvest data at scale through listing and search endpoints, and guess values that are only safe when attempts are limited, such as one-time codes, reset tokens, voucher codes or identifiers. Where requests trigger paid actions, such as SMS messages, the organisation can incur significant costs. The typical impact is limited disruption and abuse rather than direct data compromise, but it rises where a guessable secret or an expensive operation is exposed.
entries.remediation:
Apply limits at several levels, starting at the edge:

  • Enforce rate limits per client identity (user, API key or token) and per source address at the API gateway, load balancer or reverse proxy, with stricter limits on sensitive and expensive operations, and return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when they are exceeded.
  • Limit the work per request: a maximum page size enforced on the server, caps on bulk operations, maximum request body and upload sizes, and timeouts on long-running queries.
  • Apply quotas and spending limits to operations that cost money, such as a maximum number of messages per user per day.
  • Monitor request rates and alert on unusual patterns.

Most platforms provide the controls, such as rate limiting policies in Azure API Management, throttling and usage plans in Amazon API Gateway, the rate limiting middleware in ASP.NET Core, and the limit_req module in nginx:

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s; server { location /api/ { limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay; limit_req_status 429; } }

Set the limits from observed legitimate usage. Confirm the fix by repeating the burst tests and checking that excess requests are rejected, and that oversized page and body values are refused or capped.

entries.title: API Endpoint Accessible Without Authentication
entries.summary: API endpoints that return non-public data or perform actions respond to requests that carry no credentials, so anyone who can reach the API can use them.
entries.description:
The API expects callers to authenticate, but one or more endpoints process requests that carry no session cookie, token or API key, and return data or perform actions as if the caller were authorised. This usually happens because authentication is applied route by route rather than by default, so a new, internal or rarely used endpoint is left out; because a gateway protects the documented routes while the service behind it can be reached another way; or because some methods or versions of an otherwise protected endpoint are not covered.

Endpoints commonly affected include those built for a mobile application or a partner integration, internal and administrative operations, export and reporting functions, file and attachment downloads, health and diagnostic endpoints that reveal configuration, and GraphQL operations whose resolvers do not check the caller.

The weakness is identified by replaying each captured API request with the Authorization header, cookies and any API key removed, for every method, and comparing the responses with the authenticated ones. Endpoints found in client code, API documentation and older API versions should be tested in the same way, as should the service itself where it can be reached without passing through the gateway.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the API can use the affected endpoints without an account. Depending on what they do, this can expose personal or business data, often for all users at once, allow records to be created, changed or deleted, or reveal configuration and secrets that support further attacks. Because no credentials are needed, exploitation is easy to automate and cannot be traced to an account. The impact is lower where the endpoint returns only information that is public elsewhere.
entries.remediation:
Make authentication the default for the whole API:

  • Apply authentication globally, at the framework or gateway level, and mark only the endpoints that are intentionally public as anonymous. Examples are a fallback authorisation policy that requires an authenticated user in ASP.NET Core, anyRequest().authenticated() in Spring Security, and authentication middleware registered before all routes in Express.
  • Keep the list of anonymous endpoints short, documented and reviewed, and return no non-public data from them.
  • Make sure services behind a gateway cannot be reached directly, or authenticate requests in each service as well, for example by validating the token in every service.
  • Check authorisation as well as authentication on every endpoint, so that authenticated callers reach only what their role allows.
  • Add automated tests that call every route without credentials and fail if any non-public route succeeds.
// ASP.NET Core: require an authenticated user unless an endpoint allows anonymous access builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options => { options.FallbackPolicy = new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder() .RequireAuthenticatedUser() .Build(); });

Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated requests against every affected endpoint and method and checking that each returns 401 Unauthorized.

entries.title: Deprecated API Versions Still Accessible
entries.summary: Older or deprecated versions of the API remain deployed and reachable alongside the current one, without the security fixes and controls added since.
entries.description:
When an API is versioned, older versions are often left running after clients move to a new one, either deliberately for a transition period or because no one owns their retirement. These versions usually share the same data but not the same code: security fixes, authorisation checks, input validation and rate limits added to the current version are not carried back, and the old version may be missing from monitoring, from the gateway's policies and from the inventory of what is exposed. The same applies to beta, staging and test versions published on production hosts.

The weakness is identified by looking for version indicators in paths, subdomains, headers and parameters (for example /v1/ alongside /v3/, an api-version parameter, or a version in the Accept header), in older releases of mobile applications and in documentation, and by requesting lower and adjacent versions of current endpoints. Each older version found is then tested for the weaknesses fixed in the current one, such as an authorisation check, rate limit or validation rule that the old version lacks.
entries.impact: An attacker can bypass security controls added to the current API by sending the same request to an older version, for example to reach other users' data where an authorisation flaw was fixed only in the newer version, or to avoid rate limits on sign-in. Old versions may also run unpatched components and are less likely to be monitored, so abuse can go unnoticed. The impact depends on what the old version lacks: where it has the same controls as the current one, the finding is mainly one of unnecessary exposure, while a missing authorisation check would make it high.
entries.remediation:
Keep an inventory of every API version and retire old ones on a schedule:

  • Record each API, version, environment and host in an inventory with an owner, the clients that use it and a retirement date, and update it as part of each release.
  • Announce deprecation in documentation and in responses (for example with the Sunset header), then remove retired versions from routing and decommission them, rather than leaving them reachable.
  • Until a version is retired, apply security fixes to every live version, and route all versions through the same gateway policies for authentication, authorisation, rate limiting and logging.
  • Keep beta, test and staging versions off production hosts and away from production data.
  • Monitor traffic to deprecated versions to identify the remaining clients and any unexpected use.

As an interim measure, block access at the gateway to versions with known weaknesses. Confirm the fix by requesting the retired versions again and checking that they are no longer reachable, and by repeating the earlier tests against any version that remains.

entries.title: API Documentation Publicly Exposed
entries.summary: Interactive documentation or the machine-readable definition of an API that is not meant to be public, such as Swagger UI or an OpenAPI file, can be retrieved by anyone.
entries.description:
API frameworks can generate documentation from the code: an OpenAPI (Swagger) definition in JSON or YAML, an interactive Swagger UI or ReDoc page, a WSDL file for SOAP services, or a GraphQL playground. These are useful during development, but the application publishes them to anyone on its production hosts, although the API is not intended for public use. The definition lists every endpoint, method, parameter and data model the code exposes, often including internal and administrative operations and fields the client never uses. Documentation for an API that is offered to the public is not a weakness in itself.

The weakness is identified by requesting the default paths of common frameworks, such as /swagger-ui.html, /v2/api-docs and /v3/api-docs for Spring, /swagger/index.html and /swagger/v1/swagger.json for ASP.NET Core, /docs, /redoc and /openapi.json for FastAPI, and ?wsdl on SOAP endpoints, and by searching client code and responses for links to them. Scanners report it as an exposed API specification or Swagger UI. Some older Swagger UI releases have also had cross-site scripting flaws, which are reported separately where the version found is affected.
entries.impact: The documentation gives an attacker a complete and accurate map of the API, which removes much of the effort of discovering endpoints and parameters and points directly to the most sensitive operations, such as administrative and bulk functions. It does not give access to data or functions by itself: requests made from it still need whatever authentication the API enforces. On its own it is a matter of reducing exposure rather than a direct risk, and its significance rises where it reveals endpoints that prove to be vulnerable, or where its examples contain real credentials or data.
entries.remediation:
Publish API documentation only where it is intended to be public:

  • Disable the documentation endpoints in production, for example by registering Swagger only in the development environment in ASP.NET Core, setting springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false and springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false for springdoc in Spring Boot, or passing docs_url=None, redoc_url=None and openapi_url=None to FastAPI().
  • Where developers, partners or customers need the documentation, host it on a separate internal or authenticated portal, or require authentication on the documentation routes.
  • Remove real credentials, tokens and personal data from the examples in the definition.
  • Do not rely on hidden documentation for security: every endpoint must enforce authentication and authorisation whether or not it is documented.
// ASP.NET Core: expose Swagger only in development if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); }

Confirm the fix by requesting the documentation paths again from an unauthenticated, external position and checking that they are no longer served.

entries.title: GraphQL Introspection Enabled
entries.summary: The GraphQL endpoint answers introspection queries in production, returning its complete schema: every query, mutation, type and field, including ones the client never uses.
entries.description:
GraphQL includes an introspection system that lets a client ask the server for its schema, through queries on the __schema and __type fields. Development tools such as GraphiQL rely on it, and many server implementations enable it by default. The production endpoint answers introspection queries from unauthenticated or ordinary users, and so returns a full description of the API: every query, mutation and subscription with its arguments, and every type and field, including deprecated, internal and administrative operations that the client application never calls.

The weakness is identified by sending a standard introspection query to the GraphQL endpoint and checking whether the schema is returned. Tools such as InQL for Burp Suite and GraphQL Voyager, and most API scanners, send this query automatically, and scanners report the result as GraphQL introspection enabled. Endpoints are commonly found at paths such as /graphql, /api/graphql or /v1/graphql.
entries.impact: The schema gives an attacker a complete map of the API, including operations and fields the client does not use, such as administrative mutations, internal or deprecated fields and debugging queries, which are often less well protected. This removes much of the effort of discovering the attack surface and points directly to the operations most worth testing for authorisation flaws. Introspection does not give access to any data or operation by itself, as every operation it reveals still enforces whatever authorisation the server applies, but its significance rises where the schema reveals operations that prove to be exploitable.
entries.remediation:
Disable introspection in production, or restrict it to trusted users:

  • Turn introspection off in the production configuration, for example with the introspection: false option in Apollo Server, the NoSchemaIntrospectionCustomRule validation rule in servers built on graphql-js, or disable_introspection_entry_points in graphql-ruby. Other implementations offer equivalent settings.
  • Where internal developers or partners need the schema, provide it through documentation or a separate, authenticated environment, or allow introspection only for authenticated staff roles.
  • Disable GraphiQL, GraphQL Playground and similar interactive tools in production.
  • Disable field suggestions as well, since they allow much of the schema to be recovered when introspection is off.
  • Treat this as hardening: enforce authorisation in the resolvers of every sensitive query, mutation and field, so that knowledge of the schema gives no access.

Confirm the fix by sending the introspection query again, unauthenticated and as an ordinary user, and checking that the schema is no longer returned.

entries.title: GraphQL Query Depth or Batching Not Limited
entries.summary: The GraphQL server places no limit on query depth, complexity, aliases or batched operations, so one request can exhaust server resources or carry thousands of guesses.
entries.description:
A single GraphQL request can ask for a great deal of work.
