Where the schema has relationships that lead back on themselves (for example a user's posts, each post's author, and that author's posts), queries can be nested to any depth, and each level can multiply the number of records fetched. Aliases allow the same field or mutation to be requested many times in one query under different names, and many servers also accept batches: an array of separate operations in one HTTP request. The server applies no limit on query depth, complexity or cost, the number of aliases, the size of the lists returned, or the number of operations in a batch.

Two problems follow. Expensive queries can tie up the server and its database with only a few requests. And because rate limiting is usually applied per HTTP request, a single request containing hundreds of aliased or batched sign-in, verification code or voucher operations passes through it, allowing guessing attacks at scale.

The weakness is identified by sending progressively deeper nested queries and observing response times, by sending a query containing many aliases of the same field or mutation, and by sending a JSON array of operations, to see which are processed in full. Testing is kept to volumes that show the absence of limits without degrading the service.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated or ordinary user can degrade or interrupt the API for others with a small number of expensive queries, which may also increase hosting costs where resources scale automatically. Using aliases or batching, an attacker can also make thousands of attempts at passwords, one-time codes or other guessable values in a few requests, bypassing rate limits and lockout that count requests. The typical impact is limited disruption, rising where a sensitive mutation such as sign-in or code verification can be batched.
entries.remediation:
Limit the cost of each request, not just the number of requests:

  • Enforce a maximum query depth and a query complexity or cost limit, rejecting queries that exceed them before execution. Many servers provide these as options or validation rules, and libraries such as graphql-depth-limit and graphql-query-complexity provide them for graphql-js.
  • Limit the number of aliases, root fields and operations per request. Disable batching where clients do not need it (in Apollo Server, the allowBatchedHttpRequests option controls this), and cap the number of operations in a batch where they do.
  • Enforce maximum page sizes on list fields, and set execution timeouts.
  • Apply rate limits to sensitive operations, such as sign-in and code verification, per operation rather than per HTTP request, or exclude them from batching and aliasing.
  • Where the API serves only known clients, accept only persisted queries (an allowlist of operations registered in advance) instead of arbitrary queries.

Confirm the fix by repeating the deep, aliased and batched queries and checking that they are rejected before execution, and that repeated sensitive operations in one request are limited.

entries.title: GraphQL Field Suggestions Enabled
entries.summary: The GraphQL server's error messages suggest valid field and type names for misspelt ones, which lets the schema be reconstructed even when introspection is disabled.
entries.description:
When a query names a field, argument or type that does not exist, many GraphQL servers, including those built on the reference implementation graphql-js, return a validation error that states the name cannot be queried and then suggests similar valid names, introduced by 'Did you mean'. The feature helps developers, but in production it tells anyone who sends queries which names exist.

By sending queries with candidate names from a wordlist and collecting the suggestions, a tool can rebuild much of the schema, including fields and operations the client never uses, even where introspection has been disabled. Clairvoyance is a widely used tool for this.

The weakness is identified by sending a query with a deliberately misspelt field name, such as a known field with one letter changed, and checking whether the error response contains suggestions.
entries.impact: Suggestions let an attacker recover the names of fields, arguments and operations that introspection would otherwise reveal, so disabling introspection alone does not hide the schema. As with introspection, this helps an attacker find operations to test but gives no access to data or functions by itself, so it is a hardening matter unless the recovered schema leads to an exploitable operation.
entries.remediation:
Remove schema hints from error messages in production:

  • Use the server's option to disable suggestions where one exists. Where there is none, use its error formatting hook (for example formatError in Apollo Server) to remove the suggestion text from validation errors before they are returned.
  • Return generic validation errors to clients in production, and log the detail on the server instead.
  • Disable introspection in production as well, since removing one source of schema information without the other has little effect.
  • Enforce authorisation on every sensitive field and operation, so that knowledge of the schema gives no access.

Confirm the fix by sending queries with misspelt field and type names and checking that the errors no longer contain suggestions.

entries.title: API Key Passed in the URL
entries.summary: The API accepts its API key or access token as a URL query parameter, so the credential is recorded in logs, browser history and other places that keep full addresses.
entries.description:
The API expects, or accepts, its API key or access token in the query string of the request address, for example as an api_key, key, token or access_token parameter, rather than in a request header. Full request addresses are recorded in many more places than headers: web server, load balancer, proxy and content delivery network access logs, API gateway and monitoring logs, browser history and bookmarks where the request is made from a browser, and analytics and error-tracking services. Where a web page includes the address in a link or resource, the key can also be sent to other sites in the Referer header.

Because API keys are often long-lived and are not tied to a user session, a key recorded in any of these places remains useful to whoever later reads it.

The weakness is identified by observing credentials in the query strings of API requests made by the client and in documentation and code examples, and by checking whether an API that normally takes the key in a header also accepts it as a query parameter.
entries.impact: The key is exposed to anyone with access to the logs and systems that record request addresses, which commonly include operations staff, third-party providers of hosting, content delivery, monitoring and analytics, and attackers who gain access to any of them. Whoever obtains the key can call the API with the key's permissions until it is revoked, without needing the user or application it was issued to. The impact depends on what the key allows and how long it remains valid, and is greater for keys with broad or administrative access.
entries.remediation:
Send credentials in headers, never in the URL:

  • Accept API keys and tokens only in a request header, such as Authorization or a dedicated header like X-API-Key, and reject requests that supply them as query parameters, so that clients cannot fall back to the insecure form.
  • Update client applications, integrations and documentation to send the header, and announce a date after which keys in query parameters stop working.
  • Rotate every key that has been sent in a URL, as it should be assumed to be in logs already.
  • Mask or remove credential parameters in existing logs, and configure servers, gateways and monitoring tools to redact them.
  • Where a key has to be used from a browser, restrict it to the minimum permissions and to the allowed origins, and set a Referrer-Policy that does not send full addresses to other sites.

Confirm the fix by checking that requests with the key in the query string are rejected and that logs no longer contain credentials.

entries.title: Weak or Non-Expiring API Keys
entries.summary: API keys are short, predictable or derived from known values, or never expire and cannot easily be rotated, so a guessed or leaked key gives lasting access to the API.
entries.description:
API keys authenticate applications and integrations, and are often sent with every request and kept in many places: configuration files, scripts, CI/CD pipelines, mobile applications and partners' systems. The keys issued by the application are weak in one or more of these ways:

  • they are short, sequential, or derived from known values such as a user ID, email address or timestamp (for example a hash of the account's email address), so valid keys can be guessed or calculated;
  • they have no expiry date and there is no practical way to rotate them, so a key issued years ago, or held by a former employee or supplier, still works;
  • a single key is shared by many clients or users, or grants full access to the account regardless of what each client needs;
  • they are stored on the server in plain text, so a copy of the database yields every working key.

The weakness is identified by generating several keys and comparing their length, character set and structure for patterns or a relationship to account data, by decoding keys that appear encoded, by checking whether a key that has been regenerated or deleted still works, and by reviewing the expiry, scoping and rotation options the platform offers. Source code review shows how keys are generated and stored.
entries.impact: Where keys are predictable, an attacker can calculate or guess valid keys for other accounts and use the API as them. Where keys never expire and cannot be rotated, any key that leaks through code, logs, a former member of staff or a third party gives lasting access, often to everything the account can do, and the organisation may not know who holds it. The impact depends on how a key could be obtained and on its permissions, and is higher for guessable keys and for keys with administrative or cross-tenant access.
entries.remediation:
Issue keys that are random, scoped, stored safely and replaceable:

  • Generate keys from at least 128 bits, and preferably 256 bits, of a cryptographically secure random number generator, and give them no meaning. A fixed, recognisable prefix helps secret scanning tools detect leaked keys.
  • Store only a hash of each key on the server. Because a random key has far more entropy than a password, a single SHA-256 hash is sufficient, and the full key is shown to its owner once, at creation.
  • Issue a separate key for each client or integration, scoped to the permissions and, where possible, the source addresses it needs.
  • Give keys an expiry date, support more than one active key so that they can be rotated without downtime, and let owners revoke keys immediately. Revoke keys when staff or suppliers leave.
  • Log the use of each key and alert on unusual activity, such as use from new locations.
  • For machine-to-machine access, consider short-lived tokens from an OAuth client credentials flow instead of static keys.

Replace existing weak keys and revoke the old ones once clients have moved. Confirm the fix by checking that new keys show no pattern, that they expire, and that revoked and rotated keys are rejected.

entries.title: Unsafe Consumption of Third-Party APIs
entries.summary: The application trusts data and responses from third-party APIs it calls without validating them, so a compromised or impersonated provider can attack the application through them.
entries.description:
Applications increasingly depend on other APIs: payment and identity providers, address and company lookups, mapping, messaging, data enrichment and partner services. The application treats what these services return as trusted, and applies weaker checks to it than to input from its own users. Typical forms are:

  • data from the third party is used in database queries, commands, file paths or web pages without validation, parameterisation or output encoding, so it can carry injection payloads;
  • the application follows redirects returned by the third party without restriction, which can turn the integration into a route for server-side request forgery or send credentials to another host;
  • calls are made over unencrypted connections, or with certificate validation disabled;
  • there are no timeouts or limits on response size, so a slow or oversized response ties up the application;
  • callbacks and webhooks from the provider are accepted without verifying their signature or origin.

The weakness is identified through code and configuration review of the integrations, by observing outgoing requests, and, where the tester can influence data held by the third party (for example a profile, company record or address entered in the provider's service), by placing test payloads there and observing how the application handles them.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a provider, takes over a provider account, intercepts the connection, or can place data in the provider's records can use the integration to attack the application: injecting into its database or pages, redirecting its requests to internal systems, tampering with the data it relies on, or disrupting it with slow or oversized responses. Because the data arrives from a trusted partner, the attack may bypass controls applied to user input and go unnoticed. The impact depends on how the data is used, and is high where it reaches queries, commands or other users' browsers.
entries.remediation:
Treat every third-party response as untrusted input:

  • Validate data received from other APIs against a strict schema (types, lengths, formats and allowed values) before using it, and apply the same parameterised queries and output encoding as for user input.
  • Use only encrypted connections with full certificate validation to every provider, and never disable validation to work around a certificate problem.
  • Do not follow redirects from third-party APIs automatically; where a redirect is expected, allow only known destinations.
  • Set connection and response timeouts and maximum response sizes on every outbound call, and handle failures safely.
  • Verify the signature, or another proof of origin, on every webhook or callback before acting on it, and reject replayed messages.
  • Assess providers' security before integrating, keep an inventory of integrations and the data they exchange, and give each integration credentials with only the permissions it needs.

Confirm the fix by reviewing each integration against these controls and, where possible, repeating the tests with malformed, oversized, redirecting and unsigned responses from a test provider.

entries.title: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
entries.summary: A business process such as buying limited stock, booking, signing up or redeeming offers can be automated at scale through the API, with nothing to detect or limit the abuse.
entries.description:
Some business processes cause harm when they are carried out at machine speed or volume, even though each individual request is legitimate: buying limited-availability products, reserving tickets, tables or appointments, creating accounts, redeeming referral credits, vouchers or free trials, posting reviews or comments, and voting. The API exposes such a flow without anything to tell automated use from human use, or to limit how often one person can complete it, so a script can complete it far faster and more often than any genuine customer.

This is not a flaw in the logic of the flow, which works as designed, but a missing design control. It is most visible in APIs because they expose the steps of a flow directly, without the pages, timing and client-side checks that a web interface may add.

The weakness is identified by working with the organisation to list the flows whose abuse would harm the business, then scripting each flow and repeating it rapidly from one account, from several accounts and from several source addresses, and observing whether anything slows, challenges, limits or flags the activity. Testing is kept to quantities agreed with the organisation, so that it does not affect real stock or customers.
entries.impact: Attackers, including resellers and competitors, can buy up limited stock to resell it at a higher price, hold reservations so that genuine customers cannot book, create large numbers of fake accounts, harvest referral rewards, vouchers or free trials, or flood the platform with spam or fake reviews. The result is financial loss, damage to customer trust and reputation, and distorted business data. Each request is legitimate in itself, so the abuse can be hard to spot without monitoring designed for it. The impact depends on the value of the flow and the scale an attacker can reach.
entries.remediation:
Identify the flows that need protection, then add layered controls proportionate to the harm that abuse would cause:

  • Set business limits per account, payment card, delivery address and device, such as a maximum quantity of a limited item, a limit on reservations held, or one referral reward per verified person.
  • Require verified accounts for sensitive flows, for example a confirmed email address or telephone number, and consider waiting periods for new accounts.
  • Add friction where automation is likely: a CAPTCHA or similar challenge at key steps, checks on the timing between steps, and queueing for high-demand releases.
  • Use device and client signals, such as device fingerprinting and detection of headless browsers and known automation tools, or a bot management service at the edge, to identify automated clients.
  • Monitor the flows for unusual patterns, such as many accounts sharing a device, address or payment method, and be able to block and reverse abusive activity.

Confirm the fix by repeating the scripted tests and checking that the controls slow, challenge or block automated use while genuine use remains practical.

entries.title: HTTP Method Override Accepted
entries.summary: The API honours headers or parameters that change the HTTP method of a request, so controls applied to the method as sent, by a proxy, firewall or the application, can be bypassed.
entries.description:
Some frameworks let a client send a request with one HTTP method and have it processed as another, by setting a header such as X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method or X-Method-Override, or a parameter such as _method. The feature exists for clients that can send only GET and POST, such as HTML forms. Examples are the method override middleware in Express and ASP.NET Core, Rack::MethodOverride used by Ruby on Rails, the _method form field in Symfony and Laravel, and Spring's HiddenHttpMethodFilter.

The weakness arises when other components make decisions on the method as sent rather than the method the application acts on. A web application firewall, API gateway or reverse proxy that blocks DELETE or PUT, or applies different authentication or rate limits to them, sees only a POST. Access rules in the application that are keyed on the method may be evaluated before the override is applied. An implementation that honours the override on GET requests can also make state-changing operations reachable from links and cross-site requests.

The weakness is identified by sending POST and GET requests carrying each override header or parameter with the value PUT, PATCH or DELETE, and observing whether the application performs the overridden action, particularly where the same method sent directly is blocked or treated differently.
entries.impact: An authenticated user, or in some configurations an unauthenticated one, can perform operations that a front-end control was meant to block, such as deleting or replacing resources through an API gateway that allows only reads, or can avoid authentication, logging or rate limits applied to specific methods. Where the override is accepted on GET requests, state-changing actions may also become exposed to cross-site request forgery. The impact depends on the operations reachable this way and on which controls rely on the method; where no control depends on it, the feature adds little risk.
entries.remediation:
Disable method overriding where it is not needed, and make sure every control sees the effective method where it is:

  • Remove the override middleware or filter from APIs that do not serve HTML forms, for example by not calling app.UseHttpMethodOverride() in ASP.NET Core, removing the method-override middleware in Express, or leaving HiddenHttpMethodFilter disabled in Spring.
  • Where overriding is needed, accept it only on POST requests, only for the methods the application uses, and only in the one form the client needs, never on GET.
  • Apply authorisation in the application to the effective method, after the override has been resolved, rather than relying on method rules in front of it.
  • Strip override headers at the gateway or reverse proxy for routes that should not use them, or configure the gateway to evaluate the overridden method.
# nginx: remove override headers before proxying to the application # (place with any other proxy_set_header directives in the same block) proxy_set_header X-HTTP-Method-Override ""; proxy_set_header X-HTTP-Method ""; proxy_set_header X-Method-Override "";

Confirm the fix by repeating the override requests and checking that they are rejected or processed with their original method, and that front-end restrictions on methods can no longer be bypassed.

entries.title: gRPC Server Reflection Enabled
entries.summary: The gRPC server exposes the reflection service, so anyone who can connect can list every service and method and download the message definitions needed to call them.
entries.description:
gRPC services are normally called from code generated from the service's Protocol Buffers definitions (.proto files), which describe each service, method and message. The optional server reflection service lets a client ask the server for these definitions at run time, through the grpc.reflection.v1alpha.ServerReflection service or its grpc.reflection.v1 successor. It is useful for development and debugging tools, but the server enables it in production, so anyone who can connect can list every service and method it offers and obtain the full message definitions, including those of internal and administrative methods.

Reflection is turned on in code, for example with reflection.Register() in Go, ProtoReflectionService in Java, enable_server_reflection() in Python or MapGrpcReflectionService() in ASP.NET Core, often because it was copied from an example.

The weakness is identified by connecting to the gRPC port with a tool such as grpcurl (using its list and describe commands) or grpcui, or with the gRPC support in Postman, and checking whether services and methods are listed without supplying any definition files.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the gRPC endpoint obtains a complete description of the API without needing the client application or its definition files. This removes much of the effort of discovering methods and building valid requests, and points directly to internal and administrative methods worth testing. Reflection does not give access to any method by itself, as each method still enforces whatever authentication and authorisation the server applies, but its significance rises where the methods it reveals prove to lack those controls.
entries.remediation:
Register the reflection service only where it is needed:

  • Do not register reflection in production builds, or make its registration depend on the environment or on a configuration setting that is off by default, as in the example below.
  • Where operators need reflection in production, expose it only on an internal listener or network, or require authentication for it through a server interceptor or the platform's authorisation features.
  • Share the .proto files with legitimate clients through source control or documentation instead.
  • Treat this as hardening: enforce authentication and authorisation on every method, so that knowledge of the services gives no access.
// ASP.NET Core: map gRPC reflection only in development builder.Services.AddGrpcReflection(); var app = builder.Build(); if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.MapGrpcReflectionService(); }

Confirm the fix by running grpcurl's list command against the endpoint again and checking that reflection is no longer available.

entries.title: Deprecated SSL and TLS Protocols Supported
entries.summary: The service accepts SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1, protocol versions with known cryptographic weaknesses that current standards and browsers no longer permit.
entries.description:
The service accepts connections using one or more deprecated protocol versions: SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. The IETF prohibited SSL 2.0 and SSL 3.0 years ago (RFC 6176 and RFC 7568) and formally deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 in 2021 (RFC 8996). All mainstream browsers have removed support for them, and PCI DSS no longer accepts SSL or early TLS as strong cryptography.

The older versions have design weaknesses that later versions fixed. SSL 3.0 is open to the POODLE padding oracle attack, SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 to the BEAST attack on CBC-mode encryption, and SSL 2.0 to DROWN, which can also be used to decrypt modern TLS sessions on any server that shares the same RSA key. TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 also rely on MD5 and SHA-1 in their handshake and key derivation, and cannot use the authenticated encryption (AEAD) cipher suites that are now recommended.

Deprecated versions usually remain enabled because platform defaults were never changed, for compatibility with legacy clients, or on appliances and non-web services (mail, LDAPS, RDP, databases) that are configured separately from the main web servers. The versions a service accepts can be listed with testssl.sh, sslscan, SSLyze or Nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script, and vulnerability scanners usually report each deprecated version as a separate finding.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept traffic between a client and the service, for example on shared Wi-Fi or a compromised network segment, may be able to recover secrets such as session cookies from connections that use a deprecated version, and then use them to take over the user's session. POODLE and BEAST also need the victim's browser to run script that makes many repeated requests, which an attacker in that position can usually arrange. Current browsers no longer offer these versions, so the realistic exposure is to older clients, embedded devices and scripts that still negotiate them. The risk is higher where SSL 2.0 is enabled, because DROWN needs no action by the victim and can expose sessions protected by modern TLS on any server that uses the same key.
entries.remediation:
Disable SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on every TLS service, leaving only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3:

# nginx ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; # Apache httpd (mod_ssl); omit +TLSv1.3 where the build does not support it SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3
  • On Windows (IIS, RDP, AD FS, Exchange and other services that use Schannel), create the key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\TLS 1.0\Server with the DWORD values Enabled set to 0 and DisabledByDefault set to 1, repeat this for SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.1, and do the same under each version's Client key for outbound connections, then restart the server.
  • For Java services, list the old versions in the jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms security property. For load balancers, CDNs and appliances, select a TLS policy or profile that allows only TLS 1.2 and later.
  • Include mail, directory, database, VPN and management interfaces, which are often configured separately.

Before disabling a version, check server or load balancer logs for clients that still use it and arrange for them to be updated. Where an old version must remain for a short time, restrict it to the systems that need it and confirm that the server supports TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV (RFC 7507), which lets it refuse a downgraded connection from a client that supports a newer version. Confirm the fix by rescanning each service and checking that only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are accepted.

entries.title: Weak TLS Cipher Suites Supported
entries.summary: The service accepts cipher suites with weak encryption, such as RC4, Triple DES, single DES or export-grade suites, which can let an attacker recover parts of encrypted traffic.
entries.description:
The service accepts one or more cipher suites whose encryption is no longer considered adequate. The variants met most often are:

  • RC4, a stream cipher with statistical biases that allow plaintext sent repeatedly, such as a cookie or password, to be recovered from enough encrypted copies. RFC 7465 prohibits RC4 in TLS.
  • Triple DES (3DES) and other 64-bit block ciphers such as IDEA, which are open to birthday attacks once a large volume of data has been encrypted under one key in a long-lived connection (Sweet32, CVE-2016-2183).
  • Single DES and export-grade suites with 56-bit or 40-bit keys, which can be broken outright with modest resources and were abused in the FREAK and Logjam downgrade attacks.
  • Suites using MD5 for message authentication, which are not known to be broken in TLS but fall well short of current recommendations.

Weak suites usually remain because the cipher list was set years ago, is built from broad keywords, or keeps old suites for legacy clients. Whether one is actually used depends on what the client offers and whose preference order the server follows, so a server that enforces its own order and lists a weak suite early can select it even when a stronger one is available.

The accepted suites can be listed with testssl.sh, sslscan, SSLyze or Nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script. Vulnerability scanners usually report RC4 and 3DES as separate findings, the latter often under the name Sweet32.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe or intercept traffic could recover secrets sent repeatedly over connections that use a weak suite, such as session cookies, authorisation headers or passwords, and use them to access the user's account. The RC4 and Sweet32 attacks need a very large number of encryptions of the same secret, usually generated by script running in the victim's browser over many hours, so they are slow and conspicuous, but they rely on nothing beyond the cipher itself. Export-grade and single DES suites are far weaker: where a client can be made to use one, an attacker with modest computing resources can decrypt or alter the session. Current browsers no longer offer RC4, DES or export suites, which limits the exposure to older clients and non-browser software.
entries.remediation:
Remove every weak suite from the service's configuration and offer only suites with forward secrecy and authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), using an explicit list rather than broad keywords such as ALL, whose contents depend on the library version:

# nginx (TLS 1.2 suites; the TLS 1.3 suites are all strong) ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305; # Apache httpd (mod_ssl) SSLCipherSuite ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305
  • On Windows, set the content and order of the list through Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > SSL Configuration Settings > SSL Cipher Suite Order) or remove individual suites with the Disable-TlsCipherSuite PowerShell cmdlet, then restart the server.
  • For Java, make sure RC4, DES and 3DES_EDE_CBC remain in the jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms security property, as they are in current releases, and that no application setting re-enables them.
  • For load balancers, CDNs and appliances, select a TLS policy or cipher profile that excludes them.

Where a legacy client still needs an older suite, place strong suites first in the server's order and plan the client's upgrade. Confirm the fix by listing the accepted suites again and checking that no RC4, DES, 3DES, IDEA, export or MD5-based suite remains.

entries.title: NULL or Anonymous TLS Cipher Suites Supported
entries.summary: The service accepts NULL cipher suites, which send data unencrypted, or anonymous suites, which encrypt without authenticating the server, removing the protection TLS should give.
entries.description:
The service accepts cipher suites that remove one of the two protections TLS exists to provide:

  • NULL suites, such as TLS_RSA_WITH_NULL_SHA256, authenticate the server and protect the data against tampering but do not encrypt it, so the content of the session crosses the network in clear text.
  • Anonymous suites, such as TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_ECDH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA (ADH and AECDH in OpenSSL's naming), encrypt the data but use a key exchange without a certificate, so the client cannot tell whether it is talking to the genuine server.

Mainstream browsers never offer these suites, so a connection only uses one when the client offers it too, as scripts, libraries, embedded devices and other software configured with broad cipher lists sometimes do. The suites are usually enabled by mistake, through a cipher list built from broad keywords (OpenSSL's ALL, for example, includes the anonymous suites) or through an appliance's defaults. Mail servers using opportunistic STARTTLS sometimes accept anonymous suites deliberately, as unauthenticated encryption between mail servers is still better than none, and the rating should take that context into account.

The suites a service accepts can be listed with testssl.sh, sslscan, SSLyze or Nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script.
entries.impact: Where a client and the service agree on a NULL suite, anyone who can observe the traffic can read everything in the session, including credentials and session tokens. Where they agree on an anonymous suite, an attacker who can intercept the connection can complete a separate key exchange with each side and read or change all of the traffic without either side noticing. Both depend on the client offering such a suite, which limits the exposure to clients configured with broad cipher lists, but those are often automated integrations that carry credentials or sensitive data.
entries.remediation:
Remove all NULL and anonymous suites, preferably by replacing the cipher configuration with an explicit list of strong suites (ECDHE key exchange with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) rather than broad keywords:

# OpenSSL-based servers (nginx ssl_ciphers, Apache SSLCipherSuite): # where an explicit list cannot be used yet, append these exclusions !aNULL:!eNULL
  • On Windows, remove any NULL or anonymous suite from the list set through Group Policy (SSL Cipher Suite Order) or with the Disable-TlsCipherSuite cmdlet, and check that no application enables them through its own settings.
  • For Java services, make sure anon and NULL are listed in the jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms security property.
  • On load balancers and appliances, select a TLS profile that excludes them.
  • Review the cipher settings of scripts and integrations too, so that clients do not offer these suites to other services.

Where a mail server keeps anonymous suites for opportunistic encryption by design, record the decision and ensure that connections needing authentication, such as those to partner organisations, use verified certificates. Confirm the fix by listing the accepted suites again and checking that no NULL or anonymous suite remains.

entries.title: Weak Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange Parameters
entries.summary: The service uses Diffie-Hellman key exchange with a group of 1024 bits or fewer, which a well-resourced attacker could break to decrypt the sessions that rely on it.
entries.description:
The service supports ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) key exchange using a finite field group of 1024 bits or fewer. The secrecy of each session key rests on the difficulty of computing discrete logarithms in that group, and groups of this size no longer give an adequate margin.

The Logjam research in 2015 showed two practical problems. Export-grade groups of 512 bits, offered by servers that still enable DHE_EXPORT suites, can be broken quickly enough to downgrade and intercept a live connection (CVE-2015-4000). More widely, many servers use the same few standard or default 1024-bit primes, and a single large precomputation for one of those primes would let an attacker decrypt passively recorded sessions that used it, an effort considered within the reach of nation-state adversaries.

Weak groups usually come from older software defaults or a parameter file generated years ago. The group size is shown by testssl.sh, sslscan and SSLyze, and by Nmap's ssl-dh-params script, which also identifies commonly shared primes. The issue concerns only DHE suites in TLS 1.2 and earlier: TLS 1.3 negotiates only standard named groups of 2048 bits or more, and elliptic curve key exchange (ECDHE) is not affected.
entries.impact: An attacker with very large computing resources who has recorded traffic could decrypt sessions that used a weak group, exposing whatever they carried, such as credentials and session tokens. For 1024-bit groups this is beyond the reach of most attackers, so the practical risk is limited to well-resourced adversaries and to the future decryption of traffic recorded today. Where export-grade or 512-bit groups are accepted, the attack is within the means of a modest attacker who can intercept traffic, and the rating should be raised.
entries.remediation:
Prefer elliptic curve key exchange, and where finite field Diffie-Hellman must stay, use a group of at least 2048 bits:

  • Order the cipher list so that ECDHE suites come first. Where no client needs DHE, remove the DHE suites altogether, as the OWASP TLS guidance recommends for TLS 1.2.
  • Where DHE is kept, use a group of 2048 bits or more, preferably one of the standard groups defined in RFC 7919 (ffdhe2048 or ffdhe3072), and never a 1024-bit or smaller group or a DHE_EXPORT suite.
# Generate a 2048-bit group openssl dhparam -out /etc/ssl/dhparam.pem 2048 # nginx ssl_dhparam /etc/ssl/dhparam.pem; # Apache httpd (mod_ssl) SSLOpenSSLConfCmd DHParameters "/etc/ssl/dhparam.pem"
  • On Windows (Schannel), set the DWORD value ServerMinKeyBitLength under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\KeyExchangeAlgorithms\Diffie-Hellman to 0x800 (2048 bits), then restart the server.
  • For Java, raise the size with the jdk.tls.ephemeralDHKeySize system property, or remove the DHE suites.

Confirm the fix by rescanning the service and checking that every DHE suite uses a group of at least 2048 bits, or that none is offered.

entries.title: TLS Forward Secrecy Not Supported
entries.summary: The service negotiates key exchanges without forward secrecy, such as static RSA, so anyone who later obtains its private key could decrypt previously recorded sessions.
entries.description:
The service does not support, or does not prefer, cipher suites that provide forward secrecy. In suites that use RSA key exchange (named TLS_RSA_WITH_...) the client encrypts the session's secret with the server's long-term RSA public key, and the static Diffie-Hellman suites (TLS_DH_... and TLS_ECDH_...) likewise derive it from a long-term key. Anyone who later obtains the server's private key can therefore decrypt any recorded session that used one of these suites, however long ago it took place.

Suites using ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE, or DHE) create a fresh key pair for each connection and discard it afterwards, so a later compromise of the server's private key does not expose past sessions. TLS 1.3 provides forward secrecy in every full handshake, because it removed RSA and static Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

Forward secrecy is sometimes left out on purpose, because older network monitoring and intrusion detection tools decrypt traffic passively with a copy of the server's private key, which only works with RSA key exchange. Scanners report the issue when no forward secret suite is offered, or when the server's preference order leads common clients to negotiate RSA key exchange; testssl.sh lists the forward secret suites and simulates the key exchange common clients would negotiate.
entries.impact: The weakness gives an attacker nothing on its own. It matters if the server's private key is ever exposed, for example through a server compromise, a backup, a memory disclosure flaw such as Heartbleed, or a key shared with other systems: an attacker who has recorded traffic, or who records it until the key is replaced, could then decrypt those sessions and read the credentials and data they carried. Forward secrecy limits the damage of a key compromise to future traffic, which is why current guidance, such as the OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet, recommends against RSA key exchange.
entries.remediation:
Offer and prefer cipher suites with ephemeral key exchange, and remove RSA and static Diffie-Hellman key exchange where clients allow:

  • Place ECDHE suites with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 at the top of the server's cipher list, and remove the TLS_RSA_WITH_..., TLS_DH_... and TLS_ECDH_... suites once logs show that no required client depends on them. In OpenSSL cipher strings, !kRSA removes RSA key exchange.
  • Enable TLS 1.3, in which every full handshake has forward secrecy.
  • On Windows, reorder or remove the TLS_RSA_ suites through Group Policy (SSL Cipher Suite Order) or with the Disable-TlsCipherSuite cmdlet.
  • Where session tickets are used, rotate the ticket encryption keys frequently or disable tickets, because a long-lived ticket key would allow resumed sessions to be decrypted in the same way.
  • Where a monitoring tool relies on the server's private key, move it to a design that works with forward secrecy, such as inspection at the TLS-terminating proxy, before removing RSA key exchange.

Confirm the fix by rescanning the service and checking that common clients negotiate ECDHE or TLS 1.3 key exchange.

entries.title: TLS 1.3 Not Supported
entries.summary: The service does not support TLS 1.3, the current version of the protocol, so its connections cannot benefit from the newer version's stronger handshake and safer cipher suites.
entries.description:
The service supports TLS 1.2 but not TLS 1.3. TLS 1.2 remains acceptable when configured with strong cipher suites, so this is not a vulnerability in itself, but TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removes whole classes of weakness by design and is now the recommended default.

TLS 1.3 drops RSA key exchange, static Diffie-Hellman, CBC-mode and RC4 encryption, compression and renegotiation, leaving only authenticated encryption suites with forward secrecy, so many of the configuration errors reported against TLS 1.2 services cannot occur. It also encrypts more of the handshake, including the server's certificate, protects the negotiation against downgrade, and needs one fewer round trip to establish a connection.

Support depends on the TLS library and server software: OpenSSL added TLS 1.3 in its 1.1.1 release, Java in Java 11, and Windows Schannel in Windows Server 2022 and Windows 11, so services on older platforms cannot offer it without an upgrade. Its absence is shown by testssl.sh, sslscan and SSLyze, and vulnerability scanners usually report it as informational.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. Without TLS 1.3, the service relies entirely on its TLS 1.2 configuration being correct, and clients lose the extra protection of the newer protocol's encrypted handshake and built-in downgrade protection. The absence of TLS 1.3 often indicates an older TLS library or operating system, which may carry other unpatched weaknesses.
entries.remediation:
Enable TLS 1.3 alongside TLS 1.2, upgrading the TLS library, server software or operating system where it does not support the newer version:

# nginx (built against OpenSSL 1.1.1 or later) ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; # Apache httpd (mod_ssl) SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3
  • On Windows Server 2022 and later, TLS 1.3 is enabled by default in Schannel; check that it has not been disabled under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\TLS 1.3.
  • For load balancers, CDNs and cloud services, select a TLS policy that includes TLS 1.3.
  • Leave 0-RTT (early data) disabled, for example ssl_early_data off in nginx, unless the application has been reviewed for replay, because data sent as early data can be replayed by an attacker.
  • Test interception proxies, firewalls and monitoring tools on the network path, as some older middleboxes handle TLS 1.3 poorly.

Confirm the change by connecting with a TLS 1.3 client, for example openssl s_client with the -tls1_3 option, or by rescanning the service.

entries.title: Untrusted TLS Certificate
entries.summary: The service presents a certificate that clients cannot trust, such as a self-signed certificate or one from a private authority, so they cannot confirm they reached the genuine server.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service does not chain to a certification authority (CA) that clients trust. The usual causes are a self-signed certificate, often generated automatically when software or an appliance is installed; a certificate issued by an internal CA whose root certificate has not been distributed to the clients that connect; or a chain leading to a root that has been removed from trust stores.

Because the certificate cannot be verified, clients have no way to distinguish the genuine service from an impostor presenting a certificate of its own. Browsers show a full-page warning, and users who reach the service regularly learn to click through it; non-browser clients are often configured to skip certificate verification altogether so that they can connect.

The issue is shown by the browser warning, by a verification error from openssl s_client, and by testssl.sh, sslscan and vulnerability scanners, which report it under names such as SSL Certificate Cannot Be Trusted or SSL Self-Signed Certificate. A certificate from an internal CA is a problem only for clients that do not trust that CA: where all intended clients are managed devices with the internal root installed, the scanner's result reflects only the tester's own trust store, and this should be checked before the finding is reported.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept traffic, for example on shared Wi-Fi or by ARP or DNS spoofing on an internal network, can present a certificate of their own. A user accustomed to accepting the warning, or a client that does not verify certificates, will then connect through the attacker, who can read and alter everything in the session, including credentials entered at a login page or management interface. The risk is greatest for administrative interfaces and other services that carry credentials or sensitive data.
entries.remediation:
Replace the certificate with one that every intended client trusts:

  • For services reached from the internet or by unmanaged devices, use a certificate from a publicly trusted CA. Automated issuance through the ACME protocol, for example with Let's Encrypt and a client such as Certbot, removes most of the cost and effort.
  • For internal services, issue the certificate from the organisation's internal CA, such as Active Directory Certificate Services, and distribute the CA's root certificate to all managed clients, for example through Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Public Key Policies > Trusted Root Certification Authorities) or the device management platform.
  • Replace the default self-signed certificates on appliances, hypervisors, printers, management controllers and other devices, which are a common source of this finding.
  • Configure the server to send the full chain of intermediate certificates.
  • Where non-browser clients or scripts were set to skip certificate verification, re-enable it once the certificate is trusted.

For web services, HTTP Strict Transport Security then prevents browsers from offering a way past certificate warnings. Confirm the fix by connecting from a client with a standard trust store, or from a managed device for internal services, and checking that the certificate validates without a warning.

patterns.re: \bself[- ]?signed\b|\b(untrusted|not trusted|cannot be trusted|unknown (CA|certificate authority)|invalid) (SSL |TLS |X\.509 )?certificate\b|\bcertificate\b.*\b(cannot be trusted|not trusted|untrusted|unknown CA|chain of trust)\b|\buntrusted[- ]root\b

entries.title: Expired TLS Certificate
entries.summary: The service presents a TLS certificate whose validity period has ended, so clients reject it or warn their users, who may then learn to ignore certificate warnings.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service is past its expiry date (the notAfter field) and is no longer valid. Clients that check validity, which includes all browsers and most TLS libraries, reject it or show a warning. The same applies when an intermediate certificate in the chain has expired, even if the server's own certificate is current.

Expiry usually means that renewal was missed: no one was responsible for it, the reminder went to a former member of staff, or a renewed certificate was obtained but not installed on every server, load balancer or appliance that uses it. It is most common on internal services and devices that are not monitored, and on test or forgotten systems.

The issue is shown by the browser warning, by openssl s_client reporting certificate has expired, by testssl.sh and sslscan, and by vulnerability scanners, which compare the certificate's validity dates with the current date. An expired certificate on a public service also suggests that the owner's certificate inventory and renewal process are incomplete.
entries.impact: Users who meet the warning regularly learn to accept certificate errors, so an attacker able to intercept their traffic could present a certificate of their own and read or alter the session, including credentials. Clients that enforce validity, such as API integrations, mobile apps and browsers on sites protected by HTTP Strict Transport Security, cannot connect at all, which can cause an outage, and administrators may disable certificate verification in those clients to restore service, leaving them open to interception afterwards.
entries.remediation:
Renew the certificate and install it, with its full chain, everywhere it is used:

  • Obtain a new certificate, preferably for a newly generated key, and install it on every server, load balancer, proxy and appliance that presents the old one, then reload or restart each service and check the certificate actually presented.
  • Automate issuance and renewal wherever possible, using the ACME protocol (for example Certbot or the platform's built-in ACME client) for publicly trusted certificates, and certificate auto-enrolment in Active Directory Certificate Services for internal ones. The CA/Browser Forum has agreed to reduce the maximum validity of publicly trusted certificates in stages to 47 days by 2029, which makes manual renewal increasingly impractical.
  • Keep an inventory of certificates with an owner for each, and monitor expiry dates centrally, with alerts well ahead of expiry. Certificate Transparency logs can be searched to find publicly trusted certificates issued for the organisation's domains.
  • Re-enable certificate verification in any client where it was turned off as a workaround.

Confirm the fix by connecting to the service and checking the new certificate's validity dates and chain.

entries.title: TLS Certificate Hostname Mismatch
entries.summary: The service presents a TLS certificate that is not valid for the name clients use to reach it, so clients warn or refuse, and users may learn to ignore certificate warnings.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service is not valid for the host name clients use to connect. Clients compare the name they asked for with the DNS names in the certificate's Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension, and current browsers no longer accept a name that appears only in the older Common Name (CN) field. A wildcard entry matches one label only: *.example.com covers www.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com.

Common causes are a default or self-signed certificate naming a device's internal host name; a certificate for another site on the same address, because the server does not select certificates by Server Name Indication (SNI) or presents a default certificate for unrecognised names; a certificate issued for the internal name of a service that is also published externally; and services reached by IP address.

The issue is shown by the browser warning, by testssl.sh and sslscan, and by vulnerability scanners. Scanners that connect by IP address, or without sending the expected SNI name, often report a mismatch for a correctly configured service, so the finding should be confirmed using the host name that clients actually use.
entries.impact: Users who meet the warning regularly learn to accept certificate errors, so an attacker able to intercept their traffic could present a certificate of their own, which raises a similar warning, and read or alter the session, including credentials. Non-browser clients either fail to connect or, often, have host name checking disabled to make them work, which leaves them open to interception by anyone holding any certificate their trust store accepts. Where the mismatch appears only when the service is reached by IP address, and clients always use the correct name, the practical risk is low.
entries.remediation:
Present a certificate that is valid for every name clients use to reach the service:

  • Issue a certificate whose SAN lists each fully qualified name in use, including the bare domain where that is used, rather than relying on the CN.
  • Where several sites share an address, configure each virtual host with its own certificate so that the server selects it by SNI, and configure the default site to present a suitable certificate or to reject unrecognised names (in nginx, ssl_reject_handshake on in the default server block).
  • Use separate certificates for internal and external names, as the OWASP TLS guidance recommends, rather than exposing internal names in public certificates.
  • Replace the default certificates on appliances and devices with certificates issued for the names used to manage them, and give clients a DNS name to use rather than an IP address.
  • Re-enable host name verification in any client where it was disabled.

Confirm the fix by connecting with each name in use while sending the matching SNI value, for example with openssl s_client and its -servername option, and checking that the certificate validates for that name.

patterns.re: \bcertificate\b.*\b(hostname|host name|common name|CN|subject (alternative )?name)\b.*\b(mismatch|wrong|does not match|invalid|incorrect)\b|\b(wrong|mismatch(ed)?) (hostname|host name)\b.*certificate|\bcertificate with wrong hostname\b|\bmismatched[- ]ssl

entries.title: TLS Certificate Signed Using a Weak Hashing Algorithm
entries.summary: The service's certificate, or one in its chain, is signed using MD5 or SHA-1, hash algorithms broken by collision attacks, which many current clients reject.
entries.description:
A certificate presented by the service, either its own or an intermediate certificate in its chain, carries a signature made with a weak hash algorithm: typically SHA-1 (sha1WithRSAEncryption) or, on very old systems, MD5. Both hash functions are broken by collision attacks. MD5 collisions were used in 2008 to create a rogue CA certificate and later by the Flame malware to forge a code signing certificate; practical SHA-1 collisions were published in 2017 (SHAttered), followed in 2020 by a chosen-prefix collision of the kind needed to forge certificates.

Publicly trusted CAs stopped issuing SHA-1 certificates years ago, and current browsers and many other clients no longer accept SHA-1 signatures, so the finding is now met mainly on internal CAs that still sign with SHA-1, old self-signed certificates and devices with built-in certificates. The signature on a root certificate is not a concern, because clients trust a root directly rather than by checking its signature: only the signatures on the server and intermediate certificates matter, and a scanner that flags a SHA-1 root is reporting a false positive.

The signature algorithm of each certificate in the chain is shown by testssl.sh, sslscan, openssl x509 -text and vulnerability scanners.
entries.impact: An attacker able to produce a hash collision against a CA that still signs with the weak algorithm could obtain a certificate that appears validly issued for a service they do not control, and use it to intercept that service's traffic without a warning. For SHA-1 this needs a chosen-prefix collision, which is costly and requires the attacker to predict the content of a certificate the CA will sign, so it is beyond most attackers; for MD5 it is far easier. In practice the more immediate effect is that current clients reject the certificate, causing warnings that users learn to ignore, or failures that lead administrators to disable verification.
entries.remediation:
Replace any certificate signed with MD5 or SHA-1 by one signed using SHA-256 or stronger (for example sha256WithRSAEncryption or ecdsa-with-SHA256), and correct the issuing CA:

  • Reissue the server certificate, and any intermediate CA certificate signed with a weak hash, then install the new chain on every system that uses it.
  • For an Active Directory Certificate Services CA still signing with SHA-1, change its hash algorithm to SHA-256 after checking that every client and application relying on the CA supports it. For a CA whose key is held by a CNG key storage provider this is done with certutil -setreg ca\csp\CNGHashAlgorithm SHA256 followed by a restart of the Certificate Services service; a CA using a legacy cryptographic service provider must first be migrated to a key storage provider.
  • For devices with built-in certificates, install a certificate issued by a current CA, or apply firmware that supports one.
  • A trusted root certificate does not need to be replaced because of the hash used in its own self-signature.

Confirm the fix by checking the signature algorithm of each certificate the service presents, apart from the root.

entries.title: TLS Certificate With an Insufficient Key Length
entries.summary: The service's certificate uses a public key that is too short, such as an RSA key under 2048 bits, which a well-resourced attacker could break to impersonate the service.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service contains a public key shorter than current minimums: an RSA key of less than 2048 bits, most often 1024 bits and occasionally 512 or 768 bits, or an elliptic curve key on a curve smaller than P-256. NIST has not allowed RSA keys under 2048 bits for new signatures since the end of 2013, and the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements forbid publicly trusted CAs from issuing them, so the finding is now met mainly on self-signed and internal certificates, appliances that generate a key at first boot, and long-lived certificates that have never been replaced.

The security of an RSA key depends on the difficulty of factoring its modulus. The largest RSA modulus publicly factored is 829 bits (RSA-250, in 2020); 1024-bit keys have not been publicly factored but are considered within reach of well-resourced attackers, while 512-bit keys can be factored within hours using rented cloud computing.

The key size is shown by testssl.sh, sslscan, openssl x509 -text and vulnerability scanners. Devices often use the same key for several services, which should be checked as well.
entries.impact: An attacker who factors the key obtains the service's private key, and can then impersonate the service to its clients without any warning and decrypt recorded sessions that used RSA key exchange. For 1024-bit keys this is beyond the reach of most attackers, so the realistic risk is limited to well-resourced adversaries and grows over time; a 512-bit key can be broken by a modest attacker and justifies a higher rating. Some current clients also reject RSA keys under 2048 bits, which can cause connection failures and warnings that users learn to ignore.
entries.remediation:
Generate a new key pair of adequate length, have a new certificate issued for it, and retire the old key:

  • Use an RSA key of at least 2048 bits (3072 bits for keys expected to remain in use for many years) or an ECDSA key on P-256 or P-384, generated on the system that will use it.
# RSA 2048-bit key and certificate signing request openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr # ECDSA P-256 key and certificate signing request openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr
  • For internal certificates from Active Directory Certificate Services, set the minimum key size on the certificate template's Cryptography tab to 2048 or more, so that short keys cannot be requested again.
  • For appliances, regenerate the device certificate with a longer key or install one issued by the organisation's CA; where the firmware cannot support 2048-bit keys, plan its replacement.
  • Revoke the old certificate where a CA issued it, and do not reuse the old key elsewhere.

Confirm the fix by checking the key size in the certificate the service presents.

entries.title: TLS Certificate Expiring Soon
entries.summary: The service's TLS certificate is still valid but expires soon, and unless it is renewed in time clients will start to reject it or warn their users.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service is currently valid, but its expiry date (the notAfter field) falls within a short period, typically 30 to 90 days depending on the tool that reports it. This is not a weakness in itself; it is reported so that the certificate is renewed before it expires and starts to cause errors.

The finding matters most where renewal is manual, or where there is no evidence of automated renewal, monitoring or a named owner for the certificate. Certificates from automated services such as Let's Encrypt are valid for 90 days or less and are normally renewed around a month before expiry, so a short remaining lifetime on such a certificate is expected and is not a concern while renewal is working. The CA/Browser Forum has agreed to reduce the maximum validity of all publicly trusted certificates in stages to 47 days by 2029, which will make short remaining lifetimes normal.

The expiry date is shown by testssl.sh, sslscan, openssl x509 -noout -enddate and vulnerability scanners, which flag certificates that expire within a set window.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact while the certificate remains valid. If it is not renewed in time, clients will reject it or show warnings, causing an outage for automated clients and for browsers on sites that use HTTP Strict Transport Security, and teaching other users to accept certificate warnings, which an attacker able to intercept traffic could exploit.
entries.remediation:
Renew the certificate before it expires and install it, with its full chain, on every system that presents it, then reload the services and check that the new certificate is being served. To prevent a recurrence:

  • Automate issuance and renewal through the ACME protocol for publicly trusted certificates, and through certificate auto-enrolment in Active Directory Certificate Services for internal ones.
  • Keep an inventory of certificates, each with a named owner, including those on load balancers, appliances and cloud services, and monitor expiry dates centrally with alerts well before expiry.
  • Prepare for shorter certificate lifetimes, as the CA/Browser Forum schedule will make manual renewal of publicly trusted certificates impractical.

Confirm the fix by checking the validity dates of the certificate the service presents.

patterns.re: \bcertificate\b.*\b(expires? soon|expiry (date )?approaching|will expire|expiring|about to expire|expires within)\b|\bcertificate expiry\b

entries.title: Incomplete TLS Certificate Chain
entries.summary: The service does not send the intermediate certificates that link its certificate to a trusted root, so some clients cannot validate it and fail or show a warning.
entries.description:
A TLS server is expected to send its own certificate followed by the intermediate CA certificates that link it to a trusted root. The service sends an incomplete chain, usually only its own certificate, so a client that does not already hold the missing intermediate cannot build a path to a root it trusts. Related faults are a chain sent in the wrong order and an outdated intermediate left over from a previous certificate.

The fault is easily missed because desktop browsers often hide it: some fetch missing intermediates from the address in the certificate's Authority Information Access extension, and others keep a cache or preloaded list of known intermediates. Many other clients do neither, including command-line tools, programming language libraries, Android apps and API integrations, and these reject the connection.

The issue is shown by testssl.sh, by openssl s_client -showcerts, which lists exactly what the server sends and reports unable to get local issuer certificate, and by online checkers and vulnerability scanners, which report the chain as incomplete. It typically appears after a certificate is renewed or replaced and only the server certificate file is updated.
entries.impact: Affected clients cannot connect, which can break integrations, mobile apps and automated jobs while the service appears to work in a browser. The security risk is indirect: users of affected clients may be shown warnings that they learn to accept, and developers and administrators often respond to the errors by disabling certificate verification in their clients, which leaves those clients open to interception by an attacker who can present any certificate.
entries.remediation:
Configure the service to send the complete chain, from its own certificate up to, but not including, the root:

# nginx: the file holds the server certificate followed by the intermediates ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/fullchain.pem; # Apache httpd 2.4.8 and later: the intermediates can follow the server certificate SSLCertificateFile /etc/ssl/certs/fullchain.pem
  • On IIS and other Windows services, import the intermediate certificates into the local computer's Intermediate Certification Authorities store so that Windows sends them with the server certificate.
  • On load balancers and appliances, upload the intermediate certificates as the chain or CA bundle associated with the server certificate.
  • Take the intermediates from the CA's current bundle for the new certificate rather than reusing an old file, as CAs change their intermediates.
  • Add a check of the chain to the renewal process, and re-enable certificate verification in any client where it was disabled to work around the error.

Confirm the fix with openssl s_client -showcerts from a client without cached intermediates, checking that each certificate is followed by its issuer and that verification succeeds.
keywords: unable to get local issuer certificate

entries.title: Revoked TLS Certificate
entries.summary: The service presents a TLS certificate that its issuing authority has revoked, which clients checking revocation refuse, and which may mean its private key was compromised.
entries.description:
The certificate presented by the service has been revoked by the certification authority (CA) that issued it: it is listed in the CA's certificate revocation list (CRL) or reported as revoked by its Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) responder. A CA revokes a certificate when its private key is reported as compromised, when it was issued in error or in breach of the CA's rules, when its owner asks for it to be withdrawn or replaced, or when the details it certifies are no longer correct. Under the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements, publicly trusted CAs must revoke within 24 hours or five days depending on the reason, so a revoked certificate can appear with little warning.

Clients handle revocation inconsistently. Some check it and refuse the connection; many check only some certificates, ignore a failure to reach the revocation service, or do not check at all, and continue to accept the certificate. A service can therefore keep working for most users after its certificate has been revoked.

The issue is shown by testssl.sh, which checks OCSP and CRL status when run with its --phone-out option, by openssl ocsp queries to the CA's responder, and by some vulnerability scanners. The revocation reason, where the CA publishes one, indicates how serious the finding is.
entries.impact: Clients that check revocation cannot connect, which can cause an outage. If the certificate was revoked because its private key was compromised, whoever holds that key can impersonate the service to every client that does not check revocation, without any warning, and read or alter their traffic. Where the revocation was routine, for example because the certificate had been replaced, the direct risk is lower, but the service is still presenting a certificate that its CA no longer vouches for.
entries.remediation:
Replace the certificate promptly and establish why it was revoked:

  • Generate a new key pair, obtain a new certificate for it, and install it, with its chain, on every system that presents the revoked one. Do not reuse the old key.
  • Find out the revocation reason from the CA or the certificate's owner. If it was key compromise, treat it as a security incident: identify where the key was stored and how it was exposed, and replace any other certificate that shares the key.
  • If the certificate was revoked after being replaced, remove it from the systems that still present it, such as secondary servers, load balancers or disaster recovery sites.
  • Include certificate status in monitoring, so that a revocation is noticed promptly.

Confirm the fix by checking that the service presents the new certificate and that its status with the CA is good.

entries.title: Wildcard TLS Certificate in Use
entries.summary: The service uses a wildcard certificate, valid for every host name at one level of a domain, so the compromise of any system holding its key affects all of them.
entries.description:
The service presents a wildcard certificate, one whose Subject Alternative Name contains an entry such as *.example.com that is valid for any host name at that level of the domain. Wildcard certificates are convenient, but the same private key then has to be installed on every server, load balancer or appliance that uses the certificate, often including systems of very different importance and exposure.

This is not a vulnerability in itself. It is reported because it breaks the principle of least privilege: the key is only as safe as the least protected system holding it, and whoever obtains it can impersonate every host name the certificate covers, including high-value services that never held the key themselves. Shared certificates also make cross-protocol attacks such as ALPACA more likely to succeed, in which an attacker redirects a victim's TLS connection to a different service, such as a mail or FTP server, that accepts the same certificate. The NSA published guidance on these risks in 2021.

The finding is identified by inspecting the certificate's Subject Alternative Name with a browser, testssl.sh, sslscan or openssl x509 -text; its significance depends on how many systems share the key and how well each is protected.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. If the private key is stolen from any system that holds it, an attacker who can intercept traffic could impersonate any host name the certificate covers without causing a warning, and read or alter the traffic of those services. Shared keys also make the certificate harder to replace quickly after a compromise, because every system using it must be updated.
entries.remediation:
Limit where wildcard certificates are used and how widely their keys are shared:

  • Prefer a separate certificate for each service or group of related services, which automated issuance through ACME makes practical, particularly for high-value services such as identity providers, VPN gateways and payment systems.
  • Where a wildcard certificate is kept, never share it between systems of different trust levels, such as an internet-facing web server and an internal server, and limit its scope by issuing it for a subdomain (for example *.app.example.com) rather than the organisation's main domain.
  • Terminate TLS for the hosts it covers on a reverse proxy or load balancer, so that the key is held on as few systems as possible.
  • Keep a list of every system holding the key, so that all can be updated if it is compromised or expires.
  • Configure services to reject connections whose Server Name Indication or Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation values do not match the service, which defeats ALPACA-style redirection.

Confirm the position by reviewing the certificate inventory and the systems holding each wildcard key.

entries.title: OpenSSL Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)
entries.summary: The service uses an OpenSSL version vulnerable to Heartbleed, which lets anyone read chunks of the server's memory, including private keys, passwords and session data.
entries.description:
The service uses a version of OpenSSL affected by Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160): the 1.0.1 series before 1.0.1g, and 1.0.2 beta 1. The flaw is in OpenSSL's handling of the TLS and DTLS heartbeat extension. A heartbeat request carries a payload and a field stating its length, which the vulnerable code trusts without checking it against the data actually received, so a request claiming a long payload causes the server to return up to about 64 KB of its process memory in the reply.

The attack needs no authentication, can be repeated as often as the attacker likes to read different areas of memory, and leaves no trace in normal application logs. It affects any software built on a vulnerable OpenSSL, not only web servers: mail and VPN servers, appliances and embedded devices, and also clients, whose memory a malicious server can read in the same way. Statically linked or bundled copies of OpenSSL are easily missed when the operating system's own package is updated.

The vulnerability can be confirmed without disrupting the service using Nmap's ssl-heartbleed script, testssl.sh or vulnerability scanners, which send a malformed heartbeat and check whether extra memory is returned.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker anywhere on the network can repeatedly read memory from the service's process, which may contain the server's private TLS key, user names and passwords, session cookies, and the contents of other users' requests and responses. With the private key, the attacker can impersonate the service and decrypt recorded traffic that used RSA key exchange; with session cookies or passwords, they can take over user accounts. Because exploitation leaves no trace in normal logs, any secret that passed through a vulnerable service must be treated as possibly exposed.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade OpenSSL and replace any secret that may have been exposed:

  • Upgrade to a currently supported OpenSSL release from the operating system vendor or the OpenSSL project; the 1.0.1 series has long been out of support. Restart every service that uses the library, and update software and appliances that bundle their own copy through the vendor's patches or firmware.
  • Generate new private keys, obtain new certificates for them, and revoke the old certificates, as the old keys may have been read.
  • Invalidate active sessions and tokens, and require password changes for accounts that used the service while it was vulnerable, along with any other credentials or API keys that passed through it.
  • Review the host's other components, as a system this far behind on OpenSSL updates usually has other unpatched software.

Where an upgrade cannot be made at once, OpenSSL can be rebuilt without the heartbeat extension (the -DOPENSSL_NO_HEARTBEATS compile option), or the service can be restricted to trusted networks. Confirm the fix by repeating the Heartbleed check and confirming the OpenSSL version in use.

entries.title: OpenSSL ChangeCipherSpec Injection (CVE-2014-0224)
entries.summary: The service uses an OpenSSL version that accepts ChangeCipherSpec messages too early, letting an attacker in the middle force weak keys and read or alter traffic with vulnerable clients.
entries.description:
The service uses a version of OpenSSL affected by the ChangeCipherSpec (CCS) injection vulnerability (CVE-2014-0224): releases before 0.9.8za, 1.0.0 before 1.0.0m, and 1.0.1 before 1.0.1h. In the TLS handshake, the ChangeCipherSpec message tells the other side to switch to the newly agreed keys. Vulnerable versions accept this message before the master secret has been established, so an attacker in the middle of the connection can inject it early on both sides and cause them to derive their session keys from predictable values that the attacker can calculate.

The full attack works only when both ends are vulnerable. The OpenSSL advisory states that OpenSSL clients were vulnerable in all versions, but that servers were only known to be exploitable in the 1.0.1 series and the first 1.0.2 beta, so the risk depends on which clients connect: current browsers are not affected, whereas scripts, command-line tools, applications and devices built on older OpenSSL releases may be.

The vulnerability can be confirmed with Nmap's ssl-ccs-injection script, testssl.sh or vulnerability scanners, which send an early ChangeCipherSpec message and observe whether the server accepts it.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept traffic between a vulnerable client and a vulnerable server can decrypt and modify the session, exposing credentials, session tokens and data, and altering requests or responses without either side detecting it. Connections from current browsers and other unaffected clients cannot be attacked this way, so the practical exposure is to automated integrations, older applications and embedded devices built on vulnerable OpenSSL releases, which are often the clients of services that have themselves gone unpatched for years.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade OpenSSL on the server, and on any clients that connect to it, to a currently supported release; there is no configuration setting that removes the flaw:

  • Apply the operating system vendor's OpenSSL update or move to a supported release from the OpenSSL project, then restart every service that uses the library.
