  • For appliances and software that bundle their own copy of OpenSSL, apply the vendor's patch or firmware update.
  • Identify the clients that connect to the service, particularly scripts, integrations and devices, and upgrade any that use a vulnerable OpenSSL release.
  • Review the host for other outdated components, as a library this far behind on updates is rarely the only one.

Until the upgrade is complete, restrict access to the service to trusted networks where interception is less likely. Confirm the fix by repeating the CCS injection check and confirming the OpenSSL version in use.

entries.title: RSA Key Exchange Padding Oracle (ROBOT)
entries.summary: The service's handling of RSA key exchange reveals whether decrypted data was correctly padded, giving attackers an oracle to decrypt recorded sessions or sign as the server.
entries.description:
The service supports TLS cipher suites that use RSA key exchange, and its TLS implementation responds differently, through a different alert, a closed connection, a timeout or a difference in timing, depending on whether the client's encrypted key exchange message is correctly padded under PKCS #1 v1.5. This difference acts as an oracle for the adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack described by Daniel Bleichenbacher in 1998: by sending many modified versions of a captured message and observing the responses, an attacker can perform operations with the server's RSA private key without ever obtaining the key itself.

The TLS standards have required implementations to hide this difference since soon after the attack was published, but in 2017 the ROBOT research (Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat) found the flaw again in products from several major vendors, including load balancers, firewalls and TLS libraries, each of which issued its own advisory and CVE identifier. Testing distinguishes a strong oracle, which needs relatively few queries to exploit, from a weak one, which needs many more.

The issue is identified with the researchers' robot-detect tool, testssl.sh or vulnerability scanners. It affects only servers that accept RSA key exchange suites (TLS_RSA_WITH_...); TLS 1.3 removed RSA key exchange entirely.
entries.impact: An attacker who has recorded a session that used RSA key exchange can use the oracle to decrypt it, exposing credentials, session tokens and data, provided they can send the large number of queries the attack needs to the live server. The same oracle can in principle be used to create a signature with the server's key and so impersonate it, but this is much harder to complete within the time limits of a live connection. Sessions that used ECDHE key exchange cannot be decrypted this way, so the exposure is greatest where clients commonly negotiate RSA key exchange and the oracle is strong.
entries.remediation:
Remove the oracle, and preferably RSA key exchange altogether:

  • Apply the vendor's fix for the affected product, as listed in its ROBOT advisory, then restart or reload the TLS service.
  • Disable all cipher suites that use RSA key exchange (TLS_RSA_WITH_...) and keep the ECDHE suites, which also provide forward secrecy. In OpenSSL cipher strings, !kRSA removes them; on Windows, use Group Policy (SSL Cipher Suite Order) or the Disable-TlsCipherSuite cmdlet; on load balancers, select a cipher profile without them.
  • Enable TLS 1.3, which does not use RSA key exchange.
  • Where a product has no fix and RSA key exchange cannot be removed, restrict the service to trusted networks until it can be upgraded or replaced.

Confirm the fix by repeating the ROBOT test and checking that no TLS_RSA_WITH_... suite is accepted.

entries.title: Insecure TLS Renegotiation Supported
entries.summary: The service allows TLS renegotiation without the RFC 5746 secure renegotiation extension, letting an attacker in the middle inject data at the start of a victim's session.
entries.description:
TLS renegotiation lets either party start a new handshake within an existing connection, for example to request a client certificate partway through a session. In its original design, the new handshake was not cryptographically tied to the connection it took place on. An attacker in the middle could therefore open a connection to the server, send data of their choosing, and then pass the victim's own handshake through as a renegotiation of that connection: the server treats the attacker's data and the victim's as one stream, while the victim sees an ordinary new connection (CVE-2009-3555).

RFC 5746 fixed the flaw in 2010 with the renegotiation indication extension, which binds each renegotiation to the handshake before it. The finding means that the service does not support this extension yet still allows renegotiation, which usually points to a TLS library or appliance firmware that has not been updated for many years. TLS 1.3 removed renegotiation altogether.

The issue is shown by openssl s_client, which reports Secure Renegotiation IS NOT supported, and by testssl.sh, sslscan and vulnerability scanners. A separate but related finding is client-initiated renegotiation, where a server lets clients repeatedly start new handshakes and can be made to spend disproportionate processing effort, as exploited by tools such as THC-SSL-DOS (CVE-2011-1473).
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept a victim's connection can make the server process a request of the attacker's choosing as if the victim had sent it. With HTTPS, the attacker's request can be combined with the victim's session cookie or client certificate, so the server carries out an action, such as a change or a transfer, under the victim's identity. The attacker cannot read the response, which limits the direct exposure of data, though in some applications the injected request can cause the victim's data to be sent somewhere the attacker can see it. The attack needs an interception position and depends on how the application handles the combined request.
entries.remediation:
Update the TLS library or firmware so that the service supports secure renegotiation as defined in RFC 5746, and disable renegotiation wherever it is not needed:

  • Apply the operating system or appliance vendor's updates. All currently supported TLS libraries implement RFC 5746, so the finding usually indicates software that is long out of support.
  • Disable client-initiated renegotiation, which few applications need, to remove the related denial of service risk. Where server-initiated renegotiation is used only to request client certificates, consider requiring the certificate during the initial handshake instead.
  • Enable TLS 1.3, which does not support renegotiation.

Until the update is possible, restrict the service to trusted networks. Confirm the fix with openssl s_client, which should report Secure Renegotiation IS supported, and by rescanning the service.

entries.title: TLS Compression Enabled (CRIME)
entries.summary: The service supports TLS-level compression, which lets an attacker who can observe traffic and influence requests recover secrets such as session cookies (the CRIME attack).
entries.description:
The service accepts TLS-level compression, which compresses data before it is encrypted. Compression shortens repeated text, so when a secret such as a session cookie is compressed together with data an attacker can influence, the length of the encrypted record reveals whether the attacker's guess matches part of the secret. The CRIME attack, published in 2012 (CVE-2012-4929), uses this to recover a cookie a few characters at a time: the attacker makes the victim's browser send many requests with chosen content, typically through script on a page the victim visits, and watches the size of the resulting encrypted records.

Browsers disabled TLS compression in response to the attack, and TLS 1.3 removed it, so a connection is only compressed when the client also offers compression, as some older libraries and non-browser clients do. Server support usually indicates an old TLS library or a configuration that explicitly enables it.

The issue is shown by testssl.sh, which reports CRIME, and by vulnerability scanners; openssl s_client reports the compression method negotiated, provided the client build itself offers compression. A related attack, BREACH, uses HTTP-level compression of response bodies and is not prevented by disabling TLS compression.
entries.impact: Where a client negotiates compression, an attacker who can observe the encrypted traffic and cause the victim's client to send chosen requests could recover secrets carried in the compressed data, such as session cookies or authorisation headers, and use them to take over the victim's session. Current browsers do not offer TLS compression, and the attack needs both a network position and a way to drive the victim's requests, so the practical exposure is small and limited to older or non-browser clients.
entries.remediation:
Disable TLS compression on the service:

  • In Apache httpd, set SSLCompression off, which is the default in current releases.
  • In software built on OpenSSL, set the SSL_OP_NO_COMPRESSION option, or upgrade to a current OpenSSL release, in which compression is disabled by default and is only available in builds that explicitly enable it.
  • For nginx, appliances and other software with no setting for it, upgrade to a release that disables TLS compression.
  • Enable TLS 1.3, which has no compression, and remove deprecated protocol versions.

Disabling TLS compression does not address HTTP response compression; where responses that contain secrets are compressed, assess the BREACH attack separately. Confirm the fix with testssl.sh, or with an openssl s_client build that offers compression, checking that no compression is negotiated.

entries.title: SSH Weak Cryptographic Algorithms Supported
entries.summary: The SSH server offers obsolete key exchange, cipher, MAC or host key algorithms, which older clients may negotiate instead of the strong ones the server also supports.
entries.description:
The SSH server offers algorithms that are no longer considered strong enough in the negotiation that starts every connection. SSH negotiates four kinds of algorithm separately (key exchange, host key signature, cipher and message authentication code, or MAC), and the server lists every algorithm it is willing to use for each. Weak entries commonly found include:

  • key exchange methods that use the 1024-bit Diffie-Hellman group or the SHA-1 hash, such as diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1;
  • ciphers in CBC mode, RC4 (arcfour), Triple DES, Blowfish and CAST;
  • MACs based on MD5, truncated 96-bit MACs and 64-bit UMAC;
  • DSA host keys (ssh-dss), RSA signatures using SHA-1 (ssh-rsa) and RSA host keys shorter than 2048 bits.

The algorithms offered can be listed without credentials, with tools such as ssh-audit or the Nmap ssh2-enum-algos script. Scanners usually report each kind as a separate finding, for example CBC mode ciphers, weak MAC algorithms or weak key exchange algorithms enabled. Older SSH servers on network devices, appliances and embedded systems are the most common source, followed by servers whose configuration re-enables legacy algorithms for compatibility with old clients.
entries.impact: Weak algorithms are only used when both the client and the server choose them, and the negotiation itself is protected by the key exchange, so an attacker cannot simply force a modern client to use them. The risk falls on connections from older clients, scripts and devices that prefer or only support the weak algorithms. An attacker able to intercept those connections, and with considerable resources, might then decrypt or alter traffic, or impersonate the server where its host key or signature algorithm can be broken. Practical attacks against most of these algorithms in SSH remain difficult, so the issue mainly removes safety margin, but it also shows that the SSH software or its configuration has not kept pace with current guidance.
entries.remediation:
Restrict the server to strong algorithms only:

  • On OpenSSH, set the KexAlgorithms, Ciphers and MACs directives in sshd_config to explicit lists of strong algorithms, as in the example below. Check each name against the output of ssh -Q kex, ssh -Q cipher and ssh -Q mac on the server, add any post-quantum hybrid key exchange methods the installed release offers, and test the file with sshd -t before reloading, since an unknown name stops the service from starting.
  • Remove DSA host keys (the HostKey line for the DSA key), replace RSA host keys shorter than 2048 bits with Ed25519 or longer RSA keys, and remove ssh-rsa (RSA with SHA-1) from HostKeyAlgorithms where the release still offers it, leaving rsa-sha2-512 and rsa-sha2-256.
  • Where Diffie-Hellman group exchange stays enabled, remove short primes from the moduli file (/etc/ssh/moduli on most Linux distributions); 3072 bits is a common minimum.
  • On network devices and appliances, restrict the same lists with the vendor's SSH algorithm settings, or upgrade the firmware where the weak algorithms cannot be disabled.
  • Upgrade old clients, scripts and devices that need the weak algorithms, rather than keeping them enabled on the server.
KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,umac-128-etm@openssh.com

Keep chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com only on a release that supports strict key exchange, which protects it against the Terrapin attack. Until the change is made, limit SSH access to management networks. Confirm the fix with sshd -T, which prints the settings in effect, and by repeating the algorithm enumeration from the network.

entries.title: SSH Protocol Version 1 Supported
entries.summary: The SSH server still accepts version 1 of the SSH protocol, which has design flaws that version 2 corrected and is no longer supported by current SSH software.
entries.description:
The SSH server accepts connections using version 1 of the SSH protocol (SSH-1). SSH-1 was replaced by SSH-2, standardised in 2006, because of weaknesses in the protocol's design rather than in any one implementation: it protects message integrity with a CRC-32 checksum instead of a cryptographic message authentication code, which has been shown to allow data to be inserted into an encrypted session, and it relies on ciphers and key sizes now regarded as weak. Current OpenSSH releases no longer contain SSH-1 at all, so a server that offers it is usually an old release or another SSH implementation, often on a network device, appliance or embedded system.

The versions a server accepts are shown in its identification banner. A banner beginning SSH-1.99- means the server accepts both SSH-2 and SSH-1, while SSH-1.5- or similar means it accepts only SSH-1. Support can be confirmed with the Nmap sshv1 script or with a client that can still request SSH-1, and scanners report it as SSH protocol version 1 supported.
entries.impact: Published attacks against SSH-1 allow an attacker who can intercept or modify traffic to insert data into sessions and, against some implementations, to recover the session key and so read the traffic, including any passwords sent. The attack needs an intercepting position and a client that connects using SSH-1, which limits the likelihood, although a server that accepts both versions lets any client configured to prefer SSH-1 use it. Software old enough to offer SSH-1 is also likely to carry other known vulnerabilities, and SSH-1 implementations have historically been the subject of remotely exploitable flaws.
entries.remediation:
Disable SSH-1 so that only SSH-2 is accepted:

  • Upgrade the SSH server to a current, supported release; releases that no longer implement SSH-1 remove the issue entirely.
  • On older OpenSSH releases that cannot be upgraded straight away, set Protocol 2 in sshd_config and restart the service.
  • On Cisco IOS devices, use ip ssh version 2; on other network devices and appliances, use the vendor's equivalent setting, or upgrade the firmware where SSH-1 cannot be disabled.
  • Identify any clients, scripts or devices that still connect with SSH-1 and upgrade or replace them before the change, so that they do not lead to SSH-1 being re-enabled.

While the change is pending, restrict SSH on the affected systems to management networks. Confirm the fix by checking that the banner now begins SSH-2.0- and that the Nmap sshv1 script, or a client forced to use SSH-1, can no longer connect.

entries.title: SSH Password Authentication Enabled
entries.summary: The SSH server accepts password logins, so every account that can use SSH is open to password guessing and relies on the strength of a single password.
entries.description:
The SSH server allows users to authenticate with a password, through the password method, the keyboard-interactive method or both. Every account that can log in over SSH is then protected by a single factor that can be guessed, reused from another breach or captured elsewhere, rather than by a private key that never leaves the user's device.

The methods a server accepts are disclosed before authentication, so the issue can be confirmed without credentials: the Nmap ssh-auth-methods script, or ssh -v run against the server, lists them, for example publickey,password,keyboard-interactive. On most Linux systems keyboard-interactive asks for the same password through PAM, so disabling only the password method can leave password logins possible.

SSH servers reachable from the internet receive automated password guessing almost continuously, and internal servers are a common target for password spraying once an attacker has a foothold on the network.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the service can try to guess passwords for known or likely account names, use passwords exposed in other breaches, or spray common passwords across many accounts. A successful guess gives an interactive shell with that account's privileges, from which the attacker can read data, move to other systems and attempt privilege escalation. The likelihood depends on the strength of account passwords, any lockout or rate limiting in place, and whether the service is exposed to the internet. Accounts with weak or default passwords, and service accounts whose passwords are rarely changed, are the usual way in.
entries.remediation:
Require key-based or certificate-based authentication and turn off password logins:

  • Issue each administrator their own key pair, protected by a passphrase or held on a hardware token, and install the public keys before making the change.
  • In sshd_config, set PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no (ChallengeResponseAuthentication no on older releases), or set AuthenticationMethods publickey, then reload the service.
  • Check files included from /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/, such as those added by cloud images: OpenSSH uses the first value it reads for most directives, so an earlier PasswordAuthentication yes takes precedence. sshd -T prints the settings in effect.
  • Where passwords must remain for some users, add a second factor through PAM and require both with AuthenticationMethods, or allow passwords only from a management network inside a Match Address block.

As interim measures, restrict SSH to VPN or management networks with a firewall, enforce strong passwords, and block sources that repeatedly fail to log in, for example with fail2ban. Confirm the fix with the ssh-auth-methods script or ssh -v, which should list only publickey.

entries.title: SSH Root Login Permitted
entries.summary: The SSH server lets the root account log in directly, so a guessed or stolen root credential gives full control in one step and leaves no record of which administrator used it.
entries.description:
The SSH server accepts logins as root, through PermitRootLogin yes or, where root has a key, prohibit-password (formerly without-password). Administrators can then sign in to the root account directly, instead of signing in with a named account and elevating with sudo or su when they need to.

Because the root account exists on every Unix-like system, its name never has to be guessed, and it is the first account automated attacks try. Direct root logins also mean that the server's logs record only that root signed in, not which administrator it was.

The setting cannot be read reliably from the network, because OpenSSH answers a refused root login in the same way as a wrong password. It is normally identified from the configuration during an authenticated scan or build review (sshd -T shows the value in effect), or when a root password or key is obtained during testing. The OpenSSH default is prohibit-password, which still allows root to log in with a key; older releases, and some distributions and appliances, use yes.
entries.impact: An attacker who guesses, captures or finds the root password or a root private key gains complete control of the server at once: they can read and change any data, install persistent access, alter logs and use the server to attack other systems. Allowing root to log in directly removes the extra step, and the separate credential, that a named account followed by sudo would require, and it makes it harder to establish which administrator performed an action, or whether an attacker did. The risk is greater where password logins are also accepted, where the service is reachable from the internet, and where the same root password is used on several servers.
entries.remediation:
Disable direct root logins and give each administrator a named account:

  • Set PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config, check that no file included from /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ sets it earlier (OpenSSH uses the first value it reads), and reload the service. Confirm the value in effect with sshd -T | grep -i permitrootlogin.
  • Before the change, make sure each administrator has a named account with key-based login and is allowed to elevate with sudo, so that access is not lost.
  • Where an automated process genuinely needs root over SSH, use PermitRootLogin forced-commands-only and restrict its key in root's authorized_keys file with the command= and from= options, or give the process its own account with narrowly scoped sudo rules.
  • Limit who may log in at all with AllowGroups or AllowUsers.
  • Change the root password, and remove keys from root's authorized_keys file that are no longer needed.

Until the change is made, restrict SSH to management networks and monitor authentication logs for root logins. Confirm the fix by attempting to log in as root with valid credentials, which should be refused.

entries.title: SSH Terrapin Prefix Truncation (CVE-2023-48795)
entries.summary: The SSH server is vulnerable to the Terrapin attack, which lets an attacker in the network path delete messages at the start of a session and weaken its security extensions.
entries.description:
The SSH server supports a cipher or MAC mode affected by the Terrapin prefix truncation attack (CVE-2023-48795) and does not support the strict key exchange countermeasure. During the handshake, an attacker who can intercept and modify traffic can add messages before encryption starts and delete the same number of messages after it starts, without either side noticing, because the packet sequence numbers still line up. The attack is practical against the chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com cipher, and, with a lower success rate, against CBC ciphers combined with Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) MACs; AES-GCM, and MACs that are not EtM, are not affected.

The countermeasure, strict key exchange, resets the sequence numbers when encryption starts and rejects unexpected messages during the handshake. A server advertises it as kex-strict-s-v00@openssh.com in its key exchange list, and it only takes effect when the client supports it too. It was added in OpenSSH 9.6 and in many other SSH implementations at the end of 2023, and many distributions have backported it, so the version in the banner is not a reliable guide. The issue is confirmed by checking the algorithms offered and whether strict key exchange is advertised, which the researchers' Terrapin scanner and ssh-audit both do.
entries.impact: An attacker must be able to intercept and modify traffic between the client and the server, and both ends must use an affected mode without strict key exchange. Against OpenSSH the practical effect is limited: the attacker can delete the extension negotiation message sent at the start of the session, which can downgrade the signature algorithms used for public key authentication and turn off the keystroke timing obfuscation in recent OpenSSH releases. Terrapin alone does not let the attacker read the traffic or inject arbitrary data into an OpenSSH session. Some other implementations had flaws that the attack made far more serious, such as AsyncSSH, where it could log the client in to an account the attacker controls, so the impact depends on the software at both ends.
entries.remediation:
Update both ends so that strict key exchange is used:

  • Install the SSH server update that adds strict key exchange: OpenSSH 9.6 or later, the distribution's patched package, or the vendor's fixed firmware for network devices and appliances.
  • Update SSH clients and libraries as well, such as PuTTY, WinSCP, libssh, Paramiko and the Go SSH package where they are used, because the countermeasure only applies when both sides support it.

Where the server cannot be updated straight away, stop offering the affected modes. On OpenSSH, remove chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com from Ciphers, and either remove the CBC ciphers or remove the EtM MACs (names ending -etm@openssh.com) from MACs. This example removes ChaCha20-Poly1305 and the CBC ciphers:

Ciphers aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-512,hmac-sha2-256

Check that clients can still connect with the remaining algorithms, as some older clients support only the removed ones. Confirm the fix by repeating the scan, which should show strict key exchange supported or no affected mode offered.

entries.title: SMB Signing Not Required
entries.summary: The host does not require SMB signing, so NTLM authentication captured or coerced from another account can be relayed to it, and its SMB traffic can be altered in transit.
entries.description:
The host accepts SMB connections that are not signed. SMB signing adds a signature derived from the session key to every SMB message, which proves that the message came from the authenticated party and was not changed on the way. When neither the server nor the connecting client requires signing, the connection is not signed.

Without signing, an attacker who obtains NTLM authentication from a user or computer can relay it to the host and act as that account, a technique known as SMB relay or NTLM relay. Authentication is commonly obtained by poisoning name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS), by luring users to a file path that points at the attacker, or by coercing a server to authenticate, for example through the print spooler or the Encrypting File System remote protocol.

By default, domain controllers require signing of every connection to them, and Windows 11 version 24H2 Enterprise, Pro and Education require it both ways. Windows Server 2025 requires it only for the connections it makes, so a Windows Server 2025 server that is not a domain controller still accepts unsigned connections, as do earlier Windows releases and many other SMB servers, such as Samba and storage appliances. The setting is visible without credentials: the Nmap smb2-security-mode script reports Message signing enabled but not required, and NetExec can list such hosts as targets for relay tools such as ntlmrelayx.
entries.impact: An attacker on the internal network who relays the authentication of an account with administrative rights on the host gains administrative access to it, which typically allows remote command execution and the extraction of stored credentials, such as local account hashes and service account secrets, and so further movement across the network. Relaying a less privileged account gives access to the shares and services that account can use. An attacker who can intercept traffic can also alter unsigned SMB traffic, such as files or scripts read from a share. The attack needs a position on the internal network and a source of authentication, but poisoning and coercion tools make both readily achievable in most Windows networks.
entries.remediation:
Require SMB signing on every host that does not already, starting with servers and administrative workstations:

  • In Group Policy, under Computer Configuration, Windows Settings, Security Settings, Local Policies, Security Options, enable Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always) for all computers, and Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always) once servers are ready. These set RequireSecuritySignature to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters respectively.
  • For individual hosts, PowerShell sets the same values: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true and Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true.
  • On Samba, set server signing = mandatory in the [global] section of smb.conf; on storage appliances, use the vendor's equivalent setting.
  • Reduce the sources of relayable authentication as well: disable LLMNR and NBT-NS, restrict NTLM where possible, and disable the print spooler on servers that do not need it.

Signing adds processing overhead, which can reduce throughput on busy file servers, so test those before enforcing it. Confirm the fix with the Nmap smb2-security-mode script, which should report that message signing is required.

patterns: \bSMB\b.*\bsigning\b.*\b(not required|disabled|not enforced|not enabled)\b|\bmessage signing\b.*\b(disabled|not required)\b|\bSMB signing not required\b

entries.title: SMB Version 1 Enabled
entries.summary: The host supports SMB version 1, an obsolete file sharing protocol that lacks the protections of SMB 2 and 3 and has been the target of wormable exploits.
entries.description:
The host accepts connections using version 1 of the Server Message Block protocol (SMBv1, sometimes called CIFS). SMBv1 was superseded by SMB 2 with Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008, and lacks protections that later versions provide, including pre-authentication integrity, which stops an attacker downgrading a connection, encryption, stronger signing, and the blocking of insecure guest logons. Microsoft has deprecated it and no longer installs it by default in current Windows releases, but it remains enabled on older systems, on some systems upgraded from older releases, and on appliances, printers and storage devices that only support it.

The dialects a host accepts can be checked without credentials, for example with the Nmap smb-protocols script, which lists the NT LM 0.12 (SMBv1) dialect when it is supported, or with NetExec, which reports SMBv1 support for each host. Scanners report it as the SMB version 1 protocol detected or enabled. SMBv1 also tends to give unauthenticated users the host's name, domain and operating system version, which helps an attacker choose targets.
entries.impact: SMBv1 does not by itself give an attacker access, but it exposes the host to a class of serious vulnerabilities in the protocol's implementations, such as those fixed by MS17-010 and exploited in the WannaCry and NotPetya outbreaks, whenever updates are missed. Where both the client and the server support SMBv1, an attacker able to intercept traffic may be able to force a connection down to it and so remove the protections of later versions. The practical risk depends on patch levels and on how many systems on the network still use the protocol.
entries.remediation:
Remove SMBv1 from servers and clients once nothing depends on it:

  • Find remaining SMBv1 users first. Set-SmbServerConfiguration -AuditSmb1Access $true records each SMBv1 connection attempt as event ID 3000 in the Microsoft-Windows-SMBServer\Audit event log.
  • On Windows, remove the feature with Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol, which restarts the computer. To disable only the server side without a restart, use Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false.
  • On older Windows releases, set the SMB1 DWORD value to 0 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters, and disable the SMBv1 client with sc.exe config lanmanworkstation depend= bowser/mrxsmb20/nsi and sc.exe config mrxsmb10 start= disabled.
  • On Samba, set server min protocol = SMB2_02 or higher in smb.conf.
  • Upgrade or replace appliances, printers and scanners that only support SMBv1, or move them to an isolated network segment until they can be replaced.

Confirm the fix with the Nmap smb-protocols script, which should no longer list the NT LM 0.12 dialect.

entries.title: SMB Null Session Permitted
entries.summary: The host accepts anonymous (null session) SMB connections that can be used to list accounts, groups, shares or the password policy without credentials.
entries.description:
The host allows an anonymous SMB connection, known as a null session, to the IPC$ share with an empty user name and password, and answers some remote procedure calls made over it without authentication. Depending on the settings, an anonymous user can list domain or local accounts and groups, the members of administrative groups, the shares on the host and the password and lockout policy, or can translate security identifiers to names, which reveals every account by stepping through relative identifiers in turn (RID cycling).

Current Windows releases restrict anonymous enumeration by default, so the issue usually comes from relaxed security options, from legacy compatibility settings such as anonymous membership of the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group on domain controllers, or from SMB servers on other platforms, such as Samba and storage appliances. It can be confirmed with rpcclient and an empty user name, enum4linux-ng or NetExec, and scanners report it as null session or anonymous enumeration permitted. What matters is the information returned: an anonymous connection to IPC$ that returns nothing useful is not a finding in itself.
entries.impact: The information gives an attacker a list of valid account names and the lockout threshold, which together allow password spraying that stays just below the lockout limit, and shows which accounts are administrators and so worth targeting. Share names and descriptions point to where data is held. No data or system access is gained directly, and the attacker needs network access to the SMB service, but the enumeration removes much of the guesswork from the next stage of an attack.
entries.remediation:
Restrict what anonymous users can retrieve:

  • In Group Policy, under Computer Configuration, Windows Settings, Security Settings, Local Policies, Security Options, enable Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts, Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares and Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares, and disable Network access: Allow anonymous SID/Name translation and Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users.
  • Leave Network access: Named Pipes that can be accessed anonymously and Network access: Shares that can be accessed anonymously empty, or limited to entries that a documented application needs.
  • On domain controllers, remove Anonymous Logon and Everyone from the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group, after checking that no legacy application depends on them.
  • On Samba, set restrict anonymous = 2 and avoid map to guest settings that turn failed logons into guest sessions.

Test the changes on a small group of systems first, as some older applications rely on anonymous access. Confirm the fix by repeating the enumeration with an empty user name and checking that it is refused.

entries.title: SMB Guest Access Permitted
entries.summary: The SMB server accepts guest logons, so anyone on the network can read, and sometimes change, any share or file that grants access to guests or to Everyone.
entries.description:
The SMB server lets clients log on as a guest, either by naming the Guest account or by mapping failed or unknown logons to it, and then gives that session access to shares. Unlike a null session, which is limited to what the Anonymous Logon identity may do, a guest session runs as the Guest account, which on Windows is a member of the Everyone group, so it can open any share and file whose permissions allow Everyone or Guests.

On Windows the Guest account is disabled by default, so guest access there usually comes from an enabled Guest account or the legacy Guest only sharing model. It is far more common on Samba servers configured with map to guest and guest ok shares, and on storage appliances, printers and other devices that offer guest access for convenience. It can be confirmed by connecting with the Guest account, or with an arbitrary user name and an empty password, using smbclient, smbmap or NetExec, which show the session as a guest and list the shares it can read or write.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the SMB service can read the data in shares open to guests, and can add, change or delete files where those shares are writable. Writable guest shares are often used to plant malicious files, such as shortcuts that make visiting users authenticate to the attacker, or to replace documents and executable files that other people open. Microsoft also warns that clients which accept guest logons can be deceived into connecting to a malicious server without any prompt, which is why most current Windows editions refuse insecure guest logons by default; attack tools do not. The impact depends on the data in the guest-accessible shares and on whether they are writable.
entries.remediation:
Remove guest access and replace it with authenticated access:

  • On Windows, keep the Guest account disabled (Accounts: Guest account status in Security Options), set Network access: Sharing and security model for local accounts to Classic, and remove Guests and Everyone from the share and NTFS permissions of any share that holds more than public material, granting access to named groups instead.
  • On Samba, set map to guest = Never (the default) in the [global] section, and remove guest ok = yes and public = yes from share definitions.
  • On storage appliances, printers and other devices, turn off guest or anonymous access to shares in the management interface, and create accounts for the users and systems that need access.
  • Keep insecure guest logons disabled on Windows clients with the Enable insecure guest logons policy under Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Network, Lanman Workstation, so that users cannot be steered to a malicious server.

Where a device can only offer guest access, isolate it on a restricted network segment and keep nothing sensitive on it. Confirm the fix by connecting with the Guest account and with an arbitrary user name and empty password, and checking that both are refused.

entries.title: Sensitive Data in Open File Shares
entries.summary: File shares holding sensitive information grant access to broad groups such as Everyone or Domain Users, exposing it to people with no business need to see it.
entries.description:
One or more file shares hold sensitive information but grant access to broad groups, such as Everyone, Authenticated Users or Domain Users, so any member of staff, any compromised account and sometimes any device on the network can read it. Typical findings include personnel and payroll files, scanned identity documents, customer and patient records, financial exports, database and system backups, virtual machine disk images, and configuration files and scripts.

On Windows, the access a user actually has is the more restrictive of the share permissions and the NTFS permissions. Shares are often created with Everyone allowed full control at share level, so the folder permissions are the only real control, and they are frequently inherited unchanged from a permissive parent folder. Over time, data is copied into these locations without anyone reviewing who can reach it.

The issue is found by enumerating shares with an ordinary domain account and searching their contents, with tools such as Snaffler, NetExec's spider modules, smbmap or PowerView. Where the files include passwords or keys, that exposure is normally reported separately because of its direct impact.
entries.impact: Any user, or any attacker who compromises a single ordinary account, can copy the exposed data. Where it includes personal data, this may amount to a personal data breach with reporting obligations under data protection law, as well as commercial and reputational harm. Configuration files, scripts and backups often contain information that helps an attacker move further, such as server names and connection details. Where the broad access includes write permission, an attacker can also alter or delete files, plant malicious documents or executable files for other users to open, or encrypt the data. Access usually needs a valid domain account, which is a low barrier once an attacker has a foothold.
entries.remediation:
Bring share access into line with business need:

  • Remove sensitive data that does not need to be on a file share, such as old exports, backups and copies of personal data, or move it to a location restricted to the people who need it.
  • Replace Everyone, Authenticated Users and Domain Users in the NTFS permissions of sensitive folders with role-based groups, grant write access only where it is needed, and stop inheritance from permissive parent folders where necessary.
  • Give each share an owner in the business who approves who has access, and review the permissions regularly.
  • Enable access-based enumeration on shares (the share's FolderEnumerationMode set to AccessBased), so that users see only the folders they can open. This reduces discovery but does not change permissions.
  • Audit access to sensitive folders, and search file shares for sensitive data on a regular schedule, using the same kind of tooling an attacker would.

As an interim measure, restrict the specific folders found during testing. Confirm the fix by repeating the share search with an ordinary domain account and checking that the sensitive files can no longer be read.

entries.title: SMB Remote Code Execution (MS17-010, EternalBlue)
entries.summary: The host is missing the MS17-010 update for its SMBv1 server, which unauthenticated attackers can exploit with public tools to run code with SYSTEM privileges.
entries.description:
The host's SMBv1 server is missing the security update in Microsoft security bulletin MS17-010, released in March 2017, which fixed several flaws in the way the server handles specially crafted requests (CVE-2017-0143 to CVE-2017-0148). The best known exploit for them, EternalBlue, was published in April 2017 in a leak of tools widely attributed to the United States National Security Agency, and within weeks was used by the WannaCry ransomware, and later by NotPetya, to spread between networks automatically. Related exploits from the same leak, such as EternalRomance and EternalSynergy, target the same flaws.

Every Windows release of that time with the SMBv1 server was affected, from Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008 to Windows 10 and Windows Server 2016, and Microsoft also issued updates for Windows XP, Windows Server 2003 and Windows 8 although they were out of support. The issue can be identified without credentials with the Nmap smb-vuln-ms17-010 script or the corresponding Metasploit scanner module, which check for the vulnerable behaviour without exploiting it. Exploitation can crash the target with a stop error, so confirmation on a live engagement normally relies on these checks.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach TCP port 445 can run code on the host with SYSTEM privileges, the highest level on Windows, using freely available and reliable exploits. This gives complete control of the host, its data, its stored credentials and any access it has to other systems. Because no user interaction or credentials are needed, the flaws are wormable: one vulnerable host can be used to compromise every other vulnerable host it can reach, as the 2017 outbreaks showed. Failed exploitation can also crash the host. Exposure is greatest where port 445 is reachable across internal network boundaries or from the internet.
entries.remediation:
Patch the host and remove SMBv1:

  • Install the updates listed in Microsoft security bulletin MS17-010 (KB4013389), or any later cumulative update or monthly rollup for the operating system, which include the fix.
  • Disable or remove SMBv1, where the flaws are, on every system that does not need it.
  • Replace or upgrade unsupported operating systems. Where a system cannot be patched or replaced at once, isolate it on a network segment that blocks TCP port 445 from other systems.
  • Block TCP port 445 at the internet boundary and between network segments where SMB is not needed.
  • Because exploits for these flaws remain in use, check vulnerable hosts for signs of earlier compromise, such as the DoublePulsar implant that EternalBlue was used to install.

Confirm the fix by repeating the smb-vuln-ms17-010 check and by confirming the installed update level on the host.

entries.title: SMBv3 Compression Remote Code Execution (CVE-2020-0796)
entries.summary: The host is missing the fix for SMBGhost (CVE-2020-0796), a flaw in SMB 3.1.1 compression that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on it or crash it.
entries.description:
The host runs a Windows release whose SMB 3.1.1 implementation is missing the update for CVE-2020-0796, known as SMBGhost or CoronaBlue. The flaw is in the way the SMB server and client handle compressed messages, a feature introduced in Windows 10 version 1903: size values in the compression header are not checked, so a crafted message causes an integer overflow and memory corruption in the kernel. Only Windows 10 versions 1903 and 1909 and Windows Server versions 1903 and 1909 (Server Core installations) are affected, and Microsoft released the fix in March 2020.

Public exploit code followed quickly: crashing the system is straightforward, local privilege escalation exploits were published within weeks, and a remote code execution exploit was published in June 2020, prompting an alert from CISA. Network checks look for SMB 3.1.1 compression support on an affected release. Because a patched host still offers compression, such a result should be confirmed against the operating system build or the installed updates.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach TCP port 445 can crash the host, and with the published exploit can potentially run code in the kernel, giving complete control of it. The remote code execution exploit is less dependable than the denial of service, which works consistently. A local user can use the flaw to gain SYSTEM privileges, and because the SMB client is also affected, a user who connects to a malicious SMB server could have their computer compromised. The affected releases are no longer supported, so a vulnerable host is usually missing other security updates as well.
entries.remediation:
Update or upgrade the host:

  • Install the March 2020 security update for the release (KB4551762) or any later cumulative update.
  • Because Windows 10 and Windows Server versions 1903 and 1909 are no longer supported, upgrade the host to a supported release so that it continues to receive security updates.
  • Until the host can be updated, disable SMBv3 compression on the server with the workaround Microsoft published, which sets the DisableCompression DWORD value to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters, as below. The workaround does not protect the SMB client.
  • Block TCP port 445 at the internet boundary and between network segments where SMB is not needed, and block outbound SMB to the internet so that users cannot connect to malicious servers.
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters" DisableCompression -Type DWORD -Value 1 -Force

Confirm the fix by checking that the operating system build includes the March 2020 update or later.

entries.title: RDP Network Level Authentication Not Enforced
entries.summary: The Remote Desktop service does not require Network Level Authentication, so anyone who can reach it is given a Windows sign-in session before proving who they are.
entries.description:
The host's Remote Desktop service accepts connections without Network Level Authentication (NLA). With NLA, the client must authenticate through CredSSP before the server creates a session; without it, the server creates a session and shows the Windows sign-in screen to anyone who connects, and the user authenticates inside that session. NLA has been available since Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008 and is selected by default when Remote Desktop is enabled on current releases, so it is usually found turned off for compatibility with old clients or third-party tools, or so that users with expired passwords can change them at sign-in.

The security layers a server accepts can be listed without credentials with the Nmap rdp-enum-encryption script: if it reports that native RDP or SSL connections succeed, NLA is not enforced. Connecting with a client and being shown the sign-in screen, which may display the domain name and the last user to sign in, also confirms it. Scanners report it as Terminal Services or Remote Desktop not using Network Level Authentication only.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the service reaches code that runs before authentication, including session creation and the sign-in process. This widens the attack surface for pre-authentication vulnerabilities in Remote Desktop Services: Microsoft named NLA as a partial mitigation for BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) because it forces an attacker to authenticate first. Unauthenticated connections also consume server resources, which can be used to tie up sessions, and the sign-in screen can reveal the domain name and user names. Password guessing is possible with or without NLA, so the main loss is the barrier in front of pre-authentication flaws.
entries.remediation:
Require NLA for every Remote Desktop connection:

  • In Group Policy, enable Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication under Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Windows Components, Remote Desktop Services, Remote Desktop Session Host, Security.
  • On individual hosts, select Allow connections only from computers running Remote Desktop with Network Level Authentication in the Remote Desktop settings, or set the UserAuthentication DWORD value to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp.
  • Update or replace clients and tools that cannot use NLA, and give users another way to change expired passwords, such as a self-service password reset service, so that the setting does not need to be relaxed again.

Where NLA cannot be enforced at once on a host, restrict Remote Desktop access to it to management networks. Confirm the fix with the Nmap rdp-enum-encryption script, which should show only CredSSP (NLA) connections succeeding, and by checking that a client is asked for credentials before any sign-in screen appears.

patterns: \b(Network Level Authentication|NLA)\b|\bTerminal Services Doesn.t Use Network Level Authentication\b

entries.title: Weak RDP Encryption Configuration
entries.summary: The Remote Desktop service accepts the legacy RDP security layer or a low encryption level, letting an attacker in the network path intercept sessions and capture credentials.
entries.description:
The host's Remote Desktop service allows connections that use the legacy RDP security layer, also called Standard RDP Security or native RDP encryption, instead of TLS, or accepts a low encryption level. The legacy layer encrypts traffic with RC4 (Triple DES at the FIPS Compliant level) and does not authenticate the server in a way the client can verify. At the Low encryption level only data sent from the client to the server is encrypted, and at the Client Compatible level the strength is whatever the client supports.

The behaviour is controlled by two settings: the security layer (RDP, Negotiate or SSL) and the client connection encryption level (Low, Client Compatible, High or FIPS Compliant). Negotiate allows the legacy layer whenever a client asks for it, which an attacker who intercepts the connection can arrange by altering the client's request. The Nmap rdp-enum-encryption script lists the security layers the server accepts and, for the legacy layer, the encryption levels. Scanners report the issue as a Remote Desktop man-in-the-middle weakness, or as an encryption level of medium or low.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept traffic between a user and the host, for example by ARP spoofing on the same network segment, can place themselves in the middle of a Remote Desktop connection that uses the legacy layer, or force one to use it, and so capture the credentials the user types at the sign-in screen and observe or alter the session. Freely available tools automate this. Where the encryption level is Low, traffic from the server to the client, including everything displayed on screen, is not encrypted at all. The attack needs a position in the network path and a user who connects while it is in place, which in most cases limits it to the internal network.
entries.remediation:
Require TLS and strong encryption for every Remote Desktop connection:

  • In Group Policy, under Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Windows Components, Remote Desktop Services, Remote Desktop Session Host, Security, set Require use of specific security layer for remote (RDP) connections to SSL, set Set client connection encryption level to High Level, and enable Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication.
  • On individual hosts, the first two settings are the SecurityLayer (2 for SSL) and MinEncryptionLevel (3 for High) DWORD values under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp.
  • Replace the default self-signed Remote Desktop certificate with one issued by an internal certificate authority that clients trust, for example with the Server authentication certificate template policy in the same location, so that clients can verify the server.
  • Configure clients to refuse servers that cannot be authenticated, with the Configure server authentication for client policy under Remote Desktop Connection Client set to Do not connect if authentication fails.

Confirm the fix with the Nmap rdp-enum-encryption script, which should no longer report the native RDP layer as accepted.

patterns: \b(RDP|Remote Desktop|Terminal Services)\b.*\b(encryption level|man-in-the-middle|MiTM|MitM|weak encryption|FIPS|SSL certificate|TLS)\b|\bTerminal Services Encryption Level\b

entries.title: Remote Desktop Services Remote Code Execution (CVE-2019-0708, BlueKeep)
entries.summary: The host is missing the May 2019 fix for BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708), a wormable flaw in Remote Desktop Services that lets unauthenticated attackers run code as SYSTEM.
entries.description:
The host's Remote Desktop Services are missing the update for CVE-2019-0708, known as BlueKeep. The flaw is a use-after-free in the handling of virtual channels while a connection is being set up, before any authentication, so an attacker needs only network access to the Remote Desktop port. It affects Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 and Windows Server 2008 R2, and older releases such as Windows XP and Windows Server 2003; Windows 8, Windows 10 and later releases are not affected. Microsoft released fixes in May 2019, including for releases already out of support, and warned that the flaw was wormable.

The vulnerability can be identified without credentials with the Metasploit scanner module for CVE-2019-0708 or similar checks, which test for the vulnerable behaviour without exploiting it. A public Metasploit exploit module has been available since September 2019, and attacks using BlueKeep have been seen in the wild. Exploitation can crash the target with a stop error, so confirmation on a live engagement normally relies on the non-intrusive checks.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the Remote Desktop port can run code on the host with SYSTEM privileges, giving complete control of it, its data and its stored credentials. No user interaction is needed, so the flaw can be used to spread automatically between vulnerable hosts. The public exploit has to be tuned to the target environment and can crash the host instead of running code, which makes it less reliable than some other remote exploits, but it has been used in real attacks. Where Network Level Authentication is enforced, an attacker must first authenticate with a valid account, which reduces the risk from the internet but not from an attacker who already holds credentials.
entries.remediation:
Patch or retire the affected systems:

  • Install the May 2019 security update for the operating system, or any later monthly rollup, which includes the fix.
  • Plan the replacement of these releases, all of which have reached the end of support and no longer receive security fixes.
  • Until the host is patched, enable Network Level Authentication, which forces an attacker to authenticate before reaching the flaw, and disable Remote Desktop Services where they are not needed.
  • Block TCP port 3389 at the internet boundary, and restrict Remote Desktop between internal network segments to the management hosts that need it.

Confirm the fix by repeating the CVE-2019-0708 check and by confirming the installed update level on the host.

entries.title: Remote Desktop Exposed to the Internet
entries.summary: Remote Desktop can be reached directly from the internet, where it is a constant target for password guessing and a common way in for ransomware groups.
entries.description:
The Remote Desktop service (TCP port 3389 by default, and UDP 3389 where enabled) can be reached directly from the internet. Remote Desktop gives a full interactive session on the host, which makes its sign-in a high-value target: internet-facing Remote Desktop services are found by continual automated scanning and receive password guessing and credential stuffing attempts, and national cyber security agencies, including the NCSC, have named exposed Remote Desktop as one of the most common ways ransomware groups gain initial access.

Exposure is confirmed by a port scan from the internet and by connecting with a Remote Desktop client or the Nmap rdp-ntlm-info script, which, through the NTLM exchange used by Network Level Authentication, also discloses the host name, domain name and operating system build without credentials. Moving the service to a non-standard port does not prevent it being found.
entries.impact: An attacker who guesses or obtains the password of any account allowed to use Remote Desktop gains an interactive session inside the network, from which they can steal data, move to other systems and deploy ransomware. Accounts with weak or reused passwords are the usual entry point, and any future pre-authentication vulnerability in Remote Desktop Services would be exploitable directly from the internet. The likelihood rises with the number of accounts allowed to sign in and falls where an account lockout policy, strong passwords and Network Level Authentication are in place, but none of these gives the protection of a second factor.
entries.remediation:
Remove direct internet access to Remote Desktop and provide remote access through a controlled gateway:

  • Block TCP and UDP port 3389, and any other port the service listens on, at the internet boundary.
  • Provide remote access through a VPN or a Remote Desktop Gateway that requires multi-factor authentication, or through a zero trust access service, so that only authenticated users can reach Remote Desktop hosts.
  • Where direct exposure must remain for a short time, restrict it to known source addresses with firewall rules.
  • Enforce Network Level Authentication, strong passwords and an account lockout policy, and limit the Remote Desktop Users group to the accounts that need it.
  • Monitor sign-in events, including failed sign-ins (event ID 4625) and successful Remote Desktop sign-ins (event ID 4624 with logon type 10), and alert on unusual patterns.

Because exposed Remote Desktop services are attacked routinely, review the host for signs of earlier compromise. Confirm the fix with a port scan from the internet, which should no longer reach the service.

entries.title: SNMP Default Community String
entries.summary: The SNMP agent answers to a default or easily guessed community string such as public, letting anyone who can reach it read the device's management information.
entries.description:
The device's SNMP agent accepts a default or easily guessed community string, most often public for read access and private for read and write access. In SNMP versions 1 and 2c the community string is the only credential, and many network devices, printers, servers and appliances ship with these values, or have them set during installation and never changed.

With a valid community string, anyone can read the agent's management information base (MIB). Depending on the device, this exposes the system description and software version, network interfaces and addresses, routing and ARP tables, listening ports, running processes and installed software, and on Windows the local user accounts and shares. Some devices also expose configuration details or stored credentials through vendor-specific MIBs.

The issue is identified by sending requests with a list of common community strings, with tools such as onesixtyone or the Nmap snmp-brute script, and by reading the MIB with snmpwalk or the other Nmap SNMP scripts. Because SNMP uses UDP port 161, it is easily missed by port scans that cover TCP only. Where a default community also allows writing, that is reported as a writable community.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the agent can map the network from it, identify software versions with known vulnerabilities, learn user and service names, and find other systems and routes to target, without authentication and with little chance of being noticed. The value of the information depends on the device: a core router or a Windows server usually discloses far more than a printer. Where the community also grants write access, or the MIB discloses credentials, the impact is considerably higher. The agent is usually reachable only from internal networks, but a device that answers SNMP from the internet can also be used in reflection attacks against third parties.
entries.remediation:
Replace default community strings and restrict who can query the agent:

  • Disable SNMP on devices that are not monitored.
  • Where SNMP is needed, move to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption (the authPriv security level), which replaces community strings with per-user credentials.
  • Where version 2c must remain for a time, remove the public and private communities and any other defaults, and replace them with a long, random, read-only community string that is unique to the environment.
  • Restrict SNMP to the management stations that poll it: on Cisco IOS, attach an access list to the community; in Net-SNMP, give the permitted source after the community in the rocommunity directive; on the Windows SNMP Service, use Accept SNMP packets from these hosts on the Security tab. Block UDP port 161 at network boundaries.
  • Limit what each community or user can read with SNMP views, so that only the objects the monitoring system needs are exposed.

Confirm the fix by repeating the community string guessing from an untrusted network segment and checking that no response is received.

patterns: \bSNMP\b.*\b(default|public|private|guessable|weak) (community|community name|community string)s?\b|\bSNMP Agent Default Community Name\b

entries.title: SNMP Version 1 or 2c in Use
entries.summary: The device uses SNMP version 1 or 2c, which send community strings and all management data unencrypted and authenticate requests only by that shared string.
entries.description:
The device's SNMP agent accepts SNMP version 1 or version 2c. These versions have no real authentication and no encryption: each request carries a community string, which acts as a shared password, in plain text, and the replies, including everything read from the device, can be read just as easily. Because SNMP normally runs over UDP, the source address of a request is also easy to forge, so access lists based on source address give less protection against write requests than they appear to.

SNMPv3, standardised in 2002, adds a user-based security model with message authentication and encryption, and is supported by almost all current network equipment and management platforms. A device that still accepts version 1 or 2c is identified when it answers such a request made with a valid community string, or from its configuration; snmpwalk and the Nmap SNMP scripts show the version that was answered. Monitoring traffic captured on the network shows the community strings directly.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe traffic between the management systems and the devices they poll, for example from a compromised host on the same network segment or from the monitoring server itself, can capture the community strings and then read from, or where the community allows it, write to every device that shares them. Community strings are often the same across all of an organisation's devices, so one capture can expose many. The management data itself, such as interface, routing and system information, is also visible in transit. The attack needs a position where the traffic can be seen, which usually means access to the internal or management network.
entries.remediation:
Move SNMP to version 3 with authentication and encryption:

  • Configure SNMPv3 users at the authPriv security level, with SHA-based authentication (SHA-2 where the device supports it) and AES encryption, and with separate credentials for read and write access where write access is needed at all.
  • Update the monitoring and management platforms to poll with SNMPv3, then remove all version 1 and 2c communities from the devices, so that the agent no longer answers those versions.
  • Restrict SNMP to the management stations that need it, with access lists on the devices and filtering of UDP ports 161 and 162 at network boundaries, and keep management traffic on a dedicated management network where possible.
  • Where a device cannot support SNMPv3, use a long, random, read-only community string that is unique to the device or group of devices, restrict it to the polling hosts, and plan the device's replacement.

Confirm the fix by sending version 1 and 2c requests with the old community strings and checking that they are ignored, and by checking that the monitoring platform still collects data over SNMPv3.

entries.title: Writable SNMP Community
entries.summary: An SNMP community with write access is accepted, so anyone who knows or guesses it can change the device's settings, disrupt it and, on some devices, take over its configuration.
entries.description:
The device's SNMP agent accepts a community string with read and write access, so SNMP set requests made with it can change the values of writable objects in the device's management information base. The community is typically a default such as private, a guessable value or the same string as the read-only community. The objects that can be written depend on the device, but commonly include interface states and system settings and, on many network devices, vendor-specific objects that copy configuration files to or from a server.

Write access is confirmed by setting an object to its current value, such as the system contact or location, which shows that writes are accepted without changing the device's behaviour. Community strings with write access are found with the same guessing tools used for read-only ones, such as onesixtyone and the Nmap snmp-brute script, followed by a test write with snmpset.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the agent with the community string can change the device's settings, for example shutting down network interfaces, altering routing or VLAN settings where these are writable, or changing the system's identity, which can disrupt the services that depend on the device. On many routers and switches, configuration-copy objects let an attacker download the full configuration, including password hashes and keys, or upload a modified one, which gives complete control of the device. On Linux and Unix hosts running Net-SNMP, write access can allow commands to be run through the agent's extension objects. The impact ranges from disruption to full compromise of network infrastructure, depending on the device.
entries.remediation:
Remove SNMP write access unless it is genuinely needed:

  • Remove read-write communities from every device: on Cisco IOS, remove snmp-server community entries with the RW keyword; in Net-SNMP, remove rwcommunity and unneeded rwuser lines; on the Windows SNMP Service, set the community rights to READ ONLY or remove the community; on other devices, use the vendor's settings.
  • Where a management platform needs write access, provide it only through an SNMPv3 user at the authPriv level, limited by a view to the objects the platform must change and by an access list to the platform's addresses.
  • Change all community strings on the affected devices, since the write community may already be known, including any read-only community that used the same value.
  • Review the configuration of affected devices for unauthorised changes, and change any passwords and keys held in configurations that could have been copied.
  • Block UDP port 161 at network boundaries and restrict it to management networks.

Confirm the fix by attempting a harmless set request, such as writing the current system contact back, and checking that it is refused.

entries.title: Anonymous FTP Access Permitted
entries.summary: The FTP server accepts anonymous logins, so anyone who can reach it can list and download its files, and upload files where writing is allowed.
entries.description:
The FTP server accepts the anonymous (or ftp) user name with any password, by convention an email address, and gives the session access to part of the server's file system. Anonymous FTP was designed for public file distribution and is sometimes still used deliberately for that purpose, but it is often left enabled by default or for convenience on servers, network devices, printers and storage appliances that hold internal files, such as backups, configuration exports, logs, scanned documents and firmware.

The issue is confirmed by logging in as anonymous, listing the directories that can be read, and checking whether files can be uploaded or directories created. The Nmap ftp-anon script does this automatically and reports writable directories, and scanners report it as anonymous FTP login allowed. Whether it matters depends on what the anonymous user can read and write, so the finding should state what was accessible.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the service can download every file the anonymous user can read, leaving no more than an anonymous entry in the logs. The files often contain information useful to an attacker, such as configuration details, credentials in scripts or backups, and internal documents. Where anonymous uploads are allowed, the server can be used to store and distribute malicious or illegal content under the organisation's name, and if the upload directory is also served by a web server or read by an automated process, uploaded files may lead to code execution or the alteration of data. A server that only publishes files intended for the public, with no write access, presents little risk.
entries.remediation:
Disable anonymous access unless the server exists to publish public files:

  • On vsftpd, set anonymous_enable=NO in vsftpd.conf; on ProFTPD, remove the <Anonymous> section from the configuration; on IIS, disable Anonymous Authentication in the site's FTP Authentication settings; on other servers and devices, use the equivalent setting.
  • Where anonymous access is a deliberate business need, confine it to a dedicated directory that holds only public material, and disable anonymous writes (on vsftpd, anon_upload_enable=NO and anon_mkdir_write_enable=NO).
  • Move files that should not be public off the server, and change any credentials found in the files that were exposed.
  • Consider replacing FTP with HTTPS for public distribution, and with SFTP or another authenticated, encrypted method for internal transfers.

Confirm the fix by attempting an anonymous login, which should be refused, or, where anonymous access is intended, by checking that only public files are listed and that uploads fail.

entries.title: Unencrypted FTP Service
entries.summary: The FTP service sends user names, passwords and file contents unencrypted, so anyone able to observe the traffic can capture credentials and data.
entries.description:
The host runs an FTP service that accepts logins and file transfers without encryption. FTP sends the user name and password in plain text with the USER and PASS commands, and transfers file contents and directory listings over a separate data connection that is also unencrypted. Many FTP servers support FTPS, which adds TLS through the AUTH TLS command (explicit FTPS) or on a dedicated port, usually 990 (implicit FTPS), but unless TLS is required a client can still log in without it.

The issue is identified by connecting to the service, usually on TCP port 21, and checking whether a login is accepted before TLS is negotiated; the server's response to the FEAT command shows whether AUTH TLS is offered at all. Scanners report it as FTP supporting cleartext authentication. SFTP, despite the similar name, is a different protocol that runs over SSH and is not affected.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe traffic between FTP clients and the server, for example from a compromised host on the same network segment or a device on the network path, can capture the credentials used and the files transferred, and can alter files in transit. FTP accounts are often used by automated transfers whose passwords rarely change, and the same credentials frequently work on other systems, so a single capture can give lasting access. Where the service is used across the internet, the traffic is exposed on every network it crosses. The attack needs a position where the traffic can be seen.
entries.remediation:
Replace unencrypted FTP with an encrypted protocol:

  • Move transfers to SFTP (over SSH) where clients and partners support it, or to an HTTPS-based transfer service.
  • Where FTP must remain, require TLS for both the login and the data connection: on vsftpd, set ssl_enable=YES, force_local_logins_ssl=YES and force_local_data_ssl=YES; on ProFTPD, set TLSEngine on and TLSRequired on; on IIS, set the site's FTP SSL Settings policy to Require SSL connections; on other servers, use the equivalent setting.
  • Change the passwords of FTP accounts that have been used over unencrypted connections, and make sure they are not used elsewhere.
  • Restrict the service to the systems and partners that need it with firewall rules.

Confirm the fix by attempting to log in without TLS, which should be refused, and by checking with openssl s_client -starttls ftp or an FTPS client that encrypted logins and transfers work.

patterns: \bFTP\b.*\b(cleartext|clear text|unencrypted|plaintext|plain text|without TLS|no encryption|supports cleartext)\b|\bunencrypted FTP\b|\bFTP Supports Cleartext Authentication\b

entries.title: Telnet Service Enabled
entries.summary: A Telnet service is running, which sends user names, passwords and the whole session unencrypted, typically for the remote administration of devices.
entries.description:
The host or device offers remote access through Telnet, usually on TCP port 23. Telnet provides no encryption: the user name, the password and every command and response in the session cross the network in plain text. It is most often found on network equipment, printers, embedded and industrial devices and older Unix systems, where it provides the administrative command line, and it is sometimes left enabled alongside SSH.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to the port and receiving a login prompt or banner, and scanners report it as an unencrypted Telnet server. Telnet services on devices are also frequently set up with default or weak passwords, which is assessed and reported separately when found.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe traffic between an administrator and the device can capture the administrative credentials and everything done in the session, and may be able to take over the session or inject commands into it. Captured credentials for network devices often give control of routing, firewall rules and network segmentation, and are frequently reused across many devices. The service also accepts password guessing from anyone who can reach it. Attacking the traffic needs a position where it can be seen, which on internal networks is often within an attacker's reach.
entries.remediation:
Disable Telnet and use SSH version 2 for remote administration:

  • On network devices, enable SSH version 2 and allow only SSH on the management lines. On Cisco IOS, for example, generate an RSA key, set ip ssh version 2 and use transport input ssh on every line vty range.
  • On Linux and Unix systems, disable the Telnet service, whether it is started by a systemd socket unit or by inetd or xinetd, and remove the Telnet server package.
  • Where a device cannot support SSH, restrict Telnet to a dedicated management network or an out-of-band connection with access lists, and plan its replacement.
  • Change the passwords of accounts that have been used over Telnet.

Confirm the fix with a scan of TCP port 23 from the networks that could previously reach the service, and by checking that administration over SSH still works.

entries.title: Legacy r-Services Enabled (rlogin, rsh, rexec)
entries.summary: The legacy rlogin, rsh or rexec services are enabled; they send data unencrypted and can grant access based only on the client's address and claimed user name.
entries.description:
The host runs one or more of the Berkeley r-services: rexec on TCP port 512, rlogin on TCP port 513 and rsh on TCP port 514.
