These services predate SSH and have no encryption. rexec sends the user name and password in plain text, while rlogin and rsh can skip passwords entirely for connections from trusted hosts listed in /etc/hosts.equiv or in a user's .rhosts file, accepting whatever user name the client claims as long as the connection appears to come from a trusted address. A + entry in these files trusts every host or every user.

The services are now rare, but are still found on older Unix systems, specialist and industrial equipment, and clusters where scripts use rsh to run commands between nodes. They are identified by a scan of TCP ports 512 to 514 and confirmed by connecting, for example with an rsh or rlogin client, or with the Nmap rlogin-brute and rexec-brute scripts. Trust relationships are tested by connecting as common account names, including root.
entries.impact: Where trust relationships exist, an attacker who controls, or can impersonate, a trusted host can log in or run commands as any trusted user without a password, which for root gives complete control of the system. Trust based on source address can be abused by anyone who takes over a trusted host, or its address on the local network, and a wildcard entry extends it to every host. Credentials and commands sent through any of the services can be captured by anyone able to observe the traffic, and the services accept password guessing. Because the same trust files are often copied between systems, one weakness frequently extends across several hosts.
entries.remediation:
Disable the r-services and replace them with SSH:

  • Disable the rexec, rlogin and rsh services, whether they are started by systemd socket units or by inetd or xinetd entries (named exec, login and shell in /etc/inetd.conf), and remove the server package.
  • Delete /etc/hosts.equiv and every user's .rhosts file, and remove any PAM configuration that uses pam_rhosts.
  • Replace scripts and cluster tools that use rsh with SSH and key-based authentication, restricting each key to the commands and source hosts it needs.
  • Where a legacy system cannot be changed, restrict TCP ports 512 to 514 with firewall rules to the specific hosts that need them, and plan its replacement.
  • Change the passwords of accounts that have been used over these services.

Confirm the fix with a scan of TCP ports 512 to 514, and check that no .rhosts or hosts.equiv files remain, for example with find / -name .rhosts.

entries.title: Cleartext Mail and Directory Protocols in Use
entries.summary: Mail or directory services accept logins over unencrypted connections, so user credentials and data such as email can be captured by anyone able to observe the traffic.
entries.description:
One or more mail or directory services accept authentication without encryption. The protocols most often involved are POP3 (TCP port 110), IMAP (TCP port 143), authenticated SMTP mail submission (TCP ports 25 and 587) and LDAP simple binds (TCP port 389). In each case the user name and password are sent in plain text, or merely encoded in Base64 for the SMTP PLAIN and LOGIN mechanisms, and the messages or directory data that follow are also unencrypted. Many of these services support STARTTLS, but unless they require it before authentication, clients can still log in without it, and an attacker in the network path can remove the STARTTLS offer from the server's response.

The issue is identified by connecting to the service and checking whether authentication is offered or accepted before TLS: the capabilities a server advertises (CAPA for POP3, CAPABILITY for IMAP and EHLO for SMTP) show whether login is available on the unencrypted connection, and the Nmap pop3-capabilities, imap-capabilities and smtp-commands scripts report them. For LDAP, a simple bind attempted on port 389 without StartTLS shows whether it is accepted. Encryption of mail exchanged between mail servers, and LDAP signing on Active Directory, are separate matters.
entries.impact: An attacker who can observe traffic between clients and the service, for example from a compromised host on the same network segment, a shared wireless network or a device on the network path, can capture user names and passwords and read the mail or directory data exchanged. Mail clients and applications connect repeatedly with stored credentials, so passwords are exposed regularly without any action by the user. Mailbox and directory credentials are usually the user's main network credentials, and directory service accounts used by applications often have wide read access, so a single capture can lead to access well beyond the service itself. The attack needs a position where the traffic can be seen.
entries.remediation:
Require encryption before any authentication:

  • Offer the services over implicit TLS where clients support it (POP3S on port 995, IMAPS on port 993 and SMTP submission on port 465), or require STARTTLS before authentication on the standard ports.
  • On Dovecot, set ssl = required, which refuses authentication until TLS is in place. On Postfix, set smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes so that authentication is offered only after STARTTLS. On Microsoft Exchange, set the POP3 and IMAP login type to SecureLogin with Set-PopSettings and Set-ImapSettings, and allow basic authentication on receive connectors only after TLS has started.
  • For LDAP, use LDAPS on port 636 or require StartTLS, and configure the directory server to reject simple binds on unencrypted connections. On Active Directory, requiring LDAP signing causes simple binds over unencrypted connections to be rejected.
  • Update clients and applications to use the encrypted ports or STARTTLS, then close or restrict the unencrypted ports where they are no longer needed.
  • Change the passwords of accounts, particularly service accounts, that have been used over unencrypted connections.

Confirm the fix by attempting to authenticate on each unencrypted connection, which should be refused, and by checking with openssl s_client and its -starttls option that encrypted connections work.

entries.title: Open DNS Resolver
entries.summary: The DNS server answers recursive queries from any address on the internet, so it can be used to amplify denial of service attacks against third parties.
entries.description:
The DNS server performs recursive resolution, looking up names in domains it is not authoritative for, on behalf of any client that asks, including clients on the internet. Recursive service is needed only by the organisation's own users and systems; offering it to everyone makes the server an open resolver.

Open resolvers are abused for reflection and amplification attacks: an attacker sends small queries with the victim's address forged as the source, and the server sends much larger responses, such as large record sets or DNSSEC-signed answers, to the victim. Because DNS normally uses UDP, the server cannot tell that the source address is forged. An open resolver is also more exposed to cache poisoning attempts, and lets outsiders learn what is in its cache.

The issue is confirmed by sending a recursive query for a domain the server is not authoritative for from a host outside the organisation's network, for example with dig, and receiving an answer with the recursion available flag set; the Nmap dns-recursion script makes the same check. It often arises when a server that hosts the organisation's public zones also has recursion enabled, as Windows DNS Server does by default, or when the access controls on a recursive server are too broad.
entries.impact: An attacker can use the server to direct large volumes of traffic at a third party, contributing to denial of service attacks that are traced back to the organisation's network. This consumes the organisation's bandwidth and server capacity, and can lead to its addresses being placed on block lists or to complaints from the victim or upstream providers. The server's own data is not exposed beyond what can be learned about its cache, but an open resolver is a more attractive target for cache poisoning, which would redirect the organisation's own users if they rely on it.
entries.remediation:
Restrict recursion to the clients that need it, and separate public authoritative DNS from internal recursive DNS:

  • On servers that host public zones, disable recursion. On BIND, set recursion no; in the options block. On Windows DNS Server, select Disable recursion (also disables forwarders) on the Advanced tab of the server's properties, or run Set-DnsServerRecursion -Enable $false.
  • On recursive servers, allow recursion only from internal networks. On BIND, set allow-recursion and allow-query-cache explicitly, as below, because when they are not set BIND derives them from other settings such as allow-query. On Unbound, list internal ranges with access-control and keep the default refusal for everything else. On Windows DNS Server, where one server must do both jobs, use DNS policy with recursion scopes (selective recursion control) to offer recursion only to internal clients.
  • Block inbound DNS from the internet to recursive servers at the firewall.
  • On authoritative servers, enable response rate limiting where the software supports it, to reduce their usefulness for amplification.
acl internal-clients { localhost; localnets; }; options { allow-recursion { internal-clients; }; allow-query-cache { internal-clients; }; };

Add the organisation's other internal ranges to the acl. Confirm the fix by repeating a recursive query for an external domain from outside the network, which should be refused or go unanswered.

entries.title: DNS Zone Transfer Permitted
entries.summary: The DNS server allows a full zone transfer to any requester, handing over every record in the zone and with it a map of the organisation's hosts.
entries.description:
The DNS server answers zone transfer requests (AXFR) from hosts that are not its secondary servers. A zone transfer returns every record in the zone at once: host names and addresses, mail and service records, aliases and text records. Transfers exist so that secondary servers can copy a zone from the primary, and should be limited to those servers.

The issue is confirmed by requesting a transfer of each zone from each of its name servers, for example with dig axfr or host -l, or with the Nmap dns-zone-transfer script. It is common for only one of several name servers to be misconfigured, so all of them should be tested. The exposure matters most on internal DNS servers, and on external servers whose zones mix public records with internal or development host names and private addresses.
entries.impact: An attacker obtains a complete list of the zone's names and addresses in a single request, without the effort or noise of guessing names one by one. This reveals the organisation's hosts and their roles, including systems not linked from anywhere, such as test, development, remote access and management hosts, and on internal servers the layout of the internal network. The information gives no access by itself, but it makes reconnaissance faster and more complete, and points an attacker at the systems most likely to be weak.
entries.remediation:
Allow zone transfers only to the zone's own secondary servers:

  • On BIND, set allow-transfer { none; }; in the options block, as below, and in each primary zone that has secondaries, override it with an allow-transfer statement listing those servers' addresses or, better, a TSIG key they share with the primary.
  • On Windows DNS Server, on the Zone Transfers tab of each zone's properties, either clear Allow zone transfers or select Only to servers listed on the Name Servers tab or Only to the following servers. The same setting is available through the SecureSecondaries parameter of Set-DnsServerPrimaryZone. Active Directory-integrated zones replicate through Active Directory and often need no zone transfers at all.
  • For hosted DNS services and appliances, use the provider's setting to restrict or disable transfers.
  • Keep internal host names and private addresses out of zones served to the internet, using separate internal and external zones.
options { allow-transfer { none; }; };

Confirm the fix by requesting a transfer of every zone from every name server, from an address that is not a secondary, and checking that each request is refused.

entries.title: DNS Cache Snooping
entries.summary: The DNS server reveals to outside parties whether names are in its cache, letting them infer which sites and services its users have recently looked up.
entries.description:
The DNS server answers queries from its cache for parties who should not be able to see it. By sending a query with the recursion desired flag cleared, an attacker asks the server to answer only from what it already holds: an answer means that someone using the server has looked up that name recently, and the remaining time to live shows roughly when. Where non-recursive queries are refused, the same can sometimes be inferred from response times or from the time to live values in recursive answers.

Repeated over time, the technique shows which software vendors, update services, banks, suppliers and online services the organisation uses, and when. As Microsoft's guidance notes, it works even against a server that does not resolve recursively for third parties, as long as it gives them records from its cache. The issue is confirmed with dig and its +norecurse option, or with the Nmap dns-cache-snoop script, from a host that should not be using the server, and scanners report it as DNS server cache snooping remote information disclosure.
entries.impact: An attacker learns which external services the organisation's users rely on, which supports targeted phishing, for example impersonating a supplier or service the organisation is known to use, and helps in choosing exploits for the software in use. The information is indirect and limited to names that someone has recently looked up, and reaching an internal resolver usually requires a foothold on the internal network, so the impact on its own is low. It is most relevant for resolvers that can be reached from the internet.
entries.remediation:
Stop answering cache queries from parties outside the organisation:

  • Do not let untrusted networks reach recursive resolvers: block inbound DNS from the internet to them, and keep public authoritative DNS on separate servers with recursion disabled.
  • On BIND, restrict cache access to internal clients with allow-query-cache and allow-recursion.
  • On Unbound, give internal networks the allow action in access-control rather than allow_snoop, since allow refuses cache answers to non-recursive queries; reserve allow_snoop for administrators' hosts.
  • On Windows DNS Server, which allows recursion by default, Microsoft's guidance is to keep recursive servers on networks that untrusted clients cannot reach, or to disable recursion on servers that only serve their own zones.

Cache snooping by users who are entitled to use an internal resolver is generally an accepted risk. Confirm the fix by repeating the non-recursive queries from an untrusted network and checking that they are refused.

entries.title: NTP Service Usable for Amplification
entries.summary: The NTP service answers management queries such as monlist from any address, so it can be used to amplify denial of service attacks and discloses details of its clients.
entries.description:
The NTP service, usually the reference ntpd implementation, answers mode 7 (ntpdc) or mode 6 (ntpq) management queries from any address, in addition to normal time requests. The best known case is the monlist command, which returns the addresses of up to the last 600 hosts that contacted the server, so a single small request produces many large response packets. It was abused in large reflection attacks from late 2013, is tracked as CVE-2013-5211, and was removed from ntpd in version 4.2.7p26. Mode 6 queries such as readvar give a smaller but still useful amplification.

The issue is confirmed from outside the trusted network with ntpdc -n -c monlist or ntpq -c rv against the server, or with the Nmap ntp-monlist and ntp-info scripts. It is found on servers and network devices that run older ntpd releases, or that have no restrict rules limiting who may send management queries.
entries.impact: An attacker can use the server to direct large volumes of traffic at a third party with forged requests, contributing to denial of service attacks that are traced back to the organisation's network. This consumes bandwidth and server capacity, and can lead to the organisation's addresses being placed on block lists or to complaints from upstream providers. The monlist response also discloses the addresses of the server's recent clients, which can reveal internal hosts and network layout, and the mode 6 variables reveal the software version and system details. The time service itself is not compromised.
entries.remediation:
Restrict NTP to time service for untrusted clients:

  • Upgrade ntpd to a current supported release, which no longer offers monlist, and apply vendor firmware updates on network devices that run NTP.
  • Add restrict rules that allow time service but refuse management queries from everyone except the local host, as below. The noquery flag blocks mode 6 and mode 7 queries without affecting time synchronisation. Where the configuration uses pool lines, also add restrict source nomodify notrap noquery, because on current ntpd releases nopeer otherwise stops the pool servers being used.
  • On older releases that still support monlist, also add disable monitor, which turns off the feature it reports on.
  • Where the server does not need to serve time to the internet, block inbound UDP port 123 from the internet, and on network devices use NTP access groups to limit which hosts may query.
restrict default kod nomodify notrap nopeer noquery restrict -6 default kod nomodify notrap nopeer noquery restrict 127.0.0.1 restrict -6 ::1 disable monitor

Confirm the fix by repeating the monlist and readvar queries from an untrusted network and checking that they receive no response, while time requests still succeed.

entries.title: SMTP Open Relay
entries.summary: The mail server accepts mail from any sender for any external recipient without authentication and passes it on, so others can send spam and phishing through it.
entries.description:
The SMTP server relays mail for anyone: it accepts messages from senders outside the organisation addressed to recipients outside the organisation, without requiring authentication, and passes them on. A mail server should accept unauthenticated mail only for the domains it is responsible for, and relay to other domains only for authenticated users or for specific internal systems such as applications and multifunction printers.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to the server from an untrusted network and sending a message from an external address to an external mailbox under the tester's control, then checking that it arrives; some servers accept the recipient during the SMTP conversation but discard the message later, so delivery is the reliable test. The Nmap smtp-open-relay script tries a range of address forms, including older tricks such as percent-hack and source-routed addresses that some servers mishandle. Relaying that is open only to internal networks is less serious than relaying open to the internet, but still lets any compromised internal host send mail through the server.
entries.impact: Anyone can send spam, phishing and malware through the server, using the organisation's infrastructure and reputation. Because the messages come from the organisation's own mail server, they may pass sender checks such as SPF for the organisation's domain and so be more convincing to recipients, including the organisation's own staff and customers. Abuse typically leads to the server's addresses being placed on block lists, which stops legitimate mail from being delivered, and can bring complaints from recipients and providers. Open relays exposed to the internet are found and abused quickly by automated scanning.
entries.remediation:
Allow relaying only for authenticated users and named internal systems:

  • On Postfix, keep smtpd_relay_restrictions as permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, defer_unauth_destination (the default) or with reject_unauth_destination, and make sure mynetworks lists only trusted internal addresses.
  • On Microsoft Exchange, review receive connectors that accept anonymous connections: grant anonymous relay only on a dedicated connector whose remote IP ranges are limited to the specific systems that need it, never on the default internet-facing connector.
  • On Sendmail, remove RELAY entries for broad address ranges from the access database and do not use the promiscuous_relay feature; on Exim, limit relay_from_hosts to trusted addresses.
  • For devices and applications that send mail, use authenticated submission on port 587 with TLS where they support it.

Check mail logs for signs that the relay has been abused, look up the server's addresses on public block lists, and request removal once the issue is fixed. Confirm the fix by repeating the relay test from an untrusted network, which should be refused, and by checking that internal applications can still send mail.

entries.title: SMTP User Enumeration
entries.summary: The mail server's responses to the VRFY, EXPN or RCPT TO commands reveal whether a user or mailbox exists, letting outsiders build a list of valid accounts.
entries.description:
The SMTP server responds differently to valid and invalid user names, which lets anyone who can connect to it test whether accounts exist. Three commands are used: VRFY asks the server to confirm a user or mailbox, EXPN asks it to expand a mailing list into its members, and RCPT TO, which names a message's recipient, is commonly rejected straight away for unknown recipients and accepted for valid ones. The first two serve no essential purpose on a server that accepts mail from the internet. The third reflects recipient validation, which is good practice because it avoids accepting and then bouncing mail for unknown recipients, so the aim there is to slow enumeration rather than to remove the difference.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to the server and comparing its responses to known valid and invalid names, manually or with tools such as smtp-user-enum or the Nmap smtp-enum-users script, which try each method in turn. Because mailbox names usually match account names or the email addresses used to sign in elsewhere, the results are directly useful to an attacker.
entries.impact: An attacker can build a list of valid user names or email addresses, which is the starting point for password spraying against email, VPN and other internet-facing sign-in pages, and for targeted phishing. The disclosure itself gives no access, and the attacker still needs a source of candidate names, but it removes the guesswork that would otherwise make these attacks slower and noisier. The impact is greater where the same names are used to sign in to services that lack multi-factor authentication.
entries.remediation:
Remove the commands that disclose users, and slow down enumeration through recipient checks:

  • Disable VRFY and EXPN. On Postfix, set disable_vrfy_command = yes; on Sendmail, include novrfy and noexpn (or goaway) in PrivacyOptions; on other servers, use the equivalent setting.
  • Keep rejecting unknown recipients, but limit how quickly a client can test them: on Postfix, use the error limits and delays smtpd_soft_error_limit, smtpd_hard_error_limit and smtpd_error_sleep_time, together with connection rate limits; on Microsoft Exchange, keep recipient filtering with tarpitting on receive connectors, which delays responses to slow down directory harvesting.
  • Where mail is filtered by a gateway or cloud service in front of the server, make sure the internal server cannot also be reached directly from the internet.
  • Reduce the value of any names obtained by enforcing multi-factor authentication and lockout or rate limiting on the services users sign in to.

Confirm the fix by repeating the VRFY and EXPN tests, which should no longer distinguish valid users, and by checking that rapid RCPT TO guessing is slowed or the connection dropped.

entries.title: Database Service Exposed to Untrusted Networks
entries.summary: A database server accepts connections from networks that have no need to reach it, so anyone there can attempt to log in or exploit flaws in the database service.
entries.description:
The database service listens on a network interface that can be reached from networks with no need to connect to it, such as the internet, user or guest networks, or a third-party connection. Database servers are meant to be reached only by the application servers and administrators that use them, but they are often configured to accept connections on every interface, and the firewall rules in front of them do not narrow this down.

The exposure is identified by port scanning from the untrusted network and confirming the service with a protocol handshake, for example Microsoft SQL Server on TCP 1433, MySQL and MariaDB on TCP 3306, PostgreSQL on TCP 5432 or an Oracle Database listener on TCP 1521. Scanners usually report the service with its version, and several database protocols disclose the version or instance names before any login takes place.

This finding covers the network exposure of a service that still requires authentication. Missing or weak credentials and missing security updates are reported separately where found, but each is far easier to exploit when the service can be reached directly.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the service can try to guess or reuse passwords for database accounts, including built-in administrative accounts such as sa, root or postgres, and can target any unpatched vulnerability in the database's network listener without first compromising another system. A successful login gives direct access to the data the account can reach, and administrative database accounts can often read files or run operating system commands on the server. The risk is higher where the service is reachable from the internet or where weak credentials or missing patches are present, and lower where strong authentication, encrypted connections and current security updates are in place.
entries.remediation:
Make the database reachable only from the systems that need it:

  • Bind the service to the specific internal interface it needs, or to the loopback interface where the application runs on the same host, rather than to every interface. Examples are listen_addresses in PostgreSQL's postgresql.conf and bind_address in the MySQL or MariaDB server configuration.
  • Restrict the database port with network and host firewall rules so that only the application servers and named administration hosts can connect, and place database servers in a dedicated network segment.
  • Use the database's own client access rules as a second layer, for example host-based entries in PostgreSQL's pg_hba.conf, and require encrypted connections.
  • Administer databases from a management network or jump host rather than widening access, and use strong, unique passwords for every database account.
# postgresql.conf: loopback only, or add the internal address the applications use listen_addresses = 'localhost' # my.cnf (MySQL or MariaDB) [mysqld] bind_address = 127.0.0.1

As an interim measure, block the port at the perimeter and on internal firewalls for every network without a business need. Confirm the fix by repeating the port scan from each untrusted network and checking that the service no longer responds.

entries.title: MongoDB Without Authentication
entries.summary: A MongoDB server accepts connections without requiring authentication, so anyone who can reach it can read, change or delete every database it holds.
entries.description:
The MongoDB server does not have access control enabled, so it accepts commands from any client that connects without asking for credentials. MongoDB enforces authentication only when access control is switched on in its configuration, and instances created for development, carried over from old versions or started from container images without the authentication settings are often left in this state. Current releases listen only on the loopback interface by default, but this is commonly changed so that application servers can connect, which exposes the unauthenticated service to every other host that can reach the port.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to the service, normally on TCP 27017, with a client such as mongosh or the Nmap mongodb-databases script, and listing databases and collections without supplying credentials. Scanners report it as MongoDB unauthenticated access or as a database list returned to an anonymous client.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the port can read every database on the server, including personal data, credentials and application secrets stored there, and can insert, change or delete records, which could alter application behaviour or create privileged application accounts. They can also drop whole databases and add administrative MongoDB users to keep access. Automated campaigns search the internet for unauthenticated MongoDB servers, copy or delete their contents and leave ransom demands, so internet-facing instances are at particular risk. The impact is limited only by what the instance stores and by which networks can reach it.
entries.remediation:
Enable authentication and limit who can connect:

  • Create an administrative user, then enable access control by setting security.authorization: enabled in the mongod configuration file (or starting mongod with --auth) and restart the service. For replica sets and sharded clusters, also configure internal authentication between members with a keyfile or X.509 certificates.
  • Give each application its own user with a role limited to the databases and actions it needs, rather than a cluster-wide administrative role.
  • Set net.bindIp to the loopback address and the specific internal interface the application servers use, and restrict TCP 27017 with firewall rules to those servers and administration hosts.
  • Enable TLS for client and member connections.
# /etc/mongod.conf security: authorization: enabled net: port: 27017 bindIp: 127.0.0.1 # add the internal address the application servers use

Because the data may already have been read or changed, review the server's logs and data for signs of unauthorised access, and rotate any credentials or secrets stored in it. Confirm the fix by connecting without credentials and checking that listing databases is refused.

entries.title: Redis Without Authentication
entries.summary: A Redis server accepts commands without a password or access control list, letting anyone who can reach it read or change its data and often run code on the host.
entries.description:
The Redis server accepts commands from any client that connects, without requiring a password or an access control list (ACL) user. Redis is designed for trusted clients in trusted environments and has no authentication in its default configuration. Since version 3.2, protected mode restricts a password-less instance to local connections when it runs with the default settings, but it is commonly switched off, or does not apply to the configuration in use, so that application servers can connect.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to the service, normally on TCP 6379, with redis-cli or a raw TCP connection and running commands such as INFO or KEYS without authenticating. An instance that requires authentication answers with an authentication error instead. Scanners report the issue as Redis unauthenticated access, often with the server version and configuration returned by INFO.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the port can read, change or delete all data in the instance, which commonly includes session data, cached application data, queued jobs and secrets, and can erase it with commands such as FLUSHALL. Where the CONFIG command is available, an attacker can change the working directory and dump file name to write files on the server as the Redis service account, for example an SSH authorized_keys file, a cron entry or a web shell, and on some versions can load a malicious module. This often gives command execution on the host. The impact is reduced where Redis runs as a dedicated unprivileged account, where dangerous commands are blocked through ACLs, and where newer releases' protections against changing sensitive settings at runtime are left enabled.
entries.remediation:
Require authentication and restrict network access:

  • Configure ACL users (Redis 6 and later) with strong passwords and only the commands and key patterns each application needs, and disable the default user or give it a strong password. On older versions, set a long random requirepass value.
  • Deny dangerous commands such as CONFIG, MODULE, DEBUG, FLUSHALL and FLUSHDB to application users through ACL rules.
  • Bind Redis to the loopback address or a specific internal interface with the bind directive, keep protected-mode yes, and restrict TCP 6379 with firewall rules to the application servers that use it.
  • Run Redis as a dedicated unprivileged account, and enable TLS where traffic crosses untrusted networks.
# redis.conf (Redis 6 and later) bind 127.0.0.1 protected-mode yes user default off user app on >use-a-long-random-password ~app:* +@read +@write -@dangerous

Rotate any secrets held in the instance and check the host for files Redis may have been used to write. Confirm the fix by connecting without credentials and checking that commands are refused with an authentication error.

entries.title: Elasticsearch Without Authentication
entries.summary: An Elasticsearch cluster answers its REST API without credentials, so anyone who can reach it can read, change or delete the indexed data and change cluster settings.
entries.description:
The Elasticsearch cluster accepts requests to its REST API without authentication. Releases before 8.0 shipped with security features turned off unless they were configured, and clusters still running those releases, or configured with xpack.security.enabled: false, accept anonymous requests. Forks such as OpenSearch can be deployed with their security plugin disabled with the same result, and dashboards such as Kibana placed in front of an open cluster expose its data through a browser.

The issue is confirmed by sending unauthenticated HTTP requests to the API, normally on TCP 9200, and receiving data rather than an authentication error, for example from GET /_cat/indices, GET /_cluster/health or a search against an index. A secured cluster answers requests without credentials with HTTP 401. Scanners report the issue as Elasticsearch unauthenticated access or as an exposed index listing.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the API can search and download every index, which often holds application data, logs containing personal data or credentials, and other business records. They can also add, change or delete documents and whole indices and change cluster settings, and an exposed dashboard gives the same access through a browser. Exposed clusters are regularly found and wiped by automated campaigns that leave ransom notes. The impact depends on the data indexed and on which networks can reach the API, but it is normally a complete loss of the cluster's confidentiality and integrity.
entries.remediation:
Turn on Elasticsearch security and limit network access:

  • Set xpack.security.enabled: true in elasticsearch.yml on every node, configure TLS for the transport layer (which multi-node clusters need once security is on) and for the HTTP layer, and restart the cluster. Elasticsearch 8.0 and later configure security automatically when a new cluster is first started.
  • Set strong passwords for the built-in users, for example with elasticsearch-setup-passwords on releases before 8.0 or elasticsearch-reset-password on later ones, and give applications and people their own users with roles limited to the indices and actions they need.
  • Keep anonymous access disabled, and require authentication on Kibana and any other front end.
  • Bind the node to an internal address with network.host, and restrict TCP 9200 and 9300 with firewall rules to the hosts that need them.
# elasticsearch.yml on every node xpack.security.enabled: true # then configure transport and HTTP TLS certificates as the Elastic documentation describes

Review the cluster for unexpected indices, users or deleted data, and rotate any credentials found in indexed documents. Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated requests and checking that each is refused with HTTP 401.

entries.title: Memcached Exposed to Untrusted Networks
entries.summary: A Memcached server can be reached from untrusted networks without authentication, exposing cached data to reading and tampering and, over UDP, to abuse in reflection attacks.
entries.description:
The Memcached service can be reached from networks that have no need to use it. Memcached is designed to run on a trusted network beside the application servers that use it and, in its usual configuration, has no authentication: any client that can connect can issue the same commands as the application. It listens on all interfaces unless told otherwise, and releases before 1.5.6 also answered on UDP by default.

The issue is confirmed by connecting to TCP 11211 (or sending requests to UDP 11211) and issuing commands such as version or stats, then listing and retrieving cached items, for example with lru_crawler metadump all followed by get requests. Scanners report it as an accessible Memcached service and, where UDP responds, as a service that can be abused for amplification.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the service can read cached items, which may include session data, user records, tokens or query results, and can change or delete them, which could corrupt application behaviour, poison cached content or sign users out, for example with flush_all. Where UDP is enabled, an attacker can send small spoofed requests that make the server send far larger responses to a victim. CISA's guidance on UDP amplification lists Memcached with the largest amplification factor of the protocols it covers, so an exposed server is a powerful source of denial-of-service traffic against third parties. The impact depends on what the application caches and on whether the service is reachable from the internet.
entries.remediation:
Limit the service to the hosts that use it:

  • Bind Memcached to the loopback address or a specific internal interface with the -l option, and disable UDP with -U 0 unless it is genuinely required.
  • Restrict TCP 11211 with network and host firewall rules so that only the application servers that use the cache can connect, and block TCP and UDP 11211 at the perimeter.
  • Where the cache must be reached across a less trusted network, enable SASL authentication and TLS in builds that support them, or carry the traffic through an encrypted tunnel.
  • Avoid storing secrets in the cache where the application allows it.
# /etc/memcached.conf (Debian and Ubuntu) -l 127.0.0.1 -U 0 # /etc/sysconfig/memcached (Red Hat family) OPTIONS="-l 127.0.0.1 -U 0"

Confirm the fix by sending requests to TCP and UDP 11211 from an untrusted network and checking that no response is received.

entries.title: IPMI Cipher Suite Zero Authentication Bypass
entries.summary: The server's baseboard management controller accepts IPMI cipher suite 0, which performs no authentication, so any password is accepted for a valid user name.
entries.description:
The baseboard management controller (BMC) accepts IPMI 2.0 sessions that use cipher suite 0. This cipher suite selects no authentication, no integrity protection and no encryption, so the BMC opens a session for a valid user name whatever password is supplied. CISA has noted that cipher suite 0 is enabled by default on many IPMI-enabled devices, and the issue has been assigned CVE identifiers for several vendors' BMCs.

The issue is identified over the IPMI remote management protocol (RMCP+) on UDP 623, for example with the Metasploit ipmi_cipher_zero scanner, or with ipmitool using -I lanplus -C 0, a known user name such as a vendor's default administrator account and an arbitrary password. A command that succeeds, such as listing the BMC's users, confirms the bypass. Scanners report it as IPMI cipher suite zero authentication bypass.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the BMC can run IPMI commands with the privileges of the chosen account, which is usually administrator access to the BMC. They can create or change BMC users and passwords, power the server off or on, change its boot device, and then use the BMC's web interface and remote console with an account they control. Control of the BMC gives control of the server it manages, including its console and virtual media, which can be used to compromise the operating system and its data. Actions taken through the BMC are often invisible to monitoring on the host operating system.
entries.remediation:
Remove the bypass and isolate the management controller:

  • Disable cipher suite 0 on every BMC, through the vendor's BMC configuration or, on many platforms, with the cipher_privs setting of ipmitool lan set, as described in the vendor's documentation. Allow only cipher suites that provide authentication, integrity and encryption, such as cipher suite 3 or 17 where supported.
  • Disable IPMI over LAN on BMCs where it is not needed, and disable anonymous and null user accounts.
  • Apply current BMC firmware from the vendor, as several vendors have released updates that address cipher suite 0.
  • Place BMC interfaces on a dedicated management network that only administrators and management systems can reach, never on user networks or the internet.
  • Set strong, unique passwords on all BMC accounts, and review each BMC's user list for accounts an attacker may have added.

Confirm the fix by repeating the cipher suite 0 test against every BMC and checking that sessions are refused.

entries.title: IPMI 2.0 RAKP Password Hash Disclosure
entries.summary: The IPMI 2.0 RAKP handshake returns a salted password hash for any valid BMC user before authentication, which can be cracked offline to recover the password.
entries.description:
The baseboard management controller (BMC) supports IPMI 2.0 over the network, whose RMCP+ Authenticated Key-Exchange Protocol (RAKP) sends the client an HMAC computed from the requested user's password before the client has proved who it is. Any party that can reach the BMC can therefore request this value for a valid user name and try to recover the password offline. This is a weakness in the IPMI 2.0 specification itself (CVE-2013-4786) rather than a fault in one vendor's implementation, so every BMC with IPMI over LAN enabled is affected.

The issue is identified on UDP 623, for example with the Metasploit ipmi_dumphashes module, which requests hashes for a list of common user names and reports those that are valid, because the BMC answers differently for user names that do not exist. The captured values can be cracked with tools such as Hashcat, and weak or vendor-default BMC passwords are usually recovered quickly. Scanners report the issue as IPMI 2.0 RAKP remote password hash retrieval.
entries.impact: An attacker who recovers a BMC password can log in to the BMC with that account's privileges, which commonly include administration. That gives control of the server through the BMC: power control, the remote console, virtual media and BMC user management, and from there a route to the operating system and its data. The same password is often reused across a fleet of BMCs or for other systems, which widens the impact. Long, randomly generated BMC passwords make cracking impractical and are the main factor that limits this issue.
entries.remediation:
The weakness is part of the IPMI 2.0 protocol and cannot be configured away while IPMI over LAN is enabled, so reduce exposure and make the hashes useless:

  • Disable IPMI over LAN on BMCs where it is not needed, and manage them through the vendor's web interface or Redfish API over HTTPS instead.
  • Where IPMI over LAN is required, restrict UDP 623 to a dedicated management network that only administrators and management systems can reach.
  • Set long, randomly generated, unique passwords on every BMC account, kept in a password manager, and change any password that may have been captured or is a vendor default.
  • Rename or remove default accounts where the platform allows, and disable unused and anonymous accounts, so that valid user names are harder to guess.

Confirm the fix by repeating the hash retrieval test, checking that UDP 623 cannot be reached from user networks, and checking that any hashes still obtainable from the management network cannot be cracked with common wordlists.

entries.title: VNC Without Authentication
entries.summary: A VNC server allows connections without a password, giving anyone who can reach it a view of the desktop and control of the keyboard and mouse.
entries.description:
The VNC server offers the None security type, so a client can connect without supplying a password and is given the remote desktop. VNC servers support several security types and the server decides which to offer; when None is offered, authentication is skipped entirely. This is usually the result of a server installed for convenience or for a one-off support task, an embedded VNC service in an appliance or industrial human-machine interface (HMI), or a server started with authentication explicitly switched off.

The issue is confirmed by connecting with a VNC viewer, normally to TCP 5900 or a port above it for additional displays, and receiving the desktop without a password prompt. The Nmap vnc-info script and the Metasploit vnc_none_auth scanner report the security types a server offers. Scanners report the issue as VNC server unauthenticated access.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the port sees everything on the screen and can type and click as the user whose session is shown. If a user is logged in, they can open documents, run commands, read email and use any application or saved credential available to that user; if the session belongs to an administrator or a server console, this amounts to control of the system. If the screen is locked or at a login prompt, the attacker still sees what is displayed and can attempt to log in from the console. On industrial systems the attacker can operate the HMI directly, which may have physical consequences.
entries.remediation:
• Configure the VNC server to require authentication and stop offering the None security type. Prefer operating system account authentication or a TLS-protected security type to the legacy VNC password scheme, which limits passwords to eight characters and does not encrypt the session. In TigerVNC this is controlled with the SecurityTypes parameter; in RealVNC Server, through its authentication settings.
  • Bind the VNC server to the loopback interface where possible and reach it through an SSH tunnel or VPN, or restrict TCP 5900 and above with firewall rules to administration hosts.
  • Remove VNC servers that are not needed, including those installed temporarily for support, and use the organisation's approved remote administration tooling instead.
  • Where an embedded or industrial system's VNC configuration cannot be changed, isolate the device on a restricted network segment.

Confirm the fix by connecting with a VNC viewer and checking that authentication is required, and that the server no longer offers the None security type.

entries.title: Open X11 Server
entries.summary: An X Window System display server accepts connections from any host, letting an attacker capture the screen and keystrokes and send input to the user's session.
entries.description:
The X11 display server accepts client connections over the network without access control. An X server normally listens only for local connections, or uses an authorisation cookie (MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE-1) so that only clients holding the cookie can connect. Running xhost +, starting the server with the -ac option or adding broad entries to the host access list removes this protection, so any host that can reach the server's TCP port can connect as if it were a local application.

The issue is identified on TCP 6000 and the ports above it (one for each display), for example with the Nmap x11-access script, or by running a client such as xdpyinfo or xwininfo -root -tree against the remote display and receiving information instead of an authorisation error. Scanners report it as an open or unauthenticated X11 server. Current X servers and display managers normally disable TCP listening by default, so the issue is most often found on older Unix workstations, thin clients and systems where remote X was enabled deliberately.
entries.impact: An attacker who can connect can take screenshots of the whole display, record keystrokes typed into any window, including passwords, and inject keyboard and mouse events into the session. With an active session this can allow commands to be run as the logged-in user, for example by typing into an open terminal, and the attacker can close or interfere with the user's applications. The impact depends on who uses the display: an administrator's session, or one with privileged terminals open, gives a correspondingly privileged foothold.
entries.remediation:
Restore access control and stop exposing the display server:

  • Stop the X server listening on TCP: start it with -nolisten tcp, or use the display manager's setting, such as DisallowTCP=true in the [security] section of GDM's custom.conf or xserver-allow-tcp=false in LightDM's configuration.
  • Remove xhost + and -ac from start-up scripts and session files, and rely on cookie-based authorisation managed with xauth.
  • Where remote graphical applications are needed, use SSH X11 forwarding (ssh -X), which carries the connection over an authenticated, encrypted channel, or a properly authenticated remote desktop service.
  • Block TCP 6000 to 6063 with host and network firewall rules as an additional layer.
# GDM: /etc/gdm/custom.conf (/etc/gdm3/custom.conf on Ubuntu, /etc/gdm3/daemon.conf on Debian) [security] DisallowTCP=true # LightDM: /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf [Seat:*] xserver-allow-tcp=false

Confirm the fix by repeating the remote connection attempt and checking that the port is closed or the connection is refused.

entries.title: NFS Shares Exported to Any Host
entries.summary: An NFS server exports file systems to any host, so anyone on the network can mount them and, by claiming another user's ID, read or change that user's files.
entries.description:
The NFS server exports one or more directories to every host, through a wildcard (*), an over-broad network range or a malformed export line, instead of to the specific clients that need them. With the default sec=sys (AUTH_SYS) security flavour, the server does not authenticate users: it trusts the numeric user and group IDs that the client presents. An attacker who mounts the export from a system they control can therefore create a local account with any user ID and act as that user on the share. Only the root user is mapped to an unprivileged identity by default, through root_squash.

The issue is identified by listing exports with showmount -e or the Nmap nfs-showmount script, which also show the clients each export is offered to, then mounting the export from the testing system and reviewing its contents. Scanners report it as NFS shares exported to everyone or as world-readable NFS exports.
entries.impact: An attacker on any network that can reach the server can read the exported files by assuming the user IDs that own them, which commonly exposes home directories, application data, backups, SSH keys and configuration files containing credentials. Where an export is writable, they can also change or plant files as any non-root user, for example adding an SSH key to a user's home directory or altering scripts that other systems run, which can lead to code execution elsewhere. The impact depends on what is exported and whether it is writable, and is greater still where root squashing has also been disabled.
entries.remediation:
Limit each export to its clients and stop trusting client-asserted identities:

  • Export each directory only to the specific hosts or the smallest network range that needs it, and remove exports that are no longer required. In /etc/exports, make sure no space separates a client from its option list, because an option list on its own applies to every host.
  • Use Kerberos security, preferably sec=krb5p (or krb5i where encryption is not possible), so that users are authenticated rather than trusted by user ID, and do not offer sys on sensitive exports.
  • Export read-only (ro) wherever clients do not need to write, keep root_squash in place, and use all_squash for exports that should only ever be accessed anonymously.
  • Restrict TCP 2049 and the RPC services NFS relies on with host and network firewall rules.

Apply changes with exportfs -ra. Confirm the fix by listing the exports from an unauthorised host and checking that mounting is refused, and that the remaining exports require Kerberos where it has been configured.

entries.title: RPC Portmapper Exposed
entries.summary: The RPC portmapper (rpcbind) answers queries from untrusted networks, disclosing the RPC services a host runs and allowing its UDP responses to be abused for reflection attacks.
entries.description:
The RPC portmapper service, rpcbind (historically portmap), can be reached from networks that do not need it. ONC RPC services such as NFS, the NFS mount and lock daemons, NIS and various vendor services register with the portmapper, which tells clients which port each service is using. Any host that can reach TCP or UDP 111 can ask for the full list, including each service's program number, version, transport and port.

The issue is identified with rpcinfo -p or the Nmap rpcinfo script, which return the registered services. Scanners report it as RPC portmapper or rpcbind service detection and, where it answers on UDP from the internet, as a service that can be abused for distributed denial-of-service amplification. CISA's guidance on UDP amplification includes the portmapper among the protocols that can be abused in this way.
entries.impact: The service list tells an attacker which RPC services the host runs and on which ports, including services that are often weakly protected, such as NFS mount daemons and NIS, which helps them choose further attacks. Where the portmapper answers on UDP from the internet, an attacker can send it small requests with a forged source address so that it sends larger responses to a victim, contributing to denial-of-service attacks against third parties. The portmapper does not itself give access to data or systems, so the impact is limited to this disclosure and to reflection abuse.
entries.remediation:
Remove the service where it is not needed and restrict it where it is:

  • Disable rpcbind on hosts that do not run RPC services. NFS version 4 does not use it, so servers configured for NFS version 4 only can run without it. On systemd-based Linux systems, stop and disable both the service and its socket unit.
  • Where RPC services are needed, restrict TCP and UDP 111, and the ports the RPC services use, with host and network firewall rules to the clients that use them.
  • Block TCP and UDP 111 at the internet perimeter.
# systemd-based Linux, where no RPC services are needed systemctl disable --now rpcbind.service rpcbind.socket

Confirm the fix by running rpcinfo -p against the host from an untrusted network and checking that no response is received.

entries.title: UPnP SSDP Exposed to the Internet
entries.summary: A device answers UPnP SSDP discovery requests from the internet, disclosing device details and allowing its responses to be abused to amplify denial-of-service attacks.
entries.description:
The device answers Simple Service Discovery Protocol (SSDP) requests on UDP 1900 from the internet. SSDP is the discovery part of Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) and is intended for use within a local network, where devices announce themselves and answer multicast search requests. Routers, cameras, printers, media servers and other embedded devices often answer the same requests when they arrive on an internet-facing interface.

The issue is identified by sending an SSDP M-SEARCH request to the address and receiving a reply, for example with the Nmap upnp-info script. Replies typically include a SERVER header naming the operating system and UPnP software and a LOCATION URL for the device description. Scanners report it as SSDP or UPnP exposed to the internet. Where the device description and control URLs can also be reached from the internet, the UPnP control interface itself is exposed, which on some routers allows port mappings to be added remotely, and the event subscription weakness known as CallStranger (CVE-2020-12695) may also apply.
entries.impact: An attacker can send small SSDP requests with a forged source address so that the device sends much larger responses to a victim. CISA's guidance on UDP amplification lists SSDP among the protocols abused in this way, so an exposed device can be used in distributed denial-of-service attacks against third parties, consuming the organisation's own bandwidth at the same time. The replies also disclose the device type, software and versions, which helps an attacker target known vulnerabilities. The device's own data is not directly exposed unless its UPnP control interface can also be reached.
entries.remediation:
Stop the device answering discovery requests from outside the local network:

  • Disable UPnP on internet-facing interfaces of routers, firewalls and other edge devices, and disable it entirely on devices that do not need it.
  • Block inbound UDP 1900 at the perimeter firewall, together with inbound access to the UPnP description and control ports the device uses.
  • Update device firmware, and replace devices that cannot be configured to stop answering from the internet.
  • Where UPnP port mapping is used on internal routers, check that mappings cannot be requested from the internet, and review existing mappings for entries that were not created deliberately.

Confirm the fix by sending an SSDP M-SEARCH request to the device's external address and checking that no reply is received.

entries.title: Printer Management Interface Without Authentication
entries.summary: A printer's management interface allows administrative access without a password, so anyone on the network can change its settings and read the information it holds.
entries.description:
The printer or multifunction device exposes its management interface, usually the embedded web server on HTTP or HTTPS, without requiring an administrator password. Many devices ship with no administrator password set, or with administrative pages open to anyone, and the setting is not changed when the device is installed. The same devices often expose other management protocols, such as SNMP, Telnet, FTP or the raw printing port on TCP 9100 with PJL commands, which may also accept changes without authentication.

The issue is confirmed by browsing to the device's web interface and reaching configuration pages, such as network, security, address book, scan destination or firmware update settings, without being asked for credentials. Scanners, and printer-focused tools such as the Printer Exploitation Toolkit (PRET), can also identify unprotected management functions.
entries.impact: An attacker on the network can read and change the device's configuration, view address books and job logs, redirect scan-to-email or scan-to-folder destinations to capture scanned documents, change network settings, upload firmware where permitted, or make the device unavailable. Many devices store service account credentials for LDAP address book lookups, SMTP or file shares; by pointing those settings at a host they control and triggering a connection, an attacker can often capture the stored credentials (a pass-back attack), which may be valid domain credentials. The impact depends on the credentials and documents the device handles.
entries.remediation:
Protect every management interface on the device:

  • Set a strong, unique administrator password on the embedded web server and on every other management protocol the device supports, and keep it in the organisation's password manager. Apply this to every device, ideally through the vendor's fleet management tool so that new and reset devices are covered.
  • Disable management protocols and services that are not needed, such as Telnet, FTP, SNMP write access and unused printing protocols, and use HTTPS for the web interface.
  • Restrict management access to an administration network or specific administrator hosts, and place printers in their own network segment.
  • Use dedicated, least-privileged service accounts for LDAP, SMTP and scan-to-folder functions, use encrypted protocols such as LDAPS for them, and change any credentials stored on devices that were found unprotected.
  • Keep device firmware up to date.

Confirm the fix by browsing to each device's management interface and checking that configuration pages require authentication.

entries.title: Management Interface Exposed
entries.summary: An administrative interface for a device or platform can be reached from untrusted networks, exposing a high-value login and its pre-authentication code to attack.
entries.description:
A management interface, used to administer a device or platform, can be reached from networks whose users have no need to administer it, such as the internet or general user networks. Typical examples are the web, SSH or SNMP management interfaces of firewalls, VPN gateways, routers and switches, hypervisor and storage management consoles, out-of-band server management such as iLO and iDRAC, and application server administration consoles. These interfaces are intended for a small number of administrators, and vendors generally recommend placing them on a separate management network.

The exposure is identified by port scanning and by browsing to the interface from the untrusted network, where a login page or management banner is presented. Scanners usually report the product and version alongside the exposure. This finding covers the exposure of an interface that still requires authentication: default or weak credentials and missing security updates are reported separately where found.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the interface can try to guess or reuse administrator credentials and can target any vulnerability in the interface's pre-authentication code. Management interfaces of edge devices and virtualisation platforms are frequently targeted, because a single flaw or weak password there gives control of the device, the traffic it handles or every system it hosts. Exposure also reveals the product and often its version. The risk is highest for interfaces reachable from the internet and for products with a history of serious vulnerabilities, and lower where multi-factor authentication and prompt patching are in place.
entries.remediation:
Make management interfaces reachable only by administrators:

  • Remove management access from internet-facing and user-facing interfaces, for example by disabling web or SSH management on a firewall's external interface, and make management services listen only on a dedicated management network or VLAN.
  • Allow access to that network only from hardened administration workstations, jump hosts or a VPN that requires multi-factor authentication, enforced by firewall rules or device access lists.
  • Require multi-factor authentication, or central authentication with strong passwords, for administrator accounts, and use encrypted management protocols such as HTTPS and SSH rather than HTTP and Telnet.
  • Apply security updates to management software promptly, and log and alert on administrator logins.

As an interim measure, restrict access to the interface to known administrator source addresses. Confirm the fix by repeating the scan from each untrusted network and checking that the interface no longer responds.

entries.title: TFTP Service Accessible
entries.summary: A TFTP server, which has no authentication, can be reached from untrusted networks, so anyone who can guess file names can download, and sometimes upload, the files it serves.
entries.description:
A Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server can be reached from networks that have no need to use it. TFTP has no authentication or encryption: any client that can reach UDP 69 and name a file can download it, and servers configured to accept writes will also accept uploads. TFTP is commonly used to store network device configurations and operating system images, to provision IP phones and other devices, and to serve network boot files, so the files it holds are often sensitive.

TFTP has no directory listing, so the issue is confirmed by requesting likely file names, such as device configuration backups, phone provisioning files or boot files, with a TFTP client or tools such as the Nmap tftp-enum script, and by checking whether uploads are accepted. Scanners report it as a TFTP server detected or as files retrievable from a TFTP server.
entries.impact: Files retrieved from TFTP servers often contain credentials and network details, such as device passwords, SNMP community strings, VPN keys and provisioning secrets, which can be used to access network devices or other systems. Where the server accepts uploads, an attacker may be able to replace configuration files or boot images that devices load, which could give them control of those devices the next time they start or are provisioned. The impact depends on the files the server holds and whether it is writable; a read-only server holding nothing sensitive presents little risk.
entries.remediation:
Remove the service where possible and restrict it where it is needed:

  • Disable TFTP servers that are not needed, including those left running after a one-off firmware upgrade or configuration backup.
  • Where TFTP is required, for example for network boot or phone provisioning, restrict UDP 69 with firewall rules and access lists to the devices that use it, and keep the server on a management or provisioning network.
  • Run the server read-only and confined to a dedicated directory, and remove configuration backups and other sensitive files from it.
  • Move configuration transfers to authenticated, encrypted protocols such as SCP, SFTP or HTTPS, and use HTTPS-based provisioning where devices support it.
  • Change any credentials found in files that were exposed.

Confirm the fix by requesting known file names from an untrusted network and checking that no response is received.

entries.title: Rsync Modules Accessible Without Authentication
entries.summary: An rsync daemon offers modules without authentication, so anyone who can reach it can list and download their contents and, where a module is writable, change them.
entries.description:
The rsync daemon, normally on TCP 873, offers one or more modules (named directories) that can be used without a user name or password. In the daemon's rsyncd.conf, a module is protected only when it has an auth users list and a secrets file; without them, any client that can reach the service can use it, and a module set with read only = no also accepts uploads. Modules are often created for backups, website deployment or file replication between servers and left open on the assumption that the network is trusted.

The issue is confirmed by requesting the module list from the daemon with the rsync client, using an rsync:// address with no module name, which returns every module set to be listed, then listing or copying a module's contents without credentials. Unlisted modules can still be reached if their names are known or guessed. Scanners report it as rsync modules accessible without authentication.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the daemon can download the contents of open modules, which often include backups, website source code, configuration files, database dumps and private keys, and therefore credentials for other systems. Where a module is writable, they can change or add files, for example altering a website's code or a backup that will later be restored, which can lead to code execution or data corruption elsewhere. The impact depends on the contents of the modules and whether they are writable.
entries.remediation:
Require authentication and restrict access to the daemon:

  • Add auth users and a secrets file to every module that is not intended to be public, with the secrets file readable only by the daemon's account, and remove modules that are no longer used.
  • Use hosts allow to limit each module to the clients that need it, set read only = yes unless clients must write, and set list = no for modules that do not need to be advertised.
  • Restrict TCP 873 with host and network firewall rules, and block it at the perimeter.
  • Prefer rsync over SSH for transfers between servers, as the daemon protocol does not encrypt data in transit.
# /etc/rsyncd.conf [backups] path = /srv/backups auth users = backupuser secrets file = /etc/rsyncd.secrets read only = yes list = no # also add: hosts allow = (the addresses of the hosts that use this module)

Change any credentials found in files that were exposed. Confirm the fix by listing and accessing the modules from an unauthorised host without credentials and checking that access is refused.

entries.title: Java RMI or JMX Exposed Without Authentication
entries.summary: A Java RMI registry or JMX management service accepts connections from any host without authentication, which can allow remote code execution in the Java process.
entries.description:
Java Remote Method Invocation (RMI) lets a Java process publish objects whose methods other systems can call over the network, usually with an RMI registry, by default on TCP port 1099, that tells clients where each object can be reached. Java Management Extensions (JMX) commonly uses RMI as its remote transport, so that monitoring tools can read and change the managed beans (MBeans) of a running application server, message broker or other Java service. The weakness arises when remote JMX is enabled with authentication switched off, or when RMI services are reachable from networks that have no need of them.

Two properties make the exposure serious. An unauthenticated JMX service lets the caller invoke MBean operations, and on many Java versions this includes creating an MLet MBean that loads and runs Java code from a URL the caller supplies. RMI also passes arguments as serialised Java objects, so a crafted object sent to a method that accepts objects can run code during deserialisation through classes, known as gadget chains, present on the server's classpath. Java releases that include the JEP 290 serialisation filters restrict what the registry and the distributed garbage collector accept, but application methods that take object parameters remain exposed.

The weakness is identified with a service scan, where Nmap reports the RMI registry and its rmi-dumpregistry script lists the names bound in it, and confirmed with tools that enumerate and test RMI and JMX endpoints, such as remote-method-guesser and beanshooter. Vulnerability scanners report it under names such as an insecure JMX agent configuration or an exposed RMI registry.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the service may be able to run arbitrary code in the Java process, and so operating system commands with the privileges of its service account, without any credentials. Java application servers and middleware usually have broad access to application data, configuration secrets and other internal systems, so this commonly gives a foothold for further compromise. Through JMX alone, an attacker can also read and change the application's runtime settings or stop it. Success depends on the Java version, the classes available on the server and, for some techniques, whether the server can make outbound connections to the attacker.
entries.remediation:
Remove the exposure first, then add authentication where remote management is genuinely needed:

  • Disable remote JMX and RMI services that are not required. Remote JMX is switched on by JVM options such as com.sun.management.jmxremote.port in the start-up scripts or service definitions of the application; remove them where only tools on the same host need access, as local monitoring tools can attach without a network port.
  • Where remote JMX is needed, require authentication and TLS with com.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=true and com.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=true, and use the password and access files to give monitoring accounts read-only access. Never run with com.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false outside a development workstation.
  • Restrict the RMI and JMX ports with host and network firewalls so that only the management systems that need them can connect. As well as the registry port, RMI uses a second port for the exported objects, which is chosen dynamically unless it is fixed (for JMX, with com.sun.management.jmxremote.rmi.port) so that it can be filtered.
  • Keep Java up to date, set a process-wide serialisation filter with jdk.serialFilter that accepts only the classes the application expects, and remove unused libraries that provide known gadget classes.

Confirm the fix by scanning the host again from the networks that previously had access and checking that the ports are closed, or that the service rejects connections without valid credentials.

entries.title: Java Debug Wire Protocol (JDWP) Exposed
entries.summary: A Java process accepts debugger connections over the network, and because the debug protocol has no authentication, anyone who can connect can run code in it.
entries.description:
The Java Debug Wire Protocol (JDWP) is the protocol a debugger uses to control a running Java Virtual Machine. It is switched on with a start-up option such as -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:8000, or the older -Xrunjdwp form, and is intended for development. JDWP has no authentication or encryption: any client that connects to the debug port and completes the protocol's simple handshake gains full debugger control of the virtual machine.

The exposure usually arises when a debug option used during development or troubleshooting is left in a production start-up script, a container image or an application server's configuration. Ports 8000 and 5005 are common, though any port can be used. Since Java 9, an address given as a port number alone listens only on the loopback interface, so remote exposure normally reflects an explicit wildcard or host address in the option, or an older Java version.

The service is identified by connecting to the port and sending the string JDWP-Handshake, which a JDWP agent echoes back. Nmap's service detection and its jdwp-version script recognise it, and vulnerability scanners report it as an exposed Java debugging service.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the port can run arbitrary code in the Java process, and through it operating system commands with the privileges of the account the process runs as, without credentials. Public tools such as jdwp-shellifier and a Metasploit module automate this. The attacker can also read and change data held in the virtual machine's memory, including credentials, session data and keys, or stop the application. Where the process runs as root or SYSTEM, or in a container with access to its host, the compromise extends further. Exposure to the internet greatly increases the likelihood of compromise, as such ports are found by routine scanning.
entries.remediation:
Remove the debugging agent from every environment where interactive debugging is not actively taking place:

  • Remove -agentlib:jdwp, -Xrunjdwp and -Xdebug options from start-up scripts, service definitions, environment variables such as JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and JAVA_OPTS, container images and deployment manifests, then restart the affected processes.
  • Keep development and production start-up configurations separate in build and deployment pipelines, so that debug options cannot reach production by mistake.
  • Where remote debugging is genuinely needed for a period, bind the agent to the loopback interface, for example address=127.0.0.1:8000, reach it through an authenticated SSH tunnel, and remove it when the work is finished.
  • Block debugging ports at host and network firewalls, so that a debug option left in place by mistake cannot be reached.

As an interim measure, restrict the port with a firewall to the specific administrative hosts that need it. Confirm the fix by checking the running process's command line for JDWP options, and by scanning from the networks that previously had access to confirm that the port no longer answers the handshake.

entries.title: IKE Aggressive Mode With a Pre-Shared Key
entries.summary: A VPN gateway accepts IKE aggressive mode with pre-shared key authentication, which discloses a hash from which the key can be recovered by offline guessing.
entries.description:
Internet Key Exchange version 1 (IKEv1), used to set up IPsec VPNs, can establish its first phase in main mode or aggressive mode. Aggressive mode completes in three messages instead of six, but it sends the peers' identities unprotected and, when the peers authenticate with a pre-shared key (PSK), the responder's reply includes a hash computed from the key and from values that are all sent in the clear.

Anyone who obtains that reply, either by starting an exchange with the gateway or by observing an exchange between legitimate peers, can test candidate keys against the hash offline, with no further contact with the gateway and no lockout. A short or guessable key, such as a word-based phrase, can be recovered quickly. The gateway generally needs a recognised identity, such as a remote access group name, before it replies with a hash, but on some implementations identities can be guessed or enumerated from differences in its responses.

The weakness is identified with tools such as ike-scan, which sends an aggressive mode proposal (its --aggressive option, with --id for the identity) and, with --pskcrack, saves the returned values in a form that psk-crack or hashcat can attack. Vulnerability scanners report it as IKE aggressive mode with pre-shared key supported, usually on UDP port 500.
entries.impact: An attacker who recovers the key may be able to establish a tunnel as a legitimate peer where the gateway relies on the key alone, or impersonate the gateway to remote access clients and capture the user credentials they send through extended authentication (XAUTH). Any other gateway or client that shares the key is exposed too. The likelihood depends mostly on the key's strength: a long, randomly generated key cannot practically be recovered, while a short or dictionary-based one can be recovered quickly with ordinary hardware.
