Where users must also authenticate individually with strong credentials and multi-factor authentication, the key alone does not give network access.
entries.remediation:
• Disable aggressive mode, so that IKEv1 peers must use main mode, which protects identities and does not disclose a hash to an initiator that has not proved knowledge of the key. On Cisco ASA the command is crypto ikev1 am-disable, and on Cisco IOS and IOS XE it is crypto isakmp aggressive-mode disable; other gateways have an equivalent setting in their IKE or phase 1 configuration.
  • Prefer IKEv2, which has no aggressive mode and in which the responder proves knowledge of the key only after the initiator has done so.
  • Replace pre-shared keys with certificate-based authentication for site-to-site tunnels, and for remote access use a solution that authenticates each user individually with multi-factor authentication rather than relying on a shared group key.
  • Where a pre-shared key must remain, generate it randomly with high entropy, for example 32 or more random characters, use a different key for each peer, and replace any key that has been used with aggressive mode, as it may already have been captured.

Remote access clients that depend on group keys with aggressive mode will stop connecting once it is disabled, so migrate them first. As an interim measure, replace a weak key with a long random one, which makes offline recovery impractical. Confirm the fix by repeating the ike-scan aggressive mode test and checking that no hash is returned.

entries.title: PPTP VPN in Use
entries.summary: A VPN service offers the Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol (PPTP), whose MS-CHAPv2 authentication can be broken to recover the user's password hash and decrypt the session.
entries.description:
The Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol (PPTP) is a legacy VPN protocol that uses a control connection on TCP port 1723 and carries traffic in Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, IP protocol 47). It normally relies on MS-CHAPv2 to authenticate users, and on Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE), which uses the RC4 stream cipher with keys derived from the MS-CHAPv2 exchange, to protect traffic.

MS-CHAPv2 is fundamentally weak. A captured authentication exchange can be reduced to the recovery of a single 56-bit DES key, which is practical with dedicated hardware or cracking services and reveals the user's NT hash however strong the password is. With the NT hash, the captured session can be decrypted, since the MPPE keys derive from it, and the attacker can authenticate as the user. Microsoft addressed this in a 2012 security advisory, recommending that MS-CHAPv2 be encapsulated in PEAP or that a more secure VPN tunnel be used. MPPE also provides no integrity protection, so traffic can be altered in transit.

The service is identified by a port scan showing TCP port 1723 open, and confirmed with a PPTP client or Nmap's pptp-version script, which reads details from the server's reply. Vulnerability scanners report it as a PPTP VPN service detected.
entries.impact: An attacker who can capture a PPTP authentication exchange, for example on a public Wi-Fi network used by a remote worker or anywhere on the path between client and server, can recover the user's NT hash, decrypt the captured VPN traffic and then connect to the VPN as that user. Where the VPN account is a domain account, the NT hash can also be used to authenticate to internal services that accept NTLM, which extends the impact beyond the VPN. The attack needs a position from which the traffic can be observed or intercepted, and the key search needs specialised hardware or a cracking service, but it succeeds regardless of password strength.
entries.remediation:
• Decommission PPTP and move remote access to a protocol with sound cryptography and mutual authentication, such as IKEv2 with certificate or EAP authentication, or a TLS-based VPN, with multi-factor authentication for users.
  • On Windows Routing and Remote Access, disable the PPTP ports for remote access and demand-dial connections in the port properties; on firewalls and other appliances, disable the PPTP server feature.
  • Close TCP port 1723 and IP protocol 47 (GRE) at the perimeter firewall, unless GRE is needed for another purpose.
  • Treat the passwords of accounts that have connected with PPTP over untrusted networks as exposed, and reset them.

As an interim measure while the migration takes place, limit PPTP to the users who still need it, and require EAP-TLS or PEAP instead of plain MS-CHAPv2 where the clients support it. Confirm the fix by scanning from the internet and checking that TCP port 1723 is closed and no PPTP service answers.

entries.title: Cisco Smart Install Exposed
entries.summary: A Cisco switch accepts Smart Install messages on TCP port 4786 without authentication, letting anyone who can connect copy or replace its configuration and software.
entries.description:
Smart Install is a Cisco feature for zero-touch deployment of switches. A switch acting as a Smart Install client listens on TCP port 4786 for instructions from a director switch, and the protocol has no authentication, so any host that can reach the port can send the same instructions. On many switch models and software releases the client is enabled by default, so switches that were never deliberately set up for Smart Install often expose it.

Cisco describes the abuse of this feature as misuse of the protocol rather than a software flaw. An unauthenticated message can make the switch change the TFTP server it uses, copy its startup configuration to a server chosen by the sender, replace its configuration or software image and reload, and on some releases run configuration commands. Public tools, such as the Smart Install Exploitation Tool (SIET), automate these actions. The feature has also been affected by separate software vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2018-0171, a buffer overflow that allows remote code execution or a reload.

The exposure is identified by a port scan showing TCP port 4786 open on network devices, and confirmed with tools that send a harmless Smart Install query and check the reply, or on the device with show vstack config, which shows whether the client role is enabled. Vulnerability scanners report it as Cisco Smart Install detected.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the port can obtain the switch's full configuration, which typically includes password hashes or reversible passwords, SNMP community strings and details of the network's design, and can replace the configuration or software to take complete control of the switch. With that control, they can capture or redirect traffic passing through it, move between network segments and keep long-term, hard to detect access. They can also take the switch out of service. No credentials or user interaction are needed, and exposed Smart Install clients have been widely scanned for and abused, including by state-sponsored groups described in public government advisories.
entries.remediation:
Disable Smart Install wherever it is not actively used for deployment, which on most networks means every switch:

  • Run no vstack in global configuration mode on each switch, save the configuration, and verify with show vstack config. On older releases that do not support no vstack, block TCP port 4786 with an access list, as Cisco's guidance describes.
  • Block TCP port 4786 at the perimeter, and between user networks and the network device management range.
  • Upgrade to software that fixes CVE-2018-0171 and the other Smart Install vulnerabilities.
  • Where Smart Install is in use, allow port 4786 on clients only from the director, and disable the feature once deployment is complete.
  • Treat the configuration of any switch that was exposed as disclosed: change its local passwords, enable secret, SNMP communities and shared keys, and check its configuration and software image for unauthorised changes.
configure terminal no vstack end copy running-config startup-config show vstack config

Confirm the fix by scanning the switches again from the networks that previously had access and checking that TCP port 4786 no longer answers.

entries.title: Weak Cisco Password Encryption (Type 7)
entries.summary: Passwords in a Cisco device configuration are stored as type 7 values, a reversible encoding that anyone who obtains the configuration can decode instantly.
entries.description:
Cisco IOS and related platforms store some passwords in the device configuration as type 7 values, shown as password 7 or key 7 followed by a string of hexadecimal characters. Type 7 is applied by service password-encryption to passwords that would otherwise appear in clear text. It is a reversible encoding with a fixed, publicly known key, intended only to stop passwords being read by someone glancing at the configuration, and Cisco does not present it as protection against anyone who obtains the file.

The weakness is found when a configuration is reviewed, or recovered during testing from a backup, a TFTP or file server, a configuration management system or the device itself, and contains local user passwords, enable password, line passwords or keys for RADIUS, TACACS+, routing protocol authentication or VPN peers in type 7 form. Many offline tools and scripts decode these values immediately, and a device itself can be made to reveal them. Older type 5 (salted MD5) and type 4 values are also weak, though they must be cracked rather than decoded.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains a configuration file containing type 7 values can recover the passwords in clear text, which commonly gives administrative access to the device and, because network device passwords and shared keys are often reused, to other switches, routers, firewalls and authentication servers. Recovered RADIUS, TACACS+ and routing protocol keys can also help an attacker impersonate those services or interfere with routing. The attacker first needs a copy of the configuration, which limits the issue to those who can reach backups, file shares, management systems or the device, but configuration files are frequently found in such places.
entries.remediation:
• Store local account and enable passwords as strong one-way hashes, using the scrypt-based type 9 (algorithm-type scrypt) or the PBKDF2-based type 8 (algorithm-type sha256) with the secret keyword of the enable and username commands, and remove any enable password lines and username entries configured with password.
  • For keys that the device must be able to recover, such as RADIUS and TACACS+ shared secrets, use the AES-based type 6 encryption where the platform supports it, by setting a master key with key config-key password-encrypt and enabling password encryption aes.
  • Use central authentication through TACACS+ or RADIUS with individual named accounts, keeping a single local emergency account with a strong hashed secret.
  • Change every password and key that has been stored as type 7, since it must be assumed known, and remove old configuration copies from backups, TFTP servers and file shares, or restrict access to them.
  • Keep service password-encryption enabled for any values that cannot yet be converted, as it still prevents casual viewing, but do not rely on it.

As an interim measure, restrict access to configuration backups and the systems that store them. Confirm the fix by reviewing the running configuration for remaining type 7 values and enable password entries, for example with show running-config | include password.

entries.title: Unnecessary Network Services Exposed
entries.summary: Hosts expose network services that serve no business purpose, adding to the attack surface available to an attacker without any benefit to the organisation.
entries.description:
Hosts and devices often run network services that are not needed for their role, because they are enabled by default in the operating system or product, were installed for a past purpose, or were left behind after testing. Examples include default web servers and administration consoles, sample applications, legacy services such as echo, chargen, discard and finger, file sharing on systems that share no files, and remote access or monitoring agents that are no longer used.

Each listening service is code that an attacker can reach and test. Services that nobody uses are also the least likely to be patched, monitored or configured securely, so they tend to accumulate known vulnerabilities and default settings over time, and their presence discloses information about the host's role and software.

The weakness is identified by a port scan of each host, for example with Nmap, compared with the services that the host's role requires. The system owners usually need to confirm which services are unneeded, so the finding is often raised as a list of services for review. Where a needed service is weakly configured, that weakness is reported separately.
entries.impact: An unnecessary service does not in itself give an attacker access, but it adds to the number of ways in. If it has a vulnerability, a default credential or a weak configuration, it can provide an initial foothold, a route to sensitive information or a means of disrupting the host. The risk rises when the services are reachable from the internet or from large user networks, and falls when they are filtered so that only administrative systems can connect.
entries.remediation:
• For each service identified, confirm with the system owner whether it is required. Disable and uninstall services that are not, rather than only stopping them, so that they do not return after a restart or update.
  • Restrict the services that remain with host and network firewalls so that they are reachable only from the systems and networks that need them, and bind them to specific interfaces rather than all interfaces where the software allows.
  • Build systems from hardened baselines that start with the minimum services enabled, such as the CIS Benchmarks or vendor security baselines, and record the expected listening ports for each server role.
  • Scan internal and external address ranges regularly and compare the results with the recorded baseline, so that new services are noticed and reviewed.

As an interim measure, block the services at the network firewall. Confirm the fix by repeating the port scan and checking that only the expected services respond.

entries.title: Service Version Disclosure
entries.summary: Network services reveal their software name and version in banners or responses, which helps an attacker select exploits for known vulnerabilities.
entries.description:
Many network services identify themselves when a client connects or in their responses. SSH, FTP, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP servers send a greeting banner, DNS servers may answer queries for their version, SNMP agents report a system description, and management interfaces often show versions on their login pages. These frequently include the product name and exact version, and sometimes the operating system and its patch level.

The disclosure lets an attacker match each service against public vulnerability databases and exploit collections without probing it further, and focus effort on hosts that run outdated software. It is not a vulnerability in itself: where the disclosed version is affected by known vulnerabilities, those are reported separately as outdated software, and version details in web server headers are covered by a separate web application finding.

It is identified by banner grabbing and service fingerprinting, for example with Nmap version detection (-sV) or by connecting with a client such as netcat. Removing a banner does not prevent fingerprinting by behaviour, so this is a hardening measure rather than a control that stops identification.
entries.impact: The information reduces the effort needed to find exploitable weaknesses and lets an attacker choose a specific exploit rather than trying many, which makes attacks quicker and quieter. It has no direct effect on the confidentiality, integrity or availability of the host or its data. Its significance rises where the disclosed version is out of date, since an attacker can then go straight to a known exploit.
entries.remediation:
• Configure each service to send a generic greeting without product and version details, where the software allows it: for example smtpd_banner in Postfix, smtp_banner in Exim, the receive connector Banner parameter in Microsoft Exchange, ftpd_banner in vsftpd, ServerIdent in ProFTPD, and the version option in BIND, which controls the answer to version.bind queries.
  • For OpenSSH, the protocol version string includes the software version and cannot be removed without rebuilding the software; on Debian and Ubuntu, DebianBanner no in sshd_config removes the additional distribution and patch-level suffix.
  • Remove version details from SNMP system descriptions, login pages and management interfaces where the product allows it.
  • Above all, keep the disclosed software up to date, since an accurate banner on a fully patched service gives an attacker little to use, and treat banner changes as hardening rather than protection.
# Postfix (main.cf) smtpd_banner = $myhostname ESMTP # vsftpd (vsftpd.conf) ftpd_banner=FTP service ready # ProFTPD (proftpd.conf) ServerIdent on "FTP service ready" # BIND (named.conf, options block) version "not disclosed";

Confirm the fix by repeating the banner grab and version scan and checking that version numbers are no longer returned.

entries.title: ICMP Timestamp Response
entries.summary: The host answers ICMP timestamp requests, revealing the time on its system clock to any host that asks.
entries.description:
ICMP timestamp requests (type 13) and replies (type 14), defined in RFC 792, let one host ask another for its current time, given in milliseconds since midnight Universal Time. Clock synchronisation now relies on NTP, so few systems need this facility, but many operating systems and network devices still answer timestamp requests unless a firewall drops them.

A reply discloses the host's clock to within milliseconds and confirms that the host is live, which can matter where other probes are filtered. The behaviour is identified with Nmap's timestamp ping (-PP) or a tool such as hping3 (--icmp-ts), and vulnerability scanners report it as ICMP timestamp request remote date disclosure, usually with the reference CVE-1999-0524, a long-standing entry that also covers ICMP address mask replies.
entries.impact: The disclosed time has little value on its own. In uncommon cases it can assist attacks on mechanisms that depend on the clock, such as random number generators seeded with the time or time-based authentication tokens, and a reply confirms that the host exists when other probes are blocked. It does not affect the confidentiality, integrity or availability of the host or its data.
entries.remediation:
Drop ICMP timestamp requests at the network perimeter and on host firewalls, unless a specific application needs them:

  • On perimeter firewalls and routers, block inbound ICMP type 13 (timestamp request) and outbound type 14 (timestamp reply), while still allowing the ICMP types that networks need to work, such as destination unreachable, including its fragmentation needed message, and time exceeded.
  • On Linux hosts, drop the requests with iptables or nftables, as shown below.
  • On Cisco IOS devices, deny timestamp-request in the inbound interface access list.
  • Keep host clocks synchronised to a trusted time source, so that a disclosed time reveals nothing unexpected.
# iptables iptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type timestamp-request -j DROP iptables -A OUTPUT -p icmp --icmp-type timestamp-reply -j DROP # nftables (in an existing inet filter table with an input chain) nft add rule inet filter input icmp type timestamp-request drop # Cisco IOS extended access list entry deny icmp any any timestamp-request

Confirm the fix by sending a timestamp request again and checking that no reply is received.

entries.title: TCP Timestamps Enabled
entries.summary: The host includes TCP timestamps in its traffic, which on some systems lets an observer estimate how long it has been running since it was last restarted.
entries.description:
The TCP timestamp option, defined in RFC 7323 (which replaced RFC 1323), adds timestamp values to TCP segments so that hosts can measure round-trip times and reject old duplicate segments on fast connections. It is enabled by default on many operating systems, including Linux, and is a normal part of TCP.

On systems where the timestamp counter starts from a fixed value at boot and increases at a steady rate, sampling it over a short period lets an observer calculate the system's uptime, which can suggest whether updates that require a restart have been applied. Timestamps can also help to tell apart several hosts behind a load balancer or address translation device, since each keeps its own counter. Current Linux kernels add a secret random offset to the values they send, which prevents uptime being inferred, although scanners still report that the option is supported.

The option is identified from a host's responses, for example by Nmap's operating system detection, which reports an uptime guess when the values allow one, or with the --tcp-timestamp option of hping3.
entries.impact: The disclosure is minor. An uptime estimate can indicate that a host has not been restarted for a long time and may therefore lack updates that need a restart, and counting distinct timestamp sequences can reveal how many servers sit behind one address. Neither gives access to the host or affects its data, and the option itself benefits TCP performance.
entries.remediation:
For most hosts this finding can be accepted, as the option supports TCP performance and current operating systems already resist uptime inference. Where the organisation wishes to act on it:

  • On Linux, keep the default net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps = 1, which uses random offsets, rather than 2, which does not. Setting 0 disables timestamps entirely, but can reduce performance on high-speed links.
  • On Windows, timestamps can be turned off with netsh interface tcp set global timestamps=disabled.
  • On load balancers and firewalls that proxy or normalise TCP connections, use any available option to remove or rewrite TCP timestamps, so that the servers behind them cannot be told apart.
  • Keep systems patched and restart them when updates require it, so that uptime reveals little of value.

Confirm any change by repeating the scan and checking whether the timestamp option is still returned and whether an uptime estimate is still available.

entries.title: LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS Name Resolution Poisoning
entries.summary: Hosts fall back to broadcast and multicast name resolution that any device on the network can answer, so an attacker can impersonate servers and capture or relay credentials.
entries.description:
When a Windows host cannot resolve a name through DNS, it falls back to Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS), sending the query to every host on the local network. Multicast DNS (mDNS) works in a similar way and is used by many operating systems and devices. None of these protocols authenticates the answer, so any host on the same network segment can reply that it holds the requested name.

An attacker on the segment can answer these queries with tools such as Responder or Inveigh, directing the victim to connect to the attacker's machine instead. Many clients then try to authenticate automatically, so the attacker captures NTLM challenge-response hashes (NetNTLMv1 or NetNTLMv2) for offline cracking, or relays the authentication in real time to other services that do not enforce signing. The queries come from mistyped or retired server names, stale drive mappings and shortcuts, and automatic lookups such as Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD), so they occur regularly on typical networks without any deliberate user action.

The weakness is identified by listening passively for LLMNR (UDP 5355), NBT-NS (UDP 137) and mDNS (UDP 5353) queries, for example with Responder's analyse mode, and confirmed by answering them and capturing authentication attempts during an agreed test window.
entries.impact: An attacker with access to the internal network, without any credentials, can capture password hashes for the users and computers that make these lookups. Weak or common passwords can be cracked offline, giving the attacker a valid domain account. By relaying, the attacker can authenticate as the victim to other servers without cracking anything, which can lead to code execution or administrative access where the victim is privileged and the target does not require SMB or LDAP signing. The impact is greater where privileged accounts are used on ordinary workstations and where NTLMv1 is still accepted, and smaller where passwords are long and signing is enforced throughout.
entries.remediation:
• Disable LLMNR through Group Policy: set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution to Enabled, which sets the registry value EnableMulticast to 0 under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient.
  • Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP on every interface: for DHCP clients, with the Microsoft vendor-specific DHCP option 001 (Microsoft Disable Netbios Option) set to 0x2; for hosts with static addresses, in the interface's WINS settings or by setting NetbiosOptions to 2 for each interface under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NetBT\Parameters\Interfaces. Check first that no legacy application depends on it.
  • Disable mDNS where it is not needed: on Windows, set the EnableMDNS DWORD value to 0 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache\Parameters; on Linux and other systems, disable the mDNS responder, such as Avahi, where it serves no purpose.
  • Turn off automatic proxy detection where WPAD is not used, so that hosts stop looking up the WPAD name.
  • Reduce the value of any captured authentication: require SMB and LDAP signing, refuse NTLMv1, and use long passphrases for user and service accounts.

As an interim measure, monitor for poisoning with network detection rules that alert on LLMNR and NBT-NS responses from unexpected hosts. Confirm the fix by listening on each network segment again and checking that hosts no longer send LLMNR, NBT-NS or mDNS queries.

entries.title: IPv6 DHCPv6 and Router Advertisement Spoofing
entries.summary: Hosts accept IPv6 configuration from any device on the network, so an attacker can make themselves the DNS server for Windows hosts and intercept or relay their authentication.
entries.description:
Windows and most other current operating systems enable IPv6 by default and prefer it to IPv4. On networks that use only IPv4, Windows hosts still send DHCPv6 requests, many hosts listen for IPv6 router advertisements, and nothing legitimate answers either. Neither protocol authenticates the server or router, so any device on the same network segment can reply.

Tools such as mitm6 answer the DHCPv6 requests, giving the victim a link-local IPv6 address and the attacker's address as its DNS server, without advertising a route, so the victim's normal IPv4 traffic is unaffected. The attacker's DNS server then answers selected queries, such as those for WPAD or internal host names, with the attacker's own address. Victims that connect, including computer accounts, authenticate, typically with NTLM, and the attacker relays that authentication with a tool such as ntlmrelayx to services that do not enforce signing or channel binding, most damagingly LDAP on domain controllers. Rogue router advertisements, sent with tools such as those in the THC-IPv6 toolkit, can similarly redirect a host's IPv6 traffic through the attacker.

The weakness is identified by observing DHCPv6 solicitations (to UDP port 547) and router solicitations on IPv4-only segments, and confirmed by answering them with mitm6 for a short, agreed period, as the attack changes the victims' DNS settings and can disrupt them.
entries.impact: An attacker on the internal network, without credentials, can capture and relay the authentication of hosts and users on the segment. Relaying to LDAP on a domain controller that does not enforce LDAP signing and channel binding can let the attacker create computer accounts, configure delegation that lets them take over the relayed computer, or, where a privileged user's authentication is relayed, change permissions in the domain. Depending on other weaknesses, this can lead to compromise of individual hosts or of the whole domain. The attack is limited to the segments the attacker can reach directly, and it fails where relay targets enforce signing and channel binding.
entries.remediation:
• Where IPv6 is not used, stop hosts acting on rogue IPv6 configuration. Microsoft advises against disabling IPv6 entirely; instead, use Group Policy to set the predefined Windows Defender Firewall rules Core Networking - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6(DHCPV6-In) and Core Networking - Router Advertisement (ICMPv6-In) to block, and do the same for outbound DHCPv6 requests (Core Networking - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6(DHCPV6-Out)). Disabling IPv6 components with the DisabledComponents registry value also stops the attack, but Microsoft does not recommend it and it must be tested.
  • On the network, enable IPv6 first-hop security on access switches: RA Guard to drop router advertisements from host ports, and DHCPv6 Guard to drop DHCPv6 server messages from host ports. These protect every operating system, including those not managed by Group Policy.
  • Where IPv6 is in use, manage it deliberately with authorised routers and DHCPv6 servers, and apply the same switch protections.
  • Remove the value of relayed authentication: enforce LDAP signing and channel binding on domain controllers, require SMB signing, enable Extended Protection for Authentication on web services, and turn off automatic proxy detection where WPAD is not used.

Confirm the fix by running mitm6 again for a short period and checking that hosts no longer accept its replies or change their DNS server.

entries.title: No Network Access Control
entries.summary: Wired network ports give any connected device access to the internal network, without checking that the device or its user is authorised.
entries.description:
Network access control (NAC) checks a device before the network lets it communicate, most commonly with IEEE 802.1X port-based authentication, in which the switch opens the port only after the device has authenticated to a RADIUS server, typically with a machine certificate. Without it, a switch port forwards traffic for whatever is plugged in, and DHCP gives the device an address on the internal network.

The weakness is identified by connecting a test laptop to a live network port, such as one in a meeting room, reception area or unused desk, or in place of a printer, phone or other device, and checking whether it receives an address and can reach internal systems such as domain controllers and file servers. MAC address filtering or port security on its own is not access control, as an attacker can copy the MAC address of an authorised device, which is often printed on its label. Where 802.1X is deployed, testing also covers ports exempted for devices that cannot authenticate, and whether the MAC authentication bypass used for them can be abused.
entries.impact: Anyone with brief physical access to the premises, such as a visitor, contractor or intruder, can connect a laptop or leave a small implant and gain the same network reach as an employee's computer, without credentials. From there, they can carry out attacks that need internal network access, such as name resolution poisoning, credential relaying and exploitation of internal services, and an implant can give remote access long after they leave. The impact depends on how much is reachable from user network ports and how well physical access to the premises is controlled.
entries.remediation:
• Deploy IEEE 802.1X port-based authentication on access switches, with devices authenticating to a RADIUS server, such as Microsoft Network Policy Server or a dedicated NAC product, preferably with machine certificates (EAP-TLS).
  • Place devices that cannot use 802.1X, such as some printers and phones, in dedicated VLANs, and where MAC authentication bypass is used, profile the devices and limit their VLANs with access lists to the services they need.
  • Assign devices that fail or do not attempt authentication to a quarantine or guest VLAN with no access to internal systems.
  • Disable switch ports that are not in use, and assign them to an isolated VLAN.
  • Where the risk of an attacker inserting a bridge between an authorised device and the switch justifies it, use MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) with 802.1X to authenticate and encrypt traffic on the link.
  • Alert on new or unknown devices appearing on the network, for example from DHCP logs or switch port events.

As an interim measure, disable unused ports and restrict network ports in public areas such as receptions and meeting rooms. Confirm the fix by repeating the test from the same ports and checking that an unauthorised device receives no internal network access.

entries.title: Insufficient Network Segmentation
entries.summary: Internal networks are not divided into zones with controlled traffic between them, so a compromise of any one system gives an attacker direct network access to critical systems.
entries.description:
Network segmentation divides a network into zones according to the role and sensitivity of their systems, such as user workstations, servers, management interfaces, databases, payment systems and operational technology, and controls the traffic between them with firewalls or access lists so that each zone can reach only the services it needs. Where the network is flat, or zones exist but the traffic between them is not filtered, every system can reach every other.

The weakness is identified from the testing position, usually a user network port or a standard workstation, by scanning the organisation's address ranges and finding services that a user network has no need to reach: remote administration protocols such as RDP, SSH and WinRM on servers, database listeners, hypervisor and storage management, out-of-band management interfaces such as iLO, iDRAC and IPMI, network device management, backup systems, or systems in a zone that is meant to be separate. Tests of specific boundaries, such as those around a cardholder data environment, check each permitted path against the documented rules.
entries.impact: Without segmentation, an attacker who compromises any single device, for example through phishing, or who connects to the network, can reach and attack every system directly, including those that hold the most sensitive data or control the infrastructure. A single vulnerability or reused credential anywhere becomes a route to critical systems, and ransomware and other malware can spread across the whole estate. The real effect depends on the weaknesses of the systems that become reachable, but the lack of segmentation removes a layer that would otherwise contain an incident and greatly extends the reach of any initial compromise.
entries.remediation:
• Define security zones based on the role and sensitivity of systems, and document the traffic that each needs, with its source, destination, port and business reason.
  • Enforce the boundaries with firewalls or access lists that deny traffic by default and allow only the documented flows. Begin with the highest-value assets: management interfaces, domain controllers, databases, backups and any regulated or operational technology environments.
  • Put administrative interfaces, out-of-band management and network device management on a dedicated management network, reachable only from privileged access workstations or jump hosts.
  • Restrict workstation-to-workstation traffic, for example with host firewalls or private VLANs, since user devices rarely need to talk to each other.
  • Log traffic that crosses zone boundaries, and alert on denied attempts to reach sensitive zones.
  • Review the rules regularly and test the segmentation after significant changes.

Segmentation is a programme of work rather than a single change, so as an interim measure restrict access to the most sensitive systems with host-based firewalls. Confirm the fix by repeating the scan from user networks and checking that only the documented services are reachable.

entries.title: VLAN Hopping Possible
entries.summary: Switch ports can be made to carry traffic for other VLANs, through trunk negotiation or double-tagged frames, letting an attacker bypass the separation VLANs are meant to provide.
entries.description:
VLANs separate devices that share switching hardware into different broadcast domains, and organisations often rely on them to keep user, voice, server and management traffic apart. VLAN hopping is the ability of a device on an access port to send traffic into, or receive traffic from, VLANs other than the one assigned to it, so that the separation fails.

The two common forms are switch spoofing and double tagging. In switch spoofing, the attacker's device negotiates a trunk with the switch using Cisco's Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP), which is possible when the port is left in a dynamic mode such as dynamic desirable or dynamic auto; the port then carries every permitted VLAN, and the attacker can create virtual interfaces on any of them. In double tagging, the attacker sends frames with two 802.1Q tags when their access VLAN is also the native VLAN of a trunk; the first switch removes the outer tag and the next switch forwards the frame on the VLAN named in the inner tag. Double tagging works in one direction only, but lets traffic be sent to systems on the target VLAN. A related weakness is a voice VLAN that admits any device which announces itself as a phone through CDP or LLDP.

The weakness is identified by listening on an access port for DTP, CDP and LLDP frames, and confirmed with tools such as Yersinia, frogger or VoIP Hopper that attempt trunk negotiation or voice VLAN access, or by sending double-tagged frames and checking for their arrival on the target VLAN.
entries.impact: An attacker connected to a user or public network port can reach VLANs that should be isolated from it, such as server, management, voice or payment networks, and attack the systems on them directly. Where a trunk is formed, the attacker can also receive broadcast and flooded traffic from the other VLANs and use attacks that need a local network position, such as ARP spoofing, on them. The attacker needs access to an affected switch port, and double tagging alone allows only one-way traffic.
entries.remediation:
• Configure every user-facing port as a static access port and disable trunk negotiation, with switchport mode access and switchport nonegotiate.
  • On trunk ports, set trunking explicitly with switchport mode trunk and switchport nonegotiate, and allow only the VLANs the link needs with switchport trunk allowed vlan.
  • Set the native VLAN on trunks to an unused VLAN that is not assigned to any access port, or tag the native VLAN with vlan dot1q tag native where the platform supports it, and do not use VLAN 1 for user traffic.
  • Shut down unused ports and place them in an unused, isolated VLAN.
  • Protect voice VLANs with 802.1X, or limit what the voice VLAN can reach, rather than trusting CDP or LLDP announcements alone.
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 20 switchport nonegotiate ! interface GigabitEthernet1/0/48 switchport mode trunk switchport trunk native vlan 999 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30 switchport nonegotiate

Equivalent settings exist on other vendors' switches. Confirm the fix by repeating the DTP and double-tagging tests from user ports and checking that no traffic reaches other VLANs.

entries.title: ARP Spoofing Not Mitigated
entries.summary: Hosts and switches accept forged ARP replies from any device on the segment, letting an attacker place themselves between other hosts and intercept or alter their traffic.
entries.description:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps IPv4 addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses on a local network. It has no authentication, and most operating systems accept unsolicited ARP replies that update an existing cache entry. An attacker on the same network segment can therefore send forged replies that associate their own MAC address with the IP address of another host, typically the default gateway, so that traffic meant for it is sent to the attacker, who forwards it on.

Switches can prevent this with Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), which checks ARP packets on untrusted ports against the bindings between ports, MAC addresses and IP addresses that DHCP snooping has recorded, and drops those that do not match. Where these features are not enabled, ARP spoofing succeeds on any segment the attacker can join.

The weakness is identified by a controlled ARP spoofing attempt against a test host or a small, agreed set of hosts, with tools such as Bettercap, arpspoof or Ettercap, checking whether the traffic is redirected. It is tested with care, as redirecting a busy gateway's traffic through a laptop can disrupt the network.
entries.impact: An attacker on the same segment, without credentials, can intercept traffic between other hosts and their gateway or servers and, where it is not protected by encryption, read and change it. Cleartext protocols then expose credentials and data, and the attacker can downgrade weakly configured encryption, inject content or relay authentication. Strong encryption, such as TLS with proper certificate validation, limits the attacker to learning which systems communicate. Poorly executed spoofing can also interrupt communication. The attack is limited to the local segment, which makes the size and contents of each VLAN significant.
entries.remediation:
• Enable DHCP snooping on access switches, trusting only the uplinks and the ports of legitimate DHCP servers, and enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on user VLANs so that ARP packets that do not match the snooping bindings are dropped. Add static bindings or ARP access lists for hosts with fixed addresses.
  • Enable IP Source Guard where supported, so that each port can send traffic only from its assigned address.
  • Keep user VLANs small and separate from server and management VLANs, so that a spoofing attacker can reach as few systems as possible.
  • Encrypt sensitive traffic end to end with TLS, SSH and SMB signing or encryption, so that interception gains little.
  • Where switch features are not available, consider static ARP entries for the gateway on critical hosts, and use network detection tools that alert when the MAC address of a gateway changes.
ip dhcp snooping ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20 ip arp inspection vlan 10,20 ! interface GigabitEthernet1/0/48 description Uplink ip dhcp snooping trust ip arp inspection trust

Introduce Dynamic ARP Inspection in stages, as hosts with static addresses need bindings before enforcement. Confirm the fix by repeating the spoofing attempt and checking that the switch drops the forged replies.

entries.title: Cleartext Credentials Captured on the Network
entries.summary: Systems send usernames and passwords across the network without encryption, where anyone able to observe the traffic can capture and reuse them.
entries.description:
Some protocols send credentials in clear text or in a trivially reversible form such as Base64. Common examples on internal networks are Telnet, FTP, HTTP with Basic authentication or plain login forms, LDAP simple binds without TLS, POP3, IMAP and SMTP authentication without TLS, SNMP version 1 and 2c community strings, and the management protocols of printers, building systems and older applications. Database and application protocols are also often configured without encryption.

During testing, such credentials are captured either passively, from traffic that reaches the tester's network port, such as broadcast and multicast traffic and traffic on shared or mirrored segments, or actively, after redirecting traffic with techniques such as ARP spoofing. Tools such as Wireshark, tcpdump, PCredz and NetworkMiner extract usernames, passwords and community strings from captured traffic. This finding records credentials actually obtained in this way; the configuration of individual cleartext services is often reported separately.
entries.impact: Anyone in a position to observe the traffic, such as a malicious insider, an attacker with a foothold on a host in the same segment, or anyone able to connect to an unprotected network port, can obtain valid credentials without cracking anything. Depending on the accounts involved, these give access to systems, data and network devices, and the service and administrative accounts captured in this way often have broad privileges. Because the credentials are valid, their later misuse looks like legitimate activity and is difficult to detect. The scope is limited by the attacker's network position and by the protocols in use on the segments they can reach.
entries.remediation:
• For each protocol on which credentials were captured, move to an encrypted equivalent: SSH instead of Telnet, SFTP or FTPS instead of FTP, HTTPS for every web interface, LDAPS or LDAP with StartTLS instead of simple binds in clear text, IMAPS, POP3S and SMTP with STARTTLS for mail, and SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy instead of community strings.
  • Disable the cleartext versions once the encrypted ones are in use, so that clients cannot fall back to them.
  • Change every credential that was captured, as it must be treated as known, and review the recent use of those accounts.
  • Prefer authentication methods that never send the password, such as Kerberos or certificate-based authentication, and use separate, least-privileged accounts for service connections.
  • Reduce exposure while migrating by placing legacy systems on isolated segments, enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection on switches and restricting who can reach the affected services.

Confirm the fix by capturing traffic again from the same network positions and checking that no credentials can be extracted.

entries.title: Unrestricted Outbound Network Access
entries.summary: Internal systems can open connections to any address and port on the internet, so malware or an attacker can freely set up control channels and send data out.
entries.description:
Egress filtering restricts the connections that internal systems can make to the internet. Where the perimeter firewall allows all outbound traffic, or broad ranges of ports and protocols, any compromised workstation or server can connect directly to any external system on any port, including protocols that should never leave the network, such as SMB, RDP and SSH, DNS sent straight to external resolvers, and arbitrary high ports.

The weakness is identified from a workstation or server on the internal network by attempting outbound connections across a wide range of TCP and UDP ports to a system the tester controls on the internet, and recording which succeed. Testing also checks whether web traffic must pass through an authenticating proxy, whether DNS queries can reach external servers directly or only through the organisation's resolvers, and whether servers, which rarely need to browse the web, have the same outbound access as user workstations.
entries.impact: Unrestricted outbound access does not let an attacker in, but it removes a control that can stop or expose an attack after the initial compromise. Malware and intrusion tools can reach their command and control servers on whatever port suits them, data can be sent out directly over many protocols, and outbound SMB or WebDAV connections can disclose users' NTLM credentials to external servers. Servers with internet access can also download tools and be used to attack others. Where the organisation's monitoring relies on traffic passing through a proxy, direct connections bypass it.
entries.remediation:
• Change the perimeter firewall policy to deny outbound traffic by default, and allow only the destinations, ports and protocols that are needed, each recorded with an owner and a business reason.
  • Route user web traffic through a proxy or secure web gateway that authenticates users, inspects content and logs requests, and block direct outbound HTTP and HTTPS from user networks.
  • Allow DNS to the internet only from the organisation's own resolvers, and block outbound SMB (TCP 445 and 139), NetBIOS, RDP, SSH and other administrative protocols from all internal networks unless a specific system needs them.
  • Restrict servers more tightly than workstations: most need only specific update and service endpoints, and many need no internet access at all.
  • Log denied outbound connections, and alert on unusual volumes, destinations and ports, which can indicate compromise.

As an interim measure, block the highest-risk outbound protocols, such as SMB and direct DNS, and restrict servers first. Confirm the fix by repeating the outbound port test from user and server networks and checking that only the approved traffic succeeds.

entries.title: PXE Boot Exposes Credentials or Images
entries.summary: Network boot services hand operating system images and deployment settings to any device that asks, and these often contain domain credentials and other secrets.
entries.description:
Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) booting lets a computer load an operating system installer over the network, using DHCP to find a boot server and TFTP to download the boot files. Deployment platforms such as Microsoft Configuration Manager (SCCM), Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT) with Windows Deployment Services (WDS), and comparable tools on other platforms use it to build machines automatically. To do so, the boot media and deployment settings often contain credentials: the Configuration Manager network access account and task sequence variables, an account for the deployment share in MDT's Bootstrap.ini or CustomSettings.ini, and local administrator or domain join passwords in unattended setup files.

Where these services answer any device on the network without approval or a strong PXE password, an attacker can boot a virtual machine, or run a tool that sends PXE requests, retrieve the boot files and extract the credentials from them. Tools such as PXEThief automate this against Configuration Manager, recovering the media variables file and the policies it gives access to. Where a PXE password is set, the encrypted media variables file can still be taken away and the password guessed offline, so a weak password gives little protection.

The weakness is identified by observing PXE offers on the network or sending a PXE request from the testing position, retrieving the boot files over TFTP, and examining them, and any deployment shares they point to, for credentials.
entries.impact: An attacker on the internal network, without any credentials, can obtain domain credentials from the deployment configuration. The network access account and task sequence accounts are often given more rights than they need, and are sometimes members of administrative groups, so the attacker may gain broad access to systems or to the domain. Access to the deployment share can also let the attacker read the images that will be installed on new computers and, where the share is writable, alter them to plant malicious code across the estate. Images may also contain local administrator passwords shared across many machines.
entries.remediation:
• For Configuration Manager, reduce reliance on the network access account, which is no longer required in many scenarios when Enhanced HTTP or PKI certificates are used; where it remains, give it only read access to content and no interactive or administrative rights. Do not store passwords in task sequence or collection variables.
  • Set a strong, randomly generated PXE password on PXE-enabled distribution points, and disable unknown computer support where it is not needed, so that only devices already known to Configuration Manager receive a deployment.
  • For MDT and WDS, remove credentials from Bootstrap.ini, CustomSettings.ini and unattended setup files so that technicians enter them at build time, and give any deployment share account read-only access to that share and nothing more.
  • Where a domain join account is needed, use a dedicated account that can only join computers to a specific organisational unit, and give each computer a unique local administrator password after build, for example with Windows LAPS.
  • Offer PXE and TFTP only on a dedicated build network or VLAN, not on user networks.
  • Change the passwords of every account found in boot media or deployment configuration.

Confirm the fix by repeating the PXE request from user networks and checking that no boot files are served, or that the files obtained contain no usable credentials.

entries.title: Kerberoastable Service Accounts
entries.summary: User accounts with service principal names can have their Kerberos service tickets requested by any domain user and cracked offline to recover weak passwords.
entries.description:
One or more user accounts in the domain have a service principal name (SPN) registered, which allows any authenticated domain user to request a Kerberos service ticket for them. Part of each service ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the account's password, so a ticket can be taken offline and attacked to recover the password, without further contact with a domain controller and without triggering account lockout. The technique is known as Kerberoasting.

The risk depends on the strength of the password and on the encryption type. Service account passwords are often chosen by a person, set once and never changed. Where an account still accepts RC4, an attacker requests an RC4-encrypted ticket, whose key is the account's NT hash and which can be tested at very high speed; AES-encrypted tickets are slower to attack but still fall to a weak password.

Kerberoastable accounts can be listed with an LDAP query for user objects that have a servicePrincipalName value, and tools such as Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py, Rubeus and NetExec request the tickets in a form that hashcat (modes 13100, 19600 and 19700) can attack. BloodHound and PingCastle report these accounts and highlight those with privileged group membership. Computer accounts and managed service accounts also have SPNs but have long random passwords, so they are not practical targets.
entries.impact: Any domain user, or an attacker who controls any domain account or domain-joined computer, can request tickets for every Kerberoastable account and attempt to crack them at leisure. Where a password is recovered, the attacker gains every right the account holds, which commonly includes administrative access to the servers that run the service and to its data and, where the account is in a privileged group, control of the domain. The ticket requests resemble normal Kerberos traffic, although a burst of requests, particularly for RC4 tickets, can be detected. Long, randomly generated passwords and AES-only encryption make cracking impractical.
entries.remediation:
• Replace service accounts with group managed service accounts (gMSAs) wherever the application supports them. Windows generates and rotates their passwords automatically, every 30 days by default, so they cannot practically be cracked.
  • Where a user account must remain, give it a long, randomly generated password stored in a vault: Microsoft recommends at least 14 characters for service accounts, and considerably more is practical because nobody needs to type it. Change it after any suspected exposure.
  • Configure remaining service accounts to use AES only, by setting msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes (for example through the AES options on the Account tab in Active Directory Users and Computers), and then reset the password so that AES keys exist. Test first: systems that support only RC4 will fail to authenticate to the service.
  • Remove SPNs that are no longer needed, and remove service accounts from privileged groups, granting only the rights each service needs.

As an interim measure, change the passwords of privileged service accounts and of those with the oldest pwdLastSet values first. Monitor domain controllers for unusual volumes of service ticket requests (event 4769), especially with ticket encryption type 0x17 (RC4). Confirm the fix by requesting the tickets again and checking that none can be cracked against a large wordlist and rule set.

entries.title: AS-REP Roastable Accounts
entries.summary: Accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled let anyone request data encrypted with a key derived from the account's password and crack it offline.
entries.description:
One or more accounts have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, shown by the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag (0x400000) in the userAccountControl attribute and by the Do not require Kerberos preauthentication option in Active Directory Users and Computers. Normally a client must prove that it knows the password, by encrypting a timestamp with its key, before a domain controller issues a ticket-granting ticket. Without pre-authentication, the domain controller answers a request for the account from anyone, and part of its reply (the AS-REP) is encrypted with a key derived from the account's password.

The reply can be attacked offline to recover the password, a technique known as AS-REP roasting. No credentials are needed to request it, only the account name and network access to a domain controller, although any authenticated user can list every affected account with a single LDAP query.

The setting is usually found on accounts created for legacy applications or Kerberos implementations that did not support pre-authentication, or where it was changed during troubleshooting and never restored. An attacker who can write to an account's userAccountControl attribute can also set it deliberately. Impacket's GetNPUsers.py, Rubeus and NetExec identify affected accounts and retrieve replies that hashcat (mode 18200) can attack, and BloodHound and PingCastle report the flag.
entries.impact: An attacker on the internal network can obtain the encrypted reply without any credentials and attempt to crack it offline, without triggering account lockout. If the password is weak, the attacker gains the account and everything it can access; where the account is privileged or used by a service, this can lead to compromise of servers or of the domain. A long, random password makes cracking impractical, but the setting still removes a protection that otherwise applies to every account.
entries.remediation:
• List the affected accounts and confirm with each owner whether any system genuinely depends on the setting. Current Windows, Linux and macOS Kerberos clients support pre-authentication, so a genuine dependency is rare.
  • Re-enable pre-authentication by clearing Do not require Kerberos preauthentication on the Account tab in Active Directory Users and Computers, or with the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module as shown below.
  • Reset the password of every affected account, since its reply may already have been captured, and give any account that must keep the setting a long, random password.
  • Check for the flag regularly as part of directory monitoring, since it can be set again by an administrator or by an attacker preparing an account for roasting.
Get-ADUser -Filter 'DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true' | Select-Object SamAccountName Get-ADUser -Filter 'DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true' | Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false

Run the first command to review the accounts before running the second. Confirm the fix by repeating the query and requesting an AS-REP for each previously affected account, which should now fail with a pre-authentication required error.

entries.title: Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation
entries.summary: Hosts other than domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained delegation, so they cache the Kerberos tickets of users who connect and can impersonate them anywhere.
entries.description:
One or more computer or user accounts other than domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained Kerberos delegation, shown by the TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION flag (0x80000) in userAccountControl and by the Trust this computer for delegation to any service (Kerberos only) option. When a user authenticates to a service running under such an account, the user's computer sends a copy of the user's ticket-granting ticket (TGT) with the request, and the service keeps it in memory so that it can act as that user towards any other service in the domain.

Anyone who gains administrative control of the host, or the credentials of the account, can extract and reuse the TGTs of every user who connects to it. The exposure is made worse by authentication coercion: techniques that abuse the Print Spooler (MS-RPRN) or the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (MS-EFSR, PetitPotam) can make a domain controller authenticate to the host, leaving the domain controller's own TGT in memory.

The setting can be identified with an LDAP query for the flag, for example with the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module or Impacket's findDelegation.py, and BloodHound and PingCastle report it. Domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained delegation by design and are excluded from this finding.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a host with unconstrained delegation can impersonate any user whose TGT reaches it. By coercing a domain controller to authenticate to the host, the attacker obtains the domain controller's TGT, which can be used to replicate every password hash from the directory (DCSync) and so take control of the domain. Privileged users who connect to the host expose their TGTs in the same way. Exploitation needs administrative access to the host or the account's credentials first, but the setting turns compromise of one server into compromise of the domain. Accounts marked as sensitive, or in the Protected Users group, are not delegated.
entries.remediation:
• Remove unconstrained delegation from every account that is not a domain controller. Where a service genuinely needs to act on behalf of users, replace it with constrained delegation to the specific services required, or with resource-based constrained delegation configured on the target, and test the application afterwards.
  • Select Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated on privileged accounts, or add them to the Protected Users group, so that their tickets are never delegated.
  • Reduce the ways a domain controller can be made to authenticate: disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers, apply current security updates, and restrict outbound SMB and HTTP connections from domain controllers to the systems they need to reach.
  • Until the setting is removed, treat affected hosts as Tier 0: restrict who can administer them and keep privileged accounts from connecting to them.

The following commands list affected accounts other than domain controllers (primary group 516):

Get-ADComputer -Filter 'TrustedForDelegation -eq $true -and PrimaryGroupID -ne 516' -Properties TrustedForDelegation Get-ADUser -Filter 'TrustedForDelegation -eq $true' -Properties TrustedForDelegation

Confirm the fix by repeating the query and checking that only domain controllers remain.

entries.title: Constrained Delegation Allowing Privilege Escalation
entries.summary: Accounts configured for Kerberos constrained or resource-based delegation can impersonate any unprotected user, including administrators, to sensitive services.
entries.description:
One or more accounts are configured for Kerberos constrained delegation in a way that lets whoever controls the account gain privileged access to another system. Classic constrained delegation lists the services an account may access on behalf of users in its msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute; resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) instead lists, in the target's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute, the accounts allowed to delegate to it.

The configuration becomes a privilege escalation path when the delegating account can impersonate users to a sensitive service, most often on a domain controller, and particularly when protocol transition is enabled (Use any authentication protocol, shown by the TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION flag). The S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy Kerberos extensions then let the account obtain a ticket to the listed service as any user who is not protected from delegation, without that user's involvement. Because the service name in the resulting ticket is not cryptographically protected, a ticket for one service can be rewritten for another that runs under the same account, such as CIFS or LDAP on the same host. A related path exists where ordinary users can write the RBCD attribute of a computer object, which lets them grant themselves this ability over that computer.

Impacket's findDelegation.py, BloodHound (the AllowedToDelegate and AllowedToAct edges) and PingCastle identify these configurations.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains the credentials of the delegating account, or administrative control of the computer it belongs to, can impersonate any unprotected user, including domain administrators, to the services the account may delegate to. Where those services are on a domain controller this gives control of the domain; where they are on member servers it gives administrative access to those servers. Exploitation requires control of the delegating account first, which is why such accounts and their hosts need the same protection as the systems they can reach. Accounts marked as sensitive, or in the Protected Users group, cannot be impersonated in this way.
entries.remediation:
• Review every account with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo populated or the TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION flag set, and every object with RBCD configured, and remove delegation that is no longer needed.
  • Do not allow delegation to services on domain controllers or other Tier 0 systems. Where delegation is needed, limit it to the specific service on the specific host, and use Use Kerberos only rather than protocol transition unless the application requires it.
  • Protect delegating accounts and their hosts as highly privileged: use group managed service accounts or long random passwords, and restrict administrative access to the servers concerned.
  • Select Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated on privileged accounts, or add them to the Protected Users group.
  • Remove rights that let non-administrative users write msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on computer objects, such as GenericWrite or GenericAll granted to broad groups.
Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, userAccountControl Get-ADComputer -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity=*)' -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount

Confirm the fix by repeating these queries and the BloodHound analysis.

entries.title: AD CS Template Allows a Requester-Supplied Subject (ESC1)
entries.summary: A certificate template lets low-privileged users request authentication certificates for any identity they choose, such as a domain administrator.
entries.description:
An enterprise certification authority (CA) publishes a certificate template that lets the requester supply the certificate's subject, including its subject alternative name (SAN), while allowing low-privileged users to enrol and producing certificates that can be used to authenticate to Active Directory. Such a template has Supply in the request selected on its Subject Name tab (CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT in msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag), an extended key usage (EKU) that permits authentication (Client Authentication, PKINIT Client Authentication, Smart Card Logon, Any Purpose, or no EKU at all), enrolment rights for a broad group such as Domain Users, Domain Computers or Authenticated Users, and no requirement for manager approval or authorised signatures.

Because the CA issues the certificate for whichever identity the request names, any member of that group can obtain a certificate for another user, such as a domain administrator, and authenticate as that user through Kerberos (PKINIT) or Schannel. SpecterOps documented this as ESC1 in its Certified Pre-Owned research. Microsoft's strong certificate mapping changes do not prevent it, because the requester can also include the target account's security identifier (SID) in the SAN.

Certipy (certipy find -vulnerable), Certify, BloodHound and PingCastle identify such templates from the template objects and CA configuration in Active Directory, which any domain user can read.
entries.impact: Any user in a group with enrolment rights, including an account an attacker has phished or guessed, can obtain a certificate for a domain administrator and authenticate as that account, giving full control of the domain. The certificate stays valid for its whole validity period, set by the template and often a year or more, even if the impersonated account's password is changed, so it also provides durable persistence. The attack needs only standard enrolment requests and is reliable. Where enrolment is limited to Domain Computers, any user can usually still exploit it by creating a computer account, which ordinary users can do by default.
entries.remediation:
• On the affected template, select Build from this Active Directory information on the Subject Name tab instead of Supply in the request. Where the template's purpose genuinely needs a requester-supplied subject, such as web server certificates, remove the authentication EKUs and restrict enrolment to the administrators who issue those certificates.
  • Remove enrolment rights from broad groups such as Domain Users, Domain Computers and Authenticated Users, granting them only to the groups that need the template.
  • Where a template must keep these settings, require CA certificate manager approval on the Issuance Requirements tab so that each request is reviewed.
  • Stop publishing templates that are no longer needed, since an unpublished template cannot be requested.
  • Review the CA database for certificates already issued from the template with a SAN naming a different account from the requester, and revoke any that are not legitimate: a certificate remains usable after the template is fixed.

Confirm the fix by running certipy find -vulnerable again and requesting a certificate with a SAN naming another account, which should be refused or issued with the requester's own identity only.

entries.title: AD CS Template With Any Purpose or Enrolment Agent Usage (ESC2, ESC3)
entries.summary: Certificate templates open to low-privileged users issue Any Purpose or enrolment agent certificates that can be used to obtain certificates for other users.
entries.description:
An enterprise CA publishes a certificate template that low-privileged users can enrol in and whose certificates grant more than authentication as the requester. Two closely related cases, documented by SpecterOps as ESC2 and ESC3, are covered here.

In ESC2, the template has the Any Purpose EKU (2.5.29.37.0) or no EKU at all. The certificate can then be used for any purpose, including client authentication and acting as an enrolment agent, and a certificate with no EKU may also be usable to sign further certificates, which systems that trust the CA for purposes other than domain authentication could accept.

In ESC3, the template issues certificates with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1). An enrolment agent can request certificates on behalf of other users, so a low-privileged user who obtains one can then use a second template that accepts enrolment agent requests and permits authentication to obtain a certificate for any user, including a domain administrator. Schema version 1 templates, such as the default User template, accept such requests, and the CA does not restrict enrolment agents by default.

Certipy, Certify, BloodHound and PingCastle identify both conditions from the template and CA objects in Active Directory.
entries.impact: Any user with enrolment rights on the vulnerable template can obtain an enrolment agent capability, directly in ESC3 or through an Any Purpose certificate in ESC2, and use it to request a certificate for any other account, including domain administrators, giving full control of the domain. The resulting certificates remain valid until they expire or are revoked, regardless of password changes.
entries.remediation:
• Replace Any Purpose and empty EKU lists with the specific EKUs each template needs, and remove the Certificate Request Agent EKU from any template that ordinary users can enrol in.
  • Restrict enrolment on enrolment agent templates to the small group of staff or systems that act as enrolment agents, removing broad groups such as Domain Users, Domain Computers and Authenticated Users.
  • Configure enrolment agent restrictions on the CA (the Restrict enrollment agents option on the Enrollment Agents tab of the CA's properties), limiting which agents may enrol on behalf of which users and with which templates.
  • Require CA certificate manager approval on templates that must keep broad EKUs, and stop publishing templates that are not needed.
  • Review the CA database for certificates issued from these templates, and for certificates requested on behalf of other users, and revoke any that are not legitimate.

Confirm the fix by running certipy find -vulnerable again and attempting an on-behalf-of request with an enrolment agent certificate obtained by an ordinary user, which should fail.

entries.title: AD CS Certificate Template With Weak Access Control (ESC4)
entries.summary: Low-privileged users have write access to a certificate template and can reconfigure it to issue authentication certificates for any user.
entries.description:
The access control list of one or more certificate template objects in Active Directory gives low-privileged users rights that let them change the template. Templates are stored as objects under CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services in the configuration partition, and Full Control, Write Owner, Write DACL or Write Property rights (on all properties or on settings such as msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag and pKIExtendedKeyUsage), or ownership of the object, allow the holder to reconfigure it.

A user with such rights can make a published template vulnerable to ESC1, for example by enabling a requester-supplied subject and an authentication EKU and granting themselves enrolment, request a certificate for a privileged account, and then restore the original settings. SpecterOps documented this as ESC4. Such rights usually result from delegating template management to a broad group, or from nested group membership that is wider than intended.

Certipy, Certify, BloodHound and PingCastle identify these rights from the template security descriptors, which any domain user can read.
entries.impact: A user with write access to a published template can turn it into a means of obtaining a certificate for any account, including domain administrators, and so take control of the domain. The change can be made and reverted within minutes, so the template may look normal at a later review, although the modification is recorded where directory service changes are audited and the issued certificate remains in the CA database. The certificate stays valid until it expires or is revoked.
entries.remediation:
• Remove Full Control, Write Owner, Write DACL and Write Property rights on certificate templates from every principal other than the PKI administrators and built-in administrative groups, using the Security tab in the Certificate Templates console or ADSI Edit.
  • Check the owner of each template object and change it to an administrative group where it is an ordinary user or group.
  • Review the permissions of the related PKI objects as well (the Certificate Templates and Public Key Services containers, the CA objects and the NTAuthCertificates object), where similar rights also lead to compromise (ESC5).
  • Audit changes to these objects (Audit Directory Service Changes, event 5136, with a SACL on the Public Key Services container) and alert on template modifications.
  • Review the CA database for certificates issued while a template may have been altered, and revoke any that are not legitimate.

Confirm the fix by repeating the Certipy or BloodHound analysis as an ordinary user and checking that no template is reported as modifiable by low-privileged principals.

entries.title: AD CS EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Enabled (ESC6)
entries.summary: The CA accepts a requester-supplied subject alternative name on every certificate request, letting users ask for certificates that name other identities.
entries.description:
The EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag is set in the policy module settings of an enterprise CA. With the flag set, the CA accepts a subject alternative name supplied as a request attribute (for example san:upn= followed by an account name) on any request, whatever the template specifies, so every published template that permits authentication and lets ordinary users enrol, such as the default User template, behaves as though the requester could choose the identity in the certificate. SpecterOps documented this as ESC6. The flag is sometimes enabled so that web servers or devices can obtain certificates with additional names.

Since Microsoft's certificate-based authentication changes (KB5014754), CAs add the requester's security identifier (SID) to certificates built from Active Directory information, and domain controllers that enforce strong certificate mapping reject a certificate whose SAN names a different account from that SID. On fully updated domain controllers the flag is therefore normally blocked for Kerberos authentication on its own, but it becomes directly exploitable again where a template or the CA omits the SID extension, and systems that trust certificates on the strength of the SAN alone remain exposed.

Any domain user can read the flag remotely with certutil, and Certipy, Certify and PingCastle report it.
entries.impact: Where the SID extension is absent or strong mapping is not enforced, any user who can enrol in an authentication template can obtain a certificate for a domain administrator and take control of the domain. Where domain controllers fully enforce strong mapping, the flag still lets any enrolee obtain certificates naming arbitrary identities, which other systems that map certificates to users by their SAN may accept, and it turns any later weakening of the mapping into an immediate route to domain compromise.
entries.remediation:
Turn the flag off on every CA where it is set, after confirming nothing depends on it, and restart the CA service:

certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 net stop certsvc & net start certsvc
  • Check the result with certutil -getreg policy\EditFlags, which should no longer list the flag.
