  • Provide for any legitimate need for multi-name certificates, such as web servers, with a dedicated template that allows a requester-supplied subject, has no authentication EKU, and is restricted to the administrators who request such certificates.
  • Make sure every domain controller enforces strong certificate mapping (Full Enforcement, the default since the February 2025 updates), that no template sets CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION (ESC9), and that the CA has not been configured to disable the SID extension (ESC16).
  • Review the CA database for certificates issued with a SAN supplied as a request attribute, and revoke any that are not legitimate.

Confirm the fix by requesting a certificate from a user template with a SAN attribute naming another account: the certificate issued should contain only the requester's identity.

entries.title: AD CS Web Enrolment Vulnerable to NTLM Relay (ESC8)
entries.summary: An AD CS web enrolment endpoint accepts NTLM authentication without relay protection, so coerced or intercepted authentication can be relayed to obtain certificates.
entries.description:
Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) can offer HTTP-based enrolment interfaces: the Certification Authority Web Enrolment pages, normally at /certsrv/, and the Certificate Enrolment Web Service. When such an endpoint accepts NTLM authentication over plain HTTP, or over HTTPS without Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA), it cannot tell whether the authentication it receives has been relayed from another connection. An attacker who receives NTLM authentication from a computer or user can therefore relay it to the endpoint and request a certificate in the victim's name from any template the victim may use, such as the default templates for computers and domain controllers. SpecterOps documented this as ESC8 in its Certified Pre-Owned research.

The attack is usually combined with authentication coercion, in which a domain user makes a server, often a domain controller, connect to a host the attacker controls through RPC interfaces such as MS-EFSR (PetitPotam) or the print spooler's MS-RPRN. Authentication captured by poisoning name resolution can be relayed in the same way.

The weakness is identified by finding certification authorities with the web interfaces installed and checking whether each endpoint offers NTLM, through a WWW-Authenticate: NTLM or Negotiate challenge, over HTTP or over HTTPS without channel binding. Certipy reports vulnerable web enrolment as ESC8, and the relay can be demonstrated with Impacket's ntlmrelayx in its AD CS mode or with Certipy's relay command.
entries.impact: Relaying a domain controller's authentication yields a certificate for its computer account. The attacker can use the certificate to obtain a Kerberos ticket for that account through PKINIT and then replicate every password hash in the domain with DCSync, which amounts to full control of the domain. Relaying other computers or users gives control of those accounts in the same way. The certificate stays valid for the template's validity period, often a year, even if the account's password is changed, so it also provides persistence. The attack needs network access to the endpoint and a source of NTLM authentication: any domain account to trigger coercion, or a position on the local network to capture it.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the Certification Authority Web Enrolment role and the Certificate Enrolment Web Service wherever they are not needed. Domain-joined clients normally enrol through autoenrolment over RPC and do not use the web interfaces.
  • Where the web interfaces are needed, follow Microsoft's guidance in KB5005413: in IIS Manager, set Extended Protection to Required in the Advanced Settings of Windows Authentication for the CertSrv application and for the enrolment web service, and select Require SSL so that plain HTTP is refused. The enrolment web service also needs the matching extended protection setting in its web.config file, as the article describes. EPA binds the authentication to the TLS session, so relayed authentication fails.
  • Disable NTLM on these sites where clients can use Kerberos, for example by removing the NTLM provider from Windows Authentication in IIS, or by applying Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic to the certification authority servers.
  • Reduce the sources of relayable authentication: keep domain controllers up to date, disable the Print Spooler service on them and address the other coercion routes.
  • Review recently issued certificates for requests that were not expected, especially certificates for domain controller accounts issued outside normal autoenrolment, and revoke any that were not legitimately requested.

Confirm the fix by repeating the relay against each endpoint, which should be refused, and by checking that no endpoint offers NTLM over plain HTTP.

entries.title: LAPS Not Deployed
entries.summary: Local administrator passwords on domain computers are not managed by LAPS, so they are typically shared across many machines and rarely changed.
entries.description:
The Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) gives the local administrator account on each domain-joined computer a unique, random password, changes it on a schedule, and stores it in Active Directory (or Microsoft Entra ID), where only authorised accounts can read it. Windows LAPS is built into Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2019 and later when they are up to date; the older Microsoft LAPS was a separately installed component.

Where neither is deployed, or where deployment covers only part of the estate, local administrator passwords are set by a build image, a script or by hand. In practice they are the same on large groups of computers and rarely change, because there is no practical way to manage many unique passwords without such a tool.

The absence of LAPS can be confirmed with any domain account: the LAPS schema attributes are missing, or the password expiry attribute (ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime for Microsoft LAPS, msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime for Windows LAPS) is empty on most computer objects. PingCastle, BloodHound and NetExec report the coverage. Common gaps are servers excluded on purpose, computers in organisational units the policy is not linked to, and computers that cannot update their own password attributes because the permissions were not delegated.
entries.impact: Without unique local administrator passwords, an attacker who gains administrative access to one computer, for example through a vulnerability or a user with local administrative rights, can extract the local administrator's password hash and use it to authenticate to every computer that shares the password, without cracking it. A single compromised workstation then becomes administrative access across the estate, including servers where privileged users have signed in and left credentials that can be harvested. Passwords that never change also remain known to former staff and to anyone who has seen a build image or script. Exploitation needs an initial administrative foothold, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
• Deploy Windows LAPS to every domain-joined workstation and member server: extend the schema with Update-LapsADSchema, allow computers to update their own password attributes with Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission on the relevant organisational units, and configure the policy under Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > System > LAPS, with the password backup directory set to Active Directory (or Microsoft Entra ID for devices joined only to Entra ID).
  • Enable password encryption, and restrict who can read or decrypt the passwords to the administrators who need them (Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission). Review existing rights with Find-LapsADExtendedRights, since anyone who can read a password can sign in as that computer's administrator.
  • Configure a post-authentication action so the password is changed soon after it has been used.
  • Where legacy Microsoft LAPS is in use, plan its migration to Windows LAPS, and do not let both manage the same account.
  • Include servers and other exceptions explicitly rather than leaving them out.

Until coverage is complete, disable the shared local administrator account where it is not needed, and add the well-known group Local account and member of Administrators group to Deny access to this computer from the network on workstations. Confirm the fix by checking that the expiry attribute is populated and in the future on every computer object, and that Get-LapsADPassword returns a current password for a sample of computers.

entries.title: Local Administrator Password Reuse
entries.summary: The same local administrator password is set on many computers, so its hash taken from one machine gives administrative access to the others.
entries.description:
The same password, and therefore the same NT hash, is set for a local administrator account on many computers. This usually comes from a build image, a deployment script or a Group Policy setting that configured the account once for the whole estate, and it persists wherever local administrator passwords are not managed individually.

Windows accepts the NT hash in place of the password for NTLM network authentication, so a hash extracted from one computer's Security Account Manager (SAM) database can be used directly against the others without being cracked (pass-the-hash). By default, User Account Control's remote restrictions give local accounts a filtered, non-administrative token over the network, but the built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is exempt unless Admin Approval Mode is enabled for it, and the restrictions are lifted for all local accounts where LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy is set to 1.

The issue is confirmed by recovering a local administrator hash from one computer, through access gained elsewhere in the test, and authenticating with it to other hosts with a tool such as NetExec using local authentication, which reports each host where the account has administrative rights. A variant is a local administrator password that is also used for a domain account, which links workstation compromise directly to the domain.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains administrative access to any one computer can take administrative control of every other computer that shares the password, often the whole workstation estate and many servers, within minutes. From those hosts they can harvest the credentials of domain users and administrators who have signed in, disable security tools and deploy ransomware widely. Exploitation needs an initial administrative foothold on one computer, which limits the rating, but such footholds are commonly gained through phishing, local privilege escalation or another weakness.
entries.remediation:
• Give the local administrator account on every computer a unique, random password that changes regularly, using Windows LAPS (or legacy Microsoft LAPS where Windows LAPS is not available). This is the only fix that scales.
  • Prevent network use of local administrative accounts: add the well-known group Local account and member of Administrators group to the user rights Deny access to this computer from the network and Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services on workstations and member servers. The group covers every local administrative account whatever its name; Microsoft's guidance on securing local administrator accounts adds the built-in Administrator account to the same rights.
  • Remove the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, or set it to 0, wherever it has been set to 1.
  • Disable the built-in Administrator account on workstations where support staff use another managed account, and stop setting local passwords through build images and scripts.
  • Change the password of any domain account that shares the local administrator password.

Treat every computer that shared the password as exposed until the password has been changed on all of them. Confirm the fix by repeating the pass-the-hash test with the old hash, which should fail on every host.

entries.title: Excessive Membership of Privileged Groups
entries.summary: More accounts than necessary are members of groups that control Active Directory, so compromising any one of them gives control of the domain.
entries.description:
Active Directory's privileged groups give their members control of the domain or a direct route to it. Besides Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins and the built-in Administrators group, they include the operator groups: members of Backup Operators can back up the directory database from a domain controller, Server Operators can sign in to domain controllers and manage their services and files, Account Operators can change most accounts and groups that are not protected, and Print Operators can load device drivers on domain controllers. DnsAdmins, whose members can make the DNS Server service load a DLL of their choosing, is equivalent where DNS runs on domain controllers.

The finding applies when these groups contain more accounts than the organisation needs: everyday user accounts rather than separate administrative accounts, service accounts, accounts of staff who have changed role or left, disabled or unused accounts, and accounts added indirectly through nested groups. Each member is a credential whose theft gives an attacker the group's rights.

Membership, including nested membership, can be listed by any domain user, for example with Get-ADGroupMember -Recursive, BloodHound or PingCastle, and compared with the organisation's approved list of administrators.
entries.impact: Each unnecessary member adds an account through which an attacker can take control of the domain: a phished user account that is also a domain administrator, a service account with a crackable password, or a forgotten account whose password has not changed in years. Once one is compromised, the attacker can read every password hash, change any account or policy and persist in the domain. Everyday accounts with administrative rights are particularly exposed, because they are used for email and web browsing and leave credentials on ordinary workstations. The finding needs a member's credentials to be obtained before it can be exploited, which is reflected in the rating.
entries.remediation:
• Review the membership of each privileged group, including nested groups, against a documented list of who needs it and why, and remove every account that is not on the list. Keep Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins empty except while a change that needs them is being made.
  • Give administrators separate accounts for administrative work, used only for that purpose, and keep their everyday accounts unprivileged.
  • Remove service accounts from privileged groups and grant them only the rights their service needs. Where a vendor states that an application needs Domain Admins, establish the rights it actually requires.
  • Leave the Account Operators, Backup Operators, Server Operators and Print Operators groups empty unless there is a specific need, and delegate narrower rights on organisational units instead.
  • Where possible, grant administrative rights only for the time they are needed, for example with time-limited group membership through Active Directory's Privileged Access Management feature or a privileged access management product.
  • Alert on changes to privileged groups (events 4728, 4732 and 4756 record members added to security groups) and repeat the membership review regularly.

Confirm the fix by listing recursive membership again and comparing it with the approved list.

entries.title: Stale or Inactive Accounts Enabled
entries.summary: User or computer accounts that have not been used for a long time remain enabled, leaving unmonitored accounts that an attacker could take over.
entries.description:
Accounts that are no longer used remain enabled in Active Directory: accounts of staff who have left or changed role, test and temporary accounts, accounts that were created but never used, and computer accounts for machines that have been retired. Because nobody uses them, their passwords are often old, set to a known initial value, or still known to former staff and suppliers, and activity on them is unlikely to be noticed.

Inactive accounts are identified from the lastLogonTimestamp attribute, which any domain user can read, together with pwdLastSet and the date the account was created. lastLogonTimestamp is replicated between domain controllers but by default is only updated when the stored value is more than 9 to 14 days old, so it is accurate to within about two weeks; the lastLogon attribute is exact but is not replicated and must be read from every domain controller. Accounts with no sign-in for 90 days or more are commonly reported, although the threshold should follow the organisation's own policy. Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive, PingCastle and BloodHound list them.
entries.impact: An enabled but unused account gives an attacker a way in that is less likely to be noticed than a live user's account. Old and initial passwords are good candidates for password spraying, and a former employee or supplier may still know theirs. Once in, the attacker has the account's access, which may include group memberships and rights that were never removed, and can use the account to keep access over time. Stale computer accounts carry less risk, but each is another credential that can authenticate to the domain. The rating reflects that the attacker must still obtain or guess the password.
entries.remediation:
• Disable user and computer accounts that have not signed in within the period set by policy, commonly 90 days, after confirming with their owners, and delete them after a further retention period. Moving disabled accounts to a separate organisational unit makes them easier to manage.
  • Link account management to the joiners, movers and leavers process, so that accounts are disabled on a leaver's last day, and give contractor and temporary accounts an expiry date (Set-ADAccountExpiration).
  • Record an owner for every service, test and shared account and review them regularly. Service accounts can show little sign-in activity while still in use, so confirm before disabling them.
  • Alert on successful sign-ins to accounts that have been inactive, which is a common sign of misuse.

Automate the review, for example with a scheduled report of inactive accounts that are still enabled:

Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 | Where-Object Enabled | Select-Object Name, ObjectClass, LastLogonDate

Confirm the fix by running the inactivity query again and checking that no enabled account exceeds the threshold without a documented reason.

entries.title: Accounts With Passwords That Never Expire
entries.summary: Accounts are exempt from password expiry, so passwords set years ago, often on service and administrative accounts, stay valid however widely they have been exposed.
entries.description:
The Password never expires option (the DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD flag, value 0x10000, in userAccountControl) exempts an account from the maximum password age in the domain's password policy. It is commonly set on service accounts, so that a password change cannot break the services that use them, and on administrative, shared and test accounts for convenience.

Current guidance from the UK NCSC and NIST advises against forcing regular expiry of user passwords, because it encourages predictable passwords. The concern with this finding is therefore not the flag itself but what it typically hides: passwords that have not changed for years (shown by pwdLastSet), were set before the current password policy, are known to former staff or suppliers, or appear in old scripts and documentation, often on accounts with high privileges.

Any domain user can list the accounts with the LDAP filter (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=65536) or with Get-ADUser -Filter 'PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true' -Properties PasswordLastSet, and compare their password ages.
entries.impact: A password that never has to change remains valid however it is exposed: cracked offline from a Kerberos service ticket, recovered from a script or share, reused from a breach, or remembered by someone who has left. With no expiry and no review, an attacker who obtains such a password, or an insider who already knows it, can keep using it indefinitely. The impact depends on the account: for an ordinary user it is limited to that user's access, but these accounts are frequently service or administrative accounts, where it can extend to control of the systems they run or of the domain. The flag alone does not disclose a password, which keeps the rating low.
entries.remediation:
• Replace service accounts with group managed service accounts (gMSAs) wherever the service supports them. The domain sets and changes their long random passwords automatically, so the flag is not needed.
  • For service accounts that cannot use a gMSA, set a long, randomly generated password and change it on a schedule and whenever someone who knew it leaves, coordinating the change with the services that use it.
  • For user and administrative accounts, apply the same password policy as everyone else rather than exempting individual accounts. Where the organisation follows current guidance and does not force expiry, rely on long passwords, a banned password list and multi-factor authentication instead, and require a change whenever compromise is suspected.
  • Change the passwords of accounts whose pwdLastSet predates the current password policy or the departure of staff who knew them, starting with privileged accounts.
  • Record an owner and a justification for every account that keeps the flag, and review the list regularly.

Confirm the fix by running the query again and checking that each remaining account is documented and has a recent pwdLastSet value.

entries.title: Accounts Not Required to Have a Password
entries.summary: Accounts carry the PASSWD_NOTREQD flag, which lets them work with an empty password even where the domain password policy requires one.
entries.description:
The PASSWD_NOTREQD flag (value 0x0020) in an account's userAccountControl attribute lets the account work with an empty password, even where the domain's password policy requires one. The flag is not shown among the account options in Active Directory Users and Computers, so it often goes unnoticed. It is typically left by provisioning tools, scripts and migrations: an account created through LDAP without an initial password is given the flag, and tools that later enable the account often leave it in place.

The flag does not mean that the account has an empty password, only that it is allowed to. Any domain user can list flagged accounts with the LDAP filter (userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=32) or Get-ADUser -Filter 'PasswordNotRequired -eq $true'. The weakness is then confirmed by attempting to authenticate to each enabled account with an empty password, for example with NetExec, using a single attempt per account so that no account is locked out.
entries.impact: Where a flagged account has an empty password, anyone who can reach a domain controller can authenticate as that account and gain its access to the domain and its resources, without any prior foothold. Where the password is merely weak, password spraying is likely to find it. The impact depends on what the account can do: often that of a standard user, but sometimes a service or administrative account created by the same tool. The rating reflects the typical case, in which a flagged account must still be found to have an empty or weak password before it can be used.
entries.remediation:
• Find the tool or process that sets the flag, such as an account creation script, an identity management connector or a migration tool, and correct it so that new accounts are created with a password and without the flag.
  • For each flagged account that is still needed, set a password that meets the policy and then clear the flag. Clearing the flag does not change an existing password, so the reset is what removes an empty one.
  • Disable flagged accounts that are no longer needed.
  • Check for the flag regularly, since provisioning tools can set it again.

For example, to list flagged accounts and, once each has a compliant password, clear the flag:

Get-ADUser -Filter 'PasswordNotRequired -eq $true' -Properties PasswordLastSet | Select-Object SamAccountName, Enabled, PasswordLastSet Get-ADUser -Filter 'PasswordNotRequired -eq $true' | Set-ADAccountControl -PasswordNotRequired $false

Confirm the fix by running the query again, which should return no enabled accounts, and by repeating the empty-password test against the accounts that were flagged.

entries.title: Passwords Stored in Active Directory Attributes
entries.summary: Passwords are written in plain text in user or computer object attributes, such as the description field, that every domain user can read.
entries.description:
Passwords have been recorded in plain text in attributes of Active Directory objects. The most common location is the description attribute of user, service and computer accounts, where administrators note an initial or service password, followed by the info attribute (shown as Notes in Active Directory Users and Computers) and other free-text fields. Some UNIX integration and identity management tools also populate attributes such as userPassword, unixUserPassword or msSFU30Password with a password or password hash.

By default every authenticated domain user can read the description attribute of every account, so a password stored there is effectively shared with the whole organisation, and with anyone on the network where anonymous LDAP access is permitted. Other attributes may be readable just as widely, depending on the directory's permissions. None of them is protected like the account's real password, which domain controllers never return over LDAP.

The issue is identified by retrieving these attributes for all objects over LDAP and searching them for terms such as pass, pwd and pw and for values that look like passwords, with PowerShell, ldapsearch, ldapdomaindump, BloodHound or NetExec, then confirming that a candidate password authenticates.
entries.impact: Any domain user, or an attacker who has compromised one, can collect these passwords without special tools or privileges and sign in as the accounts concerned. Service accounts are frequently affected, and they often hold administrative rights over servers or the domain; user accounts noted with an initial password that was never changed are also exposed. The exposure lasts until each password is changed: removing the text from the attribute alone does not end it, because anyone may already have read it.
entries.remediation:
• Change the password of every account whose password, current or past, was found in an attribute, starting with privileged and service accounts. Treat the passwords as compromised, since they may already have been read.
  • Remove the passwords from the attributes, searching all object types rather than only users (see the example below).
  • Store service and shared account passwords in a password manager or privileged access management system with access control and auditing, and replace service accounts with group managed service accounts where possible.
  • Give new users their initial passwords by a separate channel and require a change at first sign-in, rather than recording them in the directory.
  • Where UNIX integration attributes such as userPassword or unixUserPassword are populated, establish whether they are still used, clear them if not, and restrict who can read them if they are.
  • Add a search for passwords in attributes to routine directory reviews and to the account provisioning process.

For example, to find candidate values in the description and Notes fields of every object:

Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter '(|(description=*pass*)(description=*pwd*)(info=*pass*)(info=*pwd*))' -Properties description, info | Select-Object Name, ObjectClass, description, info

Confirm the fix by repeating the search across all objects and testing that the passwords found previously no longer authenticate.

entries.title: Group Policy Preferences Passwords (MS14-025)
entries.summary: Group Policy Preferences files in SYSVOL hold cpassword values encrypted with a key Microsoft has published, so any domain user can recover the passwords.
entries.description:
Group Policy Preferences, introduced with Windows Server 2008, could set passwords through preference items for local users and groups, services, scheduled tasks, mapped drives and data sources. Each password is saved in the cpassword attribute of an XML file, such as Groups.xml, Services.xml, ScheduledTasks.xml, Drives.xml or DataSources.xml, in the policy's folder in SYSVOL. The value is encrypted with AES-256, but every installation uses the same key, which Microsoft published in its protocol documentation, so anyone who can read the file can decrypt it.

Every authenticated domain user can read SYSVOL. Security update MS14-025 (CVE-2014-1812) removed the ability to enter passwords in these preference items, but it does not remove files that already exist, so passwords set before the update remain until the preference items are deleted. They often survive in old, disabled or unlinked policies that are no longer reviewed.

The weakness is identified by searching the XML files in SYSVOL for cpassword values that are not empty, with findstr or with tools that also decrypt them, such as PowerSploit's Get-GPPPassword, NetExec's gpp_password module or Metasploit. Vulnerability scanners report it as MS14-025.
entries.impact: Any domain user can recover the passwords within seconds. They are most often the password of a local administrator account set on many computers, which gives administrative access to all of them, and sometimes the passwords of domain service accounts used by scheduled tasks or services, which may hold wider rights. Where an account's password has not changed since the preference item was created, the attacker can use it immediately; an older password may still reveal the pattern used for current ones.
entries.remediation:
• Find every XML file in SYSVOL that contains a cpassword value, including those in disabled and unlinked policies (see the example below).
  • Delete the preference items that contain passwords, or the whole policy where it is no longer needed, using the Group Policy Management Console so that the change replicates to every domain controller.
  • Change the password of every account named in those files, on every system where it is set, because the passwords must be assumed to be known.
  • Use Windows LAPS for local administrator passwords and group managed service accounts for services and scheduled tasks, instead of setting passwords through Group Policy.
  • Confirm that the systems used to manage Group Policy have the MS14-025 update (KB2962486) or run a later version of Windows that includes it, so that new passwords cannot be added.

For example, from a domain-joined computer:

findstr /S /I /M cpassword \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\SYSVOL\*.xml

Confirm the fix by repeating the search, which should find no cpassword value with content, and by testing that the recovered passwords no longer authenticate.

entries.title: Credentials in SYSVOL or NETLOGON Scripts
entries.summary: Logon, startup or deployment scripts in SYSVOL or NETLOGON contain user names and passwords that every domain user can read.
entries.description:
Scripts and files stored in the SYSVOL share, including the NETLOGON share that points to its scripts folder, contain credentials in readable form. Typical examples are logon scripts that map drives with net use and an explicit user name and password, startup scripts that set the local administrator password with net user, PowerShell that builds a credential from a plain-text string with ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText, and batch files that run tools such as PsExec with a password on the command line. Copies of installation, answer and configuration files, and old versions of scripts left in policy folders, are other sources. Passwords that are Base64-encoded or otherwise obscured are equally exposed, because the script itself must be able to recover them.

SYSVOL is replicated to every domain controller and every authenticated user can read it by default, so a credential written there is available to anyone with a domain account, often for years, because scripts are rarely reviewed once they work.

The issue is identified by reading the scripts and files in SYSVOL and NETLOGON and searching them for terms such as password, pwd, /user: and AsPlainText, manually or with tools such as Snaffler or NetExec's share spidering modules, then confirming that the credentials found are valid. Passwords in Group Policy Preferences XML files are a related issue that is reported separately.
entries.impact: Any domain user can recover the credentials and sign in as the accounts concerned. These are often accounts with elevated rights: a local administrator password applied by a startup script gives administrative access to every computer that runs it, and accounts used to join computers to the domain, map shares or run deployment tools frequently have wide permissions on servers or in the directory. Because logon scripts run everywhere and are rarely changed, the credentials are usually still valid, and changing them needs coordination with every system that depends on the script.
entries.remediation:
• Change the password of every account whose credentials were found, and assume that others have already read them.
  • Remove the credentials from the scripts and files, and delete obsolete scripts, backup copies and installation files from SYSVOL and NETLOGON. Make each change once and let replication carry it to every domain controller.
  • Redesign the tasks so that they need no stored secret: map drives with the user's own credentials, run computer startup tasks as the computer account, use Windows LAPS for local administrator passwords, and use group managed service accounts for services and scheduled tasks.
  • Where a task must run under a separate identity, retrieve the secret at run time from a secrets management service that authorises the specific computer or user, rather than storing it in the script.
  • Review new scripts before they are placed in SYSVOL, and add a periodic search for credentials there to routine directory reviews.

Confirm the fix by repeating the search of SYSVOL and NETLOGON and testing that the credentials found previously no longer authenticate.

entries.title: Credentials Found in File Shares
entries.summary: Network file shares that ordinary domain users can read hold files containing passwords, keys or other credentials.
entries.description:
File shares that ordinary domain users can read contain files with credentials. Common examples are spreadsheets and documents listing passwords; configuration files with database connection strings or service passwords, such as web.config, appsettings.json and .env files; unattended installation files such as unattend.xml and sysprep.inf; scripts; password manager databases; private keys and certificates with their passphrases; PowerShell history files in redirected profiles; and backups or virtual machine disk images that contain whole systems' credential stores.

The exposure usually arises because shares are created with broad permissions for Everyone, Authenticated Users or Domain Users, on the share, the file system or both, and files are then added over years without regard to who can read them. IT team shares, software deployment and backup locations, home drives and departmental shares with inherited permissions are frequent sources.

The issue is identified by enumerating shares with a standard domain account and searching the readable content for credential patterns with tools such as Snaffler, NetExec's spider_plus module or PowerView, followed by manual review of the matches and confirmation that the credentials are valid. The results reflect what a single account could read, so other accounts may be able to see more.
entries.impact: Any domain user, or an attacker using a compromised account, can collect the credentials and use them to sign in to the systems they protect. The impact depends on what is found: database and application service accounts give access to business data, while administrative and infrastructure credentials, which are common in IT shares and scripts, can lead directly to control of servers or the domain. Credentials kept in files also tend to be reused across systems and rarely changed. Backups and disk images can expose every credential held on the systems they capture.
entries.remediation:
• Change every credential found and remove the files, or the credentials in them. Assume the credentials have already been read.
  • Review share and NTFS permissions, removing Everyone, Authenticated Users and Domain Users from shares that hold anything other than information intended for all staff, and grant access only to the groups that need it. Access-based enumeration can also hide folders that users cannot open.
  • Move secrets used by applications and scripts into a secrets management service or the platform's own protected store, and use group managed service accounts and Windows LAPS where they remove the need for a stored password.
  • Provide an approved password manager for passwords that staff need to share, and make clear that passwords must not be kept in documents.
  • Restrict backup and virtual machine storage to the administrators who manage it.
  • Scan shares regularly for credential patterns with the same tools an attacker would use, and act on the results.

Confirm the fix by repeating the share search with a standard domain account and testing that the credentials found previously no longer work.

entries.title: NTLMv1 or LM Authentication Permitted
entries.summary: Hosts in the domain send or accept LM or NTLMv1 authentication, whose responses can be turned back into the account's NT hash regardless of password strength.
entries.description:
The Network security: LAN Manager authentication level policy (the LmCompatibilityLevel registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa) decides which NTLM response types a computer sends and, on domain controllers, which it accepts. At levels 0 to 2 a computer sends LM or NTLMv1 responses, and domain controllers accept NTLMv1 from clients unless they are set to level 5 (Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM). Legacy devices and applications, and policies lowered years ago for compatibility, are the usual causes.

NTLMv1 builds its response by using the account's NT hash as three DES keys to encrypt the server's challenge. DES keys are small enough to be recovered by brute force, and from precomputed tables where the attacker chooses the challenge and extended session security is not used, so a captured response yields the NT hash whatever the password. LM responses are weaker still. NTLMv1 also lacks the message integrity code that NTLMv2 provides, which makes its messages easier to relay to services such as LDAP.

The weakness is identified from Group Policy and registry settings, from security event 4624 on domain controllers, whose Package Name (NTLM only) field shows NTLM V1 for such sign-ins, and from responses captured during testing, which tools such as Responder label as NTLMv1.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains an NTLMv1 response, by poisoning name resolution on the local network or by coercing a computer to authenticate to them, can recover the NT hash of the account involved and use it to authenticate as that account (pass-the-hash), or crack it to reveal the password. Where servers or domain controllers themselves send NTLMv1, coercing one to authenticate gives the hash of its computer account: for a domain controller this allows every password hash in the domain to be replicated with DCSync, and for a server it allows service tickets to be forged for administrative access to it. Exploitation needs a source of authentication and some effort to recover the hash, but not a weak password.
entries.remediation:
• Set Network security: LAN Manager authentication level to Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM (level 5) on domain controllers and, once compatibility is confirmed, on all servers and workstations. The setting is under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. Level 3 on clients is a first step that stops them sending LM and NTLMv1.
  • Before refusing NTLMv1 on domain controllers, identify the clients that still use it from event 4624 records showing NTLM V1, as Microsoft's guidance on auditing NTLMv1 describes, and upgrade, reconfigure or isolate them.
  • Remove any policy that sets a lower level for systems that no longer exist or no longer need it.
  • Reduce NTLM use generally: audit it with the Network security: Restrict NTLM policies, prefer Kerberos, and require SMB and LDAP signing so that relayed authentication is rejected.

The equivalent registry setting is:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa LmCompatibilityLevel (REG_DWORD) = 5

Confirm the fix by checking the effective setting on domain controllers and a sample of hosts, and by repeating the capture: hosts should no longer send NTLMv1, and domain controllers should refuse it.

entries.title: LM Password Hashes Stored
entries.summary: Passwords are stored as LAN Manager (LM) hashes in Active Directory or local SAM databases, a format that can be cracked quickly to reveal the password.
entries.description:
The LAN Manager (LM) hash is a legacy password format kept for compatibility with very old clients. It converts the password to upper case, limits it to 14 characters, splits it into two independent seven-character halves and uses each half as a DES key to encrypt a fixed string, with no salt. Each half can therefore be cracked separately, and the whole space of seven-character upper-case strings can be searched in a short time or looked up in precomputed tables. A password of 15 or more characters cannot be stored as an LM hash.

Windows stops creating LM hashes when the policy Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change is enabled (the NoLMHash registry value), which has been the default since Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008. The setting takes effect only when each password is next changed, so LM hashes persist for accounts whose passwords have not changed since it was enabled, and are created again wherever the policy has been disabled.

The issue is identified when password hashes are extracted, from the directory database during an authorised password audit or after domain compromise, or from a computer's SAM database, and accounts have an LM hash other than the empty value aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee. It can also be found by reviewing the policy setting.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains the password hashes, for example by compromising a domain controller, a backup of the directory database or a computer's SAM database, can recover the passwords of accounts with LM hashes almost immediately, in upper case, and then use the NT hash to find the correct letter case. The NT hash alone is already enough for pass-the-hash within the domain, so the additional risk is disclosure of the plain-text password, which users often reuse on other systems, on cloud services and in later passwords. Obtaining the hashes needs high privileges, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
• Enable Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change in a policy that applies to domain controllers and to all computers (Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options), and remove any policy that disables it.
  • Require a password change for every account that still has an LM hash, since the setting takes effect only at the next change. Include service and administrative accounts, whose passwords change least often, and local accounts on computers.
  • Encourage long passphrases: a password of 15 or more characters never produces an LM hash.
  • Identify and replace any remaining system that needs LM authentication, rather than keeping LM hashes for it.

The equivalent registry setting is:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa NoLMHash (REG_DWORD) = 1

Confirm the fix at the next authorised password audit: no account should have an LM hash other than the empty value.

entries.title: LDAP Signing and Channel Binding Not Enforced
entries.summary: Domain controllers accept LDAP binds without signing, or LDAPS binds without channel binding, so relayed NTLM authentication can be used to change the directory.
entries.description:
Domain controllers do not require LDAP signing (Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements is not set to Require signing), or do not enforce channel binding for LDAP over TLS (Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements is not set to Always). Signing protects the integrity of an LDAP session on port 389, and channel binding ties authentication sent over LDAPS on port 636 to the TLS session that carries it. Without them a domain controller cannot tell whether an NTLM authentication it receives has been relayed by an attacker from a connection made to them, and it also accepts simple binds that send passwords in clear text on port 389.

The settings can be confirmed by attempting an unsigned NTLM bind on port 389 and an LDAPS bind without channel binding information, for example with NetExec or LdapRelayScan, and, where agreed, by relaying an authentication to the domain controller with ntlmrelayx. On the domain controller, Directory Service event 2887 counts the unsigned and clear-text binds received each day, and event 2889 identifies the clients once LDAP interface diagnostic logging has been raised.
entries.impact: An attacker who can obtain NTLM authentication from a user or computer, for example through name resolution poisoning or by coercing a workstation's WebDAV client to authenticate over HTTP, can relay it to a domain controller and act in the directory with the victim's rights. Relaying a computer's authentication lets the attacker configure resource-based constrained delegation or shadow credentials on that computer, giving administrative access to it; relaying an administrator's authentication can add accounts to privileged groups or grant replication rights, giving control of the domain. NTLM authentication from SMB clients normally requests signing and cannot be relayed to LDAP in this way, so the attack usually needs an HTTP source, which is reflected in the rating.
entries.remediation:
• Set Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements to Require signing in the policy applied to domain controllers (Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options).
  • Set Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements to Always, which corresponds to the LdapEnforceChannelBinding value of 2 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters.
  • Before enforcing either setting, find the clients that would fail: set the 16 LDAP Interface Events value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics to 2 on each domain controller, review event 2889, and reconfigure those clients to sign, to use LDAPS with channel binding, or to use Kerberos.
  • Keep Network security: LDAP client signing requirements at Negotiate signing or higher on all computers so that Windows clients sign their sessions.
  • Reduce relay sources: disable the WebClient service where WebDAV is not needed, and address name resolution poisoning and authentication coercion.

Confirm the fix by repeating the unsigned bind, the LDAPS bind without channel binding and the relay attempt against every domain controller; each should be rejected.

entries.title: Domain Controllers Can Be Coerced to Authenticate
entries.summary: Domain controllers expose RPC interfaces that let any domain user make them authenticate to a chosen host, where their credentials can be relayed or captured.
entries.description:
Several Windows RPC interfaces accept a path or address from the caller and make the server connect to it, authenticating as its own computer account. On domain controllers, the methods most often abused are the print spooler's MS-RPRN interface (the printer bug), the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol MS-EFSR (PetitPotam), the DFS Namespace Management Protocol MS-DFSNM (DFSCoerce) and, where the File Server VSS Agent Service is installed, MS-FSRVP (ShadowCoerce). Any authenticated domain user can call them where the corresponding service is running. Updates have closed some routes, such as unauthenticated PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942), but authenticated coercion through several of these interfaces still works on fully updated systems.

Coercion matters because of where the authentication can be sent: to AD CS web enrolment without Extended Protection for Authentication, to a host configured for unconstrained delegation that the attacker controls, or to an attacker's listener where the domain controller sends NTLMv1.

Coercer and NetExec's coercion modules test each known method. A successful test shows an incoming authentication from the domain controller's computer account at the tester's listener.
entries.impact: Coercion on its own gives an attacker only an authentication attempt, but combined with a suitable target it usually leads to control of the domain. Relaying a domain controller's authentication to AD CS web enrolment produces a certificate for the domain controller, and coercing it to authenticate to a host with unconstrained delegation exposes its Kerberos ticket-granting ticket; either allows every password hash in the domain to be replicated with DCSync. Exploitation needs a domain account, network access to the domain controller and a usable target, and the rating reflects that dependence.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the targets, which is the most effective step: enable Extended Protection for Authentication and require HTTPS on AD CS web enrolment, or remove it; remove unconstrained delegation from every host other than domain controllers; refuse NTLMv1; and require SMB signing and LDAP signing and channel binding.
  • Stop and disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers, as Microsoft recommends, and on other servers that do not need it.
  • Block the RPC interfaces that are not needed, such as MS-EFSR and MS-DFSNM, with RPC filters (netsh rpc filter) or an endpoint security product that offers equivalent controls, after testing that file encryption and DFS administration are not affected.
  • Restrict outbound connections from domain controllers to the networks and services they need, so that they cannot reach an attacker's listener over SMB or HTTP.
  • Keep domain controllers up to date, and restrict NTLM on them where the estate allows, since most relay routes depend on it.

Confirm the fix by repeating the coercion tests against each domain controller and the relay attempts against each target; no usable authentication should reach the listener.

entries.title: Print Spooler Remote Code Execution (PrintNightmare)
entries.summary: The Windows Print Spooler lets an authenticated user install a printer driver that runs as SYSTEM, giving remote code execution on unpatched or weakly configured hosts.
entries.description:
PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527, closely related to CVE-2021-1675) is a flaw in the driver installation functions of the Windows Print Spooler service, RpcAddPrinterDriverEx in MS-RPRN and RpcAsyncAddPrinterDriver in MS-PAR. An authenticated user can call them remotely and make the spooler load a DLL of their choosing, which runs as SYSTEM. The service runs by default on Windows clients and servers, including domain controllers.

Microsoft's updates from July 2021 onwards fix the flaw, and since August 2021 they restrict printer driver installation to administrators by default (RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators). An updated host can still be exploitable where that value has been set to 0 and Point and Print policy suppresses the warning and elevation prompts (NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall or UpdatePromptSettings set to 1 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint).

The weakness is identified by checking whether a host exposes the MS-RPRN and MS-PAR interfaces (for example with Impacket's rpcdump.py), its update level and the registry values above. It can be confirmed by loading a harmless DLL with a public exploit, which should be done only where agreed, because a failed attempt can stop the spooler.
entries.impact: Any domain user can run code as SYSTEM on an affected host over the network. On a domain controller this gives immediate control of the domain, including every password hash; on other servers and workstations it gives full control of the host and access to the credentials of users signed in to it. Public exploits are reliable, and the flaw has been widely exploited, including in ransomware attacks. Where the spooler cannot be reached over the network, the flaw still lets any local user become SYSTEM.
entries.remediation:
• Install the latest cumulative security update on every Windows host, starting with domain controllers and servers.
  • Stop and disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and on every server and workstation that does not need to print (see the example below, or set the service to Disabled through Group Policy).
  • Ensure that RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators is 1 or not set, and that NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall and UpdatePromptSettings are 0 or not set, under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint. Where users must install printer drivers, use the Point and Print Restrictions policy limited to approved print servers rather than suppressing the prompts.
  • On hosts that must keep the spooler running but do not share printers, disable inbound remote printing with the policy Allow Print Spooler to accept client connections (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Printers).

To disable the service with PowerShell:

Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled

Confirm the fix by checking the update level, service state and registry values, and by repeating the exploit attempt, which should be refused.

entries.title: Netlogon Elevation of Privilege (Zerologon, CVE-2020-1472)
entries.summary: A flaw in the Netlogon protocol's cryptography lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a domain controller take over its account and the domain.
entries.description:
Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) is a flaw in the Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC), which domain-joined computers use to set up a secure channel with a domain controller. The protocol computes its authentication credentials with AES in CFB8 mode and an initialisation vector fixed at zero. For about one in every 256 session keys, a client challenge and credential made entirely of zeros is then accepted, so an attacker can authenticate as any computer account, including the domain controller's own, by repeating the attempt, on average about 256 times, without knowing its password. On a vulnerable domain controller the attacker can then turn off signing and sealing for the channel and call NetrServerPasswordSet2 to change the account's password, for example to an empty one.

Microsoft addressed the flaw in two phases: the August 2020 security updates added the protection, and the February 2021 updates enforced secure RPC for all Netlogon connections unless an account is explicitly allowed by the policy Domain controller: Allow vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections. A domain controller without the August 2020 update is vulnerable, and accounts listed in that policy remain exposed.

The weakness is identified with a non-destructive check, such as the test script published by Secura, which discovered the flaw, or the equivalent NetExec module, which attempts the zero-credential authentication without changing any password. Full exploitation changes the domain controller's account password in the directory, which breaks its replication and secure channels until it is restored, so it is not performed on production systems.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker with network access to a vulnerable domain controller can take over the domain controller's computer account and use it to replicate every password hash in the domain with DCSync, gaining complete control of the domain within minutes using public tools. Exploitation in its usual form also resets the domain controller's account password, which can disrupt authentication and replication across the domain. The flaw has been widely exploited by criminal and state-sponsored groups, and CISA issued an emergency directive requiring United States federal agencies to patch it.
entries.remediation:
• Install the latest cumulative security update on every domain controller, including read-only domain controllers. Any update released since February 2021 includes the enforcement phase.
  • Check that the policy Domain controller: Allow vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections is not configured, or lists only devices that cannot yet use secure RPC, each with a documented plan for its removal.
  • Monitor the System event log on domain controllers for Netlogon events 5827 and 5828, which record denied vulnerable connections, and 5829 to 5831, which record vulnerable connections that were allowed. They identify non-compliant devices and possible exploitation attempts.
  • Upgrade or replace third-party devices and operating systems that cannot use secure RPC for Netlogon.
  • Where exploitation may already have occurred, review when the domain controllers' computer account passwords last changed and check replication health; if exploitation is confirmed, treat the domain as compromised.

Confirm the fix by repeating the non-destructive check against every domain controller, which should report that the zero-credential authentication is rejected.

entries.title: sAMAccountName Spoofing (noPac)
entries.summary: Unpatched domain controllers let a domain user rename a computer account to a domain controller's name and obtain Kerberos tickets as an administrator.
entries.description:
noPac, also called sAMAccountName spoofing, combines two Active Directory flaws that Microsoft fixed in November 2021. Under CVE-2021-42278, domain controllers did not check that a computer account's sAMAccountName ends with a dollar sign, so a computer account could be renamed to match a domain controller's name without it. Under CVE-2021-42287, when the account named in a ticket-granting ticket could no longer be found, the domain controller's Kerberos service (the KDC) searched again with a dollar sign appended, and so issued a service ticket to the domain controller's own account in which the requester could name any user.

Together they let any domain user who controls a computer account, including one created under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota of 10, clear its service principal names, rename it to a domain controller's name without the dollar sign, request a ticket-granting ticket, rename it back, and then use S4U2self to obtain a service ticket to the domain controller as a domain administrator. Public tools, including the noPac scripts, Impacket and Rubeus, automate the steps.

The weakness is identified from each domain controller's update level, and with a scanner such as the noPac tool's scan mode, which detects an unpatched KDC by requesting a ticket-granting ticket without a Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) and comparing its size with a normal one. The full attack is a definitive test but creates and renames objects in the directory.
entries.impact: Any domain user can become a domain administrator in a few steps, using the default ability to create computer accounts, and can then replicate every password hash in the domain with DCSync. The attack is reliable and public tools perform it with a single command. It needs a valid domain account and either the right to create a computer account, which domain users have by default, or write access to an existing computer account's name. Setting the machine account quota to zero raises the bar but does not remove the flaw.
entries.remediation:
• Install the November 2021 security updates, or any later cumulative update, on every domain controller. One unpatched domain controller is enough for the attack to succeed, so check them all.
  • Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota on the domain object to 0 and delegate the right to join computers to the staff and service accounts that need it, which also blocks other attacks that rely on computer accounts created by ordinary users.
  • Review computer accounts for names that lack a trailing dollar sign or resemble a domain controller's name.
  • Monitor for the attack pattern in events 4741 (a computer account was created), 4742 (a computer account was changed) and 4781 (the name of an account was changed), particularly a rename followed shortly by a rename back.

Confirm the fix by repeating the scan against every domain controller, which should show that ticket-granting tickets are always issued with a PAC.

entries.title: KRBTGT Password Not Recently Changed
entries.summary: The krbtgt account's password has not been changed for a long time, so Kerberos tickets forged with keys stolen at any point since then are still accepted.
entries.description:
Every Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) in an Active Directory domain is encrypted and signed with keys derived from the password of the built-in krbtgt account. Domain controllers accept any TGT that those keys validate, so whoever holds them can create tickets for any user, with any group memberships and lifetime, without contacting a domain controller. Tickets forged in this way are known as golden tickets.

The krbtgt password is set to a random value when the domain is created, and Windows does not change it on any schedule. Unless an administrator resets it, the same keys can stay in use for many years, through the replacement of every domain controller. Any past compromise of the domain, of a domain controller or of a backup of the directory database (ntds.dit) since the last reset will therefore have exposed keys that still work.

The issue is identified from the pwdLastSet attribute of the krbtgt account, which any domain user can read, for example with Get-ADUser krbtgt -Properties PasswordLastSet. Directory assessment tools such as PingCastle report its age, and a date close to the domain's creation shows that the password has never been reset.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtained the krbtgt keys at any time since the last reset, for example during an earlier intrusion or from an old backup, can forge tickets that make them a domain administrator or let them act as any account, and can keep doing so until the password has been reset twice. This gives a long-lived and hard-to-detect way back into full control of the domain, even after the original intrusion has been cleaned up and other passwords changed. The weakness does not give access on its own: it prolongs the effect of a compromise that has already happened, and it matters more the longer it has been since the last reset and the more incidents, administrators and backups there have been in that time.
entries.remediation:
• Reset the krbtgt password twice. Domain controllers accept tickets issued under the current and the previous key, so only the second reset invalidates a stolen key. Let the first change replicate to every domain controller and wait at least the maximum user ticket lifetime (10 hours by default) before the second, so that existing tickets expire rather than fail.
  • Use a tested procedure, such as the script Microsoft publishes for this purpose (New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1), which checks replication between the resets.
  • Reset the separate krbtgt_ accounts used by read-only domain controllers in the same way.
  • From then on, change the password at a regular interval set by policy, and promptly after any suspected compromise of the domain or a domain controller, or the departure of an administrator with domain-level rights.
  • If a compromise is suspected, carry out the double reset as part of a wider recovery that first removes the attacker's access, since an attacker who still controls a privileged account can read the new keys.

Confirm the fix by checking that PasswordLastSet shows the recent reset when queried against each domain controller, and that the account's msDS-KeyVersionNumber has increased by two.

entries.title: Users Can Add Computers to the Domain
entries.summary: Any domain user can create computer accounts, giving an attacker accounts they fully control for use in Kerberos delegation, relay and certificate attacks.
entries.description:
The domain lets ordinary users join computers to it, which creates computer accounts in the directory. Two settings control this: the ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota attribute on the domain object, which sets how many computer accounts each user may create and is 10 by default, and the Add workstations to domain user right, which the Default Domain Controllers Policy grants to Authenticated Users. Unless one of them has been changed, every domain user can create up to ten computer accounts.

The user chooses the new account's name and password, and the account is a full domain principal: it can authenticate with Kerberos and NTLM, belongs to Domain Computers, and can be given service principal names. Accounts created under the quota record their creator in the ms-DS-CreatorSID attribute.

The setting is identified by reading ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota from the domain object, which any domain user can do, and checking who holds the Add workstations to domain right. It can be confirmed by creating a computer account as a low-privileged user, for example with Impacket's addcomputer.py or Powermad, which an administrator should then remove.
entries.impact: A computer account under an attacker's control is a common building block in Active Directory attacks. It provides an account with a known password and a service principal name, which resource-based constrained delegation attacks need: where the attacker can also write to a computer object's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute, for example by relaying an NTLM authentication to LDAP, they can impersonate users on that computer, including administrators who are not protected from delegation. Such an account can also enrol in certificate templates open to Domain Computers, and creating one was a step in the noPac attack. On its own the setting gives no extra access to data; its impact comes from the other weaknesses it helps to exploit.
entries.remediation:
• Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 on the domain object, so that ordinary users can no longer create computer accounts (example below).
  • Before the change, find out how devices are joined, by service desk staff or by build and deployment tools, and delegate the Create Computer objects permission to those accounts or groups on the organisational units where new computers belong, or pre-stage computer accounts and name who may join each one.
  • Optionally, remove Authenticated Users from the Add workstations to domain right in the Default Domain Controllers Policy (Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Local Policies\User Rights Assignment); accounts with delegated permission on an organisational unit do not need it.
  • Review existing computer accounts whose ms-DS-CreatorSID is an ordinary user, and disable or delete any that do not belong to a managed device.
Set-ADObject -Identity (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName -Replace @{'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota'=0}

Confirm the fix by reading the attribute again and by attempting to create a computer account as an ordinary user, which should now fail.

entries.title: Dangerous Access Control Entries on Directory Objects
entries.summary: Low-privileged users or groups hold rights over directory objects, such as full control, permission changes or password resets, that let them take over privileged accounts.
entries.description:
Every Active Directory object has a security descriptor whose access control entries (ACEs) decide who can read and change it. Some rights give control of the object, or of what it governs, to whoever holds them: GenericAll (full control), WriteDacl (change permissions), WriteOwner (take ownership), GenericWrite or write access to sensitive attributes, the Reset Password extended right, and the right to change a group's members. Ownership of an object also carries the right to change its permissions.

The finding arises when such rights are held by principals that should not have them, particularly broad groups such as Domain Users, Authenticated Users or Everyone, or ordinary user, service and computer accounts, on objects that lead to privilege: privileged users and groups, the domain object, AdminSDHolder, Group Policy objects linked to sensitive organisational units, and organisational units holding servers or administrators. Such entries usually build up over years: service desk rights granted at the domain root, applications that add rights at installation, owners left from objects created by ordinary accounts, and rights granted through nested groups that are hard to see in the standard consoles.

Graph tools such as BloodHound, and assessment tools such as PingCastle, read the security descriptors, which any domain user can normally read, and show the attack paths they create, such as a chain of rights from ordinary users to Domain Admins.
entries.impact: An attacker who controls an account holding these rights can use them directly: reset a privileged user's password, add an account to a privileged group, write a service principal name to a user and Kerberoast it, add a key credential to its msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute and authenticate as it (shadow credentials, where the domain supports key trust), edit a Group Policy object to run code on the computers it applies to, or grant further rights, including directory replication rights at the domain root. Where a path leads to Domain Admins or an equivalent, this means full control of the domain. Because these are legitimate permissions, their use looks like ordinary administration and may go unnoticed. The impact is lower where paths only reach unprivileged objects.
entries.remediation:
• Remove each dangerous ACE that the attack paths rely on, starting with those held by broad groups and those on the domain object, AdminSDHolder, privileged groups and Group Policy objects, using the Advanced Security Settings in Active Directory Users and Computers or dsacls. Record the business need for any right that must stay.
  • Make an administrative group the owner of privileged objects, Group Policy objects and organisational units where the owner is an ordinary account.
  • Redesign delegation so that operational rights, such as password resets for the service desk, are granted to dedicated groups on the organisational units that hold ordinary users and computers, and never at the domain root or over Tier 0 objects.
  • Make changes for protected accounts and groups on AdminSDHolder: its permissions are copied to them every 60 minutes by default, overwriting edits made directly on those objects.
  • Audit changes to the security descriptors of sensitive objects (Audit Directory Service Changes, event 5136) and alert on them.

As an interim measure, where a right cannot be removed at once, reduce the membership of the group that holds it and monitor the objects concerned. Confirm the fix by repeating the BloodHound or PingCastle analysis and checking that no ordinary principal still has a path to privileged objects, and repeat the analysis periodically.

entries.title: Non-Administrative Principals With DCSync Rights
entries.summary: Accounts or groups outside the administrative tier hold directory replication rights, letting whoever controls them extract every password hash in the domain, including krbtgt.
entries.description:
Domain controllers replicate directory data, including password hashes and Kerberos keys, through the Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol (MS-DRSR). A principal holding both the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All extended rights on the domain object can ask a domain controller to replicate any account's secrets to it, from any host on the network and without running code on the domain controller. Tools such as Mimikatz (lsadump::dcsync) and Impacket's secretsdump.py do this; the technique is known as DCSync.

By default only domain controllers and the built-in administrative groups hold these rights. Others are granted them deliberately for products that synchronise passwords, such as the account Microsoft Entra Connect uses for password hash synchronisation, or by mistake through delegation at the domain root. The finding concerns principals outside the administrative tier: ordinary users and groups, service accounts protected less well than a domain administrator, and computer accounts of servers that are not domain controllers.

The rights are identified from the domain object's permissions, including rights obtained through nested groups, with BloodHound (its DCSync, GetChanges and GetChangesAll edges), PingCastle or dsacls. Where the rules of engagement allow, exploitation can be confirmed by replicating a single low-value account with the principal's credentials.
entries.impact: Anyone who controls a principal with these rights can obtain the NT hash and Kerberos keys of every account in the domain, including domain administrators and the krbtgt account. That gives full and lasting control of the domain: they can authenticate as any user with pass-the-hash and forge golden tickets that survive other password changes, and in a child domain they can use the krbtgt key to claim Enterprise Admins membership and take over the forest. Recovery means resetting every password, including krbtgt twice. The effort needed depends on how well the principal is protected: rights held by a broad group are usable by any member, while rights held by one service account first require that account to be compromised, which is often possible where its password is stored on a server or is weak.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All rights from every principal that is not a domain controller or a built-in administrative group, on the Security tab of the domain object (Advanced Features view in Active Directory Users and Computers) or with dsacls.
  • Where a product genuinely needs them, such as Entra Connect for password hash synchronisation, grant them only to a dedicated account used by that product alone, give it a long random password, and treat the account and the server it runs on as Tier 0, protected like a domain controller.
  • Remove rights left behind by decommissioned products, and check for rights granted through group nesting as well as directly.
  • Detect use of the rights: with auditing of directory service access configured for the domain object, domain controllers log event 4662 for replication requests, and requests using the Replicating Directory Changes All right (1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2) from accounts other than domain controllers indicate DCSync.
  • If there is any sign that the rights have been misused, treat the domain as compromised and plan a recovery, including a double krbtgt reset.

Confirm the fix by repeating the permissions review and checking that only domain controllers and administrative groups hold the rights; a replication attempt with the former principal should now be refused.

entries.title: Anonymous LDAP Access to Directory Data
entries.summary: Domain controllers answer LDAP searches from unauthenticated connections, letting anyone on the network list users, groups, computers and other directory data.
entries.description:
LDAP clients can bind to a directory without credentials. Active Directory always accepts such anonymous binds and lets them read the rootDSE, the entry that describes the server, its naming contexts and functional levels, which is by design. Since Windows Server 2003, anonymous connections cannot search the rest of the directory unless the seventh character of the forest-wide dSHeuristics attribute (on CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services in the configuration partition) is set to 2 and the ANONYMOUS LOGON identity is granted read access to the objects concerned. Administrators sometimes make these changes for legacy applications, printers and scanners, or Unix and Linux systems that look up users without credentials. A simple bind with a user name but an empty password is treated as anonymous and gets the same access.

The finding is confirmed when an unauthenticated search returns directory objects, for example with ldapsearch using a simple bind without credentials, or NetExec's LDAP module with an empty user name and password. Results that show only the rootDSE do not indicate this finding, although some scanners report any successful anonymous bind as an issue.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach a domain controller can read the directory without an account. Depending on the permissions granted, this typically includes user names, group memberships, computer names and attributes such as descriptions, which sometimes contain passwords. An attacker can use it to build lists of valid accounts for password spraying, to identify administrators, service accounts and servers, and to plan further attacks before holding any credentials. The impact is limited to disclosure and its extent depends on what ANONYMOUS LOGON can read; secret attributes such as password hashes are not exposed.
entries.remediation:
• Set the seventh character of dSHeuristics back to 0, leaving any other characters unchanged, or clear the attribute if no other character is in use, using ADSI Edit on CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration in the forest root domain. The change applies to every domain controller in the forest.
  • Remove access control entries that grant ANONYMOUS LOGON read access to directory objects, and remove ANONYMOUS LOGON and Everyone from groups that grant read access, such as Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access.
  • Before the change, identify the systems that rely on anonymous access, from the application owners or from network traffic, and give each a dedicated low-privileged account that binds with credentials, preferably over LDAPS or with signing.

Confirm the fix by repeating the anonymous search, which should now fail with an error stating that a successful bind must be completed on the connection before the operation can be performed.

entries.title: Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access Includes Everyone or Anonymous
