entries.summary: The Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group includes Everyone or Anonymous Logon, so unauthenticated connections can enumerate domain users, groups and policy.
entries.description:
The built-in Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group exists for compatibility with Windows NT 4.0 systems. Its members are granted read access to user and group objects throughout the domain, and its permissions on the domain object also decide whether a caller can enumerate domain accounts and groups through the Security Account Manager Remote Protocol (SAMR) on a domain controller.

Where the domain was created with permissions compatible with pre-Windows 2000 servers, or an administrator added them later, the group contains Everyone, Anonymous Logon or both. Anonymous Logon covers unauthenticated sessions directly, while Everyone covers them only where Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users is enabled, which has not been the default since Windows Server 2003. With anonymous access granted this way, a null session (an SMB connection with an empty user name and password) to a domain controller can list domain users and groups, group memberships and the password and lockout policy.

The membership is visible to any domain user in the Builtin container. Testing confirms the exposure with tools such as rpcclient (enumdomusers), enum4linux-ng or NetExec with empty credentials against each domain controller. A null session that connects but cannot enumerate does not indicate this finding.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker with network access to a domain controller can obtain the full list of domain accounts and groups, the members of privileged groups and the account lockout policy. This removes the need for credentials at the start of an attack: the account list and lockout threshold allow password spraying to be tuned to avoid lockouts, and readable attributes such as descriptions sometimes disclose more. The exposure is limited to reading directory information; secret attributes such as password hashes are not readable through this membership.
entries.remediation:
• Remove Everyone and Anonymous Logon from the Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group in the Builtin container. Keep Authenticated Users as a member unless removing it has been tested, as some applications rely on the read access it gives.
  • Check that Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users is disabled on domain controllers, and consider enabling Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares after testing, as some legacy systems rely on anonymous enumeration.
  • Identify any system that still depends on anonymous access, such as an old network appliance, and give it a dedicated low-privileged account instead; the Windows NT 4.0 systems this membership was designed for are long out of support.

Confirm the fix by repeating the null session enumeration against each domain controller, which should now be refused with an access denied error.

entries.title: Privileged Accounts Not in the Protected Users Group
entries.summary: Privileged accounts are not members of Protected Users, so their credentials can be cached on hosts, delegated, and used with NTLM and weaker Kerberos encryption.
entries.description:
Protected Users is a global security group, introduced with Windows Server 2012 R2, whose members receive protections that cannot be configured or turned off individually. When a member signs in to a device running Windows 8.1, Windows Server 2012 R2 or later, CredSSP and WDigest do not cache their plain-text credentials, NTLM does not keep their NT hash, Kerberos does not create DES or RC4 keys or keep long-term keys after the initial ticket, and no cached verifier is stored, so offline sign-in is not possible. Where the domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 or higher, domain controllers also refuse NTLM authentication for members, refuse DES and RC4 for their Kerberos pre-authentication, will not let their accounts be delegated, and limit their ticket-granting tickets to four hours.

The finding arises when members of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators, Schema Admins and other highly privileged groups are not members of Protected Users. It is identified by comparing the membership of those groups, including nested members, with that of Protected Users, which any domain user can read.
entries.impact: The group does not prevent an attack by itself; it limits what an attacker can take from a host they already control. Without it, when a privileged account signs in to a compromised computer, its NT hash can be extracted and reused for pass-the-hash or cracked long after the session ends, the account can be impersonated through Kerberos delegation, and it can be used with NTLM, where relay attacks apply. The practical effect depends on where privileged accounts sign in: where tiering keeps them off ordinary workstations and servers, the added exposure is small.
entries.remediation:
• Add the accounts of people with Tier 0 rights, and other highly privileged human accounts, to Protected Users. Test first with one or two accounts that their tools and sign-in routes still work without NTLM, RC4, delegation and cached sign-in.
  • Do not add service accounts or computer accounts: Microsoft advises against it, as the group gives them no local protection and can break the services that use them.
  • Keep a documented emergency administrative account outside the group, with its credentials stored securely, in case a configuration problem prevents members from signing in.
  • Make sure the domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 or higher, without which the domain controller protections do not apply, and that members' passwords have been changed since the domain reached the Windows Server 2008 level, so that their accounts have AES keys.
  • Also set Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated on all privileged accounts.

Confirm the fix by checking the group's membership and, after signing in with a member account, using klist to confirm that its ticket-granting ticket expires four hours after issue.
keywords: account is sensitive and cannot be delegated

entries.title: WDigest Authentication Enabled
entries.summary: WDigest is configured to keep users' passwords in LSASS memory in a recoverable form, so anyone with administrative access to the host can read them in clear text.
entries.description:
WDigest is the Windows security support provider for HTTP Digest and SASL Digest authentication. Because these protocols compute each response from the user's password, WDigest keeps the password of every user who signs in in the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS), encrypted with keys that LSASS also holds, so it can be recovered in clear text.

Windows 8.1, Windows Server 2012 R2 and later versions do not keep these credentials by default. The update for Microsoft security advisory 2871997 brought the UseLogonCredential registry value, under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest, to earlier versions so that the behaviour could be turned off there. The finding arises when UseLogonCredential is set to 1, which turns caching back on in any version and is a known step attackers take to collect passwords at later sign-ins, or when older systems such as Windows Server 2008 R2 do not have it set to 0.

The setting is identified from the registry or Group Policy, or on a test by extracting credentials from LSASS with tools such as Mimikatz (sekurlsa::wdigest), which show clear-text passwords for users who signed in while caching was enabled.
entries.impact: An attacker with administrative access to an affected system can read the clear-text passwords of users who have signed in to it while caching was enabled, interactively or over Remote Desktop, including administrators. Clear-text passwords can be used with services that do not accept password hashes, such as VPNs, webmail and cloud services that share the directory password, remain valid until changed, and reveal how users construct their passwords. The attacker must already have administrative rights on the host, and only accounts that sign in to it are exposed.
entries.remediation:
• Set UseLogonCredential to 0 (REG_DWORD) under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest on every system, through Group Policy Preferences or configuration management. The WDigest Authentication setting in the MS Security Guide administrative template from Microsoft's security baselines manages the same value.
  • Where the value is found set to 1 without a documented reason, treat it as a possible sign of compromise: find out how it was set, and reset the passwords of accounts that signed in while it was in place.
  • Monitor the value for changes with endpoint detection tools or registry auditing.
  • Replace systems running Windows versions that are out of support.
reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest /v UseLogonCredential /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

Passwords already cached remain in memory until the user signs out or the system restarts. Confirm the fix by reading the value and, where permitted, checking that a credential dump taken after new sign-ins shows no clear-text WDigest passwords.

entries.title: LSA Protection Not Enabled
entries.summary: LSASS does not run as a protected process, so any process with administrative rights can read its memory or load code into it to steal credentials.
entries.description:
The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) holds credential material for signed-in users, such as NT hashes and Kerberos tickets, and loads authentication packages, security support providers and password filters. Without LSA protection it runs as an ordinary process, so any process running with administrative rights and the debug privilege can open it, read its memory or load code into it.

LSA protection, often called RunAsPPL after its registry value, runs LSASS as a protected process light. Processes that are not protected, including those running as administrator or SYSTEM, can then no longer read its memory or inject code into it, and LSASS only loads plug-ins and drivers that carry a Microsoft signature. The protection is configured with the RunAsPPL value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa, or through Group Policy on versions that include the setting.

The finding is identified from the registry or policy, from the System event log, where WinInit event 12 is recorded at start-up when LSASS runs as a protected process, or on a test when a tool such as Mimikatz can read LSASS memory without first loading a driver.
entries.impact: The absence of LSA protection does not give an attacker access on its own. Once they have administrative rights on a host, it lets them dump LSASS with common tools, such as Mimikatz, ProcDump or the MiniDump function of comsvcs.dll, and recover the hashes and Kerberos tickets of users signed in there for pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket, or install a malicious security support provider to capture passwords at later sign-ins. With the protection enabled, the attacker has to load a kernel driver to remove it, which is more likely to be blocked or detected but remains possible. The value of what can be stolen depends on which accounts sign in to the host.
entries.remediation:
• Enable LSA protection on all supported Windows systems, starting with servers and workstations where privileged accounts sign in, with the Group Policy setting Computer Configuration\Administrative Templates\System\Local Security Authority\Configure LSASS to run as a protected process where it is available, or by setting RunAsPPL to 1 (REG_DWORD), and restart.
  • On devices with UEFI and Secure Boot, the value 1 also stores the setting in a UEFI variable, so it cannot be turned off from the registry alone. This resists tampering, but should be planned for before deployment.
  • Before enforcing it on systems that run third-party authentication, smart card or security software, use audit mode (AuditLevel set to 8 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\LSASS.exe) and review Code Integrity events 3065 and 3066 for plug-ins that would fail to load.
  • Combine it with Credential Guard where supported, which protects hashes and tickets even from code running in the kernel, and with monitoring of access to LSASS.
reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

Confirm the fix after a restart by finding WinInit event 12 in the System log, which records that LSASS started as a protected process, and, where permitted, by checking that an attempt to read its memory from an administrative session is refused.

entries.title: Credential Guard Not Enabled
entries.summary: Credential Guard is not running, so NT hashes and Kerberos tickets held in LSASS memory can be extracted by an attacker with administrative rights on the host.
entries.description:
Credential Guard uses virtualisation-based security (VBS) to isolate secrets that would otherwise be held in the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). NTLM password hashes, Kerberos ticket-granting tickets and credentials stored by applications as domain credentials are kept in an isolated process, LsaIso.exe, which the operating system cannot read even with kernel-level privileges; LSASS calls it when it needs to use them.

Credential Guard needs a 64-bit processor with virtualisation extensions and second level address translation, Secure Boot, and an edition of Windows that supports it, such as Enterprise or Education, or Windows Server. Windows 11 version 22H2 and later turn it on by default on devices that meet the requirements, but it is often absent on servers, older builds and devices where it has been turned off. Microsoft does not recommend it on domain controllers, where it adds no protection, so the finding concerns workstations and member servers.

Its status is shown by msinfo32 (Virtualization-based security Services Running), by the presence of the LsaIso.exe process, or by the Win32_DeviceGuard WMI class, whose SecurityServicesRunning property includes the value 1 when Credential Guard is running.
entries.impact: Without Credential Guard, an attacker who gains administrative rights on a host can extract the NT hashes and Kerberos tickets of users signed in there from LSASS memory and reuse them elsewhere with pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket, a standard way of moving through a network towards privileged accounts. Credential Guard prevents that extraction, though not other ways of capturing credentials, such as keylogging. The added risk depends on which accounts sign in to the host and on other controls such as tiering, and is small where privileged accounts never sign in to ordinary systems.
entries.remediation:
• Enable Credential Guard on supported workstations and member servers, starting with those where administrators sign in, through Computer Configuration\Administrative Templates\System\Device Guard\Turn On Virtualization Based Security, with Credential Guard Configuration set to Enabled with UEFI lock, or Enabled without lock where it may need to be turned off remotely later. Microsoft Intune and other management tools offer the same setting.
  • Check hardware and firmware support (virtualisation extensions enabled in firmware, Secure Boot) and the Windows edition, and plan the replacement of devices that cannot run it.
  • Test before wide deployment: with Credential Guard running, NTLMv1, MS-CHAPv2, Digest and CredSSP cannot use the signed-in credentials for single sign-on, and Kerberos unconstrained delegation and DES encryption are not supported, so some Wi-Fi and VPN configurations and legacy applications may need changes.
  • Do not enable it on domain controllers.
  • Combine it with LSA protection and with tiering, which keeps privileged credentials off hosts where they could be captured in other ways.

Confirm the fix after a restart with msinfo32, or with the following query on a sample of devices, which should return a list that includes 1:

(Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesRunning

entries.title: Excessive Cached Domain Credentials
entries.summary: Windows hosts keep verifiers for many recent domain sign-ins, which an attacker with administrative access can extract and try to crack, including those of administrators.
entries.description:
So that users can sign in when no domain controller can be reached, Windows stores a verifier for each of the most recent domain accounts to sign in interactively, known as cached domain credentials or DCC2 (MS-Cache v2) hashes. The number kept is set by Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case domain controller is not available), stored as CachedLogonsCount under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon, and is 10 by default.

The verifiers are held in the SECURITY registry hive. They cannot be used for pass-the-hash, but an attacker with administrative rights on the host can extract them with tools such as Impacket's secretsdump.py or Mimikatz (lsadump::cache) and attack them offline, for example with hashcat. The algorithm applies PBKDF2 with 10,240 iterations, so cracking is slow and mainly succeeds against weak or common passwords.

The finding is reported where hosts cache more entries than they need, particularly servers, which rarely need to work without a domain controller, and where the cached entries include privileged accounts. It is identified from the policy or registry value, and on a test by listing the cached entries on a compromised host.
entries.impact: An attacker with administrative access to a host can extract the verifiers of the accounts that last signed in to it, which on servers and shared workstations can include administrators and service desk staff, and try to crack them offline. A cracked password works anywhere the account is valid and may lead to privilege escalation. The risk is limited by the slow hashing algorithm, which protects long and unusual passwords, and by the need for administrative access to the host first.
entries.remediation:
• Reduce Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache (Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Local Policies\Security Options) to 0 on servers that always have a domain controller available, and to a small number such as 1 or 2 on laptops and other devices that need offline sign-in.
  • Keep a local administrator account managed by Windows LAPS on servers, so that administrators can still sign in if no domain controller can be reached.
  • Add privileged accounts to Protected Users, whose members' verifiers are not cached, and keep privileged accounts off hosts where they are not needed.
  • Require long passwords or passphrases for administrative accounts, so that any verifier that is extracted resists cracking.

Confirm the fix by checking the effective value on a sample of hosts, for example with gpresult or by reading CachedLogonsCount in the registry.

entries.title: Weak Domain Password Policy
entries.summary: The domain password policy allows short passwords or does not lock accounts after repeated failures, making passwords easier to guess and to crack.
entries.description:
The password and account lockout settings in the Default Domain Policy apply to every domain account, unless a fine-grained password policy overrides them for particular users or groups; password settings in Group Policy objects linked to organisational units affect only local accounts. The finding arises when these settings do not require passwords strong enough to resist guessing and cracking. Common examples are a minimum length of eight characters or fewer (the default is seven), no account lockout (the default threshold of 0 never locks accounts), a threshold so high that it does not slow guessing, and storage of passwords with reversible encryption.

Complexity rules on their own do little: users meet them with predictable patterns, such as a season and a year followed by a symbol, and frequent forced changes encourage the same patterns. Short passwords that meet the rules can be cracked quickly from captured material such as Kerberoasting output, NTLMv2 challenge responses and dumped NT hashes.

The domain policy can be read by any domain user, for example with Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy, net accounts /domain or NetExec's --pass-pol option, and fine-grained policies with Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy where the account in use can read them. Where in scope, an audit of extracted password hashes shows the resulting password quality directly.
entries.impact: A weak policy makes password guessing and cracking more likely to succeed. Without lockout, an attacker can try many passwords against each account through any service that authenticates against the domain; even with lockout, password spraying (a few common passwords tried against every account) succeeds where short passwords are allowed. Short passwords also make captured hashes more likely to be cracked offline. Each recovered password gives the attacker that user's access, and may belong to a privileged or service account. The actual exposure depends on the passwords users choose and on whether multi-factor authentication protects remote access.
entries.remediation:
• Raise the minimum password length, for example to at least 14 characters for user accounts, and encourage passphrases such as three random words. Use fine-grained password policies (password settings objects) to set longer minimums for administrators and service accounts, and where a minimum beyond what the domain policy setting accepts is wanted.
  • Set an account lockout threshold, for example between 5 and 10 failed attempts, with a lockout duration and counter reset time of at least 15 minutes, balancing protection against guessing with the risk of deliberate lockouts.
  • Block common and breached passwords, as current NCSC and NIST guidance recommends, for example with Microsoft Entra Password Protection for Active Directory Domain Services or another password filter on the domain controllers.
  • Disable Store passwords using reversible encryption in the policy and on individual accounts, and reset the passwords of any accounts that had it.
  • Once length and blocklist checks are in place, consider dropping frequent forced expiry for user accounts, which the same guidance advises against, and require a change whenever compromise is suspected.
  • Require multi-factor authentication for remote and administrative access, which limits the value of a guessed password.

Existing passwords only have to meet a new policy when they are next changed. Confirm the fix by reading the effective policies again, and track adoption through password age or a later password audit.

entries.title: Domain Trust Without SID Filtering
entries.summary: A trust to another domain or forest does not filter security identifiers, so an attacker who controls the trusted side can claim privileged group membership in this domain.
entries.description:
When a user from a trusted domain accesses resources across a trust, their Kerberos ticket or NTLM authentication carries the security identifiers (SIDs) of their groups, and can also carry SIDs from the account's sIDHistory attribute. SID filtering is the check by which the trusting domain discards SIDs that do not belong to the trusted domain, so that the trusted domain can only make claims about its own principals. Without it, administrators of the trusted domain, or an attacker who controls it, can add the SIDs of the trusting domain's groups, such as a group with administrative rights there, to an account's sIDHistory or to a forged ticket, and receive those groups' rights across the trust.

SID filtering is applied by default to external and forest trusts created by Windows Server 2003 and later domain controllers. It is removed when quarantine is turned off on an external trust (the /quarantine:no option of netdom trust) and relaxed when SID history is enabled on a forest trust (/enablesidhistory:yes), which lets some SIDs from the trusting forest through, potentially including groups with administrative rights. Both are usually done to support a migration and then left in place. Trusts between domains in the same forest are not filtered: the forest, not the domain, is the security boundary.

Trust settings can be read by any domain user from the trust objects' trustAttributes or with Get-ADTrust, are reported by tools such as PingCastle, and are displayed by netdom trust with the /quarantine or /enablesidhistory option and no value.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains administrative control of the trusted domain, which may be less well protected than this one (for example a partner's domain, an acquired company's domain or an old domain kept for a migration), can use it to gain privileged access to the trusting domain. On an external trust with quarantine disabled, they can claim membership of the trusting domain's groups and gain the rights those groups hold there, including administrative rights. Where SID history is enabled on a forest trust, the impact depends on which groups with administrative rights can still be claimed. Only the trusting side is at risk, and only after the trusted side has been compromised; the risk grows with the number of such trusts and the weakness of the domains on the other side.
entries.remediation:
• Enable SID filtering on every external trust with the /quarantine:yes option of netdom trust, run with administrative credentials for the trusting domain.
  • Disable SID history on forest trusts (/enablesidhistory:no) once any migration that needed it has finished, and remove sIDHistory values from migrated accounts after confirming that resources no longer depend on them.
  • Before enabling filtering, check that no access across the trust relies on SID history or on SIDs from outside the trusted domain, as that access will stop working.
  • Remove trusts that are no longer needed, and for those that remain, use selective authentication, so that accounts from the trusted domain can only authenticate to the servers they are explicitly allowed to use.
  • Where two environments must be separated administratively, keep them in separate forests, since domains in the same forest cannot be isolated from each other.

Confirm the fix by displaying the trust settings again with netdom trust or Get-ADTrust, and by repeating the trust checks of the assessment tool used.

entries.title: Outdated Domain Functional Level
entries.summary: The domain or forest runs at an old functional level, which keeps legacy behaviour and prevents the use of security features that require a newer level.
entries.description:
The domain and forest functional levels determine which Active Directory features are available, and cannot be higher than the oldest Windows Server version run by any domain controller in the domain or forest. A domain or forest left at an old level cannot use features introduced since, even when every domain controller has been upgraded, and an old level often indicates that domain controllers running unsupported versions of Windows Server remain, or did until recently.

Security-related features that depend on the domain functional level include AES encryption for Kerberos and fine-grained password policies (Windows Server 2008); the domain controller options that always provide claims and require Kerberos armouring, also called FAST (Windows Server 2012); the domain controller protections of the Protected Users group, and authentication policies and silos (Windows Server 2012 R2); and the automatic rolling of NTLM secrets for accounts that require smart card sign-in (Windows Server 2016). The Active Directory Recycle Bin, which helps recovery, needs the Windows Server 2008 R2 forest functional level.

The levels are shown by the domainFunctionality and forestFunctionality attributes of the rootDSE, which can be read without authentication, by Get-ADDomain and Get-ADForest, and by most directory assessment tools.
entries.impact: An outdated functional level does not expose the domain to a specific attack. Its effect is to withhold protections, such as the domain controller side of Protected Users and authentication policy silos, that limit credential theft and the misuse of privileged accounts, and it can point to legacy domain controllers that no longer receive security updates, which are a more serious issue in their own right. It is therefore rated as informational.
entries.remediation:
• Upgrade or replace every domain controller running a Windows Server version that is out of support or older than the target level, then demote the old ones and remove any that no longer exist from the directory.
  • Raise the domain functional level, then the forest functional level, to the highest level that all domain controllers support, with Active Directory Domains and Trusts or the Set-ADDomainMode and Set-ADForestMode cmdlets, as a member of Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins respectively.
  • Plan the change: a raised level can only be lowered in limited cases, so confirm with application owners that nothing depends on legacy behaviour, and check that no domain controller runs an older version.
  • After raising the level, adopt the features it allows, such as Protected Users for administrators and authentication policy silos for Tier 0 accounts.

Confirm the fix with (Get-ADDomain).DomainMode and (Get-ADForest).ForestMode, or by reading the rootDSE attributes again.

entries.title: Privileged Accounts Used on Workstations (Tiering Not Enforced)
entries.summary: Domain administrators and other highly privileged accounts sign in to workstations and ordinary servers, leaving credentials that an attacker who compromises those hosts can steal.
entries.description:
When an account signs in to a Windows host interactively, over Remote Desktop, with RunAs, or as a service or scheduled task, reusable credential material such as its NT hash or Kerberos tickets is held on that host, at least while the session lasts, and anyone with administrative control of the host can extract it. Network sign-ins used by most remote management tools do not leave such material. The tiered administration model addresses this by grouping systems into tiers, with Tier 0 for the identity infrastructure (domain controllers, certificate services, directory synchronisation and similar systems), Tier 1 for servers and applications, and Tier 2 for workstations, and by never letting accounts that control a higher tier sign in to a lower one.

The finding arises when this separation is not in place: members of Domain Admins and other Tier 0 groups use their privileged accounts for everyday work or sign in with them to workstations and member servers, service desk staff use domain administrator rights to support users, or privileged accounts run services and scheduled tasks on ordinary servers. It is identified from the sessions of privileged users on workstations and servers (for example with BloodHound's session collection), from privileged credentials recovered from hosts compromised during the test, and from the absence of controls such as authentication policy silos or deny sign-in rights for privileged groups.
entries.impact: Compromising any workstation or server where a privileged account has signed in, through phishing, an unpatched vulnerability or a reused local administrator password, can give an attacker that account's credentials and with them control of the domain. This is a common route to domain compromise in internal tests and in real intrusions: it needs no weakness in Active Directory itself, only administrative access to one of the many hosts that privileged credentials pass through. The risk grows with the number of hosts where privileged accounts sign in and the number of staff who hold those rights, and is reduced, though not removed, by Credential Guard, LSA protection and the Protected Users group.
entries.remediation:
• Give administrators separate accounts for each tier they manage, and a standard account for email and web browsing, and use Tier 0 accounts only on Tier 0 systems.
  • Enforce the separation technically: in Group Policy objects linked to workstation and member server organisational units, add Tier 0 groups to the Deny access to this computer from the network, Deny log on as a batch job, Deny log on as a service, Deny log on locally and Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services user rights, and use authentication policies and silos to restrict where Tier 0 accounts can sign in.
  • Provide privileged access workstations for Tier 0 administration, and give service desk staff delegated rights over workstations and ordinary users instead of domain administrator rights.
  • Run services and scheduled tasks on ordinary servers with dedicated least-privilege accounts, preferably group managed service accounts, and never with Tier 0 accounts.
  • Where higher-tier staff must connect to lower-tier systems over Remote Desktop, use a lower-tier account, or Restricted Admin mode or Remote Credential Guard, which do not leave reusable credentials on the target.
  • Add privileged users to Protected Users, and enable Credential Guard and LSA protection, as supporting controls.

As an interim measure, reduce the membership of Tier 0 groups, and reset the passwords of privileged accounts after cleaning up the hosts where they were used. Confirm the fix by repeating session collection and by reviewing sign-in events (event 4624) for privileged accounts on systems outside Tier 0.

entries.title: Service Accounts With Domain Administrative Rights
entries.summary: Accounts that run services, tasks or applications are members of Domain Admins or similar groups, so compromising any system that uses them compromises the domain.
entries.description:
Service accounts are domain accounts used by applications, services, scheduled tasks and scripts rather than by people. The finding arises when such an account is a member of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators or another group with domain-wide control, directly or through nested groups, usually because installation was easier that way or a vendor asked for it, and the rights were never reduced.

Service account credentials are unusually exposed. Windows stores the password of each service configured to run as a domain account in the LSA secrets of every host that runs it, and scheduled tasks set to run without the user signed in also keep their password on the host; a local administrator can recover these in clear text. Accounts with service principal names can be Kerberoasted by any domain user. Service account passwords are often old, set never to expire, shared between teams and systems, and copied into scripts, configuration files and application databases.

The issue is identified by listing the members of privileged groups, including nested members, for example with Get-ADGroupMember -Recursive, BloodHound or PingCastle, and recognising service accounts among them from their names, descriptions, service principal names, password age and sign-in patterns.
entries.impact: Compromising the account gives the attacker domain administrator rights. Because its password is held on every host where it runs, administrative access to any one of those hosts, which may be ordinary application servers, is enough; where it has a service principal name and a crackable password, any domain user may be able to obtain it by Kerberoasting. Service accounts are seldom monitored as closely as named administrators, so their misuse may go unnoticed. The risk grows with the number of hosts that use the account and the weakness of its password.
entries.remediation:
• For each service account in a privileged group, establish the rights the application actually needs, grant those specifically (for example administrative rights on the application's own servers, or delegated permissions on particular organisational units), and remove the account from the privileged group.
  • Where a vendor states that domain administrator rights are needed, ask for the specific permissions the product uses.
  • Replace ordinary user accounts with group managed service accounts where the application supports them: the domain generates long random passwords for them and changes them automatically, every 30 days by default, and no administrator needs to know them.
  • Where an ordinary account must remain, give it a long random password, deny it interactive and Remote Desktop sign-in, and limit the hosts where it is used.
  • Treat any service account that truly needs Tier 0 rights, such as one used by a directory synchronisation or domain controller backup product, as part of Tier 0: use it only on Tier 0 systems and protect and monitor it like a domain administrator.
  • After reducing the rights, change the account's password, as it may already have been exposed.

Confirm the fix by listing the privileged groups' membership again and checking that no service account remains, and by confirming with the application owners that their services still work.

entries.title: Excessive Microsoft Exchange Permissions in Active Directory
entries.summary: Exchange security groups hold broad write permissions in the domain, in older deployments including the right to change its permissions, so control of Exchange can become control of the domain.
entries.description:
Exchange Server setup prepares Active Directory by creating security groups in the Microsoft Exchange Security Groups organisational unit and granting them extensive permissions across the domain. In the default shared permissions model, the Exchange Windows Permissions group, which contains Exchange Trusted Subsystem and through it the computer account of every Exchange server, can modify many attributes of users and groups throughout the domain, and in older deployments it also holds WriteDacl on the domain object itself.

With WriteDacl on the domain object, a member can grant any account the directory replication rights used by DCSync. The PrivExchange research published in January 2019 showed that an Exchange server could be made to authenticate to an attacker, who relayed that authentication to LDAP to grant exactly these rights. Microsoft's cumulative updates of February 2019 reduced the permissions, but only where the domain is prepared again with the updated setup, so they persist in domains not prepared since, and in forests where Exchange was removed or its mailboxes moved to Exchange Online without its groups and permissions being cleaned up. Members of Exchange's administrative role groups, such as Organization Management, can by default change the membership of these groups, which extends the exposure to every Exchange administrator.

The permissions are identified with BloodHound, which shows the paths from Exchange groups and servers to the domain, or by reviewing the permissions on the domain object and the membership of the Exchange groups.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains control of an Exchange server, for example through one of the remote code execution vulnerabilities that have affected internet-facing Exchange servers, or of an account in an Exchange administrative role group, can use these permissions to change users and groups across the domain and, where WriteDacl on the domain object remains, grant themselves replication rights and extract every password hash in the domain. Exchange servers and Exchange administrators are then, in effect, part of the most privileged tier, whether or not that is recognised. Where the domain-level permission has been removed, the remaining rights over users and groups still allow significant changes, though not always a direct path to domain control.
entries.remediation:
• Install the latest cumulative update for the Exchange version in use and run its Active Directory preparation (Setup.exe /PrepareAD, with the licence acceptance parameter that version requires), which applies Microsoft's reduced permissions. Then check the domain object and remove any WriteDacl still granted to Exchange groups.
  • Where Exchange is no longer used on premises, decommission the remaining servers following Microsoft's guidance, and remove the permissions and groups it created once nothing depends on them.
  • Consider Active Directory split permissions (Setup.exe /PrepareAD /ActiveDirectorySplitPermissions:true), which removes Exchange's ability to create security principals and change most of their attributes, where recipients can be managed with Active Directory tools instead.
  • Treat Exchange servers and the members of Exchange administrative role groups as Tier 0: keep the role groups' membership to a minimum, restrict who can sign in to the servers, apply security updates promptly, and expose to the internet only the services that are needed.
  • Monitor changes to the domain object's security descriptor (Audit Directory Service Changes, event 5136) and to the membership of the Exchange groups.

Confirm the fix by repeating the BloodHound analysis and checking that no Exchange group or server holds WriteDacl, WriteOwner or full control on the domain object, and that no remaining path leads from Exchange to privileged groups.

entries.title: Users Can Create ADIDNS Records
entries.summary: Any domain user can add records to Active Directory-integrated DNS zones, so an attacker can make unused or wildcard names resolve to a host they control and intercept traffic.
entries.description:
Active Directory-integrated DNS zones store each record as a dnsNode object in the directory, and access to them is controlled by Active Directory permissions. By default, Authenticated Users hold the Create all child objects permission on these zones, so that domain computers can register their own records through secure dynamic update. The same permission lets any domain user create a record for any name that does not yet exist, either with a dynamic DNS update or by writing a dnsNode object directly over LDAP, and become that record's owner. Records that already exist and belong to other accounts cannot be changed in this way.

Attackers use this to add a wildcard record (*), which answers for every name in the zone that has no record of its own, or records for names that clients still look up but that no longer exist, such as decommissioned servers referenced in scripts and drive mappings. Unlike LLMNR and NetBIOS name poisoning, this works across subnets, does not depend on those protocols being enabled, and is served to every client by the domain's own DNS servers.

The permission is identified by reviewing the security of the zone objects in the DomainDnsZones and ForestDnsZones application partitions, and of any zones stored in the domain partition. It can be confirmed by adding a test record as an ordinary user, for example with Powermad or the dnstool.py script from krbrelayx, and removing it afterwards.
entries.impact: An attacker with any domain account can redirect clients that look up unused names, or any name that does not exist in the zone, to a host they control. They can then capture NTLM authentication from those clients to crack offline or relay to other services, and serve their own content to clients that connect. The effect depends on what clients look up and on the protection of the services they authenticate to, and is greatest where SMB and LDAP signing are not required and NTLM is widely used. A wildcard record also changes the answer for every mistyped or missing name, which can disrupt applications and draw attention.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the Create all child objects permission held by Authenticated Users on each Active Directory-integrated zone (on the zone's Security tab in DNS Manager, or with ADSI Edit), and grant it only to the principals that must register new records, such as Domain Computers or the account the DHCP servers use to register records on behalf of clients. Test the change on one zone first, as it stops other accounts from registering new names.
  • Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0, so that an attacker cannot create a computer account to regain the permission through Domain Computers.
  • Find clients that still look up names that no longer exist, for example from DNS server analytical logs, and correct their configuration.
  • Audit the creation of dnsNode objects (Audit Directory Service Changes, event 5137) in the DNS application partitions, and alert on wildcard records and on records created by user accounts rather than computers or DHCP servers.
  • Reduce the value of any intercepted authentication by requiring SMB signing, enforcing LDAP signing and channel binding, and restricting NTLM.

Confirm the fix by attempting to add a record as an ordinary user, which should now be refused, and by checking that computers still register their records and that no unexpected wildcard records remain in any zone.

entries.title: Unquoted Service Path
entries.summary: A Windows service's executable path contains spaces but is not quoted, so Windows may run a program planted earlier in that path with the service's privileges.
entries.description:
The path to a Windows service's executable, held in the service's ImagePath registry value, contains spaces but is not enclosed in quotation marks. When the service starts, Windows cannot tell where the file name ends and the arguments begin, so it tries each space-separated part of the path in turn, adding .exe. For a service installed at C:\Program Files\Vendor App\Service Host\svc.exe, Windows first looks for C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe, and so on, before it reaches the intended file.

The weakness can be exploited only where a standard user can write to one of the directories searched first. The system drive's root folder and C:\Program Files do not allow this by default, but software installed into a folder created elsewhere, such as directly under the system drive, often inherits permissions that let any authenticated user create files there. A program placed at one of the earlier candidate paths runs with the service's privileges, commonly LocalSystem, the next time the service starts.

Unquoted paths are found by reviewing the service configuration, for example with sc qc or Get-CimInstance Win32_Service, and are reported by credentialed vulnerability scans and by local enumeration tools such as WinPEAS and PowerUp. Testing then establishes whether any directory in the path is writable by unprivileged users, and whether those users can restart the service or must wait for a reboot.
entries.impact: Where a directory earlier in the path is writable, a local user without administrative rights can plant an executable that Windows runs in place of the service, with the service account's privileges. Most affected services run as LocalSystem, so this normally gives full control of the host, including access to stored credentials and the ability to disable security tools. Exploitation needs local access and usually a service restart or reboot, which the attacker may have to wait for. Where no directory in the path is writable by unprivileged users, the weakness cannot be exploited until permissions change, but it remains a latent risk.
entries.remediation:
Correct the service definition and the permissions around it:

  • Enclose the executable path in double quotation marks in the service's ImagePath value, under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services in the key named after the service, leaving any arguments outside the quotation marks. The same change can be made with sc.exe config and its binPath= option.
  • Report the defect to the software vendor so that the installer quotes the path, and check again after upgrades or reinstallation, which may restore the unquoted value.
  • Remove write access for non-administrative users from every directory in the path, and install services under C:\Program Files where possible.

A corrected value looks like this:

"C:\Program Files\Vendor App\Service Host\svc.exe" -service

As an interim measure, removing write access for users from the intermediate directories prevents exploitation until the path is corrected. Confirm the fix by listing services again and checking that no service path containing a space is unquoted, and that no directory in any service path is writable by standard users.

entries.title: Weak Service Permissions
entries.summary: A Windows service's configuration, executable or registry key can be changed by unprivileged users, letting them run code with the service's privileges.
entries.description:
A Windows service can be reconfigured or replaced by users who are not administrators. Three forms are common: the service's own access control list grants rights such as SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG, WRITE_DAC or SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS to broad groups such as Everyone, Authenticated Users or Users; the service executable, or a DLL or script it loads, sits in a directory those groups can write to; or the service's registry key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services can be modified by them.

The cause is usually a third-party installer that sets permissive access control lists, or software installed outside the protected Program Files folders. The weakness is identified by reviewing service, file and registry permissions, for example with Sysinternals accesschk, sc sdshow, icacls and the PowerShell Get-Acl cmdlet, and local enumeration tools such as WinPEAS and PowerUp report it automatically. It is confirmed by showing that a standard user can change the service's binary path, replace its executable or alter its registry values.
entries.impact: A local user can make the service run a command or program of their choosing, for example by pointing its binary path at a command that adds them to the local Administrators group, and then starting the service or waiting for a reboot. Services commonly run as LocalSystem, so the user gains full control of the host, including stored credentials, security tooling and any data on it. Where administrators sign in to the host, the credentials obtained can extend the compromise to other systems.
entries.remediation:
Close every route by which an unprivileged user can influence the service:

  • Reset the service's security descriptor so that only SYSTEM and Administrators hold rights that change its configuration or permissions. Standard users should hold at most the rights to query the service and, where there is a business need, to start or stop it.
  • Remove write, modify and full control permissions for Everyone, Authenticated Users, Users and similar groups from the service executable, the directory that contains it, and any DLLs, scripts or configuration files it loads.
  • Remove write access for those groups from the service's registry key and its subkeys.
  • Enforce the corrected permissions through Group Policy, in the System Services, File System and Registry nodes under Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings, so that reinstallation does not restore the weak settings, and report the defect to the vendor.

As an interim measure, disable the affected service where it is not needed. Confirm the fix by repeating the permission checks as a standard user and verifying that the service configuration, executable and registry key can no longer be changed.

entries.title: Writable Executables or Directories in System Paths
entries.summary: Executables, or directories that privileged processes search for programs and DLLs, such as those in the system PATH, can be modified by unprivileged users.
entries.description:
Standard users can write to executables, or to directories, from which privileged processes load code. The common cases are a directory in the system-wide PATH environment variable that Users or Authenticated Users can write to, often added by development tools or runtimes installed outside C:\Program Files; program or script files run by services, scheduled tasks or other users that any user can modify; and application directories that a privileged process searches for DLLs.

When a privileged process starts a program or loads a DLL by name rather than by full path, Windows searches a sequence of directories, and the system PATH directories come last in the standard DLL search order. A file planted in a writable directory on that route can be loaded in place of a missing or legitimate component. The same weakness exists on Linux and other Unix-like systems where a directory in the PATH used by root, or by scripts root runs, is writable by other users, or where root runs programs which other users are able to change.

The weakness is identified by checking the permissions of each PATH directory and of the files that privileged processes run, for example with icacls, Sysinternals accesschk or find with its -writable test, and local enumeration tools such as WinPEAS, PowerUp and linPEAS report it.
entries.impact: A local user can plant or modify a program or DLL that a privileged process later runs, and so gain that process's privileges. When the process belongs to a service or a root job, this gives full control of the host. Exploitation depends on a privileged process loading from the writable location, which may only happen at a service restart or reboot, and on the attacker knowing which file name it looks for. Where the modified file is run by other users instead, the attacker gains their privileges and access.
entries.remediation:
• Remove write, modify and full control permissions for non-administrative users and groups from every directory in the system PATH, and from executables, scripts and DLLs run by services, scheduled tasks and administrators. On Linux, make such files and directories owned by root and not writable by group or other users.
  • Remove directories from the system PATH that do not need to be there, and install software into protected locations such as C:\Program Files or root-owned system directories.
  • Where a directory must stay writable for an application, take it out of the system PATH and run the application by its full path.
  • Ask vendors to load components by full path and to use the restricted DLL search options the platform provides.

For example, to stop a tools directory inheriting write access for all authenticated users while keeping read and execute access:

icacls "C:\Tools" /inheritance:d icacls "C:\Tools" /remove:g "Authenticated Users" icacls "C:\Tools" /grant:r "Users:(OI)(CI)RX"

As an interim measure, monitor the affected directories for new executable and DLL files. Confirm the fix by repeating the permission checks as a standard user.

entries.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Enabled
entries.summary: The Windows Installer policy AlwaysInstallElevated is enabled, so any user can install a package that runs with SYSTEM privileges.
entries.description:
The Windows Installer policy Always install with elevated privileges is enabled for both the computer and the user. When the AlwaysInstallElevated registry value is set to 1 under both HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer and HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer, Windows Installer runs every installation package with SYSTEM privileges, whoever starts it. The setting is sometimes enabled so that users can install software without help from IT, but it applies to any package, including one an attacker builds.

The weakness is identified by querying the two registry values, for example with reg query, or by reviewing the resultant Group Policy, and local enumeration tools such as WinPEAS and PowerUp report it. It is confirmed by installing a harmless test package as a standard user and showing that its custom action runs as SYSTEM. Microsoft's own documentation warns that the setting is equivalent to granting full administrative rights.
entries.impact: Any local user, or any malware running as one, can obtain SYSTEM privileges by installing a crafted Windows Installer package with a single command, with no vulnerability or user interaction needed. This gives full control of the host: the attacker can create administrator accounts, extract stored credentials, disable security tools and persist. Where the policy is applied to many computers through Group Policy, every one of them is affected in the same way.
entries.remediation:
• Set both Always install with elevated privileges policies to Disabled: the one under Computer Configuration\Administrative Templates\Windows Components\Windows Installer and the one under User Configuration\Administrative Templates\Windows Components\Windows Installer. Remove any Group Policy Preferences items or scripts that write the registry values directly.
  • Deliver software through a managed route that installs with administrative rights centrally, such as Microsoft Intune, Configuration Manager or Group Policy software installation assigned to computers, or through an endpoint privilege management product, rather than letting users elevate any package.
  • After policy refresh (gpupdate /force), confirm that both values are absent or set to 0:
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

The elevation applies only when both values are set, so disabling the computer policy is an effective interim measure while software deployment moves to a managed route. Confirm the fix by repeating the test package installation as a standard user and checking that it runs without elevated rights.

entries.title: Autologon Credentials Stored in the Registry
entries.summary: Windows automatic logon is configured with the account's password stored in plain text in the registry, where local users can read it.
entries.description:
The host is configured to sign an account in automatically at start-up, and the account's password is held in clear text in the DefaultPassword value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon, alongside AutoAdminLogon, DefaultUserName and DefaultDomainName. This configuration is common on kiosks, digital signage, shared terminals, laboratory machines and servers that run an application in an interactive session.

Standard users can normally read the Winlogon key, so anyone who can run commands on the host can recover the password with a simple registry query. The weakness is identified with reg query or by local enumeration tools such as WinPEAS, Seatbelt and PowerUp, and credentialed scans may report it. The same credentials are sometimes also present in the Windows Setup answer files used to build the host. Automatic logon configured with the Sysinternals Autologon tool instead stores the password as an LSA secret, which only administrators can read.
entries.impact: Any local user, or malware running as one, can obtain the password of the automatic logon account. The impact depends on that account: where it is a local or domain account with administrative rights, which is common on application servers and kiosks set up for convenience, the password gives full control of the host and possibly of others. Even a low-privileged domain account gives an attacker a valid identity on the wider network, and the password may be reused elsewhere.
entries.remediation:
• Remove automatic logon where it is not essential: set AutoAdminLogon to 0 and delete the DefaultPassword value, then change the exposed account's password, which must be treated as compromised.
  • Where automatic logon is required, use a dedicated local account with only the rights the kiosk or application needs, never an administrative or general-purpose domain account, and configure it with the Sysinternals Autologon tool rather than the plain-text registry value.
  • Remove any copies of the credentials from Windows Setup answer files and deployment files left on the host.
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword /f reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v AutoAdminLogon /t REG_SZ /d 0 /f

Confirm the fix by querying the Winlogon key as a standard user and checking that no DefaultPassword value is returned, and that the old password no longer works.

entries.title: Standard Users With Local Administrator Rights
entries.summary: Accounts used for everyday work are members of the local Administrators group, so anything they run can take full control of the host.
entries.description:
User accounts used for everyday work, such as email and web browsing, are members of the local Administrators group on their workstations or on servers. Membership may be granted directly, through a domain group added to the local group by Group Policy, or by leaving the first account created during setup as an administrator. In some estates a broad group such as Domain Users is an administrator on every workstation.

User Account Control runs an administrator's programs with a filtered token until elevation is approved, but Microsoft does not treat it as a security boundary: the user can approve the prompt, and malware can bypass it with well-known techniques. The weakness is identified by reviewing the membership of the local Administrators group, for example with net localgroup administrators or whoami /groups, or by collecting group membership across the domain with tools such as BloodHound, which also shows where a single group grants administrative rights to many hosts.
entries.impact: Any malware or attacker that gains code execution as one of these users, for example through a phishing attachment or a malicious download, can take full control of the host: disable endpoint protection, install drivers and persistence, and extract credentials from memory and the registry. Credentials of other users and administrators who have signed in to the host can then be used to move to other systems. Where a domain group is an administrator on many hosts, one compromised account gives administrative access to all of them, which is a common route to wider domain compromise.
entries.remediation:
• Remove standard user accounts and broad groups from the local Administrators group on every host. Manage the group's membership centrally with Group Policy Restricted Groups, Group Policy Preferences (Local Users and Groups) or an Intune account protection policy, so that local changes are reverted.
  • Give IT staff who need administrative rights a separate administrative account, used only for administration and never for email or browsing, or use an endpoint privilege management product that elevates approved tasks without granting full rights.
  • Where a user needs particular software, deploy it centrally or allow that specific elevation, rather than granting administrative rights.
  • Manage the built-in local administrator account's password with Windows LAPS so that it is unique on each host.

Removing domain-wide groups from the local group is a quick interim step while individual exceptions are worked through. Confirm the fix by reviewing the local Administrators membership on a sample of hosts after policy refresh.

entries.title: User Account Control Disabled or Weakened
entries.summary: User Account Control is disabled or configured so that administrators' programs gain full rights without a prompt, removing a barrier to malware and remote misuse.
entries.description:
User Account Control (UAC) is turned off, or configured so that it no longer separates administrators' everyday programs from administrative ones. The settings involved are held under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and set by the matching Group Policy security options:

  • EnableLUA set to 0, which disables User Account Control: Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode and turns UAC off, so every program an administrator runs has full rights.
  • ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin set to 0 (Elevate without prompting), which lets programs gain full rights silently.
  • PromptOnSecureDesktop set to 0, which shows the prompt on the normal desktop, where malicious software can more easily imitate or interfere with it.
  • LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy set to 1, which gives local administrator accounts full rights over the network and removes the restriction that blocks remote administration with local accounts.

The weakness is identified by reading these values with reg query or from the resultant Group Policy, and configuration review tools and credentialed scans report them.
entries.impact: Malware or an attacker running as an administrator's account gains full administrative rights immediately, without the user seeing or approving a prompt, so a single phishing payload opened by an administrator can disable security tools, extract credentials and persist. Where remote restrictions are removed, a password or hash for any local administrator account can be used to run commands on the host over the network, which makes reuse of a local administrator password across hosts far more damaging. Microsoft does not treat UAC as a security boundary and bypass techniques exist, so the main effect is to remove a layer that stops much commodity malware rather than to open a new route on its own.
entries.remediation:
Restore the Windows defaults or stricter values through Group Policy, under Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Local Policies\Security Options:

  • User Account Control: Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode: Enabled.
  • User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode: Prompt for consent on the secure desktop, or Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop.
  • User Account Control: Switch to the secure desktop when prompting for elevation: Enabled.
  • User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users: Automatically deny elevation requests, where standard users should not elevate.

Set LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy to 0 or remove it, for example with the Apply UAC restrictions to local accounts on network logons setting from Microsoft's security baseline templates, and make local administrator passwords unique on each host. A change to EnableLUA takes effect after a restart. Confirm the fix by checking the registry values after policy refresh and confirming that an administrator's programs run with a filtered token until elevation is approved.

entries.title: Full Disk Encryption Not Enabled
entries.summary: The host's disks are not encrypted, so anyone with physical access to the device or its drive can read and alter its data and operating system offline.
entries.description:
The operating system volume, and possibly other fixed or removable drives, are not protected with full disk encryption such as BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS or LUKS on Linux. Anyone who obtains the device, or removes its drive, can read the file system from another operating system without signing in, because the operating system's access controls apply only while it is running.

Laptops and other portable devices are most exposed, through loss or theft, but servers and workstations in shared or poorly controlled locations, and drives sent for repair or disposal, carry the same risk. A related weakness is encryption that depends on the TPM alone: it protects a drive removed from the device, but offers less protection against an attacker who holds the whole device, because the device unlocks the drive at start-up without any user input.

The weakness is identified with manage-bde -status or Get-BitLockerVolume on Windows, fdesetup status on macOS and lsblk or cryptsetup status on Linux, or during a build review by booting the device from external media and reading the disk.
entries.impact: An attacker with physical access, for example to a lost or stolen laptop, can read every file on the disk, including documents, email caches, browser data and saved credentials. Password hashes for local accounts and cached domain credentials can be extracted for cracking, and passwords stored as LSA secrets, such as those of service accounts, can be recovered. The attacker can also alter the operating system offline, for example replacing an accessibility program to obtain a SYSTEM prompt at the sign-in screen, or planting malware that runs when the device is returned. Loss of an unencrypted device holding personal data may also need to be reported as a personal data breach.
entries.remediation:
• Enable full disk encryption on all laptops, and on desktops and servers that hold sensitive data: BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS and LUKS on Linux. Encrypt fixed data drives as well as the operating system volume, and use BitLocker To Go or a device control policy for removable drives.
  • On portable Windows devices, require pre-boot authentication (TPM and PIN) where the threat model includes theft of a device that is switched on or asleep, and configure BitLocker through Group Policy (Computer Configuration\Administrative Templates\Windows Components\BitLocker Drive Encryption) or Intune.
  • Store recovery keys in Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID or another protected escrow before encryption starts, and restrict who can read them.
  • Use the XTS-AES encryption method, and enforce encryption through device compliance policies so that unencrypted devices are reported or blocked from corporate resources.

As an interim measure, encrypt laptops and other devices that leave the office first, and make sure lost devices can be wiped remotely. Confirm the fix by checking the protection status on each device type and by attempting to read the drive from external media.

entries.title: Application Allowlisting Not Enforced
entries.summary: No application control policy is enforced, so users and malware can run any program or script, including unapproved code saved in user-writable locations.
entries.description:
No application control policy restricts which programs, scripts and libraries can run, so users, and any malware acting as them, can run any executable, script or installer they can write to disk, including files saved in their profile, temporary folders, downloads or removable media. Partial deployments are also common: a policy left in audit mode, rules that cover executables but not scripts, installers or DLLs, broad path rules that allow user-writable folders, or no protection against signed Windows binaries that can be misused to run other code.

Application allowlisting, delivered on Windows by App Control for Business (formerly Windows Defender Application Control) or AppLocker, and on Linux by tools such as fapolicyd or by mounting writable file systems with noexec, allows only approved software to run. Its absence is identified by reviewing the effective policy, for example with Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective or by checking for an active App Control policy, and by running a harmless unapproved executable and script as a standard user from a user-writable directory.
entries.impact: Malware delivered by phishing, malicious downloads or removable media runs without restriction, and an attacker with access to a user's session can run their own tools for discovery, credential theft and lateral movement. Application control is one of the most effective defences against commodity malware and ransomware, so without it the host relies on detection by endpoint protection alone. The weakness gives an attacker no access in itself, and code that runs is limited to the privileges of the user whose session runs it.
entries.remediation:
• Deploy application control in audit mode first to build an inventory of the software in use, then enforce it. On Windows, App Control for Business is the stronger option; AppLocker can be used where it is already established.
  • Base rules on publisher signatures or file hashes rather than paths, and never allow execution from user-writable locations such as user profiles, %TEMP%, download folders and removable media.
  • Cover scripts (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript and HTML applications), Windows Installer packages and, where practical, DLLs, as well as executables.
  • Apply Microsoft's recommended block rules for signed Windows binaries that can be misused to run arbitrary code, and keep them current.
  • On Linux servers, use fapolicyd or an equivalent, and mount /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm and home directories with noexec where workloads allow.

Manage policies centrally through Group Policy, Intune or configuration management, and review audit events before each tightening. As an interim measure, enforce rules that block execution from user-writable paths, which stops much commodity malware with little disruption. Confirm enforcement by repeating the test with an unapproved executable and script.

entries.title: Endpoint Protection Absent or Disabled
entries.summary: The host has no working anti-malware or endpoint detection and response protection, or it is disabled, out of date or weakened by broad exclusions.
entries.description:
No anti-malware or endpoint detection and response (EDR) product is running on the host, or the product installed is not protecting it. Common variants are real-time protection turned off; signatures or engine many days out of date; an agent installed but not reporting to its management console; a product left in passive mode after another was removed; tamper protection disabled, so that local administrators or malware can turn protection off; and exclusions so broad, such as whole drives, user-writable folders or common script types, that malicious files are never scanned.

Servers, particularly Linux servers and systems built outside the standard image, are the most frequent gaps. The weakness is identified from the management console's coverage reports and on the host itself, for example with Get-MpComputerStatus and Get-MpPreference for Microsoft Defender Antivirus, or the agent's service status on other platforms. During testing it is confirmed when a harmless test file, such as the EICAR test string, or common attack tools are written to disk or run without being blocked or raising an alert.
entries.impact: Known malware, ransomware and attack tools run without being blocked, and the security team receives no alert, so an intrusion that begins on this host is less likely to be detected or contained before it spreads. The weakness does not give an attacker access in itself: the attacker still needs a way to run code, such as a phishing payload or a compromised account. Its effect is to remove a primary layer of defence and visibility, which raises the likely impact of any other weakness on the host.
entries.remediation:
• Install a supported anti-malware and EDR product on every host, including servers and Linux systems, and confirm through the management console that each agent is reporting, up to date and in active mode.
  • Enable real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection and automatic updates, and enable tamper protection so that settings cannot be changed locally, even by administrators.
  • Review exclusions: remove broad folder, drive and file type exclusions, keep only those a vendor documents for a specific product, and restrict who can view and change them.
  • On Windows, enable attack surface reduction rules, first in audit mode and then in block mode, where the product supports them.
  • Alert on hosts that stop reporting, and add an endpoint protection check to the build process so that new hosts are not missed.

As an interim measure, make sure Microsoft Defender Antivirus, which is built into current Windows versions, is not disabled on hosts that have no other product. Confirm the fix by checking the protection status on the host and repeating the test file check.

entries.title: Host Firewall Disabled
entries.summary: The host's built-in firewall is turned off for one or more network profiles, so every listening service is reachable from any network the host joins.
entries.description:
The host-based firewall, such as Windows Defender Firewall on Windows or nftables, iptables, firewalld or ufw on Linux, is disabled or set to allow all inbound connections, so every network service the host offers can be reached by anything that can route to it. On Windows the firewall has separate Domain, Private and Public profiles, and a common variant is one profile turned off, for example the Public profile used on untrusted networks, or the Domain profile disabled by Group Policy to simplify troubleshooting.

A host firewall complements network firewalls by restricting connections between hosts on the same network segment, which network devices often do not filter. The weakness is identified with Get-NetFirewallProfile or netsh advfirewall show allprofiles on Windows and the relevant firewall tool's status command on Linux, or by scanning the host from an adjacent system and finding services that a host firewall would normally block, such as SMB, RPC or remote management on workstations.
entries.impact: Services that should only be reachable from management systems, such as file sharing, remote management and RPC, are exposed to every system on the same network, including other compromised workstations, untrusted guest or public networks, and attackers who have gained a foothold. This widens the opportunity to exploit vulnerable or misconfigured services and to move laterally with stolen credentials. Exploitation still depends on a weakness in an exposed service, so the main effect is to increase the reach and speed of an attack.
entries.remediation:
• Enable the host firewall for every profile and set the default inbound action to block. On Windows, enforce this through Group Policy (Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security) or Intune, so that it cannot be turned off locally.
  • Allow inbound connections only for the services each role needs, and limit management protocols to the addresses of management systems and administrative workstations.
  • Where locally created rules are not needed, stop them from taking effect alongside central policy, using the profile setting that controls local rule merging.
  • On Linux, enable and persist the firewall service, for example with systemctl enable --now firewalld or ufw enable, with a default policy that denies inbound traffic.

As an interim measure, enable the firewall with rules that allow the services currently in use, and tighten the rules afterwards. Confirm the fix by checking each profile's status and repeating the scan from an adjacent host.

entries.title: PowerShell Version 2 Enabled
entries.summary: The Windows PowerShell 2.0 engine is installed, so attackers can run PowerShell without the logging and anti-malware scanning that later versions provide.
entries.description:
The deprecated Windows PowerShell 2.0 engine is still installed as an optional Windows feature alongside the current version. PowerShell 2.0 does not support script block logging, the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) that lets endpoint protection inspect scripts, or the constrained language mode that application control applies to later versions. Anyone who can run PowerShell can start the old engine with powershell.exe -Version 2 and run commands that these controls would otherwise record or block, a technique known as a downgrade attack.
