The engine depends on .NET Framework 3.5, so it can start only where that is also installed, although .NET Framework 3.5 is often added for older applications. Microsoft deprecated PowerShell 2.0 in 2017 and has since begun removing it from Windows. The weakness is identified with Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root on client versions of Windows or Get-WindowsFeature PowerShell-V2 on Windows Server, and confirmed by starting the old engine and checking $PSVersionTable.
entries.impact: An attacker who can already run commands on the host as any user can run PowerShell scripts and tools without script block logging and without AMSI scanning, which makes malicious activity less likely to be detected or blocked. It also lets them step outside the constrained language mode that application control applies to PowerShell. The weakness grants no access or privilege on its own, and it requires .NET Framework 3.5 to be present.
entries.remediation:
Remove the PowerShell 2.0 engine from every host where no application depends on it, through configuration management, Intune or the build process:

# Windows client versions Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root -NoRestart # Windows Server Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name PowerShell-V2
  • Where an application still needs PowerShell 2.0, plan its upgrade and keep the old engine only on the hosts that run it.
  • Remove .NET Framework 3.5 where no application needs it, which also prevents the old engine from starting.
  • Enable PowerShell script block logging, forward the events centrally, and alert on process command lines that request version 2, which detects downgrade attempts on hosts not yet fixed.

Confirm the fix by checking the feature state and by running powershell.exe -Version 2, which should no longer start a version 2 session.

entries.title: PowerShell Logging Not Enabled
entries.summary: PowerShell script block, module and transcription logging are not enabled, so PowerShell activity leaves little record for detection or investigation.
entries.description:
Windows PowerShell and PowerShell 7 can record the code they run, but this logging is not enabled through policy, so only limited detail of PowerShell activity is recorded. The settings concerned are Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging, which records the content of scripts and commands as they run (event 4104 in the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log); Turn on Module Logging, which records pipeline execution details (event 4103); and Turn on PowerShell Transcription, which writes a text record of each session to a chosen folder. Without script block logging enabled, only script blocks that PowerShell itself judges suspicious are logged.

Related weaknesses are an operational log too small to hold more than a short period of activity, logs kept only on the host where an attacker can clear them, and PowerShell 7 installed without its separate policy settings. The weakness is identified by reviewing the values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell or the resultant Group Policy, and by running a test command and checking which events are recorded.
entries.impact: An attacker who runs PowerShell on the host, which is common in both commodity malware and targeted intrusions, leaves little record of what was run, so the activity is less likely to be detected, and an investigation may be unable to establish what was done, which data was accessed or which other systems were contacted. The weakness gives an attacker no access in itself; it reduces the organisation's ability to detect and respond to an intrusion that has already begun.
entries.remediation:
Enable PowerShell logging through Group Policy under Computer Configuration\Policies\Administrative Templates\Windows Components\Windows PowerShell, or the equivalent Intune settings:

  • Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging: Enabled.
  • Turn on Module Logging: Enabled, with * as the list of module names.
  • Turn on PowerShell Transcription: Enabled, writing to a protected folder or network share that users can add to but not read or alter.
  • For PowerShell 7, install its policy templates and enable the matching settings, or select the option in those templates to follow the Windows PowerShell policy.

Increase the maximum size of the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log, forward the events to a central log platform or SIEM, and build detections for suspicious content. Logged script blocks can contain secrets, so restrict access to the logs and consider Protected Event Logging. Confirm the fix by running a test command and checking that event 4104 records its content, both on the host and in the central platform.

entries.title: Insufficient Security Event Logging
entries.summary: The host's audit policy and log settings do not record key security events, or keep them only briefly and locally, so attacks may go unseen and uninvestigated.
entries.description:
The host does not record enough security-relevant activity to detect or investigate an attack. Typical gaps on Windows are an audit policy that relies on the limited defaults, so that events such as process creation with command lines, changes to local group membership, and new services and scheduled tasks are not logged; a Security log small enough to overwrite itself within hours or days; and no forwarding of events to a central platform. On Linux the equivalents are auditd not installed, or running without rules for privileged commands and changes to authentication files, and system journals that are not persistent or not sent off the host.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the effective audit policy with auditpol /get /category:* together with log sizes and retention, checking auditctl -l and the logging configuration on Linux, and confirming whether the actions performed during testing appear in the host's logs and in the organisation's central log platform.
entries.impact: Attacker activity on the host, such as privilege escalation, creation of accounts and services, credential theft and lateral movement, may not be recorded, or the record may be overwritten or deleted before anyone reviews it. The organisation is then less likely to detect an intrusion while it is in progress, and may be unable to establish its scope, which data was affected and whether the attacker remains, which also affects its ability to meet notification duties. The weakness gives an attacker no access in itself, but increases the impact of any intrusion.
entries.remediation:
• Configure an advanced audit policy through Group Policy (Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Advanced Audit Policy Configuration) based on a recognised baseline, such as Microsoft's audit policy recommendations or the CIS Benchmarks, and enable Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings.
  • Record at least logon and account lockout events, credential validation, account and group management, process creation with command lines (Include command line in process creation events), service and scheduled task creation, audit policy changes and log clearing.
  • Increase the size of the Security log and other important logs so that they hold several days of activity locally.
  • Forward events to a central log platform or SIEM, using Windows Event Forwarding or an agent, so that they survive deletion on the host, and keep them for a defined retention period.
  • On Linux, install and enable auditd with rules for privileged commands, identity and authentication files and sudo use, and forward system and audit logs off the host.
  • Synchronise the clocks of all hosts so that events can be correlated.

Confirm the fix by performing a set of test actions and checking that each appears, with enough detail, in the central platform.

entries.title: Removable Media Not Restricted
entries.summary: Users can read from and write to USB storage and other removable media without restriction, so data can be copied off the host and untrusted files brought in.
entries.description:
No device control policy restricts the use of removable storage such as USB drives, memory cards, external disks and phones connected as storage. Any user, or anyone with access to an unlocked session, can copy data from the host to a device they take away, and can bring in and open files from a device of unknown origin. Related gaps are the absence of an encryption requirement for removable drives, no logging of what is copied, and no restriction on other classes of device that connect over USB.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the device control configuration, such as the Group Policy settings under Computer Configuration\Administrative Templates\System\Removable Storage Access, an Intune or endpoint protection device control policy, or USBGuard or kernel module restrictions on Linux, and by connecting a test storage device during a build review to show that files can be written to and read from it.
entries.impact: A malicious insider, or an attacker with brief physical access to an unlocked session, can copy sensitive data to removable media without technical restriction, often leaving no record of what was taken. Removable media is also a route for malware into the organisation, including into networks that are otherwise isolated. The person must be able to sign in, or find a session left unlocked, and the data at risk is limited to what that account can reach, so the risk is greatest on hosts that hold or can access sensitive data.
entries.remediation:
• Decide which users and roles need removable storage, and block it for everyone else, or allow read access only, using the Removable Storage Access Group Policy settings, Intune device control or the device control feature of the endpoint protection product.
  • Where removable storage is allowed, permit only approved, organisation-issued devices, identified by device instance or serial number where the product supports it, and require encryption, for example with the BitLocker policy that denies write access to removable drives not protected by BitLocker.
  • Scan removable media automatically when it is connected, keep AutoPlay turned off, and log file copies to removable devices where the endpoint product supports it.
  • On Linux, use USBGuard to allow only authorised devices, or block the usb-storage kernel module where storage devices are never needed.

Confirm the fix by connecting an unapproved storage device as a standard user and checking that it cannot be read from or written to, as the policy intends.

entries.title: Firmware Settings Not Protected
entries.summary: The UEFI or BIOS setup has no administrator password, so anyone with physical access can change the boot order and turn off firmware security features.
entries.description:
The firmware setup interface (UEFI or BIOS) is not protected by an administrator or supervisor password, so anyone at the keyboard can enter it during start-up and change its settings. With access to setup, a person can enable booting from USB devices or the network, change the boot order, and turn off Secure Boot, the TPM, virtualisation support and other security features the vendor provides. Related weaknesses are a one-time boot menu that allows external boot devices without a password, and a single firmware password used across the whole estate and widely known among staff.

The weakness is identified during a build review by restarting the device and entering firmware setup or the boot menu, or with the vendor's management tools, which report whether an administrator password is set.
entries.impact: An attacker with physical access can boot the device from their own media. Where the disk is not encrypted, this gives them full read and write access to its contents and to the operating system. Where disk encryption is in place, booting another operating system does not unlock the disk, and turning off Secure Boot normally causes BitLocker to require its recovery key, so the main risk becomes the quiet weakening of platform protections as one step in a longer attack. The risk is therefore greatest when combined with missing disk encryption or pre-boot authentication.
entries.remediation:
• Set a firmware administrator (supervisor) password on all devices, applying it at scale with the vendor's management tools, and store the passwords in a password vault with access limited to the support staff who need them.
  • Use a unique password for each device, or at least for each group of devices, so that one disclosed password does not unlock the whole estate.
  • Disable booting from external media and the network unless required, put the internal disk first in the boot order, and protect the one-time boot menu with the same password.
  • Enable Secure Boot and the TPM, and turn on any firmware write protection the vendor offers.
  • Keep firmware up to date through the vendor's update process.

As an interim measure, make sure the affected devices have full disk encryption with pre-boot authentication. Confirm the fix by restarting a sample of devices and checking that firmware setup and the boot menu require the password.

entries.title: Secure Boot Not Enabled
entries.summary: UEFI Secure Boot is disabled, so the firmware will start boot loaders and other early boot code without checking that a trusted publisher signed them.
entries.description:
UEFI Secure Boot is a firmware feature that checks the digital signature of each piece of code the firmware loads before the operating system, such as the boot loader, UEFI drivers and option ROMs, against keys and hashes held in the firmware's signature databases, and refuses to run code that is not trusted or has been revoked. The operating system then extends that chain of trust to its kernel and early drivers. When Secure Boot is disabled, when the device boots in legacy BIOS mode (often labelled CSM, the Compatibility Support Module), or when the firmware is left in Setup Mode with no platform key installed, these checks are not made and any boot code on the system will run.

The state can be confirmed on Windows with the System Information tool (msinfo32, Secure Boot State) or the PowerShell cmdlet Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, and on Linux with mokutil --sb-state; endpoint management and configuration review tools also report it. It is commonly found on older hardware, on systems originally installed in legacy BIOS mode, on virtual machines created without Secure Boot support, such as Hyper-V generation 1 virtual machines, and on Linux hosts where it was turned off to allow unsigned kernel modules or drivers to load.
entries.impact:
An attacker who has already gained administrative or root rights on the operating system, or who has physical access to the device, can install a bootkit: malicious code in the boot loader or the EFI system partition that runs before the operating system and its security software. Code running at that stage can tamper with the operating system as it loads, hide from endpoint protection, and survive the removal of the attacker's other footholds. Disabling Secure Boot also weakens protections built on it, such as virtualisation-based security on Windows and the kernel lockdown that many Linux distributions apply when Secure Boot is on.

The weakness does not by itself give an attacker access or privileges, which is why it is rated low; its significance lies in the stealth and persistence it allows after another compromise.
entries.remediation:
Enable Secure Boot on every device whose hardware and operating system support it, and keep it enabled:

  • In the UEFI firmware settings, set the boot mode to UEFI only, with legacy or CSM boot disabled, and enable Secure Boot with the platform's default keys. Windows devices installed in legacy BIOS mode first need their system disk converted from MBR to GPT, which the MBR2GPT tool can do without reinstalling.
  • Set a firmware administrator password so that Secure Boot cannot be turned off again without authorisation.
  • On Linux, where Secure Boot was disabled to load unsigned kernel modules, sign the modules with a local key and register that key as a Machine Owner Key (mokutil --import) instead.
  • For virtual machines, use a type that supports Secure Boot, such as Hyper-V generation 2 virtual machines, VMware virtual machines with EFI firmware, Azure Trusted Launch or Google Cloud Shielded VM, and enable it in the template.
  • Report and enforce the setting centrally, for example with an Intune compliance policy that requires Secure Boot, so that devices that drift are found.
  • Keep firmware and the Secure Boot revocation list (dbx) up to date, since old boot managers with known flaws remain trusted until they are revoked.

Where older hardware cannot support Secure Boot, restrict administrative rights on it, protect its firmware with a password and include it in the hardware replacement plan. Confirm the fix with Confirm-SecureBootUEFI, which should return True, or msinfo32 on Windows, and with mokutil --sb-state on Linux.

entries.title: Screen Lock Not Enforced
entries.summary: Devices are not set by policy to lock after a period of inactivity, so an unattended session stays open to anyone with physical access.
entries.description:
The device is not configured by central policy to lock the user's session after a period of inactivity. Unless users remember to lock their screens each time they step away, an unattended workstation or laptop stays signed in, and anyone who can reach it can use the session with the user's identity and access. Related forms are a timeout that is very long, one that users can change or switch off, and a screen saver that starts without requiring the user to sign in again when it ends.

On Windows the lock is normally enforced through the security policy Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit or the screen saver policies under User Configuration\Administrative Templates\Control Panel\Personalization; on macOS through a configuration profile; and on Linux desktops through settings such as the GNOME idle-delay and lock-enabled keys. The weakness is identified by reviewing the effective policy on a sample of devices, for example with gpresult or the device management console, and by leaving a session idle to see whether it locks. Physical security reviews often find it directly, as unlocked and unattended devices.
entries.impact:
Anyone with physical access to an unattended, unlocked device can act as the signed-in user: reading and sending email, opening files and internal applications, approving requests in the user's name, or running commands. A keystroke-injection device plugged into an unlocked session can install malware or create persistence within seconds. Where the user has administrative rights, the whole device and everything that account can reach is exposed.

Exploitation needs physical presence at a moment when a device has been left unlocked, so the risk is greatest in shared offices, public areas and for staff who work in public places, and lowest where physical access is tightly controlled.
entries.remediation:
Enforce an automatic lock on every workstation and laptop through central policy, so that protection does not depend on each user:

  • Windows: set Computer Configuration\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Local Policies\Security Options\Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit to the organisation's chosen timeout. The CIS Benchmarks recommend 900 seconds (15 minutes) or less, but not 0, which turns the limit off. The screen saver policies Enable screen saver, Password protect the screen saver and Screen saver timeout achieve the same per user, and Intune offers equivalent settings for managed devices.
  • macOS: deploy a configuration profile that starts the screen saver after the chosen idle time and requires a password immediately when it starts or the display sleeps.
  • Linux desktops: set the GNOME keys org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay and org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled as system defaults through dconf and lock them so that users cannot change them, or use the equivalent for the desktop in use.
  • Use shorter timeouts for privileged access workstations and for devices in public areas.
  • Remind staff to lock their screen whenever they leave the device (Windows logo key + L on Windows, Control + Command + Q on macOS).

Confirm the fix by checking the applied policy on a sample of devices and leaving a test session idle beyond the timeout to confirm that it locks and requires authentication to resume.

entries.title: Credentials Stored in Files on Disk
entries.summary: Passwords, keys or tokens are kept in readable files on the host, such as scripts, configuration files and notes, where other users or an attacker can recover them.
entries.description:
Credentials are stored in clear text, or in a form that can be reversed without any secret, in files on the host's local disk, and the files can be read by users or processes that should not have them. Common examples are scripts and batch files with embedded passwords; application and service configuration files holding database connection strings, API keys or cloud access keys; deployment answer files such as unattend.xml left behind after installation; shell and PowerShell command history; backup copies of configuration files; and documents, spreadsheets and text files in which users record passwords. Values that are only base64-encoded, as in many answer files, are no better protected than plain text.

The weakness is identified once access to the host has been obtained, by searching readable file systems for credential patterns, manually or with tools such as winPEAS, linPEAS, Seatbelt or LaZagne, and by checking who can read the files found. It covers files on the host itself; credentials found on file shares, in SYSVOL scripts and in directory attributes are reported under their own findings.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the files obtains the credentials and the access that goes with them. Where they belong to a service account, a local or domain administrator, a database or a cloud account, a low-privileged user or an attacker with a foothold on the host can escalate privileges and move to other systems without exploiting any vulnerability, and activity carried out with valid credentials is harder to distinguish from legitimate use. The impact depends on the privileges of the accounts concerned and on who can read the files: it is greatest when the files are readable by all users and when the same credentials are used on other systems.
entries.remediation:
Remove credentials from files and give the processes that need them a protected source instead:

  • Search the affected host, and others built from the same image or managed by the same scripts, for stored credentials, and remove them from scripts, configuration files, answer files, history files and documents. Delete deployment answer files, such as those under C:\Windows\Panther, once the build is complete.
  • Change every credential that was found, since it must be presumed known, and review the recent use of the accounts concerned.
  • Supply secrets to scripts, services and applications through a mechanism designed for it: a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager; group Managed Service Accounts for Windows services and scheduled tasks; managed identities or instance roles for cloud workloads; or the operating system's protected credential store where a secret must stay on the host.
  • Where a configuration file has to contain a secret, restrict its permissions to the account that uses it and to administrators, and use the platform's protected configuration where one exists, such as encrypted sections in an ASP.NET web.config file.
  • Provide users with an approved password manager so that passwords are not kept in documents.
  • Add secret scanning to build pipelines, and periodic scans of hosts, so that new occurrences are found early.

Confirm the fix by repeating the search with the same tools and checking that the credentials found earlier no longer work.

entries.title: Credentials Saved in Web Browsers
entries.summary: Users save passwords in the web browser's built-in password manager, from which malware or anyone able to run code as the user can recover them.
entries.description:
Users save the usernames and passwords they enter into websites and web applications in the web browser's built-in password manager, which fills them in on later visits. Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Mozilla Firefox keep saved credentials in files in the user's profile. The files are encrypted, but with keys the browser can use without asking the user for anything, so code running as that user can generally recover every saved password in clear text. Firefox can add protection with its optional Primary Password, which is not set by default.

The weakness is identified during a host review, or after access to a device has been obtained, by examining browser profiles for saved logins, through the browser's own password list or with tools such as LaZagne or SharpChrome, and by reviewing browser policy to see whether saving passwords is permitted. Corporate credentials are often stored alongside personal ones, and where users sign in to the browser with a personal account and turn on synchronisation, saved credentials are copied to that account and to every device signed in to it.
entries.impact: An attacker who runs code as the user, for example through a malicious attachment or download, or who gains administrative control of the device, can extract every saved credential in one step. Information-stealing malware is built to do exactly this. The credentials often include access to internal applications, cloud services, network device interfaces and suppliers' portals, as well as personal accounts whose passwords may be reused for corporate ones, so the compromise of a single workstation can lead to access well beyond it. Credentials synchronised to a personal browser account are also exposed on devices the organisation does not manage.
entries.remediation:
Stop corporate credentials being saved in browsers and give users a managed alternative:

  • Disable the built-in password manager by policy: set PasswordManagerEnabled to disabled for Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome through Group Policy, Intune or the Chrome Enterprise console, and set OfferToSaveLogins and PasswordManagerEnabled to false in Firefox's enterprise policies. Disabling saving does not remove passwords already stored, so have users move them to the approved password manager and delete them from the browser.
  • Prevent synchronisation of corporate browsing data to personal accounts, with the SyncDisabled policy or by restricting browser sign-in to corporate accounts with RestrictSigninToPattern.
  • Provide an enterprise password manager protected by a strong primary password and multifactor authentication, so that users have an approved place to keep the credentials they need.
  • Change the passwords of accounts whose credentials were saved on devices that may have been compromised, starting with administrative and shared accounts, and keep administrative accounts out of everyday browsers altogether.
  • Reduce the number of passwords there are to save by using single sign-on, and require multifactor authentication so that a stolen password alone is not enough.

Confirm the fix by checking the browser's policy page (edge://policy, chrome://policy or about:policies) on a sample of devices and checking that no saved credentials remain in their profiles.

entries.title: Operating System Not Hardened to a Recognised Baseline
entries.summary: The operating system largely keeps its default settings instead of following a recognised security baseline, leaving unnecessary features and weak settings in place.
entries.description:
Operating systems ship with settings chosen largely for compatibility, and several protections are off or relaxed by default. Organisations close that gap by applying a recognised security baseline, such as the CIS Benchmarks, the Microsoft security baselines, the DISA Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs) or a vendor's hardening guide, and by keeping hosts compliant with it. The host reviewed does not follow such a baseline: comparing its configuration with one shows a significant number of settings that differ, with no documented reason.

Typical deviations include legacy protocols and authentication methods still enabled, such as SMBv1, LLMNR, NetBIOS name resolution or NTLMv1; unnecessary services, features and software installed; weak audit and logging settings; permissive local security policy and user rights; and, on Linux, permissive kernel parameters, unneeded network services and lax file permissions. Individual deviations with a significant impact are normally reported as findings of their own; this finding records that hardening is not managed as a whole. It is identified by comparing the configuration with a baseline, using tools such as CIS-CAT, OpenSCAP or those in Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit, or by reviewing the effective Group Policy and configuration files manually.
entries.impact: No single deviation from a baseline need be serious, but together they make attacks easier at every stage: they give an attacker more services to target, more ways to capture or relay credentials, more routes to escalate privileges and fewer records of what was done. A configuration that is not managed against a baseline also drifts over time and differs between hosts, so a weakness corrected on one system often remains on others. The practical impact depends on the specific deviations found, which should be read alongside this finding.
entries.remediation:
Adopt a recognised baseline and manage hosts against it as a continuing process:

  • Choose a baseline for each operating system in use, such as the relevant CIS Benchmark Level 1 profile, the Microsoft security baselines or a DISA STIG, and record each setting the organisation deliberately departs from, with the reason and the risk owner.
  • Test the baseline on a representative group of systems, then apply it centrally: Group Policy or Intune security baselines for Windows (Windows Server 2025 can also apply Microsoft's baselines through OSConfig), and configuration management tools such as Ansible, Puppet or Chef, or hardened build profiles, for Linux.
  • Build new systems from hardened images or templates so that they are compliant from the start.
  • Remove features, services and software that are not needed, such as SMBv1 and PowerShell 2.0, and disable legacy name resolution and authentication protocols once their remaining dependencies have been dealt with.
  • Measure compliance regularly with a tool such as CIS-CAT, OpenSCAP or Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit, and treat deviations as defects to be corrected.

While the baseline is rolled out, prioritise the individual deviations reported elsewhere in the assessment. Confirm the fix by repeating the comparison against the chosen baseline and checking that any remaining differences are documented exceptions.

entries.title: Insecure sudo Configuration
entries.summary: sudo rules let a user run commands as root that can be turned into a full root shell, such as editors, interpreters, writable scripts or wildcard arguments.
entries.description:
The sudo policy on the host, in /etc/sudoers and the files under /etc/sudoers.d, lets a user or group run commands as root, or as another privileged account, in a way that grants more than was intended. Many seemingly harmless tools can start a shell, run other commands, or read and write any file: editors such as vi and nano, pagers such as less, interpreters such as python and perl, and utilities such as find, tar, awk, git and package managers. Allowing any of these to run as root is, in effect, allowing a root shell.

Other common forms are rules that allow ALL commands to accounts that do not need full administration, wildcards in permitted command arguments or paths, rules that run scripts or binaries the user can modify, NOPASSWD on broad rules, and settings that pass environment variables such as LD_PRELOAD through to the command (env_keep or the SETENV tag). The weakness is identified by running sudo -l as each test account, reviewing the sudoers files, and checking the permitted commands against references such as GTFOBins; enumeration scripts such as linPEAS flag likely misconfigurations.
entries.impact: A user permitted to run such a command can become root and take full control of the host: reading and changing all data on it, including /etc/shadow and other users' SSH keys, installing persistence, disabling logging and security tools, and using the host's trust relationships to reach other systems. Where the rule applies to a service account or to a group with many members, compromise of any of those accounts, for example through a vulnerable web application running as the service account, becomes a root compromise. A rule that requires the user's password protects only as long as that password is not known to the attacker.
entries.remediation:
Grant each user only the specific commands they need, in a form that cannot be used to escape to a shell:

  • Review every rule in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d, editing only with visudo, and remove rules that are no longer needed or that grant ALL to accounts that do not need full administration.
  • Do not permit editors, pagers, interpreters, general file utilities or package managers to run as root. To let a user edit a root-owned file, grant sudoedit for that file rather than an editor.
  • Specify commands by full path with fixed arguments, avoid wildcards, and permit only scripts and binaries that are owned by root and not writable by anyone else, in directories that others cannot write to.
  • Keep env_reset enabled (the default), do not add variables such as LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH or PYTHONPATH to env_keep, and do not use the SETENV tag.
  • Require the user's password for rules that grant significant privilege, and consider the NOEXEC tag to stop permitted commands starting further commands, bearing in mind that it does not stop them reading or writing files.
  • Keep the sudo package up to date and send its logs to central logging.

Confirm the fix by running sudo -l as each affected user and checking that none of the permitted commands can be used to obtain a shell or write arbitrary files.

entries.title: Dangerous SUID or SGID Binaries
entries.summary: Executables that can run commands or write files have the SUID or SGID bit set, so any local user can use them to act as root or another privileged account.
entries.description:
On Linux and other Unix-like systems, an executable with the set-user-ID (SUID) bit runs with the privileges of the file's owner rather than those of the user who starts it, and one with the set-group-ID (SGID) bit runs with the privileges of its group. A small number of system utilities, such as passwd, need this to carry out one narrow task safely. When the bit is set on a root-owned executable that can do more than that, such as a shell, an interpreter, an editor, a file utility such as find or cp, or a debugging tool, any local user can use it to run commands, read files or overwrite files as root.

The same weakness arises from custom or third-party SUID executables that call other commands without full paths, load libraries from writable locations or trust environment variables or user input, and from SUID utilities with known vulnerabilities. File capabilities such as cap_setuid on an interpreter have the same effect. The weakness is identified by listing SUID and SGID files, for example with find / -perm -4000 -type f and find / -perm -2000 -type f, and capabilities with getcap -r /, then comparing the results with what the distribution installs and checking unusual entries against references such as GTFOBins.
entries.impact: Any user who can log in to the host or run code on it, including through a compromised service account or web application, can gain the privileges of the file's owner, usually root, and with them full control of the host: reading and changing all data, harvesting credentials and keys, installing persistence and hiding activity. An SGID executable gives the privileges of its group, which can be enough to read sensitive files or to reach root by another route. No user interaction or special conditions are needed, and public references describe the technique for most common utilities.
entries.remediation:
Keep the SUID and SGID bits only on executables that need them and are designed for it:

  • List every SUID and SGID file on the host and compare the list with what the distribution installs. Remove the bit from anything that does not need elevated privileges (chmod u-s or chmod g-s), and never set it on shells, interpreters, editors or general utilities as a convenience. Remove unneeded file capabilities with setcap -r.
  • Where users need to perform a specific privileged action, grant it through a narrowly scoped sudo rule or a dedicated service rather than a SUID copy of a general-purpose tool.
  • For custom SUID executables that must remain, review the code: call other commands by full path, set a safe environment, drop privileges as soon as they are no longer needed and validate all input. Keep the file and its directory owned by root and not writable by others.
  • Mount file systems that hold user data, temporary files and removable or network media, such as /tmp, /var/tmp, /home and NFS mounts, with the nosuid option so that SUID files placed there are ignored.
  • Monitor for new SUID and SGID files with file integrity monitoring or a scheduled comparison against a known list, and keep packages that include SUID utilities up to date.

Confirm the fix by repeating the search and checking that every remaining SUID or SGID file is expected and cannot be used to run commands or write files as its owner.

entries.title: Writable Scheduled Tasks or Cron Jobs
entries.summary: A scheduled task or cron job runs with high privileges, but its definition, or the script or binary it runs, can be changed by a low-privileged user.
entries.description:
Scheduled tasks on Windows, and cron jobs and systemd timers on Linux, often run with high privileges, as SYSTEM, root or a service account. A task is only as safe as the files it depends on. Where a low-privileged user can modify the task definition, the script or binary it runs, a file or module that the script loads, or a directory on its search path, they can make the task run their own commands with its privileges the next time it starts.

Typical examples are scripts kept in application or shared directories that all users can write to, cron entries that run scripts from user-writable locations, crontab files or /etc/cron.d entries that are writable by others, scripts that call other commands without full paths while the job's PATH includes a writable directory, and cron scripts that pass a wildcard to a command such as tar in a writable directory, where crafted file names are read as options. The weakness is identified by listing tasks (schtasks /query /fo LIST /v or Get-ScheduledTask on Windows; /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.*, user crontabs and systemctl list-timers on Linux), checking the permissions on every file and directory each task uses, for example with icacls or ls -l, and watching for short-lived processes with a tool such as pspy.
entries.impact: A low-privileged user, or an attacker who has compromised such an account or a web application on the host, can run commands with the privileges of the task, typically SYSTEM or root, and so take full control of the host. Because the task runs on a schedule, the change also provides persistence that survives reboots and may run unnoticed alongside the task's normal work. The attacker may have to wait for the next scheduled run, and where the task's account has rights on other systems, such as a domain service account, the impact extends beyond the host.
entries.remediation:
Protect everything a privileged task uses to the same level as the account it runs as:

  • Make the task's scripts, binaries, configuration files, included modules and the directories that contain them writable only by administrators or root. On Windows, remove write and modify rights for Users, Authenticated Users and Everyone; on Linux, make sure the files are owned by root and are not group- or world-writable.
  • Keep scripts for privileged tasks in protected locations, such as a directory under C:\Program Files or /usr/local/sbin, rather than in user, temporary or shared application directories.
  • In scripts, call commands by full path, set a safe PATH at the top of the crontab or script, and do not pass bare wildcards to commands that accept options (prefix them with ./ or use -- so that file names cannot be read as options).
  • Restrict who can create and change tasks: keep /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d and the /etc/cron.* directories owned by root and not writable by others, use /etc/cron.allow where users do not need their own crontabs, and check that task definitions under C:\Windows\System32\Tasks cannot be changed by standard users.
  • Run each task with the least privilege it needs, for example a dedicated account or a group Managed Service Account, rather than SYSTEM or root.

Confirm the fix by repeating the permission checks, as a standard user, on every file and directory each task uses.

entries.title: World-Writable Sensitive Files
entries.summary: Files that affect how the system or its services behave can be changed by every local user, because write access to them is granted to all.
entries.description:
Files and directories on the host can be written to by all users, through the write permission for other users on Linux and Unix, or write access for Everyone, Users or Authenticated Users on Windows, although their content affects the security of the system, of a service or of other users. Typical examples are configuration files of services and applications, files that privileged processes read or include, log files relied on for auditing, login and environment scripts such as those in /etc/profile.d, systemd unit files and, in the most serious cases, system files such as /etc/passwd. World-writable directories without the sticky bit, in which any user can delete or replace other users' files, are a related form. Executables run directly by privileged services and scheduled tasks are covered by the findings for those.

These permissions usually come from installation scripts, quick fixes to access problems (such as chmod 777), archives extracted with their original permissions, or permissive defaults in third-party software. They are identified with searches such as find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 and find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 on Linux, or with icacls and Sysinternals AccessChk on Windows, followed by working out which process uses each file and with what privileges.
entries.impact: Any local user, or an attacker who has compromised any account or service on the host, can change these files. Depending on the file, that lets them alter a service's behaviour or point it at a resource they control, plant commands that a privileged process or another user later runs, remove evidence from logs, corrupt data, or deny service by emptying or breaking a file the system needs. Where the file is read or run with root or SYSTEM privileges, as with /etc/passwd, a systemd unit or a login script, the result is full control of the host. The impact therefore depends on which files are affected and what uses them.
entries.remediation:
Remove write access for all users from every file and directory that affects security, and stop it returning:

  • For each world-writable file and directory found, identify its owner and what reads or runs it. Remove the write permission for other users where it is not needed (chmod o-w) and set ownership to the account that should maintain the file. On Windows, remove write and modify rights for Everyone, Users and Authenticated Users with icacls or Group Policy file system settings.
  • Where several accounts genuinely need to write to a file, grant access to a specific group instead, and make sure no privileged process reads or runs it.
  • Set the sticky bit (chmod +t) on shared directories that must stay writable, such as /tmp, so that users cannot delete or rename each other's files.
  • Correct the source of the permissions in installation scripts, deployment tooling and packages, and use a restrictive default umask, such as 027, for services and users.
  • Check the integrity of files that were world-writable, since they may already have been changed, and restore any that differ from a known good copy.
  • Add a regular check for world-writable files to configuration compliance scanning or file integrity monitoring.

Confirm the fix by repeating the search and checking that every remaining world-writable location is expected, and that such directories have the sticky bit set.

entries.title: Linux Kernel With Known Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities
entries.summary: The running Linux kernel has publicly known flaws that let a local user gain root, because kernel updates are missing or the host has not been restarted into them.
entries.description:
The host runs a Linux kernel affected by one or more publicly disclosed vulnerabilities that allow a local, unprivileged user to gain root privileges. Kernel flaws of this kind are found regularly, in areas such as memory management, file systems, networking subsystems and namespaces, and many have public exploits. Well-known examples are Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195), Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) and the nf_tables use-after-free CVE-2024-1086, all of which appear in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.

A common cause is that kernel updates have been installed but the host has not been restarted, so the vulnerable kernel is still running. Others are distributions or kernel series that no longer receive updates, vendor kernels on appliances that are not updated through the normal package channels, and live patching that covers only some flaws. The weakness is identified by comparing the running kernel (uname -r) with the distribution's security advisories, through an authenticated vulnerability scan, or with tools such as linux-exploit-suggester. Findings are confirmed against the vendor's advisories, because distributions often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.
entries.impact: Any user who can run code on the host, including through a compromised web application, service account or container, can become root and take full control of it: reading and changing all data, harvesting credentials and keys, installing persistence such as malicious kernel modules, and disabling security tools and logging. Because containers share the host's kernel, some of these flaws can also be used to escape from a container to the host. Exploitation needs the ability to run code locally, which is why the issue is usually rated high rather than critical, but reliable public exploits make it straightforward once that is obtained.
entries.remediation:
Install the distribution's kernel security updates and make sure the patched kernel is the one running:

  • Update the kernel package through the distribution's package manager, such as apt, dnf or zypper, and restart the host so that the new kernel is loaded. Check afterwards that uname -r reports the patched version.
  • Schedule regular maintenance windows for kernel updates and restarts, and report hosts whose running kernel is older than the newest installed one, for example with needs-restarting -r on Red Hat based systems or the /var/run/reboot-required file on Ubuntu.
  • Where restarts must be rare, use the vendor's live patching service, such as Ubuntu Livepatch, Red Hat kpatch or SUSE Live Patching, as an interim measure, while still restarting into fully updated kernels periodically.
  • Replace distributions and kernel series that no longer receive security updates.
  • Reduce exposure while patching: restrict shell access and local code execution to those who need it, keep containers unprivileged, and consider restricting unprivileged user namespaces, which many recent kernel exploits rely on, where applications do not need them (for example through the user.max_user_namespaces sysctl or the distribution's own controls).
  • Prioritise flaws listed in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.

Confirm the fix by checking the running kernel version against the vendor's advisories and repeating the vulnerability scan.

entries.title: NFS Export With no_root_squash
entries.summary: An NFS export is configured with no_root_squash, so root on any permitted client has root access to the exported files and can plant set-user-ID executables.
entries.description:
By default, an NFS server maps requests made by the root user (user ID 0) on a client to an unprivileged anonymous user, usually nobody, a behaviour known as root squashing. The no_root_squash option in /etc/exports turns this off for an export, so root on a client is treated as root on the exported file system. With the usual sec=sys (AUTH_SYS) security, the server trusts the user ID that the client sends, so anyone with root on a machine the export permits, which may be a machine of their own on a permitted network, can act as root on the export.

The option is often set so that administration, backups or hypervisors using the export as a datastore work, and is found on Linux NFS servers and storage appliances. It is identified by reviewing /etc/exports or the output of exportfs -v on the server, or from a permitted client by mounting the export as root and checking whether files created there remain owned by root, and whether root-owned files with restrictive permissions can be read. Exports open to any host are reported separately; this finding concerns the squashing of root.
entries.impact: An attacker with root on a permitted client can read, change and delete every file on the export regardless of its permissions, including other users' data, SSH keys and configuration files. They can also place a root-owned executable with the set-user-ID bit on the export: any user who can run it on the NFS server, where the export is a local file system, or on another client that mounts the export without the nosuid option, gains root on that host. A low-privileged foothold on such a host is therefore enough to become root. Where the export holds home directories, system files or virtual machine images, the result can be full compromise of the server and its clients.
entries.remediation:
Restore root squashing and limit which clients can mount the export:

  • Remove no_root_squash from the export's options in /etc/exports so that the default root_squash applies, or state root_squash explicitly, and apply the change with exportfs -ra. Consider all_squash for exports that only need anonymous or single-account access.
  • Where one client genuinely needs root access, such as a backup server or a hypervisor, allow no_root_squash only for that client's specific address in its own export entry, never for a network range or wildcard, and keep that traffic on a dedicated, segregated storage network.
  • Restrict every export to the specific hosts that need it, and export read-only (ro) where clients only need to read.
  • Mount NFS exports on clients with the nosuid and nodev options.
  • Where clients cannot be trusted to assert user identities, use Kerberos security (sec=krb5, krb5i or krb5p) so that access depends on authenticated users rather than on the user ID the client sends.
  • Search exports that had the option for unexpected set-user-ID files and for changes to sensitive files, since they may already have been abused.

Confirm the fix with exportfs -v on the server, and from a permitted client by checking that a file created as root on the export is owned by the anonymous user.

entries.title: Users in the docker Group
entries.summary: Accounts in the docker group can control the Docker daemon, which runs as root, and so can gain full root access to the host without a password.
entries.description:
On Linux, the Docker daemon (dockerd) normally runs as root and takes commands through the Unix socket /var/run/docker.sock, which is owned by root and the docker group. Adding a user to the docker group, which Docker's installation guidance offers as a way to run Docker commands without sudo, gives that user full control of the daemon. Docker's own documentation states that only trusted users should be allowed to control the daemon, and that the docker group grants root-level privileges.

Control of the daemon amounts to control of the host, because a member can start a container that mounts the host's root file system, runs in privileged mode or shares the host's process and network namespaces, and then change any file on the host from inside it. The same applies to any account or service that can write to the Docker socket, and to the equivalent sockets of other container engines running as root, such as rootful Podman's API socket or containerd's socket. The weakness is identified by listing the group's members (getent group docker) and checking the socket's permissions; it is often found on build servers, developer machines and hosts where an application or monitoring agent was given access to Docker. A socket mounted into a container, and a daemon API exposed over the network, are reported separately.
entries.impact: Any member of the group, or an attacker who compromises a member's account or a process running as it, can become root on the host with a single command, without a password and without exploiting any vulnerability, for example by running a container that mounts the host's / directory. From there they have full control of the host and its data, and of every container on it, including the secrets and credentials those containers hold. Group membership is also easy to overlook in access reviews, because it does not appear among the host's administrative accounts or sudo rules.
entries.remediation:
Treat membership of the docker group as equivalent to root, and limit it accordingly:

  • Remove every account that does not need to administer Docker from the group (for example with gpasswd -d), and keep the remaining members to administrators who would be trusted with root.
  • Where users need to run containers without administering the host, use Docker in rootless mode or rootless Podman, so that the daemon and containers run under the user's own account rather than as root.
  • Do not give applications, monitoring agents or CI runners access to the Docker socket unless they are trusted with root; where they need only some information, put a proxy in front of the socket that allows only the API calls they need.
  • Keep the socket owned by root and the docker group with mode 660, and monitor changes to the group's membership and the use of privileged containers and host mounts, for example with audit rules on the socket and the Docker binaries.
  • Where finer control is needed over which Docker API requests a user may make, use an authorisation plugin for the daemon.

Confirm the fix with getent group docker, and by checking as a former member that Docker commands are refused.

entries.title: Unprotected or Shared SSH Private Keys
entries.summary: SSH private keys are readable by others, have no passphrase, or are shared between people or systems, so anyone with a copy can log in wherever the key is trusted.
entries.description:
An SSH private key is a credential: whoever holds it can authenticate to every system that lists the matching public key in an authorized_keys file. The weakness covers keys that are not adequately protected or controlled. Keys may be stored without a passphrase, so that the file alone is enough to log in; kept with permissions that let other users read them, or copied into backups, shared drives, source code repositories, container images or virtual machine templates; or shared, with one key pair used by several administrators, or copied to many hosts and service accounts so that one key opens many systems.

It is identified during host reviews and after gaining access to a system, by searching for private key files, such as id_rsa, id_ecdsa and id_ed25519, PuTTY .ppk files, and files containing a BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY or similar header, and checking their permissions; by testing whether a key found is encrypted, for example with ssh-keygen -y -f, which asks for a passphrase only when the key has one; and by comparing authorized_keys entries across hosts to find keys that are reused or belong to people who have left.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains a usable copy of a key can log in as the key's account to every system that trusts it, without a password, and their access looks like that of the legitimate user. Keys belonging to root, administrators, deployment systems or service accounts often give privileged access to many servers at once, which makes them a common route for moving across Linux and Unix estates. A key without a passphrase can be used immediately, and one with a weak passphrase can be cracked offline. Shared keys also prevent the organisation from attributing actions to individuals or revoking one person's access without affecting others, and because plain SSH keys do not expire, they often remain trusted long after the person or system that needed them has gone.
entries.remediation:
Protect each private key, give every person and system its own, and control where keys are trusted:

  • Restrict private key files to their owner (chmod 600, in a ~/.ssh directory with mode 700) and remove keys from shared locations, readable backups, repositories, images and templates. Treat any key found in such a place as compromised: remove its public key from every authorized_keys file and issue a new key pair.
  • Protect interactive users' keys with a strong passphrase (ssh-keygen -p adds one to an existing key) and use ssh-agent so that it is not typed for every connection. Better still, keep keys on hardware security keys, using the ed25519-sk or ecdsa-sk key types, or on smart cards, so that the private key cannot be copied.
  • Give every administrator their own key and named account, and every automated process its own key, restricted in authorized_keys with options such as from=, command= and restrict.
  • Keep an inventory of trusted keys, review authorized_keys files regularly and remove the keys of leavers and retired systems. Consider an SSH certificate authority, which issues short-lived certificates instead of permanent keys and removes the need to distribute authorized_keys files.
  • Where users should not add their own keys, set AuthorizedKeysFile to a root-owned location.

Confirm the fix by repeating the search for private keys, checking that those found are protected, and checking that keys exposed earlier no longer grant access.

entries.title: Missing Microsoft Windows Security Updates
entries.summary: Windows hosts are missing security updates that Microsoft has released, leaving known and often actively exploited operating system vulnerabilities unfixed.
entries.description:
One or more Windows hosts have not installed security updates that Microsoft has already released. Microsoft publishes Windows security fixes on the second Tuesday of each month, and for current Windows releases each monthly update is cumulative, so a host that has missed one update usually lacks every fix released since it was last updated. The fixes typically address remote code execution in network-facing components, elevation of privilege flaws that let a standard user or service account gain SYSTEM rights, and weaknesses in authentication and cryptographic components.

The condition is usually identified by an authenticated vulnerability scan, which reads the installed updates and file versions on each host and reports one result for each missing update or advisory, so a single host several months behind can produce dozens of results with one cause. Unauthenticated scans infer missing updates from the behaviour of exposed services and are less reliable. Results can be confirmed from the host's update history or with Get-HotFix.

Some fixes are shipped disabled and take effect only once a registry value is set, as with the signature padding check for CVE-2013-3900 (EnableCertPaddingCheck); scanners report these as missing even on fully updated hosts until the setting is applied. Hosts usually fall behind because they are outside the scope of the update management tool, their Windows Update agent is failing, or a deferral or exclusion was never removed.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach a host with missing updates can use published exploits for the unfixed vulnerabilities. Depending on which updates are missing, this can mean running code on the host remotely without credentials, or a standard user, or malware running as one, gaining full administrative control of the host and harvesting the credentials stored on it for lateral movement. Windows vulnerabilities are among the most numerous in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, and exploits for many of them are built into commodity attack tools and ransomware. The risk is greatest for domain controllers, internet-facing servers and hosts used by many people, and grows the longer updates are outstanding. Network restrictions and endpoint protection may block particular exploits but do not remove the vulnerabilities.
entries.remediation:
Bring every host up to date and keep it there:

  • Install the latest cumulative security update on each affected host, with any servicing stack update Microsoft lists as a prerequisite, and restart the host so that the update takes effect. Microsoft's Security Update Guide lists each update and the CVEs it fixes.
  • Find out why each host fell behind, for example a failing Windows Update agent, a host missing from the scope of WSUS, Configuration Manager, Intune or Windows Update for Business, or a pause or deferral that was never lifted, and correct the cause rather than updating the host once by hand.
  • Apply any registry or configuration change that an advisory requires before its fix is active, and add it to the build standard so that new hosts receive it.
  • Run a patch management process with defined timescales, for example installing high and critical updates within 14 days of release as Cyber Essentials requires, sooner for vulnerabilities that are being exploited or are listed in the KEV catalogue, and report on hosts that are not current.

Where a host cannot be updated promptly, restrict its network exposure to the systems that need it, disable services and features it does not use, and monitor it closely until the update is installed. Confirm the fix by repeating the authenticated scan and checking that each host reports the current cumulative update.

patterns.re: ^KB\d{6,7}:|^MS\d{2}-\d{3}:|\bMicrosoft Windows\b.*\b(Security Update|Cumulative Update|Multiple Vulnerabilities|Remote Code Execution|Elevation of Privilege)\b|\bSecurity Updates? for (Microsoft )?Windows\b|\bWindows (10|11|Server \d{4})\b.*\b(Security Update|Cumulative Update)\b

entries.title: Unsupported Windows Operating System
entries.summary: Hosts run a Windows release that Microsoft no longer supports, so vulnerabilities discovered in it are never fixed.
entries.description:
One or more hosts run a release or edition of Windows that has passed the end of its support lifecycle. Once a release reaches end of support, Microsoft stops publishing security updates for it, except to organisations that pay for Extended Security Updates (ESU) where Microsoft offers them for that release. Every vulnerability found in Windows after that date remains unfixed on these hosts, and because later releases share much of the same code, the details published with each monthly update for supported releases often show attackers where the unsupported release is also vulnerable.

Unsupported hosts are identified from the operating system version reported by authenticated scans, by fingerprinting SMB, RDP and other services during unauthenticated scans, and from Active Directory, whose computer objects record the operating system of every domain-joined host. Such hosts usually also lack updates released before the end of support, and they lack security features that later releases enable by default.

Common causes are servers hosting a legacy application that has not been migrated, specialist equipment controlled by an embedded Windows computer, such as laboratory, manufacturing or medical devices, and hosts left running after a migration. Hosts covered by a current ESU subscription still receive security updates for its term, which should be checked before the finding is reported.
entries.impact: An unsupported host is permanently exposed to every Windows vulnerability disclosed after its end of support, including remotely exploitable flaws in network services and privilege escalation flaws that turn any foothold into full control of the host. An attacker on the same network can often compromise such a host with public exploit code and no credentials, then use it as a base for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Because no fix will be released, the exposure grows over time, and current security products may also stop supporting the platform. The impact is greatest where the host holds sensitive data, is reachable from untrusted networks, or is trusted by other systems.
entries.remediation:
Remove unsupported Windows releases from the estate:

  • Upgrade or replace each affected host with a supported Windows release, migrating the application or function it provides. Use Microsoft's lifecycle pages to confirm support dates and plan future migrations well before the next end-of-support date.
  • Where a migration cannot be completed before support ends, subscribe to Extended Security Updates where Microsoft offers them for that release and install the ESU updates every month. ESU is time-limited and buys time to migrate; it is not a replacement for migration.
  • For a host that must remain, such as one that controls specialist equipment, isolate it: place it in its own network segment, allow only the connections it needs, block internet access, email and web browsing from it, disable unused services and monitor it closely, as the NCSC's guidance on obsolete products describes.
  • Record each remaining unsupported host as an accepted risk with an owner and a replacement date, and review the decision regularly.

Confirm the fix by checking the operating system version of each host in a new authenticated scan and in Active Directory.

patterns.re: \b(Microsoft )?Windows (Server )?(2000|2003|2008( R2)?|2012( R2)?|XP|Vista|7|8\.1|8|10)\b.*\b(Unsupported|End of Life|SEoL|EOL|no longer supported)\b|\bUnsupported Windows OS\b|\bMicrosoft Windows\b.*\bSEoL\b

entries.title: Missing Linux Package Security Updates
entries.summary: Linux hosts have not installed security updates from their distribution, leaving known vulnerabilities in the kernel and installed packages unfixed.
entries.description:
One or more Linux hosts have outstanding security updates from their distribution's repositories. Distributions such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian, Ubuntu and SUSE publish fixed packages, with security advisories listing the CVEs each update fixes, for the kernel, the C library, OpenSSH, sudo, polkit, OpenSSL and the many other packages a host runs. The updates still have to be installed on each host, and a kernel update has no effect until the host is restarted or live-patched.

The finding is normally identified by an authenticated scan that compares installed package versions with the distribution's advisories, or locally with commands such as dnf updateinfo list --security, apt list --upgradable or zypper list-patches --category security. Scanners report one result per advisory, so a host that has not been updated for some months can produce many results with a single cause. Unauthenticated scans that judge vulnerability from the version a service announces are unreliable on Linux, because distributions backport security fixes into the versions they ship without changing the upstream version number; such results should be confirmed against the distribution's own advisory or the package changelog.

A common variant is a host whose packages are current but which is still running an older kernel because it has not been restarted since the update was installed.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains a foothold on the host, for example through a web application flaw or a stolen low-privileged account, can use public exploits for unpatched local vulnerabilities to gain root access; the polkit pkexec flaw CVE-2021-4034, for instance, gave any local user root on most distributions with a reliable public exploit. Missing updates to network-facing packages can also allow remote compromise or denial of service without credentials. Root access exposes all data, keys and credentials on the host and supports persistence and lateral movement. The risk is highest for internet-facing hosts and hosts shared by many users or services, and lower where the outstanding updates affect packages that are installed but not used.
entries.remediation:
Install the outstanding updates and keep hosts current:

  • Apply all security updates from the distribution's repositories using its package manager or the organisation's patch management tooling, for example dnf upgrade --security on Red Hat-based distributions or apt upgrade on Debian-based ones. Then restart services that use updated libraries, and reboot hosts that received a kernel update or apply it with a supported live-patching service.
  • Automate security updates where the service allows it, for example with unattended-upgrades on Debian and Ubuntu or dnf-automatic on Red Hat-based distributions, and patch other hosts within defined timescales, sooner for vulnerabilities that are being exploited.
  • Check that each host is subscribed to the correct repositories, including the distribution's security repository and any paid extended maintenance channel, and that internal mirrors are synchronised.
  • Remove packages that are not needed, which reduces both the attack surface and the volume of future updates.

Confirm the fix by repeating the authenticated scan and checking that the running kernel (uname -r) matches the latest installed kernel.

families.family: (Ubuntu|Debian|Red Hat|CentOS|Oracle Linux|Amazon Linux|SuSE|Fedora|Alma Linux|Rocky Linux|Alpine Linux|Scientific Linux|Gentoo|Slackware|Virtuozzo|Photon OS|Mandriva) Local Security Checks$

entries.title: Unsupported Linux Distribution
entries.summary: Hosts run a Linux distribution release that no longer receives security updates, so vulnerabilities in its kernel and packages will not be fixed.
entries.description:
One or more hosts run a Linux distribution release that has reached the end of its security support. Each distribution publishes a lifecycle for its releases: Red Hat Enterprise Linux and SUSE Linux Enterprise offer long support periods with paid extensions, Ubuntu LTS releases receive standard security maintenance followed by optional Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro, and Debian releases are followed by a period of Long Term Support. Once a release falls outside every support period available to the organisation, no further fixed packages are published, and vulnerabilities in the kernel and every installed package accumulate.

The finding is identified from /etc/os-release or equivalent files during authenticated scans, or from service banners and package versions that reveal the release during unauthenticated ones. Hosts on an unsupported release usually also lack the last updates published before support ended, and their repositories may have moved to archive servers, which breaks routine updating. Interim releases with short support periods, such as non-LTS Ubuntu releases and Fedora, become unsupported quickly and are a common cause, as are appliances and container images built on an old base.

Where the organisation holds a paid extended support subscription for the release, the host may still be receiving fixes; this should be confirmed before the finding is reported.
entries.impact: An unsupported release leaves every vulnerability disclosed after its end of support permanently unfixed. Over time this typically includes local privilege escalation flaws in the kernel and system utilities, which let any foothold become root access, and flaws in network-facing packages such as OpenSSH, web servers and the C library, which can allow remote compromise or denial of service. Exploits for many such flaws are public. Root access exposes all data and credentials on the host and makes it a base for lateral movement. The exposure only grows with time, and current releases of security tools and applications may stop installing on the platform.
entries.remediation:
Move each affected host to a supported release:

  • Upgrade in place using the distribution's supported upgrade path, such as do-release-upgrade on Ubuntu or leapp on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, or rebuild the host on a supported release and migrate its applications and data, testing the applications first.
  • Where a migration cannot be completed in time, buy the distribution's extended support offering, such as Ubuntu Pro Expanded Security Maintenance or Red Hat's Extended Life Cycle Support, and confirm that the host is receiving updates from it.
  • For a host that must stay on an unsupported release, isolate it in its own network segment, allow only the connections it needs, remove unnecessary packages and services, and monitor it closely, recording the risk with an owner and a replacement date.
  • Track the end-of-support dates of every release in use, rebuild container images and appliances on supported bases, and plan upgrades well before support ends.

Confirm the fix by checking /etc/os-release on each host and repeating the authenticated scan.

patterns.re: \bUnix Operating System Unsupported Version Detection\b|\b(Ubuntu|Debian|CentOS|Red Hat Enterprise Linux|RHEL|SUSE|SLES|Fedora|Oracle Linux|Amazon Linux|Alpine|FreeBSD)\b.*\b(Unsupported|End of Life|SEoL|EOL|no longer supported)\b

entries.title: Unsupported Software Version in Use
entries.summary: A product is running a release that its vendor or project no longer supports, so vulnerabilities found in it will not be fixed.
entries.description:
One or more systems run a release of an application, server product, framework or runtime that its vendor or open-source project no longer supports. Most vendors support each release line, major version or branch for a published period and then stop issuing security fixes for it, and many open-source projects support only their most recent branches. An unsupported release receives no fixes for vulnerabilities disclosed after its end of support, and advisories for newer releases frequently describe flaws that also exist in the unsupported release but will never be fixed there.

The finding is usually identified from the version a service announces in its banner or headers, from installed software inventories during authenticated scans, or from files on disk, compared with the vendor's published end-of-life dates, and scanners typically report it as a single result per product. Version detection should be confirmed where possible, because some vendors and Linux distributions continue to support an old version under their own long-term support arrangements, and a paid extended support contract may also cover the release.

Typical examples are web and application servers, databases, programming language runtimes, content management systems, management agents and appliance software left on a release line that has reached end of life.
entries.impact: Every vulnerability disclosed in the product after its end of support remains permanently exploitable, and advisories for supported releases give attackers a ready list of flaws to try. Depending on the product and its exposure, this can lead to remote code execution, data theft or denial of service, frequently without authentication where the service faces the internet. Unsupported releases are also excluded from vendor assistance during an incident and may not run on supported operating systems, which can hold back the wider estate. The risk rises with internet exposure, the sensitivity of the data the product handles and the time since support ended.
entries.remediation:
Move to a supported release and keep track of support dates:

  • Upgrade the product to a release line that its vendor currently supports, following the vendor's upgrade path and testing dependent applications first. Where the product has been abandoned, replace it with a maintained alternative.
  • Where an upgrade cannot be completed promptly, obtain extended security support from the vendor or a reputable third party if available, and confirm that its fixes are being installed.
  • Reduce exposure in the meantime: restrict network access to the product to the users and systems that need it, remove it from the internet where possible, disable unused features, and monitor it for signs of attack. A web application firewall or intrusion prevention rule can block known exploits for some flaws but is not a fix.
  • Maintain a software inventory that records each product's version and end-of-support date, review it regularly, and budget for upgrades before support ends.

Confirm the fix by checking the version reported by the product and repeating the scan.

entries.title: Outdated OpenSSH
entries.summary: The SSH service runs an OpenSSH release that is missing published security fixes.
entries.description:
The SSH service runs a release of OpenSSH that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities. OpenSSH flaws fixed over the years include a signal handler race in the server that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution as root on glibc-based Linux systems (CVE-2024-6387, known as regreSSHion), username enumeration, denial of service, and flaws in the client, ssh-agent and scp that matter where the host is also used to connect to other systems. Many of these issues apply only with particular configurations or platforms.

The finding is normally raised from the version string the server sends at the start of every connection, such as SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_ followed by a version and often a distribution package suffix, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. This method is unreliable for OpenSSH supplied by Linux distributions and BSDs, which backport security fixes without changing the upstream version number, so a server announcing an old version may be fully patched. Results should therefore be confirmed against the distribution's own advisories or package changelog, or by an authenticated check of the installed package. Builds embedded in appliances and network devices are updated by the device vendor and follow its advisories.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the vulnerabilities actually present.
