Most published OpenSSH flaws allow information disclosure such as username enumeration, denial of service, or attacks that need a non-default configuration or a user connecting to a malicious server. The most serious, such as CVE-2024-6387, allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code as root, although exploiting that flaw requires many connection attempts over an extended period. SSH services exposed to the internet or to untrusted networks are the most at risk, and restricting access to SSH considerably reduces the likelihood of exploitation.
entries.remediation:
Update OpenSSH through the source it was installed from:

  • On Linux and BSD hosts, install the latest OpenSSH package from the distribution's security updates and restart the sshd service. Do not replace a distribution package with a source build just to satisfy a version check, as this removes the host from the distribution's future updates.
  • Where OpenSSH was built from source, upgrade to the current upstream release from the OpenSSH project and rebuild it with the same configuration. On appliances and network devices, apply the vendor's software update.
  • Restrict access to SSH with firewall rules or an allowlist of management networks, avoid exposing it directly to the internet, and use key-based authentication.
  • Use configuration workarounds published for a specific advisory only as a temporary measure and with their side effects understood; for example, setting LoginGraceTime 0 prevents code execution through CVE-2024-6387 but leaves the server open to connection exhaustion.

Confirm the fix by checking the installed package against the distribution's advisory for each reported CVE, or by checking the announced version where OpenSSH was built from source.

patterns.re: ^OpenSSH\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bregreSSHion\b|CVE-2024-6387

entries.title: Outdated Apache HTTP Server
entries.summary: The web server runs an Apache HTTP Server release that is missing published security fixes.
entries.description:
The web server runs a release of Apache HTTP Server (httpd) that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities. The Apache project's security pages list each flaw, its severity and the release that fixes it. Past issues include path traversal that allowed files outside the document root to be read and, where CGI was enabled, code to be run (CVE-2021-41773 and its incomplete fix), server-side request forgery and request smuggling through mod_proxy, flaws in mod_rewrite, mod_lua and the HTTP/2 module, and denial of service. Many apply only when a particular module or configuration is in use.

The finding is usually raised from the version in the Server response header or on default error pages, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. Linux distributions such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Debian backport security fixes into the httpd version they ship without changing its version number, so a server announcing an old version may be fully patched; results should be confirmed against the distribution's advisories or, better, by an authenticated check of the installed package. Apache httpd is also embedded in other products, such as management consoles and appliances, where it is updated by the product's vendor.
entries.impact: An attacker can use public exploits for the unfixed vulnerabilities against the web server, which is usually internet-facing. Depending on the flaws and the modules in use, this can allow files outside the web root to be read, code to be run on the server, requests to be smuggled past front-end controls, internal systems to be reached through the proxy, or the service to be taken offline. Several httpd vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-41773, have been widely exploited and are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. Code execution runs with the privileges of the httpd worker account, so a hardened configuration and least privilege limit the impact but do not remove it.
entries.remediation:
Update httpd through the channel it was installed from:

  • Where httpd comes from the operating system, install the distribution's latest httpd or apache2 package and restart the service. Do not replace it with a source build just to satisfy a version check.
  • Where it was built from source or comes from a third-party package, upgrade to the current release of a supported branch from the Apache HTTP Server project, review the changes affecting the modules in use, and restart. Where httpd is embedded in another product, apply that vendor's update.
  • Disable modules that are not needed, such as mod_proxy, mod_cgi and mod_lua, and keep Require all denied on the filesystem root directory, which limited the impact of past path traversal flaws.
  • Set ServerTokens Prod and ServerSignature Off to stop the version being advertised; this hides the version but does not fix anything.
  • Subscribe to the Apache httpd announcements or the distribution's security notices so that future fixes are applied promptly.

Where an update must wait, a web application firewall rule can block known exploit patterns for a specific advisory as an interim measure. Confirm the fix by checking the installed package or the version reported by httpd -v or apache2ctl -v against the advisories.

patterns.re: ^Apache (HTTP Server|httpd|2\.\d)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bApache HTTP Server\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated nginx
entries.summary: The web server or reverse proxy runs an nginx release that is missing published security fixes.
entries.description:
The web server or reverse proxy runs a release of nginx that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities. The nginx project lists each advisory with the vulnerable and fixed versions and its own severity rating. Most nginx advisories affect particular modules or features rather than the core server, for example the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 implementations, the mp4 module, the DNS resolver, the mail proxy and SSL session handling, and they typically allow a worker process to be crashed, fragments of memory to be disclosed or, less often, memory to be corrupted. Whether an advisory applies therefore depends on the modules built in and the configuration.

The finding is usually raised from the version in the Server header or on default error pages, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version, without checking whether the affected module is enabled. Linux distributions backport fixes into the nginx version they ship without changing the version number, so results should be confirmed against the distribution's advisories or an authenticated check of the installed package. nginx is also embedded in many products, such as Kubernetes ingress controllers, load balancers and appliances, which are updated by their vendors.
entries.impact: An attacker who can send requests to the server can exploit unfixed flaws in the modules in use. The usual result is denial of service, as crafted requests repeatedly crash worker processes, or the disclosure of fragments of worker memory that may contain other users' data or headers. A small number of flaws, such as memory corruption in the resolver, could in principle allow code execution with the worker's privileges, although this has rarely been demonstrated. Where nginx fronts many applications, an outage affects all of them. The risk is low where the affected modules are not enabled.
entries.remediation:
Update nginx through the channel it was installed from:

  • Where nginx comes from the operating system, install the distribution's latest nginx package and reload or restart the service.
  • Where it comes from the nginx project's own packages or a source build, upgrade to the current stable or mainline release, rebuilding any third-party modules against it.
  • Where nginx is part of another product, such as an ingress controller or appliance, apply that product's update.
  • Disable modules and features that are not needed, such as HTTP/3, the mail proxy or mp4, and set server_tokens off; to stop the version being advertised; hiding the version does not fix anything.
  • Where an advisory gives a configuration workaround, such as disabling an affected feature, apply it until the update can be installed.

Confirm the fix with nginx -v or the installed package version, checked against the advisory for each reported CVE.

patterns.re: ^nginx\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated PHP
entries.summary: A web server runs a PHP release that is missing security fixes or belongs to a branch that no longer receives them.
entries.description:
A web server runs a release of PHP that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a release branch that has reached end of life. The PHP project supports each release branch with bug and security fixes for two years, then with fixes for critical security issues only for a further two years, after which the branch receives no fixes at all. Past PHP vulnerabilities include memory corruption in built-in functions and extensions, a flaw in the FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM) that allowed remote code execution in some configurations (CVE-2019-11043), and argument injection in PHP-CGI on Windows (CVE-2024-4577); both of these were widely exploited.

The finding is usually raised from the X-Powered-By header, error pages or exposed phpinfo() output, or from installed packages in an authenticated scan, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. Linux distributions backport fixes into the PHP version they ship without changing its version number, and some keep branches that the PHP project has retired supported for the life of their own release, so results should be confirmed against the distribution's advisories. Many PHP flaws are reachable only when the application passes attacker-controlled data to the affected function, while others, such as those in PHP-FPM and PHP-CGI, depend on how PHP is connected to the web server.
entries.impact: Depending on the vulnerabilities present and how the application uses PHP, an attacker may be able to run code on the web server, read files or memory, or cause denial of service. Flaws in PHP-FPM and PHP-CGI can be exploited directly over HTTP without any weakness in the application, and both CVE-2019-11043 and CVE-2024-4577 are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. Code execution runs with the privileges of the PHP or web server account and typically exposes the application's source code, configuration secrets such as database credentials, and the data it handles. On a branch that has reached end of life, newly found flaws will remain unfixed.
entries.remediation:
Move to a supported, current PHP release:

  • Upgrade to the latest release of a PHP branch that is still supported, as listed by the PHP project, or install the distribution's latest PHP packages where PHP comes from the operating system. Test the application first, as moving between branches can remove deprecated functions.
  • Where the application cannot yet run on a supported branch, use a distribution or vendor that still provides security fixes for the branch in use, and plan the code changes needed to upgrade.
  • Run PHP through PHP-FPM or the web server's PHP module rather than as a CGI binary, and keep the web server's PHP handler configuration in line with the PHP and web server documentation.
  • Set expose_php = Off in php.ini to remove the X-Powered-By header, and remove any phpinfo() pages; this hides the version but does not fix anything.

Confirm the fix by checking the version with php -v and the version the web server actually uses, which can differ where several PHP versions are installed, then repeat the scan.

patterns.re: ^PHP\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bPHP (Unsupported|end of life)|^PHP\b.*(argument injection|CVE-\d)

entries.title: Outdated OpenSSL
entries.summary: A service or application uses an OpenSSL release that is missing security fixes or belongs to a series that is no longer supported.
entries.description:
A service or application uses a release of the OpenSSL cryptographic library that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a release series that the OpenSSL project no longer supports. OpenSSL implements TLS and other cryptography for web servers, mail servers, VPNs and a great many applications, so its flaws are often reachable by anyone who can open a connection. The project rates each issue from Low to Critical. Most recent issues allow denial of service, such as the infinite loop in certificate parsing tracked as CVE-2022-0778, while others have allowed process memory to be read or, rarely, corrupted.

The finding is raised from version strings, such as the OpenSSL version that some web servers include in their Server header, from installed packages in authenticated scans, or from library files bundled with applications, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. Linux distributions backport OpenSSL fixes without changing the version number and continue to support series that the OpenSSL project has retired, so results based on the version alone should be confirmed against the distribution's advisories. Applications that bundle their own copy of OpenSSL, including many on Windows, are not updated by the operating system and are a common source of genuine findings.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the vulnerabilities present and how the library is used. Most allow an unauthenticated attacker to crash a service or tie up its processor during the TLS handshake or certificate processing, causing denial of service. Some have allowed fragments of process memory, which can contain private keys, session data or credentials, to be read, as Heartbleed did, and a few have allowed memory corruption that could lead to code execution. Because OpenSSL processes connections before any authentication takes place, every exposed TLS service is reachable by an attacker. Where the release series is no longer supported, newly found flaws will remain unfixed.
entries.remediation:
Update OpenSSL wherever it is present:

  • Where OpenSSL comes from the operating system, install the distribution's latest OpenSSL packages, then restart every service that loads the library, or reboot the host, so that no process keeps using the old copy in memory; tools such as needrestart on Debian-based systems and needs-restarting on Red Hat-based ones list the processes affected.
  • Where an application or appliance bundles its own copy of OpenSSL, apply the vendor's update, and ask the vendor for one where none exists.
  • Where OpenSSL is built from source or statically linked into in-house software, upgrade to the current release of a supported series, preferably a long-term support series, and rebuild the software that uses it.
  • Move off release series that the OpenSSL project no longer supports, unless the distribution or a paid extended support arrangement still provides fixes for them.

Confirm the fix with openssl version or the installed package version for system copies, and by checking the library version that each affected service actually loads, then repeat the scan.

patterns.re: ^OpenSSL\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Apache Tomcat
entries.summary: An application server runs an Apache Tomcat release that is missing security fixes or a major version that has reached end of life.
entries.description:
An application server runs a release of Apache Tomcat that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a major version that has reached end of life. The Tomcat project publishes a list of fixed vulnerabilities for each supported major version, linking each fix to its source change but never providing binary patches, so fixes are obtained by upgrading. Past Tomcat issues include file read and inclusion through the AJP connector (CVE-2020-1938, known as Ghostcat), code execution through JSP files (CVE-2017-12617) or session files (CVE-2025-24813) uploaded when the default servlet allowed writes, request smuggling, session fixation, information disclosure and denial of service. Many depend on a non-default configuration, such as an exposed AJP port, writes enabled on the default servlet or file-based session persistence.

The finding is usually raised from the version shown on default error pages, the default home page and the documentation and manager applications, or from an authenticated scan of the installation's files, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version, seldom checking the configuration it depends on. Tomcat packaged by Linux distributions may carry backported fixes without a version change, and Tomcat embedded in other products or in applications, such as Spring Boot applications, is updated through those products and their dependency management.
entries.impact: Depending on the vulnerabilities and the configuration, an attacker may be able to read application files and configuration, including credentials, run code on the server by uploading a JSP file or abusing session persistence, smuggle requests past front-end controls, or cause denial of service. Several of these flaws, including Ghostcat and CVE-2025-24813, are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. Code execution runs with the privileges of the account that runs Tomcat, which in poorly hardened installations is root or SYSTEM. The risk is greatest where Tomcat is internet-facing or its AJP connector or management applications are reachable from untrusted networks.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade Tomcat and remove risky configuration:

  • Upgrade to the latest release of a currently supported Tomcat major version, as listed by the Apache Tomcat project, migrating applications off any major version that has reached end of life. Where Tomcat comes from a distribution package, install its latest update; where it is embedded in an application, update the Tomcat dependency and rebuild.
  • Disable the AJP connector if it is not needed, or bind it to the loopback interface and set a secret on it, and never expose it to untrusted networks.
  • Keep the default servlet read-only, with its readonly parameter at the default of true, and remove the example, documentation, manager and host-manager applications from production or restrict them to administrators' networks.
  • Run Tomcat under a dedicated low-privileged account.

Confirm the fix by checking the version with the version.sh or version.bat script in the installation's bin directory, reviewing the configuration changes above, and repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \bApache Tomcat\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Apache Log4j Remote Code Execution (Log4Shell)
entries.summary: An application uses an Apache Log4j 2 version whose message lookups let anyone who can get text logged run code on the server (Log4Shell).
entries.description:
The application uses a version of the Apache Log4j 2 logging library (log4j-core) that is vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228, known as Log4Shell. Vulnerable versions evaluate lookup expressions found in logged data, including the jndi lookup. If attacker-supplied text that the application logs, such as a username, a search term or the User-Agent header, contains an expression beginning ${jndi:ldap:// followed by the address of a server the attacker controls, Log4j connects to that server, which can return a reference that makes the application load and run attacker-supplied Java code. Where the Java runtime blocks remote class loading, exploitation relies on classes already present in the application, which is often still possible. The first fix was incomplete in certain non-default configurations, which was tracked as CVE-2021-45046.

The vulnerability can be confirmed actively by placing a JNDI expression that points at a server the tester controls into headers, parameters and other inputs and watching for the resulting DNS or LDAP callback, which also reveals vulnerable systems further along the processing chain, such as log processors that handle the data later. It can be found passively by searching file systems for log4j-core JAR files, including copies nested inside WAR, EAR and fat JAR files, and through software composition analysis. Log4j is embedded in a very large number of commercial and open-source products, so vendor advisories must also be checked. The older, end-of-life Log4j 1.x branch is not affected by this flaw but has unfixed vulnerabilities of its own.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can get a string logged by a vulnerable application can typically run arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the application, gaining full control of its data and a foothold in the hosting environment. Exploitation needs only a single request and was automated by attackers within hours of disclosure; Log4Shell is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue and has been used to deploy ransomware, cryptocurrency miners and backdoors. Even where code execution is blocked, a lookup can leak environment variables, such as cloud credentials, through the DNS request. Internal systems that log data originating from the internet are as exposed as internet-facing ones.
entries.remediation:
Remove vulnerable Log4j 2 versions from every application:

  • Upgrade log4j-core to a release that the Apache Log4j security page lists as fixing both CVE-2021-44228 and CVE-2021-45046 for the Java version in use, rebuild and redeploy the application, and replace copies shaded or nested inside other archives.
  • For commercial and open-source products that embed Log4j, apply the vendor's fixed release or documented mitigation.
  • Where an upgrade cannot be made immediately, remove the JndiLookup class from the log4j-core JAR as an interim measure, as shown below. Setting log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups was found not to protect every configuration and should not be relied on.
  • Restrict outbound connections from servers to the internet, which blocks the LDAP and RMI callbacks that exploitation needs, and monitor DNS and proxy logs for jndi lookups.
  • Treat internet-facing systems that were vulnerable for any period as potentially compromised: review them for web shells, unexpected accounts and outbound connections, and rotate the credentials they held.
zip -q -d log4j-core-*.jar org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class

Confirm the fix by rescanning file systems for vulnerable log4j-core versions and repeating the callback test against every input that was affected.

entries.title: Outdated Microsoft SQL Server
entries.summary: A SQL Server instance is missing Microsoft security updates or runs a release that is out of support.
entries.description:
A Microsoft SQL Server instance has not had the security updates that Microsoft has released for it, or runs a release that has passed the end of its support. Microsoft services each supported SQL Server release through cumulative updates (CUs) and, where needed, general distribution release (GDR) security updates, and publishes the vulnerabilities each one fixes in its Security Update Guide. Past SQL Server vulnerabilities include remote code execution, elevation of privilege that lets a database user gain higher rights within the instance, and flaws in the client drivers and providers installed alongside it.

The finding is identified from the build number, which an authenticated scan reads from the installation and which can also be retrieved over the network from the instance's pre-login response or the SQL Server Browser service on UDP port 1434, compared with the build that includes each fix. Scanners report one result per missing update. Hosts often run several instances, or shared components such as client drivers, at different update levels, and SQL Server Express instances installed silently with third-party applications are a frequent source of findings because they sit outside normal database management.
entries.impact: An attacker with network access to the instance, typically holding a database login or able to reach it through an application, can use the unfixed vulnerabilities to escalate privileges within SQL Server, run code on the server, or crash the service. Elevated rights in SQL Server usually lead to operating system command execution, through features such as xp_cmdshell or SQL Server Agent jobs, with the rights of the service account, and to access to every database on the instance. The impact is greatest where the service runs as a privileged domain account or the instance holds sensitive data, and is reduced where network access to the instance is tightly restricted.
entries.remediation:
Apply Microsoft's updates and stay on a supported release:

  • Install the latest security update for the instance's release, choosing the cumulative update or GDR package according to the servicing path the instance is already on, as Microsoft's guidance explains, and restart the service. Update every instance on the host and the shared client components.
  • Opt in to Microsoft Update, or include SQL Server in WSUS or the organisation's patch management tool; SQL Server security updates are offered through Windows Update only when Microsoft Update is enabled.
  • Upgrade instances on releases that have passed end of support to a supported release, or obtain Extended Security Updates where Microsoft offers them.
  • Remove unused instances, run the service under a low-privileged account, keep xp_cmdshell disabled, and restrict access to the database port to the application servers and administrators that need it.

Confirm the fix by running SELECT @@VERSION; on each instance and comparing the build with the update that fixes each reported CVE.

patterns.re: \b(Microsoft )?SQL Server\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated MySQL or MariaDB
entries.summary: A MySQL or MariaDB server runs a release that is missing security fixes or is no longer supported.
entries.description:
A MySQL or MariaDB database server runs a release that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a release series that no longer receives fixes. Oracle publishes MySQL fixes in its quarterly Critical Patch Updates, which typically list many MySQL Server flaws, and MariaDB publishes the CVEs fixed in each of its releases. Most of these flaws let an authenticated user crash the server or make it hang, while a smaller number allow unauthorised reading or modification of data, privilege escalation, or exploitation of vulnerable components bundled with the server, such as its TLS library.

The finding is usually raised from the version string the server sends in its greeting before authentication, or from installed packages in an authenticated scan, and scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. Linux distributions backport fixes into the version they ship, so results based on the greeting alone should be confirmed against the distribution's advisories. Because Oracle's advisories describe each flaw only briefly, the privileges and server component needed to exploit each one should be checked before judging its relevance.
entries.impact: A user with a database account, including an application's own account if the application is compromised, can use the unfixed flaws to stop the database repeatedly, causing an outage for every application that relies on it. Some flaws allow such a user to read or change data beyond their privileges or to escalate to administrative rights. Very few MySQL or MariaDB vulnerabilities are exploitable without credentials, so the risk is considerably higher where the database port is exposed to untrusted networks or where weak or shared database credentials are in use. Where the release series is unsupported, the number of unfixed flaws grows over time.
entries.remediation:
Update the database server and limit who can reach it:

  • Install the latest release of the series in use, from Oracle or MariaDB, or the distribution's latest packages, following the vendor's upgrade notes, and restart the server. For MySQL, apply each quarterly Critical Patch Update promptly after its release.
  • Move release series that have reached end of life, as published by Oracle and the MariaDB project, to a supported series, testing applications first.
  • Restrict network access to the database port to the application servers and administrators that need it, and never expose it to the internet.
  • Give application accounts only the privileges they need, remove anonymous and unused accounts, and limit administrative accounts to local or management connections.

Confirm the fix by running SELECT VERSION(); and comparing the result with the fixed version for each reported CVE, or by checking the installed package against the distribution's advisories.

patterns.re: \b(Oracle MySQL|MySQL|MariaDB)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated PostgreSQL
entries.summary: A PostgreSQL server runs a minor release that is missing security fixes, or a major version that is no longer supported.
entries.description:
A PostgreSQL server runs a minor release that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a major version that has reached end of life. The PostgreSQL project supports each major version for five years and releases fixes, including security fixes, at least once every three months as minor releases, which it recommends always installing. Recent PostgreSQL vulnerabilities have mostly needed a database login and allowed privilege escalation, for example by causing a command run by a more privileged user to execute a less privileged user's code, along with SQL injection through the client library's quoting functions (CVE-2025-1094), bypasses of row security and disclosure of server memory.

The finding is identified from installed packages in an authenticated scan or with SELECT version();, as PostgreSQL reports its version only after authentication and unauthenticated scanners can infer it only approximately. Scanners report one result per advisory affecting that version. Linux distributions and managed database services backport or apply fixes on their own schedules, so results should be confirmed against the provider's advisories. Copies of PostgreSQL bundled with other products, and the libpq client library used by applications, also need updating.
entries.impact: A user with a database login can use the unfixed flaws to gain the privileges of another role, up to superuser, or to read data that row security should hide. A PostgreSQL superuser can run operating system commands as the database service account, for example with COPY ... TO PROGRAM, so privilege escalation within the database usually leads to control of the database host and every database on it. Few PostgreSQL flaws are exploitable without credentials, so the risk is greatest where untrusted users or compromised applications hold logins, or where the database port is reachable from untrusted networks. Unsupported major versions accumulate unfixed flaws over time.
entries.remediation:
Keep each server on the current minor release of a supported major version:

  • Install the latest minor release for the major version in use, from the PostgreSQL project's packages or the distribution, and restart the server. Minor releases do not need a dump and restore, but their release notes can list extra steps, such as rebuilding certain indexes, which should be followed.
  • Upgrade major versions that have reached end of life, using pg_upgrade or a dump and restore, after testing applications.
  • Update client libraries such as libpq on application servers, and apply the provider's maintenance updates for managed database services.
  • Restrict access with pg_hba.conf and network controls to the hosts and users that need it, avoid granting superuser rights or the ability to create objects in shared schemas to application and untrusted roles, and keep the number of superusers small.

Confirm the fix with SELECT version(); on each server, compared with the minor release that fixes each reported CVE.

patterns.re: \bPostgreSQL\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Microsoft Exchange Server
entries.summary: An on-premises Exchange server is missing Microsoft's security updates, runs a cumulative update too old to receive them, or runs an unsupported release.
entries.description:
An on-premises Microsoft Exchange Server is missing security updates (SUs) that Microsoft has released, runs a cumulative update (CU) too old to receive them, or runs an Exchange release that has passed the end of its support. Microsoft releases SUs only for the most recent one or two CUs of each release, so a server on an older CU cannot be secured until its CU is updated. Exchange servers are a frequent target because they are usually reachable from the internet through Outlook on the web, ActiveSync and Autodiscover, hold extensive rights in Active Directory, and store the organisation's email.

The finding is identified by an authenticated scan that reads the installed build, by Microsoft's Exchange Server Health Checker script, or remotely from the build number that Outlook on the web and other endpoints expose, and scanners report one result per missing update. Some updates also require manual steps after installation, such as enabling Extended Protection or applying configuration changes, which the Health Checker reports separately. Hybrid deployments often keep an on-premises Exchange server for recipient management, which also needs updating.
entries.impact: Unpatched Exchange servers have been mass-exploited repeatedly. Flaws such as ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855) and ProxyShell (CVE-2021-34473) let unauthenticated attackers on the internet run code on the server as SYSTEM, read any mailbox and install web shells, and are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. Because Exchange holds high privileges in Active Directory, compromise of the server commonly leads to compromise of the domain, alongside theft of the organisation's email. Several Exchange flaws have been exploited before a fix was released or within days of one, so any delay is particularly dangerous for internet-facing servers.
entries.remediation:
Bring every Exchange server to a supported, fully updated state:

  • Install the latest CU for the Exchange release in use, then the latest SU for that CU, on every Exchange server, including hybrid management servers, following Microsoft's update guidance.
  • Run the Exchange Server Health Checker after updating and complete any manual actions it reports, such as enabling Extended Protection.
  • Migrate servers running an Exchange release that has passed end of support to a supported release or to Exchange Online.
  • Limit internet exposure to the services users need, publish them through a pre-authenticating gateway where possible, and never expose remote PowerShell or the Exchange administration interfaces to the internet.
  • Where an update cannot be installed immediately, apply Microsoft's published mitigation for the specific vulnerability, which the Exchange Emergency Mitigation service can apply automatically on supported builds, and check the servers for indicators of compromise.

Confirm the fix by running the Health Checker and checking that each server reports the latest SU with no outstanding actions.

patterns.re: \bExchange Server\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bProxy(Logon|Shell|NotShell)\b|\bMicrosoft Exchange\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Microsoft SharePoint Server
entries.summary: An on-premises SharePoint Server farm is missing Microsoft's security updates or runs a release that is out of support.
entries.description:
An on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server farm has not installed the security updates Microsoft has released for it, or runs a SharePoint release that has passed the end of its support. Microsoft publishes SharePoint Server security updates monthly; they must be installed on every server in the farm and followed by the SharePoint Products Configuration Wizard or PSConfig, which upgrades the farm's databases. Past SharePoint vulnerabilities include remote code execution through unsafe deserialisation and server-side code injection, many of which need only an authenticated site user, and authentication bypass. In 2025 a deserialisation flaw that needed no authentication (CVE-2025-53770, part of the attacks known as ToolShell) was exploited against many internet-facing farms before a fix was available.

The finding is identified by an authenticated scan that reads the installed patch level, or from the farm's build number, which SharePoint returns in the MicrosoftSharePointTeamServices response header, compared with Microsoft's list of SharePoint updates, and scanners report one result per missing update. Servers on which updates were installed but the configuration wizard was not run can report inconsistent versions, and Central Administration shows the patch status of every server in the farm.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the farm, usually with any authenticated user account and sometimes with none, can use the unfixed flaws to run code on the SharePoint servers with the rights of the farm's service accounts. This gives access to every site and document in the farm and to its configuration, including the ASP.NET machine keys that protect its authentication data, which attackers have stolen in order to keep access after patching. SharePoint farms usually run under privileged service accounts in Active Directory, so compromise can extend into the domain. Internet-facing farms are at greatest risk, and CVE-2025-53770 is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue.
entries.remediation:
Bring the farm to a supported, fully updated state:

  • Install the latest security updates that Microsoft lists for the SharePoint release in use on every server in the farm, then run the SharePoint Products Configuration Wizard or PSConfig on each server.
  • Migrate farms running a SharePoint release that has passed end of support to a supported release or to SharePoint Online.
  • Enable the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) integration with a compatible anti-malware product, as Microsoft recommends, so that malicious requests can be detected and blocked.
  • After installing the fix for a vulnerability that was exploited, rotate the farm's ASP.NET machine keys with Set-SPMachineKey and Update-SPMachineKey and restart IIS on every server, as Microsoft advised for CVE-2025-53770, and check the servers for signs of compromise.
  • Avoid exposing the farm directly to the internet where external access is not needed, or publish it through an authenticating gateway.

Confirm the fix by checking product and patch installation status for every server in Central Administration and repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \bSharePoint\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Microsoft Office
entries.summary: Hosts run Microsoft Office builds that are missing security updates, or an Office release that is out of support.
entries.description:
Microsoft Office installations on one or more hosts are missing security updates, or are an Office release that has passed the end of its support. Microsoft releases Office security fixes monthly. Microsoft 365 Apps and recent volume-licensed Office releases are installed with Click-to-Run and update themselves from an update channel, such as Current Channel, Monthly Enterprise Channel or Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel, unless updates are disabled, deferred or pointed at an internal source that is not kept current. Older MSI-based releases receive updates through Microsoft Update or WSUS. Office vulnerabilities are mainly memory corruption and logic flaws triggered when a user opens, or in some cases previews, a crafted document, workbook, presentation or email.

The finding is identified by an authenticated scan that compares the installed Office build with the builds listed in Microsoft's security update notes, and scanners report one result per missing monthly update. Hosts on the Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel legitimately run older feature versions and should be compared with that channel's latest security build rather than with Current Channel. Office installations on terminal servers and virtual desktop hosts, and separately installed products such as Visio and Project, are commonly missed.
entries.impact: An attacker can send a crafted Office document by email or host it on a website and, if a user on an affected host opens it, run code with that user's privileges, gaining a foothold on the network. Office flaws are a long-standing phishing vector: the Equation Editor flaw CVE-2017-11882 was still used in malware campaigns years after its fix, and many Office vulnerabilities are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The impact rises where users have local administrator rights, and falls where macros and external content are restricted, Protected View is enforced, and attack surface reduction rules stop Office applications from creating child processes.
entries.remediation:
Keep every Office installation on a current, supported build:

  • For Click-to-Run installations, ensure automatic updates are enabled and come from a source that is kept current, such as Microsoft's content delivery network, Configuration Manager or Intune, and choose an update channel the organisation can keep up with; Monthly Enterprise Channel delivers one predictable update each month.
  • For MSI-based installations, enable Microsoft Update for other Microsoft products and approve Office security updates in WSUS or the patch management tool.
  • Migrate installations of Office releases that have reached end of support to a supported release.
  • Find hosts where updates have stalled, for example because Office has been left open for long periods or a Group Policy setting disables updates, and correct the cause.
  • Reduce the impact of future flaws by blocking macros in files from the internet, enforcing Protected View, and enabling attack surface reduction rules where Microsoft Defender is used.

Confirm the fix by checking the build under File, Account in an Office application or in the management tool's update compliance reports, and repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \b(Microsoft (Office|Word|Excel|PowerPoint|Outlook|Access|Visio|Project|Publisher|OneNote|365 Apps)|Office 365|Microsoft 365 Apps)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated .NET Framework or .NET Runtime
entries.summary: Hosts run .NET Framework or .NET runtimes that are missing Microsoft security updates or have reached end of support.
entries.description:
One or more hosts have .NET Framework or .NET (formerly .NET Core) runtimes that are missing security updates, or .NET runtimes from release lines that have passed the end of their support. .NET Framework is a component of Windows and receives monthly security updates through Windows Update and WSUS. .NET runtimes are installed separately and side by side, often several versions on one host, and each release line is supported for a fixed period; Microsoft releases their security updates on Patch Tuesday, and they reach hosts only if Microsoft Update or another deployment tool installs them. Applications published as self-contained carry their own copy of the runtime and are fixed only when the application is rebuilt.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans that read installed runtime and file versions, or with dotnet --list-runtimes, and scanners report one result per missing update or unsupported runtime. Old runtimes are often left behind after an application moves to a newer one and remain installed but unused. Past .NET vulnerabilities include remote code execution, denial of service and request smuggling in ASP.NET Core and its Kestrel web server, security feature bypass and elevation of privilege.
entries.impact: The impact depends on which runtime is affected and how it is used. Flaws in ASP.NET Core and the runtime libraries can let an unauthenticated attacker take down or, in some cases, compromise a web application running on the vulnerable runtime. Flaws in .NET Framework have allowed code execution when a user opens a crafted file, or elevation of privilege on the host. Runtimes that are installed but not used by any application present little direct risk, although they remain on the host and are reported by every scan. Release lines past end of support receive no further fixes.
entries.remediation:
Update the runtimes in use and remove the rest:

  • Install the latest .NET Framework updates through Windows Update, WSUS or the patch management tool as part of the monthly Windows update cycle.
  • Install the latest patch release for every supported .NET and ASP.NET Core runtime in use, and enable Microsoft Update or the organisation's deployment tooling so that future updates arrive automatically.
  • Move applications on release lines past end of support to a supported one, preferably a long-term support release, then uninstall the old runtimes.
  • Rebuild and redeploy self-contained applications and container images with the latest runtime patch.
  • Uninstall runtimes and SDKs that no application uses.

Confirm the fix with dotnet --list-runtimes and the host's update history, and by repeating the scan.

patterns.re: (\.NET (Framework|Core|\d)|\bASP\.NET Core\b|\.NET Runtime)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Web Browsers
entries.summary: Hosts run web browser versions that are missing security fixes, leaving users open to compromise from malicious or compromised websites.
entries.description:
One or more hosts run versions of Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox or other browsers that are missing security fixes. Browser vendors release security updates very frequently, weekly in Chrome's case, and many fix memory corruption in the rendering and JavaScript engines that can be triggered simply by visiting a web page. Several such flaws are exploited in the wild each year before or shortly after a fix is released. Browsers update themselves by default, but an update takes effect only when the browser restarts, and updating can be blocked by policy, by a broken update service, or by installations that the user cannot update.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans that read installed browser versions, by management tool inventories, or from the browser's About page, and scanners report one result per missing release. Common variants are browsers left open for weeks so that a downloaded update waits for a restart, per-user installations in user profiles that central tools do not manage, unsupported browsers still installed on older hosts, and desktop applications built on frameworks such as Electron that embed their own copy of a browser engine.
entries.impact: An attacker can compromise a user of an affected browser by luring them to a malicious page, or by placing malicious content on a legitimate site or advertisement, with no further action needed from the user. Exploiting the renderer gives code execution inside the browser's sandbox, and combining it with a sandbox escape or an operating system flaw gives control of the host with the user's privileges, from which the attacker can steal session cookies and saved credentials and move further into the network. Browser flaws such as the WebP image vulnerability CVE-2023-4863 have been exploited in the wild, and many are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue.
entries.remediation:
Keep browsers current and make sure updates take effect:

  • Leave automatic updates enabled and enforce them with enterprise policies for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, including a relaunch policy that requires a restart within a few days of an update being downloaded.
  • Manage browsers centrally with the organisation's deployment tool, remove per-user installations that bypass it, and remove browsers that are not needed.
  • Remove unsupported browsers, using Microsoft Edge's Internet Explorer mode for legacy sites that still need it.
  • Update desktop applications that embed browser engines, such as those built on Electron, when their vendors release fixes.
  • Limit the impact of future flaws with browser and endpoint protections, such as site isolation and exploit protection, and by not giving users local administrator rights.

Confirm the fix by checking the browser versions reported by the management tool or the browser's About page, and repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \b(Google Chrome|Mozilla Firefox|Firefox ESR|Microsoft Edge|Apple Safari|Chromium)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Java Runtime
entries.summary: Hosts or applications use a Java runtime that is missing security updates or comes from a release line that is no longer supported.
entries.description:
One or more hosts or applications use a Java runtime (JRE or JDK) that is missing security updates, or a Java release line that its provider no longer supports. Oracle publishes Java SE fixes in its quarterly Critical Patch Updates, and OpenJDK builds from other providers, such as Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft and Red Hat, release matching updates on the same schedule; each provider supports particular release lines for its own published period. Java vulnerabilities affect the core libraries, cryptography, networking and serialisation, and include flaws such as CVE-2022-21449, which allowed forged ECDSA signatures to pass verification.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans that find Java installations and read their version files, and scanners report one result per missing quarterly update. Hosts frequently have several runtimes: older versions left behind by earlier installers, private runtimes bundled inside applications, and JDKs installed by developers and build tools. Bundled runtimes are updated only by the application's vendor. Some scanners rate Java findings for the worst case of a browser plug-in running untrusted applets, a deployment model that has since been retired, so the rating should reflect how the runtime is actually used.
entries.impact: The impact depends on how the runtime is used. Where a server application processes untrusted data with an affected Java API, such as a web service parsing attacker-supplied input, an unauthenticated attacker may be able to cause denial of service, bypass cryptographic checks or, for some flaws, run code. Where a desktop runtime opens untrusted content, a user who opens a crafted file or application may be compromised. Many Java flaws are difficult to exploit and need specific conditions, but runtimes on unsupported release lines accumulate unfixed vulnerabilities, including in TLS and certificate handling.
entries.remediation:
Keep each runtime on the latest update of a supported release line:

  • Install the latest quarterly update for every Java runtime in use, from Oracle or the OpenJDK provider the organisation has chosen, and deploy it through the patch management tool.
  • Move applications on release lines the provider no longer supports to a supported long-term support release, after testing.
  • Uninstall runtimes that are no longer needed, including old versions left by earlier installers, and remove Java from hosts that do not need it.
  • Ask vendors of applications that bundle their own runtime for updated releases, and rebuild in-house applications and container images with the updated runtime.
  • Check the licence terms of the provider's builds before deploying updates widely, as the terms for Oracle's JDK have changed over time.

Confirm the fix with java -version for each installed runtime and by repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \b(Oracle )?(Java SE|Java Runtime|JRE|JDK|OpenJDK|Java\b(?! (RMI|Debug)))\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Adobe Acrobat or Reader
entries.summary: Hosts run Adobe Acrobat or Acrobat Reader builds that are missing security updates, so a crafted PDF opened by a user could run code.
entries.description:
One or more hosts run builds of Adobe Acrobat or Adobe Acrobat Reader that are missing security updates, or a product track that Adobe no longer supports. Adobe publishes security bulletins for Acrobat and Reader regularly, and most of their fixes address memory corruption, such as use-after-free and out-of-bounds write flaws, that can be triggered by opening a crafted PDF file. Acrobat and Reader are distributed in a Continuous track, which updates frequently and, by default, silently, and a Classic track, which receives quarterly updates; Classic releases reach end of support on fixed dates.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans that read the installed product version, and scanners report one result per missing security bulletin. Updates commonly fail to arrive where automatic updating has been disabled in an enterprise deployment and nothing replaces it, where a Classic track installation has been left in place after its end of support, or where users have installed Reader themselves outside central management.
entries.impact: An attacker can send a crafted PDF by email or host it on a website and, if a user on an affected host opens it, run code with that user's privileges, gaining a foothold on the network. PDF files are routinely accepted and opened in business, which makes this an effective phishing vector, and Acrobat and Reader vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-26369 have been exploited in the wild and are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. Reader's Protected Mode sandbox makes exploitation harder, and removing administrative rights from users limits what a successful exploit gains.
entries.remediation:
Keep Acrobat and Reader current and supported:

  • Update every installation to the latest build of a supported track, using Adobe's updater or the organisation's patch management tool, and install future updates within the timescales of the patch management process.
  • Leave automatic updates enabled for Continuous track installations, or distribute Adobe's updates promptly where the enterprise configuration disables them.
  • Replace installations on Classic tracks that have reached end of support with a supported release.
  • Remove installations that users added outside central management, or bring them under it.
  • Keep Protected Mode and Protected View enabled, and disable Acrobat JavaScript where it is not needed, using the enterprise configuration settings that Adobe documents.

Confirm the fix by checking the version under Help, About in the product or in the management tool's inventory, and repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \bAdobe (Acrobat|Reader)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bAdobe (Acrobat|Reader)\b.*\bAPSB\d

entries.title: Outdated Third-Party Desktop Software
entries.summary: Hosts have third-party desktop applications, such as archivers, media players, editors and meeting clients, that are missing security updates.
entries.description:
One or more workstations or servers have third-party desktop applications installed that are missing security updates published by their vendors. Typical examples are file archivers, media players, text and image editors, PDF tools, collaboration and meeting clients, remote access tools, and utilities installed for a single task and then forgotten. Unlike operating system updates, these applications often fall outside the organisation's patch management process: each has its own update mechanism, some have none, and many are installed by users into their own profiles.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans or software inventories that compare installed versions with vendors' advisories, and scanners report one result per missing update or advisory for each product. The most significant results are flaws triggered when a user opens a crafted file, such as the WinRAR vulnerability CVE-2023-38831, which was exploited in the wild, and privilege escalation flaws in the background services and updaters that some applications install with SYSTEM or root rights. Portable copies and old installers left in download folders may also be reported.
entries.impact: An attacker can send a crafted file, such as an archive, media file or document, and if a user opens it in an affected application, run code with the user's privileges. Flaws in privileged services or updaters can let a local user or malware gain administrative control of the host. Vulnerabilities in common desktop tools, including CVE-2023-38831, are listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The risk depends on how widely each application is used and whether it handles files from outside the organisation; little-used software still adds attack surface without benefit.
entries.remediation:
Bring third-party software under patch management:

  • Update each affected application to the latest release from its vendor, and remove applications that are not needed, including unused versions, portable copies and software installed for one-off tasks.
  • Extend the patch management process to third-party applications using a deployment tool that supports them, such as Intune, Configuration Manager with third-party update catalogues, or the Windows Package Manager (winget), and set timescales for applying their security updates.
  • Maintain a software inventory and an approved software list, and use application control, such as AppLocker or App Control for Business, to stop users installing unapproved or per-user software.
  • Remove local administrator rights from standard users, which limits both the installation of unmanaged software and the impact of a successful exploit.

Confirm the fix by checking installed versions in the software inventory and repeating the authenticated scan.

patterns.re: \b(7-Zip|WinRAR|Notepad\+\+|VLC|VideoLAN|Zoom (Client|Workplace|Meetings)|Wireshark|PuTTY|WinSCP|FileZilla|TeamViewer|Foxit|LibreOffice|OpenOffice|KeePass|Webex|AnyDesk|iTunes|VMware (Workstation|Player|Tools)|Citrix Workspace|Slack|Git for Windows)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Node.js
entries.summary: A server runs a Node.js release that is missing security fixes or whose release line has reached end of life.
entries.description:
A server or application runs a release of Node.js that predates fixes for one or more published vulnerabilities, or a Node.js release line that has reached end of life. The Node.js project issues security releases for all supported release lines together, announced in advance on its blog, and stops fixing each major release line at the end of its planned maintenance period. Past Node.js vulnerabilities include HTTP request smuggling in the built-in HTTP parser, denial of service through crafted HTTP/2 traffic, flaws in TLS and certificate handling, path traversal and command injection on Windows, and bypasses of the permission model.

The finding is identified by authenticated scans that read the installed version, or with node --version, since Node.js applications rarely announce the runtime version over the network, and scanners report one result per missing security release. Node.js is commonly present in several places on one host: installed from the distribution or from the project's own binaries, through version managers such as nvm, inside container images, and bundled with desktop or development tools, and each copy must be updated separately. Whether a given flaw is exploitable depends on the application using the affected API or feature.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach the application can exploit the unfixed flaws that its code paths use. The typical results are denial of service, which takes the single-threaded application offline, and request smuggling, which can bypass controls enforced by a front-end proxy or poison shared caches. A smaller number of flaws have allowed data exposure or code execution under particular conditions. Once a release line reaches end of life it receives no further security fixes, so newly disclosed flaws remain exploitable for as long as it is used.
entries.remediation:
Keep each Node.js runtime on a current, supported release:

  • Upgrade to the latest release of the release line in use, and move applications on end-of-life lines to an active long-term support (LTS) line, testing dependencies first.
  • Rebuild container images on an updated Node.js base image and redeploy them; updating the host does not update its containers.
  • Update every copy of Node.js on each host, including those installed by version managers and bundled with tools, and remove those that are not needed.
  • Follow the Node.js security release announcements and schedule the update as soon as a release is pre-announced.
  • Run the application behind a reverse proxy that normalises HTTP requests and enforces request limits, which reduces exposure to parser and denial of service flaws.

Confirm the fix with node --version on each host and in each image, and by repeating the scan.

patterns.re: \bNode\.js\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Jenkins
entries.summary: The Jenkins automation server, or plugins installed on it, are older than the releases that fix publicly documented security vulnerabilities.
entries.description:
The Jenkins controller, or one or more of its plugins, is running a release older than the versions named in published Jenkins security advisories. Jenkins core and its large plugin ecosystem receive security fixes frequently, and the advisories regularly cover cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery, missing permission checks and credential exposure, and at times flaws that allow files to be read or code to be run on the controller. Fixes are delivered in new weekly and Long-Term Support (LTS) releases rather than as patches for older releases, so an installation that has not been upgraded stays exposed.

The core version is normally identified from the X-Jenkins HTTP response header, which Jenkins returns on most pages, or from the page footer, and is compared with the advisories. Plugin versions are not usually visible without authentication, so outdated plugins are confirmed from the plugin manager or from the security warnings that Jenkins itself shows administrators when an installed component is named in a published advisory. Some advisories cover plugins for which no fix has been released; these remain vulnerable however recently they were updated.

A notable example is CVE-2024-23897, in which the command line interface parser replaced an argument beginning with @ with the contents of the named file. Unauthenticated attackers could read the first lines of files on the controller, or whole files where anonymous read access was granted, and in some configurations could reach code execution using secrets read this way.
entries.impact: Jenkins controllers usually hold credentials for source code repositories, artefact registries, cloud accounts and deployment targets, and can run code on every connected agent. An attacker who exploits a flaw in core or a plugin may therefore be able to read stored secrets, run commands on the controller or its agents, alter build jobs to insert malicious code into software the organisation builds and ships, and move into the environments its pipelines deploy to. The real exposure depends on the specific missing fixes, the plugins installed, whether anonymous read access or self sign-up is enabled and whether the instance is reachable from the internet. Many flaws need an authenticated user, but low-privileged accounts are often easy to obtain where access is granted broadly.
entries.remediation:
Bring Jenkins core and every plugin up to date, and keep them there:

  • Upgrade the controller to the latest release of the LTS line, or of the weekly line if that is a deliberate choice, and update all plugins through the plugin manager in the same change window, as plugin updates often depend on a recent core. Check the Java version that the new release requires before upgrading.
  • After the upgrade, review the security warnings shown under Manage Jenkins. Remove any plugin that an advisory lists as having no fix, and any plugin that is no longer needed, as each installed plugin adds attack surface.
  • Subscribe to the Jenkins security advisories and schedule regular updates, since new advisories are published often. Test upgrades on a staging copy of the controller where builds are business-critical.

Reduce exposure while upgrades are prepared: keep the controller off the internet unless it must be reachable, restrict access to it through a VPN or an IP allowlist, disable anonymous read access and self sign-up, and block the command line interface endpoint at the reverse proxy where it is not used. If there is reason to think the instance was exploited, rotate the credentials stored in Jenkins after upgrading, as secrets read before the fix remain valid. Confirm the fix by checking the version in the X-Jenkins header and in the plugin manager against the latest advisories, and by confirming that no security warnings remain.

patterns.re: \bJenkins\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Atlassian Confluence or Jira
entries.summary: A self-managed Confluence or Jira installation runs a release older than those fixing published Atlassian security advisories, some of which are actively exploited.
entries.description:
A self-managed installation of Atlassian Confluence or Jira is running a release that predates fixes published in Atlassian's security advisories, or a release that Atlassian no longer supports. These products are attractive targets because they are often reachable from the internet and hold an organisation's internal documentation and project information, and frequently credentials pasted into pages or tickets.

Confluence in particular has had several critical flaws that let an unauthenticated attacker run code on the server or take administrative control, including the OGNL injection flaws CVE-2021-26084 and CVE-2022-26134, the template injection flaw CVE-2023-22527, and the access control flaws CVE-2023-22515 and CVE-2023-22518, which allowed attackers to create administrator accounts. All of these have been exploited in real attacks. Jira has also had critical flaws, such as the template injection flaw CVE-2019-11581, alongside regular fixes for server-side request forgery, information disclosure and cross-site scripting.

The version is usually visible without authentication, in the footer and page metadata of Confluence and in the footer and the /rest/api/2/serverInfo endpoint of Jira, and is compared with the affected and fixed releases in each advisory. Fixes are delivered in new releases, and Atlassian's security bug fix and end of life policies set which release lines receive them. Atlassian has also ended support for its Server products, so an instance on a Server licence no longer receives security fixes at all.
entries.impact: The most serious flaws let an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server with the privileges of the Confluence or Jira service, or create an administrator account, from anywhere the application can be reached. That gives access to all of the content the instance holds, including restricted spaces and projects, any credentials or sensitive documents stored in it, and its local user accounts. The server can then be used as a foothold into the internal network, and compromised Confluence servers have been used to deploy ransomware. Instances reachable from the internet are at the greatest risk, as exploitation of these flaws has been automated and widespread soon after disclosure; internal instances remain exposed to anyone who can reach them on the network.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade to a supported, fixed release and keep to a regular update cycle:

  • Upgrade Confluence and Jira to the latest release of a supported Long Term Support line, or to the latest feature release, as listed in Atlassian's security advisories. Do not remain on a release that has reached end of life, as it will not receive fixes.
  • Where the instance runs on a Server licence, plan the move to a supported self-managed edition or to Atlassian's cloud service, because Server products no longer receive security fixes.
  • Subscribe to Atlassian's security advisories and treat critical advisories for internet-facing instances as emergencies, applying the fix or the published mitigation within days.
  • Keep installed Marketplace apps up to date as well, as they run inside the application and receive their own fixes.

As an interim measure, remove direct internet access to the instance, or place it behind a VPN or an authenticating reverse proxy until it is upgraded, and apply any temporary mitigation that Atlassian publishes for a specific flaw. Because the most serious flaws have been exploited at scale, an instance that ran a vulnerable release while reachable from the internet should be checked for signs of compromise, such as unexpected administrator accounts, new files in the installation directory and unusual processes started by the service account. Confirm the fix by checking the version shown by the application against the fixed releases in each relevant advisory.

patterns.re: \b(Atlassian )?(Confluence|Jira|Bitbucket|Bamboo)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated VMware ESXi or vCenter Server
entries.summary: VMware ESXi hosts or vCenter Server run builds older than those fixing published VMware security advisories, exposing the whole virtualisation platform.
entries.description:
VMware ESXi hosts, or the vCenter Server that manages them, are running builds older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in VMware security advisories (VMSAs), or a major version that is no longer supported. Because vCenter controls every host and virtual machine it manages, and ESXi runs the virtual machines themselves, both are high-value targets.

vCenter Server has had several flaws that allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to it to run code on the appliance, including CVE-2021-21972 in a vSphere Client plugin, CVE-2021-22005 in the Analytics service and CVE-2023-34048, an out-of-bounds write in its DCERPC implementation. ESXi has had heap overflow flaws in its OpenSLP service, such as CVE-2021-21974, which was linked to widespread ransomware attacks on unpatched hosts, and CVE-2024-37085, through which anyone able to create or rename a domain group called ESX Admins gains full administrative access to hosts joined to Active Directory. Several of these have been exploited in real attacks.

Version and build numbers are returned without authentication by the vSphere web services API at /sdk, which is how scanners identify missing updates, and can be confirmed in the vSphere Client. Older major versions have reached the end of general support and no longer receive routine security fixes.
entries.impact: Code execution on vCenter Server gives an attacker control of every host and virtual machine it manages: they can power machines off, copy or delete virtual disks, clone sensitive servers such as domain controllers to extract credentials offline, and create accounts for persistent access. Administrative access to ESXi gives the same control over that host's virtual machines, and ransomware groups target ESXi specifically because encrypting its datastores takes many servers offline at once. These interfaces are usually on internal networks, so an attacker typically needs a foothold inside first, but some are exposed to the internet, and CVE-2024-37085 needs only enough Active Directory rights to create or rename a group.
entries.remediation:
Update vCenter Server and ESXi to the fixed builds listed in the relevant VMware security advisories, and move off unsupported versions:

  • Update vCenter Server first and then the ESXi hosts, following VMware's supported update sequence and interoperability guidance, and use vSphere Lifecycle Manager or an equivalent process to keep every host at the same patched build.
  • Plan an upgrade to a supported major version for any host or vCenter instance on a release that has reached the end of general support.
  • Subscribe to VMware security advisories and treat critical advisories for vCenter and ESXi as urgent.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned. Make vCenter, the ESXi host client, SSH and other management services reachable only from a dedicated management network or jump hosts, never from user networks or the internet. Disable the SLP service on ESXi hosts where it is not needed, following VMware's published workaround. For hosts joined to Active Directory, review the host advanced settings that control the administrators group, so that membership of a domain group called ESX Admins does not silently grant full access. Enable lockdown mode where it fits operational needs. Confirm the fix by checking the build numbers reported by the vSphere Client or the /sdk API against the fixed builds in each advisory.

patterns.re: \bVMware (ESXi|vCenter|vSphere|Cloud Foundation)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bVMSA-\d

entries.title: Outdated Citrix NetScaler ADC or Gateway
entries.summary: A NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway appliance runs a build older than those fixing published Citrix security bulletins, several of them exploited at scale.
entries.description:
A NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway appliance (formerly Citrix ADC and Citrix Gateway) is running a build older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in Citrix security bulletins, or a release line that has reached end of life. These appliances usually sit at the network edge, providing remote access, load balancing and authentication for internal applications, so they are reachable from the internet by design and are among the most heavily targeted devices.

Notable flaws include CVE-2019-19781, a path traversal that led to unauthenticated code execution; CVE-2023-3519, an unauthenticated code execution flaw; and CVE-2023-4966, known as Citrix Bleed, a memory disclosure flaw that leaked session tokens from appliances configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server, letting attackers take over authenticated sessions without passwords or multi-factor authentication. A similar memory overread, CVE-2025-5777, followed. All of these have been exploited in real attacks, several as zero-days or soon after disclosure.

The exact build is not always displayed, but remote checks can often infer it from resources served by the Gateway login page. A credentialed check, or the output of show version on the appliance, gives a definitive answer.
entries.impact: Exploitation of these flaws gives an unauthenticated attacker on the internet either control of the appliance or the ability to hijack users' remote access sessions. From the appliance, an attacker can capture credentials as users sign in, read its configuration and stored secrets, and reach the internal applications and networks it fronts, which is why compromised NetScaler appliances have been a common entry point for ransomware and espionage. Session tokens stolen through memory disclosure remain usable until the sessions end, so upgrading alone does not remove access an attacker has already gained. The risk is lower only where the vulnerable feature, such as a Gateway or AAA virtual server, is not configured.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade every appliance to a fixed build on a supported release line, then deal with any earlier compromise:

  • Install the fixed build named in each relevant Citrix security bulletin on all appliances, including high availability partners. Replace or upgrade appliances on a release line that has reached end of life, as these do not receive fixes.
