  • After upgrading for a session token disclosure flaw, terminate all active and persistent sessions using the commands given in the bulletin, as tokens stolen earlier stay valid until those sessions are ended.
  • Check for signs of compromise using the indicators published by Citrix and national cyber security agencies, such as unexpected files in the web directories, new accounts and unexplained configuration changes. Where compromise is suspected, rebuild the appliance from a clean image and rotate every credential, certificate key and secret held in its configuration.
  • Subscribe to Citrix security bulletins and treat critical bulletins for internet-facing appliances as emergencies.

As an interim measure, restrict the management interface (the NSIP, and any SNIP with management access enabled) to a management network, and disable Gateway, AAA and other virtual servers that are not needed. Confirm the fix by checking the build reported by show version against the fixed builds in each bulletin.

patterns.re: \b(Citrix|NetScaler)\b.*\b(ADC|Gateway)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bCitrix Bleed\b|\bCitrixBleed\b

entries.title: Outdated Fortinet FortiOS
entries.summary: A FortiGate or other FortiOS device runs a build older than those fixing published Fortinet advisories, including actively exploited SSL VPN and admin interface flaws.
entries.description:
A FortiGate firewall, or another device running FortiOS, is on a build older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in Fortinet's PSIRT advisories, or on a release branch that has reached end of support. FortiOS provides the firewall, the SSL VPN and the administrative web interface on these devices, so a flaw in it usually affects a system that faces the internet.

FortiOS has had a series of critical flaws in its SSL VPN service, including the path traversal CVE-2018-13379, which exposed files holding VPN users' credentials, and the heap overflow and out-of-bounds write flaws CVE-2022-42475, CVE-2023-27997 and CVE-2024-21762, which allow unauthenticated code execution. The administrative interface has had authentication bypass flaws such as CVE-2022-40684 and CVE-2024-55591, the latter giving super-admin rights through crafted requests to a Node.js websocket module. These flaws have been exploited by both criminal and state-sponsored groups.

The build is not always visible from outside the device, but remote checks infer it from the SSL VPN and administrative login pages; a credentialed check or the output of get system status gives a definitive answer. Fortinet has also reported attackers keeping read-only access to previously compromised devices after they were updated, so the current build alone does not show that a device is clean.
entries.impact: Exploitation of the SSL VPN or administrative interface flaws gives an unauthenticated attacker on the internet control of the firewall itself, or the credentials of VPN users. With that, they can change firewall policy, create administrator and VPN accounts, capture traffic and credentials passing through the device, and use the VPN to enter the internal network as a trusted user, which is why compromised FortiGate devices are a frequent starting point for ransomware and espionage. SSL VPN flaws are only reachable where that service is enabled, and administrative interface flaws need the management interface to be reachable by the attacker, but both are common on internet-facing devices.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade FortiOS to a fixed build on a supported branch and check for earlier compromise:

  • Install the fixed build named in each relevant Fortinet PSIRT advisory, following Fortinet's recommended upgrade path between builds, and upgrade or replace devices whose branch or hardware model has reached end of support.
  • Check for the indicators of compromise published by Fortinet and national cyber security agencies. Where compromise is suspected, restore a known-good configuration after a clean upgrade and reset all administrator and VPN user passwords, VPN pre-shared keys and certificates held on the device, as credentials taken earlier remain valid.
  • Subscribe to Fortinet PSIRT advisories and treat critical advisories for internet-facing devices as emergencies.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned: remove HTTP, HTTPS and SSH from the allowaccess list of internet-facing interfaces so that the administrative interface is reachable only from a management network, and limit administrator logins to known addresses with the trusthost settings on each administrator account. Disable the SSL VPN where it is not used, and require multi-factor authentication for VPN users. Confirm the fix by checking the build reported by get system status against the fixed builds in each advisory.

patterns.re: \b(Fortinet|FortiOS|FortiGate|FortiProxy)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bFG-IR-\d

entries.title: Outdated Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS
entries.summary: A Palo Alto Networks firewall runs a PAN-OS release older than those fixing published security advisories, including exploited GlobalProtect and management interface flaws.
entries.description:
A Palo Alto Networks firewall, or a Panorama management server, is running a PAN-OS release older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in the vendor's security advisories, or a release that has reached end of life. PAN-OS provides the firewall, the GlobalProtect remote access portal and gateway, and the management web interface, so flaws in it often affect systems that are reachable from the internet.

Critical examples include CVE-2024-3400, a command injection in GlobalProtect that allowed unauthenticated attackers to run code as root on affected configurations, and CVE-2024-0012, an authentication bypass in the management web interface that, chained with the privilege escalation flaw CVE-2024-9474, gave unauthenticated attackers root access. Both were exploited as zero-days. Other flaws, such as the SAML authentication bypass CVE-2020-2021, affected devices only when particular authentication settings were in use, so the exposure from a given release depends on the features enabled.

The version is not always visible from outside, but remote checks infer it from the GlobalProtect portal or the management interface. A credentialed check, or the output of show system info, gives a definitive answer.
entries.impact: Exploitation of these flaws gives an unauthenticated attacker root-level control of the firewall. They can then change security policy, create administrator and VPN accounts, read the configuration and the credentials and keys it holds, intercept traffic passing through the device, and use it as a trusted route into the internal network. Firewalls are hard to inspect and are rarely covered by endpoint monitoring, so attackers can keep access for long periods. Management interface flaws are only reachable where that interface is exposed to the attacker, which Palo Alto Networks advises against, while GlobalProtect flaws affect internet-facing portals and gateways by design.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade PAN-OS to a fixed release and confirm the device was not compromised:

  • Install the fixed maintenance or hotfix release named in each relevant advisory on every firewall and Panorama instance, and upgrade any device on a PAN-OS release that has reached end of life.
  • Restrict the management web interface and SSH to a dedicated management network or a small set of trusted administrative addresses, using the permitted IP addresses of the management interface and interface management profiles, and never enable management access on internet-facing interfaces.
  • Where a device ran an exploited release while exposed, check for the indicators of compromise published by Palo Alto Networks and national cyber security agencies, and follow the vendor's recovery guidance, which may include a private data reset or a factory reset, before rotating the administrator, VPN and certificate credentials stored on it.
  • Subscribe to the vendor's security advisories and treat critical advisories for internet-facing devices as emergencies.

As an interim measure, apply any Threat Prevention signatures or configuration workarounds that an advisory provides, recognising that they are not a substitute for the fixed release. Confirm the fix by checking the release reported by show system info against the fixed versions in each advisory.

patterns.re: \bPAN-OS\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bPAN-SA-\d

entries.title: Outdated Ivanti Connect Secure
entries.summary: An Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliance runs a release older than those fixing published Ivanti advisories, including flaws exploited for unauthenticated code execution.
entries.description:
An Ivanti Connect Secure appliance (formerly Pulse Connect Secure) is running a release older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in Ivanti's security advisories, or a release line that has reached end of support. Connect Secure provides SSL VPN access to internal networks, so it faces the internet by design, and it has been one of the most heavily targeted remote access products.

Notable flaws include CVE-2019-11510, an unauthenticated arbitrary file read in Pulse Connect Secure that exposed cached credentials and session data; the chain of CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2024-21887, a command injection, which together gave unauthenticated attackers code execution; and the stack-based buffer overflows CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-22457, each allowing unauthenticated remote code execution. All were exploited in real attacks, several as zero-days, and some intrusions were attributed to state-sponsored groups.

The release can sometimes be inferred remotely from the appliance's web pages, but is confirmed reliably from the administrative console or a credentialed check. Ivanti provides an Integrity Checker Tool to look for signs of compromise, but national cyber security agencies have reported cases in which it did not detect one, so a clean result is not proof that an appliance is unaffected.
entries.impact: Exploitation gives an unauthenticated attacker on the internet root-level control of the appliance. Attackers have used this to deploy web shells and credential-harvesting code, capture the usernames and passwords of users signing in to the VPN, read session data and the appliance's configuration, and move into the internal network as a trusted remote user. Some malware deployed on these appliances was designed to survive upgrades, and national agencies have warned that access may persist even after a factory reset. The appliance is rarely covered by endpoint monitoring, so access can last unnoticed for long periods. Multi-factor authentication for VPN users does not prevent exploitation of the pre-authentication flaws.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade to a fixed, supported release, and treat any exposed appliance that ran a vulnerable release as possibly compromised:

  • Install the fixed release named in each relevant Ivanti security advisory, and migrate appliances on a release line or hardware platform that has reached end of support, as these will not receive fixes for new flaws.
  • Run both the internal and the external Integrity Checker Tool, and review the appliance and its logs for indicators of compromise published by Ivanti and national cyber security agencies.
  • Where compromise is suspected or cannot be ruled out, follow Ivanti's recovery guidance, which includes a factory reset before applying the fixed release. Then reset the passwords of local accounts and of directory service accounts used by the appliance, revoke and reissue its certificates and keys, and reset the passwords of users who signed in while it was exposed.
  • Subscribe to Ivanti security advisories and treat critical advisories for these appliances as emergencies.

As an interim measure, apply any mitigation file that Ivanti publishes for a specific flaw, restrict the administrative interface to a management network, and forward the appliance's logs to a central system so that tampering on the device cannot hide activity. Confirm the fix by checking the release shown in the administrative console against the fixed versions in each advisory.

patterns.re: \b(Ivanti|Pulse) (Connect Secure|Policy Secure|Secure)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Cisco IOS or ASA Software
entries.summary: A Cisco router, switch or firewall runs IOS, IOS XE or ASA software older than the releases that fix published Cisco security advisories.
entries.description:
A Cisco network device is running a release of IOS, IOS XE or Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) software older than those that fix vulnerabilities published in Cisco security advisories, or a release that has reached the end of software maintenance. Cisco publishes advisories for these platforms regularly, many of them in scheduled bundled publications, covering flaws in features such as the web user interface, SNMP, the SSL VPN, IKE and the handling of crafted network traffic.

Most flaws need a particular feature to be enabled and reachable, and many cause the device to reload rather than give control of it, but some have been severe. In IOS XE, CVE-2023-20198 let an unauthenticated attacker create a privileged account through the web user interface, and CVE-2023-20273 then allowed commands to be run as root; together they were used to implant large numbers of internet-facing devices. ASA software has had flaws in its web services and VPN, such as the path traversal CVE-2020-3452, and ASA devices were targeted in an espionage campaign that used CVE-2024-20353 and CVE-2024-20359.

The release is confirmed with show version or a credentialed scan; remote checks infer it from SNMP or the VPN web service and are less reliable. Cisco's Software Checker can then list the advisories that apply to a given release.
entries.impact: The effect depends on the missing fixes and the features in use. At worst, an unauthenticated attacker can take full control of a router, switch or firewall, then change its configuration, capture or redirect traffic, harvest credentials and use it as a hidden foothold, since network devices are rarely monitored as closely as servers. More commonly, the flaws allow an attacker to reload the device or exhaust its resources, interrupting the network services that depend on it. Devices with management services, VPN or the web user interface exposed to the internet face the greatest risk, and flaws reachable only from internal networks still matter to an attacker who already has a foothold.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade each device to a fixed release that Cisco still maintains:

  • Use the Cisco Software Checker and the relevant advisories to find a release that fixes all applicable vulnerabilities, preferring Cisco's suggested release for the platform, and upgrade every device running an affected release.
  • Replace hardware that has reached end of software maintenance or end of support, as it will not receive fixes for new flaws.
  • Subscribe to Cisco security advisories, and plan for the scheduled bundled publications as well as urgent out-of-cycle advisories.

Reduce exposure while upgrades are planned: disable features that are not needed, such as the IOS XE web user interface (no ip http server and no ip http secure-server) and unused VPN or web services on ASA; limit SSH and SNMP access to management networks with access control lists; and keep management interfaces off the internet. Where a device ran an exploited release while exposed, check it against the indicators of compromise in Cisco's advisory before relying on the upgrade, as attacker-created accounts and some implants can persist after an upgrade. Confirm the fix by checking show version against the fixed releases in each advisory.

patterns.re: \bCisco (IOS|IOS XE|IOS XR|ASA|Adaptive Security Appliance|Firepower|FTD|NX-OS)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)|\bcisco-sa-

entries.title: Outdated Samba
entries.summary: A Samba file server or domain controller runs a release older than those that fix published Samba security advisories.
entries.description:
A host is running a version of Samba, the open source implementation of SMB file sharing and of Active Directory domain controller services, that is older than the releases that fix vulnerabilities published in Samba security advisories, or a release series that the Samba project no longer maintains. Samba is common on Linux file servers, network attached storage devices and appliances, and is sometimes used as an Active Directory domain controller.

Samba vulnerabilities range from denial of service and information disclosure to remote code execution. Well-known examples include CVE-2017-7494, which allowed a client able to write to a share to upload a shared library and cause the server to load and run it, and CVE-2021-44142, an out-of-bounds heap read and write in the vfs_fruit module used for Apple client compatibility, which could lead to code execution as root. Many other flaws affect only domain controller deployments or need an authenticated user, so the exposure depends on how Samba is configured.

The version can sometimes be read from the server's SMB responses, and is otherwise confirmed from the installed package on the host. Linux distributions often backport security fixes into older version numbers, so a version string alone can overstate the risk; the distribution's own advisories, or a credentialed check of the package release, give a reliable answer. The Samba project maintains only a few release series at a time, and older series stop receiving security fixes.
entries.impact: The most serious flaws let an attacker who can reach the SMB service, and in some cases write to a share, run code on the server, often as root, giving access to every share and file it holds and a foothold for moving further into the network. On a Samba Active Directory domain controller, flaws can allow privilege escalation within the domain or forged authentication, which affects every system that trusts the domain. Other flaws allow an attacker to crash the service or read data they should not see. The risk is greatest where SMB is reachable from untrusted networks, where guest or anonymous write access is allowed, and on appliances whose Samba version depends on vendor firmware updates.
entries.remediation:
Update Samba to a release that contains all published fixes:

  • Apply the distribution's latest Samba security updates through the package manager or, where Samba is built from source, upgrade to the latest release of a series that is still maintained. Plan a move off any series that no longer receives security fixes.
  • For network attached storage devices and appliances, install the vendor's latest firmware, as the Samba version is controlled by the vendor, and replace devices that no longer receive updates.
  • Subscribe to Samba security announcements or the distribution's security advisories.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned: block SMB (TCP port 445, and 139 where NetBIOS is used) at network boundaries so that it is reachable only by the clients that need it; remove guest access and anonymous write access to shares; and disable optional modules that are not needed, for example by removing fruit from the vfs objects setting where Apple clients do not use the share. Some advisories give a specific configuration workaround, such as setting nt pipe support = no in the global section of smb.conf for CVE-2017-7494; use these only as a stopgap, as they can disable features that Windows clients expect. Confirm the fix by checking the installed package release against the distribution's advisories, or the Samba version against the fixed releases in each Samba advisory.

patterns.re: ^Samba\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated ISC BIND
entries.summary: A DNS server runs a version of ISC BIND older than the releases fixing published ISC advisories, most often flaws that let a remote attacker stop the service.
entries.description:
A DNS server is running a version of ISC BIND 9 older than the releases that fix vulnerabilities published in ISC's security advisories, or a branch that ISC no longer supports. BIND is one of the most widely used DNS servers, acting as an authoritative server, a recursive resolver or both.

Most BIND vulnerabilities let a remote attacker stop the named process, for example by triggering an assertion failure with a crafted query or response, or exhaust its CPU or memory. CVE-2015-5477, in which a crafted TKEY query crashed the server, is a long-standing example, and the KeyTrap issue CVE-2023-50387 showed how crafted DNSSEC data could tie up validating resolvers. Many flaws affect only resolvers, or only servers with particular features enabled, so the exposure depends on the server's role and configuration. Flaws allowing cache poisoning or code execution are rarer.

BIND returns its version in response to a CHAOS-class TXT query for version.bind unless its configuration changes this, and scanners compare that string with ISC's advisories. Linux distributions backport fixes into older version numbers, so the distribution's advisories or a credentialed check of the package release give a reliable answer. ISC supports a limited number of stable and Extended Support Version branches at a time, and older branches stop receiving fixes.
entries.impact: An attacker who can send queries to the server, or cause it to receive crafted responses, can usually stop it from answering. For an authoritative server, that makes the organisation's domains fail to resolve for external users, interrupting websites, email and other services; for an internal resolver, it can stop users and systems from reaching anything by name. The effect normally lasts until the service restarts, but repeated attacks can keep it down. Servers that answer queries from the internet, and resolvers that accept recursive queries from untrusted networks, are most exposed. Confidentiality and integrity are rarely affected, though the rarer cache poisoning flaws could let an attacker redirect users to systems they control.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade BIND to a supported release that contains all published fixes:

  • Apply the distribution's latest BIND security updates through the package manager or, where BIND is built from source, upgrade to the latest release of a branch that ISC still supports. Plan the move off any branch that has reached end of life.
  • Subscribe to ISC's security advisories or the distribution's announcements; ISC usually releases each fix for all supported branches at the same time.
  • Where the server runs on an appliance, install the vendor's latest firmware, as the BIND version is controlled by the vendor.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned: limit recursion to internal clients with allow-recursion, keep authoritative and recursive roles on separate servers, restrict zone transfers to known secondary servers, and apply any configuration workaround that an advisory gives. Setting the version option to a neutral string hides the version from casual queries, but it fixes nothing and is no substitute for upgrading.

options { allow-recursion { localhost; localnets; }; version "not disclosed"; };

Confirm the fix by checking the installed package release against the distribution's advisories, or the version reported by named -v against the fixed releases in each ISC advisory.

patterns.re: \b(ISC BIND|BIND 9|BIND \d)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Exim
entries.summary: A mail server runs a version of the Exim mail transfer agent older than the releases that fix published Exim security vulnerabilities.
entries.description:
A mail server is running a version of Exim, a mail transfer agent widely used on Linux and Unix systems and the default on some distributions, older than the releases that fix published Exim security vulnerabilities. Exim usually accepts SMTP connections from the internet, and parts of it run with root privileges, so flaws in it can be serious.

Exim has had several flaws that allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to run code on the server. CVE-2019-10149 allowed commands to be run through a crafted recipient address and was exploited by a state-sponsored group; CVE-2019-15846 allowed code execution as root through a crafted TLS Server Name Indication value; and CVE-2023-42115 was an out-of-bounds write in the handling of SMTP authentication. A set of 21 flaws reported together by researchers, known as 21Nails, included both remote code execution and local privilege escalation issues. Some of these flaws need particular features to be enabled, such as TLS or a specific authentication method, so the exposure depends on the configuration.

Exim announces its version in the SMTP banner by default, which is how scanners identify it. Linux distributions backport fixes into older version numbers, so the distribution's advisories or a credentialed check of the package release give a reliable answer; an Exim build compiled from source and not updated since is the clearest case.
entries.impact: Exploitation of the remote flaws gives an unauthenticated attacker on the internet code execution on the mail server, in several cases as root. With that, they can read and alter all mail passing through or stored on the server, harvest credentials, send mail that appears to come from the organisation, and use the server as a foothold into the internal network. Exim flaws have been exploited at scale soon after details were published. Where the missing fixes need features that are not enabled, or only allow local privilege escalation, the risk is lower, but it rises sharply if another flaw gives an attacker a local foothold.
entries.remediation:
Upgrade Exim to a release that contains all published security fixes:

  • Apply the distribution's latest Exim security updates through the package manager or, where Exim is built from source, upgrade to the current Exim release, and keep to a regular update cycle.
  • Where Exim is bundled with a hosting control panel or appliance, update it through that product's supported update mechanism, and replace systems that no longer receive updates.
  • Subscribe to the Exim announcements list or the distribution's security advisories.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned: disable authentication methods, protocols and features that are not used, accept SMTP connections from the internet only on servers that need to receive external mail, and apply any configuration workaround given in an advisory. The version can be removed from the SMTP banner with the smtp_banner option, but this only hides the version and does not reduce the risk. Confirm the fix by checking the version reported by exim -bV, or the installed package release, against the fixed versions in the relevant advisories.

patterns.re: ^Exim\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Outdated Device Firmware
entries.summary: Network-connected devices such as printers, cameras, switches or management controllers run firmware older than vendor releases that fix known vulnerabilities.
entries.description:
One or more network-connected devices are running firmware older than the latest release from the vendor, and the vendor's advisories or release notes list security fixes in the newer releases. Devices commonly affected include printers, IP cameras, network switches and wireless access points, uninterruptible power supply and environmental monitoring cards, storage appliances, and server baseboard management controllers such as iDRAC and iLO. Firmware updates are often left out of routine patching because they are applied manually, need downtime or are owned by a facilities or third-party team.

Device firmware typically bundles an embedded operating system, a web server, SSH or Telnet services and libraries such as OpenSSL, so it can inherit vulnerabilities from any of these as well as from the vendor's own code. Published flaws in such devices range from information disclosure and denial of service to authentication bypass and unauthenticated code execution.

The firmware version is usually identified from the device's web management interface, SNMP system description or service banners, and compared with the vendor's advisories. Devices whose model has reached end of life receive no further firmware updates and are better treated as unsupported hardware.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the device and the flaws left unfixed. An attacker on the network can typically use known flaws to read the device's configuration and any credentials stored in it, such as directory, email or SNMP accounts, change its settings, disrupt it or, in the worse cases, run code on it. Compromised devices are rarely monitored, so they make durable footholds for persistence and for reaching other systems, and a compromised management controller gives control of the server it manages. Devices reachable from the internet, or from user networks rather than a management network, are most at risk.
entries.remediation:
Bring device firmware into the organisation's vulnerability management process:

  • Install the latest firmware released by the vendor on each affected device, obtained from the vendor's official support site and checked against the published hash or signature where one is given, following the vendor's upgrade path between releases.
  • Keep an inventory of network-connected devices, including model, firmware version and owner, so that new vendor advisories can be matched to the devices they affect.
  • Subscribe to the vendors' security advisories and review firmware at least as often as other patching, with a faster route for critical advisories.
  • Replace devices whose model has reached end of life and no longer receives firmware updates.

Reduce exposure while updates are planned: place device management interfaces on a dedicated management network, block access to them from user networks and the internet, disable services that are not needed such as Telnet, FTP and unused web interfaces, and change any default credentials. Confirm the fix by checking the firmware version reported by each device against the latest vendor release and its advisories.

patterns.re: \b(iLO|iDRAC|BMC|firmware)\b.*(?:<|<=|prior to|before|older than|multiple vulnerabilities|vulnerabilit|remote code|denial of service|security update|\bRCE\b|\bSEoL\b|unsupported|end of life|\bEOL\b|outdated|obsolete)

entries.title: Amazon S3 Bucket Publicly Accessible
entries.summary: An Amazon S3 bucket's policy or access control lists let anyone on the internet, or any AWS account, list or read its objects.
entries.description:
One or more Amazon S3 buckets grant access to the public. A bucket policy statement with "Principal": "*" and no restricting condition, or an access control list (ACL) grant to the predefined AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers groups, allows requests that are not made by an identity in the bucket owner's account. The AuthenticatedUsers group is often misunderstood: it means anyone signed in to any AWS account, not users of the owner's account.

Exposure may be limited to reading known objects (s3:GetObject), may include listing the bucket's contents (s3:ListBucket), or may extend to writing, overwriting or deleting objects, or to reading and changing the bucket's ACL. Where S3 Block Public Access is enabled on the bucket or the account, such grants are blocked or ignored, so a public bucket also has those settings switched off.

The issue is confirmed by requesting the bucket and its objects without credentials, for example with the AWS CLI's --no-sign-request option, or with credentials from an unrelated AWS account. IAM Access Analyzer for S3, the AWS Config managed rules s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and s3-bucket-public-write-prohibited, Security Hub, Prowler and ScoutSuite all report such buckets. Since April 2023 new buckets have Block Public Access enabled and ACLs disabled by default, but buckets created earlier, and buckets whose settings were later changed, are still commonly found with public grants.
entries.impact: Anyone who finds the bucket can download its contents. Bucket names are often predictable from the organisation's name, domains or application code, and are routinely discovered by automated scanning, so a public bucket should be assumed to have been found. The effect depends on what the bucket holds: backups, database exports, logs, documents and personal data lead to a data breach, and configuration files or credentials can give access to other systems. Where write access is also granted, an attacker can alter or replace objects, such as scripts or files served to a website's visitors, or delete data.
entries.remediation:
Remove public access from every bucket that is not intended to serve public content:

  • Remove bucket policy statements that grant access to "Principal": "*" without a restricting condition, and grant access instead to named IAM principals or, for other accounts, to specific account or role ARNs.
  • Disable ACLs by setting S3 Object Ownership to Bucket owner enforced, after moving any access that still depends on ACLs into the bucket policy and resetting the bucket ACL to the default private ACL. Once ACLs are disabled, AllUsers and AuthenticatedUsers grants no longer have any effect.
  • Enable all four S3 Block Public Access settings on the bucket, and at account level so that every bucket is covered.
  • Where content must be public, such as website assets, keep only that content in a dedicated bucket and serve it through Amazon CloudFront with origin access control rather than from a public bucket.
  • Where files must be shared with specific people, use presigned URLs with a short expiry instead of public grants.

Treat any data that was publicly readable as disclosed: review S3 server access logs or CloudTrail data events, where enabled, for unauthenticated requests, rotate any credentials found in the bucket, and assess whether breach notification is required. Confirm the fix by repeating unauthenticated requests to the bucket and its objects, which should be refused, and by checking that IAM Access Analyzer reports no remaining public or unintended cross-account access.

entries.title: S3 Block Public Access Not Enabled
entries.summary: S3 Block Public Access is not enabled for the account or for buckets, so a mistaken bucket policy or ACL could make data public with nothing to stop it.
entries.description:
S3 Block Public Access is a set of four settings that override bucket policies and access control lists (ACLs) to prevent public access. BlockPublicAcls rejects requests that would add a public ACL; IgnorePublicAcls makes S3 ignore public ACLs already present on a bucket and its objects; BlockPublicPolicy rejects bucket and access point policies that grant public access; and RestrictPublicBuckets limits a bucket with a public policy to AWS service principals and authorised users in the owner's account. The settings can be applied to individual buckets, to a whole account, where they cover every bucket and access point it owns, and across an AWS organisation through an organisation-level S3 policy. Where levels differ, S3 applies the most restrictive combination.

The finding is raised when some or all of the settings are off at account level, so that buckets rely on their own settings and on every bucket policy and ACL being correct. Since April 2023 new buckets have all four settings enabled by default, but they can be switched off when a bucket is created or later, and buckets created earlier often have none. A bucket that is private today can then become public through a single policy or ACL change, made by mistake or by a deployment template.

The settings are reviewed with aws s3control get-public-access-block for the account and aws s3api get-public-access-block for each bucket, or in the S3 console. Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub report accounts and buckets without them.
entries.impact: On its own, the absence of these settings exposes nothing. It removes the guardrail that would stop a bucket becoming public through a misconfigured bucket policy, a public ACL on an uploaded object or a permissive infrastructure template, which are common causes of data exposure in AWS. Where buckets hold sensitive data, a single such change would expose it to anyone on the internet without any warning or block. The risk is greater in accounts where many people or pipelines can change bucket policies or upload objects with ACLs.
entries.remediation:
Enable all four Block Public Access settings at account level, and keep them enabled on each bucket:

aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
  • Before enabling the settings, identify buckets that legitimately serve public content, using IAM Access Analyzer for S3 or the access column in the S3 console, and move that content behind Amazon CloudFront with origin access control so that the buckets themselves need no public access.
  • In an AWS organisation, attach an S3 policy that blocks all public access at the root or organisational unit level, so that every member account, including new ones, inherits the setting centrally.
  • Restrict the s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock and s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock permissions to administrators, and consider a service control policy that denies them, so the settings cannot be switched off casually.
  • Disable ACLs on buckets with the S3 Object Ownership setting Bucket owner enforced.

Confirm the fix with aws s3control get-public-access-block showing all four settings as true for the account, and by checking that Security Hub or Prowler no longer report the settings as disabled.

entries.title: IAM Users Without MFA
entries.summary: IAM users who can sign in to the AWS Management Console have no multi-factor authentication device, so a stolen or guessed password alone gives access.
entries.description:
One or more IAM users have a console password but no multi-factor authentication (MFA) device. IAM supports passkeys and FIDO security keys, virtual authenticator applications and hardware TOTP tokens; without one, the console accepts the user's password alone.

The weakness is identified from the IAM credential report, where the password_enabled column is true and mfa_active is false, or from the user list in the IAM console. Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub report it as a failed check. Users who have access keys but no console password are not covered by this check, although IAM policies can still require MFA for their API calls through the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition key.

The finding is most significant for users with administrative or broad permissions, and in accounts where IAM users are the main way people sign in, rather than federation through IAM Identity Center or another identity provider that can enforce MFA centrally.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains an affected user's password, through phishing, reuse of a password exposed in another breach, or guessing, can sign in to the console as that user. They also need the account ID or alias and the user name, which are often found in documentation, emails or code repositories. The attacker gains whatever the user's permissions allow, which for an administrative user means control of the account: reading and deleting data, creating users and access keys for persistence, and running resources at the organisation's expense. The impact is limited where the user's permissions are narrow.
entries.remediation:
Require MFA for every IAM user who can sign in to the console:

  • Register an MFA device for each affected user, preferring phishing-resistant passkeys or FIDO security keys for administrative users. IAM allows more than one MFA device per user, so a backup device can be registered.
  • Attach a policy that denies all actions other than those needed to manage the user's own MFA device unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true, so that a user who has not set up MFA can do nothing else in the console.
  • Remove console passwords from users who do not need console access, and delete IAM users that are no longer used.
  • For the longer term, move people to federated access through IAM Identity Center or an external identity provider that enforces MFA, so that individual IAM users with passwords are no longer needed.

Confirm the fix by generating a new credential report (aws iam generate-credential-report, then aws iam get-credential-report) and checking that no user has password_enabled set to true with mfa_active set to false.

entries.title: AWS Root User Used or Holding Access Keys
entries.summary: The AWS account's root user has active access keys or is used for routine work, exposing credentials with unrestricted control of the account.
entries.description:
Every AWS account has a root user, identified by the email address used to create the account, with complete access to all resources and to billing. IAM policies cannot limit it; in a member account of an AWS organisation, service control policies can. AWS's guidance is that the root user should not be used for everyday tasks, should have no access keys, and should be protected with MFA.

The finding covers two related conditions. The first is root access keys: the IAM credential report shows access_key_1_active or access_key_2_active as true on the <root_account> row, which means long-term keys with full control of the account are stored somewhere, often in scripts, CI systems or a workstation's credentials file. The second is routine use: the credential report shows recent password_last_used or key use for the root user, or CloudTrail records events whose userIdentity type is Root for tasks that do not require it.

Testers also check whether the root user has MFA (mfa_active in the same report) and, in an AWS organisation, whether centralised root access has been enabled so that member accounts hold no root credentials at all.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains a root access key, or the root password where MFA is absent, has unrestricted control of the account. They can read and destroy all data, create users and roles for persistence, disable CloudTrail and other monitoring, change the account's contact and payment details, and close the account. Root activity is not constrained by IAM permissions, so least-privilege controls do not limit the damage. Routine use of the root user also increases the chance of its credentials being phished or captured on an administrator's workstation, and weakens accountability, because actions are recorded against the account rather than a named person.
entries.remediation:
Remove root access keys and limit the root user to the few tasks that require it:

  • Delete the root access keys from the root user's security credentials page, after identifying from the credential report and CloudTrail what used them and moving those processes to IAM roles or other short-term credentials.
  • Protect the root user with MFA, preferably a passkey or FIDO security key, and hold its password and MFA device under controlled custody for break-glass use.
  • Use IAM Identity Center or IAM roles for all administration, and reserve the root user for the tasks that only it can perform.
  • In an AWS organisation, enable trusted access for IAM and then centralised root access for member accounts (aws iam enable-organizations-root-credentials-management and aws iam enable-organizations-root-sessions), remove member accounts' root credentials, and carry out the rare privileged root tasks through short-term sessions from the management account using sts:AssumeRoot.
  • Alert on root user activity, for example with an Amazon EventBridge rule or a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on CloudTrail events where userIdentity.type is Root.

Confirm the fix with a new credential report showing no active root access keys and mfa_active as true for the root user, and with no unexplained root activity in CloudTrail.

entries.title: Overly Permissive IAM Policies
entries.summary: IAM policies grant principals far broader permissions than they need, such as all actions on all resources, or permissions that let them raise their own privileges.
entries.description:
IAM policies attached to users, groups or roles grant more than the principals' tasks require. Common forms are statements with "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*", the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy attached to workloads or to people's everyday identities, service-wide wildcards such as iam:*, s3:* or kms:*, and NotAction statements that allow far more than intended.

A less obvious form is a policy that looks limited but allows privilege escalation. Permissions such as iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, iam:CreateAccessKey on other users, or iam:PassRole combined with the ability to create or update EC2 instances, Lambda functions or other compute resources, let a principal grant itself, or act with, the permissions of a more privileged identity.

The issue is identified by reviewing the policies attached to each principal, for example from aws iam get-account-authorization-details, and with tools that model escalation paths, such as Prowler, ScoutSuite, PMapper and Pacu. IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings show permissions that have not been used, which helps separate what principals need from what they merely hold.
entries.impact: Any compromise of an over-privileged principal, whether a user's leaked access key, a role's credentials taken from a compromised EC2 instance or Lambda function, or a CI/CD pipeline's credentials, gives the attacker the excess permissions as well. Where a principal holds administrative or escalation permissions, a foothold that should have been contained becomes control of the account: access to all data, creation of new users and keys for persistence, disabling of logging and, where roles are trusted by other accounts, movement into them. The more principals hold such permissions, the more routes an attacker has to that outcome.
entries.remediation:
Reduce each principal to the permissions it needs:

  • Replace "Action": "*" and service-wide wildcards with the specific actions and resource ARNs each principal uses. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from a principal's CloudTrail activity, and its unused access findings show unused services, actions, roles and keys.
  • Remove AdministratorAccess from workloads and from people's everyday identities, and give administrators separate roles that they assume only when needed.
  • Restrict IAM write actions and iam:PassRole to the few principals that manage IAM, limit iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs, and use the iam:PassedToService condition key to control which services roles can be passed to.
  • Apply permissions boundaries to principals that can create roles or users, and in an AWS organisation use service control policies to set limits that no policy in an account can exceed.
  • Validate policies before deployment with IAM Access Analyzer policy checks or an escalation-path tool such as PMapper.

Confirm the fix by repeating the policy review and escalation-path analysis, and checking that no principal outside the intended administrators can reach administrative permissions.

entries.title: Long-Lived IAM Access Keys Not Rotated
entries.summary: IAM users hold long-term access keys that have not been rotated for a long time, extending the period in which a leaked key can still be used.
entries.description:
IAM user access keys are long-term credentials: an access key ID and secret access key that remain valid until they are deactivated or deleted. One or more active keys have not been rotated within the period set by the organisation's policy, commonly 90 days, as in the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Keys that have not been used for months, and users with two active keys, are often found alongside them.

Long-lived keys tend to spread. They are copied into scripts, CI/CD variables, configuration files, developers' workstations and sometimes source code repositories, where they remain usable long after the person or system that needed them has moved on. Without rotation, a key exposed at any point in that history may still work.

The issue is identified from the IAM credential report, which records access_key_1_last_rotated and access_key_1_last_used_date (and the same for the second key) for each user, or with aws iam list-access-keys and aws iam get-access-key-last-used. Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub report keys older than 90 days and keys that are not used.
entries.impact: An attacker who finds an old key, in a repository, a backup, a decommissioned server or a former employee's device, can call AWS APIs with the user's permissions from anywhere, without MFA unless policies require it. The calls are recorded in CloudTrail, but are hard to tell apart from the key's legitimate use unless source addresses are monitored. The impact depends on the user's permissions: keys belonging to administrative or automation users can give control of the account, while narrowly scoped keys limit what can be done.
entries.remediation:
Prefer short-term credentials, and rotate or remove the long-term keys that remain:

  • Replace access keys wherever possible: IAM roles for workloads running on AWS, IAM Identity Center for people using the CLI, OIDC federation for CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, and IAM Roles Anywhere for servers outside AWS.
  • Delete keys that are not used, finding them from access_key_1_last_used_date in the credential report or from IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings.
  • Rotate keys that must remain: create a second key, update every place the old key is used, deactivate the old key, confirm that nothing has failed, then delete it.
  • Keep remaining keys in a secrets manager rather than in files or pipeline variables, and give each key's user only the permissions it needs.
  • Monitor key age, for example with the AWS Config managed rule access-keys-rotated, and alert when a key exceeds the agreed period.

Confirm the fix with a new credential report showing no active key older than the agreed period and no active keys that are unused.

entries.title: IAM Policies Attached Directly to Users
entries.summary: IAM users have policies attached directly rather than receiving permissions through groups or roles, which makes permissions harder to review and keep consistent.
entries.description:
Permissions are granted to individual IAM users by attaching managed policies to them or embedding inline policies in them, rather than through IAM groups or through roles assumed by federated identities. Each user's permissions then have to be reviewed one by one, and people with the same job often end up with different access as one-off changes accumulate.

The issue is identified with aws iam list-attached-user-policies and aws iam list-user-policies for each user, or from aws iam get-account-authorization-details. It is a check in the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, Security Hub and Prowler, which report every user with a directly attached or inline policy.

The finding concerns how permissions are managed rather than what they allow: a policy attached directly to a user is no more permissive than the same policy attached to a group. Its practical effect is that excessive or outdated permissions are more likely to go unnoticed during access reviews and when people change role or leave.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. Permissions spread across individual users are harder to audit, so users are more likely to keep access they no longer need after a change of role, and the access reviews that would catch an over-privileged account are slower and less reliable. This increases the effect of any later compromise of an affected user's credentials.
entries.remediation:
Manage permissions through groups and roles:

  • Create IAM groups for each job function, attach the required managed policies to the groups and add users to the right groups, then detach the policies from the users and delete their inline policies.
  • Prefer customer managed policies to inline policies, so that each policy is defined once, versioned and reused.
  • For the longer term, move people to IAM Identity Center or another identity provider with permission sets or roles, which removes the need for individual IAM users.
  • Include IAM in periodic access reviews, using IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings to remove permissions that are not used.

Confirm the fix by checking that aws iam list-attached-user-policies and aws iam list-user-policies return no policies for any user.

entries.title: Overly Permissive IAM Role Trust Policy
entries.summary: An IAM role's trust policy lets principals outside the intended set assume it, such as any AWS account, a third party without an external ID, or any repository using an OIDC provider.
entries.description:
A role's trust policy (its AssumeRolePolicyDocument) defines who may assume it. One or more roles trust a wider set of principals than intended. Typical forms are:

  • A principal of "AWS": "*" or "*" without restricting conditions, which lets an identity in any AWS account assume the role.
  • Trust in a third party's whole account without an sts:ExternalId condition, which exposes the role to the confused deputy problem: any customer of that third party can ask its service to act against the role.
  • Trust in an OIDC identity provider, such as token.actions.githubusercontent.com for GitHub Actions, without a condition on the token's sub claim restricting it to the organisation's repositories and branches, so that workflows in other repositories can assume the role.
  • Trust in another account's root ARN where only one specific role in that account should be trusted.

The issue is identified by reviewing trust policies with aws iam get-role and from IAM Access Analyzer external access findings, which report roles that can be assumed from outside the account or organisation. Prowler and ScoutSuite also flag wildcard and condition-less trust. It can be confirmed by attempting sts:AssumeRole from an unrelated account controlled by the tester.
entries.impact: Where a role can be assumed from outside the intended set, an attacker who learns its ARN, made up of the account ID and role name, which are often guessable or exposed in code and documentation, can obtain temporary credentials for it from their own AWS account or code repository. They then hold all of the role's permissions without having compromised any of the organisation's credentials. Cross-account roles used by deployment pipelines and third-party tools often have broad permissions, so the result can be control of the account. The activity appears in CloudTrail under the role's name, which makes it easy to mistake for legitimate use.
entries.remediation:
Restrict every trust policy to the specific principals that need the role:

  • Replace wildcard principals with the exact role or account ARNs that must assume the role. Where a wildcard is needed for technical reasons, add conditions such as aws:PrincipalOrgID or aws:PrincipalAccount that limit it to the organisation's own accounts.
  • For roles assumed by third-party services, require the unique external ID that the vendor issues for the organisation, with an sts:ExternalId condition.
  • For OIDC federation, require the expected aud claim and restrict the sub claim to the specific repositories and branches or environments that deploy, using StringEquals or a narrowly scoped StringLike.
  • Review the permissions of cross-account roles as well, and give each only the access its task requires.
  • Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyser for the account or organisation, and treat new findings as alerts.

Confirm the fix by repeating the assumption attempt from an unrelated account, which should be denied, and by checking that no unintended external access to the role is reported.

entries.title: CloudTrail Not Enabled in All Regions
entries.summary: No CloudTrail trail records management events in every AWS Region, so API activity in some Regions, and activity older than 90 days, is not kept for investigation.
entries.description:
AWS CloudTrail records API calls made in an account. Without any configuration, the CloudTrail event history shows the last 90 days of management events in each Region, but it keeps nothing longer, does not include data events such as reads of S3 objects, and cannot be sent to a central log store or used to raise alerts. A durable record needs a trail, or a CloudTrail Lake event data store, delivering events to storage the organisation controls.

The finding is raised when there is no trail, or when trails cover only some Regions. A trail created through the API or CLI covers only its own Region unless IsMultiRegionTrail is set, and activity in other Regions, which an attacker may choose precisely because nobody watches them, then goes unrecorded. Related weaknesses often found at the same time include trails that are not logging, event selectors that exclude management events, log file integrity validation being disabled, and a log bucket that the account's own administrators can alter or delete.

The configuration is reviewed with aws cloudtrail describe-trails and aws cloudtrail get-trail-status in each Region, and is reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub, which check for a multi-Region trail recording management events.
entries.impact: An attacker with access to the account can work in Regions without a trail, or rely on events ageing out of the 90-day event history, knowing that their actions will not be retained. Without a complete record, the organisation may be unable to establish what an intruder did, which data they reached, or whether they created persistence such as new users, access keys or roles, and may be unable to meet its obligations to investigate and report a breach. The weakness gives no access on its own; its effect is on detection and response once another weakness has been exploited.
entries.remediation:
Create a multi-Region trail, or an organisation trail covering every account, and protect its logs:

aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail --s3-bucket-name "$LOG_BUCKET" --is-multi-region-trail --enable-log-file-validation --kms-key-id "$KMS_KEY_ARN" aws cloudtrail start-logging --name org-trail
  • In an AWS organisation, create the trail from the management account or a delegated administrator with --is-organization-trail, so that it covers every member account and member accounts cannot change or delete it.
  • Deliver logs to a bucket in a dedicated log archive account, with a bucket policy that lets only CloudTrail write to it, S3 Versioning enabled and, where required, S3 Object Lock to prevent deletion.
  • Enable log file integrity validation, and encrypt logs with a KMS key whose policy restricts decryption to the people who investigate incidents.
  • Add data events for sensitive S3 buckets and other high-value resources, and send events to the organisation's SIEM or to CloudWatch Logs, with alerts on high-risk actions such as StopLogging, DeleteTrail and root user activity.

Confirm the fix with aws cloudtrail describe-trails showing IsMultiRegionTrail as true, and aws cloudtrail get-trail-status showing that the trail is logging and delivering recently.

entries.title: GuardDuty Not Enabled
entries.summary: Amazon GuardDuty is not enabled, or not in every Region and account, so activity such as credential misuse, reconnaissance and crypto-mining is not detected.
entries.description:
Amazon GuardDuty is AWS's managed threat detection service. Once enabled in a Region, it analyses CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS query logs, which it reads from its own independent streams without the account having to enable those logs, and raises findings for activity such as the use of EC2 instance credentials from outside AWS, API calls from known malicious addresses, unusual console sign-ins, port scanning and communication with crypto-mining or command-and-control infrastructure. Optional protection plans extend it to S3 data events, EKS audit logs, runtime monitoring of EC2, ECS and EKS workloads, malware scanning, RDS login activity and Lambda network activity.

GuardDuty is enabled per Region, through one detector per account in each Region, and in an AWS organisation is normally managed from a delegated administrator account that enables it for every member. The finding is raised when there is no detector in one or more Regions, when a detector is suspended, or when member accounts are not enrolled. It is confirmed with aws guardduty list-detectors and aws guardduty get-detector in each Region, or in the GuardDuty console of the delegated administrator, and is reported by Prowler and Security Hub.
entries.impact: Without GuardDuty or an equivalent detection capability, an intruder using stolen credentials, a compromised instance or an exposed resource can operate for longer before anyone notices. Common attacks on AWS accounts, such as the use of leaked access keys, theft of instance role credentials and deployment of crypto-mining resources, raise GuardDuty findings soon after they begin when it is enabled. The weakness gives no access on its own; it reduces the organisation's ability to detect and contain a compromise, which raises the impact of other weaknesses. The risk is lower where an equivalent third-party detection service covers the account.
entries.remediation:
Enable GuardDuty in every Region, including Regions the organisation does not use, since attackers favour unwatched Regions:

  • In an AWS organisation, designate a security account as the GuardDuty delegated administrator and turn on automatic enablement for all existing and new member accounts, in each Region.
  • Enable the protection plans relevant to the estate, such as S3 Protection for accounts holding sensitive data and Runtime Monitoring for EC2, ECS and EKS workloads.
  • Send findings to the people who will act on them, for example through Amazon EventBridge to a ticketing or paging system, or through Security Hub to a SIEM, and define how high-severity findings are handled.
  • Where Regions are not used at all, also consider denying them with a service control policy.

Confirm the fix with aws guardduty list-detectors returning an enabled detector in every Region, and by checking in the delegated administrator that all member accounts are enabled. GuardDuty's sample findings can be used to check that alerts reach their destination.

entries.title: AWS Config Not Enabled
entries.summary: AWS Config is not recording resource configuration in every Region, so changes to resources are not tracked and configuration rules and most Security Hub checks cannot run.
entries.description:
AWS Config records the configuration of supported resources, such as security groups, IAM roles, S3 buckets and EC2 instances, as configuration items each time they change, and keeps a history of those changes and of the relationships between resources. Config rules and conformance packs evaluate the recorded configuration against policy, and AWS Security Hub relies on Config for most of its security checks.

Config is enabled per Region by a configuration recorder and a delivery channel. The finding is raised when no recorder exists, when it is stopped, when it records only a narrow set of resource types, or when Regions are left out. IAM users, groups, roles and customer managed policies are global resources and are normally recorded in a single Region to avoid duplicates. The configuration is reviewed with aws configservice describe-configuration-recorders and aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status in each Region, and is reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub.
entries.impact: Without Config, the organisation has no reliable record of how its resources were configured at a given time. After an incident it may be unable to establish when a security group was opened, a bucket policy changed or a role's permissions widened, and, together with CloudTrail, by whom. Misconfigurations introduced by mistake or by an attacker are not detected by Config rules, and Security Hub cannot assess most of its controls. The weakness gives no access on its own; it weakens detection, investigation and assurance.
entries.remediation:
Enable AWS Config in every Region in use, recording all supported resource types:

  • Create a configuration recorder that records all supported resource types (allSupported set to true), include the global IAM resource types in one Region only, and start it with aws configservice start-configuration-recorder.
  • Deliver configuration history and snapshots to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account.
  • In an AWS organisation, deploy Config to all accounts and Regions centrally, for example with AWS Control Tower or CloudFormation StackSets, and use an aggregator in the security account to view every account together.
  • Deploy Config rules or conformance packs for the organisation's key controls, such as public S3 buckets, unrestricted security groups and unencrypted volumes, and enable Security Hub on top of Config.
  • Where cost is a concern, use daily recording for resource types that change frequently rather than leaving them unrecorded.

Confirm the fix with aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status showing the recorder recording, with a successful last status, in each Region.

entries.title: VPC Flow Logs Not Enabled
entries.summary: VPC Flow Logs are not enabled, so there is no record of network connections to and from resources in the VPC for investigating intrusions or data exfiltration.
entries.description:
VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic through the network interfaces in a VPC: source and destination addresses and ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether the traffic was accepted or rejected by security groups and network ACLs. They do not capture packet contents. A flow log can be created for a whole VPC, a subnet or a single network interface, and published to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Amazon Data Firehose.

The finding is raised when VPCs hosting workloads have no flow log, or when flow logs record only rejected traffic, which shows blocked scanning but not the connections an attacker actually made. It is confirmed with aws ec2 describe-flow-logs and aws ec2 describe-vpcs in each Region, and reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub. Amazon GuardDuty analyses flow data from its own stream even where flow logs are not enabled, but that data is not available to the organisation for its own investigations.
entries.impact: Without flow logs, investigators cannot establish which hosts a compromised instance connected to, whether data left the VPC and where it went, or which internal systems an attacker reached through lateral movement. Attempts to reach exposed services cannot be reviewed after the event. The weakness gives no access on its own; it limits the organisation's ability to detect and scope a compromise.
entries.remediation:
Enable flow logs for every VPC that hosts workloads, capturing all traffic:

aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids "$VPC_ID" --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type s3 --log-destination "$LOG_BUCKET_ARN"
  • Send flow logs to a central S3 bucket in a log archive account, or to CloudWatch Logs where alerting is needed, and keep them for a period that meets the organisation's investigation and regulatory needs.
  • Consider a custom log format with fields beyond the default, such as pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr and flow-direction, which help where traffic passes through NAT gateways or load balancers.
  • Deploy flow logs centrally across accounts and Regions, for example with CloudFormation StackSets or an AWS Config remediation, so that new VPCs are covered automatically.
  • Make the logs searchable, for example with Amazon Athena or the organisation's SIEM, so that they can be used during an incident.

Confirm the fix with aws ec2 describe-flow-logs showing an active flow log with traffic type ALL for each VPC, and that records are arriving at the destination.

entries.title: Security Groups Allow Unrestricted Access to Administrative Ports
entries.summary: Security group rules allow inbound connections from any internet address to administrative services such as SSH and RDP on AWS instances.
entries.description:
One or more security groups allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to ports used for remote administration, typically SSH (TCP 22) and RDP (TCP 3389), and sometimes WinRM (TCP 5985 and 5986) or the management interfaces of other software. Where the group is attached to an instance or other resource with a public IP address, the service is reachable from the whole internet. Rules allowing all ports or all protocols from anywhere have the same effect and are often found alongside them.

Such rules are usually created for convenience during set-up, for administrators working from changing locations, or by launch wizards that offer to open SSH or RDP to anywhere, and then remain in place.

The issue is identified by reviewing security group rules with aws ec2 describe-security-groups, together with the network interfaces they are attached to, and by scanning the public addresses from outside. Prowler, ScoutSuite, Security Hub and AWS Trusted Advisor all report unrestricted administrative ports.
entries.impact: Exposed SSH and RDP services are quickly found by internet-wide scanning and are subjected to continual password guessing and credential stuffing. An attacker who guesses or reuses a valid password, holds a leaked SSH key, or exploits a vulnerability in the service gains interactive access to the instance, and from there to its data, to its IAM role credentials through the instance metadata service, and to other systems it can reach. The risk is greater where password authentication is enabled, the service software is out of date or the instance's IAM role is broad; it is lower where only key-based authentication is accepted and the software is current.
entries.remediation:
Remove internet-wide access to administrative ports:

  • Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint for administrative access. Neither needs inbound rules from the internet: Session Manager needs no inbound ports at all, authenticates users through IAM and can log sessions.
  • Where direct SSH or RDP is still needed, restrict each rule's source to the organisation's VPN or bastion address ranges, or to a managed prefix list maintained for administrators, never 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0.
  • Remove public IP addresses from instances that do not need them, and place them in private subnets.
  • Prevent recurrence with AWS Config rules such as restricted-ssh and restricted-common-ports, AWS Firewall Manager security group policies, or checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines.
  • Harden the services themselves: key-based SSH authentication only, Network Level Authentication for RDP, and current patches.

Confirm the fix by reviewing the rules again and by scanning the instances' public addresses from outside the organisation's network, expecting the ports to be filtered.

entries.title: EC2 Instance Metadata Service Version 1 Enabled
entries.summary: EC2 instances still accept Instance Metadata Service version 1 requests, so a request forgery flaw in a hosted application can be used to steal the instance's IAM role credentials.
entries.description:
The EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS), reachable from an instance at http://169.254.169.254, provides information about the instance, including temporary credentials for its IAM role. Version 1 (IMDSv1) answers simple GET requests. Version 2 (IMDSv2) requires a session token, obtained with a PUT request carrying the X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds header and then sent with each request in an X-aws-ec2-metadata-token header. The token response is limited by a network hop limit, and token requests carrying an X-Forwarded-For header are refused.

When an instance's HttpTokens metadata option is optional, both versions are accepted. An application on the instance that can be made to fetch a URL chosen by an attacker, through server-side request forgery (SSRF), an open proxy or a misconfigured reverse proxy, can then be used to read /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ and the role's credentials, because such flaws can usually send a plain GET but not the PUT with a custom header that IMDSv2 needs. Whether a new instance accepts IMDSv1 depends on the AMI's ImdsSupport value, the account-level default for the Region and the launch parameters, so instances launched from older AMIs or by older templates often still allow it.

The setting is reviewed with aws ec2 describe-instances (MetadataOptions.HttpTokens) and reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite and Security Hub. The CloudWatch metric MetadataNoToken shows whether IMDSv1 is still being used.
entries.impact: IMDSv1 is not exploitable on its own; it turns another flaw into credential theft. Where an SSRF or proxy flaw exists in an application on the instance, an unauthenticated attacker can obtain the instance role's temporary credentials and use them from anywhere to call AWS APIs with the role's permissions, which are often broad: reading S3 buckets, secrets and parameters, or changing infrastructure. The credentials remain valid for hours and can be refreshed by repeating the request. The impact depends on the role's permissions, and is greatest on internet-facing instances whose applications fetch URLs or proxy requests.
entries.remediation:
Require IMDSv2 on every instance, after confirming that the software on it supports it:

aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id "$INSTANCE_ID" --http-tokens required --http-endpoint enabled
  • Use the MetadataNoToken CloudWatch metric to find instances still making IMDSv1 calls, and update old AWS SDKs, CLI versions and agents that do not support IMDSv2 before enforcing it.
  • Set the account-level default for new launches in each Region (aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-defaults --http-tokens required), set ImdsSupport to v2.0 on custom AMIs, and set HttpTokens to required in launch templates and infrastructure code.
  • Keep the PUT response hop limit (HttpPutResponseHopLimit) at 1 unless containers on the instance need the metadata service, in which case 2 is normally sufficient.
  • Disable the metadata endpoint (--http-endpoint disabled) on instances that do not use it, and stop IMDSv1 returning with service control policies that deny ec2:RunInstances unless ec2:MetadataHttpTokens is required, and deny ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions to everyone but administrators.
  • Fix any SSRF or proxy flaws found in the applications, and limit each instance role to the permissions it needs.

Confirm the fix with aws ec2 describe-instances showing HttpTokens as required for every instance, and by checking from the instance that a metadata request without a token is refused with HTTP 401.

entries.title: Unencrypted EBS Volumes or Snapshots
entries.summary: EBS volumes or snapshots are stored unencrypted, so their contents are not protected by KMS key permissions and unencrypted snapshots can be shared or made public.
entries.description:
Amazon EBS encryption protects a volume's data at rest, its snapshots, and data moving between the volume and its instance, using a KMS key: either the AWS managed key aws/ebs or a customer managed key. One or more volumes or snapshots are unencrypted. A volume's encryption is fixed when it is created, and snapshots of an unencrypted volume, and volumes restored from those snapshots, are also unencrypted unless encryption is requested when they are copied or restored.

EBS encryption by default is an account setting that applies to each Region separately. When it is off, volumes are created unencrypted unless encryption is requested at launch, which is how unencrypted volumes usually arise. Turning it on has no effect on existing volumes.

The issue is identified with aws ec2 describe-volumes and aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self (the Encrypted attribute) and aws ec2 get-ebs-encryption-by-default in each Region, and is reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite, Security Hub and AWS Config rules such as encrypted-volumes.
entries.impact: AWS protects the physical storage media in either case, so the practical value of encryption here is as an additional access control. An unencrypted snapshot can be copied, shared with another AWS account or made public by anyone with the relevant EC2 permissions, and the whole disk, including files, databases and any credentials stored on it, can then be read by mounting it. A snapshot encrypted with a customer managed key can be used only by principals that the key policy allows, cannot be made public, and cannot be used by another account until the key is shared with it. Unencrypted storage may also breach regulatory or contractual requirements for encryption at rest.
entries.remediation:
Turn on encryption by default and replace unencrypted volumes and snapshots:

  • Enable EBS encryption by default in every Region in use (aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default), preferably with a customer managed KMS key set as the default (aws ec2 modify-ebs-default-kms-key-id), so that all new volumes are encrypted.
  • Encrypt existing volumes by taking a snapshot, copying it with encryption enabled (aws ec2 copy-snapshot --encrypted --kms-key-id), creating a new volume from the encrypted copy and swapping it in during a maintenance window, or by rebuilding instances from encrypted AMIs.
  • Replace unencrypted snapshots that must be kept with encrypted copies, then delete the unencrypted originals.
  • Restrict customer managed key policies so that only the roles that use the volumes can decrypt them, and limit who can change snapshot sharing (ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute).
  • Enable block public access for EBS snapshots in each Region as an additional guard.
