Confirm the fix with aws ec2 get-ebs-encryption-by-default returning true in each Region, and with describe-volumes and describe-snapshots showing no unencrypted resources remaining in use.

entries.title: RDS Instance Publicly Accessible
entries.summary: An Amazon RDS database instance is publicly accessible and its security group admits connections from the internet, exposing the database to password guessing and attack.
entries.description:
An RDS DB instance has PubliclyAccessible set to true. Its DNS endpoint then resolves to a public IP address from outside the VPC, and where the instance's subnets route to an internet gateway and its security group allows the database port from wide ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0, the database listener is reachable from the internet. The same applies to Aurora DB instances.

Public access is sometimes enabled deliberately for developers, reporting tools or third parties connecting from outside AWS, and sometimes arises from defaults: when PubliclyAccessible is not specified, RDS makes non-Aurora instances public if no DB subnet group is given, and makes instances public if the subnet group named default is used.

The issue is identified with aws rds describe-db-instances (the PubliclyAccessible attribute and the attached security groups), by resolving the endpoint from outside the VPC, and by scanning for the database port. Prowler, ScoutSuite, Security Hub and the AWS Config rule rds-instance-public-access-check report it.
entries.impact: An internet-facing database is exposed to automated password guessing against the master user and other accounts, to exploitation of vulnerabilities in the database engine, and to denial of service. An attacker who obtains valid credentials, for example from a leaked application configuration file, can read, change or delete all the data the account can reach, without needing any foothold in the organisation's network. The risk is lower where the security group admits only specific trusted addresses, IAM database authentication is used and TLS is enforced, and higher where the database holds personal or financial data.
entries.remediation:
Remove the database from the internet:

  • Set PubliclyAccessible to false (aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --no-publicly-accessible --apply-immediately) and place the instance in a DB subnet group made up of private subnets.
  • Restrict the security group to the application tier's security groups and specific administrative sources, never 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Give administrators and external tools access through a VPN, AWS Systems Manager port forwarding through a host in the VPC, or AWS PrivateLink, rather than through public exposure.
  • If the instance has been exposed, rotate the master password and other database credentials, store them in AWS Secrets Manager, and consider IAM database authentication.
  • Enforce TLS for client connections through the instance's parameter group, for example rds.force_ssl for PostgreSQL and SQL Server, or require_secure_transport for MySQL and MariaDB.

Confirm the fix with aws rds describe-db-instances showing PubliclyAccessible as false, and by checking that the endpoint resolves to a private address and that the port cannot be reached from outside.

entries.title: Public EBS or RDS Snapshots
entries.summary: EBS or RDS snapshots are shared publicly, so any AWS account can copy them and read the full contents of the disks or databases they hold.
entries.description:
EBS snapshots and manual RDS DB snapshots can be shared with other AWS accounts or made public. A public EBS snapshot has a createVolumePermission grant to the group all, and a public RDS snapshot has the value all in its restore attribute. Any AWS account can then find the snapshot among public snapshots, copy it, create a volume or restore a database from it, and read the data.

Public snapshots are usually created by mistake, for example while trying to share with a single account, or by scripts and templates that set public permissions. Only unencrypted snapshots can be made public; encrypted snapshots can be shared only with specific accounts.

The issue is identified with aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self --restorable-by-user-ids all and aws rds describe-db-snapshot-attributes, and can be confirmed from an unrelated account by listing public snapshots owned by the organisation's account ID. Prowler, ScoutSuite, Security Hub and AWS Trusted Advisor report public snapshots, and researchers and attackers are known to search public snapshots for credentials and data.
entries.impact: A public snapshot gives anyone with an AWS account a complete copy of the disk or database as it was when the snapshot was taken: application data, personal data, password hashes, configuration files, private keys and cloud credentials stored on the volume. No authentication to the organisation is needed, and a copy cannot be recalled once taken. Credentials found in the snapshot can lead to further compromise of the organisation's systems. Where a snapshot was public for any length of time, its contents should be treated as disclosed.
entries.remediation:
Remove public permissions and prevent them being granted again:

  • Remove public sharing from each EBS snapshot (aws ec2 modify-snapshot-attribute --snapshot-id "$SNAPSHOT_ID" --attribute createVolumePermission --operation-type remove --group-names all) and each RDS snapshot (aws rds modify-db-snapshot-attribute --db-snapshot-identifier "$SNAPSHOT_ID" --attribute-name restore --values-to-remove all).
  • Enable block public access for EBS snapshots in every Region (aws ec2 enable-snapshot-block-public-access --state block-all-sharing), which also stops snapshots that are already public from being publicly available.
  • Enable EBS encryption by default and encrypt RDS instances, since encrypted snapshots cannot be made public.
  • Share snapshots only with specific account IDs, restrict ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute and rds:ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute to administrators, and consider a service control policy that denies public sharing.
  • Treat the contents of any snapshot that was public as disclosed: rotate the credentials and keys it contained and assess whether breach notification is required.

Confirm the fix by repeating the searches for public snapshots, and with aws ec2 get-snapshot-block-public-access-state showing block-all-sharing in each Region.

entries.title: Secrets in Lambda Environment Variables
entries.summary: Lambda functions hold passwords, API keys or other secrets in environment variables, where anyone able to read the function's configuration sees them in clear text.
entries.description:
Lambda environment variables are a convenient place for configuration, and are often used for database passwords, API keys, signing secrets and tokens for third-party services. Lambda encrypts them at rest, with an AWS managed key unless a customer managed key is set, but returns them decrypted to anyone who can read the function's configuration and, where a customer managed key is set, is allowed to decrypt with it: lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration and lambda:GetFunction return them in clear text, the Lambda console displays them, and they are usually also present in the infrastructure code, templates and pipelines that deploy the function.

Read access to function configuration is widely granted, including through broad read-only roles given to developers, support staff, auditors and monitoring tools. Inside the function, the values are ordinary process environment variables, so a code injection, path traversal or similar flaw that can read the environment (for example /proc/self/environ) also discloses them.

The issue is identified by reviewing function configurations with aws lambda get-function-configuration or aws lambda list-functions, and with secret scanners. Prowler checks Lambda environment variables for secrets.
entries.impact: Anyone with read access to the function's configuration, or an attacker who exploits a flaw in the function's code, obtains the secrets and can use them directly against the systems they protect, such as databases, payment providers, email services or other APIs, usually from anywhere and without further authentication. Those systems often sit outside AWS's own access controls and logging, so their misuse may go unnoticed. The impact depends on what the secrets unlock, and is greater where the same secrets are shared across environments or functions.
entries.remediation:
Move secrets out of environment variables and into a secrets store:

  • Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or as SecureString parameters in Systems Manager Parameter Store, and retrieve them at runtime, for example with the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, which caches values to limit API calls.
  • Allow each function's execution role to read only its own secrets, and restrict who can read or change those secrets.
  • Rotate every secret that has been held in an environment variable, since it must be assumed to have been seen by everyone with read access to the function.
  • Where an environment variable must still hold a sensitive value, encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key before deployment and decrypt it in the function code, so that the console and API show only ciphertext.
  • Limit lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration and lambda:GetFunction to those who need them, and add secret scanning to deployment pipelines.

Confirm the fix by reviewing each function's configuration again and checking that no secrets remain in its environment variables or in the infrastructure code that deploys it.

entries.title: KMS Key Rotation Not Enabled
entries.summary: Automatic rotation is not enabled for customer managed KMS keys, so the same key material is used indefinitely, contrary to common key management policies.
entries.description:
AWS KMS can rotate the key material of customer managed symmetric encryption keys automatically. When rotation is enabled, KMS creates new key material on a schedule, every 365 days by default and configurable between 90 and 2,560 days, and uses it for new encryption, while keeping earlier material so that existing data can still be decrypted. The key's ID, ARN and policy do not change, so applications are unaffected. On-demand rotation is also available. AWS managed keys are rotated automatically every year and cannot be configured.

One or more customer managed symmetric encryption keys do not have automatic rotation enabled. This is shown by aws kms get-key-rotation-status, and reported by Prowler, ScoutSuite, Security Hub and the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Automatic rotation is not available for asymmetric keys, HMAC keys, keys with imported key material or keys in a custom key store, so those should be excluded from the finding or handled by manual rotation.

KMS key material is generated and used within hardware security modules and does not leave them unencrypted, so the risk that rotation addresses, compromise of the key material itself, is small. The finding is mainly one of alignment with key management policy and compliance requirements.
entries.impact: There is no direct impact. Without rotation, all data encrypted under a key since its creation depends on a single piece of key material, so a compromise of that material, unlikely given how KMS protects it, would expose more data. Rotation does not protect against the more realistic risk of misuse of the key through permissive key policies or IAM permissions, which allow decryption of all the data whatever the rotation state.
entries.remediation:
Enable automatic rotation for customer managed symmetric encryption keys:

aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id "$KEY_ID" --rotation-period-in-days 365
  • Choose a rotation period that meets the organisation's key management policy; KMS accepts 90 to 2,560 days.
  • Use on-demand rotation (aws kms rotate-key-on-demand) where key compromise is suspected or a policy requires an immediate change.
  • For keys with imported key material, import new key material and rotate it on demand, or create a new key and move the alias to it.
  • Review key policies and grants at the same time, since who can use a key matters more to its security than how often its material changes.

Confirm the fix with aws kms get-key-rotation-status returning KeyRotationEnabled as true for each key.

entries.title: Azure Storage Account Allows Anonymous Blob Access
entries.summary: The storage account permits anonymous read access to blob containers, so anyone who knows or guesses a container's address can read, and sometimes list, the files in it.
entries.description:
Azure Blob Storage can serve data to clients that present no credentials at all. Two settings control this: the storage account's AllowBlobPublicAccess property (Allow Blob anonymous access in the portal) must permit it, and each container then has its own anonymous access level. A container set to the Blob level lets anyone read a file whose name they know, and a container set to the Container level also lets anyone list every file it holds.

The weakness is confirmed by sending an unauthenticated request for a container on the account's blob endpoint, adding ?restype=container&comp=list to ask for a listing, and by downloading files without credentials. Storage account and container names are often guessable from the organisation's name and environment names, and tools such as MicroBurst enumerate both. Microsoft Defender for Cloud and cloud posture tools report accounts that permit anonymous access.

Storage accounts created recently disallow anonymous access by default, so the finding is most common on older accounts, on accounts deployed from templates that enable the property, and on accounts where a container was made public deliberately for website assets and later used for other data.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can download every file in a public container, and list the container's contents where the Container level is set, without needing any credential. Exposed containers commonly hold backups, database exports, logs, documents and configuration files, and configuration files often contain further secrets, such as connection strings or storage account keys, that widen the attacker's access. The impact depends on what the containers hold: a container of intentionally public images matters little, while one holding personal data may also amount to a reportable data breach. Anonymous access is read only, so it does not by itself let an attacker change or delete data.
entries.remediation:
Disallow anonymous access at the account level, which overrides every container's own setting:

  • Set Allow Blob anonymous access to Disabled in the storage account's Configuration settings, and set allowBlobPublicAccess to false in the templates and scripts that deploy it.
  • Before the change, check whether any client legitimately depends on anonymous reads: the account's transaction metrics can be split by authentication type to show anonymous requests.
  • Where content genuinely must be public, keep it in a dedicated storage account that holds nothing else, or give clients time-limited shared access signatures, preferably user delegation SAS tokens.
  • Prevent recurrence with an Azure Policy assignment, at management group level, that audits or denies storage accounts permitting anonymous blob access.
  • Treat anything that was exposed as disclosed: review the account's logs for anonymous reads where logging was enabled, and rotate any secrets found in the exposed files.

With the Azure CLI:

az storage account update --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --allow-blob-public-access false

As an interim measure, set the access level of each public container to Private. Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated listing and download requests and confirming that they are refused.

entries.title: Storage Account Shared Key Access Enabled
entries.summary: The storage account accepts requests signed with its account keys, static secrets that give full access to all of its data and bypass Microsoft Entra ID controls.
entries.description:
Every Azure storage account has two account keys. A request signed with either key (Shared Key authorisation) is given full access to all data in the account's blobs, files, queues and tables, and either key can sign shared access signatures (SAS) that grant any part of that access. The keys do not expire, are not tied to a user or application, and are outside Microsoft Entra ID controls such as multifactor authentication, Conditional Access and role assignments scoped to a single container. Shared Key authorisation is permitted unless the account's AllowSharedKeyAccess property has been explicitly set to false.

The keys can be listed by any principal that holds the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action permission, which common management roles such as Owner, Contributor and Storage Account Contributor include. A user with management rights over the account can therefore read all of its data through the keys even where no data access role has been assigned to them.

The setting is read from the account's configuration, for example with az storage account show. During testing, keys and connection strings that contain them are frequently found in application settings, source code, pipeline variables and configuration files.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains an account key, from a leaked connection string, a configuration file or a compromised developer workstation, can read, change and delete all data in the account from anywhere the account's network rules allow, without multifactor authentication and without their identity appearing in the logs. Keys remain valid until they are rotated. The setting does not expose data by itself: an attacker must first obtain a key or hold a management role that can list the keys, and network restrictions on the account limit where a key can be used from.
entries.remediation:
Move every client to Microsoft Entra ID authorisation, then disallow Shared Key authorisation:

  • Give applications managed identities, or service principals where they run outside Azure, and grant them data roles at the narrowest scope that works, such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor on a single container.
  • Replace account and service SAS tokens with user delegation SAS tokens, which are signed with Entra ID credentials rather than an account key.
  • Find the remaining key-based clients before the change: the account's transaction metrics can be split by authentication type, and its resource logs record how each request was authorised.
  • Set Allow storage account key access to Disabled in the account's Configuration settings, and set the property in the templates and scripts that deploy it.
  • Prevent recurrence with an Azure Policy assignment that audits or denies storage accounts permitting Shared Key access.
az storage account update --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --allow-shared-key-access false

Where some workloads still need keys for now, keep the keys in Azure Key Vault rather than in code or configuration files, rotate both keys on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure, restrict the account's network access, and limit which roles can list the keys. Confirm the fix by sending a request signed with an account key and confirming that it is refused, while requests authorised through Entra ID still succeed.

entries.title: Network Security Group Allows Unrestricted Access to Management Ports
entries.summary: A network security group rule lets SSH, RDP or other administrative ports be reached from any internet address, exposing those services to password attacks and exploits.
entries.description:
Network security groups (NSGs) filter traffic to Azure virtual machines and subnets. An inbound rule whose source is Any, 0.0.0.0/0 or the Internet service tag, and whose destination ports include an administrative service, exposes that service to the whole internet whenever the virtual machine has a public IP address or sits behind a load balancer rule that forwards the port. The ports most often found are TCP 22 (SSH) and TCP 3389 (RDP), followed by WinRM (TCP 5985 and 5986) and database ports.

Such rules often originate in the virtual machine creation wizard, where allowing selected public inbound ports creates a rule open to all source addresses, and are left in place after the initial set-up. An NSG can be associated with both a subnet and a network interface, and inbound traffic must be allowed by both, so the effective security rules of each network interface are what matter.

The exposure is identified by reviewing NSG rules or the effective security rules, and confirmed by scanning the public addresses from outside the organisation's network. Microsoft Defender for Cloud and cloud posture tools report it as management ports open to the internet.
entries.impact: Exposed SSH and RDP services are quickly found by internet-wide scanning and then face continuous password guessing, password spraying and credential stuffing. A weak or reused password, or an unpatched vulnerability in the service, gives an attacker interactive access to the virtual machine and, from there, to the virtual network, any managed identity assigned to the machine and other systems it can reach. The risk is lower where SSH accepts only keys, RDP requires Network Level Authentication with strong passwords and the services are fully patched, but the exposure still gives every attacker on the internet an unrestricted opportunity to try.
entries.remediation:
Remove internet-wide access to administrative ports:

  • Delete the rule, or restrict its source to the specific address ranges administrators connect from, such as the organisation's VPN egress addresses. Never use Any, 0.0.0.0/0 or Internet as the source for an administrative port.
  • Provide administrative access through Azure Bastion, which connects to virtual machines over their private addresses so that SSH and RDP need no public exposure, or through a VPN or ExpressRoute connection.
  • Where occasional direct access is unavoidable, use just-in-time VM access in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which opens the port only to the requesting address and only for a limited time.
  • Remove public IP addresses from virtual machines that do not need them.
  • Prevent recurrence with Azure Policy and with checks in infrastructure-as-code pipelines that reject inbound rules allowing administrative ports from any source.
  • Harden the services themselves: key-based SSH authentication only, Network Level Authentication for RDP, strong unique passwords and current patches.

For example, to restrict an existing rule's source with the Azure CLI:

az network nsg rule update --resource-group "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" --name "$RULE" --source-address-prefixes "$ADMIN_RANGE"

Confirm the fix by reviewing the effective security rules of each network interface and by scanning the public addresses from outside the organisation's network, expecting the ports to be filtered.

entries.title: Microsoft Entra ID MFA Not Enforced for All Users
entries.summary: Microsoft Entra ID does not require multifactor authentication for every user, so a stolen or guessed password alone is enough to sign in to some accounts.
entries.description:
Multifactor authentication (MFA) for a Microsoft Entra ID tenant is enforced either by security defaults or by Conditional Access policies. The finding applies where neither requires MFA for every user signing in to every resource, so that some accounts can sign in with a password alone. Common causes are security defaults switched off without equivalent Conditional Access policies, policies that target only administrators or selected groups, policies left in report-only mode, broad exclusions for groups, service accounts or trusted network locations, and policies that cover only some applications.

A related gap is incomplete registration. Where users have not yet registered an MFA method and are allowed to register one at their next sign-in, an attacker who knows the password can register their own method and keep the account.

The weakness is identified by reviewing security defaults, the Conditional Access policies and their exclusions, and the sign-in logs, where interactive sign-ins that needed only single-factor authentication show which accounts and applications are not covered. The Conditional Access What If tool, and tools such as MFASweep run with a test account, show which combinations of application, client and location accept a password alone. Microsoft's mandatory MFA for Azure management and the Microsoft administration portals does not cover users' sign-ins to Microsoft 365 services such as Exchange Online, SharePoint and Teams.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains the password of an account not covered by MFA, through phishing, password spraying, credential stuffing with passwords leaked from other services, or malware on a user's device, can sign in as that user from anywhere. They can then read and send the user's email, open their OneDrive and SharePoint files and Teams chats, use the account for convincing internal phishing, and set up persistence such as mailbox rules or application consents. Where the account holds an administrative role, the attacker may gain control of the tenant. The impact is smaller where only a few low-privileged accounts are uncovered, or where sign-in risk policies and smart lockout disrupt password attacks.
entries.remediation:
Require MFA for every user and every resource, with as few exclusions as possible:

  • Where the tenant has Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licences, create a Conditional Access policy that targets all users and all resources and grants access only with multifactor authentication or, better, an authentication strength. Exclude only the emergency access accounts, and run the policy in report-only mode briefly before turning it on.
  • Where the tenant has no such licences, enable security defaults, which require every user to register for MFA, prompt users for MFA when Microsoft judges it necessary and always prompt administrators.
  • Block legacy authentication, which cannot perform MFA and would otherwise remain a way around the policy.
  • Require phishing-resistant methods, such as FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business or certificate-based authentication, for administrative roles through an authentication strength.
  • Protect MFA registration with a Conditional Access policy on the Register security information user action, for example allowing it only from trusted locations or compliant devices, and use a Temporary Access Pass to onboard new users.
  • Review every exclusion. Replace service accounts that sign in with passwords by managed identities or service principals, and remove trusted-location exclusions.

As an interim measure, enable Microsoft Entra ID Protection sign-in risk policies where licensed, and review the sign-in logs for successful single-factor sign-ins. Confirm the fix with the What If tool and by signing in with a test account from an untrusted network, expecting an MFA prompt, then check that the sign-in log shows MFA was required.

entries.title: Legacy Authentication Not Blocked
entries.summary: The tenant does not block legacy authentication, so any service that still accepts a username and password over an older protocol can be signed in to without MFA.
entries.description:
Legacy authentication is the term Microsoft Entra ID uses for sign-ins from clients that send a username and password directly, over protocols such as IMAP, POP3, authenticated SMTP, Exchange ActiveSync with basic authentication, and older Office clients. These clients cannot perform multifactor authentication (MFA), so a sign-in that succeeds over one of them is single-factor, whatever MFA policies apply to modern clients.

The finding is raised where no Conditional Access policy blocks the legacy client types (Exchange ActiveSync clients and other clients) and security defaults, which would block them, are switched off. Microsoft has been retiring basic authentication from Exchange Online, which reduces but does not remove the exposure: the risk depends on which protocols and services in the tenant still accept a password alone.

It is identified by reviewing the Conditional Access policies and security defaults, and by filtering the sign-in logs by client app to show legacy sign-ins, successful and failed. Repeated failures from unfamiliar addresses usually indicate password spraying. Exchange Online settings such as SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled and the per-mailbox POP and IMAP settings show which protocols remain available, and tools such as MFASweep test which endpoints accept a password alone.
entries.impact: Where any legacy protocol still accepts a password, an attacker can password spray it, or use stolen passwords against it, without meeting an MFA prompt. A successful sign-in can give access to the user's mailbox, for example by downloading mail over IMAP or sending mail as the user through authenticated SMTP. Legacy protocols have long been a favoured route for password spraying precisely because they bypass MFA. The impact is limited to what the remaining protocols allow, and is low where basic authentication is already switched off for every protocol the tenant uses.
entries.remediation:
• Create a Conditional Access policy that targets all users, excluding only the emergency access accounts, and all resources, with the client apps condition set to Exchange ActiveSync clients and other clients, and the grant control set to block access. Run it in report-only mode first and review which sign-ins it would block.
  • Where the tenant has no Conditional Access licences, enable security defaults, which block legacy authentication.
  • Switch off protocols that are not needed in Exchange Online: disable SMTP AUTH for the organisation and enable it only on mailboxes that need it, and disable POP and IMAP on mailboxes that do not use them. For example, to disable them everywhere before re-enabling the exceptions:
Set-TransportConfig -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled $true Get-CASMailbox -ResultSize Unlimited | Set-CASMailbox -PopEnabled $false -ImapEnabled $false
  • Move devices and applications that send mail, such as printers and line-of-business systems, to OAuth or to a connector-based relay, and update or replace clients that cannot use modern authentication.

Confirm the fix by filtering the sign-in logs for legacy client apps and finding no successful sign-ins, and by attempting an IMAP or authenticated SMTP sign-in with a test account, expecting it to be refused.

entries.title: Excessive Global Administrators
entries.summary: More accounts than necessary hold the Global Administrator role, so compromising any one of them gives an attacker full control of the Microsoft Entra ID tenant.
entries.description:
Global Administrator is the most privileged role in Microsoft Entra ID. It can manage every aspect of the directory and of the Microsoft services that rely on it, assign any role to any account, and elevate its access to manage all Azure subscriptions and management groups in the tenant. Microsoft recommends keeping fewer than five Global Administrators and using less privileged roles for everyday administration.

Tenants frequently hold many more, because the role was given to every member of an IT team, to staff who needed it once, to accounts of former staff or third-party support providers, or to service accounts. Members of role-assignable groups that hold the role, and eligible assignments in Privileged Identity Management, count as well as direct active assignments. Related weaknesses often accompany the finding: Global Administrator accounts also used for email and browsing, accounts synchronised from on-premises Active Directory rather than cloud-only, and accounts without phishing-resistant MFA.

The finding is identified by listing the role's assignments under Roles and administrators in Microsoft Entra ID, or through Microsoft Graph, and comparing each holder's duties with the role's scope.
entries.impact: Every Global Administrator account is a route to complete control of the tenant, so each additional holder increases the chance that one is phished, has a weak password, signs in from a compromised device or is misused by its owner. An attacker who compromises any one of them can read all mail and files, create accounts and credentials for persistence, change authentication and federation settings, disable security controls and logging, and take control of linked Azure subscriptions. The likelihood is reduced, but not removed, where the accounts are cloud-only, protected by phishing-resistant MFA and activated only when needed.
entries.remediation:
• Reduce the number of Global Administrators to the minimum, fewer than five, including at least two cloud-only emergency access accounts that are kept for break-glass use and monitored for any sign-in.
  • Reassign everyone else to the least privileged role for their tasks, such as User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator, Exchange Administrator, SharePoint Administrator or Security Reader, using Microsoft's guidance on least privileged roles by task.
  • Make the remaining assignments eligible rather than permanent with Privileged Identity Management, requiring MFA, a justification and approval on activation.
  • Use dedicated, cloud-only administrative accounts that are not used for email or everyday work, and require phishing-resistant MFA for administrative roles through Conditional Access.
  • Review privileged role assignments regularly with access reviews, and alert on new assignments to the role.

Confirm the fix by listing the role's active and eligible assignments again, including group-based assignments, and checking that each remaining holder is justified.

entries.title: Privileged Roles Assigned Permanently
entries.summary: Privileged directory and Azure roles are assigned permanently rather than activated when needed, so the accounts hold administrative rights at all times.
entries.description:
Administrative roles in Microsoft Entra ID, such as Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator and Exchange Administrator, and privileged Azure roles such as Owner, User Access Administrator and Contributor, can be assigned in two ways. A permanent active assignment gives the account the role's rights at all times. An eligible assignment, managed through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), gives no rights until the user activates the role for a limited period, and activation can require multifactor authentication, a justification and approval, and is logged and can raise alerts.

The finding applies where privileged roles are held through permanent active assignments, either because PIM is not licensed (it requires Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance) or because it is licensed but assignments were made, or left, as permanent. It is identified in PIM by reviewing the active assignments for Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resources and groups managed through PIM, and looking for assignments with no end date. Emergency access accounts are a deliberate exception and should be the only permanent holders.
entries.impact: Standing privilege means that anyone who compromises an administrator's password, session cookie or token, for example through adversary-in-the-middle phishing or malware on the administrator's device, immediately holds that administrator's full rights, with no further prompt, approval or alert. It also widens the window for misuse by the administrators themselves. With eligible assignments an attacker would also have to pass the activation requirements, and the activation itself would be recorded and could alert defenders. The impact depends on the roles concerned and is greatest for tenant-wide directory roles and subscription-level Azure roles.
entries.remediation:
• Licence PIM for the accounts that hold privileged roles, then convert each permanent active assignment to an eligible assignment, for Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles and role-assignable groups.
  • Configure each role's settings: require MFA, or a Conditional Access authentication context, on activation; require a justification; require approval for the most privileged roles; keep the maximum activation duration short; and send notifications when roles are activated.
  • Give eligible assignments an end date where the need is temporary, and review them regularly with access reviews.
  • Remove privileged roles that are not needed at all, rather than making them eligible.
  • Keep two cloud-only emergency access accounts with permanent Global Administrator assignments, excluded from the activation requirements and monitored for any use.

Where PIM cannot be licensed straight away, reduce the number of privileged role holders, require phishing-resistant MFA for administrative roles through Conditional Access, and alert on changes to role assignments. Confirm the fix by reviewing the active assignments in PIM and finding no permanent privileged assignments other than the emergency access accounts.

entries.title: Guest Users With Excessive Directory Access
entries.summary: Guest accounts can read more of the Microsoft Entra ID directory than they need, such as every user and group, or hold roles and group memberships beyond their purpose.
entries.description:
Guest users are external identities, such as suppliers and partners, invited into a Microsoft Entra ID tenant through B2B collaboration. What they can see of the directory is set by the Guest user access restrictions option in the external collaboration settings. The most inclusive choice gives guests the same access as members, letting them enumerate every user, group, group membership, device and application. The default choice limits guests' access to the properties and memberships of directory objects, and the most restrictive choice limits them to their own objects.

The finding applies where guests have member-level directory access, and it is often accompanied by related weaknesses: invitation settings that let any user, or even guests, invite further guests from any domain; guests holding Microsoft Entra roles or Azure role assignments; guests left in sensitive groups and Teams long after the work ended; and guests with no MFA requirement.

It is identified by reviewing the external collaboration settings and the roles and group memberships held by guest accounts, and confirmed by signing in as a guest and enumerating the directory through Microsoft Graph or with tools such as AzureHound and ROADtools.
entries.impact: A guest account controlled by an attacker, whether through a compromised supplier account or a malicious individual at a partner organisation, can map the organisation: every user name and job title for phishing and password spraying, the members of administrative and sensitive groups, and the applications and devices in use. This makes later attacks faster and better targeted. Where guests also hold roles, group memberships or Azure permissions they no longer need, the attacker gains that access too. The impact is limited to directory information where no such roles or memberships exist.
entries.remediation:
• Set Guest user access restrictions to the most restrictive choice, so that guests see only their own directory objects, or at least to the default limited choice.
  • Restrict who can invite guests to users in specific administrator roles, such as Guest Inviter, or at most to members, and limit invitations to approved partner domains through the collaboration restrictions.
  • Remove Microsoft Entra roles and Azure role assignments from guests unless a documented need exists, and review guests' group and Teams memberships.
  • Run regular access reviews of guest accounts and remove those no longer needed.
  • Require MFA for guests through Conditional Access.

Confirm the fix by signing in as a test guest and checking that other users, groups and their memberships can no longer be enumerated.

entries.title: Users Can Consent to Applications
entries.summary: Users can grant third-party applications access to organisational data without an administrator's review, which consent phishing exploits to gain lasting access to mail and files.
entries.description:
Applications that integrate with Microsoft Entra ID request permissions, such as reading the signed-in user's mail or files, and a user can consent to delegated permissions on their own behalf if the tenant allows it. This is governed by the user consent settings for enterprise applications, which can allow users to consent to any application, allow consent only to applications from verified publishers and only for permissions classified as low impact, or not allow user consent at all. The finding applies where users can consent to applications from any publisher, or to permissions that reach mail, files or other sensitive data.

Consent phishing, also called an illicit consent grant, abuses this. The attacker registers a multi-tenant application with a convincing name, requests permissions such as mail and file access together with offline access, and sends users a link to the genuine Microsoft sign-in and consent page. A user who accepts gives the application tokens for their data. No password is disclosed and MFA is not bypassed, because the user signs in normally, which makes the attack hard for users to recognise.

The setting is reviewed in Microsoft Entra ID under Enterprise applications, in the consent and permissions settings, and existing delegated permission grants are reviewed for unfamiliar applications or applications holding broad permissions.
entries.impact: A user who consents to a malicious application gives the attacker an access token and, with offline access, a refresh token that lets the application read the user's mail, files or other granted data through Microsoft Graph without the user being present. The access does not depend on the user's password, so it is not removed by a password reset, and it continues until the consent is revoked or the application is disabled. Successful consent phishing typically leads to data theft and to further phishing from the compromised mailbox. The impact is limited to the permissions the user was able to grant and the data that user can reach, and the attack needs the user to accept the consent prompt.
entries.remediation:
• Change the user consent setting so that users can consent only to applications from verified publishers, and only for permissions classified as low impact, or disable user consent entirely where the organisation prefers every application to be approved.
  • Classify only genuinely low-risk permissions, such as basic sign-in and profile permissions, as low impact.
  • Enable the admin consent workflow, so that users can request access to applications they cannot consent to, and assign reviewers who assess each request against the permissions it asks for.
  • Review existing grants: list delegated permission grants and application role assignments, remove those that are unused or unexpected, and disable and investigate any application that appears malicious, revoking the affected users' sessions.
  • Monitor the audit logs for consent activity, and alert on consent to applications that request high-impact permissions.

Train users to recognise consent prompts and to report unexpected requests for access to their data. Confirm the fix by signing in as a standard user and attempting to consent to a test multi-tenant application that requests mail access, expecting the consent to be refused or routed to an administrator for approval.

entries.title: Azure Key Vault Publicly Accessible or Over-Permissive
entries.summary: The key vault accepts connections from any network and grants more identities, or broader rights, than needed, so one compromised identity can read the secrets it holds.
entries.description:
Azure Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates, which often include database passwords, API keys and storage connection strings for several applications. Access is controlled in two layers. The network layer decides where the vault can be reached from: public network access can be allowed from all networks, restricted to selected virtual networks and IP address ranges, or disabled in favour of private endpoints. The data layer decides who can read or change the vault's contents, through either Azure role-based access control (RBAC) or the older vault access policy model.

The finding applies where a vault holding sensitive material is reachable from all networks and grants access more widely than needed. Common examples are broad roles such as Key Vault Administrator or Key Vault Secrets Officer assigned at subscription or resource group scope; access policies granting every permission to many users and applications; one shared vault holding the secrets of several applications and environments; and vaults using the access policy model, where any principal with Contributor rights over the vault can add an access policy that grants itself full access to the contents.

It is identified by reviewing the vault's networking settings, permission model, role assignments and access policies, and confirmed by using an identity obtained during testing to list and read secrets from outside the organisation's network.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises any identity with read access to the vault, such as a user, an application's credentials or the managed identity of a compromised workload, can retrieve every secret that identity can reach and use those secrets to access the databases, storage accounts and services they protect. Because a vault often serves several applications, one over-permissive assignment can expose credentials well beyond the system first compromised. Public network access lets the attacker do this from anywhere, whereas network restrictions would force them to operate from an allowed network. Microsoft Entra ID authentication is always required, so the vault is not open to anonymous access.
entries.remediation:
• Use the Azure RBAC permission model, and grant data roles at the vault scope or narrower: Key Vault Secrets User for applications that only read secrets, Key Vault Crypto User for applications that use keys, and administrative roles such as Key Vault Administrator only to the few people who manage the vault. Map existing access policies to roles before switching.
  • Remove role assignments and access policies that are not needed, and assign roles to groups or managed identities rather than to individual users.
  • Use a separate vault for each application and environment, so that each workload's identity can reach only its own secrets.
  • Disable public network access and reach the vault through private endpoints, or restrict it to the virtual networks and address ranges that need it. Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass the firewall only where a service depends on it.
  • Limit who holds Owner, User Access Administrator or Contributor over the vault, since these roles can change its network rules and, depending on the permission model, who can read its contents.
  • Send the vault's AuditEvent logs to a Log Analytics workspace or SIEM, and alert on unusual secret reads.
az keyvault update --name "$VAULT" --resource-group "$RG" --enable-rbac-authorization true az keyvault update --name "$VAULT" --resource-group "$RG" --public-network-access Disabled

Rotate any secret that an over-permissive identity could have read. Confirm the fix by reviewing the vault's role assignments and networking again, and by attempting to read secrets with a test identity that holds no data role, and from an address outside the allowed networks, expecting both to be refused.

entries.title: Azure SQL Firewall Allows Broad Access
entries.summary: The Azure SQL server's firewall admits connections from the whole internet, or from all of Azure, so its database logins are exposed to password attacks from anywhere.
entries.description:
An Azure SQL Database logical server accepts connections on its public endpoint, a host name under database.windows.net on TCP 1433, only from addresses its firewall allows. Server-level IP rules apply to every database on the server, and database-level rules apply to a single database. The finding applies where the rules admit far more than the clients that need access: a rule covering 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255, very large address ranges, or the setting Allow Azure services and resources to access this server, which is stored as a rule from 0.0.0.0 to 0.0.0.0 and admits connections from any address inside Azure, including resources in other organisations' subscriptions.

Broad rules are usually added for convenience during development, for clients with changing addresses, or to let Azure services connect without private networking. The same pattern is found on the public endpoint of Azure SQL Managed Instance and on the firewalls of Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL.

It is identified by reviewing the server and database firewall rules, or the sys.firewall_rules and sys.database_firewall_rules views, and confirmed by connecting from an unrelated address: a refused connection returns an error stating that the client's address is not allowed, while a permitted one reaches the login stage.
entries.impact: Anyone on the internet, or anyone with an Azure resource where all of Azure is allowed, can attempt to log in to the server. SQL authentication logins with weak or reused passwords can then be guessed, and credentials leaked from connection strings in code, configuration files or compromised workstations can be used from anywhere. A successful login gives the attacker whatever that login can do, which for the server administrator or an application account is commonly full read and write access to the data. The impact is lower where only Microsoft Entra authentication is allowed, passwords are strong and logins have limited rights, but the firewall then provides no defence in depth.
entries.remediation:
• Remove rules that cover the whole internet or very large ranges, and allow only the specific addresses that need direct access, reviewing both server-level and database-level rules.
  • Prefer private connectivity: reach the server through a private endpoint and disable public network access, or use virtual network rules for clients inside Azure.
  • Switch off Allow Azure services and resources to access this server unless a specific service needs it and cannot use private connectivity.
  • Enable Microsoft Entra-only authentication, so that SQL authentication logins cannot be used, and give applications managed identities rather than passwords.
  • Require a minimum TLS version of 1.2, and enable Microsoft Defender for SQL to alert on brute-force attempts and unusual access.

For example, broad rules can be removed with Transact-SQL, the first statement in the master database for a server-level rule and the second in the user database for a database-level rule:

EXECUTE sp_delete_firewall_rule N'AllowAll'; EXECUTE sp_delete_database_firewall_rule N'AllowAll';

Confirm the fix by listing the firewall rules again and by attempting a connection from an address outside the allowed ranges, expecting it to be refused.

entries.title: App Service Accepts Unencrypted HTTP
entries.summary: The App Service app serves content over plain HTTP instead of redirecting to HTTPS, so its traffic can be read or altered by anyone positioned on the network path.
entries.description:
Azure App Service apps, including function apps and deployment slots, answer on both HTTP and HTTPS unless the HTTPS Only setting is enabled, in which case HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS. The finding applies where HTTPS Only is off, so pages, API responses, form submissions and cookies travel unencrypted whenever a user or client follows an http:// link, types the address without a scheme, or is configured with an HTTP address. It applies to the default azurewebsites.net host name and to any custom domains.

It is identified by requesting the app over HTTP and observing that content is returned rather than a redirect to HTTPS, and confirmed in the app's configuration, where the httpsOnly property is false. Related settings are usually reviewed at the same time: the minimum TLS version for HTTPS connections, and the FTP state, where All allowed lets deployment credentials and files be sent over unencrypted FTP.

The redirect alone does not add an HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) header, so even with HTTPS Only enabled a browser's first request can still be made over HTTP unless the application itself sends HSTS.
entries.impact: An attacker able to observe or intercept the traffic, for example on a shared or untrusted Wi-Fi network or through a compromised network device, can read data sent over HTTP, including session cookies that lack the Secure attribute, credentials submitted through forms and personal data in responses. They can also alter responses to inject malicious script or redirect users, and can keep users who start on HTTP from ever reaching the HTTPS site. The attack needs a position on the network path and a user or client that uses HTTP, so the impact is lower for APIs whose clients are configured with HTTPS addresses only.
entries.remediation:
• Enable HTTPS Only on every app and deployment slot, so that HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS.
  • Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 or higher.
  • Set the FTP state to FTPS only or, preferably, Disabled, and deploy through pipelines that use authenticated HTTPS endpoints.
  • Send an HSTS header from the application, for example with app.UseHsts() in ASP.NET Core, once every page and subdomain is confirmed to work over HTTPS.
  • Bind a valid certificate to each custom domain, for example an App Service managed certificate, so that HTTPS works on every host name.
  • Prevent recurrence with an Azure Policy assignment that audits or denies apps without HTTPS Only, and set the property in deployment templates.
az webapp update --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP" --https-only true az webapp config set --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP" --min-tls-version 1.2 --ftps-state Disabled

Confirm the fix by requesting the app over HTTP, expecting a redirect to HTTPS, and by checking that HTTPS responses include a Strict-Transport-Security header.

entries.title: Over-Privileged Managed Identity
entries.summary: A managed identity attached to a VM, app or automation resource holds far broader roles than its workload needs, so anyone who runs code on that resource inherits those rights.
entries.description:
Managed identities give Azure resources, such as virtual machines, App Service and Functions apps, Automation accounts, Logic Apps and container workloads, an identity in Microsoft Entra ID without stored credentials. Code running on the resource requests tokens for the identity from a local endpoint: the Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 on virtual machines, or the endpoint named in the IDENTITY_ENDPOINT environment variable on App Service and Functions. Whatever roles the identity holds are therefore available to any code, and any person, able to run commands on the resource.

The finding applies where an identity holds far more than its workload needs. Common examples are Owner, Contributor or User Access Administrator at subscription or resource group scope; broad data roles such as Key Vault Administrator or Storage Blob Data Owner across many resources; Microsoft Graph application permissions that can change the directory or assign roles; and one user-assigned identity shared by many unrelated resources.

It is identified by listing each identity's Azure role assignments at every scope, its Microsoft Graph application permissions and any directory roles, and by mapping who can run code on the resources that use it. Tools such as AzureHound show these paths. During a test, a token is typically requested from the endpoint on a compromised resource and used to enumerate what the identity can do.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains code execution on the resource, through a vulnerability in the application, server-side request forgery that can reach the token endpoint with the required header, or a stolen deployment credential, can obtain tokens for the identity and use them from anywhere until they expire. With Owner or Contributor at subscription scope they can read and change every resource in the subscription, extract secrets and data and deploy their own resources, and with Owner or User Access Administrator they can grant access to other identities for persistence. The same path lets users who can run commands on the resource, for example through VM Run Command or a code deployment, escalate to the identity's privileges. The impact is limited where the identity's roles are narrow and scoped to the resources the workload uses.
entries.remediation:
• Inventory every managed identity with its Azure role assignments at all scopes, Microsoft Graph application permissions and directory roles, and record what each workload actually needs.
  • Replace broad roles with the narrowest built-in or custom role at the narrowest scope, for example Storage Blob Data Reader on one storage account or Key Vault Secrets User on one vault, rather than Contributor on a subscription.
  • Remove Owner, User Access Administrator and high-impact Graph permissions from workload identities unless the workload's purpose genuinely requires them, and document any exception.
  • Give each workload its own identity rather than sharing one user-assigned identity across unrelated resources.
  • Treat the ability to run code on a resource as equivalent to holding its identity: restrict the roles that allow VM Run Command, extension installation, code deployment and runbook editing on resources with privileged identities.
  • Fix server-side request forgery and code execution weaknesses in the workloads, and monitor managed identity sign-in logs and the Activity Log for unexpected actions.
az role assignment list --assignee "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --all --output table

Confirm the fix by listing the identity's role assignments again and, with a token obtained on the resource, checking that actions outside the workload's needs are refused.

entries.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Plans Not Enabled
entries.summary: The subscription relies only on Defender for Cloud's free posture features, so threat detection for servers, storage, databases, key vaults and other workloads is not running.
entries.description:
Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides free foundational posture management, which assesses configuration against its recommendations, and paid Defender plans that add threat detection and protection for specific kinds of workload. These include Defender for Servers, Storage, Databases, Containers, App Service, Key Vault, Resource Manager and APIs. Each plan is enabled per subscription, and while a plan is off, Defender for Cloud raises no security alerts for that kind of resource.

The finding applies where the plans relevant to a subscription's resources are switched off, for example Defender for Servers on a subscription with virtual machines, or Defender for Storage where sensitive data is held. Without them, activity such as brute-force attempts against SQL logins, malware uploaded to storage, unusual access to key vault secrets and suspicious management operations goes undetected unless another tool covers it.

It is identified in Defender for Cloud's environment settings, which list each subscription's plans and their status, or with az security pricing list, where plans that are off show the Free tier.
entries.impact: The absence of these plans does not in itself let an attacker into the environment, but it removes a layer of detection that would otherwise alert the organisation to attacks in progress against its Azure workloads. Attackers can then remain in the environment for longer, and the organisation may learn of a compromise only from its consequences. The impact is lower where equivalent detection comes from other tools, such as endpoint detection and response on servers and a monitored SIEM that receives the relevant logs.
entries.remediation:
• Enable the Defender plans that match the resources in each subscription, prioritising production and internet-facing workloads: typically Servers, Storage, Databases, Key Vault, Resource Manager, App Service and Containers.
  • Apply the plans consistently through Azure Policy at management group level, so that new subscriptions are covered automatically.
  • Configure email notifications to the security contacts for alerts of an appropriate severity, and stream alerts to the organisation's SIEM, for example through the Microsoft Sentinel connector or continuous export.
  • Define who triages Defender for Cloud alerts and how quickly, so that alerts lead to action.
  • Review the foundational posture recommendations, which remain available without paid plans, and remediate the high-severity ones.

Where cost prevents enabling every plan, start with the subscriptions that hold the most sensitive data or the most exposed workloads, and record the compensating detection for the rest. Confirm the fix with az security pricing list showing the Standard tier for the required plans, and by generating sample alerts in Defender for Cloud to check that notifications reach the right people.

entries.title: Activity Log Not Retained or Exported
entries.summary: The subscription's Activity Log is kept only for Azure's default 90 days and is not sent to a workspace, storage or SIEM, limiting investigation of and alerting on management actions.
entries.description:
The Azure Activity Log records management operations on a subscription's resources, such as creating, changing and deleting resources, role assignments, policy decisions and security alerts, together with who performed them and from where. Azure keeps these events for 90 days and then deletes them. To keep them for longer, query them alongside other logs or alert on them, a diagnostic setting on the subscription must send them to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, an event hub or a partner solution.

The finding applies where no such diagnostic setting exists, or where it sends only some categories or sends them to a destination with short retention. It is identified in Azure Monitor, under the Activity Log's diagnostic settings for each subscription, or with az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list.

Similar gaps are common for Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, which are kept for at most 30 days by default, and for resource logs, which are not collected at all unless a diagnostic setting is configured on each resource.
entries.impact: Without the exported log, an investigation that begins more than 90 days after an attacker's first actions cannot establish what they changed, which accounts they used or how they gained access, and no alert fires when sensitive operations occur, such as new role assignments, deleted diagnostic settings or changes to network rules. This lengthens the time an attacker can operate unnoticed and weakens the organisation's ability to scope and report an incident. The log remains available for 90 days, which limits the impact for incidents that are detected quickly.
entries.remediation:
• Create a diagnostic setting on every subscription that sends all Activity Log categories to a central Log Analytics workspace, and keep the data for as long as the organisation's incident response and regulatory needs require.
  • Where long-term or tamper-resistant retention is needed, also send the log to a storage account with an immutability policy, or stream it to the organisation's SIEM through an event hub or a native connector such as Microsoft Sentinel's.
  • Enforce the setting with Azure Policy at management group level, so that new subscriptions are covered automatically.
  • Export Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, and the resource logs of key services such as Key Vault, to the same workspace.
  • Create alerts for sensitive operations, including role assignment changes, deletion of policies and diagnostic settings, and network rule changes, and restrict who can change or delete diagnostic settings and the workspace.

Confirm the fix by listing the subscription's diagnostic settings and by querying the AzureActivity table in the workspace for recent events.

entries.title: Entra Connect Server Not Protected as Tier 0
entries.summary: The Microsoft Entra Connect server is administered and protected like an ordinary server, although compromising it can lead to control of both Active Directory and the Entra ID tenant.
entries.description:
Microsoft Entra Connect Sync synchronises identities from on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID. Its server holds credentials for highly privileged accounts: an Active Directory connector account which, when password hash synchronisation is enabled, has the directory replication permissions needed to read every password hash in the domain, and a cloud synchronisation identity that can create and change synchronised users in Entra ID. The credentials are stored encrypted in the synchronisation database, and an administrator of the server can recover them with publicly available tools such as AADInternals. Microsoft therefore advises treating the server as a Tier 0 component, protected to the same standard as domain controllers.

The finding applies where the server is managed like an ordinary member server: its computer object sits in a general server organisational unit, it receives the same Group Policy as other servers, accounts and groups outside Tier 0 are members of its local Administrators or ADSyncAdmins groups, it is administered from ordinary workstations, it runs other software or has unrestricted internet access, or its virtualisation host and backups are managed by staff outside Tier 0. The same applies to staging servers and to servers running pass-through authentication agents.

It is identified by reviewing the server's local group memberships, organisational unit, linked Group Policy and logon rights, and by attack path analysis with tools such as BloodHound, which show principals outside Tier 0 with administrative paths to it.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains administrative access to the server, for example by compromising a server administrator, a backup operator or a management agent that is not held to Tier 0 standards, can extract the connector credentials. With the Active Directory connector account they can replicate the password hashes of every account in the domain, including the krbtgt account and domain administrators, which amounts to full domain compromise. Through the synchronisation service they can also change synchronised identities in Entra ID, and where pass-through authentication runs on the server they can intercept or bypass cloud sign-ins. A compromise of the server therefore becomes a compromise of both the on-premises and the cloud identity systems.
entries.remediation:
• Manage the server as Tier 0: move its computer object to the Tier 0 organisational unit, apply Tier 0 Group Policy, and allow only Tier 0 administrators to sign in to it or administer it, from privileged access workstations.
  • Remove every account and group outside Tier 0 from its local Administrators and ADSyncAdmins groups, and from the permissions on its computer object, its organisational unit and its linked Group Policy objects.
  • Apply the same protection to staging servers, servers running pass-through authentication agents, any remote SQL Server holding the synchronisation database, and the virtualisation hosts, storage and backups that hold any of these machines.
  • Keep the server dedicated to its role: no other applications, no web browsing, outbound internet access restricted to the Microsoft endpoints it needs, Microsoft Entra Connect kept on a current supported version, and prompt operating system patching.
  • Give the Active Directory connector account only the permissions its configured features need, and monitor the server and its accounts closely, for example with Microsoft Defender for Identity, alerting when the connector account is used from any machine other than the synchronisation server.

Where the full tier model will take time, start by removing administrators outside Tier 0 and restricting interactive and remote logon to the server. Confirm the fix by repeating the attack path analysis and finding no route from principals outside Tier 0 to the server.

entries.title: SharePoint and OneDrive Allow Anonymous Sharing Links
entries.summary: SharePoint and OneDrive let users create Anyone links, which give access to files and folders to whoever holds the link, without signing in or being identified.
entries.description:
The external sharing settings for SharePoint and OneDrive decide how far users can share content outside the organisation. The most permissive level, Anyone, lets users create links that work for whoever holds them, with no sign-in, so the person opening the content is never identified. The other levels require recipients to authenticate: new and existing guests, existing guests only, or only people in the organisation. OneDrive's level cannot be more permissive than SharePoint's, and individual sites can be restricted further but cannot exceed the organisation-wide level.

The finding applies where the organisation-wide level is Anyone, particularly where Anyone links do not expire, can grant edit rights or can be created for folders, or where an Anyone link is the default link type offered to users. Once created, a link can be forwarded, pasted into tickets and chats, saved in browser history or published, and it keeps working for anyone who finds it until it expires or is removed.

It is identified in the organisation's SharePoint sharing settings, or with Get-SPOTenant, where SharingCapability is ExternalUserAndGuestSharing, and in the audit log, which records the creation and use of anonymous links.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains an Anyone link, whether through a forwarded email, a compromised mailbox, a public post or a search engine, can open the shared content without an account, and the organisation cannot tell who did so. A shared folder exposes everything later placed in it, and an edit link lets the holder change or replace content, for example to plant malicious documents for colleagues to open. Exposed content may include personal data, making the exposure a reportable breach. The attacker needs the link itself, which is long and random, so the exposure depends on how widely such links are created and how carefully they are handled.
entries.remediation:
• Lower the organisation-wide external sharing level for SharePoint and OneDrive to New and existing guests or more restrictive, so that every external recipient signs in and is identified.
  • Where Anyone links are needed for a specific business purpose, allow them only on designated sites, and set the link options so that they expire within a short period, give view-only access and, where possible, cannot be created for folders.
  • Set the default link type to people in the organisation or specific people, so that users do not create Anyone links by default.
  • Restrict external sharing to members of specific security groups where only some staff need it, and require MFA for guests through Conditional Access.
  • Review existing Anyone links using the audit log and sharing reports, and remove those that are no longer needed.

For example, with the SharePoint Online Management Shell:

Set-SPOTenant -SharingCapability ExternalUserSharingOnly Set-SPOTenant -DefaultSharingLinkType Internal

Where Anyone links must remain for now, set RequireAnonymousLinksExpireInDays, and set FileAnonymousLinkType and FolderAnonymousLinkType to View. Confirm the fix by attempting, as a standard user, to create an Anyone link, and finding that the option is not offered.

entries.title: Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log Not Enabled
entries.summary: Microsoft Purview audit is not recording user and administrator activity, so actions across Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and Entra ID leave no searchable trail.
entries.description:
The Microsoft 365 unified audit log, searched through Microsoft Purview Audit, brings together records of user and administrator activity across the tenant's services: mailbox access and changes, file access, sharing and downloads in SharePoint and OneDrive, Teams activity, Microsoft Entra ID administration and changes to security settings. It is the main source of evidence when investigating a compromised account or a suspected data breach in Microsoft 365.

Audit recording is on by default for most organisations, but it can be switched off, and older tenants or tenants configured by scripts are sometimes found with it disabled. A related organisation-wide setting controls mailbox auditing, and individual mailboxes can be excluded from auditing.

The finding is identified in Exchange Online PowerShell, where Get-AdminAuditLogConfig reports UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled as False, or in the Purview portal, which offers to start recording user and admin activity while it is off. Get-OrganizationConfig shows through AuditDisabled whether mailbox auditing is disabled for the whole organisation.
entries.impact: Without the audit log, the organisation cannot establish what an attacker did with a compromised account: which emails were read or forwarded, which files were downloaded or shared, which mailbox rules were created and which settings were changed. This hampers containment, prevents the organisation from scoping a breach accurately, and may leave it unable to show regulators or affected people what data was accessed. It also removes the data that alert policies and SIEM integrations depend on, so attacks in progress go unnoticed. The log cannot be enabled retrospectively: activity that occurs before recording is switched on is never captured.
entries.remediation:
Turn on audit recording, either from the Audit page of the Microsoft Purview portal or in Exchange Online PowerShell, and make sure mailbox auditing is not disabled for the organisation:

Set-AdminAuditLogConfig -UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled $true Set-OrganizationConfig -AuditDisabled $false
  • Review mailboxes excluded from auditing through mailbox audit bypass associations, and remove exclusions that are not justified.
  • Check that the retention period meets investigation and regulatory needs. Where it does not, use Audit (Premium) retention policies, or export the records to a SIEM through the Office 365 Management Activity API or the Microsoft Sentinel connector for longer retention and correlation.
  • Create alert policies or SIEM detections for high-risk activity, such as new forwarding rules, mailbox permission changes, mass downloads and changes to the audit configuration itself.
  • Restrict the roles that can change the audit configuration, and alert on any change to it.

Confirm the fix by running Get-AdminAuditLogConfig again and by searching the audit log for a test activity performed after the change, allowing time for records to appear.

entries.title: Automatic External Mail Forwarding Permitted
entries.summary: Exchange Online lets mailboxes automatically forward mail to external addresses, which attackers use after compromising an account to keep receiving its mail.
entries.description:
Exchange Online can automatically forward a mailbox's incoming mail to another address through inbox rules created by the user, through the forwarding option in Outlook on the web, or through forwarding set by an administrator. Automatic forwarding to external recipients is governed by the outbound spam filter policies, whose Automatic forwarding rules setting can be left system-controlled, which blocks external forwarding, switched on, or switched off. Remote domain settings can also allow or block automatically forwarded messages to particular domains.

The finding applies where a policy covering some or all users sets automatic forwarding to On, so that mail can be forwarded to any external address without review. Forwarding is a hallmark of business email compromise: after taking over a mailbox, attackers commonly create a rule that forwards all mail, or mail containing words such as invoice or payment, to an address they control, often alongside rules that hide replies from the user.

It is identified with Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy, where AutoForwardingMode is On, with Get-RemoteDomain, and by testing: a rule that forwards to an external mailbox either delivers the message or produces a non-delivery report stating that external forwarding is not allowed. Existing forwarding is found in mailbox properties and inbox rules.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a mailbox, even briefly, can set up forwarding that keeps delivering copies of incoming mail to them after the password is reset and their sessions are revoked, unless the rule is found and removed. This gives them a lasting view of conversations, which supports invoice fraud, further phishing and data theft. Insiders can use the same mechanism to move business mail out of the organisation. The impact is limited to mail received by the affected mailboxes, and it requires either access to a mailbox or the user's own action to create the rule.
entries.remediation:
• Set automatic forwarding to Off, or to system-controlled, in the default outbound spam filter policy and in every custom policy, and allow forwarding only through a custom policy scoped to named mailboxes with an approved business need.
  • Block automatic forwarding in the default remote domain, and allow it only for specific partner domains where required.
  • Remove existing external forwarding: review mailbox forwarding settings and inbox rules that forward or redirect mail to external addresses, and investigate any that were not created for a known purpose as a possible compromise.
  • Alert on the creation of forwarding and redirect rules, for example through Microsoft Defender alert policies or SIEM detections based on the audit log.
Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity Default -AutoForwardingMode Off Set-RemoteDomain -Identity Default -AutoForwardEnabled $false

Confirm the fix by creating an inbox rule that forwards to an external test mailbox and checking that the message is not delivered and a non-delivery report is returned.

entries.title: Cloud Storage Bucket Publicly Accessible
entries.summary: A Cloud Storage bucket grants access to allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers, so anyone on the internet, or anyone with any Google account, can read and sometimes list its objects.
entries.description:
Access to Cloud Storage buckets and objects is granted through IAM policies and, on buckets that still use fine-grained access control, through access control lists (ACLs). Two special principals make data public: allUsers means anyone on the internet, and allAuthenticatedUsers means anyone signed in to any Google account, not only users in the organisation. A bucket is publicly accessible when either principal is granted a role on it, such as Storage Object Viewer, or when its objects carry ACL entries granting either principal read access.
