The weakness is confirmed by requesting the bucket and its objects without credentials at https://storage.googleapis.com/ followed by the bucket name: where the grant includes listing, the response is an XML index of every object. Bucket names share a global namespace and often follow the organisation's or project's name, so they can be guessed, and tools such as GCPBucketBrute enumerate them. Google Cloud's own security findings and cloud posture tools report public buckets.

Public write access is less common but more serious: a role that lets allUsers create or overwrite objects allows anyone to upload content, such as malware or altered website files.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can download every object in the bucket, and list its contents where listing is granted, without any identity of their own being involved. Public buckets commonly expose backups, exports, logs and configuration files, and configuration files often contain credentials, such as service account keys, that give further access to the project. Where write access is public, the attacker can also plant or replace content. The impact depends on the data: a bucket of intentionally public website assets matters little, while one holding personal data may also amount to a reportable breach.
entries.remediation:
• Remove every allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers binding from the bucket's IAM policy, and grant access instead to specific users, groups or service accounts.
  • Enforce public access prevention on the bucket, which blocks any public grant through IAM or ACLs, and enforce it across the organisation or folder with the constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention organisation policy constraint.
  • Enable uniform bucket-level access, so that object ACLs cannot grant access that the bucket's IAM policy does not show.
  • Where content genuinely must be public, keep it in a dedicated bucket that holds nothing else, or give recipients time-limited signed URLs.
  • Treat anything that was exposed as disclosed, and rotate any credentials found in the bucket.
gcloud storage buckets remove-iam-policy-binding "gs://$BUCKET" --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer gcloud storage buckets update "gs://$BUCKET" --public-access-prevention

Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated listing and download requests and confirming that they are refused.

entries.title: Uniform Bucket-Level Access Not Enabled
entries.summary: The bucket uses fine-grained access control, so individual objects can carry their own ACLs that grant access the bucket's IAM policy does not show.
entries.description:
Cloud Storage offers two ways of controlling access to a bucket's objects. With uniform bucket-level access, only IAM policies apply, set on the bucket or inherited from the project, folder and organisation. With fine-grained access control, each object can also carry its own access control list (ACL), which can grant read or write access to users, groups, project roles, or the public principals allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers.

The finding applies where buckets use fine-grained access control without a need for it. Access granted through object ACLs does not appear in the bucket's IAM policy, so a review of IAM alone can miss objects that are shared more widely, including objects uploaded with a predefined ACL such as publicRead. Auditing per-object ACLs across many objects is impractical, and mistakes made at upload time persist unnoticed.

It is identified from each bucket's configuration, for example with gcloud storage buckets describe, where uniform bucket-level access is shown as disabled, and from the organisation policies in force, where the constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess constraint is not enforced.
entries.impact: The setting does not expose data by itself. Its consequence is that object-level grants, including accidental public grants, can exist without being visible in the bucket's IAM policy, so objects may be readable by people the organisation believes have no access. An attacker who learns or guesses the name of such an object can read it. The risk is greatest for buckets that receive uploads from many systems or users, and lowest where public access prevention is enforced, since that blocks public ACLs regardless of this setting.
entries.remediation:
• Before switching, review the bucket's object ACLs and move any access that is genuinely needed into IAM bindings on the bucket, because object ACLs stop applying once uniform access is enabled.
  • Enable uniform bucket-level access on each bucket. It can be reversed within 90 days, after which it becomes permanent.
  • Enforce the constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess organisation policy constraint so that new buckets are created with uniform access.
  • Enforce public access prevention as well, so that no public grant can be made through either mechanism.
gcloud storage buckets update "gs://$BUCKET" --uniform-bucket-level-access

Confirm the fix by describing each bucket and checking that uniform bucket-level access is enabled, and that objects which should not be shared can no longer be read by principals outside the bucket's IAM policy.

entries.title: User-Managed Service Account Keys in Use
entries.summary: Service accounts have user-managed keys, long-lived private key files that let whoever holds them act as the service account from anywhere until the key is deleted.
entries.description:
A Google Cloud service account can authenticate with keys managed by Google, which are used internally and rotated automatically, or with user-managed keys, which are downloaded as JSON files containing a private key. A user-managed key does not expire unless an expiry is enforced by organisation policy, is not bound to any device or network, and lets whoever holds the file obtain tokens for the service account from anywhere, with no further authentication.

Key files tend to spread: they are copied onto developer workstations, committed to source code repositories, built into container images, stored in CI/CD variables and passed between teams, and the organisation often cannot say how many copies of a key exist or who holds them. Google recommends avoiding user-managed keys wherever a keyless alternative exists.

The finding is identified by listing each service account's keys with gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --managed-by=user, by reviewing key age and recent use, and by checking whether the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation organisation policy constraint is enforced. During testing, key files are frequently recovered from repositories, file shares and build systems.
entries.impact: Anyone who obtains a key file can act as the service account, with all of its permissions, from any network until the key is disabled or deleted, and their activity appears in the logs as the service account rather than as a person. Where service accounts hold broad roles, a single leaked key can expose data or infrastructure across a project or the whole organisation. Where key creation is not restricted, an attacker who gains suitable IAM permissions can also create new keys as a persistent backdoor. The impact depends on the permissions of the affected service accounts and on how widely the key files have travelled.
entries.remediation:
• Replace user-managed keys with keyless alternatives: attach service accounts to Compute Engine, Cloud Run and other resources so that code obtains short-lived tokens from the metadata server; use Workload Identity Federation for workloads in other clouds, on premises and in CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions; and use service account impersonation for administrators and tools.
  • Delete keys that are unused or no longer needed, starting with the oldest and those of the most privileged service accounts.
  • Enforce the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation and constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload organisation policy constraints, with documented exceptions only for projects that genuinely cannot avoid keys.
  • Where a key must remain, store it in a secrets manager rather than in code or images, rotate it regularly by creating a new key and deleting the old one, consider enforcing a maximum key lifetime by organisation policy, and limit who holds roles that can create keys.
  • Monitor the Admin Activity audit logs for key creation, and alert on keys created outside the approved process.
gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account="$SA_EMAIL" --managed-by=user gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete "$KEY_ID" --iam-account="$SA_EMAIL"

Confirm the fix by listing user-managed keys again and finding none outside the documented exceptions, and by checking that the organisation policy prevents new keys from being created.

entries.title: Default Compute Service Account With the Editor Role
entries.summary: The Compute Engine default service account still holds the project-wide Editor role, so any compromised workload running as it can change most resources in the project.
entries.description:
When the Compute Engine API is enabled in a project, Google Cloud creates the Compute Engine default service account, named with the project number followed by -compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com, and, unless the constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts organisation policy constraint is enforced, grants it the basic Editor role on the project. Virtual machines use this account unless another is chosen, and other services, such as Cloud Run, also run as it by default. Editor allows a principal to create, change and delete most resources in the project and to read most of its data.

Code running on a virtual machine obtains tokens for its service account from the metadata server, at http://metadata.google.internal/, by sending the header Metadata-Flavor: Google. On Compute Engine, the instance's access scopes also limit what the token can do: the default scopes restrict most APIs, while the scope allowing full access to all Cloud APIs lets the token use everything the Editor role permits. Workloads configured with full access, and services that do not use access scopes, can use the whole role.

The finding is identified by reviewing the project's IAM policy for the default service account's Editor binding, and the service account and scopes configured on each instance and service.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains code execution on any workload running as the default service account, or who can make it send requests to the metadata server through server-side request forgery that allows the required header, can obtain a token and use it from anywhere until it expires. With the Editor role and unrestricted scopes, they can read data in Cloud Storage, BigQuery and other services, change or delete resources, and deploy their own workloads for persistence. With the default scopes, the token is largely limited to reading Cloud Storage and writing logs and metrics, which can still expose the project's stored data. The Editor role cannot change the project's IAM policy.
entries.remediation:
• Create a dedicated, user-managed service account for each workload, grant it only the predefined or custom roles it needs, and attach it to the workload in place of the default service account.
  • Remove the Editor role from the Compute Engine default service account once no workload depends on it, testing first in a non-production project, and disable the account if nothing uses it.
  • Enforce the constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts organisation policy constraint so that default service accounts in new projects receive no roles automatically.
  • Do not combine broad roles with the scope allowing full access to all Cloud APIs, and use narrow IAM roles rather than access scopes as the main way of limiting access.
  • Restrict who can attach service accounts to resources, which the Service Account User role allows, since attaching a privileged service account to a new resource is a privilege escalation path.
gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" --member="serviceAccount:$PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" --role=roles/editor

Confirm the fix by reviewing the project's IAM policy, expecting no Editor binding for default service accounts, and by checking each instance's attached service account and scopes.

entries.title: Basic Owner or Editor Roles Granted
entries.summary: Users, groups or service accounts hold the basic Owner or Editor role, which grants broad rights over almost every resource in the project, folder or organisation.
entries.description:
Google Cloud's basic roles, Owner, Editor and Viewer, predate its predefined roles and apply across almost every service. Editor allows a principal to create, change and delete most resources and to read most data in its scope. Owner adds the ability to manage IAM policies, and so to grant any role to anyone. Google recommends against using basic roles where predefined or custom roles can be used instead, particularly in production.

The finding applies where Owner or Editor is granted to users, groups or service accounts that need far narrower access, for example developers who deploy one service, support staff who restart instances, or automation that writes to one bucket. Grants made at folder or organisation level are inherited by every project beneath, multiplying their effect, and grants to accounts outside the organisation's domain, such as personal Gmail accounts, are a related and common weakness.

It is identified by reviewing the IAM policies of the organisation, folders and projects, for example with gcloud asset search-all-iam-policies filtered on roles/owner and roles/editor. The IAM role recommender compares the permissions each principal holds with those it has actually used, and suggests smaller roles.
entries.impact: Every principal holding a basic role is a route to broad control of the resources in its scope. An attacker who compromises one of these accounts, through phishing, a leaked service account key or a compromised workload, can read and change data, deploy resources and, with Owner, grant themselves or others further access for persistence. Because the roles are far wider than the holders' duties, a compromise that should have been contained to one service affects the whole project or more. The impact is greatest for grants at organisation or folder level and for service accounts used by exposed workloads.
entries.remediation:
• Replace each Owner and Editor grant with the predefined or custom roles that cover the holder's actual duties, granted at the narrowest scope that works. The IAM role recommender's suggestions are a good starting point.
  • Reserve Owner for a small, named administrative group, preferably granted only temporarily through Privileged Access Manager or IAM Conditions with an expiry, and remove basic roles from service accounts.
  • Remove basic role grants at organisation and folder level unless there is a documented need, since they apply to every project beneath.
  • Grant roles to groups rather than to individual users, and enforce the constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains organisation policy constraint so that roles can be granted only to identities in the organisation's own domains.
  • Alert on IAM policy changes that grant basic roles, using the Admin Activity audit logs.
gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" --member="user:$USER_EMAIL" --role=roles/editor

Confirm the fix by searching the IAM policies again and finding basic role grants only where they are documented and approved.

entries.title: VPC Firewall Rules Allow Unrestricted Access to Management Ports
entries.summary: A VPC firewall rule lets SSH, RDP or other administrative ports be reached from any internet address, exposing those services to password attacks and exploits.
entries.description:
VPC firewall rules control which traffic reaches Compute Engine instances. Every VPC network has implied rules that deny all ingress and allow all egress, so inbound access exists only where a rule allows it. An ingress rule whose source range is 0.0.0.0/0 and whose ports include an administrative service exposes that service to the whole internet on every targeted instance that has an external IP address. The ports most often found are TCP 22 (SSH) and TCP 3389 (RDP), followed by WinRM and database ports.

A common cause is the default network that Compute Engine creates in new projects unless an organisation policy prevents it. It comes with pre-populated rules, including default-allow-ssh and default-allow-rdp, which allow TCP 22 and TCP 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0 to every instance in the network. Rules added during troubleshooting and never removed, and rules that target all instances rather than specific network tags or service accounts, are also common.

The exposure is identified by reviewing the firewall rules and hierarchical firewall policies that apply to each network, and confirmed by scanning the instances' external addresses from outside the organisation's network. Cloud posture tools report it as open SSH or RDP ports.
entries.impact: Exposed SSH and RDP services are quickly found by internet-wide scanning and then face continuous password guessing, password spraying and credential stuffing. A weak password, a leaked SSH private key or an unpatched vulnerability in the service gives an attacker interactive access to the instance and, from there, to the VPC network, the instance's attached service account and other systems it can reach. The risk is lower where SSH accepts only keys, RDP requires Network Level Authentication with strong passwords and the services are fully patched, but the exposure still gives every attacker on the internet an unrestricted opportunity to try.
entries.remediation:
• Delete the rule, or restrict its source ranges to the specific addresses administrators connect from. On the default network, delete default-allow-ssh and default-allow-rdp, or delete the default network entirely once nothing depends on it.
  • Provide administrative access through Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding, which needs ingress only from IAP's address range, 35.235.240.0/20, and authorises each connection through IAM, so that instances need no external IP address for administration.
  • Remove external IP addresses from instances that do not need them, and restrict new ones with the constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess organisation policy constraint.
  • Prevent recurrence with hierarchical firewall policies at organisation or folder level that deny administrative ports from 0.0.0.0/0, and with the constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation constraint for new projects.
  • Harden the services themselves: OS Login or key-based SSH authentication only, Network Level Authentication for RDP, and current patches.
gcloud compute firewall-rules delete default-allow-ssh default-allow-rdp gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-ssh-from-iap --network="$NETWORK" --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:22 --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20

Enable firewall rules logging on the administrative rules that remain, to record connections. Confirm the fix by reviewing the effective firewall rules for each instance and by scanning the external addresses from outside the organisation's network, expecting the ports to be filtered.

entries.title: Cloud SQL Instance Publicly Accessible
entries.summary: The Cloud SQL instance has a public IP address whose authorised networks include 0.0.0.0/0, so its database port accepts connections from anywhere on the internet.
entries.description:
A Cloud SQL instance can have a private IP address inside a VPC network, a public IP address, or both. With a public IP address, direct connections are accepted only from the address ranges listed as authorised networks, while connections made through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or the Cloud SQL language connectors are authorised through IAM instead. The finding applies where the authorised networks include 0.0.0.0/0 or other very large ranges, so that the database port (TCP 3306 for MySQL, 5432 for PostgreSQL or 1433 for SQL Server) accepts connections from anywhere.

The setting is usually added so that developers, reporting tools or applications with changing addresses can connect without private networking. It is often found together with instances that do not require SSL/TLS, and with built-in database users, such as root or postgres, that have weak passwords.

It is identified by reviewing each instance's connection settings, for example with gcloud sql instances describe, and confirmed by connecting to the public address from outside the organisation's network. Google's recommender also flags instances whose authorised networks include 0.0.0.0/0.
entries.impact: Anyone on the internet can attempt to log in to the database. Built-in or application users with weak or reused passwords can be guessed, and credentials leaked from connection strings in code, configuration files or compromised workstations can be used from anywhere. A successful login gives the attacker whatever that user can do, which for the built-in administrative users and most application accounts is full read and write access to the data. Where SSL/TLS is not required, credentials and data may also cross the internet unencrypted. The impact is lower where passwords are strong and users have limited rights, but the instance then has no network-level defence.
entries.remediation:
• Remove 0.0.0.0/0 and other broad ranges from the authorised networks, leaving only the specific addresses that genuinely need direct access.
  • Prefer private connectivity: give the instance a private IP address, connect from inside the VPC network, and remove the public IP address once nothing depends on it.
  • Where a public IP address must remain, connect through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or a Cloud SQL connector, which authorise connections through IAM and encrypt them, with no authorised networks configured.
  • Require encrypted connections through the instance's SSL mode, use IAM database authentication where the database engine supports it, and set strong, unique passwords for built-in users.
  • Prevent recurrence with the constraints/sql.restrictAuthorizedNetworks and constraints/sql.restrictPublicIp organisation policy constraints.
gcloud sql instances patch "$INSTANCE" --clear-authorized-networks gcloud sql instances patch "$INSTANCE" --ssl-mode=ENCRYPTED_ONLY

Confirm the fix by describing the instance again and by attempting a direct connection to its public address from outside the organisation's network, expecting it to be refused.

entries.title: Data Access Audit Logs Not Enabled
entries.summary: Data Access audit logs are not enabled for sensitive services, so reads of data and secrets, and many data changes, are not recorded in Cloud Audit Logs.
entries.description:
Cloud Audit Logs record activity in Google Cloud in several streams. Admin Activity logs, which record configuration changes such as IAM policy updates and resource creation, are always written and cannot be disabled. Data Access logs, which record API calls that read resource configuration or metadata (ADMIN_READ) and calls that read or write user-provided data (DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE), are disabled by default for most services, BigQuery being the main exception, because they can be voluminous.

The finding applies where Data Access logs are not enabled for services that hold sensitive data, such as Cloud Storage, Secret Manager, Cloud KMS, Cloud SQL and Firestore. Without them there is no record of who read an object in a bucket, accessed a secret version or used a key to decrypt data.

It is identified on the Audit Logs page of the console's IAM settings, or in the auditConfigs section of the organisation, folder and project IAM policies, which lists the services and log types enabled.
entries.impact: The gap does not by itself let an attacker in, but it leaves the organisation unable to determine what data an attacker read after compromising an account, a key or a workload, or to detect unusual reads of secrets and sensitive buckets as they happen. Investigations then have to assume that everything reachable was accessed, which widens the scope of any breach notification. The impact is lower where data access is recorded at another layer, such as by the application itself, or where the projects concerned hold no sensitive data.
entries.remediation:
• Enable DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE logs, and ADMIN_READ where useful, for services that hold sensitive data, at organisation or folder level so that every project inherits the configuration.
  • Manage volume and cost by enabling the logs selectively, by service and project, and by exempting well-understood high-volume principals, rather than leaving the logs off.
  • Route audit logs through an aggregated sink to a central logging project, a locked log bucket with retention set to the organisation's needs, or the organisation's SIEM, and restrict who can change sinks and log buckets.
  • Create alerts for sensitive data access, such as reads of high-value secrets or unusually large volumes of object reads.

For example, the following entry in an IAM policy enables Data Access logs for Cloud Storage:

auditConfigs: - auditLogConfigs: - logType: ADMIN_READ - logType: DATA_READ - logType: DATA_WRITE service: storage.googleapis.com

Confirm the fix by reading a test object or secret and finding the corresponding Data Access entry in Logs Explorer.

entries.title: OS Login Not Enforced
entries.summary: Linux instances accept SSH keys stored in project or instance metadata instead of OS Login, so SSH access is not tied to IAM and is not removed when a user's access ends.
entries.description:
Compute Engine Linux instances can control SSH access in two ways. With metadata-managed keys, public keys are added to the project or instance metadata and the guest environment creates matching local accounts, typically with sudo rights. With OS Login, enabled by setting the enable-oslogin metadata key to TRUE, access is granted through IAM roles such as roles/compute.osLogin and roles/compute.osAdminLogin, Linux accounts are tied to Google identities, and access ends when the role is removed or the user is suspended.

The finding applies where OS Login is not enabled, or is enabled at project level but switched off on individual instances, and the constraints/compute.requireOsLogin organisation policy constraint is not enforced. Metadata keys persist after the person who added them leaves, are not linked to an identity the organisation manages, and can be added by anyone with permission to change instance or project metadata. OS Login does not apply to Windows instances.

It is identified by reviewing project and instance metadata, for example with gcloud compute project-info describe and gcloud compute instances describe, for the enable-oslogin key and for ssh-keys entries, and by checking the organisation policies in force.
entries.impact: Without OS Login, SSH access cannot be reliably revoked or audited through IAM. Keys belonging to former staff, contractors or decommissioned systems remain valid on every instance that trusts them, and a stolen private key keeps working until someone finds and removes it from metadata. A principal able to edit metadata can add their own key and gain administrative access to instances without holding any SSH-specific role, a technique attackers use for persistence. Exploitation requires either a valid private key or permission to change metadata, as well as network access to the instance's SSH port.
entries.remediation:
• Enable OS Login across each project by setting enable-oslogin to TRUE in project metadata, and enforce it with the constraints/compute.requireOsLogin organisation policy constraint so that individual instances cannot opt out.
  • Grant roles/compute.osLogin, or roles/compute.osAdminLogin only where administrative rights are needed, to groups rather than individuals, on the projects or instances they need.
  • Enable OS Login 2-step verification with the enable-oslogin-2fa metadata key for administrative access.
  • Once OS Login is in use, remove the keys held in project and instance metadata.
  • Restrict who can change instance and project metadata, and combine OS Login with Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding so that SSH is not exposed to the internet.
gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata enable-oslogin=TRUE

Confirm the fix by checking that the organisation policy is enforced and that metadata keys are no longer accepted, and by signing in with an account that holds an OS Login role and with one that does not, expecting only the first to succeed.

entries.title: Project-Wide SSH Keys Allowed
entries.summary: Instances accept SSH keys stored in project-wide metadata, so a single key, or anyone able to edit project metadata, gains access to every Linux instance in the project.
entries.description:
Where Compute Engine instances use metadata-managed SSH keys rather than OS Login, keys can be stored in instance metadata, which applies to one instance, or in project metadata under ssh-keys, which applies to every Linux instance in the project. An instance accepts project-wide keys unless its metadata sets block-project-ssh-keys to TRUE. Where project-wide keys are not blocked, gcloud compute ssh adds the user's key to project metadata by default, so keys accumulate there as people connect to different instances.

The finding applies where instances, particularly sensitive ones, accept project-wide keys. Each key in project metadata then grants access to every instance in the project, typically with sudo rights, and the list is rarely reviewed, so it often contains keys of former staff and contractors. Any principal with permission to change project metadata can add a key and reach every instance.

It is identified by listing project metadata with gcloud compute project-info describe and checking each instance's metadata for block-project-ssh-keys. The issue does not arise where OS Login is enforced, since metadata keys are then ignored.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains any private key listed in project metadata, or any principal able to edit project metadata, can sign in to every Linux instance in the project, including those that should be reachable only by a small team. A single compromised key or workstation therefore exposes the whole project rather than one instance, and removing a departed user's access means finding their key among many. Exploitation requires a valid private key or metadata permissions, as well as network access to the instances' SSH port.
entries.remediation:
• Prefer OS Login, enforced through the constraints/compute.requireOsLogin organisation policy constraint, so that SSH access is granted through IAM and metadata keys are ignored.
  • Where metadata keys must still be used, set block-project-ssh-keys to TRUE on each instance, and add only the keys that instance needs to its own metadata.
  • Remove the ssh-keys entries from project metadata once no instance relies on them, and check any that remain against current staff and systems.
  • Restrict who can change project metadata, and monitor the Admin Activity audit logs for metadata changes.
gcloud compute instances add-metadata "$INSTANCE" --zone="$ZONE" --metadata block-project-ssh-keys=TRUE

Confirm the fix by checking each instance's metadata, and by attempting to sign in to a protected instance with a key held only in project metadata, expecting the sign-in to fail.

entries.title: Serial Port Access Enabled
entries.summary: Interactive serial console access is enabled on Compute Engine instances, giving an administrative route to them that firewall rules and network restrictions do not control.
entries.description:
Compute Engine instances have virtual serial ports, and setting the serial-port-enable metadata key to TRUE, on an instance or across a project, enables interactive access to the instance's serial console. Users then connect through Google's serial console gateway, for example with gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port, which reaches the instance's console regardless of its network configuration, including instances with no external IP address and instances whose VPC firewall rules block all ingress.

Google's documentation warns that the interactive serial console does not support IP-based access restrictions: once it is enabled, connections can be attempted from any address by anyone holding an authorised SSH key and the instance's details, and the console then presents the operating system's own login prompt. The console remains available even when the instance's network or SSH service has failed, which is why it is enabled for troubleshooting, and it is often left enabled afterwards, sometimes together with local passwords created for console login.

It is identified by reviewing project and instance metadata for serial-port-enable, and by checking whether the constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess organisation policy constraint is enforced.
entries.impact: The serial console provides an administrative route to the instance that bypasses the VPC firewall rules, Identity-Aware Proxy and any other network-level restrictions the organisation relies on to control administrative access. An attacker who obtains an authorised SSH key, or the IAM permissions needed to add one, together with valid operating system credentials, can reach the instance's console from anywhere and act with the rights of the account they log in as, which is often an administrative one. The exposure is limited by the need for both a key accepted by the gateway and an operating system login, but those are then the only controls protecting the console.
entries.remediation:
• Disable interactive serial port access by removing the serial-port-enable metadata key, or setting it to FALSE, on every instance and at project level.
  • Enforce the constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess organisation policy constraint at organisation or folder level, and allow temporary exceptions at project level only while troubleshooting a specific instance, removing them afterwards.
  • Remove local passwords created for console login once troubleshooting is complete.
  • Restrict who can change instance and project metadata, since that permission can re-enable the console, and alert on metadata changes that enable it, using the Admin Activity audit logs.
  • Provide routine administrative access through OS Login and Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding instead.
gcloud compute instances add-metadata "$INSTANCE" --zone="$ZONE" --metadata serial-port-enable=FALSE gcloud compute project-info add-metadata --metadata serial-port-enable=FALSE

Confirm the fix by reviewing the metadata and the organisation policy, and by attempting to connect with gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port, expecting the connection to be refused.

entries.title: Privileged Containers
entries.summary: One or more containers run in privileged mode, which removes most of the isolation between the container and the node it runs on.
entries.description:
One or more containers run in privileged mode, set with securityContext.privileged: true in a Kubernetes pod specification or the --privileged option of docker run. A privileged container receives every Linux capability and access to the node's devices, and runs largely outside the confinement that the container runtime normally applies, such as seccomp filtering and mandatory access control profiles. Root in a privileged container therefore has almost the same power as root on the node.

Privileged mode is often found on monitoring, logging, networking and storage agents that need some access to the node, and on containers that build images or run Docker inside a container. It can be identified by reviewing workload manifests and pod specifications, for example in the output of kubectl get pods -A -o yaml, by inspecting containers with docker inspect, or from inside a container, where a full effective capability set (CapEff) in /proc/self/status and the node's disks visible under /dev indicate privileged mode. Configuration scanners and Kubernetes benchmark tools report it as a failed check.

Settings that grant part of the same power, such as added capabilities like SYS_ADMIN or allowPrivilegeEscalation: true, should be reviewed at the same time.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains code execution in a privileged container, for example through a vulnerability in the application it runs, can escape to the node with little effort, by mounting the node's disk, loading kernel modules or abusing kernel interfaces exposed to the container. Root on a node gives access to every other container scheduled on it, together with their secrets and service account tokens, and to the node's own cluster credentials, which may allow further movement through the cluster. The main limit on the impact is the effort needed to compromise the container first.
entries.remediation:
Remove privileged mode from every workload that does not strictly need it:

  • Set privileged: false, or remove the field, in each container's securityContext, drop all capabilities and add back only those the workload is known to need.
  • Where an agent genuinely needs access to the node, give it the narrowest access that works, such as one capability, one device or one read-only path, instead of full privilege, and run it in a dedicated namespace that few people can deploy to.
  • Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and use the runtime's default seccomp profile.
  • Enforce the Baseline or Restricted Pod Security Standard on namespaces through Pod Security Admission, or an equivalent policy engine, so that new privileged pods are rejected.
securityContext: privileged: false allowPrivilegeEscalation: false capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault

Where privileged mode cannot be removed at once, restrict those workloads to dedicated nodes with taints and node selectors, limit who can execute commands in them, and monitor them closely. Confirm the fix by searching all pod specifications for privileged: true and checking that only documented exceptions remain.

entries.title: Containers Running as Root
entries.summary: Containers run their processes as root, so compromising the application gives an attacker root inside the container and makes an escape to the node easier.
entries.description:
One or more containers run their processes as root (user ID 0). A container runs as the user its image specifies, and many images set no USER instruction and so run as root; Kubernetes keeps that user unless runAsUser or runAsNonRoot is set in the pod's or container's securityContext.

Unless user namespaces are in use, root in a container is the same user ID as root on the node. The container's capability set, seccomp profile and other runtime controls still restrict it, but files the node shares with the container, such as mounted volumes, are accessed as root, and many container escape techniques and runtime vulnerabilities, for example the runc flaw CVE-2019-5736, require root inside the container.

The issue can be confirmed by running id in the container, by reviewing the image's USER instruction and the pod's securityContext, or from configuration scanners and Kubernetes benchmark tools, which report containers that may run as root.
entries.impact: Running as root does not by itself break the container's isolation, but it removes a layer of defence. An attacker who compromises the application gains full control of the container, including every file in it, and can install tools or change the application. Where the container also has added capabilities or a writable host mount, or runs on an unpatched kernel or container runtime, root in the container makes an escape to the node considerably more likely.
entries.remediation:
Run every container as a dedicated non-root user:

  • Create an unprivileged user in the image and select it with a USER instruction, using a numeric user ID so that Kubernetes can verify it is not root.
  • Set runAsNonRoot: true and explicit runAsUser and runAsGroup values in the pod or container securityContext, so that the kubelet refuses to start a container that would run as root.
  • Combine this with allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and dropping all capabilities, so the process cannot regain root through setuid binaries. Where the application listens on a port below 1024, have it listen on a higher port and map the Service port to it.
  • Enforce the Restricted Pod Security Standard on application namespaces so that new workloads must run as non-root.
  • Where a workload must run as root, use user namespaces (hostUsers: false) on clusters that support them, or Docker's rootless mode or user namespace remapping, so that root in the container is not root on the node.
securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 runAsGroup: 10001 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false capabilities: drop: ["ALL"]

Confirm the fix by running id in each affected container, and by checking that a test pod running as root is rejected in namespaces that enforce the Restricted standard.

patterns: \b(image|container) user should not be .?root|\b(container|containers|pod) (is |are )?running as root\b|\brunAsNonRoot\b

entries.title: Containers Sharing Host Namespaces
entries.summary: Pods share the node's process, network or IPC namespace, so their containers can see and interact with the node's processes and network traffic.
entries.description:
Containers are normally isolated from the node through Linux namespaces. Setting hostPID: true, hostNetwork: true or hostIPC: true in a pod specification, or --pid=host, --network=host or --ipc=host with Docker, removes that isolation for the corresponding resource, so the pod shares it with the node itself.

In the node's process namespace, a container can see every process on the node with its command line and, with enough privileges, read process memory and environments or enter other processes' namespaces. In the node's network namespace, it uses the node's interfaces directly: it can reach services listening only on the node's loopback address, capture the node's traffic if it holds the NET_RAW capability, which Docker and containerd grant by default, and may not be subject to network policies, depending on the network plugin. The node's IPC namespace exposes shared memory used by processes on the node.

The settings can be found in pod specifications or with configuration scanners. They are common on node agents for monitoring, logging and networking, where they may be justified, and are rarely needed by application workloads.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a container that shares host namespaces can collect credentials and other secrets from the command lines and environments of the node's processes, reach services that listen only on the node, including cloud instance metadata services that may be blocked for ordinary pods, and capture unencrypted traffic to and from other pods on the node. Combined with privileged mode or added capabilities, the host process namespace allows a direct escape to the node, for example by entering the namespaces of a host process with nsenter.
entries.remediation:
• Remove hostPID, hostNetwork and hostIPC from every workload that does not need them; application workloads almost never do.
  • Where a workload needs to receive traffic on the node's address, publish it through a Service, for example of type NodePort or LoadBalancer, instead of using the host network.
  • For node agents that genuinely need host namespaces, document the exception, run them in a dedicated namespace that few people can deploy to, do not combine host namespaces with privileged mode or added capabilities, and drop NET_RAW where packet capture is not needed.
  • Enforce the Baseline or Restricted Pod Security Standard, both of which forbid host namespaces, on all other namespaces.

Confirm the fix by listing pods that set any of the three fields to true and checking that only documented exceptions remain.

entries.title: Sensitive hostPath Mounts
entries.summary: Pods mount sensitive directories or files from the node's filesystem, giving their containers access to node configuration, credentials or runtime sockets.
entries.description:
A hostPath volume mounts a file or directory from the node's own filesystem into a pod. When the path is sensitive, such as the root directory, /etc, /root, /home, /proc, /sys, /dev, the kubelet's directory /var/lib/kubelet, or the directories holding the container runtime's data and sockets, the container gains access to data and interfaces that belong to the node rather than to the workload.

Mounts are writable unless readOnly: true is set on the volume mount, and a writable mount of a sensitive path lets the container change the node's configuration directly. Even a read-only mount can expose the kubelet's credentials, the secrets and service account tokens of other pods on the node, and keys stored on the node.

These volumes can be found by reviewing pod specifications or with configuration scanners. Some node agents use them legitimately, for example log collectors that read container logs, so each mount should be judged on its path, whether it is writable and what the workload needs.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a container with a writable mount of a sensitive node path can usually take over the node, for example by adding a cron job, a systemd unit or an SSH key, or by changing files that the node runs as root. A read-only mount can still give them node and cluster credentials that allow further movement through the cluster. Taking over one node exposes every workload scheduled on it.
entries.remediation:
• Remove hostPath volumes from application workloads, and use persistent volumes, emptyDir, ConfigMaps, Secrets or projected volumes for the data they need.
  • Where a node agent needs host files, mount the narrowest specific path rather than a parent directory, set readOnly: true on the volume mount wherever possible, and never mount the root directory, the kubelet's directory or container runtime sockets.
  • Run such containers as a non-root user, so that file permissions on the node still apply to them.
  • Enforce the Baseline or Restricted Pod Security Standard, which forbid hostPath volumes, on every namespace that does not need them, and where exceptions are required use a policy engine that allows only specific approved paths.
volumes: - name: app-logs hostPath: path: /var/log/app type: Directory containers: - name: log-collector volumeMounts: - name: app-logs mountPath: /logs readOnly: true

Confirm the fix by listing every hostPath volume in the cluster and checking that each remaining path is specific, read-only where possible, and documented.

entries.title: Docker Socket Mounted Into a Container
entries.summary: A container has the Docker daemon's socket mounted, which lets anyone in the container control Docker on the host and so gain root on it.
entries.description:
The Docker daemon is controlled through a Unix socket, normally /var/run/docker.sock, which offers the full Docker Engine API to any process that can connect to it. Through the API, a client can create and start containers with any settings, including privileged containers that mount the host's root filesystem. Mounting this socket into a container, with -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock or a hostPath volume, therefore gives that container control of the host.

Mounting the socket read-only does not help, because the API remains reachable through it. The same applies to the sockets of other container runtimes, such as containerd's /run/containerd/containerd.sock and CRI-O's /var/run/crio/crio.sock, and to mounts of a parent directory that contains them.

The mount is common in CI/CD runners, monitoring agents, reverse proxies that discover containers, and container management tools. It can be found in pod specifications and Compose files, or from inside a container by locating the socket and querying it, for example with curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/version.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains code execution in the container, or can influence the requests it sends to Docker, can start a new privileged container with the host's filesystem mounted and so gain root on the host. From there they can read the data and secrets of every other container, tamper with images and workloads, and use the host's own credentials to move further into the environment. On a Kubernetes node, this means the compromise of the node and every pod scheduled on it.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the socket mount from every container that does not strictly need it; most applications never need to talk to the container runtime.
  • For CI/CD builds, use an image builder that does not need the host's daemon, such as a rootless or daemonless builder, or run builds on dedicated hosts that hold nothing else of value.
  • Where a tool only needs information about containers, give it a narrower interface, such as the Kubernetes API with a read-only role, or a filtering proxy in front of the socket that allows only the specific API calls it needs.
  • Where Docker is used directly, consider rootless mode, so that control of the daemon does not mean root on the host.
  • Prevent new mounts of runtime sockets with the Baseline Pod Security Standard, which forbids hostPath volumes, or with a policy engine rule.

As an interim measure, restrict the affected workloads to dedicated nodes and limit who can deploy them or execute commands in them. Confirm the fix by searching pod specifications and Compose files for docker.sock, containerd.sock and crio.sock, and checking that no running container has them mounted.

entries.title: Docker Engine API Exposed Without Authentication
entries.summary: The Docker Engine API is reachable over the network without authentication, so anyone who can reach it can run containers on the host and gain root on it.
entries.description:
The Docker daemon can be configured to accept API requests over TCP, with a -H tcp:// option for dockerd or a hosts entry in its configuration. Unless it is also configured for mutual TLS, the API on that port requires no authentication, and without TLS it is not encrypted either. Docker's current documentation says that exposing the API over HTTP without TLS is no longer permitted and stops the daemon at startup; older releases accept it. By convention, port 2375 is used for the unprotected API and port 2376 for the TLS-protected one. The same weakness exists when TLS is enabled without client certificate verification (--tls without --tlsverify), because any client can then connect.

The exposure is confirmed by requesting /version or /info from the port, which return details of the engine and the host, or by pointing the Docker client at the port with its -H option and listing containers. Network scanners and internet search engines identify the service from these responses, and exposed Docker APIs are routinely found and abused by automated cryptomining campaigns.
entries.impact: Anyone who can reach the port has full control of the Docker daemon, which runs as root. They can list, stop and inspect containers, read their environment variables, logs and files, pull and run their own images, and start a privileged container with the host's root filesystem mounted, which gives them root on the host. Exposed APIs are commonly used to deploy cryptocurrency miners and as a foothold into the wider network.
entries.remediation:
• Stop the daemon listening on TCP unless remote access is genuinely required: remove the tcp:// entries from its -H options and from hosts in /etc/docker/daemon.json, so that it listens only on its local Unix socket.
  • Where remote access is needed, use the Docker client's SSH transport (a DOCKER_HOST value beginning ssh://), or configure mutual TLS with --tlsverify, --tlscacert, --tlscert and --tlskey, so that only clients holding a certificate from a dedicated certificate authority are accepted. Treat those client certificates as root credentials for the host.
  • Restrict the port with a host or network firewall to the management hosts that need it.
  • If the port has been reachable from an untrusted network, check the host for signs of compromise, such as unknown containers, images, users or scheduled tasks.
dockerd --tlsverify --tlscacert=ca.pem --tlscert=server-cert.pem --tlskey=server-key.pem -H=0.0.0.0:2376

Confirm the fix by checking from another host that port 2375 is closed and that port 2376, if used, refuses clients that do not present a valid certificate.

entries.title: Kubernetes API Server Allows Anonymous Access
entries.summary: The Kubernetes API server accepts unauthenticated requests and authorises them to reach more than basic health and version information.
entries.description:
The Kubernetes API server treats requests that carry no credentials, and are not rejected by another authentication method, as coming from the user system:anonymous in the group system:unauthenticated. Anonymous authentication is enabled by default, and in a default cluster these identities may only read a few discovery and health endpoints, such as /version, /healthz, /livez and /readyz.

The weakness arises when authorisation rules grant them more: a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated, often added while troubleshooting, or the AlwaysAllow authorisation mode, which permits every request. Unauthenticated users can then list namespaces, pods and other resources, and in the worst cases read Secrets or create workloads.

It can be confirmed by sending requests without an Authorization header to the API server, usually on port 6443 or 443, for example for /api/v1/namespaces or /api/v1/pods, and by reviewing role bindings for those subjects with kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o wide. A 403 Forbidden response naming system:anonymous shows that anonymous authentication is enabled but not authorised for that resource.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the API server can read whatever the anonymous bindings allow. Read access to pods, ConfigMaps and other objects reveals the cluster's structure, images and environment variables, which often contain credentials, and read access to Secrets yields service account tokens and application credentials that can lead to full compromise of the cluster. Where the bindings allow creating or changing workloads, the attacker can run code in the cluster directly. The risk is greatest when the API server is reachable from the internet.
entries.remediation:
• Remove every RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding whose subjects include system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated, apart from the default system:public-info-viewer binding and, on kubeadm clusters, kubeadm:bootstrap-signer-clusterinfo, which new nodes need to read the public cluster-info ConfigMap when joining with a bootstrap token.
  • Make sure the API server uses the Node and RBAC authorisation modes and never AlwaysAllow.
  • Where nothing depends on anonymous requests, start the API server with --anonymous-auth=false. Check health checks and load balancer probes first, as some rely on anonymous access to the health endpoints; newer Kubernetes releases can instead limit anonymous access to named endpoints through the authentication configuration file.
  • Restrict network access to the API server to administrators, nodes and the systems that need it, rather than exposing it to the internet.
kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(any(.subjects[]?; .name == "system:anonymous" or .name == "system:unauthenticated")) | .metadata.name'

Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated requests and checking that only the health and version endpoints respond, or that every request is refused with 401 Unauthorized.

entries.title: Kubelet API Accessible Without Authentication
entries.summary: The kubelet API on a node accepts unauthenticated requests, letting anyone who can reach it list pods and run commands in any container on that node.
entries.description:
The kubelet, the agent that runs on every Kubernetes node, exposes an HTTPS API, by default on port 10250, which the API server uses to read container logs, run commands in containers and forward ports. If the kubelet accepts anonymous requests and authorises every request, which is what its command-line defaults do (--anonymous-auth=true with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow), anyone who can reach the port can use this API. Common installers and managed services configure the kubelet more securely, so the weakness is mostly found on manually built, customised or older clusters.

It can be confirmed by requesting the /pods endpoint on port 10250 without credentials: a list of pods confirms the exposure, while 401 Unauthorized shows that anonymous access is disabled. Tools such as kubeletctl automate these checks. The kubelet's read-only port, conventionally 10255, serves pod and node information over plain HTTP without any authentication wherever it is enabled.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach an exposed kubelet can list every pod on the node and run commands in any of its containers through the /run and /exec endpoints, without any Kubernetes credentials and without the requests appearing in the API server's audit log. Commands in containers give access to their data, secrets and service account tokens, and a privileged pod on the node leads to control of the node itself. Every exposed node exposes every workload scheduled on it.
entries.remediation:
• Disable anonymous access and delegate authorisation to the API server, in the kubelet configuration file or with the equivalent flags (--anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=Webhook and --client-ca-file).
  • Configure the API server to authenticate to kubelets with a client certificate (--kubelet-client-certificate and --kubelet-client-key) and grant that identity only the kubelet API permissions it needs.
  • Disable the read-only port by setting readOnlyPort: 0.
  • Restrict access to port 10250 on every node to the control plane and the monitoring systems that need it.
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration authentication: anonymous: enabled: false webhook: enabled: true x509: clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt authorization: mode: Webhook readOnlyPort: 0

Restart the kubelet on each node after the change, then confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated requests to ports 10250 and 10255.

entries.title: etcd Exposed Without Authentication
entries.summary: The etcd database that holds the Kubernetes cluster's state accepts connections without client certificate authentication, exposing every Secret and object in the cluster.
entries.description:
etcd is the key-value store in which the Kubernetes API server keeps the entire state of the cluster, including every Secret, the definition of every workload and the cluster's access control rules. Kubernetes protects it with mutual TLS: etcd should accept client connections, by default on port 2379, only from clients presenting a certificate issued by its own certificate authority, and treat peer connections between etcd members, on port 2380, in the same way.

The weakness arises when etcd listens on a reachable interface without client certificate authentication (--client-cert-auth with a trusted CA), or over plain HTTP, so that anyone who can connect can read and write its keys. Kubernetes stores its objects under the /registry prefix, and Secrets are not encrypted in etcd unless encryption at rest has been configured on the API server.

It can be confirmed by connecting with etcdctl without a client certificate, for example listing keys with etcdctl get /registry --prefix --keys-only, or by requesting the /version endpoint. Network scanners identify the service on its default ports.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach etcd can read every Secret in the cluster, including application credentials, cloud keys and any long-lived service account tokens, and can change the cluster's stored state directly, for example to grant themselves administrative rights, bypassing the API server's authentication, authorisation and admission controls entirely. This amounts to full control of the cluster, and often of the cloud and infrastructure accounts whose credentials it holds.
entries.remediation:
• Require client certificate authentication on etcd: set --client-cert-auth=true with --trusted-ca-file, serve TLS with --cert-file and --key-file, and protect peer traffic in the same way with --peer-client-cert-auth=true, --peer-trusted-ca-file, --peer-cert-file and --peer-key-file.
  • Use a certificate authority dedicated to etcd, and give the API server its own client certificate through --etcd-cafile, --etcd-certfile and --etcd-keyfile.
  • Bind etcd only to the interfaces it needs, and allow ports 2379 and 2380 only from the API servers and the other etcd members with a host or network firewall.
  • Configure encryption at rest for Secrets on the API server, and protect etcd backups and snapshots as carefully as etcd itself.
  • If etcd has been reachable by untrusted parties, treat every Secret in the cluster as compromised and rotate it.

Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated etcdctl connection from outside the control plane and checking that it is refused.

entries.title: Kubernetes Dashboard Exposed
entries.summary: The Kubernetes Dashboard is reachable from an untrusted network, where it may allow cluster management without credentials or through an over-privileged account.
entries.description:
The Kubernetes Dashboard is an optional web interface for managing a cluster. It acts on the cluster with the credentials that users sign in with or, where its login can be skipped, with the permissions of its own service account. Many installation guides grant that service account broad rights, sometimes cluster-admin, so that the Dashboard works without a token.

The weakness arises when the Dashboard is published beyond the administrators who need it, through a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service, an Ingress, or kubectl proxy bound to a public interface. It is most serious when the skip option is enabled (--enable-skip-login), when the Dashboard's service account is privileged, or in versions before 1.10.1, which allowed authentication to be bypassed (CVE-2018-18264). An exposed Dashboard was the starting point of well-publicised compromises in which attackers ran cryptocurrency miners in cloud Kubernetes clusters.

It can be identified from the Dashboard's login page or interface on an exposed address, from the Services and Ingresses in its namespace, and by testing whether the interface can be used without signing in and what its service account is allowed to do.
entries.impact: Where the Dashboard can be used without credentials, an attacker can do whatever its service account permits, which can include viewing workloads, logs and configuration, reading Secrets and, where the account is privileged, deploying containers and taking control of the cluster. Where a token is required, the exposure still gives an attacker on an untrusted network a route to a powerful administrative interface, which leaked tokens or a future vulnerability in the Dashboard could open.
entries.remediation:
• Remove the Dashboard and, where a web interface is still needed, move to a maintained alternative such as Headlamp. The Dashboard project has been archived and will receive no further updates or security fixes.
  • Do not publish it through public LoadBalancer or NodePort Services or Ingresses. Reach it through kubectl port-forward or kubectl proxy on the administrator's own machine, or behind an authenticating proxy with multi-factor authentication on an internal network.
  • Disable the skip option and require users to sign in with their own identity rather than a shared token, so that their own RBAC permissions apply.
  • Reduce the Dashboard's own service account to the minimum permissions it needs, and remove any cluster-admin binding to it.
  • If the Dashboard has been usable without authentication, review the cluster for unknown workloads and rotate the Secrets it could read.

Confirm the fix by checking from an untrusted network that the Dashboard is no longer reachable, and from inside the network that it cannot be used without signing in.

entries.title: Overly Permissive Kubernetes RBAC
entries.summary: Kubernetes roles grant users, groups or service accounts more access than they need, such as wildcard rights or permissions that allow escalation to cluster administrator.
entries.description:
Kubernetes role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions through Roles and ClusterRoles, which RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings attach to users, groups and service accounts. The weakness arises when these grants are broader than the subject needs, for example cluster-admin bound to application service accounts or to broad groups such as system:authenticated, or roles that use the * wildcard for verbs or resources.

Several permissions amount to, or lead quickly to, full control even when they look narrow: listing or reading Secrets across the cluster; creating pods or workload resources, which allows a pod to run as any service account in the namespace and, without Pod Security Admission, to run privileged; the escalate, bind and impersonate verbs; the nodes/proxy subresource; creating service account tokens; approving certificate signing requests; and changing admission webhooks. Membership of the system:masters group bypasses RBAC entirely.

Excessive permissions are identified by reviewing roles and bindings, by testing what each identity can do with kubectl auth can-i --list and its --as option, and with RBAC analysis tools that flag risky permissions and escalation paths.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains the credentials of an over-privileged identity, such as a service account token taken from a compromised pod or a leaked CI/CD credential, gains its permissions. Depending on the grant, this allows reading every Secret in the cluster, running code in other workloads, creating privileged pods that take over nodes, or granting themselves cluster administrator rights, and from there reaching any cloud or external system whose credentials the cluster holds.
entries.remediation:
• Inventory all bindings, for example with kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o wide, and remove those that are not needed, starting with cluster-admin and wildcard grants.
  • Give each workload its own service account with a namespaced Role that lists only the resources and verbs it uses, and avoid ClusterRoleBindings for application identities.
  • Restrict the high-risk permissions listed above to a small number of administrative identities, and do not add users to system:masters.
  • Use groups from an external identity provider with short-lived credentials for human access, and review bindings regularly and whenever staff change roles.
  • Enforce Pod Security Admission so that permission to create pods does not imply control of nodes.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: read-app-settings namespace: app rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["configmaps"] resourceNames: ["app-settings"] verbs: ["get"]

Confirm the fix by repeating kubectl auth can-i --list for the affected identities and checking that only the intended permissions remain.

entries.title: Secrets in Plain Environment Variables or ConfigMaps
entries.summary: Credentials are placed in plain environment variables or ConfigMaps instead of being handled as secrets, so anyone who can read workload definitions can read them.
entries.description:
Workloads receive credentials, such as database passwords, API keys and tokens, as literal values in the environment variables of their pod specifications, or from ConfigMaps. Both are stored and shown as ordinary configuration: anyone with read access to the pods, deployments or ConfigMaps in the namespace can see the values with kubectl get -o yaml or kubectl describe, and the values also appear in the manifests, Helm values and repositories used to deploy the workload. Kubernetes documents that ConfigMaps provide no secrecy or encryption.

Environment variables add further exposure even when their values come from a Secret: they are inherited by child processes, visible in the process environment under /proc, and often included in crash reports, debug pages and logs.

The issue is identified by reviewing manifests and the output of kubectl get pods,deployments,configmaps -A -o yaml for credential-like names and values, and with secret scanning tools run against manifests, images and repositories. Kubernetes Secrets are themselves only base64-encoded and are stored unencrypted in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured, so moving a value into a Secret is necessary but not sufficient.
entries.impact: Anyone with read access to workload configuration, which is usually granted far more widely than access to Secrets, can obtain the credentials and use them against the databases, cloud services and third-party APIs they protect. The values also tend to leak through repositories, CI/CD logs and diagnostic output, and are rarely rotated, so a single exposure can give lasting access. The impact depends on what the credentials unlock.
entries.remediation:
• Move credentials into Kubernetes Secrets, or preferably an external secrets manager integrated through a CSI driver or an operator, and remove them from pod specifications, ConfigMaps, images and repositories.
  • Mount secrets as files in read-only volumes rather than environment variables where the application allows it.
  • Restrict get, list and watch on Secrets to the identities that need them, remembering that permission to create pods in a namespace also allows its Secrets to be read.
  • Enable encryption at rest for Secrets on the API server, preferably with a KMS provider, and rewrite existing Secrets so that they are stored encrypted.
  • Rotate every credential that has been held in plain configuration, since it should be assumed to be exposed.
volumes: - name: db-credentials secret: secretName: db-credentials containers: - name: app volumeMounts: - name: db-credentials mountPath: /var/run/secrets/app readOnly: true

Confirm the fix by checking that no credential values remain in pod specifications, ConfigMaps or deployment repositories, and that the rotated credentials are read only from their new location.

entries.title: No Kubernetes Network Policies
entries.summary: The cluster has no network policies, so every pod can connect to every other pod and service, and to external networks, without restriction.
entries.description:
By default, Kubernetes allows all network traffic between pods, across all namespaces, and from pods to any destination the node can reach. NetworkPolicy resources restrict this by selecting pods and defining which incoming and outgoing connections they accept, but only where the cluster's network plugin enforces them; creating a policy has no effect on a plugin that does not.

The weakness arises when no policies are defined, or when policies cover only a few workloads. Pods that no policy selects remain open in both directions, which is why a default deny policy in each namespace is the usual starting point. It is identified by listing policies with kubectl get networkpolicies -A, checking which namespaces have none, and testing from a pod whether services in other namespaces, the nodes, the cloud instance metadata service and the internet can be reached.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises one pod, for example through an application vulnerability, can reach every other workload in the cluster, including databases, internal APIs and administrative interfaces assumed to be internal, as well as the kubelet on each node and, in cloud clusters, often the instance metadata service and the credentials it issues. Unrestricted egress also lets them download tools and send data out. Network policies do not prevent the first compromise, but their absence lets it spread.
entries.remediation:
• Confirm that the cluster's network plugin enforces NetworkPolicy, and move to one that does if not.
  • Apply a default deny policy for ingress and egress in every application namespace, then add policies that allow only the connections each workload needs, selected by pod and namespace labels.
  • When restricting egress, allow DNS lookups to the cluster DNS service, and block the cloud instance metadata address (169.254.169.254) for pods that do not need it.
  • Limit egress to the internet to the destinations each workload needs, through an egress gateway or proxy where possible.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny-all spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress

Confirm the fix by repeating the connection tests from a pod in each namespace and checking that only the intended connections succeed.

entries.title: Service Account Tokens Mounted Unnecessarily
entries.summary: Pods receive a Kubernetes service account token they do not need, which an attacker who compromises the pod can use to call the Kubernetes API.
entries.description:
By default, Kubernetes mounts a token for the pod's service account into every container, at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, so that the workload can call the Kubernetes API. Most application workloads never call the API, yet still receive the token because automountServiceAccountToken is not set to false on the pod or its service account.

In current Kubernetes versions the mounted token is time-limited and bound to the pod, and the default service account has no permissions beyond basic discovery unless they have been granted. The weakness matters most where workloads share the default service account and someone has granted it permissions, or where a workload's own service account holds rights that the workload rarely uses.

It can be identified by reviewing pod and service account specifications, or from inside a container by checking for the token file and testing what it allows with kubectl auth can-i --list or direct API requests.
entries.impact: An attacker who gains code execution in the pod can read the token and act on the Kubernetes API as the service account, from inside the cluster or from anywhere the API server is reachable. With default permissions this gives little more than information about the API, but where the account has been granted rights, it can allow reading Secrets, changing workloads or escalating further. Removing unneeded tokens takes away a step that many container compromises rely on.
entries.remediation:
• Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on service accounts, including the default service account of each namespace, and on pods that do not call the Kubernetes API. A value set on the pod takes precedence over the service account's.
  • Give each workload that does need the API its own service account with a minimal Role, rather than using or granting rights to default.
  • Where a workload needs a token for another audience, such as a secrets manager or cloud identity federation, use a projected service account token volume with that audience and a short expiry.
  • Remove long-lived service account token Secrets that are no longer needed.
apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: default namespace: app automountServiceAccountToken: false

Confirm the fix by checking that the token file is absent from the affected containers.

entries.title: Pod Security Admission Not Enforced
entries.summary: No namespace enforces a Pod Security Standard, so anyone able to create pods can run privileged containers or mount the node's filesystem.
entries.description:
Pod Security Admission is the built-in Kubernetes admission controller that checks pods against the Pod Security Standards: Privileged, which is unrestricted; Baseline, which blocks known privilege escalations such as privileged containers, host namespaces, hostPath volumes and capabilities beyond a default set; and Restricted, which also requires non-root users, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation and a seccomp profile. It replaced PodSecurityPolicy, which was removed in Kubernetes 1.25.

Each namespace selects a level through labels for three modes: enforce rejects violating pods, while audit and warn only record or display violations. A namespace without an enforce label falls back to the cluster default, which is Privileged unless the admission configuration sets another level. The weakness exists when no namespace, or only a few, enforce Baseline or Restricted, and no other policy engine, such as Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy rules, enforces equivalent controls.

It is identified by listing namespace labels with kubectl get namespaces --show-labels, reviewing the API server's admission configuration, and attempting to create a test pod that violates Baseline in an application namespace.
entries.impact: Without enforcement, any user, pipeline or compromised workload that can create pods in a namespace can run a privileged pod, share the node's namespaces or mount its filesystem, and so gain root on a node, from where every pod scheduled there and the credentials they hold are exposed. Kubernetes' own guidance notes that users who can run privileged pods can use them to gain node access, and recommends enforcing Baseline or Restricted wherever pod creators are not fully trusted. Exploitation requires an identity that can create workloads, such as a developer or CI/CD credential or an over-privileged service account.
entries.remediation:
• Label every application namespace to enforce at least Baseline, and Restricted wherever the workloads allow it; pin the policy version with the -version labels if upgrades must not change behaviour.
  • Before enforcing, apply the level in warn and audit mode, or run a server-side dry run, to find existing pods that would be rejected, and fix or document them.
  • Keep Privileged only for system namespaces whose components need it, and restrict who can create pods there.
  • Set a cluster-wide default of Baseline in the PodSecurity admission configuration, so that new namespaces are protected without labels.
  • Restrict who can change namespace labels, since the labels are the control.
kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns --all pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: app labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted

Confirm the fix by attempting to create a privileged test pod in each application namespace and checking that it is rejected.

entries.title: Container Images With Known Vulnerabilities
entries.summary: Container images in use contain operating system packages or libraries with publicly known vulnerabilities for which fixes are available.
entries.description:
Container images bundle an operating system userland and application dependencies, which stay at the versions present when the image was built.
