Unless images are rebuilt and redeployed regularly, they accumulate packages and libraries with publicly known vulnerabilities, even when the application code itself has not changed. Images based on full distributions also carry many packages the application never uses, such as shells, compilers and package managers, and images whose base distribution has reached end of life receive no fixes at all.

The weakness is identified by scanning images, in registries or as deployed, with tools such as Trivy or Grype, which compare installed package versions with vulnerability databases and report CVE identifiers, severities and fixed versions. Scanner output needs interpretation: a vulnerability matters most when the affected component is reachable by an attacker, for example a network-facing library or the runtime the application uses, and much less when it sits in a package that is never executed.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach a vulnerable component may be able to exploit it to run code in the container, read data or cause a denial of service, depending on the vulnerability. Code execution in a container exposes its data, secrets and service account token, and is the usual first step towards attacking the node and the rest of the cluster. The real risk depends on which vulnerabilities are exploitable in the way the image is used, which is why remotely exploitable flaws in network-facing components deserve priority.
entries.remediation:
• Rebuild images regularly from updated base images and dependency versions, and redeploy them, rather than running images built once; automate this in the CI/CD pipeline.
  • Scan images in the pipeline and fail builds that introduce critical or high-severity vulnerabilities with available fixes, and rescan deployed images continuously as new vulnerabilities are published.
  • Use minimal base images, such as distroless or slim variants that contain only what the application needs, and keep package managers and shells out of production images.
  • Replace base images whose distribution is no longer supported.
  • Prioritise fixes by exploitability, starting with network-facing components and vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild, such as those in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.
  • Use admission policies to stop images that fail scanning, or that come from unapproved registries, from running.

Confirm the fix by rescanning the deployed images and checking that the reported vulnerabilities are gone or formally accepted.

entries.title: Unpinned Container Image Tags
entries.summary: Workloads reference container images by mutable tags such as latest rather than by digest, so the code that runs can change without review.
entries.description:
A container image reference such as nginx:latest or app:1.4 names a tag, which the registry maps to an image and which can be moved to a different image at any time. Only a digest reference, @sha256: followed by the image's hash, identifies one exact, immutable image. When a pod specification gives no tag, latest is used, and Kubernetes then checks the registry for a newer image every time a container starts.

With mutable tags, the code that runs depends on when each node pulled the image: different nodes can run different versions of the same workload, a rollback may not restore the previous code, and a change pushed to the tag, whether a routine upstream update, a mistake or a malicious push by someone with access to the registry or the upstream project, reaches production on the next restart without passing through review. The same applies to FROM lines in Dockerfiles. The issue is identified by reviewing image references in manifests, Helm charts and Dockerfiles for tags without digests, particularly latest.
entries.impact: The weakness does not let an attacker in by itself. It means that anyone who gains the ability to push to a tag the cluster uses, in the organisation's registry or an upstream public repository, can have their image run in the cluster without any deployment change, and it makes it harder to establish which code was running at the time of an incident. Unreviewed upstream updates can also introduce vulnerabilities or break workloads.
entries.remediation:
• Reference images by digest in production manifests, optionally keeping the tag for readability in the form name:tag@sha256: followed by the digest, and have the CI/CD pipeline resolve and update digests when it deploys a new version.
  • Pin base images in Dockerfiles by digest as well, and update them deliberately, for example through automated pull requests, so that updates are reviewed and tested.
  • Never deploy latest to production; use unique version tags and enable tag immutability in the registry where it is supported.
  • Restrict who can push to production repositories, and verify image signatures at admission where images are signed.

Confirm the fix by checking that every image reference in the deployed manifests includes a digest.

entries.title: Sensitive Data Stored Insecurely on the Device
entries.summary: The app stores sensitive data, such as tokens or personal data, on the device in a readable form instead of protecting it with the platform's secure storage.
entries.description:
The application stores sensitive information, such as authentication tokens, passwords, personal data or cryptographic keys, in a form that anyone with access to the device's file system can read. Common locations are Android SharedPreferences files, SQLite databases and other files in the app's data directory or in shared external storage, and on iOS property lists such as UserDefaults, databases, caches and files created without a suitable Data Protection class. Data the app encrypts itself is equally exposed when the key is stored beside it or built into the app.

The app's private storage is protected by the operating system's sandbox and, by default, by device encryption only until the device is first unlocked after a restart, but it can be read on a rooted or jailbroken device, by malware that has gained root, from some device backups and with forensic tools, while files in Android's shared storage may be readable by other apps. Testing confirms the issue by using the app's features, extracting its data directory and reviewing the files for sensitive values, as described for the storage controls (MASVS-STORAGE) of the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard.
entries.impact: An attacker with access to the device's storage, through physical possession of an unlocked or rooted device, a backup, or malware with elevated privileges, can read the stored data. Session or refresh tokens let them act as the user without knowing their password, often for long periods, and stored personal data may need to be treated as a breach. The need for privileged access to the device limits the likelihood, but lost, shared and rooted devices make it a realistic scenario.
entries.remediation:
• Store as little sensitive data on the device as possible, and keep long-lived secrets on the server.
  • Keep keys in the platform's protected key stores, the Android Keystore (hardware-backed where available) and the iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, and use them to encrypt any sensitive data the app must store; store small secrets such as tokens directly in the Keychain with a restrictive accessibility class such as kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly.
  • On iOS, give files containing sensitive data the NSFileProtectionComplete protection class, noting that the app then cannot read them while the device is locked, for example from background tasks; on Android, keep them in app-specific internal storage rather than shared storage.
  • Exclude sensitive files from backups, and delete cached responses, temporary files and stored data at logout.
  • Use short-lived access tokens that the server can revoke, so that stored tokens have limited value.

Confirm the fix by repeating the extraction of the app's data after using its sensitive features and checking that no sensitive values can be read.

entries.title: Hard-Coded Secrets in the Application Package
entries.summary: The application package contains secrets such as API keys, credentials or private keys that anyone who downloads the app can extract.
entries.description:
The application includes secrets in its code or resources, such as API keys for backend or third-party services, cloud access keys, client secrets, passwords or private keys. Mobile application packages are distributed to anyone who installs the app and can be unpacked and decompiled with freely available tools, such as apktool and jadx for Android apps or a disassembler for iOS apps, so any value shipped in the package should be treated as public.

Secrets are found in source code, string resources, configuration files, native libraries and the JavaScript bundles of cross-platform frameworks. Obfuscation and string encryption slow the search but do not prevent it, because the app must recover the value at runtime, where it can be read with dynamic instrumentation tools such as Frida. Testing identifies candidate secrets with automated scanners and manual review, and then checks what each one grants.

Not every key in an app is a secret: some identifiers are designed to be public, such as Firebase configuration values, whose security depends on server-side rules, and keys that the provider restricts to the app's package and signing certificate. The finding concerns values that grant access on their own.
entries.impact: An attacker who extracts a secret can use it directly against the service it belongs to, from anywhere, with whatever permissions it carries. Depending on the secret, this can expose other users' data, allow messages or payments to be sent at the organisation's expense, give access to cloud resources, or allow forging of tokens the backend trusts. Because the same secret ships in every copy of the app, revoking it breaks existing installations, which often leaves it valid for a long time.
entries.remediation:
• Remove secrets from the app. Calls that need a secret should go through the organisation's backend, which authenticates the user and holds the secret itself.
  • Where the app must call a service directly, use per-user or per-device credentials issued by the backend after authentication, with short lifetimes and narrow scopes, instead of a shared static key.
  • Restrict any key that must remain in the app to the minimum permissions, and to the app's package name and signing certificate or bundle identifier where the provider supports it.
  • Revoke and replace every secret found in released versions, since they must be considered compromised, and check the services' logs for misuse.
  • Add secret scanning to the build pipeline so that new secrets are caught before release.

Platform attestation services, such as Play Integrity and App Attest, can help a backend recognise requests from genuine installations, but they do not make embedded secrets safe. Confirm the fix by decompiling the new release and searching it for the removed secrets, and by checking that the old values have been revoked.

entries.title: Cleartext Network Traffic Permitted
entries.summary: The app's network security settings permit unencrypted HTTP connections, so traffic to some or all endpoints can be read or changed on the network.
entries.description:
Android and iOS both block unencrypted HTTP connections from apps by default and allow apps to relax this in configuration. On Android, cleartextTrafficPermitted="true" in the network security configuration, globally or for specific domains, or the manifest attribute android:usesCleartextTraffic="true", permits cleartext; the default blocks it only for apps targeting Android 9 (API level 28) or higher. On iOS, App Transport Security exceptions in Info.plist, such as NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads for a domain, permit HTTP connections.

The finding is raised when these exceptions are present, and is more serious when the app actually sends sensitive data, such as credentials, tokens or personal information, over HTTP. Testing identifies it by reviewing the manifest, the network security configuration and Info.plist, and by capturing the app's traffic through an intercepting proxy to see which requests use HTTP. Lower-level networking APIs and some third-party libraries do not honour the platform setting, so traffic capture is needed to be sure.
entries.impact: An attacker on the same network as the user, such as public Wi-Fi, or elsewhere on the network path, can read any data the app sends over HTTP and change the responses it receives. Depending on the traffic, this can expose credentials and session tokens, leak personal data, or let the attacker inject content into the app, such as altered information, malicious links or scripts in WebViews. Where only non-sensitive resources use HTTP the impact is limited, but the permissive setting leaves room for future mistakes.
entries.remediation:
• Serve every endpoint the app uses over HTTPS, and remove the cleartext exceptions.
  • On Android, set cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" in the base-config of the network security configuration, referenced from the manifest's android:networkSecurityConfig attribute, remove domain exceptions, and do not set android:usesCleartextTraffic="true".
  • On iOS, remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads and per-domain NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads keys, so that App Transport Security applies to all connections.
  • Where an exception is unavoidable, for example for a third-party resource that cannot use HTTPS, limit it to that specific domain and make sure no sensitive data passes over it.
<network-security-config> <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" /> </network-security-config>

Confirm the fix by capturing the app's traffic while exercising all of its features and checking that no request uses HTTP.

entries.title: Improper TLS Certificate Validation in the App
entries.summary: The app accepts TLS certificates without validating them properly, so an attacker on the network can intercept its encrypted traffic with a certificate of their own.
entries.description:
The application overrides or weakens the platform's TLS certificate validation, so that it accepts certificates that are self-signed, issued by an untrusted authority, expired or issued for a different host name. Typical causes are a custom Android X509TrustManager whose checkServerTrusted method does nothing, a HostnameVerifier that always returns true, a WebView onReceivedSslError handler that calls proceed(), an iOS URLSession delegate that accepts any server trust, or a networking library option that disables validation. These are often added during development to work with test servers and left in release builds.

Testing confirms the weakness by routing the app's traffic through an intercepting proxy whose certificate the device does not trust: a correctly built app refuses the connection, while a vulnerable one continues and its traffic can be read. Static analysis tools and code review find the patterns above, and Google Play warns developers about some of them.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept the device's traffic, for example on public Wi-Fi or through a rogue access point, can present their own certificate, decrypt the app's HTTPS traffic and change it, without any warning to the user. This exposes credentials, session tokens and all data the app exchanges with its servers, and lets the attacker manipulate responses. TLS provides no protection for the affected connections, so the impact is equivalent to unencrypted traffic.
entries.remediation:
• Remove custom trust managers, host name verifiers and error handlers that weaken validation, and rely on the platform's default validation, which checks the certificate chain, validity period and host name.
  • On Android, use the network security configuration for legitimate customisation, such as trusting a private certificate authority for specific domains, and its debug-overrides element for test certificates, which applies only to debuggable builds.
  • On iOS, do not override server trust evaluation in URLSession delegates; where custom evaluation is needed, call the system evaluation (SecTrustEvaluateWithError) first and reject the connection if it fails.
  • In WebViews, cancel the request on certificate errors instead of proceeding.
  • Review third-party networking libraries and cross-platform framework settings for options that disable validation.

Confirm the fix by repeating the interception test with an untrusted certificate and checking that every connection fails.

entries.title: Certificate Pinning Not Implemented
entries.summary: The app trusts any certificate that chains to an authority trusted by the device, without pinning the keys of its own servers.
entries.description:
Certificate pinning restricts the certificates or public keys an app accepts for its own servers to a known set, instead of any certificate issued by any authority the device trusts. Without pinning, an attacker who can get a certificate for the app's domains trusted by the device, through a compromised or coerced certificate authority, a malicious configuration profile, or a root certificate installed by the user or a device management system, can intercept the app's TLS traffic.

Current platforms reduce this risk without pinning: Android apps targeting Android 7.0 (API level 24) or higher do not trust user-installed certificate authorities by default, and iOS requires a user-installed root certificate to be explicitly trusted in settings. Pinning is therefore an additional layer, which the OWASP MASVS includes among its network controls (MASVS-NETWORK) for apps that handle highly sensitive data, rather than a baseline requirement.

Testing identifies the absence of pinning by installing an intercepting proxy's root certificate as trusted on a test device, as a system certificate on Android, and observing that the app's traffic can be intercepted.
entries.impact: The absence of pinning does not by itself expose traffic. It matters only where an attacker can also get a rogue certificate trusted by the user's device, which requires a compromised authority, control of device management, or persuading the user to install and trust a profile; in that case the attacker can read and change the app's traffic. Without pinning, it is also easier for others to inspect the app's API traffic on their own devices.
entries.remediation:
• Decide whether pinning is justified by the app's risk; apps handling payments, health data or other highly sensitive information are the usual candidates.
  • Pin the public key (a SHA-256 hash of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo) of the server or of the issuing certificate authority rather than a leaf certificate, include at least one backup pin for a key not yet in use, and plan how pins will be rotated before keys change, since a wrong pin stops the app connecting.
  • On Android, use the pin-set element of the network security configuration, with an expiration date, or OkHttp's CertificatePinner; on iOS, use the NSPinnedDomains key in Info.plist or a maintained pinning library.
  • Pin only the organisation's own domains, not third-party services whose keys it does not control.

Confirm the fix by repeating the interception test with a trusted proxy certificate and checking that pinned connections fail, and test the backup pin before relying on it.

entries.title: Exported Android Components Without Protection
entries.summary: Android activities, services or broadcast receivers are exported without a permission, so any other app on the device can start or call them.
entries.description:
Android app components (activities, services, broadcast receivers and content providers) can be exported, which lets other apps start or call them. A component is exported when android:exported="true" is set in the manifest or, for apps targeting versions before Android 12 (API level 31), implicitly when it declares an intent filter. Apps targeting Android 12 or higher must set the attribute explicitly on components with intent filters. Content providers are covered by a separate finding.

The weakness arises when an exported component that performs a sensitive action or returns data is not protected by a permission, ideally one with the signature protection level, and does not validate the intents it receives. Typical examples are internal activities that skip the login screen, services that act on the user's behalf, and receivers that trust broadcast data. Intent redirection, where an exported component forwards an intent it received to an internal component, extends the problem to components that are not exported themselves.

Testing lists exported components from the decoded manifest, with tools such as apktool, jadx or drozer, and sends crafted intents to them, for example with adb shell am start or adb shell am broadcast, to observe their behaviour.
entries.impact: A malicious app installed on the same device, which needs no special permission, can invoke the exposed functionality. Depending on the component, it may open screens that should require authentication, trigger actions such as payments or account changes without the user's intent, read data the component returns, or crash the app. The attack requires the user to install the malicious app, which limits the likelihood but is realistic for widely used apps.
entries.remediation:
• Set android:exported="false" on every component that other apps do not need to use.
  • Protect components that must be exported, such as those shared between apps from the same developer, with a custom permission declared with android:protectionLevel="signature".
  • Treat every incoming intent as untrusted input: validate its action, data and extras, check that the user is authenticated before performing sensitive actions, and do not forward received intents to other components without checking them.
  • Use explicit intents for communication within the app, and make PendingIntent objects immutable with FLAG_IMMUTABLE where they are handed to other apps.
<permission android:name="com.example.app.permission.INTERNAL" android:protectionLevel="signature" /> <activity android:name=".AccountActivity" android:exported="true" android:permission="com.example.app.permission.INTERNAL" />

Confirm the fix by repeating the intent tests from adb or a separate test app and checking that protected components refuse them.

entries.title: Insecure Content Provider
entries.summary: An Android content provider is accessible to other apps without adequate permissions or input handling, exposing the app's data to any app on the device.
entries.description:
Content providers share an app's data with other apps through content:// URIs. A provider is accessible to other apps when it is exported, which was the default for apps targeting Android 4.1 (API level 16) or lower and otherwise requires android:exported="true". The weakness arises when an exported provider has no read or write permission, or one that any app can obtain, or grants URI permissions too broadly, so that other apps can query, insert, update or delete its data.

Providers backed by SQLite databases are also prone to SQL injection through the projection, selection and sort order arguments, which can expose tables the provider was not meant to share, and providers that serve files through openFile are prone to path traversal when they build file paths from the URI.

Testing enumerates providers and their URIs from the manifest and code, and queries them from adb, for example with adb shell content query --uri, from a test app, or with drozer's provider modules, which also test for injection and traversal.
entries.impact: A malicious app on the same device can read the data the provider exposes, which often includes the user's personal data, messages or account information, and where write operations are available, change or delete it. SQL injection or path traversal can extend this to the app's whole database or to private files such as stored tokens. The attacker needs the user to install their app, but needs no special permission.
entries.remediation:
• Set android:exported="false" on providers that are used only within the app.
  • For providers other apps must use, require android:readPermission and android:writePermission, with the signature protection level where the consumers are the developer's own apps, and use path-permission elements to restrict sensitive paths.
  • Grant temporary access to individual URIs with android:grantUriPermissions and intent flags rather than exporting the whole provider.
  • Pass selection values as arguments rather than building SQL strings, validate projections and sort orders against an allowlist, and consider SQLiteQueryBuilder with a projection map and strict mode.
  • For files, use FileProvider with narrowly scoped paths, and canonicalise and check any path built from a URI.

Confirm the fix by repeating the queries and injection tests from a separate app and checking that they are refused or return only the intended data.

entries.title: Application Built as Debuggable
entries.summary: The released app is built with debugging enabled, letting anyone with access to the device attach a debugger to it and read its private data.
entries.description:
The application is distributed with debugging enabled. On Android this is the android:debuggable="true" attribute of the manifest's application element, which the build system sets automatically for debug builds; on iOS it is the get-task-allow entitlement, present in builds signed for development.

A debuggable Android app accepts debugger connections over ADB and JDWP, and allows run-as to run commands as the app's own user, which gives direct access to its private data directory without rooting the device. On iOS, the entitlement allows a debugger to attach to the running app. Debug builds may also include extra logging, test endpoints or relaxed security settings, such as the debug overrides of the Android network security configuration.

The issue is identified from the decoded manifest or the app's entitlements, for example with apktool, aapt dump badging or codesign -d --entitlements. Google Play does not accept debuggable builds, so the finding usually concerns apps distributed outside the store, enterprise builds and test builds released to users.
entries.impact: Anyone with access to an unlocked device with USB debugging enabled, or to a device they control, can attach a debugger to the app, read and change its memory and variables, bypass client-side checks such as PIN or biometric gates, and on Android read every file in its private storage with run-as, including tokens and databases. Debugging also makes reverse engineering and tampering easier. The need for access to the device limits the likelihood.
entries.remediation:
• Build release versions with debugging disabled: do not set android:debuggable in the manifest, and leave the debuggable setting of the Gradle release build type false.
  • Sign iOS builds for distribution with a distribution profile, which does not include get-task-allow.
  • Add a check to the release pipeline that fails if the packaged manifest or entitlements allow debugging.
  • Remove debug-only code, logging and test endpoints from release builds.

Confirm the fix by inspecting the released package's manifest or entitlements, and by checking that run-as fails for the app's package on a test device.

entries.title: Android Backup Enabled for Sensitive Data
entries.summary: The Android app allows its private data to be included in backups and device transfers, which can expose stored tokens and personal data outside the device.
entries.description:
Android can copy an app's private data into backups: Auto Backup to the user's Google account, device-to-device transfers when the user sets up a new device, and on older versions the adb backup command. This is controlled by the android:allowBackup attribute of the manifest's application element, which defaults to true, and refined by android:fullBackupContent (Android 11 and lower) and android:dataExtractionRules (Android 12 and higher), which include or exclude specific files.

The weakness arises when backups are enabled and the app stores sensitive data, such as session tokens, keys or personal data, without excluding it. For apps targeting Android 12 (API level 31) or higher, adb backup no longer includes app data, which removes the easiest extraction route, but cloud backups and device-to-device transfers still copy it. Testing reviews the manifest and backup rules and, where possible, creates and inspects a backup of the app's data.
entries.impact: An attacker with access to the user's unlocked device can transfer the app's data to a device they control, or for older apps extract it with adb backup, and then read the stored data or restore it to take over the user's session. Data can also be altered before it is restored, if the app trusts it. The need for access to the unlocked device, or to the user's backup account and screen lock, limits the likelihood.
entries.remediation:
• Set android:allowBackup="false" if the app has no data that users need restored, or exclude sensitive files with backup rules. For apps targeting Android 12 or higher, android:allowBackup="false" does not stop device-to-device transfers on some manufacturers' devices, so exclude sensitive files in the device-transfer rules as well.
  • Define android:dataExtractionRules, with separate cloud-backup and device-transfer sections, for Android 12 and higher, and android:fullBackupContent for earlier versions, excluding tokens, keys, caches and other sensitive files.
  • Keep encryption keys in the Android Keystore, whose keys are not included in backups, so that encrypted data that is backed up cannot be decrypted elsewhere.
  • Bind sessions to the device where possible, so that restored tokens are not accepted from another device.
<data-extraction-rules> <cloud-backup> <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="session.xml" /> <exclude domain="database" path="app.db" /> </cloud-backup> <device-transfer> <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="session.xml" /> <exclude domain="database" path="app.db" /> </device-transfer> </data-extraction-rules>

Confirm the fix by creating a backup or device transfer of a test installation and checking that the excluded files are absent.

entries.title: Insecure WebView Configuration
entries.summary: The app's WebViews are configured so that web content they load can reach native app functions or local files, or can load untrusted pages.
entries.description:
WebViews display web content inside the app, and their settings decide what that content can do. The weakness arises when a WebView that can load content an attacker influences, such as pages over HTTP, arbitrary URLs passed in intents or deep links, or third-party content, is also given powers beyond those of a normal browser tab.

On Android, the risky settings include JavaScript bridges added with addJavascriptInterface, which expose app methods to every script in the page; setAllowFileAccess, setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs and setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs, which let pages read local files; and URL handlers such as shouldOverrideUrlLoading that load any URL they are given. On iOS, the equivalents are script message handlers registered on a WKWebView, broad file access granted through loadFileURL, and the deprecated UIWebView. Passing session tokens into pages through URLs or JavaScript widens the exposure.

Testing reviews the WebView configuration in code, checks whether attacker-controlled content can be loaded, for example through a deep link or by intercepting HTTP traffic, and then establishes what that content can reach.
entries.impact: Script running in an affected WebView, whether it arrives through a vulnerable page, a manipulated deep link or intercepted traffic, can call the exposed native methods, read the app's local files or the user's session tokens, and present convincing phishing content inside the trusted app. Depending on what the bridge exposes, this can lead to account compromise or actions performed as the user. The attacker needs a way to get content into the WebView, which usually requires user interaction or a position on the network.
entries.remediation:
• Load only the organisation's own content over HTTPS in WebViews that have bridges or file access, validate URLs against an allowlist of hosts before loading them, and open other links in the system browser.
  • Expose as few native methods as possible through JavaScript bridges, check the origin of each call, and never expose methods that return tokens or perform sensitive actions without confirmation.
  • Disable JavaScript where it is not needed, and disable file access with setAllowFileAccess(false), leaving the file URL access settings off; serve local content through WebViewAssetLoader instead.
  • On iOS, use WKWebView, limit the read access given to loadFileURL to the specific directory needed, and check the frame's origin in script message handlers.

Confirm the fix by attempting to load attacker-controlled content into each WebView and checking that it is refused or cannot reach native methods or files.

entries.title: Insecure Deep Link Handling
entries.summary: The app acts on deep links without validating their source or parameters, so a crafted link can open sensitive screens, trigger actions or load attacker content.
entries.description:
Deep links let other apps, web pages and messages open specific screens of an app through custom URL schemes, Android App Links or iOS Universal Links. Any app or web page can send a link to a custom scheme, and custom schemes are not owned by any app, so another app can register the same scheme and receive links intended for the real one; App Links and Universal Links avoid this only when the association with the organisation's domain is verified.

The weakness arises when the app trusts the link: it performs actions, such as changing settings, making payments or linking accounts, without confirmation; opens screens that should require authentication; loads a URL from a parameter into a WebView, sometimes with the user's session; or passes parameters into file paths, queries or internal intents without validation. Links that carry OAuth authorisation codes or tokens through a custom scheme can be intercepted by another app registered for the same scheme.

Testing lists the link handlers from the Android manifest's intent filters and from the iOS Info.plist and associated domains, then opens crafted links, for example with adb shell am start -d or from a web page, and observes the app's behaviour.
entries.impact: An attacker who persuades a user to open a crafted link, for example in a message or on a web page, can make the app perform actions on the user's behalf, bypass screens that should require authentication, display phishing content inside the trusted app, or, through a WebView, steal session tokens. Where codes or tokens pass through custom schemes, a malicious app on the device can capture them. The attack requires user interaction, which limits but does not prevent it.
entries.remediation:
• Treat all deep link data as untrusted input: validate the host, path and every parameter against what the target screen expects, and reject anything else.
  • Require the user to be authenticated, and to confirm, before performing any state-changing or sensitive action that a link initiates.
  • Do not load URLs from link parameters into WebViews unless they match an allowlist of the organisation's own hosts, and never attach session tokens to them.
  • Prefer verified Android App Links (android:autoVerify="true" with a Digital Asset Links file) and iOS Universal Links (with an apple-app-site-association file) over custom schemes, especially for links that carry codes or tokens, and use PKCE in OAuth flows.

Confirm the fix by repeating the crafted links and checking that each one is rejected or requires authentication and confirmation.

entries.title: Sensitive Data in Device Logs
entries.summary: The app writes sensitive data such as tokens, credentials or personal information to the device's system log, where it can be read outside the app.
entries.description:
The application writes sensitive information, such as passwords, session tokens, API responses containing personal data, or cryptographic material, to the platform's logging facilities: Android's Log class and System.out, which appear in logcat, or iOS's NSLog and the unified logging system. Logging statements added during development are often left in release builds, and third-party libraries can log network traffic in detail when verbose logging is enabled.

Since Android 4.1, ordinary apps cannot read other apps' log entries, but logs remain readable over ADB and in bug reports, and on iOS through the Console app or a sysdiagnose from a connected device. Crash reporting and analytics services may also collect log output and send it to third parties.

Testing exercises the app's features, particularly login, payment and profile functions, while monitoring adb logcat or the macOS Console, and reviews the code for logging calls that include sensitive variables.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the device's logs, such as a person with access to an unlocked device with USB debugging enabled, support staff collecting bug reports, or a third-party analytics service, can obtain the logged data. Logged tokens and credentials allow the user's account to be taken over, and logged personal data creates a data protection exposure. The need for access to the device or to collected reports limits the likelihood.
entries.remediation:
• Remove logging of sensitive data from the code, and avoid logging full requests, responses or objects that may contain it.
  • Route logging through a wrapper that is disabled in release builds, and on Android strip logging calls from release builds with an R8 or ProGuard -assumenosideeffects rule for android.util.Log.
  • On iOS, use the unified logging system (Logger or os_log), which treats interpolated strings and objects as private by default, and do not mark sensitive values as public.
  • Disable verbose logging in third-party networking and SDK libraries in release builds, and review what crash reporting services collect.
-assumenosideeffects class android.util.Log { public static int v(...); public static int d(...); public static int i(...); }

Confirm the fix by repeating the monitored test against a release build and checking that no sensitive values appear in the logs.

entries.title: Root or Jailbreak Detection Absent
entries.summary: The mobile application runs normally on rooted or jailbroken devices, without detecting or responding to the weakened platform security.
entries.description:
The application does not check whether the device it runs on has been rooted (Android) or jailbroken (iOS), and behaves the same on a compromised device as on a standard one. Rooting and jailbreaking remove operating system protections that the application otherwise relies on, such as the separation between application sandboxes and the restrictions that stop debuggers and instrumentation frameworks attaching to other applications' processes.

The weakness is confirmed by installing the application on a rooted or jailbroken test device and observing that it starts and operates normally, with no warning, restriction or report to its server. Static review of the decompiled package shows whether common checks are present, such as searches for su binaries, root management applications, test-keys builds or jailbreak file paths, or the use of platform attestation such as the Play Integrity API. Static analysers such as MobSF can indicate whether known root detection code is present.

Where detection exists but is weak, testing typically finds a single check made at launch, which public tools defeat without customisation, such as objection (android root disable, ios jailbreak disable) or root-hiding modules for Magisk. The OWASP MASVS places these controls in its resilience group (MASVS-RESILIENCE), which applies where an application's threat model includes reverse engineering and tampering, as is common for banking, payment and content protection applications.
entries.impact: The absence of detection does not expose data by itself. It removes a layer that would make it harder for someone in control of a device, whether a researcher or an attacker studying the application, to instrument it at runtime, bypass client-side controls such as certificate pinning or biometric checks, and read the application's private storage. It also means that users whose devices have been rooted or jailbroken, sometimes by malware, receive no warning that the protections around their data are weakened. Detection can always be bypassed by a determined attacker, so its value lies in raising the effort required rather than in preventing attacks.
entries.remediation:
Decide from the application's risk whether resilience controls are warranted. For applications that handle payments, financial data or other high-value functions:

  • On Android, use the Play Integrity API and evaluate its verdicts on the server, not in the application: request an integrity token for sensitive actions, decode and verify it through Google's servers, and act on the device integrity verdict (for example MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY). The SafetyNet Attestation API it replaces is deprecated.
  • On iOS, combine local jailbreak checks with App Attest, which lets the server confirm that requests come from a genuine instance of the application. App Attest does not detect jailbreaks by itself.
  • Implement several independent local checks (files, binaries, writable system locations, hooking frameworks and debuggers), run them at different points rather than once at launch, and protect them with obfuscation so that hooking one function cannot disable them all. A maintained library or commercial runtime protection product is usually more resilient than in-house code.
  • Respond proportionately and enforce the response on the server: warn the user, restrict high-risk functions such as payments or credential changes, and record the event, rather than relying only on the application closing.
  • Do not treat detection as a security boundary. Data and functions must remain protected by server-side controls and the platform keystores even when detection is bypassed.

Confirm the fix on rooted and jailbroken test devices, including with off-the-shelf bypass tools, and check that the server receives and acts on the integrity signals.

entries.title: Code Obfuscation Not Applied
entries.summary: The application's code is shipped without obfuscation, so decompiling it gives readable class, method and field names that make its logic easy to study.
entries.description:
The application package is built without code obfuscation, so its compiled code can be turned back into readable source with freely available tools. Android applications written in Java or Kotlin compile to DEX bytecode, which decompilers such as jadx reconstruct closely, including the original class, method and field names unless a tool such as R8 has renamed them. Cross-platform frameworks often ship code in an even more accessible form, such as the JavaScript bundle of a Cordova application or the .NET assemblies of a Xamarin or .NET MAUI application. iOS applications compile to native code, which is harder to read, but Objective-C class and method names are kept in the binary for the runtime and can be listed with tools such as class-dump, and other symbol names remain unless the release build is stripped.

The weakness is identified by decompiling the release build and finding meaningful names throughout the application's own code, debug information such as source file names and line numbers, and descriptive strings that explain its logic. Tools such as APKiD, which MobSF includes, identify known obfuscators and packers in Android packages.

Obfuscation is a resilience measure that raises the cost of reverse engineering. It does not protect secrets embedded in the code, which are a separate finding.
entries.impact: Without obfuscation, an attacker can quickly understand how the application works: its API endpoints and parameters, how requests are signed, how client-side checks such as root detection or certificate pinning are implemented, and where keys and tokens are handled. This shortens the work needed to find other weaknesses, to bypass client-side controls with instrumentation tools, to build automated clients that imitate the application, or to produce repackaged copies for fraud. The absence of obfuscation does not directly expose data, and obfuscation only delays a capable reverse engineer, so the finding is informational unless the application depends on its code staying secret.
entries.remediation:
Enable obfuscation for every release build, and keep broad exceptions from undoing it:

  • On Android, turn on R8 code shrinking and obfuscation in the release build type, and keep -keep rules as narrow as possible, limited to classes reached through reflection, serialisation or native code. A rule that keeps a whole package removes most of the benefit.
  • Keep the mapping file that R8 produces private, and upload it to the Play Console so that crash reports can still be read.
  • For Flutter, build with --obfuscate and --split-debug-info. For other cross-platform frameworks, use the framework's release optimisation and an obfuscator suited to its code format.
  • On iOS, strip symbols from release builds using Xcode's symbol stripping build settings (such as Strip Linked Product and Strip Style), and avoid self-describing names for security-relevant classes and methods.
  • For applications with high-value logic, consider a commercial protector that adds string encryption, control flow obfuscation and anti-tampering, as R8 renames identifiers but does not encrypt strings.
  • Move secrets and security decisions to the server, as obfuscation hides them only from casual inspection.
// Android, module build.gradle.kts android { buildTypes { release { isMinifyEnabled = true isShrinkResources = true proguardFiles( getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"), "proguard-rules.pro" ) } } }

Confirm the fix by decompiling the release build with jadx, or a disassembler for iOS, and checking that the application's own classes and methods no longer carry meaningful names.

entries.title: Sensitive Screens Not Protected From Capture
entries.summary: Screens showing sensitive data are not protected, so their content can be captured in screenshots, screen recordings or the app switcher's preview image.
entries.description:
Screens that display sensitive information, such as account details, card numbers, personal data, one-time codes or recovery phrases, are not protected from the operating system's screen capture features. Their content can therefore be recorded in user screenshots, which are saved to the photo library and often synchronised to cloud storage, in screen recordings and casting sessions, and by applications the user has allowed to capture the screen.

Both platforms also keep an image of each application's last screen for the recent apps or app switcher view. On iOS, the system takes this snapshot as the application moves to the background and stores it in the application's data container, so a sensitive screen that is not hidden first is shown in the switcher and remains on disk.

On Android, the weakness is confirmed when screenshots of sensitive screens succeed and the recent apps view shows their content; the decompiled code shows whether FLAG_SECURE is set on the relevant windows. On iOS, it is confirmed by sending the application to the background from a sensitive screen and checking the app switcher, and by examining the stored snapshot images on a test device. The OWASP MASVS covers this under secure use of the user interface.
entries.impact: Sensitive data shown on unprotected screens can be obtained by anyone who later sees the device's screenshots, its synchronised photo library or its app switcher, by someone recording or casting the screen, or by a malicious application the user has allowed to capture the screen. On iOS, someone with access to the device's file system, for example through a forensic extraction, can recover the stored snapshot images. Exploitation needs physical access, access to the user's photo storage or a malicious application with screen capture consent, so the risk is low for most applications and higher for those showing payment card data, credentials or recovery phrases.
entries.remediation:
Protect every screen and window that displays sensitive data:

  • On Android, set FLAG_SECURE on the window of each sensitive activity before its content is shown. This blocks screenshots and screen recording, keeps the content off non-secure displays and blanks the recent apps preview. Dialogues and pop-up windows created with the classic view system have their own windows, so check that the flag reaches them too.
  • On iOS, hide or blur sensitive views when the scene is about to resign active or enter the background (sceneWillResignActive(_:) and sceneDidEnterBackground(_:), or the application delegate equivalents), and restore them when it becomes active again, so that the stored snapshot contains no sensitive data.
  • On iOS, watch the screen's isCaptured state and hide sensitive content while the screen is being recorded or mirrored. Apple provides no supported way to block user screenshots, and workarounds that rely on undocumented behaviour can break with any update, so mask the most sensitive values and reveal them only on request.
  • Avoid showing full values where they are not needed, such as complete card numbers.
// Android, in the activity's onCreate, before setContentView window.setFlags( WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE )

Confirm the fix by attempting screenshots and screen recordings on each sensitive screen, and by checking the recent apps view and, on iOS, the stored snapshots.

entries.title: Sensitive Input Cached by the Keyboard
entries.summary: Sensitive fields allow keyboard learning and suggestions, so typed values can be kept in the keyboard's learned data and offered back as predictive text.
entries.description:
Mobile keyboards learn words typed into text fields to improve autocorrection and predictive suggestions. The application does not mark its sensitive input fields, such as account numbers, memorable information, security answers, personal details or confidential search terms, to opt out of this learning, so values typed into them can be stored in the keyboard's learned data on the device and offered later as suggestions, including in other applications.

The risk is greater with third-party keyboards. On Android, the active keyboard, which may be one the user installed from any developer, receives everything typed into the field, and on iOS a custom keyboard that the user has granted full access can send what is typed off the device. iOS always uses the system keyboard for secure text entry fields, but not for ordinary fields that hold sensitive data.

The weakness is confirmed by typing a distinctive value into each sensitive field, then typing its first characters in another application and checking whether it is suggested. Code review shows the input attributes: on Android, the inputType and imeOptions of each field; on iOS, the autocorrectionType and isSecureTextEntry properties.
entries.impact: Someone who later uses the device, or watches its screen, may be shown sensitive values as typing suggestions, and an attacker with access to the device's file system through a forensic extraction may recover them from the keyboard's stored data. A malicious or compromised third-party keyboard can collect values as they are typed. The data exposed is limited to what was typed into unprotected fields, and exploitation needs physical access to the device or a malicious keyboard the user has installed, so the risk is low.
entries.remediation:
Mark every field that takes sensitive input so that keyboards do not learn or suggest its contents:

  • On Android, add textNoSuggestions to the inputType of sensitive text fields and set flagNoPersonalizedLearning in imeOptions, which asks the keyboard not to learn from the field. Use a password input type (textPassword or numberPassword) for secrets such as passwords and PINs.
  • On iOS, set autocorrectionType to .no on sensitive fields, and set isSecureTextEntry to true on secrets, which also prevents copying and forces the system keyboard.
  • Where third-party keyboards are a concern, an iOS application can refuse them by returning false for the keyboard extension point in application(_:shouldAllowExtensionPointIdentifier:). For the most sensitive values, such as PINs, an in-app keypad avoids the device keyboard entirely.
<!-- Android layout --> <EditText android:id="@+id/memorableWord" android:inputType="text|textNoSuggestions" android:imeOptions="flagNoPersonalizedLearning" /> // iOS memorableWordField.autocorrectionType = .no pinField.isSecureTextEntry = true

These attributes are requests that some keyboards may ignore, so they reduce rather than remove the risk. Confirm the fix by repeating the suggestion test with the system keyboard and with the third-party keyboards in common use among the application's users.

entries.title: Biometric Authentication Bypass
entries.summary: The application's biometric check is a client-side success or failure event rather than a cryptographic unlock, so instrumenting the app bypasses it.
entries.description:
The application uses fingerprint or face recognition to protect access, but treats the result as a simple success or failure event instead of binding it to a cryptographic key. On Android this is typically a BiometricPrompt call without a CryptoObject, where the application proceeds as soon as onAuthenticationSucceeded is called; on iOS, a call to LAContext.evaluatePolicy whose Boolean result decides whether to continue. Because the decision is made in the application's own code, anyone who can instrument the application can call the success path directly or change the result, without presenting a matching biometric.

Related variants include a session token or password stored outside the Keystore or Keychain protections and released after the check, keys that remain usable after new fingerprints or faces are added to the device, and a fallback to the device passcode where the design intended biometrics only.

The weakness is confirmed on a rooted or jailbroken test device, or with an instrumented build, by hooking the biometric callbacks with Frida (for example with objection's ios ui biometrics_bypass command or public Android scripts) and showing that the protected screen or function opens without a valid biometric. Code review shows whether the keys used after authentication require user authentication in the Android Keystore, or whether the secrets are protected by a biometric access control in the iOS Keychain.
entries.impact: An attacker who has the device can reach the account inside the application without the owner's biometric, then view the data and use the functions the check protected, such as payments or changes to account details. Exploitation needs physical possession of the device and the ability to instrument the application, which in practice means the device is already rooted or jailbroken, or, for the related variants, that the attacker knows the device passcode. Remote exploitation is not possible. The impact is higher where the biometric check is the only barrier to high-value actions.
entries.remediation:
Bind biometric authentication to a key that the platform's secure hardware releases only after a successful match, and make the application depend on that key:

  • On Android, generate a key in the Android Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) and, on Android 11 and later, setUserAuthenticationParameters(0, KeyProperties.AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG), keep setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true), and pass a Cipher or Signature using that key to BiometricPrompt as a CryptoObject. Use the authenticated object to decrypt the stored token or to sign a server challenge.
  • On iOS, store the secret in the Keychain with an access control created by SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags using .biometryCurrentSet and the kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly accessibility class, so that reading it requires a current biometric match, or use a Secure Enclave key to sign a server challenge.
  • Prefer designs in which the server verifies a signature made with the protected key, so that a bypass inside the application gains nothing, and keep server-side session expiry and step-up checks for high-risk actions.
  • Allow the passcode fallback only where the design intends it.

Confirm the fix by repeating the instrumentation bypass and checking that the protected function fails because the key or secret cannot be used without a real biometric match, and that adding a new fingerprint or face invalidates access.

entries.title: Tapjacking
entries.summary: Sensitive controls accept touches while another app's window covers them, so a malicious overlay can trick the user into tapping them unknowingly.
entries.description:
Tapjacking is an Android user interface attack, comparable to clickjacking on the web. A malicious application that the user has installed draws a window over the target application. The overlay shows misleading content but lets the user's taps pass through to the target's controls beneath it, or covers only part of the screen so that the user taps an exposed control without understanding what it does. The user believes they are interacting with the harmless content, but their taps confirm actions in the target application, such as approving a payment, granting a permission or changing a setting.

The application is affected when its sensitive views accept touches while their window is wholly or partly obscured by another application's window. Android 12 and later block touches that pass through most opaque overlays from other applications, which reduces the risk on current devices, but touches through sufficiently translucent overlays, and touches beside an overlay that covers only part of the screen, are still delivered, and older versions lack this protection.

The weakness is identified by reviewing layouts and code for filterTouchesWhenObscured or for checks on the obscured flags of touch events, and confirmed with a proof-of-concept overlay application on a device running an affected Android version. iOS does not allow applications to draw over other applications, so the finding applies to Android.
entries.impact: An attacker who persuades the user to install a malicious application, and in most cases to grant it permission to display over other applications, can trick the user into performing actions in the target application that they did not intend, such as confirming a transaction or approving a request. The attack cannot read data directly, needs the user's interaction at the right moment, and is largely limited by the protections in current Android versions, so the risk is low. It is higher for applications in which a single tap completes a high-value action.
entries.remediation:
Discard touches on sensitive controls whenever another window covers them:

  • Set android:filterTouchesWhenObscured="true" on views that confirm sensitive actions, or on the root layout of sensitive screens, or call setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true) in code.
  • Because that setting does not cover a partial overlay that leaves the touched point uncovered, also reject touch events that carry FLAG_WINDOW_IS_PARTIALLY_OBSCURED (Android 10 and later) as well as FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED on the most sensitive controls.
  • On Android 12 and later, call setHideOverlayWindows(true) on the window of the most sensitive screens, declaring the HIDE_OVERLAY_WINDOWS permission, to hide other applications' overlays while the screen is shown.
  • Require an explicit confirmation step with re-authentication for high-value actions, so that a single misdirected tap cannot complete them.
// Kotlin, in a custom view that guards a sensitive control override fun onFilterTouchEventForSecurity(event: MotionEvent): Boolean { val obscured = MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED or MotionEvent.FLAG_WINDOW_IS_PARTIALLY_OBSCURED if ((event.flags and obscured) != 0) return false return super.onFilterTouchEventForSecurity(event) }

Confirm the fix with an overlay test application on the oldest Android version the application supports, checking that taps through or beside the overlay are ignored.

entries.title: Sensitive Data Exposed Through the Clipboard
entries.summary: Sensitive values can be copied to, or are placed on, the system clipboard, where other applications, keyboards and synchronised devices can read them.
entries.description:
The application allows sensitive values, such as passwords, one-time codes, account or card numbers and recovery phrases, to be copied from its fields, or places them on the clipboard itself through copy buttons, without limiting how long they stay there or where they can go. The clipboard is shared across the device: on Android the keyboard in use and the application in the foreground can read it, and on iOS the application in the foreground can request its contents. Apple's Universal Clipboard can also make copied content available on the user's other nearby Apple devices, and clipboard managers and keyboards with a clipboard history may keep copies.

Current versions of both platforms restrict reading by background applications and alert the user when an application reads content copied elsewhere, but the keyboard and an application in the foreground can still obtain it, and a copied value stays on the clipboard until it is replaced unless an expiry is set.

The weakness is identified by attempting to copy from each sensitive field, by reviewing the application's use of the clipboard APIs, and by monitoring the clipboard while the application is used, for example with objection's android clipboard monitor and ios pasteboard monitor commands.
entries.impact: A malicious application the user opens, a malicious or compromised keyboard, or a clipboard history feature can obtain values the user copied, which may include credentials or one-time codes that give access to the account, or recovery phrases that give control of funds. Copied values may also appear on the user's other devices, or in the clipboard preview that recent Android versions display. Exploitation needs a malicious application or keyboard on the device, or access to a synchronised device, and the user must first copy the value, so the risk is low for most applications.
entries.remediation:
Keep sensitive values off the clipboard, and limit their exposure where copying is a deliberate feature:

  • Use password input types for secrets (textPassword on Android, isSecureTextEntry on iOS), which do not allow their contents to be copied. For other sensitive fields, remove the copy and cut actions, for example with a custom selection action mode callback on Android or by overriding canPerformAction(_:withSender:) on iOS.
  • Where the application offers a copy button for a sensitive value, mark the content as sensitive on Android with ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE so that the clipboard preview hides it, and clear it with clearPrimaryClip() once it is no longer needed.
  • On iOS, write such values with the localOnly option, which keeps them off Universal Clipboard, and an expirationDate, so that they are removed automatically.
  • Do not offer copying for recovery phrases and other long-term secrets.
// Android val clip = ClipData.newPlainText("", value) clip.description.extras = PersistableBundle().apply { putBoolean(ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE, true) } clipboardManager.setPrimaryClip(clip) // iOS UIPasteboard.general.setItems( [["public.utf8-plain-text": value]], options: [.localOnly: true, .expirationDate: Date().addingTimeInterval(60)])

Confirm the fix by attempting to copy from each sensitive field, and by monitoring the clipboard while using the application's copy features.

entries.title: Misconfigured Firebase Database or Storage
entries.summary: Firebase Security Rules give anyone, or any signed-in user, access to the app's database or storage, so its data can be read, and often changed, directly.
entries.description:
Mobile applications that use Firebase talk directly to the Firebase Realtime Database, Cloud Firestore and Cloud Storage for Firebase, using project details bundled in the application. These details, including the API key, are not secrets: Firebase relies on Security Rules, written by the developer and deployed with the project, to decide who may read and write each path, document or file. The weakness arises when those rules allow public access, such as a Realtime Database rule of ".read": true, test mode rules that allow all access until a date, or rules that accept any signed-in user (auth != null) while anyone can create an account or sign in anonymously.

The weakness is identified by extracting the project details from the application package (the values from google-services.json in an Android application's resources, or GoogleService-Info.plist in an iOS application) and querying the services directly. A Realtime Database that returns data, rather than a permission denied error, when .json is appended to its address is publicly readable, and similar requests to the Firestore and Cloud Storage REST interfaces show whether documents and files can be listed or read. Write access, and the access gained by creating an account through the Firebase Authentication interface with the bundled API key, are then tested without altering existing data.
entries.impact: Anyone on the internet who extracts the project details from the application can read the data the rules expose, which commonly includes other users' personal data, messages, uploaded documents and images, and sometimes internal configuration or credentials. Where write access is also open, an attacker can alter or delete records, plant content that other users are shown, or upload files to the project's storage at the organisation's cost. No authentication or user interaction is needed, the data can be downloaded in bulk with simple requests, and exposure of personal data may need to be handled as a personal data breach.
entries.remediation:
Rewrite the Security Rules so that access is denied unless a rule explicitly grants it to the right user:

  • Grant access per user or per role, for example by matching the path or document owner to auth.uid or request.auth.uid, rather than allowing any request or any signed-in user. Use custom claims or stored role records for shared data.
  • Remove test mode and other time-limited open rules, and validate the shape, type and size of written data in the rules.
  • Do not treat sign-in as authorisation where email sign-up or anonymous sign-in is enabled, as anyone can create an account with the bundled API key.
  • Enforce App Check for the database, Firestore and Storage to reject requests that do not come from the genuine application. This reduces scripted abuse but does not replace correct rules.
  • Keep rules in version control, test them with the Firebase Local Emulator Suite before deployment, and deploy them with the Firebase CLI.
// Realtime Database { "rules": { "users": { "$uid": { ".read": "$uid === auth.uid", ".write": "$uid === auth.uid" } } } } // Cloud Firestore rules_version = '2'; service cloud.firestore { match /databases/{database}/documents { match /users/{userId} { allow read, write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId; } } }

Review what was exposed while the rules were open, check for data altered or files uploaded by others, and assess whether a personal data breach occurred. Confirm the fix by repeating the unauthenticated requests and the requests from a second test account, which should all be refused.

entries.title: Outdated Minimum Platform Version Supported
entries.summary: The application can be installed on operating system versions that no longer receive security updates and lack protections it may rely on.
entries.description:
The application declares a minimum platform version, the minSdk value on Android or the deployment target on iOS, old enough to allow installation on operating system releases that no longer receive security updates. Users on those releases remain exposed to publicly known vulnerabilities in the operating system and its components, and the application runs there without platform protections introduced in later versions.

On Android, for example, devices before Android 7.0 trust user-installed certificate authorities by default and do not support network security configuration, devices before Android 5.0 cannot receive WebView updates separately from the operating system, and TLS 1.2 is not enabled by default before Android 5.0. Google's monthly Android Security Bulletins cover only recent Android releases, and Apple issues security fixes mainly for the current iOS release, back-porting some fixes to older ones.

The weakness is identified from the package: the minimum SDK version in the decoded AndroidManifest.xml or in the output of aapt dump badging, and the MinimumOSVersion key in the iOS application's Info.plist. Static analysers such as MobSF report a low minimum SDK version. The finding concerns the oldest version permitted, not the target SDK version, which decides which newer platform behaviours the application opts in to.
entries.impact: Users running unsupported operating system versions can have their devices, and with them the application's data, compromised through known vulnerabilities, for example by a malicious application that gains elevated privileges or through flaws in outdated system components. The application's own protections, such as certificate validation that relies on platform defaults, may also be weaker on those versions. The risk depends on how many users run old versions and on whether an attacker can reach them, usually through a malicious application or a hostile network, so it is low for most applications and higher for those handling payments or sensitive personal data.
entries.remediation:
Align the minimum supported platform with versions that still receive security updates:

  • Raise minSdk in the application's Gradle configuration, and the minimum deployment target (IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET) in Xcode, to versions that are still patched, weighing this against the share of users on older versions shown by the application's analytics.
  • Adopt a documented policy for reviewing the minimum version, for example whenever a platform version stops receiving security updates, and tell users in advance when support for a version will end.
  • Where older versions must remain supported for a period, do not rely on platform defaults that have since changed: enable TLS 1.2 or later explicitly, and restrict trust to the system certificate authorities, or pin certificates, in the application's own networking code, as network security configuration has no effect before Android 7.0. Consider warning users of unpatched devices, for example by reading Build.VERSION.SECURITY_PATCH on Android, and restricting high-risk functions for them.
  • For high-risk applications, check device integrity on the server, for example with the Play Integrity API, before allowing sensitive operations.

Confirm the fix by checking the minimum version declared in the next release build's manifest or Info.plist, and that installation is refused on a device running an older version.

entries.title: Weak Cryptography in the Application
entries.summary: The application encrypts, hashes or generates random values with weak algorithms, insecure modes, fixed keys or predictable randomness, so its protection can be undone.
entries.description:
The application uses cryptography in a way that does not provide the protection intended. Typical cases in mobile applications include obsolete algorithms such as DES, 3DES or RC4; AES in ECB mode, which reveals patterns in the data and is what common providers apply when Cipher.getInstance("AES") is called without a mode; fixed or all-zero initialisation vectors and reused GCM nonces; keys written into the code or derived from constants or device identifiers; MD5 or SHA-1 used for integrity checks or to protect passwords; RSA without OAEP padding; and non-cryptographic random number generators, such as java.util.Random, used for keys, tokens or nonces. Custom schemes, such as XOR with a fixed value or Base64 encoding presented as encryption, are also common.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the decompiled code for the algorithms, modes and key sources passed to the platform's cryptographic APIs, which static analysers such as MobSF often flag, and confirmed at runtime by hooking those APIs with Frida to capture the keys, initialisation vectors and plaintext actually used. A key that is the same on every installation, or that can be recomputed from public values, shows that the protection can be reversed by anyone who has the application package.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains data the application has protected, from the device's storage, a backup or intercepted traffic, can decrypt it when the key is fixed or recoverable from the package, or infer its content from repeated patterns when ECB mode is used. Weak hashes and integrity checks may let an attacker alter data or messages without detection, and predictable random values may let them guess tokens or keys. Obtaining the protected data usually requires access to the device, its backups or the network path, which limits the risk, but a single extracted key typically affects every user of the application.
entries.remediation:
Replace custom and weak constructions with current algorithms provided by the platform, and keep keys out of the application package:

  • Use authenticated encryption, AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, with a unique random nonce for every encryption. On Android, use the Android Keystore or a vetted library such as Tink; on iOS, use CryptoKit.
  • Generate keys on the device inside the Android Keystore, or the iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, so that they cannot be extracted, rather than embedding them in code. Where a key must be shared with the server, issue it per user over an authenticated channel.
  • Use SHA-256 or stronger for integrity, HMAC for message authentication, and Argon2id or PBKDF2 with the parameters in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet where a key is derived from a password.
  • Use SecureRandom on Android and SecRandomCopyBytes on iOS for every security-relevant random value.
  • Use OAEP padding with RSA keys of at least 2048 bits.
  • Re-encrypt existing stored data with the new scheme when the application updates, and treat any key that has shipped in a package as exposed.
// Android: AES-GCM key held in the Android Keystore val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance( KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore") keyGenerator.init( KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder("data_key", KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT) .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM) .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE) .setKeySize(256) .build()) val key = keyGenerator.generateKey() val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding") cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key) // store cipher.iv with the ciphertext

Confirm the fix by repeating the code review and runtime hooking, checking that keys differ between installations and cannot be read from the package, and that no weak algorithm or mode remains.

entries.title: WEP Encryption in Use
entries.summary: A wireless network is protected with Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP), whose key can be recovered from captured traffic within minutes using freely available tools.
entries.description:
One or more wireless networks use Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) to encrypt traffic. WEP combines a shared key with a 24-bit initialisation vector (IV) and encrypts each frame with the RC4 stream cipher. The IV space is small, IVs are sent in cleartext and repeat quickly, and some IV values leak information about the key, so an attacker who collects enough frames can calculate the key itself. WEP's integrity check is a CRC-32 checksum rather than a cryptographic one, so frames can also be altered or forged without detection.

Statistical attacks such as PTW, implemented in tools including aircrack-ng, recover a 104-bit key from tens of thousands of captured frames. Where the network is quiet, an attacker can replay captured frames, such as ARP requests, to make the access point generate the traffic needed, so recovery normally takes minutes. Key length makes no practical difference, and the shared-key authentication option exposes keystream rather than adding protection.

WEP is identified from beacon frames during a wireless survey: tools such as airodump-ng and Kismet report the network's encryption as WEP. It is most often found on networks kept for legacy devices, such as older handheld scanners, printers, or industrial and medical equipment that cannot use anything stronger.
entries.impact: An attacker within radio range, including outside the building where the signal reaches, can recover the key without any credentials, then decrypt all traffic on the network, both live and previously captured, and join it as a legitimate client. From there they can reach every system the wireless network can reach, intercept and alter unprotected traffic, and attack connected devices. Because the key is shared, it stays exposed until it is changed on every device.
entries.remediation:
WEP cannot be configured securely and should be removed:

  • Reconfigure the network to use WPA3, either WPA3-Personal (SAE) or WPA3-Enterprise, as certified by the Wi-Fi Alliance. Where some clients do not yet support WPA3, use WPA2 with AES-CCMP only, or WPA2/WPA3 transition mode, with TKIP disabled.
  • Replace or upgrade devices that only support WEP, checking first for vendor firmware that adds WPA2 or WPA3 support.
  • Where a legacy device cannot be replaced immediately, move it to a dedicated SSID and VLAN, allow only the specific traffic it needs through a firewall, and monitor that segment until the device is retired.
  • Once WEP is removed, treat the old key as compromised, and change any credentials that crossed the network without another layer of encryption.

Confirm the fix with a wireless survey showing that no SSID advertises WEP, and by checking that any remaining legacy segment cannot reach other internal networks.

entries.title: WPA or TKIP Encryption in Use
entries.summary: A wireless network allows the original WPA protocol or its TKIP cipher, which is deprecated and allows limited decryption and forging of frames.
entries.description:
One or more wireless networks offer the original version of WPA, or allow the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP) as a cipher, either on its own or alongside AES-CCMP in a mixed WPA/WPA2 configuration. TKIP was designed as a temporary fix that could run on hardware built for WEP.
