It still uses the RC4 stream cipher, and relies on a weak message integrity check called Michael, backed by countermeasures that shut the network down briefly when repeated integrity failures are detected.

Published attacks, starting with the Beck-Tews attack and refined since, allow an attacker within range to decrypt short frames such as ARP packets, recover the Michael key for one direction of traffic, and then inject a limited number of forged frames. They do not reveal the network key, but they show that TKIP no longer provides the protection it was designed for. TKIP has been deprecated in the IEEE 802.11 standard and is not used by WPA3.

In a mixed configuration, the group cipher used for broadcast and multicast traffic is TKIP, so even clients that use AES-CCMP for their own traffic depend on it. Clients using TKIP are also limited to legacy data rates, because the high-throughput rates of 802.11n and later are not permitted with it. The configuration is identified from beacon frames during a wireless survey, where tools such as airodump-ng report the cipher as TKIP, or as CCMP and TKIP.
entries.impact: An attacker within radio range can decrypt some short frames and inject a small number of forged frames into the network, which can be used to redirect or disrupt traffic, for example by poisoning ARP caches. The attacks are slow and constrained, and do not recover the pre-shared key or give network access on their own, which limits the impact. Keeping TKIP enabled also holds the network back from WPA3, and usually indicates legacy clients whose other security settings deserve review.
entries.remediation:
Remove WPA and TKIP from every SSID:

  • Configure each network for WPA3 where clients support it, or WPA2 with AES-CCMP as the only cipher. WPA2/WPA3 transition mode allows a gradual move while still excluding TKIP.
  • Before disabling TKIP, identify the clients that negotiate it from the wireless controller's client list, then update their drivers or firmware, reconfigure them for AES-CCMP, or replace them.
  • Where a legacy device can only use TKIP, give it a dedicated SSID and network segment with firewall rules that allow only the traffic it needs, and plan its replacement.

Confirm the fix with a wireless survey showing that no SSID advertises WPA or the TKIP cipher, and that clients still connect using AES-CCMP.

entries.title: Open Wireless Network
entries.summary: A wireless network uses no encryption or authentication, so anyone in range can join it and read traffic that is not protected by another layer such as TLS.
entries.description:
One or more wireless networks are open: clients associate without a key or credentials, and frames travel over the air unencrypted. Open networks are usually provided for guests or the public, often with a captive portal that asks users to accept terms or sign in. A captive portal controls who may use the network but encrypts nothing, and the session it grants is usually tied to the client's MAC address, which another device in range can copy to inherit it.

Anyone within range can capture every frame on an open network passively, without connecting. Traffic that is not encrypted at a higher layer, such as HTTP, DNS lookups, cleartext mail protocols and some device management traffic, is readable in full. Because clients have no way to authenticate an open network, they also connect readily to a rogue access point that broadcasts the same network name (an evil twin), particularly devices that have joined the network before and reconnect automatically.

An open network is identified during a wireless survey, where tools such as airodump-ng report its encryption as OPN. The risk depends on what the network is for and what it can reach: an open network that reaches internal systems or carries corporate traffic is considerably more serious than an isolated guest network.
entries.impact: An attacker in range can join the network, read any traffic that is not protected by TLS or a VPN, and impersonate the network with an evil twin to intercept or alter users' connections, for example to present fake sign-in pages. If the network reaches internal systems, joining it also gives the attacker a foothold on those systems without any credentials. Devices on the network are exposed to every other user of it.
entries.remediation:
Decide what each open network is for, then protect it accordingly:

  • For networks used by staff or corporate devices, use WPA3-Enterprise or WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X, or at least WPA3-Personal, rather than an open network.
  • For guest and public networks, enable Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, defined in RFC 8110) where access points and clients support it. It encrypts each client's traffic without a password, though it does not authenticate the network, so it does not prevent evil twins. Alternatively, use WPA3-Personal with a key given to guests, which stops passive capture by anyone without the key and stops other users decrypting each other's traffic.
  • Isolate guest networks from internal systems, enable client isolation, and route their traffic directly to the internet.
  • Make sure corporate services used over any wireless network enforce TLS, and require a VPN for corporate devices on networks the organisation does not control.

Confirm the fix with a wireless survey showing the intended security on each SSID, and by checking from the guest network that internal ranges cannot be reached.

entries.title: Weak WPA2 Pre-Shared Key
entries.summary: A WPA2-Personal network uses a guessable pre-shared key, which can be cracked offline from a captured handshake or PMKID to gain access to the network.
entries.description:
A wireless network protected with WPA2-Personal uses a pre-shared key (PSK) that is weak enough to be guessed: for example a dictionary word, the organisation's name with a year or number, an address, a default key printed on the device, or a short key. Every user and device shares the same key, it often stays unchanged for years, and staff who leave continue to know it.

WPA2-Personal lets an attacker test guesses offline, without interacting with the network after the initial capture. The attacker records the four-way handshake when a client connects, and can force a client to reconnect by sending spoofed deauthentication frames where protected management frames are not enforced. Many access points also include a value called the PMKID in the first handshake message, which an attacker can obtain directly from the access point with no client present. Either capture can be attacked with tools such as hashcat, which tests guesses at high speed on ordinary graphics hardware, so a key built from words, names, dates or common patterns is likely to be recovered from wordlists and rules within hours or less.

The finding is confirmed when the key is recovered from a captured handshake or PMKID during testing.
entries.impact: Once the key is recovered, an attacker in range can join the network as if they were an authorised device and reach every system the network can reach. Because WPA2-Personal does not provide forward secrecy, the key also lets them decrypt the traffic of other clients whose handshakes they capture, including traffic recorded before the key was cracked. The access lasts until the key is changed on every device, and the attack can be carried out from outside the premises where the signal reaches.
entries.remediation:
Replace the weak key and reduce dependence on a single shared secret:

  • For networks used by staff or corporate devices, move to WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, so each user or device authenticates with its own credentials or certificate and access can be revoked individually.
  • Where a pre-shared key must remain, enable WPA3-Personal (SAE), which resists offline guessing from captured exchanges and gives each session its own keys. In WPA2/WPA3 transition mode, clients that still connect with WPA2 remain open to the offline attack, so the key must be strong regardless.
  • Set a long, randomly generated key, for example of 20 or more random characters, held in a password manager, rather than one derived from words, names or dates.
  • Change the key whenever staff who know it leave. Vendor features that issue a separate pre-shared key per device or per user allow individual keys to be revoked without reconfiguring every device.
  • Restrict what the network can reach, so that a recovered key gives as little access as possible.

Confirm the fix by repeating the handshake or PMKID capture and confirming that the new key resists the same wordlist and rule-based attack, or that the network now uses SAE or 802.1X.

entries.title: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) Enabled
entries.summary: An access point has Wi-Fi Protected Setup enabled, whose eight-digit PIN can be brute-forced or, on some devices, derived offline to reveal the network's key.
entries.description:
Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is enabled on one or more access points or wireless routers. WPS was designed to let users connect devices without typing the network key, using either a push button or an eight-digit PIN. The PIN method has a design flaw (CVE-2011-5053): the last digit is a checksum, and the access point confirms the first four digits and the next three separately, so an attacker needs at most 11,000 guesses to find the PIN rather than the ten million its length suggests. Tools such as Reaver and Bully automate the attack.

A separate weakness, known as Pixie Dust, affects devices whose WPS implementation generates predictable random values. On those devices the PIN can be calculated offline from a single exchange, in seconds, with pixiewps. Once the PIN is known, the access point hands over the network's WPA pre-shared key however strong it is, and because the PIN is often fixed, changing the key does not remove the exposure.

WPS is identified from the information element that access points include in their beacons and probe responses: tools such as wash and airodump-ng list WPS-enabled access points, their WPS version and whether the PIN method is locked. Some access points slow or lock out repeated PIN attempts, which stretches a brute-force attack from hours to days, though many only pause for a period rather than disabling WPS. It is most often found on small office routers, branch equipment, printers and unmanaged access points.
entries.impact: An attacker within range who recovers the PIN obtains the network's pre-shared key, and can then join the network, reach every system it can reach and decrypt other clients' traffic. On some devices the PIN can also be used to change the access point's wireless settings. How quickly this happens depends on the device: seconds on models affected by Pixie Dust, hours where no lockout is applied, and days or longer where lockouts are enforced, which is why the typical case is rated below a weak pre-shared key.
entries.remediation:
Disable WPS, and in particular its PIN method, on every access point and router:

  • Turn off WPS in each device's management interface or configuration. On small office and consumer routers it is often enabled by default.
  • Confirm with a wireless scan that the access point no longer advertises WPS, because some devices have been found to keep responding to WPS after it was disabled in their interface. Update the firmware of, or replace, any device that cannot disable it.
  • Once WPS is disabled, change the pre-shared key, since it may already have been recovered.
  • Where devices need simple onboarding, use a method that does not rely on a static PIN, such as Wi-Fi Easy Connect, or provision them through a management platform.
  • Include WPS in configuration baselines and periodic wireless surveys, so that it is not re-enabled by firmware updates or new equipment.

Confirm the fix with wash or airodump-ng showing no WPS information element for the organisation's access points.

entries.title: WPA2-Enterprise Clients Do Not Validate the Server Certificate
entries.summary: Wireless clients do not check the RADIUS server's certificate, so a rogue access point can impersonate the corporate network and capture users' domain credentials.
entries.description:
The corporate wireless network uses WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise with a password-based EAP method, typically PEAP with MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS, but some or all clients do not validate the certificate that the RADIUS server presents. These methods protect the user's credentials inside a TLS tunnel, and the tunnel is only as trustworthy as the client's check that the server certificate was issued by the expected certification authority to the expected server name. Where that check is missing, the client completes the tunnel with any server.

The weakness is exploited with an evil twin: an access point broadcasting the corporate network name, backed by the attacker's own RADIUS server, using tools such as hostapd-mana or EAPHammer. Clients that roam to it, attracted by a stronger signal or pushed off the genuine network with deauthentication frames, send the user's MSCHAPv2 challenge and response, which can then be cracked offline. Some clients can be negotiated down to methods such as EAP-GTC that reveal the password in cleartext.

Typical causes are profiles configured by hand on personal devices, Windows profiles with server validation turned off, older Android settings that allowed a choice not to validate, and profiles that ask users whether to trust an unknown certificate, which many users accept. The weakness is confirmed by running a test access point with an untrusted certificate and observing which clients complete authentication against it.
entries.impact: An attacker within range of any affected device, including in a car park, a station or a hotel used by staff, can capture domain credentials without any prior access. MSCHAPv2 responses for weak or common passwords are cracked quickly, and the protocol's design allows the account's NT hash to be recovered with significant computing effort whatever the password's strength. The credentials give access to the corporate wireless network and to every other service that accepts the account, such as email, VPN and remote desktop, unless multi-factor authentication or certificate-based access prevents it.
entries.remediation:
Make every client verify the RADIUS server before sending credentials:

  • Deploy wireless profiles centrally, through Group Policy for domain-joined Windows devices and through mobile device management, such as Microsoft Intune, for laptops, phones and tablets, rather than letting users configure them.
  • In each profile, enable server certificate validation, specify the certification authority that issued the RADIUS server certificate (preferably an internal CA used for this purpose), and specify the exact server names the certificate must contain.
  • Disable the option that lets users trust new servers or certification authorities when prompted, so that a rogue server causes the connection to fail rather than a prompt.
  • Move to EAP-TLS, where each device authenticates with its own certificate, so that there is no password for a rogue access point to capture. Where passwords remain, require multi-factor authentication on remote services that accept the same accounts.
  • Keep unmanaged devices off the corporate network and give them a separate guest network.

As an interim measure, enable wireless intrusion detection to alert on access points broadcasting the corporate network name. Confirm the fix by repeating the rogue access point test and confirming that no client completes authentication.

entries.title: Guest Wireless Network Not Isolated
entries.summary: The guest wireless network can reach internal systems, so anyone given or able to obtain guest access can attack the corporate network.
entries.description:
The wireless network provided for visitors is not adequately separated from the organisation's internal network. A client connected to the guest network can reach internal address ranges and services, for example file shares, intranet sites, directory services, printers, or the management interfaces of the wireless infrastructure itself. Common causes are a guest SSID bridged to an internal VLAN, routing between the guest and corporate networks without restrictive firewall rules, internal DNS servers handed to guests, and rules that block some internal ranges but not others.

Guest networks are, by design, used by people the organisation does not control: visitors, contractors, staff's personal devices, and anyone who has been told the guest key or can see it displayed in reception or a meeting room. Many are open or protected only by a captive portal, and the signal frequently reaches beyond the building.

The weakness is identified by connecting to the guest network and attempting to reach internal ranges with host discovery and port scanning, and by checking which DNS servers, gateways and routes are provided. Access to any internal service from the guest network, other than one deliberately offered such as a guest printer, shows that isolation is incomplete.
entries.impact: Anyone able to join the guest network, possibly from outside the building, can discover and attack internal systems as though they were on the corporate network, without needing corporate credentials. The impact depends on what is reachable: exposed management interfaces, unauthenticated services or unpatched systems could lead to compromise of internal hosts, and internal DNS can reveal the structure of the network. Malware on visitors' devices can also reach internal systems.
entries.remediation:
Treat the guest network as an untrusted, internet-only network:

  • Place guest traffic on a dedicated VLAN or virtual routing instance with no route to internal networks, or tunnel it to a controller or firewall in a DMZ.
  • At the firewall, deny all traffic from the guest network to internal and management address ranges, including all RFC 1918 ranges, and allow only the outbound internet traffic guests need. Write the policy as a default deny rather than a list of blocked subnets.
  • Give guests public DNS resolvers or a dedicated guest resolver, not internal DNS servers.
  • Block guest access to the management interfaces of the wireless controller, access points and other network devices.
  • Enable client isolation on the guest SSID, and apply bandwidth limits and acceptable use terms.
  • Where guests genuinely need an internal service, such as a printer, publish only that service through a specific firewall rule.

Confirm the fix by connecting to the guest network and scanning internal and management ranges, confirming that nothing internal responds.

entries.title: Wireless Client Isolation Not Enabled
entries.summary: Devices connected to the same wireless network can communicate directly with each other, so one connected device can scan and attack the others.
entries.description:
Client isolation is not enabled on one or more wireless networks, so devices connected to the same SSID can send traffic directly to one another. The feature, called client isolation, AP isolation or peer-to-peer blocking depending on the vendor, makes the access point or controller drop traffic between wireless clients, so that each client can only communicate with the network beyond it.

Without isolation, a connected device can discover the other clients, reach any services they expose, such as file sharing, remote desktop or web interfaces, and carry out attacks that rely on sharing a network segment, such as ARP spoofing or answering broadcast name resolution requests (LLMNR and NBT-NS) to capture credentials. This matters most on guest and public networks, where users and devices are untrusted, and on corporate networks where laptops have local services enabled.

The weakness is identified by connecting a test device to the network and confirming that other wireless clients respond to discovery and connection attempts. Isolation applied on each access point does not by itself stop traffic between clients on different access points that share a VLAN, so testing from more than one access point can show partial isolation.
entries.impact: An attacker who can join the network, which on a guest network may need no more than the displayed key, can attack other connected devices directly, capture credentials through spoofing and poisoning attacks, and exploit services exposed on users' laptops and phones. The impact depends on the other clients and requires the attacker to be connected first, which is why it is rated low on its own, but it often provides the starting point for more serious attacks.
entries.remediation:
Enable client isolation on every SSID where clients have no need to communicate with each other, which includes all guest and public networks:

  • Turn on the vendor's client isolation or peer-to-peer blocking setting for the SSID. Where the network spans several access points, also enable the equivalent controller-wide setting, or use private VLANs or access control lists, so that isolation applies between access points too.
  • On corporate networks where some peer-to-peer traffic is required, such as wireless printing or screen casting, allow only those specific flows with access control lists rather than leaving clients open to each other.
  • Reduce what clients expose by enabling host firewalls on managed devices and disabling unneeded sharing services.

Confirm the fix by connecting two test devices to the network, including on different access points, and confirming that neither can reach the other.

entries.title: Protected Management Frames Not Enabled
entries.summary: Wireless networks do not use 802.11w Protected Management Frames, so forged deauthentication frames can disconnect clients at will.
entries.description:
Protected Management Frames (PMF), defined in IEEE 802.11w, are not enabled or not required on one or more wireless networks. Without PMF, management frames such as deauthentication and disassociation frames are not authenticated, so any device in range can forge them using the address of the access point or of a client, and the recipient acts on them.

Tools such as aireplay-ng and mdk4 send forged deauthentication frames to disconnect a single client or every client of an access point, repeatedly if required. Attackers use this to disrupt wireless service, to force clients to reconnect so that their handshakes can be captured for offline cracking of a pre-shared key, and to push clients off the genuine network towards an evil twin access point.

PMF can be disabled, optional (capable) or required. In optional mode, clients that support PMF are protected and older clients are not. PMF is mandatory in WPA3 and optional in WPA2. The setting is identified from the RSN information element in beacons, which shows whether management frame protection is capable or required, and confirmed by sending forged deauthentication frames to a test client.
entries.impact: An attacker within range can disconnect chosen clients, or all clients of an access point, for as long as they keep sending frames, disrupting wireless users and any devices that depend on the wireless network. More often the technique supports other attacks, by forcing reconnections that expose handshakes for cracking or that move clients to a rogue access point. Radio jamming can disrupt any wireless network and PMF does not prevent it, but forged frames are far easier, cheaper and more targeted.
entries.remediation:
Enable PMF, and require it wherever clients support it:

  • Migrate SSIDs to WPA3-Personal or WPA3-Enterprise, which make PMF mandatory. During migration, WPA2/WPA3 transition mode applies PMF to the clients that connect with WPA3.
  • On WPA2 networks, set PMF to required where all clients support it, and to optional where some do not. Identify the remaining clients without PMF support from the controller, and plan their upgrade or replacement.
  • Enable wireless intrusion detection on the controller to alert on deauthentication floods and on access points broadcasting the organisation's network names.

Confirm the fix by checking that beacons advertise management frame protection as required, and that a test client stays connected when forged deauthentication frames are sent to it.

entries.title: Rogue Access Point Detected
entries.summary: An unauthorised access point is connected to the internal network, providing a wireless route into it that bypasses the organisation's wireless and physical controls.
entries.description:
A wireless access point that is not part of the organisation's managed infrastructure was found connected to the internal network. Typical examples are a consumer router plugged into a desk or meeting room network port, a printer or other device broadcasting its own wireless network while connected to the wired network, a laptop sharing its wired connection as a hotspot, or a device deliberately placed by an intruder. Such devices are usually installed with default or weak settings: open, protected by a default or simple key, or with Wi-Fi Protected Setup enabled.

A rogue access point bridges the wired network to anyone in radio range. It sits outside the controls applied to the managed wireless network, such as 802.1X authentication, client isolation and monitoring, and its presence shows that the port it uses accepts unknown devices.

Rogue access points are identified by surveying the wireless networks visible from the premises and correlating them with the wired network, for example by matching wireless and wired MAC addresses, by tracing the switch port the device is connected to, or by connecting to the unknown network and checking whether internal addresses are reachable. Wireless intrusion detection on enterprise controllers performs the same correlation automatically. Neighbouring organisations' networks are not rogue access points unless they connect to the organisation's network.
entries.impact: An attacker in range, possibly outside the building, can connect to the rogue access point and gain a position on the internal network without passing any authentication, giving the same starting point as plugging into an internal network port. From there they can discover and attack internal systems and intercept traffic. The rating assumes the access point is open or weakly protected, as is typical; a well-secured unauthorised access point is less exposed but still escapes central management and monitoring.
entries.remediation:
Remove the device and address the conditions that allowed it:

  • Locate the access point through the switch's port and MAC address tables, disconnect it, and establish who installed it and why. Where it was meeting a genuine business need, provide that through the managed wireless network.
  • Enforce network access control on wired ports, such as 802.1X port authentication, so that unknown devices are not given internal network access, and disable unused switch ports.
  • Enable rogue access point detection in the wireless controller or a dedicated wireless intrusion prevention system, with alerts for unknown access points seen on the wired network and for access points broadcasting the organisation's network names. Use automatic containment with care, because transmitting deauthentication frames at networks that do not belong to the organisation can be unlawful in some jurisdictions.
  • State in policy that only the IT function may connect network equipment, and include periodic wireless surveys in security testing, as recommended in NIST SP 800-153.

Confirm the fix with a further wireless survey, and by checking that the port no longer gives network access to an unknown device.

entries.title: Corporate Wireless Signal Available Outside the Premises
entries.summary: The organisation's wireless networks can be received from public areas outside the premises, letting attackers target them without entering the building.
entries.description:
The organisation's corporate wireless networks can be received, with enough signal strength to connect or to capture traffic, from areas outside its control, such as car parks, streets, public spaces and neighbouring buildings. This is identified during a wireless survey by walking or driving the perimeter with a laptop or phone and recording where each SSID and access point can be detected, and at what signal strength.

Some leakage beyond the walls is unavoidable and is not a weakness in itself. It matters because it removes the need for physical access: every attack against the wireless network, such as capturing handshakes, guessing a pre-shared key, setting up an evil twin to capture credentials, or exploiting a weak configuration, can be carried out discreetly from outside the premises, often from a vehicle, and with directional antennas that extend the range further.
entries.impact: On its own this has no direct impact, and it is reported for information. It extends the area an attacker can operate from, so any other wireless weakness, such as a weak key, an open network or clients that do not validate the server certificate, can be exploited without entering the building and with little chance of being noticed.
entries.remediation:
Reduce unnecessary coverage, and make sure the networks remain secure when they can be reached from outside:

  • Review access point placement and transmit power so that coverage serves the occupied areas, using a predictive or on-site survey. Place access points away from external walls and windows where possible, and consider directional antennas at the perimeter.
  • Rely on strong authentication rather than signal containment: WPA3-Enterprise or WPA2-Enterprise with certificate-validating clients, ideally using EAP-TLS, and WPA3-Personal or long random keys where a pre-shared key is unavoidable.
  • Use wireless intrusion detection to alert on attacks and on access points imitating the organisation's network names, and, when designing network segmentation, allow wireless clients to reach only the hosts and subnets they need, as NIST SP 800-153 recommends.

Confirm the effect by repeating the perimeter survey after any changes.

entries.title: SPF Record Missing or Permissive
entries.summary: The domain has no SPF record, or one that authorises too many senders or fails to evaluate, so receivers cannot tell legitimate mail from forged mail using it.
entries.description:
Sender Policy Framework (SPF, RFC 7208) lets a domain owner publish, in a DNS TXT record, the servers that are allowed to send email using the domain in the envelope sender (the SMTP MAIL FROM address, also known as the return path). Receiving mail servers compare the connecting server's IP address with the record and use the result as evidence of whether a message is genuine. SPF also underpins DMARC, which relies on an aligned SPF or DKIM result to protect the From address that recipients see.

The weakness takes several forms: no SPF record at all; a record ending in +all, which authorises every server on the internet, or ?all, which asserts nothing; mechanisms that authorise far more than the organisation's own senders, such as broad IP ranges or include entries for services no longer used; records that need more than ten DNS lookups to evaluate, or more than one SPF record for the same name, both of which cause a permanent error so that SPF gives no protection; and domains and subdomains that send no email but do not publish v=spf1 -all. A record ending in ~all (soft fail) is common, and acceptable alongside an enforced DMARC policy. The record is checked with a DNS query, such as dig TXT or nslookup -type=txt, and an SPF validation tool.
entries.impact: Without an effective SPF record, an attacker can send email that claims to come from the domain, and receiving servers have less evidence on which to reject or flag it. This supports phishing and fraud against the organisation's staff, customers and suppliers, and can harm the domain's reputation. SPF checks only the envelope sender, so the visible From address is protected only through DMARC: where an enforced DMARC policy and DKIM signing are in place, a weak SPF record mainly affects deliverability, but where DMARC is missing or not enforced, SPF is one of the few signals receivers have. Success also depends on each recipient's own filtering.
entries.remediation:
Publish an accurate SPF record for every domain and subdomain, and pair it with DKIM and DMARC:

  • List every service that sends email using the domain, including the main mail platform, marketing, ticketing and billing services and on-premises applications, and publish a single TXT record that authorises only those. For example, a domain whose only sender is Microsoft 365 publishes the record below; other services document the include value to add.
v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all
  • End the record with -all (fail), or with ~all (soft fail) where an enforced DMARC policy is in place; never use +all or ?all.
  • Keep evaluation within ten DNS lookups by removing entries for services no longer used and avoiding the ptr mechanism, and publish only one SPF record per name.
  • For domains and subdomains that never send email, publish v=spf1 -all together with a DMARC policy of reject.
  • Deploy DKIM signing and an enforced DMARC policy, since SPF on its own does not protect the From address that recipients see.

Confirm the fix by querying the TXT record and checking it with an SPF validation tool, then sending a test message through each legitimate service and checking that the receiving server records an SPF pass in the Authentication-Results header.

entries.title: DMARC Policy Missing or Not Enforced
entries.summary: The domain has no DMARC record, or one with a policy of none, so receivers are not told to reject or quarantine mail that forges the domain in the From address.
entries.description:
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC, RFC 7489) is published as a DNS TXT record at _dmarc under the domain. It tells receiving mail servers what to do with a message whose visible From address uses the domain but which does not pass SPF or DKIM in alignment with that address: deliver it as normal (p=none), treat it as suspicious (p=quarantine) or reject it (p=reject). It also asks receivers to send aggregate reports (rua) showing which servers send mail as the domain. DMARC is the control that protects the From address recipients see; a forged message can pass SPF or DKIM on its own by using the attacker's own domain in the envelope sender or signature.

The weakness covers a missing record; a policy of none left in place after the monitoring period; a pct value below 100, which under RFC 7489 applies the policy to only part of the failing mail; a subdomain policy of sp=none, which leaves subdomains unprotected; and records with syntax errors, which receivers ignore. It is identified with a DNS query for the _dmarc TXT record and a review of its policy tags.
entries.impact: Without an enforced DMARC policy, an attacker can send email showing the organisation's exact domain in the From address, and receivers that would honour a policy deliver it. Such messages are used for phishing, invoice and payment fraud and impersonation of senior staff, and towards customers and suppliers they are more convincing than lookalike domains because the address is genuine. Many receiving services apply their own checks and may still flag some forged mail, so the effect varies by recipient, but the organisation has no control over that. Without a record the organisation also receives no reports of who is sending mail as its domain.
entries.remediation:
Publish a DMARC record for every domain and move it to an enforced policy:

  • Make sure every legitimate sender passes SPF or DKIM in alignment with the From domain, preferably DKIM, which survives forwarding.
  • Publish a record in monitoring mode with aggregate reporting to a mailbox or reporting service, for example:
_dmarc.example.com. TXT "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"
  • Review the aggregate reports, correct or authorise any legitimate sender that fails, then move to p=quarantine and then p=reject, with pct at 100 or omitted.
  • Set a subdomain policy (sp=quarantine or sp=reject) unless subdomains publish their own records, and publish v=DMARC1; p=reject for domains that send no mail at all, including parked domains.
  • Use a DMARC reporting tool or service to read the reports, as the raw XML is hard to review at volume.

Confirm the fix by querying the _dmarc record and checking that the policy is quarantine or reject and applies to all mail, then sending a test message that fails alignment from an outside server and checking that a major mailbox provider rejects or quarantines it.

entries.title: DKIM Not Configured
entries.summary: Outgoing email is not signed with DKIM for the organisation's domain, so receivers cannot verify that messages came from it and were not altered.
entries.description:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM, RFC 6376) lets a sending mail system add a digital signature to each message, covering the body and selected headers, and publish the matching public key in DNS under a selector name below _domainkey in the domain. Receiving servers check the signature against the published key to confirm that the message was sent by a system holding the domain's private key and was not altered on the way. A valid DKIM signature for the From domain also satisfies DMARC, and unlike SPF it normally survives forwarding.

The weakness is reported when messages sent from the domain carry no DKIM signature, or are signed only for the email provider's own default domain rather than the organisation's, so that the signature is not aligned with the From address. Related forms are signing keys shorter than 1024 bits, which current standards say receivers must not treat as valid, and selectors left published for keys that are no longer used. It is identified by examining the headers of messages sent from the domain (DKIM-Signature and Authentication-Results) and by querying the selector records named in them, as selector names cannot be listed from DNS.
entries.impact: Without DKIM, receivers cannot confirm that a message claiming to come from the domain is genuine and unaltered, and DMARC has to rely on SPF alone. Because SPF fails when mail is forwarded, organisations without DKIM often cannot move DMARC to an enforced policy without losing legitimate mail, which leaves the domain open to spoofing for longer. Missing DKIM can also reduce deliverability, as large mailbox providers expect senders to authenticate their mail. On its own, the absence of DKIM does not let an attacker forge mail that passes an enforced DMARC policy, which is why it is rated low.
entries.remediation:
Sign all outgoing mail with a DKIM key for the organisation's own domain:

  • Enable DKIM signing for the organisation's domain on every system that sends mail as it. In Microsoft 365, publish the two selector CNAME records shown for the domain in the Microsoft Defender portal and then enable signing; in Google Workspace, generate a key in the Admin console, publish the TXT record it provides and start authentication; for on-premises servers and third-party senders, follow the product's DKIM instructions.
  • Use RSA keys of 2048 bits where the platform and DNS provider support them, and never shorter than 1024 bits.
  • Rotate keys periodically using a new selector, and remove the records of retired selectors once mail signed with them is no longer in transit.
  • Check that third-party services sign with the organisation's domain rather than their own, so that the signature aligns with the From address.
  • Once DKIM is in place, use DMARC reports to confirm that all legitimate mail passes, and move DMARC to an enforced policy.

Confirm the fix by sending a message through each sending service to an external mailbox and checking that the Authentication-Results header shows dkim=pass for the organisation's domain.

entries.title: MTA-STS Not Configured
entries.summary: The domain publishes no MTA-STS policy, so servers sending it email fall back to unencrypted or unverified delivery if an attacker interferes with the connection.
entries.description:
Email between mail servers is protected by STARTTLS, which is opportunistic: a sending server encrypts the connection if the receiving server offers it, and usually does not check the receiving server's certificate. An attacker who can intercept the connection can remove the STARTTLS offer so that the message is sent in clear text, or present a certificate of their own, and most sending servers will carry on. SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS, RFC 8461) lets a domain tell senders that its mail servers support TLS with valid certificates, so that senders which support MTA-STS refuse to deliver over an unencrypted or unverified connection.

A policy has two parts: a DNS TXT record at _mta-sts under the domain, and a policy file served over HTTPS from the host mta-sts under the domain, at the path /.well-known/mta-sts.txt, listing the permitted MX host names and a mode of testing or enforce. The finding is reported when no policy exists, or when one is left in testing mode, in which senders report failures but still deliver. It is usually paired with SMTP TLS Reporting (TLS-RPT, RFC 8460), a _smtp._tls TXT record that asks senders to report delivery problems. DANE for SMTP (RFC 7672) gives similar protection to domains signed with DNSSEC.
entries.impact: The absence of MTA-STS does not expose mail by itself: it removes a protection against an attacker who is already able to intercept or redirect traffic between the sending and receiving mail servers, for example through a compromised network or provider on the path, or by tampering with DNS answers for the domain's MX records. Such an attacker could read or alter inbound email in transit by downgrading the connection, without the sender or recipient noticing. Because that position is hard to obtain, the finding is rated informational, as a recommended hardening measure.
entries.remediation:
Publish an MTA-STS policy, with TLS reporting, for each domain that receives email:

  • Make sure every MX host supports STARTTLS with a certificate from a public certification authority that is valid for the MX host name. Hosted platforms such as Exchange Online and Gmail already meet this for their MX hosts.
  • Publish the policy file at /.well-known/mta-sts.txt on the mta-sts host under the domain, served over HTTPS with a valid certificate, starting in testing mode, for example:
version: STSv1 mode: testing mx: mail.example.com max_age: 86400
  • Publish the two DNS records, changing the id value whenever the policy changes:
_mta-sts.example.com. TXT "v=STSv1; id=1" _smtp._tls.example.com. TXT "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tls-reports@example.com"
  • Review the TLS reports, then change the mode to enforce, raise max_age to a period of weeks, and change the id.
  • Where the domain is signed with DNSSEC, consider publishing DANE TLSA records for the MX hosts as well, for senders that support DANE.

Confirm the fix by retrieving the policy file and DNS records and checking them with an MTA-STS validation tool, and by checking that the TLS reports show successful sessions.

entries.title: SMTP STARTTLS Not Supported
entries.summary: The domain's inbound mail server does not offer STARTTLS, so email delivered to it from other mail servers crosses the internet unencrypted.
entries.description:
Mail servers exchange email over SMTP on TCP port 25. The STARTTLS extension (RFC 3207) lets a sending server upgrade the connection to TLS before transferring the message, and mail servers on the internet generally do so whenever the receiving server offers it. The mail exchanger (MX) host for the domain does not advertise STARTTLS in its response to EHLO, or advertises it but cannot complete the TLS handshake, so senders deliver messages to it in clear text.

It is identified by connecting to each MX host on port 25, for example with openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect or swaks --tls, and examining the EHLO response and the handshake. Causes include older or misconfigured mail servers and gateways, a certificate that was allowed to lapse with TLS switched off rather than renewed, and secondary or backup MX hosts that were not configured like the primary. This finding concerns delivery between mail servers; clear-text client protocols such as POP3, IMAP and authenticated SMTP submission are covered separately.
entries.impact: Email sent to the organisation travels unencrypted between the sender's server and the MX host. An attacker able to observe that traffic, for example on a compromised network segment, at a provider on the path, or on the same network as either server, can read the messages, including any attachments, personal data or credentials they contain, and could alter them in transit. Obtaining such a position is not easy, which limits the likelihood, but interception would go unnoticed. Without STARTTLS the domain also cannot adopt MTA-STS, and senders whose policies require TLS for the domain will not deliver to it.
entries.remediation:
Enable STARTTLS on every MX host for the domain:

  • Install a certificate that is valid for the MX host name, issued by a public certification authority, and enable STARTTLS on the SMTP service. For example, in Postfix set smtpd_tls_security_level = may with smtpd_tls_cert_file and smtpd_tls_key_file; in Exim set tls_advertise_hosts = * with tls_certificate and tls_privatekey; and in Exchange Server assign the certificate to the SMTP service with Enable-ExchangeCertificate and its -Services SMTP parameter.
  • Configure protocol versions and cipher suites in line with the organisation's TLS standard, preferring TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
  • Apply the same configuration to secondary and backup MX hosts and to any mail gateway or filtering service in front of the server.
  • Keep TLS opportunistic for inbound mail in general, so that the few senders without TLS are not rejected, unless policy requires otherwise, and publish an MTA-STS policy so that senders which support it insist on TLS.
  • Monitor certificate expiry, since senders that validate certificates, such as those applying MTA-STS, will not deliver to a host whose certificate has expired.

Confirm the fix by connecting to each MX host on port 25 and checking that STARTTLS is advertised and the handshake completes with a valid certificate.

entries.title: Internal Email Spoofing Possible
entries.summary: Email from outside the organisation that claims to come from an internal address is accepted and delivered to staff as though it were internal.
entries.description:
The organisation's mail system accepts messages from the internet whose sender address uses one of the organisation's own domains, and delivers them to users' inboxes as though they had been sent internally. Staff therefore receive what appears to be email from colleagues, senior managers or internal systems, often without the warnings applied to other external mail.

It typically arises where the domain's DMARC policy is not enforced; where the mail gateway or platform does not apply the domain's own SPF, DKIM and DMARC results to inbound mail; where an allow rule or connector trusts any message from the organisation's own domain; or where a mail server or relay accepts unauthenticated messages for local delivery from any source. In Microsoft 365 a common route is Direct Send, which lets devices and services submit mail to the tenant's MX endpoint without authentication, using an internal sender address. It is confirmed by sending test messages from an external server, with the organisation's domain in both the envelope sender and the From header, to an internal mailbox (for example with swaks), and recording whether they are delivered, quarantined or rejected and how they are displayed.
entries.impact: An attacker can send email that appears to come from a named colleague, a senior manager or an internal service such as IT support or payroll. Because people tend to trust messages from inside their own organisation, and the message may carry no external warning, such email is effective for credential phishing, malware delivery, requests to change payment details and requests for sensitive information. No access to the organisation's systems is needed. The likelihood of success depends on users' awareness and on other filtering, and the impact on what the deceived user can do or disclose.
entries.remediation:
Stop the mail system accepting unauthenticated mail from outside that claims an internal sender:

  • Enforce DMARC on the organisation's domains (p=quarantine or p=reject), with SPF and DKIM in place, and make sure the inbound gateway or platform applies that policy to mail arriving from outside.
  • Add an inbound rule that rejects or quarantines messages from outside the organisation that use an internal domain in the envelope sender or From address, with exceptions only for named, authenticated services that are allowed to send as the domain.
  • Remove allow rules, safe sender entries and connector settings that trust the organisation's own domain or bypass filtering for it.
  • In Microsoft 365, move devices and services that use Direct Send to authenticated submission or a partner connector, then block Direct Send with Set-OrganizationConfig -RejectDirectSend $true, and keep spoof intelligence enabled in the anti-phishing policy.
  • On on-premises servers, restrict anonymous relay and receive connectors to the gateways and devices that need them.
  • Enable external sender tagging, for example with Set-ExternalInOutlook in Exchange Online, so that staff can see when a message did not originate internally.

Confirm the fix by repeating the test from an external server and checking that spoofed internal messages are rejected or quarantined.

entries.title: Dangerous Attachments Delivered by Email
entries.summary: The email filtering service delivers attachments that can run code when opened, such as executables, scripts, disk images or macro-enabled documents.
entries.description:
The organisation's email filtering delivers attachments of types that can run code on the recipient's device when opened. Such types include executables and installers (.exe, .scr, .msi), scripts (.js, .vbs, .hta, .ps1, .bat), shortcut and help files (.lnk, .chm), disk images (.iso, .img, .vhd), OneNote files, HTML files used for phishing and HTML smuggling, and Office documents containing macros. Attackers often place these inside ZIP or other archives, sometimes password-protected so that the filter cannot inspect them, or rename them, to get past filters that check only the outer file or its extension.

The weakness is identified by sending a set of harmless test files of each type, on their own, renamed and inside archives, from an external account to a test mailbox, and recording which are delivered. Because results depend on the gateway's file type rules, malware scanning and sandboxing together, a type that is delivered is reported even if a later control on the endpoint might stop it, as one layer of defence is missing.
entries.impact: An attacker can deliver malicious files directly to staff, and a single user opening one may run malware with that user's privileges, giving the attacker remote access to the device and a foothold in the internal network; this is a common first step in ransomware attacks. Whether a delivered file leads to compromise depends on further controls: endpoint protection, application control, the blocking of macros in files from the internet, and the user recognising the threat. The risk is greater where users have local administrator rights or endpoint controls are weak, and lower where application control would stop the file running.
entries.remediation:
Block attachment types the organisation does not need to receive, and inspect the rest:

  • Configure the mail gateway or platform to block or quarantine executable, script, shortcut, disk image and similar file types, identified by their content rather than only their extension. In Microsoft 365 this is the common attachments filter in the anti-malware policy, whose list of file types can be extended; other gateways have equivalent file type rules. Check how the chosen service treats files inside archives, and extend the rules to them where possible.
  • Quarantine password-protected archives and other attachments that cannot be scanned, or release them only after review, unless there is a business need to receive them.
  • Open permitted attachments in a sandbox before delivery where the service offers it, such as Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
  • On endpoints, keep macros in Office files from the internet blocked (the default in current Microsoft 365 Apps, which can be enforced with the Block macros from running in Office files from the Internet policy), and use attack surface reduction rules and application control to stop files received by email from running.
  • Provide a sanctioned way to exchange file types that are blocked, such as an approved file transfer service, so that staff do not look for workarounds.
  • Make it easy for staff to report suspicious attachments, and train them to do so.

Confirm the fix by repeating the test with the same set of files and checking that each blocked type is quarantined or rejected, on its own and inside archives.

entries.title: Microsoft 365 User Enumeration
entries.summary: Microsoft 365 and Entra ID respond differently to valid and invalid usernames, so anyone on the internet can confirm which email addresses are real accounts.
entries.description:
Several public Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra ID endpoints reveal, without authentication, whether a username or email address belongs to an account in the organisation's tenant. Examples include the GetCredentialType request made by the Microsoft sign-in page, which returns an IfExistsResult value; the error codes returned by sign-in and token endpoints, which differ between an unknown user (AADSTS50034) and a wrong password (AADSTS50126); requests to a user's OneDrive address, which return different responses for existing and unknown users once OneDrive has been provisioned; Autodiscover; and Microsoft Teams external search, where external access is allowed.

Microsoft treats this as part of how the service works, and tenants cannot switch most of it off. It is identified by submitting known valid and invalid addresses and comparing the responses, manually or with tools such as o365spray, TeamFiltration or AADInternals, and is usually combined with names gathered from public sources to build a list of valid accounts. Username enumeration in the organisation's own web applications is reported separately.
entries.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can confirm which staff email addresses are valid accounts, and from them the username format. The list itself discloses little, but it makes password spraying, credential stuffing with leaked passwords and targeted phishing more efficient, because effort is spent only on real accounts. The risk therefore depends mostly on the controls that protect the accounts: where every account requires multifactor authentication and legacy authentication is blocked, a valid username gives the attacker little; where some accounts can sign in with a password alone, it brings account compromise closer.
entries.remediation:
The behaviour cannot be removed entirely, so the aim is to make a list of valid usernames of little use to an attacker:

  • Require multifactor authentication for every account through Conditional Access or security defaults, preferring phishing-resistant methods for administrators.
  • Block legacy authentication protocols, which cannot enforce multifactor authentication and are commonly used for password spraying.
  • Enable Microsoft Entra Password Protection with a custom banned password list containing the organisation's name and common local terms, and review the Smart Lockout settings.
  • Restrict Microsoft Teams external access to named partner domains where open federation is not needed, which removes one enumeration route.
  • Monitor sign-in logs for password spraying, such as many failed sign-ins across different accounts from the same source, and use Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk policies where licensed.
  • Disable or remove accounts that are no longer used, since they are attractive targets once enumerated.

As the enumeration itself will remain possible, confirm the remediation by checking that a password spraying test against the enumerated accounts is stopped by multifactor authentication, lockout or Conditional Access.

entries.title: Subdomain Takeover
entries.summary: A DNS record for a subdomain points to a cloud or hosting resource that no longer exists, so anyone can claim that resource and serve their own content on the subdomain.
entries.description:
Organisations often point subdomains at third-party services with CNAME or other records, for example at a cloud web application, a storage bucket website, a content delivery network endpoint or a hosted platform. When the service is cancelled or the resource deleted but the DNS record is left in place, the record is described as dangling. If the provider lets any customer create a resource with the same name, an attacker can register it, and the organisation's subdomain then serves content the attacker controls.

Services where this has been possible include Azure resources referenced by their default host names, Amazon S3 website endpoints and GitHub Pages; whether a takeover works depends on how each provider checks ownership, which changes over time. A records pointing to released cloud IP addresses, and NS records delegating to deleted DNS zones, create the same risk. The weakness is identified by resolving the organisation's known subdomains and looking for records that point to unclaimed resources or that return the provider's error page for a missing resource, then confirming, where the rules of engagement allow, by claiming the resource with harmless content. Community references such as the can-i-take-over-xyz list record which services are affected.
entries.impact: An attacker who takes over the subdomain can serve any content under the organisation's domain name and can usually obtain a valid TLS certificate for it, since certification authorities validate control of a name through the content or DNS it serves. They can host convincing phishing pages and malware, capture cookies scoped to the parent domain, which browsers send to every subdomain, and abuse trust that the organisation's applications place in their own subdomains, such as cross-origin (CORS) rules, Content Security Policy sources and OAuth redirect addresses. Malicious content on the organisation's own domain can also cause significant reputational harm, even where no data is taken.
entries.remediation:
Remove the dangling record and stop new ones appearing:

  • Delete or correct the affected DNS record immediately. If someone else has already claimed the resource, removing the record is the quickest way to take the name back out of their control.
  • Make DNS part of decommissioning: remove the DNS record before deleting the resource it points to, not after.
  • Keep an inventory of DNS records linked to the resources and owners they belong to, and check every CNAME, A and NS record regularly for targets that no longer exist.
  • Use the provider's ownership verification where it exists, such as the asuid TXT record for Azure App Service custom domains, and in Azure DNS use alias records that point to the resource itself, which become empty when the resource is deleted.
  • Avoid wildcard DNS records that point to third-party services, and do not scope session cookies to the parent domain unless that is required.
  • Review logs and content for the period the subdomain was exposed, and check Certificate Transparency logs for certificates issued for it that the organisation did not request, asking the issuing authority to revoke any found.

Confirm the fix by resolving the subdomain and checking that the record no longer exists or points to a resource the organisation controls.

entries.title: DNSSEC Not Enabled
entries.summary: The domain's DNS zone is not signed with DNSSEC, so resolvers cannot verify that the answers they receive for it are genuine.
entries.description:
DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add digital signatures to DNS records. A validating resolver checks each signature against the zone's public key, and that key against a Delegation Signer (DS) record held in the parent zone, building a chain of trust up to the DNS root. Answers that have been forged or altered fail validation and are discarded. When a zone is not signed, or is signed but has no DS record at the parent, resolvers have no way to tell a genuine answer for it from a forged one.

It is identified by querying the zone for DNSKEY records and the parent for a DS record, for example with dig +dnssec or delv, or with a DNSSEC analysis tool. Signing is configured with the organisation's DNS hosting provider and domain registrar, many of which support it. DNSSEC protects the integrity and authenticity of DNS answers, not their confidentiality, and protects users only when their resolvers validate.
entries.impact: Without DNSSEC, a resolver can be given false answers for the domain by an attacker who can intercept or spoof DNS traffic, or who poisons a resolver's cache, so that users and systems are sent to servers the attacker controls. Such attacks need a privileged network position or a vulnerable resolver, and for web traffic their effect is largely contained by TLS certificate validation, so the absence of DNSSEC is rated informational, as a recommended hardening measure. It matters more for services that rely on DNS without other authentication, and it is a prerequisite for DANE, which uses DNS to protect email transport.
entries.remediation:
Sign the zone and publish its DS record at the parent:

  • Enable DNSSEC signing with the DNS hosting service, many of which, including Amazon Route 53 and Cloudflare, offer managed signing, or on the organisation's own authoritative servers, for example with a dnssec-policy in BIND or zone signing in Windows Server DNS.
  • Publish the DS record for the zone's key signing key through the domain registrar, and check that the chain of trust validates from the root.
  • Use a current algorithm such as ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (algorithm 13), and plan key rollovers, preferably automated by the provider, since expired signatures or a failed rollover make the domain unresolvable for validating resolvers.
  • Enable DNSSEC validation on the organisation's own recursive resolvers, so that internal users are protected when resolving other signed domains.
  • Once the zone is signed, consider DANE TLSA records for the mail servers.

Confirm the fix with a DNSSEC analysis tool or delv, checking that answers for the zone validate.

entries.title: CAA Record Not Configured
entries.summary: The domain publishes no CAA record, so every publicly trusted certification authority is permitted to issue TLS certificates for it.
entries.description:
CAA records, defined in RFC 8659, let a domain owner name in DNS the certification authorities (CAs) that may issue certificates for the domain and its subdomains. Publicly trusted CAs are required by the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements to check CAA records before issuing, and to refuse when they are not named. When no CAA record applies to a name, any publicly trusted CA may issue a certificate for it, subject to its usual validation.

It is identified by querying the domain for CAA records (for example dig CAA); a CA looks for a record at the name in the certificate and then at each parent domain in turn, using the first it finds. The issue property controls ordinary certificates, issuewild controls wildcard certificates, and iodef gives an address for reports of refused requests. CAs that support them can also honour parameters that restrict issuance further, such as accounturi and validationmethods, defined in RFC 8657.
entries.impact: The absence of a CAA record does not expose anything by itself. It removes a check that could stop a certificate being issued for the domain by a CA the organisation does not use, for example to an attacker who briefly controls a subdomain's content or DNS, or through a CA's validation error. A certificate obtained that way could support impersonation of the organisation's services or interception of their traffic. Because the attacker must still pass the CA's domain validation, and issued certificates appear in Certificate Transparency logs, the finding is rated informational, as a recommended hardening measure.
entries.remediation:
Publish CAA records naming the CAs the organisation uses:

  • Identify every CA that issues certificates for the domain and its subdomains, including those used by hosting, content delivery and email services on the organisation's behalf, from the certificate inventory and Certificate Transparency logs.
  • Publish CAA records at the organisation's domain with an issue entry for each CA, an issuewild entry if wildcard certificates are needed (or issuewild ";" to forbid them), and an iodef contact, for example:
example.com. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" example.com. CAA 0 issue "digicert.com" example.com. CAA 0 issuewild ";" example.com. CAA 0 iodef "mailto:security@example.com"
  • Where a subdomain uses a different CA, publish CAA records at that subdomain, which take precedence over the parent's.
  • Add the CAA records to the process for changing certificate provider, so that renewals and new requests are not refused.
  • Monitor Certificate Transparency logs for certificates issued for the organisation's domains.

Confirm the fix by querying the CAA records for the domain and its main subdomains, and checking that the CAs named match those in use.

entries.title: Hard-Coded Credentials in the Client
entries.summary: The desktop client contains credentials, such as a database password or API key, that any user with a copy of the application can extract and reuse.
entries.description:
The thick client application contains credentials embedded in its executable files, libraries or bundled configuration files, for example a database connection string with a username and password, a service account password, an API key or a client secret. The same credentials are present in every installed copy, so they are effectively known to every user who has the application, and to anyone who obtains the installer.

Credentials in a client cannot be kept secret from its users. .NET and Java applications decompile to readable source with tools such as dnSpy, ILSpy and JD-GUI, native binaries reveal strings with simple utilities, and configuration files such as app.config are often plain text. Credentials that are encrypted or obfuscated within the client are no better protected, because the client must also contain the key or routine to recover them, and they are visible in memory and often in network traffic whenever the application uses them.

The weakness is identified by decompiling or extracting strings from the application's files, reviewing its configuration files and observing its connections to back-end services, then confirming that the recovered credentials are accepted by the service they belong to.
entries.impact: Any user of the application, or anyone with a copy of it, can use the embedded credentials directly against the back-end service, outside the application and its restrictions. Shared database and service accounts typically have access to all of the application's data, so this usually means reading and changing every record rather than only the user's own, with the activity attributed to the shared account instead of the individual. The credentials cannot be revoked for one user, and changing them requires a new release to every installation.
entries.remediation:
Remove shared secrets from the client and authenticate each user individually:

  • Move access to back-end resources behind a server-side API that authenticates each user, for example with Windows integrated authentication or an OAuth 2.0 flow that issues per-user tokens, and that holds any service credentials itself, out of users' reach.
  • Where the client must connect to a database directly, use each user's own Windows account (integrated security) with only the permissions that user needs, rather than a shared SQL login.
  • Treat the exposed credentials as compromised: change them, review the service's logs for use from unexpected hosts, and remove them from every released version and from source control.
  • Where the client must keep a per-user secret, such as a refresh token, protect it with the operating system's facilities, such as the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) with user scope, rather than with a key held in the application.

As an interim measure, reduce the privileges of the embedded account to the minimum the application needs, and restrict which hosts can use it. Confirm the fix by decompiling the new release and confirming that no usable credentials remain.

entries.title: DLL Search Order Hijacking
entries.summary: The application loads DLLs from locations that users can write to, so code placed there runs inside the application when it starts.
entries.description:
The application loads one or more dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) without specifying a full path, so Windows searches a sequence of directories for them, and at least one directory searched before the genuine copy, or in place of a DLL that does not exist, can be written to by users who should not control the application's code. A DLL with the expected name placed there is loaded into the application's process, and its code runs with the application's privileges.

With the default safe search mode, Windows looks in the application's own directory first, then the system and Windows directories, then the current working directory and the directories listed in the PATH environment variable; system libraries on the KnownDLLs list are always loaded from the system directory. Common causes are an application installed outside Program Files, for example in a folder at the root of the system drive or in the user's profile, whose directory standard users can write to; an application that tries to load DLLs that do not exist, which are then sought in every location, including writable PATH entries; and installers or updaters that run from writable folders such as Downloads or temporary directories.

The weakness is identified by monitoring the application's DLL loads with Process Monitor, filtering for load attempts that return NAME NOT FOUND or that resolve to unprotected directories, checking those directories' permissions, and confirming exploitation by placing a test DLL that records its execution.
entries.impact: An attacker who can write to the affected directory gets code execution inside the application whenever it starts. Where the directory is writable only by the user who runs the application, this gives persistence and lets the attacker's code run inside a trusted, possibly signed, process that application control may allow, which is the typical case rated here. Where the application is started by other users or administrators, runs as a service or is launched elevated, the same weakness gives privilege escalation and should be rated higher.
entries.remediation:
Make the application load libraries only from trusted, protected locations, following Microsoft's guidance on dynamic-link library security:

  • Install the application under Program Files, or another directory where only administrators and SYSTEM can write, and make sure the installer does not loosen those permissions.
  • At start-up, call SetDefaultDllDirectories with LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32, adding LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR only when the application directory is protected, so that the current directory and PATH are no longer searched. Add any other trusted directories with AddDllDirectory, which are searched only when LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS is also specified.
  • Load libraries with LoadLibraryEx and the LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_* flags, or with a fully qualified path, rather than by name alone, and remove attempts to load DLLs that are not shipped.
  • Run installers and updaters only from protected locations, and remove user-writable directories from the system PATH.

For example:

SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32); HMODULE h = LoadLibraryExW(L"helper.dll", NULL, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR);

Libraries that the executable imports statically are resolved before any of this code runs, so a protected installation directory remains essential. As an interim measure, correct the permissions on the affected directories so that standard users cannot write to them. Confirm the fix by repeating the Process Monitor review and the test DLL placement.

entries.title: Sensitive Data Stored Insecurely by the Client
entries.summary: The client stores credentials, tokens or sensitive data on the local system in cleartext or in a form that is easily reversed.
entries.description:
The thick client stores sensitive information on the local system without adequate protection. Typical examples are saved usernames and passwords, session or refresh tokens, connection strings, encryption keys, and business or personal data cached for offline use. They are found in configuration files, the registry (under HKEY_CURRENT_USER or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE), local databases such as SQLite or Access files, log files, temporary files and exported reports.

Protection is often absent or only apparent: values stored in cleartext, Base64 encoded, obscured with a simple XOR, or encrypted with a key held in the application itself, all of which can be reversed by anyone who can read the files and the client. Data written to shared locations, such as C:\ProgramData or a folder at the root of the system drive, is frequently readable by every user of the computer, which matters on shared workstations and terminal servers.

The weakness is identified by using the application while monitoring the files and registry keys it writes, for example with Process Monitor, then reviewing those locations and their permissions for sensitive values, and by decompiling the client to understand any encoding or encryption it applies.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the stored data, including malware running as the user, other users of a shared computer where permissions allow, or anyone who obtains the device or a backup of it, can recover the information. Recovered credentials and tokens let them sign in to the application or its back-end services as the user, potentially from elsewhere, and cached data may include personal or commercially sensitive records. The attacker needs some access to the system first, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Store as little as possible locally, and protect what remains with the operating system's facilities:

  • Do not store users' passwords. Where the client needs to remember a sign-in, store a revocable token with a limited lifetime instead.
  • Protect secrets that must be kept with the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI), for example through the ProtectedData class in .NET with user scope, or with Windows Credential Manager, rather than with a key held in the application.
  • Keep cached data to what is needed, encrypt local databases with a key protected by DPAPI, and delete temporary files and caches when they are no longer needed.
  • Write per-user data to the user's own profile rather than to shared locations, and set restrictive permissions on any file or registry key the application creates.
  • Make sure logs and diagnostic output do not record credentials, tokens or sensitive data.

Confirm the fix by repeating the review of files and registry keys written during use, including after sign-out.

entries.title: Unencrypted Client-Server Traffic
entries.summary: The client communicates with its server without encryption, exposing credentials and data to anyone able to observe or intercept the traffic.
entries.description:
The thick client sends and receives data over the network without encryption. Common forms are web services called over HTTP rather than HTTPS, database connections where encryption is not required, for example to SQL Server or MySQL, and proprietary TCP protocols that send data in cleartext or under a simple encoding. Some clients use TLS but accept any certificate, which leaves the same exposure to an attacker who can intercept the connection.

The traffic typically includes users' credentials or session tokens, the application's business data, and the requests that drive server-side actions. Because thick clients are often deployed on internal networks, cleartext protocols tend to be accepted on the assumption that the internal network is trusted.

The weakness is identified by capturing the application's traffic with Wireshark, or routing it through an intercepting proxy, and reviewing what is visible. Where the traffic is not HTTP, tools that intercept arbitrary TCP connections show whether requests can also be altered in transit.
entries.impact: An attacker with a position on the network path, for example on the same network segment using ARP spoofing, or with control of a network device, can read credentials and data as they pass, and in many cases alter requests and responses to change what the client or server does. The attacker needs that network position first, which limits the rating, but on flat internal networks and shared wireless networks it is often easy to obtain.
entries.remediation:
Encrypt and authenticate every connection between the client and its servers:

  • Use TLS 1.2 or later for all client-server communication, with the client validating the server certificate's chain and host name. For web services, use HTTPS only and disable cleartext endpoints on the server.
  • For direct database connections, configure the server to require encryption and the client to require it too, without trusting any certificate presented. For SQL Server this means setting Encrypt=True and TrustServerCertificate=False in the connection string, with a valid certificate installed on the server.
  • Replace custom encoding in proprietary protocols with TLS, or carry the protocol inside a TLS connection.
  • Where the server needs to know which clients are genuine, add mutual TLS.

As an interim measure, restrict the client-server traffic to a dedicated network segment or an IPsec-protected path. Confirm the fix by capturing the traffic again and confirming that it is encrypted, and that an intercepting proxy presenting an untrusted certificate is rejected.

entries.title: Authorisation Enforced Only by the Client
entries.summary: The server relies on the desktop client to restrict what each user can do, so a user who alters the client or calls the server directly can bypass those restrictions.
entries.description:
The application decides what each user may see and do in the client rather than on the server.
