The client hides menu items, disables buttons or filters data according to the user's role, but the server accepts the corresponding requests from any authenticated user, or trusts a role or permission value that the client sends.

Everything in a thick client is under the control of the person running it. A user can decompile, modify or patch the client, change values in memory or in local configuration files, re-enable hidden controls with tools that manipulate the user interface, or bypass the client entirely by sending requests straight to the server once its protocol is understood from intercepted traffic. Any restriction that exists only in the client can therefore be removed.

The weakness is identified by signing in as a low-privileged user, capturing or replaying requests that only a higher-privileged role should be able to make, and observing that the server processes them. It is also found by modifying the client, for example by changing a role check in a decompiled assembly with dnSpy, or by editing a server response that tells the client which features to enable.
entries.impact: Any authenticated user can perform actions and reach data reserved for more privileged roles, such as viewing other users' records, changing configuration or approvals, or carrying out administrative functions, limited only by what the server will do on request. Because the server records these as legitimate requests from that user, misuse may go unnoticed. The attacker needs a valid account, which is why this is rated high rather than critical.
entries.remediation:
Enforce every authorisation decision on the server:

  • For every request, have the server establish the user's identity from its own authenticated session, and check the user's role and permissions against the action and the specific record before doing anything. Never accept a role, permission or user identifier from the client as the basis for a decision.
  • Apply the checks centrally, for example in middleware or a common service layer, and deny by default, so that a new function cannot be added without a check.
  • Keep client-side restrictions only as a usability feature, consistent with the server's rules.
  • Where the client connects directly to a database, move business logic and authorisation into a server-side API or, as an interim step, into stored procedures that check the caller's permissions.
  • Add automated tests that call each function as each role and confirm that unauthorised calls are refused.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests as a low-privileged user, outside the client, and confirming that the server refuses them.

entries.title: Client Connects Directly to the Database
entries.summary: The desktop client connects straight to the back-end database, so users can bypass the application and query or change the data directly.
entries.description:
The application uses a two-tier design in which the desktop client connects straight to the back-end database, such as Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle or MySQL, and runs queries itself. The database therefore has to accept connections from every user's workstation, using either a shared account whose credentials are held in the client, or each user's own database or Windows login. Business rules and access restrictions are applied by the client, while the database account it uses is usually granted read and write access to all of the application's tables.

Because users can connect to the same database with their own tools, such as SQL Server Management Studio, sqlcmd or the ODBC connection in a spreadsheet, the restrictions in the client do not apply to them. SQL Server application roles, whose activation password is held in the client, do not change this, because the password can be recovered from the client.

The weakness is identified by observing the client's connections, recovering the connection details from its configuration, files or traffic, then connecting to the database directly with a standard tool as a low-privileged application user and reviewing what can be read and changed.
entries.impact: Any user of the application, and anyone who obtains the connection details, can read and change data across the whole application regardless of the role they hold in it. That typically includes other users' records, personal data and financial information, and the ability to alter or delete records in ways that bypass the application's validation and audit trail. Depending on the database account's privileges, it may also give a route to further compromise of the database server.
entries.remediation:
Move data access behind a server-side tier that enforces the application's rules:

  • Introduce an application server or API that the client calls, which authenticates each user, enforces authorisation and business rules, and alone holds the credentials used to connect to the database. Restrict the database to accept connections only from that tier.
  • Until that is in place, use each user's own Windows account rather than a shared login, and grant users EXECUTE permission only on stored procedures that apply the application's checks, with no direct access to tables.
  • Use database features such as row-level security to limit which records each user can reach, and apply least privilege to every database account.
  • Where the client must remain two-tier, publish it through a remote application platform, such as Remote Desktop Services, so that only those servers need network access to the database, and block the database port from users' workstations.
  • Require encrypted connections to the database, and audit direct access to it.

Confirm the fix by attempting to connect to the database directly from a workstation with a user's credentials, and confirming that the connection is refused or limited to the intended procedures.

entries.title: Sensitive Data Retained in Memory
entries.summary: The client keeps passwords, keys or other secrets in process memory in cleartext for longer than needed, where they can be read from a memory dump.
entries.description:
The application holds sensitive values in its process memory in cleartext for longer than it needs them: for example the user's password after sign-in has completed, database credentials, encryption keys, tokens, or sensitive records that remain after the screen showing them has closed. Values can also persist in memory that has been freed but not cleared, in several copies made by the runtime, and in files that capture memory, such as crash dumps, the page file and the hibernation file.

Managed runtimes make this hard to avoid. Strings in .NET and Java are immutable and cannot be cleared, and the garbage collector may copy them before they are released, so a password handled as a string can remain in memory for the life of the process. In native code, a call to clear a buffer that is not used afterwards may be removed by the compiler's optimiser.

The weakness is identified by using the application, then creating a dump of its process, for example with Task Manager or ProcDump, and searching it for known secrets such as the password used to sign in. Tools that inspect live process memory show the same.
entries.impact: An attacker who can read the process memory, which requires code running as the same user or administrative rights, or who obtains a crash dump or the device's storage, can recover the secrets. In most cases an attacker with that access could capture the same information in other ways, such as by logging keystrokes, which limits the rating. The exposure matters more where memory holds secrets the user does not otherwise see, such as shared service credentials or keys protecting other users' data.
entries.remediation:
Hold secrets in memory only as long as they are needed, and clear them afterwards:

  • Do not keep the user's password after authentication; exchange it for a token or session and discard it.
  • In .NET, hold secrets in byte or character arrays rather than strings, and clear them with CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory or Array.Clear as soon as they have been used. Microsoft advises against relying on SecureString in new code, as it offers limited protection on modern .NET.
  • In native code, clear buffers with SecureZeroMemory, or an equivalent the compiler will not remove, rather than memset.
  • Avoid holding shared or server-side secrets in the client at all, which also removes them from its memory.
  • Configure crash reporting so that full memory dumps of the application are not created or sent automatically, and protect any dumps that are kept.

Confirm the fix by repeating the memory dump after the same actions and searching for the same values.

entries.title: Insecure Software Update Mechanism
entries.summary: The client downloads and installs updates without verifying they are authentic, so an attacker who can intercept or alter them can run code on every client.
entries.description:
The application's update mechanism does not establish that an update genuinely comes from the vendor before installing it. Typical forms are an updater that fetches its update manifest or package over HTTP; one that uses HTTPS but accepts any certificate; one that checks only a hash supplied in the same unprotected response; and one that installs whatever it finds in a network share or folder that users can write to. Updaters often run with administrative or SYSTEM privileges, for example as a Windows service, so that they can replace the application's files.

The weakness is identified by observing the update process: capturing its traffic to see how it locates and downloads updates, reviewing the update client in a decompiler to see what it verifies, and checking the permissions of any share or directory it installs from. Exploitation is confirmed by serving a modified update, from an intercepting proxy or a test server the client is directed to, and observing that the client installs and runs it. Related variants include the absence of protection against downgrade to an older, vulnerable version, and verification carried out on a file in a user-writable location that can be swapped after it has been checked.
entries.impact: An attacker able to intercept or redirect the client's update traffic, for example from the same network segment with ARP or DNS spoofing, or anyone able to write to the update location, can make every affected client run their code, often with SYSTEM privileges where the updater runs as a service. This gives full control of the affected workstations at once. The attacker needs a network position or access to the update source first, which is reflected in the rating.
entries.remediation:
Make the client verify every update cryptographically before it is used:

  • Sign update packages and manifests, and have the updater verify the signature against the vendor's own key or certificate, built into the client, before doing anything else with the package. For Windows installers and executables, verify the Authenticode signature with WinVerifyTrust and check that the signer is the expected publisher, not merely that a valid signature is present.
  • Download updates over HTTPS with full certificate validation, as an additional layer rather than a replacement for signatures.
  • Reject updates whose version is lower than the installed one, unless a rollback is deliberately authorised.
  • Download and verify updates in a directory that only the updater can write to, and install from that same copy, so the file cannot be swapped between check and use.
  • Run the updater with the least privilege it needs, and restrict write access to any update share to the release process.
  • Consider an established packaging and update format that already signs and verifies packages, such as MSIX.

Confirm the fix by repeating the test with a modified update and an unsigned update, and confirming that both are rejected.

entries.title: Binaries Not Code-Signed
entries.summary: The application's executables, libraries or installers are not digitally signed, so their origin and integrity cannot be verified by users, Windows or security tools.
entries.description:
Some or all of the application's executable files, libraries and installers carry no Authenticode digital signature, or carry a signature that is invalid, or that expired without a timestamp. A signature identifies the publisher and lets Windows, users and security tools confirm that a file has not been altered since it was signed.

Without signatures, a modified or replaced binary looks the same as the genuine one. Windows identifies the publisher as unknown in elevation prompts, which teaches users to accept such warnings; application control policies cannot trust the application by publisher, and must rely on path rules, which trust anything placed in the folder, or hash rules, which break with every release; and security tools have less information to tell legitimate files from tampered ones.

The weakness is identified by checking the signature of each executable, DLL and installer, for example with the PowerShell Get-AuthenticodeSignature cmdlet, Sysinternals sigcheck or signtool verify, or the Digital Signatures tab of each file's properties. Third-party libraries shipped with the application should be checked too.
entries.impact: An attacker who can replace the application's files, or distribute a modified installer, can do so without the change being detectable through signature checks, and users have no reliable way to tell a genuine copy from a tampered one. The absence of signatures does not by itself give access, which is why it is rated low, but it removes a control that would expose tampering, and weakens application allowlisting.
entries.remediation:
Sign every file the application ships, as part of the build and release process:

  • Obtain a code signing certificate from a trusted certification authority, with its private key generated and held in a hardware security module or a cloud signing service, and restrict who and what can use it.
  • Sign all executables, DLLs, installers and scripts with Authenticode using SHA-256, and timestamp every signature so that it remains valid after the certificate expires. With SignTool, the /fd SHA256, /tr and /td SHA256 options apply a SHA-256 signature and an RFC 3161 timestamp from the certification authority's timestamp server.
  • Ask the suppliers of bundled third-party components for signed versions.
  • Verify signatures in the release pipeline before publishing, and publish the expected publisher name so that users and administrators can check it.
  • Once the application is signed, use publisher rules for it in application control policies, such as App Control for Business or AppLocker.

Confirm the fix by checking the signatures of every file in a new installation.

entries.title: Missing Binary Exploit Mitigations
entries.summary: Some of the application's binaries are built without exploit mitigations such as ASLR, DEP or Control Flow Guard, making any memory corruption flaw easier to exploit.
entries.description:
One or more of the application's executables or DLLs were built without the exploit mitigations that Windows supports. Each is set at compile or link time: address space layout randomisation (ASLR, the /DYNAMICBASE linker option, with /HIGHENTROPYVA for 64-bit binaries), Data Execution Prevention (DEP, /NXCOMPAT), Control Flow Guard (CFG, /guard:cf), stack buffer security checks (/GS) and, for 32-bit binaries, safe exception handlers (/SAFESEH). Current Microsoft toolchains enable several of these by default, so their absence usually points to an old compiler, another toolchain, options deliberately disabled, or third-party components shipped with the application.

These mitigations do not fix vulnerabilities; they make memory corruption flaws such as buffer overflows much harder to turn into code execution. ASLR applies per module, so a single DLL without it, loaded at a predictable address, can give an attacker the known code locations they need even when every other module is protected. The issue matters most for native C and C++ components that parse files or network data; managed .NET and Java code is far less exposed, though the native libraries it loads are not.

The settings are identified by inspecting each binary's headers, for example with dumpbin /headers or tools such as winchecksec and PESecurity; on Linux, checksec reports the equivalent ELF protections.
entries.impact: Missing mitigations give an attacker nothing on their own, and the finding is reported for information. If a memory corruption vulnerability exists or is later found in an affected binary, for example in its handling of a crafted file or network message, the missing mitigations make reliable exploitation, and therefore code execution in the context of the user or service running the application, considerably easier.
entries.remediation:
Rebuild the affected binaries with the platform's exploit mitigations enabled:

  • For Microsoft Visual C++, compile with /GS and /guard:cf, and link with /DYNAMICBASE, /HIGHENTROPYVA (64-bit), /NXCOMPAT, /guard:cf and, for 32-bit builds, /SAFESEH. Remove any options that disable them, such as /DYNAMICBASE:NO.
  • For other toolchains, use the equivalents, such as position-independent executables, non-executable stacks and full RELRO for GCC and Clang on Linux.
  • Ask the suppliers of third-party DLLs for builds with these mitigations, or replace components that cannot be rebuilt.
  • Add a check to the build pipeline that fails a release when a binary lacks the required settings.

As an interim measure, Windows Exploit Protection can enforce DEP and mandatory ASLR for the application's processes, configured per application in Windows Security or with the Set-ProcessMitigation cmdlet after testing for compatibility; it cannot add Control Flow Guard to binaries not compiled for it. Confirm the fix by inspecting the headers of every shipped binary.

entries.title: Insecure Named Pipe or IPC Permissions
entries.summary: A named pipe or other local IPC endpoint used by the application accepts connections from any local user, exposing privileged functions or data to them.
entries.description:
The application exposes an inter-process communication (IPC) endpoint with permissions that let users who should not use it connect to it. Thick clients commonly pair a user interface running as the signed-in user with a background service running as SYSTEM or another privileged account, and the two communicate through a named pipe, a local TCP port, a WCF or .NET remoting endpoint, a COM server or shared memory. If the endpoint accepts any local user, and the service does not itself check who is calling, any user can send it commands.

Named pipes created with a NULL DACL grant full access to everyone, and even the default security descriptor gives read access to Everyone and the anonymous account. A TCP port bound to the loopback address is still reachable by every user and process on the computer. Exposed commands frequently include actions such as running an update from a given path, writing configuration or files, or starting processes, which a standard user can then trigger with the service's privileges. A related variant is pipe squatting, where an attacker creates a pipe with the expected name before the genuine server does.

The weakness is identified by enumerating the application's pipes and ports, for example with Sysinternals accesschk and pipelist or the process's open handles, reviewing their security descriptors, and connecting as a standard user to send messages captured from, or reconstructed from, the client.
entries.impact: Any local user, or malware running as one, can invoke the functions the endpoint exposes with the privileges of the process behind it. The typical result is unauthorised access to data or settings held by the service; where an exposed function can write files, install updates or start processes, it becomes full privilege escalation to SYSTEM, and the finding should then be rated high. The attacker needs local access to the computer, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Restrict who can reach the endpoint, and check the caller on every request, following Microsoft's guidance on named pipe security and access rights:

  • Create named pipes with an explicit security descriptor that grants access only to the accounts that need it, never a NULL DACL, and set PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS unless network access is required. Create the first instance with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE, so that creating the pipe fails, rather than silently joining it, if another process has already taken the name.
  • In the server, identify the caller, for example with GetNamedPipeClientProcessId or by impersonating the client with ImpersonateNamedPipeClient and checking its token, and authorise each command against that identity.
  • Expose only the operations the user interface genuinely needs, and treat every message as untrusted input: validate paths, refuse arbitrary file locations and command lines, and require signed packages for any update operation.
  • For local TCP, WCF and remoting endpoints, require authentication and authorisation on the endpoint itself rather than relying on it being local.
  • Run the service with the least privilege it needs.

Confirm the fix by repeating the enumeration and attempting the same commands as a standard user.

entries.title: Secrets Committed to Source Control
entries.summary: Passwords, API keys, tokens or private keys are stored in a source code repository or its history, where anyone with read access to the repository can use them.
entries.description:
Credentials have been committed to a source code repository: for example database passwords in configuration files, cloud access keys, API tokens, private keys, or .env files holding the application's secrets. Anyone who can read the repository, including every developer, contractor and integrated service with access to it, can therefore read the secrets, whether or not their role needs them.

Removing a secret in a later commit does not remove it from the repository. It stays in the commit history, in other branches and tags, in forks and clones, and in copies held by build systems, until the history is rewritten everywhere. Secrets in a repository that is, or has ever been, public must be assumed to have been collected, as public repositories are scanned continuously for credentials.

The weakness is identified by scanning the full history of each repository with tools such as gitleaks or TruffleHog, or with the hosting platform's secret scanning, and by reviewing configuration files, deployment scripts and infrastructure templates. Each secret found is then checked to see whether it is still valid. This finding concerns the repository itself; secrets embedded in code delivered to browsers or devices, and repositories exposed through a web server, are separate issues.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains read access to the repository, through a compromised developer account, a leaked access token, an insider, a third party with access or the repository being made public, gains every secret in it at once. Depending on what they unlock, that may give direct access to production databases, cloud accounts, payment or messaging services and other internal systems, often with the broad privileges that service accounts tend to hold, and without passing the controls that protect user sign-in, such as multi-factor authentication. The impact is greatest for long-lived credentials to production systems, and lower where the secrets are for test environments or have already been revoked.
entries.remediation:
Treat every committed secret as compromised, and move secrets out of source code:

  • Revoke or rotate each exposed secret at its source first, then review the target system's logs for use of the old credential. Deleting the file or rewriting history does not make an exposed secret safe.
  • Store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager, such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault or Google Cloud Secret Manager, or in the CI/CD platform's protected secret store, and have the application or pipeline retrieve them at run time. Prefer workload identities and short-lived credentials where the platform supports them.
  • Keep local configuration files such as .env out of the repository with .gitignore, and commit only templates with dummy values.
  • Enable secret scanning on the hosting platform, with push protection where it is available, and add a pre-commit hook such as gitleaks so that new secrets are blocked before they are pushed.
  • Where history must be cleaned, for example before a repository is made public, rewrite it with a tool such as git filter-repo and have every clone and fork replaced. This is in addition to rotation, not instead of it.

Confirm the fix by rescanning the full history of every repository and checking that each secret found earlier has been revoked and no longer works.

entries.title: Hard-Coded Cryptographic Keys
entries.summary: Encryption or signing keys are written into source code or shipped inside the application, so anyone who obtains the code can decrypt its data or forge what it signs.
entries.description:
The application uses cryptographic keys that are written into its source code, configuration committed with the code or compiled binaries, instead of being generated for each environment and held in a protected key store. Typical examples are an AES key used to encrypt data or cookies, a secret used to sign session tokens or JSON Web Tokens, a framework's signing key such as an ASP.NET machine key, and a private key bundled with the software.

A hard-coded key is the same in every environment and every installation built from the code, cannot be rotated without a new release, and is known to everyone who can read the source or extract it from a binary, including former staff and anyone who obtains a copy of the code. Keys copied from documentation, code samples or framework defaults are worse still, as they are already public: Apache Shiro's default key for its remember-me cookie (CVE-2016-4437) and publicly disclosed ASP.NET machine keys have both been used to forge serialised data that applications accepted, leading to remote code execution.

The weakness is identified by source code review and static analysis that looks for key material in literals and configuration, by decompiling or extracting strings from distributed binaries, and by testing whether tokens or ciphertext produced with a recovered key are accepted. Hard-coded passwords and API keys, and weak signing secrets, are related but separate issues.
entries.impact: Anyone who recovers the key can decrypt the data it protects, whether stored in a database, held in files or sent over the network, and can forge whatever it signs or authenticates, such as session cookies, password reset tokens or API tokens, typically gaining access as any user, including administrators. Where the key protects serialised objects, forging them can lead to code execution on the server. Because the same key is shared by every installation, one disclosure affects every deployment and all data previously protected with it. Exploitation requires access to the key, from the source code or a distributed binary, and to the data or interface it protects.
entries.remediation:
Remove keys from the code and replace them with keys that are generated per environment and managed separately:

  • Generate new random keys for each environment and store them in a key management service or hardware security module, such as AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault or Google Cloud KMS, or in a secrets manager, and load them at run time. Where the platform allows, perform encryption and signing inside the key management service so that the application never holds the raw key.
  • Rotate every key that has been hard-coded: re-encrypt data protected with the old key, invalidate sessions and tokens signed with it, and treat it as public from then on.
  • For frameworks with their own signing keys, set a unique, randomly generated key in protected configuration rather than a value copied from documentation or another installation, for example a unique machine key for ASP.NET or a configured cipher key for Apache Shiro's remember-me feature.
  • Design for rotation: record which key version protected each item, and support more than one active key during a changeover.
  • Add static analysis and secret scanning to the build so that new key material in code is blocked.

Confirm the fix by checking that no key material remains in the source, configuration or built artefacts, and that tokens or ciphertext created with the old key are rejected.

entries.title: Third-Party Dependencies With Known Vulnerabilities
entries.summary: The application includes third-party libraries or packages at versions with publicly known vulnerabilities, some of which may be exploitable through the application.
entries.description:
The application includes open source or commercial libraries, frameworks or packages at versions affected by publicly disclosed vulnerabilities for which fixed versions are available. This applies to server-side packages, for example from npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems or Composer, to client-side JavaScript libraries served to browsers, and to the dependencies of those dependencies, which often outnumber the packages the developers chose directly and are easily overlooked.

The weakness is identified by software composition analysis tools such as OWASP Dependency-Check, npm audit, pip-audit or the hosting platform's dependency alerts, which compare the declared and resolved package versions with vulnerability databases, or during testing from version strings in served files. Not every reported vulnerability is exploitable: many affect only a function or configuration that the application does not use, so each finding needs triage to decide whether the vulnerable code is reachable. Vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, or with public exploit code, deserve priority.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the vulnerable component and how the application uses it, and ranges from cross-site scripting through an outdated client-side library to remote code execution through a server-side framework or parser. Where a vulnerable function is reachable with input an attacker controls, published details and exploit code make exploitation straightforward, and widely used components are scanned for at internet scale. Where the vulnerable code is not reachable, the immediate risk is low, but the outdated component makes future fixes harder to apply quickly.
entries.remediation:
Update the affected components and put dependency management on a continuous footing:

  • Upgrade each affected dependency to a version that fixes the reported vulnerabilities, including transitive dependencies, using the package manager's override or resolution feature where a direct dependency has not yet updated. Replace components that are no longer maintained.
  • Commit lock files so that builds use known versions, and rebuild and redeploy after updating; for client-side libraries, update the files actually served to browsers.
  • Add software composition analysis to the CI/CD pipeline and the repository so that changes introducing or keeping vulnerable versions are flagged, and use automated update tools to raise upgrade requests.
  • Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) for each application, so that newly disclosed vulnerabilities can be matched to affected systems quickly.
  • Set target times for fixing by severity, with known exploited vulnerabilities fixed first.

Where an upgrade cannot be made quickly, record the reason, confirm whether the vulnerable code is reachable, and consider a compensating control such as a web application firewall rule for the specific flaw. Confirm the fix by rerunning the composition analysis against the built application and checking that the reported versions are no longer present.

entries.title: Use of Weak Cryptographic Algorithms
entries.summary: The code uses broken or outdated cryptographic algorithms, modes or key sizes, such as DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1 or ECB mode, to protect data or check its integrity.
entries.description:
The application's code uses cryptographic algorithms, modes or key sizes that are broken or no longer considered strong enough for their purpose. Common examples are encryption with DES, Triple DES or RC4; block ciphers in ECB mode, which reveals patterns in the data; CBC mode without integrity protection, which can allow padding oracle attacks; MD5 or SHA-1 used for digital signatures or integrity checks, or message authentication built by simply hashing a secret with the data; RSA keys shorter than 2048 bits, or RSA encryption with the older PKCS#1 v1.5 padding rather than OAEP; and home-made schemes such as XOR obfuscation or custom ciphers.

These choices are usually found by source code review or static analysis, searching for algorithm names and cipher settings passed to cryptographic APIs, for example Cipher.getInstance("DES") in Java, or Cipher.getInstance("AES"), which defaults to ECB mode in the standard Java provider. In testing they can show as ciphertext that repeats for repeated input, or as tokens whose structure reveals the algorithm. Some uses are acceptable, such as MD5 as a non-security checksum, so each occurrence is judged by what the algorithm protects. Password storage and TLS configuration are covered by separate findings.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains data protected with a weak algorithm, for example from a database backup, a stolen file or intercepted traffic, may be able to decrypt it, recover patterns in it or modify it without detection, and may be able to forge signatures or integrity checks that the application relies on. The effort required varies: weaknesses in RC4 and ECB mode can be exploited with modest resources, while attacks on SHA-1 or Triple DES need much greater effort or large volumes of data. The impact depends on the sensitivity of the protected data, whether the attacker can obtain it and how long it must stay protected, as attacks only improve over time.
entries.remediation:
Replace weak algorithms with current, well-reviewed ones from a standard library:

  • For symmetric encryption, use AES in an authenticated mode such as GCM, or ChaCha20-Poly1305, with a unique nonce for every encryption and keys of at least 128 bits, or 256 bits where long-term protection is needed.
  • For integrity and signatures, use SHA-256 or stronger, HMAC for message authentication, and RSA with keys of at least 2048 bits and PSS or OAEP padding, or elliptic curve algorithms such as ECDSA with P-256, or Ed25519.
  • Use a high-level, misuse-resistant library such as libsodium or Google Tink, or the platform's recommended API, rather than assembling primitives by hand, and never use custom algorithms.
  • Make algorithms configurable and versioned so that they can be replaced without re-engineering, and plan the move to post-quantum algorithms for data that must stay protected for many years.
  • Re-encrypt stored data, and re-issue signatures and tokens created with the weak algorithm, then retire the old keys.

Add rules for banned algorithms to static analysis in the build pipeline so that new uses are caught. Confirm the fix by reviewing the code paths that were reported and checking that data written after the change uses the new algorithm.

entries.title: Insecure Randomness for Security Values
entries.summary: Tokens, identifiers or keys that must be unguessable are generated with a non-cryptographic random number generator whose output can be predicted.
entries.description:
The application generates values that must be unpredictable, such as session identifiers, password reset and email verification tokens, one-time codes, API keys, nonces or encryption keys, with a general-purpose pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) that is not designed for security. Examples include Math.random() in JavaScript, java.util.Random in Java, System.Random in .NET, Python's random module, and rand() or mt_rand() in C and PHP. These generators produce output that looks random but is fully determined by a small internal state or seed.

Depending on the generator, an attacker who observes enough outputs can recover its state and predict past and future values, and generators seeded with predictable values such as the current time can be brute-forced over a far smaller range than the token's length suggests. Related weaknesses include tokens built from timestamps, counters or hashes of predictable data, and output from a secure generator truncated to too few characters.

The weakness is usually found by source code review, tracing where each security value is created. In testing it can show as tokens that share structure or increase over time; collecting a large sample and analysing it, for example with the sequencer in Burp Suite, can reveal low entropy, although a sample that appears random does not prove that the generator is secure.
entries.impact: An attacker who can predict security values can forge them instead of having to steal them: for example, predicting a password reset token issued to another user to take over their account, guessing valid session identifiers, or deriving encryption keys or nonces. Exploitation usually requires the attacker to collect several outputs of the same generator, for instance by requesting tokens for their own account, and some knowledge of the generator, which makes it harder than many other attacks, but tools exist to recover the state of common generators. The impact depends on what the value protects, and is greatest for password reset tokens, session identifiers and keys.
entries.remediation:
Generate every security-sensitive value with a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG) provided by the platform:

  • Use crypto.randomBytes() in Node.js and crypto.getRandomValues() in browsers; java.security.SecureRandom in Java; RandomNumberGenerator in .NET; the secrets module in Python; random_bytes() and random_int() in PHP; and the operating system's generator, such as getrandom() on Linux, in C.
  • Give tokens at least 128 bits of randomness, and encode the random bytes directly rather than deriving tokens from timestamps, counters, user data or hashes of predictable values.
  • Use the framework's own session management and token features where they exist, as these already use a secure generator.
  • Do not seed secure generators with fixed or predictable values, and do not swap them for a faster general-purpose generator for performance.
  • Once the change is deployed, invalidate tokens, sessions and keys issued by the weak generator, and give single-use tokens a short expiry.

Add a static analysis rule that flags non-cryptographic generators in security-relevant code. Confirm the fix by reviewing the code that creates each security value and by analysing a fresh sample of tokens.

entries.title: Use of Unsafe Memory Functions
entries.summary: C or C++ code uses functions such as strcpy, strcat, sprintf or gets that do not check buffer sizes, risking buffer overflows when input is longer than expected.
entries.description:
The application's C or C++ code, or native code within another application such as a mobile or desktop client, uses library functions that write to memory without checking the size of the destination buffer. The classic examples are gets(), which cannot be used safely at all and has been removed from the C standard, and strcpy(), strcat(), sprintf(), vsprintf() and scanf() with an unbounded %s conversion. Functions such as memcpy() and strncpy() are unsafe when the length passed to them comes from the input or is miscalculated, and strncpy() also leaves the destination without a terminating null character when the source is too long.

Whether a particular call is exploitable depends on whether data from outside the program can reach it and exceed the buffer. The finding therefore covers both calls where an overflow has been shown to be reachable and calls whose safety rests on assumptions elsewhere in the code, which later changes can break.

Unsafe functions are found by source code review and static analysis, such as compiler warnings, clang-tidy, Flawfinder or Cppcheck, which flag each use, and in compiled binaries by listing the functions they import. Each occurrence is then reviewed to judge whether its input is bounded, and fuzzing can confirm whether an overflow can be triggered.
entries.impact: Where input an attacker controls can overflow the buffer, memory next to it is overwritten. The most likely result is a crash and denial of service, but an overflow can also corrupt data that controls the program's behaviour and, in the worse cases, let an attacker run code with the privileges of the process, for example as a network service or with elevated rights on the local system. Modern compiler and operating system protections, such as stack canaries, address space layout randomisation and non-executable memory, make code execution considerably harder but do not prevent it in every case. The risk is highest in code that parses network data or files from untrusted sources.
entries.remediation:
Replace unbounded memory operations with bounded ones, and check every length:

  • Remove all uses of gets(), replacing it with fgets().
  • Replace sprintf() and vsprintf() with snprintf() and vsnprintf(), checking the return value for truncation, and give every %s conversion in the scanf() family a field width.
  • Replace strcpy() and strcat() with bounded operations that always terminate the string, such as snprintf(), or strlcpy() and strlcat() where the platform provides them, and validate the length of input before copying it.
  • Check that the length passed to memcpy() and similar functions can never exceed the destination size, and check size calculations for integer overflow.
  • In C++, use std::string, std::vector and other standard containers instead of raw character arrays, and consider writing new components that parse untrusted input in a memory-safe language.

Build with the compiler's hardening options, such as stack protection, _FORTIFY_SOURCE, position-independent executables and full RELRO, and enable warnings and static analysis rules that flag banned functions in the build. These protections reduce the chance of exploitation while code is being fixed, but do not replace the fix. Confirm the fix by rerunning static analysis and fuzzing the affected input paths.

entries.title: Untrusted Input in CI/CD Workflows
entries.summary: A CI/CD workflow puts attacker-controllable data, such as pull request titles or branch names, into scripts it runs, or runs untrusted code with access to secrets.
entries.description:
A CI/CD pipeline handles data or code from people outside the trusted team in a way that lets them run commands in the pipeline. The most common form in GitHub Actions is script injection: a workflow inserts an expression that reads event data, such as github.event.issue.title, github.event.pull_request.title or github.head_ref, directly into a run: step. The expression is substituted into the script before the shell runs it, so a title or branch name containing shell syntax becomes part of the command. The same pattern occurs on other platforms wherever commit messages, merge request details or other event data are interpolated into scripts.

A second form, often called a pwn request, is a workflow triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run, which runs in the context of the base repository with access to its secrets and, depending on settings, a token that can write to it, and which checks out and builds code from an untrusted pull request, so that build scripts, tests or package install hooks written by the contributor run with those privileges. Self-hosted runners that accept jobs from untrusted pull requests carry a similar risk.

The weakness is identified by reviewing workflow definitions, helped by tools such as zizmor, actionlint or CodeQL's workflow queries, for event data used inside scripts and for privileged triggers that check out untrusted code. Where in scope, it can be confirmed by opening an issue or pull request whose title contains a harmless marker command and observing it in the workflow log.
entries.impact: An attacker who can trigger the workflow can run commands on the build runner with the workflow's permissions. They can typically read every secret available to the job, such as cloud credentials, package registry tokens and deployment keys, and, where the workflow token has write permissions, use it to push code or create releases. Where the pipeline publishes packages, container images or releases, the attacker can insert malicious code into software that customers or other teams install, turning one injection into a supply chain compromise. In public repositories anyone with an account on the platform can usually open an issue or pull request, which raises the severity considerably; in private repositories the attacker needs to be, or to have compromised, a contributor.
entries.remediation:
Treat all event data and contributed code as untrusted in every workflow:

  • Never interpolate event data directly into scripts. Pass it to the step through an env: entry and refer to it in the script as a quoted shell variable, such as "$TITLE", so that the shell treats it as data rather than code.
  • Avoid pull_request_target and workflow_run for jobs that check out or build code from pull requests. Build untrusted code with the unprivileged pull_request trigger, and keep privileged steps, such as commenting or publishing, in separate jobs that do not run contributed code.
  • Set the workflow token's permissions to read-only by default and grant write scopes only to the jobs that need them.
  • Require approval before workflows run for pull requests from outside contributors, and do not use self-hosted runners for public repositories or untrusted pull requests.
  • Add a workflow linter such as zizmor or actionlint to the repository's checks so that new injection points are flagged before they are merged.

Where a vulnerable workflow may already have been triggered by an outsider, rotate the secrets it could reach and review recent releases and commits made by the pipeline. Confirm the fix by reviewing every workflow for remaining event data in scripts and privileged triggers, and by repeating the marker test.

entries.title: Secrets Exposed in CI/CD Logs or Configuration
entries.summary: Credentials used by build and deployment pipelines appear in job logs, pipeline definitions, unprotected variables or build artefacts readable by people who should not have them.
entries.description:
Secrets used by a CI/CD pipeline, such as cloud keys, deployment credentials, registry tokens and signing keys, can be read by people or systems that do not need them, because they appear in places with broader access than the secret store. Common causes are build steps that print environment variables or run in verbose or debug mode, writing credentials to job logs; secrets written in plain text into pipeline definitions such as .gitlab-ci.yml, a Jenkinsfile or workflow files; pipeline variables not marked as masked, protected or secret, so that every project member can view them in the settings; and secrets baked into build artefacts, container image layers or cached files.

Masking in job logs is a safety net rather than a control. Platforms mask only values they know to be secret and that appear exactly as stored, so a secret that is encoded, split, transformed or written to a file can still appear in full. Logs and artefacts are often kept for long periods and are readable by everyone with access to the project and, in public projects, by anyone.

The weakness is identified by reviewing pipeline definitions and variable settings, and by searching job logs and downloaded artefacts for credential patterns with secret scanning tools. Each secret found is checked to see whether it is still valid.
entries.impact: Anyone who can read the logs, settings or artefacts, which often includes every developer, contractor and integration with access to the project, and for public projects anyone on the internet, can collect the secrets and use them directly. Pipeline credentials usually have wide reach, such as deployment rights to production, write access to package registries or cloud administration roles, so their exposure can lead to changes to production systems, access to data or tampering with released software. The impact is greatest for long-lived credentials with broad permissions, and lower where secrets are short-lived or scoped to test environments.
entries.remediation:
Rotate exposed secrets, and keep secrets out of logs, definitions and artefacts:

  • Revoke or rotate every secret found in logs, pipeline definitions, variables or artefacts, then delete the affected logs and artefacts. Rotation is what makes an exposed secret safe; deletion alone is not enough.
  • Hold secrets only in the platform's secret store or an external secrets manager, marked as masked and, where supported, protected so that they are available only to protected branches and environments. Remove secrets written into pipeline definitions.
  • Prefer short-lived credentials obtained at run time through OpenID Connect federation with the cloud provider to long-lived keys stored in the pipeline.
  • Stop commands from printing secrets: avoid echoing environment variables, disable verbose or debug output in steps that handle credentials, and register any derived value with the platform's masking feature.
  • Use the build tool's secret mounts rather than build arguments or files copied into images, and check that artefacts and image layers contain no credentials.
  • Limit who can read job logs and artefacts, and set retention periods that match operational needs.

Confirm the fix by rescanning recent logs, pipeline definitions and artefacts, and checking that each secret found earlier has been revoked.

entries.title: Over-Privileged CI/CD Pipeline Credentials
entries.summary: Build and deployment pipelines run with credentials far broader than their tasks need, so any compromise of a pipeline gives wide control of cloud, code and production systems.
entries.description:
The credentials that a CI/CD pipeline uses grant far more access than the pipeline's tasks need. Typical examples are a cloud service principal or IAM role with owner or administrator rights over a whole subscription or account; one deployment credential shared by development, test and production; a repository token with write access to every repository in the organisation; a workflow token with broader write permissions than the job uses; Kubernetes service accounts bound to cluster-admin; and self-hosted runners shared between projects of different trust levels, or that keep credentials and files between jobs.

Over-privilege does not give an attacker access by itself, but it decides how much damage follows from any compromise of the pipeline, whether through injection into a workflow, a malicious or compromised dependency or build tool, a stolen developer account or exposed pipeline secrets. Because pipelines run code from many sources automatically, they are a common target.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the roles and permissions assigned to pipeline identities, service connections and tokens, the scope of deployment credentials for each environment and the runner configuration, and by comparing them with what each job actually does.
entries.impact: An attacker who can run code in, or steal credentials from, an over-privileged pipeline gains everything those credentials allow rather than only what the job needed. That can include administrative control of cloud accounts, read and write access to every repository, the ability to publish packages and container images, and direct access to production systems and data. Persistent runners shared between projects let a compromise of one low-value project reach the secrets and builds of others. The attacker still needs a way into the pipeline first, but once inside, the excess privileges turn a contained incident into an organisation-wide one.
entries.remediation:
Apply least privilege to every identity and credential a pipeline uses:

  • Give each pipeline, and where possible each job, its own identity scoped to the specific resources it deploys to, with separate credentials for each environment, and remove owner, administrator and wildcard permissions.
  • Replace long-lived keys with short-lived credentials issued through OpenID Connect federation, with trust conditions that limit them to specific repositories, branches and environments.
  • Set workflow token permissions to read-only by default at organisation or repository level, and grant write scopes explicitly in the jobs that need them.
  • Protect production deployments with environment protection rules or approval gates, so that only reviewed code from protected branches can use production credentials.
  • Use ephemeral, single-use runners where possible, keep self-hosted runners separate for different trust levels, and do not leave cloud credentials on runner hosts.
  • Review pipeline identities regularly, using the cloud provider's access analysis tools to remove permissions that are never used.

Confirm the fix by listing the effective permissions of each pipeline identity and token, and checking that they match the documented needs of the jobs that use them.

entries.title: Dependency Confusion Possible
entries.summary: Internal package names are not reserved on public registries and builds can fetch from both, so an attacker can publish a same-named public package that is installed instead.
entries.description:
The organisation uses private packages whose names are not registered on the corresponding public registry, and its package managers are configured so that a request for one of those names may be satisfied from the public registry. An attacker who learns an internal package name can publish a package with the same name and a higher version number publicly, and a developer workstation or build server may then install it in place of the internal package. This attack, known as dependency confusion or namespace confusion, has been demonstrated against many large organisations.

Typical causes are pip used with --extra-index-url, which consults the public index as well as the private one and may choose the higher version from either; npm packages without a scope, or with a scope that is not mapped to the private registry in .npmrc; NuGet configurations with several package sources and no package source mapping; and registry proxies that merge public and private feeds for the same names. Internal package names often leak through public repositories, JavaScript bundles and source maps, error messages and published manifests such as package.json.

The weakness is identified by listing the private package names in manifests and lock files, checking whether each name is unclaimed on the public registry, and reviewing package manager and registry configuration. It can be confirmed without harm by checking which registry a clean install resolves each name from; publishing a test package to a public registry should only be done with explicit agreement.
entries.impact: A malicious package installed this way runs the attacker's code on developer workstations and build servers, often immediately through install scripts, with access to source code, credentials and the build environment. From a build server, the attacker can steal pipeline secrets and insert code into the software the organisation builds and ships. Exploitation needs the attacker to learn an internal package name and to wait for a build or install to pick up the package, but it needs no access to the organisation's systems, and automated builds make the timing reliable once those conditions are met.
entries.remediation:
Make every internal package resolve only from the private registry:

  • Use a scope or namespace that the organisation owns for all internal packages, such as an npm organisation scope, and map that scope to the private registry in the project and user .npmrc files.
  • For Python, install from a single private index that proxies the public one, using --index-url rather than --extra-index-url, and configure the proxy so that internal names are never fetched from the public registry.
  • For NuGet, enable package source mapping so that internal package ID prefixes can come only from the private feed, and reserve the prefix on the public registry where possible.
  • Register placeholder packages, or claim the namespace, on public registries for internal names that cannot be scoped.
  • Commit lock files with integrity hashes and install with commands that honour them, such as npm ci, so that builds do not silently resolve new versions.
  • Configure registry proxies and repository managers so that private and public packages with the same name are never merged.

Confirm the fix by checking, for each internal package name, that a clean install resolves it from the private registry and that the name on the public registry is claimed or blocked.

entries.title: Unpinned Third-Party Dependencies or Actions
entries.summary: Builds pull third-party actions, packages or images by mutable tags or version ranges, so a change by an upstream owner or attacker is used automatically without review.
entries.description:
The build references third-party code by a name that can be changed after the fact, rather than by an immutable identifier. In GitHub Actions and similar systems, workflows use actions by tag or branch, such as @v4 or @main, which the action's owner, or anyone who compromises the action's repository, can move to point at different code. Elsewhere, package manifests use version ranges without a committed lock file, install commands ignore the lock file, scripts download and run tools from a URL without checking a hash, and Dockerfiles build from base images by tag, such as latest.

Each build then runs whatever the upstream source provides at that moment, with the build's secrets and permissions. This was shown in the compromise of the widely used tj-actions/changed-files action (CVE-2025-30066), in which an attacker repointed the action's existing version tags to a malicious commit that wrote CI/CD secrets to workflow logs, affecting workflows that ran the action by tag during that time.

The weakness is identified by reviewing workflow files, manifests, lock files, Dockerfiles and build scripts for references that are not pinned to a full commit SHA, an exact version with an integrity hash or an image digest. Container image tags in deployment manifests are covered by a separate finding.
entries.impact: If an upstream project, its maintainer's account or its release process is compromised, the malicious version is pulled into the organisation's builds automatically, without any change in its own repositories. The code then runs with the build's access to source code, secrets and publishing rights, and can steal credentials or insert malicious code into released software. Exploitation depends on an attacker first gaining control of an upstream component, which is outside the organisation's control and not an everyday event, but such compromises do happen and affect every consumer at once. Unpinned references also make builds unreproducible, so it is hard to establish afterwards exactly what code ran.
entries.remediation:
Pin every third-party reference to an immutable identifier, and update it deliberately:

  • Reference GitHub Actions and similar reusable workflow components by full-length commit SHA, with the version in a comment for readability, and turn on any policy setting the platform offers that requires SHA pinning.
  • Commit lock files with integrity hashes for every package manager, and install with commands that fail if the lock file does not match, such as npm ci, pip install --require-hashes or dotnet restore --locked-mode.
  • Pin base images in Dockerfiles by digest rather than by tag, and verify the checksum or signature of any tool downloaded during the build.
  • Use an automated dependency update tool to propose updates to pinned versions as reviewable pull requests, so that pinning does not leave components out of date.
  • Prefer actions and packages from verified, well-maintained publishers, and copy critical third-party actions into the organisation's own repositories where practical.

Confirm the fix by reviewing workflows, manifests and Dockerfiles for remaining mutable references, and by checking that builds fail when a lock file or hash does not match.

entries.title: Insecure Infrastructure-as-Code Configuration
entries.summary: Infrastructure templates such as Terraform, CloudFormation, Bicep or Kubernetes manifests define resources with insecure settings that are deployed wherever they are used.
entries.description:
The organisation's infrastructure-as-code templates, such as Terraform, CloudFormation, Azure Bicep or ARM templates, Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts, define resources with insecure settings. Common examples are storage buckets or blob containers allowing public access; security groups or firewall rules open to the internet on administrative ports such as SSH, RDP or database ports; identity policies with wildcard actions or resources; storage, databases and disks without encryption; logging and versioning turned off; containers that run privileged or as root; and secrets written into templates or variable files.

Because templates are reused, a single insecure module or default is copied into every environment built from it, and manual fixes made in the console are overwritten at the next deployment. Terraform state files are a related concern: they hold resource attributes, often including secrets, in plain text, so state kept in a repository or an openly readable bucket exposes them.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the templates manually and with static analysis tools such as Checkov, Trivy or KICS, and by comparing what the templates define with the deployed resources. These tools report many low-impact items, so each result is judged on what the resource holds and whether it is reachable.
entries.impact: The impact depends on the misconfiguration and the resource. Public storage can expose data to anyone on the internet; administrative services open to the internet invite password attacks and exploitation of unpatched flaws; and broad identity policies let an attacker who compromises one workload or credential reach far more. Since templates are deployed repeatedly, the same weakness is often present in every environment, including production, and returns after manual correction. Template findings that have not been deployed, or that apply to resources holding no sensitive data, carry less immediate risk.
entries.remediation:
Fix the templates, and make secure settings the default in the deployment process:

  • Correct the insecure settings in the templates and shared modules rather than in the deployed resources, then redeploy so that every environment picks up the change: block public access to storage, restrict inbound rules to known address ranges or private access paths, replace wildcard permissions with specific actions and resources, enable encryption and logging, and run containers unprivileged as a non-root user.
  • Remove secrets from templates and variable files, reference them from a secrets manager, and rotate any that were committed.
  • Store Terraform state in a remote backend with encryption, restricted access and locking, never in the repository.
  • Run an infrastructure-as-code scanner in the CI/CD pipeline and fail builds on high-severity findings, recording any accepted exception with a reason and an owner.
  • Enforce key rules at deployment time as well, using cloud policy services or Kubernetes admission control, so that insecure resources are blocked even if they bypass the pipeline.
  • Detect drift between the templates and the deployed resources, so that manual changes are found and reconciled.

Confirm the fix by rescanning the templates and checking the deployed resources for the corrected settings.

entries.title: Branch Protection Not Enforced
entries.summary: Main and release branches accept direct pushes, force pushes or unreviewed merges, so a single account can change the code that is built and deployed without review.
entries.description:
The repositories' default and release branches, which feed builds and deployments, are not protected by enforced rules on the hosting platform. Typical gaps are that contributors can push directly to the branch without a pull or merge request; that changes can be merged without approval from another reviewer or, where the platform allows it, with the author's own approval; that required status checks, such as tests and security scans, are not enforced; that force pushes and branch deletion are allowed, so history can be rewritten; that administrators are exempt from the rules; and that code owner review is not required for sensitive paths such as pipeline definitions and infrastructure code.

Without these controls, a single account, whether a developer acting alone, an insider or an attacker with a stolen token, can place code into the branch that is built and deployed, and can change or remove pipeline definitions and their security checks along with it. Rules that exist but are not enforced, for example rules on a branch name pattern that does not match the release branch, or rules that apply only to some users, give the same result.

The weakness is identified by reviewing branch protection rules or rulesets on GitHub, protected branch settings on GitLab, or branch policies in Azure Repos for each repository that feeds production, and by checking the audit log for direct pushes and bypasses. Where agreed, it can be confirmed by attempting a direct push of a harmless change with a test account that has ordinary write access.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises one developer account or access token, or a malicious insider, can push malicious code, such as a backdoor or code that steals data or credentials, into the branch that is built and released, without anyone else seeing it first. Where the branch deploys automatically, the change can reach production within minutes, and force pushes can then remove the evidence from the branch history. The attacker needs write access to the repository, so the weakness exposes nothing by itself, but it removes the review that would otherwise stop a single compromised account from changing production software.
entries.remediation:
Enforce protection on every branch that feeds builds and deployments:

  • Require changes to reach the default and release branches through pull or merge requests, with at least one approval from someone other than the author, and dismiss existing approvals when new commits are pushed.
  • Require status checks, such as builds, tests and security scans, to pass before merging, and require branches to be up to date with the target branch.
  • Block force pushes and branch deletion, and apply the rules to administrators as well, keeping any bypass to a small, audited break-glass group.
  • Require code owner review for sensitive paths, such as CI/CD workflow files, infrastructure templates and authentication code, using a CODEOWNERS file.
  • Apply the rules at organisation level, for example through organisation rulesets, so that new repositories are protected by default, and consider requiring signed commits.
  • Limit write access to the people who need it, and require multi-factor authentication for every account with access to the organisation's repositories.

Review the audit log for direct pushes and bypasses made before the rules were enforced. Confirm the fix by checking the rules on each repository that feeds production, and by confirming that a direct push to a protected branch is rejected.

entries.title: Prompt Injection
entries.summary: User input can override the instructions given to a large language model, making it ignore its restrictions, reveal data or misuse the tools it can call.
entries.description:
The application passes user input to a large language model (LLM) together with the instructions that define its behaviour, such as the system prompt, retrieved content and descriptions of the tools it may call. The model processes all of this as a single stream of text and cannot reliably tell the developer's instructions from instructions written by the user. A user can therefore write input that overrides the intended behaviour: telling the model to ignore its previous instructions, assigning it a new role, framing a request as fiction or a test, or hiding the request through encoding, another language or a series of harmless-looking messages.

The weakness exists wherever the application relies on the model's instructions to limit what a user can obtain or do. Instructions such as "only discuss the customer's own orders" or "never reveal internal data" guide the model; they are not security controls, and prompt injection removes them.

Prompt injection is confirmed by showing that crafted input causes behaviour the application was designed to prevent, such as disclosing the system prompt or data held in the model's context, calling tools with arguments the user chose, or producing content the application's policy forbids. Because model output varies, payloads are repeated and varied, and open-source tools such as garak, PyRIT and promptfoo can run large sets of attempts. Injection through content the model reads from other sources is the related weakness of indirect prompt injection.
entries.impact: An attacker can make the model act outside the limits the application set for it, within everything the model can reach. Depending on the design, this includes reading the system prompt and any data placed in the model's context, retrieving other users' records through tools that do not enforce the user's own permissions, performing actions such as sending messages or changing records, and producing harmful or misleading content under the organisation's name. The impact is limited where the model sees only the current user's data and its tools enforce authorisation independently, and is greatest where the model holds broad data access or can act without confirmation.
entries.remediation:
No current technique prevents prompt injection reliably, so design the application on the assumption that a user can make the model do anything it is capable of:

  • Enforce authorisation outside the model. Tools and data sources should act with the signed-in user's own permissions, checked by the back end on every call, so that the model can never obtain more than the user could request directly.
  • Give the model only the data and tools the feature needs, and require explicit user confirmation, showing the exact parameters, before actions that change data, spend money or send messages.
  • Keep instructions in the system or developer role of the model provider's API and user input in the user role, rather than joining them into one prompt, and mark external content clearly. This reduces, but does not remove, the risk.
  • Add input and output screening, such as classifier-based prompt attack detection and filters for sensitive data in responses, as defence in depth, and limit input length.
  • Log prompts, responses and tool calls, monitor for injection attempts, and throttle users who trigger them repeatedly.
  • Include adversarial prompt testing in the release process for every change to prompts, models or tools.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original payloads and variations of them, and by checking that whatever instruction the model follows, it cannot reach data or actions beyond the user's own permissions.

entries.title: Indirect Prompt Injection
entries.summary: Instructions hidden in content an LLM reads, such as web pages, emails or documents, are followed as if they came from the user, acting with the user's access.
entries.description:
The application gives a large language model (LLM) content from sources outside the user's control, such as web pages it browses, emails and calendar invitations it summarises, documents users upload or share, search and retrieval results, and responses from tools or other systems. An attacker who can place text in any of those sources can include instructions in it. When the model processes the content on a user's behalf, it may follow those instructions as if the user had given them, because it cannot reliably distinguish data from instructions.

The instructions are often hidden from people: white or tiny text, HTML comments, document metadata, the alternative text of images, or text inside images for models that read them. Common goals are to make the model send data from the conversation to the attacker, for example by producing a Markdown image or link whose address contains that data, to call tools such as email, file or ticketing functions, or to give the user false information or a malicious link.

The weakness is confirmed by placing a harmless test instruction in content the application will process, such as a shared document, a web page or an email to a test mailbox, then using the feature as an ordinary user and showing that the model follows the instruction. Testing should cover each content source and each tool the model can call, and whether the interface loads images or links from external addresses in model output.
entries.impact: An attacker who never interacts with the application can act with the access of the user whose assistant reads the poisoned content. Depending on the tools available, this can mean disclosure of the conversation, files or mailbox contents the assistant can see, actions taken in the user's name such as sending emails or changing records, or manipulation of the answers the user relies on. The user only has to use the feature normally, and assistants that process incoming content automatically need no action from the user at all. The impact is limited where the model cannot call tools while handling untrusted content and the interface does not fetch external resources named in model output.
entries.remediation:
Treat all content the model reads from outside the application's control as untrusted, and design so that instructions in it cannot cause harm:

  • Restrict what the model can do while untrusted content is in its context: limit it to read-only tools, or require explicit user confirmation, showing the exact parameters, before any action that sends data or changes state.
  • Close the common exfiltration channels: do not render images or follow links in model output that point to arbitrary external domains, enforce an allowlist of domains, and apply a Content Security Policy that restricts image and connection sources in the chat interface.
  • Run tools with the user's own permissions and enforce authorisation in the back end, so that an injected instruction cannot reach more than the user can.
  • Separate and mark untrusted content in the prompt, for example by enclosing it in clearly labelled delimiters or transforming it (techniques sometimes called spotlighting). These reduce, but do not remove, the risk.
  • Screen retrieved content and model output with classifier-based injection detection, and log tool calls together with the content that preceded them, so that attacks can be investigated.

Confirm the fix by repeating the planted-content tests for each source and tool, checking that no data leaves through rendered content and that no action completes without the user's informed confirmation.

entries.title: Sensitive Information Disclosure by an LLM
entries.summary: The LLM feature reveals data the user should not see, such as other people's personal data, confidential records or credentials, from its training data, context or tools.
entries.description:
A large language model (LLM) can only reveal what it has been given, but applications often give it more than the user in front of it should see. Sensitive information reaches the model's responses through several routes: personal or confidential data included in training or fine-tuning data, which the model may reproduce; data placed in its context, such as the system prompt, conversation memory shared between users, retrieved documents, or tool results that contain more fields than the task needs; and faults in session handling or caching that show one user's conversation to another.

The weakness is identified by asking for data belonging to other users or to the organisation, by probing for memorised training content, for example by giving the start of a record and asking the model to continue it, and by examining the raw API responses and tool results behind the conversation, which often contain more than the interface displays. Responses that contain personal data, credentials, internal identifiers or confidential documents the test account is not entitled to see confirm the finding.

Retrieval that ignores document permissions, and leakage of the system prompt itself, are separate findings; this one covers the wider exposure of sensitive data through the model.
entries.impact: A user, or an attacker with an ordinary account, may obtain other people's personal data, confidential business information or credentials by asking the model for them, or may receive them unprompted. The attacker cannot always choose what is revealed, particularly for memorised training data, which limits the impact in many cases. It is greater where the model's context or tools have broad access to customer records, or where credentials disclosed by the model give access to other systems, and exposure of personal data may need to be handled as a personal data breach.
entries.remediation:
Control what reaches the model, and treat everything it can see as visible to the user:

  • Minimise the data used for training and fine-tuning, and remove or pseudonymise personal and confidential data before use.
  • Apply the user's permissions before data enters the context: retrieve and pass only records the user is entitled to, and return only the fields the task needs from tools and APIs.
  • Keep credentials and secrets out of prompts and context entirely; tools should authenticate in the back end.
  • Isolate conversation history, memory and caches per user and per tenant, and test session handling for leakage between users.
  • Screen model output for personal data, payment card numbers and secrets with a data loss prevention filter before it is displayed, as defence in depth.
  • Review the model provider's data handling terms, including retention and any use of inputs for training, configure the service accordingly, and record the processing in the organisation's privacy documentation.

Confirm the fix by repeating the original requests from a low-privileged test account, and by checking the raw API responses as well as the displayed answers.

entries.title: System Prompt Leakage
entries.summary: Users can extract the instructions given to the LLM, revealing internal rules, tool details and any sensitive data placed in them.
entries.description:
