The system prompt, also called the developer message or pre-prompt, holds the instructions that define how the application's large language model (LLM) behaves: its role, rules and restrictions, the tools it may call and sometimes reference data. Users can usually make the model reveal it, by asking it to repeat or translate the text above the conversation, to summarise its instructions, to output them in a code block or another encoding, or through role play. Instructions telling the model to keep its prompt secret are not a reliable control.

Disclosure matters because of what the prompt contains and how the application relies on it. Prompts found in testing often hold internal business rules, such as discount or approval limits, details of internal tools and APIs, names of staff or systems, and occasionally credentials or connection details. Where the prompt carries security rules, such as which users may see which data, reading it shows an attacker exactly what to work around.

The weakness is confirmed by extracting the prompt through the conversation, often in several fragments, and checking that the result is consistent across attempts. A related and more serious variant is found by inspecting traffic: some applications build the system prompt in client-side code and send it with each request, where it can be read and also changed.
entries.impact: An attacker learns how the assistant is configured, which makes prompt injection and other attacks easier to craft, and obtains any sensitive information the prompt contains, such as internal business rules, system details or credentials that may give access to other services. Where the prompt is sent from the client, the attacker can also replace it and remove the application's restrictions altogether. Where the prompt contains only behavioural instructions, the direct impact is limited to assisting further attacks.
entries.remediation:
Assume that the system prompt will be read, and make sure that reading it gives an attacker nothing of value:

  • Remove credentials, keys, connection strings, internal addresses and personal data from the prompt. Tools should authenticate in the back end with credentials the model never sees.
  • Move security decisions out of the prompt: enforce authorisation, limits and business rules in application code and in the tools' back ends, so that knowing or bypassing an instruction changes nothing.
  • Build the prompt on the server, and never accept it, or any part of it, from the client.
  • Where the prompt has commercial value, accept that it cannot be fully protected. Output filters that detect prompt text, or a canary string embedded in the prompt, in responses can reduce casual extraction as defence in depth.
  • Monitor conversations for extraction attempts.

Confirm the fix by repeating the extraction attempts, reviewing whatever prompt text can still be obtained for sensitive content, and checking client requests for prompt content.

entries.title: Excessive Agency Granted to an LLM
entries.summary: An LLM is given more tools, permissions or freedom to act than its task needs, so manipulated or mistaken output can cause damaging actions.
entries.description:
The application lets a large language model (LLM) take actions by calling tools, functions, plugins or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the model has more agency than its purpose requires. The weakness takes three common forms. Excessive functionality: tools offer operations the feature does not need, such as a mailbox tool that can send and delete as well as read, or general-purpose shell, SQL or HTTP request tools. Excessive permissions: tools connect to other systems with a privileged service account rather than the identity of the user being served, often with access to every user's data. Excessive autonomy: actions that change data, spend money or send messages run without anyone confirming them.

On its own, excessive agency is a design flaw. It becomes exploitable when the model's behaviour is manipulated through direct or indirect prompt injection, or simply when the model misunderstands a request.

The weakness is identified by enumerating the tools available to the model, from their definitions in API traffic or configuration or by asking the model to describe them; by establishing which identity and permissions each tool uses in the systems it reaches; and by attempting, through crafted prompts, to make the model use tools outside their intended purpose, for example against another user's records, while checking whether any confirmation step intervenes.
entries.impact: An attacker who can influence the model, directly or by planting content it reads, can make it carry out any action its tools allow, with the tools' privileges. Depending on the tools, this can mean reading or changing other users' data, sending messages or emails in the organisation's name, deleting records, making purchases or running commands on the systems the tools reach. The impact is bounded by the tools and permissions granted, and is limited where every tool acts with the current user's own permissions and high-impact actions need the user's confirmation.
entries.remediation:
Limit what the model can do to the minimum the feature needs, and enforce those limits outside the model:

  • Remove tools and operations the feature does not use, and prefer narrow, purpose-built tools, such as one that looks up an order belonging to the current user, to general shell, SQL, file system or HTTP request tools.
  • Run tools with the identity of the user being served, through delegated authorisation such as OAuth with narrowly scoped tokens, and enforce authorisation in the systems the tools call, never through instructions to the model. Where a service account is unavoidable, give it least-privilege, preferably read-only, access.
  • Require explicit user confirmation, showing the exact action and parameters, before any action that changes data, spends money, sends messages or reaches outside the organisation.
  • Validate tool arguments against strict schemas and allowlists, apply rate and spending limits to actions, and run any code execution in an isolated sandbox without network access to internal systems.
  • Log every tool call with the identity, the parameters and the preceding conversation, and alert on unusual patterns.
  • Review the permissions of each MCP server and plugin, and the scopes of the tokens given to them, before connecting them.

Confirm the fix by repeating the attempts to misuse each tool, checking that out-of-scope calls fail in the back end and that consequential actions wait for the user's confirmation.

entries.title: Improper Handling of LLM Output
entries.summary: LLM output is passed to browsers, databases, shells or other interpreters without validation or encoding, so manipulated output becomes an injection attack.
entries.description:
The application treats text generated by a large language model (LLM) as trusted and passes it, without validation or encoding, to components that interpret it. Because anyone who influences the model's input, through direct or indirect prompt injection, can steer its output, this turns the model into a route for classic injection attacks against those components.

Common cases include model output rendered as HTML or Markdown in a web interface, leading to cross-site scripting or to data leaving through images and links that the browser loads; generated SQL or other query languages run directly against a database; output passed to a shell, eval, a code interpreter or a template engine; output used to build file paths or URLs that the server then opens or fetches, leading to path traversal or server-side request forgery; and output placed into emails or messages sent to other people.

The weakness is identified by tracing where model output goes in the application, and confirmed by prompting the model to produce a payload suited to each destination, such as an HTML element with an event handler, a query with an extra clause or a URL pointing at an internal address, and showing that the payload takes effect. Reviewing the Markdown renderer's configuration, including whether it allows raw HTML, and the Content Security Policy of the chat interface shows the browser-side exposure.
entries.impact: The impact is that of the injection the output reaches. Generated queries or commands run with the application's privileges can expose or alter the whole database or run code on the server; script injected into the chat interface runs in the session of the user viewing it and can steal their data or act as them; and server-side requests built from output can reach internal services. An attacker needs a way to influence the model's output, which a signed-in user usually has directly and an outside attacker may have through content the model reads. The impact is lower where output only reaches a browser with strict encoding and a restrictive Content Security Policy.
entries.remediation:
Treat model output as untrusted input, and handle it as the application would any other user-supplied data:

  • Encode output for the context it is placed in. Render Markdown with raw HTML disabled, sanitise any HTML with a maintained library such as DOMPurify, restrict images and links to approved domains, and apply a restrictive Content Security Policy to the interface.
  • Never pass output to eval, a shell or a template engine. Where generated code must run, run it in an isolated, short-lived sandbox without access to secrets or internal networks.
  • Rather than running generated SQL, have the model return structured parameters, validated against a JSON schema, which the application places into fixed, parameterised queries. Where free-form queries are a requirement, run them with a read-only database account limited to the permitted tables and rows.
  • Validate file names, paths and URLs taken from output against strict allowlists before use.
  • Use the model provider's structured output features to constrain responses to the expected format, and reject output that does not match it.

Confirm the fix by repeating the payload tests for each destination and checking that the payloads are displayed or rejected as data rather than interpreted.

entries.title: Unbounded Consumption of LLM Resources
entries.summary: The LLM feature sets no effective limits on request rates, input size, output length or agent steps, so users can exhaust its capacity or run up costs.
entries.description:
Every request to a large language model (LLM) consumes computing capacity and, with hosted models, money charged per token processed. The application does not limit that consumption effectively: users can send requests without a rate limit or quota, submit inputs as large as the model's context window allows, request outputs without a cap on their length, upload large documents for processing, or start agent tasks that call the model and its tools repeatedly with no limit on steps or time.

The weakness is identified by sending repeated and concurrent requests and checking for throttling, submitting very large inputs, asking for unusually long outputs, and giving agent features open-ended or self-repeating tasks, while observing response times and the token usage that many model APIs report with each response. The absence of throttling responses, such as HTTP 429, and of per-user quotas confirms the finding.

The same lack of limits allows heavy automated querying intended to copy a model's behaviour, for example to train a substitute model, which matters to organisations whose own models are a commercial asset.
entries.impact: A user or attacker can degrade or deny the LLM feature for everyone, either by saturating a self-hosted model or by exhausting the request and token quotas the model provider applies to the organisation's account, and can run up significant usage charges, an effect sometimes called denial of wallet. Heavy querying may also be used to extract the behaviour of a proprietary model. Exploitation needs only access to the feature, often through a free or low-cost account. Provider quotas and spending limits cap the cost, but reaching them causes the same outage for legitimate users.
entries.remediation:
Set and enforce limits at every point where consumption can grow:

  • Apply per-user, per-tenant and per-address rate limits and daily token quotas in the application's back end or API gateway, returning HTTP 429 when they are reached.
  • Limit input size before calling the model, by characters or tokens, and limit uploaded file sizes and page counts for document features.
  • Set a maximum output length on every model call with the provider's output token parameter.
  • Cap agent loops by number of steps, tool calls, elapsed time and total tokens per task, and stop tasks that exceed them.
  • Limit concurrent requests per user, set timeouts, and queue work rather than accepting unlimited parallel requests.
  • Configure budgets, alerts and, where the provider supports them, hard spending limits, and monitor usage per user to detect abuse quickly.
  • Require authentication for model endpoints, and do not expose details that help model extraction, such as token probabilities, unless they are needed.

Confirm the fix by repeating the rate, size, length and agent tests, and checking that each limit is enforced on the server and reported clearly to the user.

entries.title: Retrieval Without Access Control
entries.summary: The assistant retrieves documents for its answers without applying the requesting user's permissions, so users can obtain content they are not authorised to see.
entries.description:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer from an organisation's own content: documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings and stored in a vector database or search index, and the chunks most similar to a question are retrieved and placed into the prompt. The weakness arises when retrieval does not apply the permissions of the user asking. Content is often ingested with a service account that can read everything, the source system's access controls are not carried into the index, and every query searches the whole index, so the assistant quotes or summarises documents the user could not open directly.

Variants include an index shared between customers of a multi-tenant service without a tenant filter, filters built from values the client supplies, such as a tenant or user identifier in the request, permissions captured once at ingestion and never updated when access is removed, and documents deleted at source that remain in the index.

The weakness is confirmed with two accounts of different access, by asking the assistant about content only the more privileged account may see, for example using a distinctive phrase from a restricted document, and checking both the answer and the citations or retrieved chunks the API returns, which often contain more than the answer shows. Testing should also alter any filter values sent by the client.
entries.impact: Any user of the assistant can obtain information from every document in the index by asking the right questions, which may include human resources records, financial results, legal advice, customer data or, in multi-tenant services, other customers' content. The attacker needs only an ordinary account, and the assistant's ability to search and summarise makes sensitive material easy to find. The impact depends on what has been indexed, and is greatest where whole file shares, mailboxes or intranet sites were added without review; exposure of personal data may need to be handled as a personal data breach.
entries.remediation:
Make retrieval return only what the requesting user is entitled to see, enforced in the retrieval layer rather than by the model:

  • Store access control information with every chunk at ingestion, such as the permitted users or groups and the tenant, taken from the source system.
  • Filter every retrieval query by the authenticated user's identity and group memberships, resolved on the server from the session, so that unauthorised chunks are never retrieved. Never take filter values from the request, and never rely on filtering the model's answer afterwards.
  • In multi-tenant services, use a separate index or namespace per tenant, or a mandatory tenant filter applied in the data access layer.
  • Synchronise permission changes and deletions from the source systems promptly, and re-check access against the source at query time where it supports this.
  • Where possible, search through the source system's own search interface with the user's delegated token, so that its permission checks apply.
  • Review what is indexed, and exclude repositories whose content should not be available through the assistant.

Confirm the fix by repeating the two-account tests, including with altered client-supplied filters, and checking that restricted content appears in neither the answer nor the retrieved sources.

entries.title: Users Submitted Credentials to a Phishing Page
entries.summary: During a phishing exercise, users entered their credentials into a fake sign-in page, and the authentication in use could not stop those credentials being reused.
entries.description:
During a simulated phishing campaign, a number of recipients followed a link in an email and entered their usernames and passwords, and in some cases multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, into a sign-in page controlled by the tester. The page imitated a service the organisation uses, such as Microsoft 365, and the emails used pretexts typical of real attacks, such as a shared document, a parcel delivery or a security alert.

A successful credential phish shows that several layers did not stop the attack: email filtering delivered the message, web filtering allowed the page, recipients did not recognise the warning signs, and the authentication in use could not distinguish the tester from the genuine user. The last point matters most. Passwords alone, and one-time codes or push approvals entered or accepted through a fake page, can be relayed by readily available adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits, which also capture the session cookie issued after sign-in. Only phishing-resistant methods, such as FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication, cannot be relayed through a fake site in this way.

The finding reflects the controls that failed, not the individuals involved. Well-crafted phishing deceives a proportion of users in every organisation, so defences must assume that some submissions will happen.
entries.impact: An attacker who obtains valid credentials can sign in as those users to email, file storage and other internet-facing services, read and send mail as them, and use their access to send further phishing internally, commit payment fraud, or gain a foothold for wider compromise. Where a session cookie or MFA code is relayed in real time, multi-factor authentication that is not phishing-resistant gives no protection. The attack requires a user to act, but needs no prior access.
entries.remediation:
Combine technical, procedural and awareness controls, starting with those that make a submitted password useless:

  • Deploy phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys, Windows Hello for Business or certificate-based authentication, starting with administrators and staff with access to sensitive data or payments, and enforce it through conditional access.
  • Require sign-ins to come from managed, compliant devices where practical, so that stolen credentials or session cookies cannot be used from an attacker's computer.
  • Strengthen email and web filtering, with link checking at the time of click, blocking of newly registered domains and impersonation protection.
  • Make reporting easy, with a report button in the mail client, and act on reports quickly by removing the message from other mailboxes and blocking the site.
  • Run regular awareness training with realistic exercises that show how to recognise fake sign-in pages, and that praise reporting rather than penalising mistakes.
  • Prepare the response: for affected accounts, reset passwords, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, review mailbox rules and registered MFA methods, and check sign-in logs.

Confirm improvement through follow-up exercises that measure submission and reporting rates, and by verifying that phishing-resistant methods are enforced.

entries.title: Users Ran a Payload Delivered by Phishing
entries.summary: During a phishing exercise, users opened a file or link that ran the tester's payload, and email and endpoint controls did not prevent it from running.
entries.description:
During a simulated phishing campaign, a number of recipients opened an attachment or followed a link and ran a payload supplied by the tester, which then connected back to the tester's infrastructure. Payloads used in such exercises, as in real attacks, include shortcut (LNK) files, scripts, HTML Application files, disk image and archive files containing executables, installers, documents that abuse trusted features, and files assembled in the browser through HTML smuggling to get past email filtering.

Each successful execution shows that several layers failed together: email or web filtering delivered the file, the endpoint allowed an untrusted file from the internet to run, endpoint protection did not block or contain it, and the user did not recognise the lure. Because only one user needs to run a payload for an attacker to gain a foothold, resilience depends on technical controls that stop execution regardless of the user's decision, rather than on every user making the right choice every time.

The finding describes the controls that did not prevent execution, not the individuals involved; convincing lures deceive a proportion of users in every organisation.
entries.impact: An attacker gains code execution on the user's workstation with that user's privileges, and with it access to the user's files, email and browser sessions, and a foothold on the internal network from which to move laterally, escalate privileges and deploy ransomware. A single successful execution is often enough. The attack requires a user to open the file or link, which is reflected in the rating.
entries.remediation:
Prevent untrusted code from running whatever the user does, and support users in spotting and reporting lures:

  • Enforce application control, such as App Control for Business or AppLocker, so that only approved software can run, starting by blocking execution from user-writable locations such as Downloads and temporary folders.
  • Enable Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction rules, or the equivalent controls in other endpoint products, such as those that block executable content from email and webmail, and Office applications creating child processes.
  • Block risky attachment types at the email gateway, including executables, scripts, HTML Application, shortcut, disk image and macro-enabled files.
  • Change the default handler for script file types such as .js, .vbs, .wsf and .hta, so that they open in a text editor rather than running.
  • Remove local administrator rights from standard users, and make sure endpoint detection and response alerts are monitored and acted on.
  • Run regular awareness training and exercises that encourage prompt reporting, and give users a simple report button.

Confirm improvement by repeating the exercise with the same payload types and confirming that they are blocked.

entries.title: Staff Disclosed Information or Credentials by Phone
entries.summary: During telephone social engineering, staff disclosed internal information or credentials to an unverified caller posing as a colleague, supplier or IT support.
entries.description:
During telephone social engineering (vishing) testing, staff disclosed information or took actions for a caller whose identity they had not verified. Typical pretexts are a member of the IT service desk resolving a fault, a new or remote colleague who cannot reach a system, a senior manager with an urgent request, or a supplier updating its details. Callers often spoof the displayed number to match an internal or known external one, and use details gathered from public sources to sound credible.

What is disclosed in such tests ranges from internal details useful for later attacks, such as staff names, roles, internal systems, software in use and procedures, to passwords, MFA codes, approval of authentication prompts, or installation of remote support software at the caller's request.

The finding shows that procedures for verifying callers are missing, not widely known, or not practical to follow under pressure, so that a familiar-sounding name, a displayed number or the use of internal terminology was accepted as proof of identity. It reflects the process and awareness controls in place, not the individuals who answered.
entries.impact: Disclosed information helps an attacker craft convincing phishing and further calls and choose targets. Disclosed passwords or MFA codes, an approved authentication prompt, or installed remote support software give the attacker direct access to accounts or workstations, with the impact of a successful credential phish. The attack requires staff interaction but no prior access, and can be repeated against many staff at little cost.
entries.remediation:
Give staff a simple, supported way to verify callers, and remove the opportunities a convincing caller can exploit:

  • State clearly, and repeat regularly, that the IT service desk and other staff will never ask for a password or MFA code, or ask a user to approve a prompt they did not start.
  • Introduce a callback procedure: for any request involving credentials, access, payments or personal data, end the call and ring the person back on a number taken from the internal directory or supplier records, never one the caller gives.
  • Configure push-based MFA to use number matching, and move towards phishing-resistant methods, so that codes and approvals cannot be passed to a caller.
  • Restrict remote support tools to approved software started through the service desk's own process.
  • Run awareness training with realistic scenarios, and make it easy and blame-free to report suspicious calls so that others can be warned.

Confirm improvement through a follow-up vishing exercise using similar pretexts.

entries.title: Help Desk Reset Credentials Without Verifying Identity
entries.summary: The help desk reset a password or MFA method for a caller without adequately verifying their identity, allowing an impostor to take over the account.
entries.description:
During social engineering testing, the IT service desk reset an account's password, or registered a new multi-factor authentication (MFA) method or removed an existing one, for a caller impersonating the account holder, after checks that an attacker could pass. Typical checks are the user's name, username, employee number, job title, manager or date of birth: information that is often available publicly, through social media or from earlier calls, and that confirms knowledge rather than identity.

Help desks are under pressure to resolve requests quickly, and an impostor exploits that with plausible urgency, such as a lost phone before an important meeting. Attackers have used this approach in widely reported intrusions against large organisations, often targeting privileged users, because a successful reset hands over a working account and frequently bypasses MFA altogether.

The finding is identified by contacting the service desk by phone, chat or email with a pretext and the information an attacker could gather, and recording which checks were applied and what the desk agreed to do. It reflects the verification procedure and the tools available to the desk, not the analysts who followed it.
entries.impact: An attacker can take over any account they can name, including those of administrators and staff with access to sensitive systems or payments, gaining all the access the account holds, with MFA either reset in their favour or bypassed. Because the reset is a legitimate support action, it may not be noticed until the real user is locked out. The attack needs no prior access, only a convincing caller and publicly available information.
entries.remediation:
Verify identity, not knowledge, before any credential or MFA change:

  • Adopt a verification procedure based on something an impostor cannot easily obtain, such as a callback to the phone number held in the HR system, a prompt sent to an already registered MFA method, confirmation from the user's line manager through a separate channel, or a video call matching the caller to their photo identification.
  • Prefer self-service password reset that requires the user's existing registered methods, so that the help desk is needed only when those are lost.
  • Where the desk must restore access, issue a time-limited credential, such as a Microsoft Entra Temporary Access Pass, delivered only through a verified channel, rather than setting a password over the phone.
  • Apply stricter checks and a second approver for privileged accounts, and never reset administrative accounts on the strength of a phone call alone.
  • Notify users through their existing channels whenever their password or MFA methods change, and alert the security team to resets of privileged accounts.
  • Train help desk staff on the procedure and on common pretexts, and support them in refusing requests that do not pass it.

Confirm improvement by repeating the test with the same pretexts.

entries.title: Tailgating Into Secure Areas
entries.summary: An unauthorised person could enter controlled areas by following authorised staff through access-controlled doors without being challenged.
entries.description:
Access-controlled areas could be entered without a valid credential by following authorised staff through a door or gate (tailgating), or by being let through by them (piggybacking), without being challenged. Common enablers are staff holding doors open for others out of courtesy, doors that stay open long enough for a second person to pass, side and rear entrances such as smoking areas and loading bays that receive less scrutiny, and the routine presence of visitors and contractors moving around the building.

A single door controlled by a card reader admits everyone who passes while it is open, so it depends on people's willingness to challenge strangers. That willingness is limited in most organisations, particularly when the intruder carries props such as a coffee, a delivery, a ladder or a high-visibility jacket, or appears to be on a phone call.

The finding is identified by attempting entry at controlled doors during busy and quiet periods and recording where entry succeeded, and whether anyone questioned it. It reflects the physical controls and the challenge culture in place, not the individuals who held the door; courtesy is behaviour that organisations generally encourage, and the controls need to work with it.
entries.impact: An intruder inside controlled areas can reach unattended equipment and documents, connect devices to the network or to unlocked workstations, steal laptops and storage media, and install covert devices that give remote access to the internal network, bypassing many perimeter and network controls. The impact depends on what the area contains, and is greatest for server rooms and network equipment rooms. The attack requires physical presence and relies on staff behaviour, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Combine physical controls that limit entry to one person per credential with a culture that supports challenge:

  • At main entrances and for sensitive areas, install controls that admit one person at a time, such as speed gates, turnstiles or interlocking doors, staffed or monitored by security or reception.
  • Fit door-held-open and forced-door alarms to controlled doors, shorten door closing times, and monitor the alarms in real time.
  • Secure secondary entrances such as fire exits, loading bays and smoking areas, so that they cannot be used for entry or propped open unnoticed.
  • Require visible identification for staff, contractors and visitors, with distinct visitor badges, so that people without one stand out.
  • Train staff to politely challenge or report people they do not recognise, give them a simple way to call security, and support them when they do, including making clear that challenging senior staff is welcome.
  • Use guidance from national protective security bodies, such as the UK National Protective Security Authority (NPSA), when choosing entry controls.

Confirm improvement through repeat physical testing at the same entrances.

entries.title: Access Badges Can Be Cloned
entries.summary: Staff access cards use low-frequency proximity technology that transmits a fixed number without authentication, so cards can be read covertly and cloned.
entries.description:
The organisation's access control system uses 125 kHz low-frequency proximity cards, such as HID Prox, EM4100-family or Indala cards. These cards transmit a fixed identifier whenever a reader powers them, with no encryption and no challenge-response authentication, so the reader has no way to tell a genuine card from a copy. Some legacy high-frequency cards, such as MIFARE Classic and older HID iCLASS cards using the standard keys, rely on broken or publicly known cryptography and have the same practical weakness.

An attacker can read a card from a short distance with a handheld device such as a Proxmark3, or from further away with a concealed long-range reader, for example while standing next to the card holder in a queue or lift, then write the identifier to a blank writable card or emulate it. The reader accepts the copy with no indication that it is not genuine.

The weakness is identified by reviewing the card technology in use, reading a test card supplied by the organisation, cloning it, and confirming that readers accept the clone. Multi-technology readers deserve particular attention, because they often continue to accept the old low-frequency cards after more secure cards have been issued.
entries.impact: An attacker who clones a card gains the same physical access as its holder, without forcing entry or relying on tailgating, and can return repeatedly. Cloning the card of a facilities, IT or security staff member can give access to server rooms and other sensitive areas. Use of the clone is logged under the genuine holder's name, which hinders detection and investigation. The attack requires physical proximity to a card holder, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Replace the card technology, and add a second factor where the risk justifies it:

  • Migrate to cards that use mutual cryptographic authentication with keys diversified per card, such as MIFARE DESFire EV2 or EV3, or HID Seos or iCLASS SE, with keys managed by the organisation or its installer under a documented process rather than left at default values.
  • Once all cards are replaced, reconfigure multi-technology readers to reject the old low-frequency format, and check that no reader still accepts it.
  • Require a PIN or biometric in addition to the card at entrances to sensitive areas, such as server and equipment rooms.
  • Configure the access control system to alert on anomalies, such as the same card used at distant doors within a short time, or out-of-hours use.
  • As a short-term measure, issue shielded card sleeves, and advise staff not to wear badges visibly outside the premises.

Confirm the fix by attempting to read and clone a card of the new type, and confirming that readers reject the copy.

entries.title: Unattended Unlocked Workstations
entries.summary: Workstations were found unattended and unlocked, giving anyone who reached them the signed-in user's access to email, files and applications.
entries.description:
Workstations were found unattended with the user's session unlocked, in offices, meeting rooms or shared areas. The screen had either not been locked by the user on leaving, or had not locked automatically because the inactivity timeout was long or not enforced. Some kiosk and shared machines are also left signed in under a shared or generic account for convenience.

An unlocked session gives anyone who reaches the keyboard the user's full access: their email, files, open applications and browser sessions, and the ability to run commands. Little time is needed, because a device that emulates a keyboard can type a prepared sequence of commands within seconds of being plugged in.

The finding is identified by walking through the premises during and outside normal hours and recording workstations left unlocked, where they were, and how long they remained so, optionally demonstrating access in a harmless way. It reflects the technical settings and clear screen practice in place, not the individuals concerned.
entries.impact: Anyone with physical access, such as a visitor, contractor, cleaner or intruder, can read and send email as the user, open files and applications, approve transactions, install malware or remote access tools, and copy data, with all activity attributed to the user. The impact grows with the user's privileges, and is greatest for administrators and staff handling payments or sensitive data. The attacker must be physically present, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Make locking automatic, and make manual locking a habit:

  • Enforce an inactivity lock through Group Policy or device management, for example with the Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit security policy setting, set to a short period, commonly 15 minutes or less, and shorter in public-facing areas. Configure the equivalent setting on macOS and other platforms.
  • Consider Windows Dynamic Lock, which locks the computer when a paired phone moves out of range, and smart card removal policies for shared workstations in clinical or operational settings.
  • Replace shared, always signed-in accounts on kiosks with individual sign-in or a locked-down kiosk mode.
  • Promote locking with the Windows key and L as part of a clear screen policy, through awareness messages and regular walkthroughs, treating findings as process feedback rather than individual blame.

Confirm improvement by checking that the policy applies to all workstations and by repeating the walkthrough.

entries.title: Sensitive Information Left Unattended
entries.summary: Sensitive documents, written passwords or other confidential information were left unattended where visitors, contractors or intruders could see or take them.
entries.description:
Sensitive information was found unattended and unsecured on the premises: for example documents containing personal or commercial data left on desks and printers, passwords written on notes attached to monitors or under keyboards, whiteboards in meeting rooms left showing confidential plans, unlocked drawers and filing cabinets with keys left in them, unsecured laptops and storage media, and confidential waste in ordinary bins.

Information left in these ways is available to anyone who can reach the area, including visitors, contractors, cleaners and intruders, and sometimes to people outside through windows. Photographs taken with a phone leave no trace.

The finding is identified by walking through work areas, meeting rooms, print areas and waste points, during and after working hours, and recording what is visible or accessible without opening anything locked. It reflects the clean desk arrangements and the storage and disposal facilities provided, not the individuals concerned.
entries.impact: Exposed information can include personal data, whose exposure may need to be reported as a data breach, commercially sensitive material, and details that support further attacks, such as staff names, internal systems and procedures. Written passwords can give direct access to accounts. The attacker needs physical access to the area, and what they obtain is limited to what happens to be left out, which is why it is rated low.
entries.remediation:
Provide the means, set the expectation, and check that it is followed:

  • Adopt and communicate a clean desk and clear screen policy covering documents, written credentials, whiteboards, laptops and storage media.
  • Provide lockable storage for each user, confidential waste bins or shredders near work areas and printers, and secure printing that releases documents only when the user is at the printer.
  • Replace written passwords with a supported password manager, and make sure users have a way to recover forgotten passwords that does not encourage writing them down.
  • Require laptops to be locked away or secured with cable locks when unattended, and enforce full disk encryption.
  • Carry out periodic walkthroughs, particularly at the end of the day, and feed findings back as reminders rather than blame.

Confirm improvement through repeat walkthroughs.

entries.title: Live Network Ports in Public Areas
entries.summary: Network ports in public or visitor areas give any connected device access to the internal network without authentication.
entries.description:
Live network ports were found in areas that visitors or the public can reach, such as reception, meeting rooms, training rooms, corridors and shared kitchens, and a device connected to them was given an address on the internal network without any authentication. Ports used by devices in those areas, such as IP phones, printers, screens and video conferencing equipment, give the same access when the device is unplugged and a laptop connected in its place.

Where network access control is in place, it is often based only on MAC addresses, which can be copied from a label or from the device being replaced, or it covers only some ports. Once connected, an attacker can carry out any attack available to an internal device, or leave a small concealed device with its own mobile data connection to give them remote access to the internal network afterwards.

The finding is identified by connecting a test laptop to ports in accessible areas, and in place of accessible devices, and recording whether it receives an internal address and can reach internal systems.
entries.impact: An attacker who can spend a few minutes in a public or visitor area can gain a position on the internal network without credentials, the starting point for most internal attacks, such as capturing credentials through name resolution poisoning and attacking internal services. A concealed device left connected turns this into persistent remote access. The impact depends on what the connected network can reach and on the internal network's own defences.
entries.remediation:
Make sure that ports in accessible areas give unknown devices no internal access:

  • Disable switch ports that are not in use, and re-enable them only through a change request.
  • Deploy 802.1X port-based network access control, preferably with certificate-based EAP-TLS for corporate devices, and place unauthenticated devices in a restricted VLAN with no internal access.
  • For devices that cannot use 802.1X, such as some printers and phones, use MAC authentication bypass only with device profiling and a VLAN that allows just the traffic those devices need, and alert when a known MAC address appears on an unexpected port.
  • Where visitors need wired connectivity in meeting rooms, connect those ports to the guest network rather than the corporate one.
  • Use switch port security features to limit the number of devices per port, and alert on link changes on ports in public areas.
  • Where practical, move network points out of public areas or fit lockable covers.

Confirm the fix by repeating the connection test on each accessible port.

entries.title: Users Connected Unknown Removable Media
entries.summary: Users connected removable media of unknown origin, such as USB drives left in or near the premises, to organisational computers and opened files on them.
entries.description:
USB storage devices left where staff would find them, such as car parks, reception areas and shared spaces, or sent to staff, were connected to organisational computers and the files on them opened. The devices carried harmless tracking files or payloads that reported back when opened, labelled to invite curiosity, for example as salary information or confidential documents.

Current versions of Windows no longer run programs automatically from USB drives, so the attack relies on the user opening a file, which can be a shortcut, script, document or executable disguised as something else. Devices that look like storage but present themselves to the computer as a keyboard, typing commands as soon as they are connected, need no further action at all, and are not stopped by controls that block storage devices only.

The finding shows that devices of unknown origin can be connected and used, and that endpoint controls did not stop their content running. It reflects the device control, application control and awareness measures in place, not the individuals who connected the devices.
entries.impact: A connected device can run an attacker's code on the workstation with the user's privileges, giving the same foothold as a successful phishing payload: access to the user's data and a route into the internal network. Removable media also offers a way to take data out of the organisation and to reach systems that are not connected to the internet. The attacker must deliver a physical device and depends on someone connecting it, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Control which devices can be used, stop their content from running, and tell staff what to do with found devices:

  • Restrict removable storage with device control, for example Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device control or the Group Policy settings under System > Removable Storage Access, allowing only approved, encrypted devices where there is a business need.
  • Enforce application control, and enable the attack surface reduction rule that blocks untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB.
  • Turn off AutoPlay for all drives through Group Policy.
  • Consider device installation restrictions that block new keyboard-class devices on sensitive systems, accepting the support impact, and monitor for new devices being installed.
  • Tell staff to hand found devices to the IT or security team unopened, and include removable media in awareness training.

Confirm improvement by checking that an unapproved device is blocked on a sample of workstations, and through a repeat exercise.

entries.title: Visitors Not Escorted or Challenged
entries.summary: Visitors, or people posing as visitors or contractors, could move around the premises without an escort and were not challenged in areas they had no reason to be in.
entries.description:
A person posing as a visitor, contractor, interviewee or delivery driver could enter the premises and move into areas beyond those they had reason to visit, without an escort and without being challenged. Common contributing factors are visitors being signed in without identity checks or confirmation from the person they are visiting, visitor badges that do not stand out or need not be worn, escorting rules that lapse once the visitor has been met at reception, and contractors whose arrival is not checked against a work order or an expected list.

Pretexts that suggest legitimate business, such as maintenance, IT support, fire safety inspection or cleaning, are particularly effective, because staff are used to such people moving around unescorted.

The finding is identified by attempting entry under a pretext and recording which checks were applied at reception, whether an escort was provided, which areas could be reached, and whether anyone questioned the visitor's presence. It reflects the visitor management procedure and the challenge culture, not the individuals involved.
entries.impact: An unescorted visitor has the same opportunities as an intruder who has tailgated in, with less risk of being questioned: they can reach unattended workstations and documents, connect devices to the network, and take equipment or information. Because they entered through the front door, their presence may later be hard to distinguish from legitimate visits. The attacker must be physically present, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Make visitor management a consistent process from arrival to departure:

  • Pre-register visitors and confirm each one with their host before admitting them; check contractors and suppliers against a work order or an expected list, using contact details already held rather than any offered on arrival.
  • Check photo identification at sign-in, and issue dated, clearly distinguishable visitor badges that must be worn visibly and returned on departure.
  • Require hosts to collect visitors from reception and escort them at all times outside public areas, and make hosts accountable for this.
  • Use the access control system to limit where visitor badges can open doors, if they open any.
  • Train staff to approach people they do not recognise, or who are not wearing a badge, and to call security when in doubt, and support them when they do.
  • Use guidance from national protective security bodies, such as the UK National Protective Security Authority (NPSA), when designing the procedure.

Confirm improvement through repeat physical testing using similar pretexts.

entries.title: Excessive Information Available Publicly
entries.summary: Information published by the organisation and its staff gives attackers what they need to plan targeted phishing, impersonation and other attacks.
entries.description:
Open source intelligence (OSINT) gathering found more information about the organisation publicly available than its business needs justify, which an attacker could combine to plan targeted attacks. Typical findings include staff names, roles and reporting lines from professional networking sites; the email address format and lists of valid addresses; the technologies and versions in use, described in job adverts or staff profiles; usernames, internal paths and software details in the metadata of published documents; and photographs on social media showing identity badges, screens, desks or building interiors.

Much of this information is published deliberately or by staff in good faith, and some must remain public. The weakness lies in the aggregate: together it lets an attacker choose convincing pretexts, identify staff in finance, IT and administrative roles, guess usernames for password spraying, tailor malware to the technologies in use, and imitate badges and branding.

The finding is identified by searching public sources as an attacker would, including search engines, social media, company registries, job sites, code repositories and document metadata, and assessing which information would help an attack.
entries.impact: The information gives no access on its own, but it makes phishing, vishing, help desk impersonation and password spraying more convincing and better targeted, and therefore more likely to succeed. The rating reflects the indirect nature of the impact; specific items, such as credentials or internal network details, may justify a separate finding with a higher rating.
entries.remediation:
Reduce unnecessary detail, and prepare staff for the attacks it enables:

  • Remove metadata from documents before publication, for example with the Document Inspector in Microsoft Office or a tool such as exiftool, and build this into the publishing process.
  • Review job adverts, case studies and website content for technical detail, such as product names and versions, that their purpose does not require.
  • Give staff guidance on what not to share online, such as photographs showing badges, screens or office interiors, and details of internal systems and processes, and explain why.
  • Use role-based contact addresses on public material instead of individuals' addresses where practical.
  • Make sure staff in commonly targeted roles, such as finance, IT support and executive assistants, receive training on the pretexts that public information makes possible.
  • Repeat OSINT reviews periodically, and monitor for new exposures.

Confirm improvement through a repeat OSINT review.

entries.title: Corporate Credentials Exposed in Public Breach Data
entries.summary: Usernames and passwords for the organisation's email addresses appear in publicly available breach data, and may still work on its services.
entries.description:
Searches of publicly available breach data found credentials associated with the organisation's email domains: email addresses together with passwords, either in cleartext or as hashes that can be cracked. They typically come from breaches of third-party websites where staff registered with their work address, and increasingly from logs collected by information-stealing malware on personal or work devices, which can also capture session cookies.

The exposure matters because people reuse passwords, or change them predictably, for example by incrementing a number or a year. An attacker can try exposed passwords and their obvious variations against the organisation's internet-facing services, such as Microsoft 365, VPN gateways, remote desktop gateways and webmail, in credential stuffing and password spraying attacks. Services that accept a password alone, including legacy protocols that cannot use multi-factor authentication, are most at risk.

The finding is identified by searching breach data sources for the organisation's domains and, where agreed in scope, checking whether exposed credentials or close variants are still accepted. Even passwords no longer in use can reveal the patterns users follow when choosing new ones.
entries.impact: Where an exposed password, or a predictable variation of it, is still valid and the service does not require a second factor, an attacker can sign in as the user from anywhere, with access to their email and files and possibly remote access to the network. Many exposed passwords are old or no longer valid, and multi-factor authentication blocks their use where it is enforced, which is why the typical case is rated medium; confirmed valid credentials justify a higher rating.
entries.remediation:
Make exposed passwords useless, and keep watching for new exposures:

  • Enforce multi-factor authentication, preferably phishing-resistant, on every internet-facing service, and block legacy authentication protocols that cannot use it.
  • Force a password change for accounts whose exposed credentials may still be in use, and review their sign-in logs for unexpected activity.
  • Check new and changed passwords against lists of known breached passwords and common patterns, for example with Microsoft Entra Password Protection and a custom banned password list, and enable leaked credential detection where the identity platform offers it.
  • Ask staff not to use work email addresses or passwords for personal services, and provide a password manager so that unique passwords are practical.
  • Monitor breach data sources for the organisation's domains, and act on new exposures promptly.
  • Apply sign-in protections such as smart lockout, and alert on password spraying.

Confirm the fix by checking that exposed credentials are no longer accepted, and that MFA is enforced on all external services.

entries.title: Weak or Bypassable Physical Locks
entries.summary: Doors, cabinets or other physical barriers protecting sensitive areas use locks or fittings that can be opened quickly without the key or credential.
entries.description:
Locks and door hardware protecting sensitive areas or equipment could be opened or bypassed quickly without the key or access credential. Typical findings are latches that can be pushed back with a thin tool through the gap between door and frame (shimming or slipping); lever handles that can be operated from the other side of the door with a tool passed underneath it or through a letterbox; request-to-exit sensors that release a door when triggered from outside through a gap; push-bar exits that can be reached from outside; low-security cylinders and wafer locks that can be picked or bypassed in seconds; combination locks left at default codes; and network cabinets and server racks fitted with locks that share a widely available key.

Many of these weaknesses lie in how doors and fittings are installed rather than in the lock itself, and they bypass electronic access control entirely, leaving no record that the door was opened.

The finding is identified by inspecting doors, frames, locks and exit hardware on the routes to sensitive areas and, where agreed in scope, attempting non-destructive bypass techniques and recording how long each took.
entries.impact: An intruder can enter server rooms, network equipment rooms, offices and storage areas, or open cabinets, without leaving signs of forced entry and often without triggering any alarm. That gives direct access to equipment, data and storage media, and the opportunity to install covert network devices. The attacker must already be on site, often in a semi-public area, which limits the rating.
entries.remediation:
Assess the barriers on the route to each sensitive area as a whole, and strengthen the weakest point first:

  • Fit latch guards or anti-shim plates, and use deadlocking latches that cannot be pushed back once the door is closed.
  • Close gaps under and around doors with thresholds, door sweeps and seals, and protect inside lever handles where under-door tools could reach them.
  • Position and adjust request-to-exit sensors so that they cannot be triggered from outside, and protect push-bar exits from being reached through gaps.
  • Replace low-security cylinders and locks on sensitive doors and cabinets with products tested to a recognised security standard, using guidance such as that from the UK National Protective Security Authority (NPSA), with a restricted key system and a key register.
  • Change default combinations, and replace common keys on network cabinets and racks with unique or electronically controlled locks.
  • Fit door contacts and alarms to sensitive doors, so that opening without a valid access event is detected.

Confirm improvement by repeating the bypass attempts after the changes.

entries.title: Firmware Updates Not Signed or Verified
entries.summary: A device installs firmware updates without checking a cryptographic signature, so anyone able to supply an update can run their own code on it.
entries.description:
A firmware update mechanism should confirm, before installing an image, that it was produced by the manufacturer and has not been altered, normally by checking a digital signature against a public key held in protected storage on the device. Where the device accepts any correctly formatted image, or checks only a checksum such as a CRC or an unkeyed hash supplied with the image, anyone who can deliver an image can install modified firmware.

Updates reach devices in several ways, each with its own exposure: an image uploaded through the device's web or management interface, an image fetched automatically from the manufacturer over an unencrypted or unauthenticated connection, an update pushed by a management platform, or an image loaded from removable media or a service port. The weakness is identified by obtaining a genuine image, modifying it, for example by changing a file in its file system after unpacking it with tools such as binwalk, recalculating any checksums, and observing whether the device accepts it, or by intercepting the automatic update process. Reviewing the update code in the firmware can also show whether a signature is checked at all, and whether older, vulnerable images can be installed in place of newer ones.
entries.impact: An attacker able to supply an update, through an exposed management interface, by intercepting the device's update traffic, or with brief physical access, can install firmware of their choice. This gives complete and persistent control of the device that survives reboots and factory resets, which can be used to steal the data and credentials it handles, to change what it does, to attack other systems from a trusted position, or to make it permanently unusable. Where many devices share an update channel, one compromise of that channel can affect all of them. The attacker's route for delivering an image determines how easily this can be done.
entries.remediation:
• Sign every firmware image with a private key kept in a hardware security module or an equivalent protected signing service, and verify the signature on the device before any part of the image is written, using a public key held in read-only or otherwise protected memory.
  • Anchor the check in a secure boot chain, so that the bootloader also verifies the firmware at every start-up and a modified image cannot run even if it is written by another route.
  • Deliver updates over an authenticated, encrypted channel, such as TLS with certificate validation, while relying on the signature rather than the channel for integrity.
  • Prevent rollback to older, vulnerable versions with a version counter that the update process enforces.
  • Restrict who can trigger updates: require authenticated administrative access to update interfaces, and keep those interfaces off untrusted networks.

Where the devices are bought rather than built, raise the issue with the manufacturer and ask for signed updates. As an interim measure, restrict network access to the devices' management interfaces, obtain updates only from the manufacturer's official source over HTTPS, and check any published hash before installing. Confirm the fix by attempting to install a modified image again and checking that the device rejects it.

entries.title: Hard-Coded Credentials in Device Firmware
entries.summary: Device firmware contains fixed passwords, keys or tokens shared by every unit, which anyone who extracts them can use to access devices or the services they connect to.
entries.description:
Hard-coded credentials are passwords, private keys, API keys or tokens built into a device's firmware, rather than created for each device or set by its owner. Typical examples are a root or support account password in the firmware's /etc/shadow or /etc/passwd file, an account accepted by a Telnet, SSH or web service that the owner cannot change or disable, a private key for TLS or SSH shared by every device of the model, and credentials or keys that the device uses to reach the manufacturer's cloud services.

Because every unit runs the same image, the credentials are the same on every device, and anyone can recover them from a firmware image downloaded from the manufacturer's website, captured during an update, or read from the device's flash memory. The weakness is identified by extracting the file system with tools such as binwalk, searching it for password files, keys, configuration files and strings in binaries, cracking any password hashes found, and testing the recovered credentials against the device's services.
entries.impact: An attacker who recovers the credentials can use them against every device that runs the firmware, often with administrative or root access, to take control of the device, read the data it handles, change its behaviour or use it to reach other systems. Shared private keys let the attacker impersonate devices or decrypt their traffic, and embedded cloud credentials can expose the manufacturer's service and other customers' data. The owner usually cannot remove the credentials without a firmware fix. The effort needed depends on whether the credentials are stored in clear text or as hashes that must be cracked, and on whether the services that accept them are reachable.
entries.remediation:
The root cause lies in the firmware, so the full fix rests with the manufacturer or development team:

  • Remove all fixed passwords and shared keys from firmware. Require the owner to set a unique password on first use, or generate a unique password for each device during manufacture, and allow every account to be changed or disabled.
  • Generate keys and certificates on each device, or provision them individually during manufacture, and keep them in protected storage such as a secure element or TPM where the hardware has one.
  • Remove debug and support accounts, and the services that accept them such as Telnet, from production firmware.
  • Give each device its own credentials for cloud services, so that a key extracted from one device cannot be used to reach others or the wider service.
  • Scan firmware builds for embedded secrets before release.

For consumer products sold in the UK, the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure regime has prohibited universal default passwords since April 2024, and ETSI EN 303 645 sets the same expectation. Where the devices are bought rather than built, report the issue to the manufacturer and apply its fix when available; as an interim measure, change any credentials the device allows to be changed, disable unneeded services, and place the devices on a restricted network segment so that their services cannot be reached from user networks or the internet. Confirm the fix by examining the updated firmware and checking that the credentials are gone and no longer work.

entries.title: Hardware Debug Interfaces Accessible
entries.summary: A device's circuit board exposes debug interfaces such as UART, JTAG or SWD, giving anyone with physical access a console, memory access or a way to read and change the firmware.
entries.description:
Embedded devices are built with hardware debug interfaces for development and manufacturing: UART serial consoles, JTAG and Serial Wire Debug (SWD) for controlling the processor, and sometimes direct access to the flash memory chips. In production units these are often left active, with their pins brought out to labelled headers, unpopulated pads or test points on the circuit board.

A UART console commonly shows the boot process and offers a bootloader prompt, such as that of U-Boot, and a login prompt or root shell on the running system. JTAG and SWD, unless locked by the processor's security settings, allow the processor to be halted and its memory and flash to be read or written, which exposes the firmware, keys and credentials and can allow protections such as secure boot to be bypassed. The weakness is identified by opening the device, locating candidate pins from board markings and voltage measurements, or with tools such as JTAGulator, then connecting a USB serial adapter or debug probe and testing what access is offered.
entries.impact: An attacker with brief physical access and the casing open can obtain a shell or full control of the processor, extract the firmware and any secrets stored on the device, such as Wi-Fi keys, credentials, certificates and cloud access keys, and modify the firmware to keep control. Secrets shared by every unit, once extracted from one device, can be used against all of them remotely, which is often the most serious consequence. The need for physical access limits the threat for devices in secure locations, and raises it for devices installed in public places or on customer premises.
entries.remediation:
• Disable debug interfaces in production units: lock JTAG and SWD through the processor's debug protection settings, such as read-out protection levels or eFuses, before shipping, and remove or disable the UART console in production firmware and in the bootloader.
  • Where a console must remain for servicing, require authentication with a credential unique to each device, and disable the bootloader's interactive prompt or protect it with a password.
  • Remove debug headers and test points from production boards where possible, though this only slows an attacker and is not a control on its own.
  • Store secrets in a secure element or the processor's protected key storage rather than in readable flash, and avoid secrets shared across all units, so that extracting one device's contents does not compromise others.
  • Enable secure boot so that modified firmware cannot run.

Where the devices are bought rather than built, raise the issue with the manufacturer. As an interim measure, install devices where they cannot easily be reached, use tamper-evident seals or enclosures, and change any credentials that may have been extracted. Confirm the fix by connecting to the interfaces again and checking that no console, memory access or debug control is available.

entries.title: Unauthenticated Industrial Protocols Exposed
entries.summary: Industrial control devices accept read, write and control commands over protocols such as Modbus/TCP, DNP3 or S7comm from any host that can reach them, without authentication.
entries.description:
Many industrial protocols were designed for closed, trusted networks and have no authentication. Modbus/TCP (TCP 502), DNP3 (TCP 20000), Siemens S7comm (TCP 102), EtherNet/IP with CIP (TCP 44818) and BACnet/IP (UDP 47808), among others, accept commands from any device that can reach them. Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), remote terminal units, protection relays, building management controllers and protocol gateways will act on requests to read process values, write to registers and coils, change setpoints, download or upload control logic, or stop and start the controller, as far as the protocol and device support them.

Secure variants exist, such as DNP3 Secure Authentication, Modbus/TCP Security and CIP Security, as do access protection and password features in many controllers, but installed equipment often does not support them or they are not enabled.

The weakness is identified by scanning for these services and identifying devices with read-only queries, for example with Nmap scripts such as modbus-discover, s7-info, enip-info and bacnet-info, or with dedicated industrial security tools. On live industrial systems, testing is limited to passive or read-only checks agreed with the asset owner, as even well-formed requests can disrupt fragile devices.
entries.impact: An attacker who can reach these services, from the corporate network or wherever else they are exposed, can read process data and, with knowledge of the process, change setpoints, force outputs, alter or replace control logic, or stop controllers. The consequences extend beyond data: production can be halted, equipment damaged and, in safety-related processes, people or the environment harmed. Safety instrumented systems and physical interlocks may limit the worst outcomes, but should not be relied on as a defence against deliberate manipulation. Exposure to the internet greatly increases the likelihood of attack, as such services are routinely catalogued by internet-wide scanning.
entries.remediation:
• Make these services reachable only from the systems that need them, such as the engineering workstations, HMIs and historians in the same zone, with firewalls between the corporate and OT networks and within the OT network, following a zone and conduit model such as that of IEC 62443. Never expose them to the internet, and provide remote support through a secure remote access solution with multi-factor authentication.
  • Where the devices and protocols support it, enable authentication and integrity protection, such as DNP3 Secure Authentication, CIP Security, Modbus/TCP Security, or the controller's access protection and password features, and use key switches or equivalent controls that block program changes while the controller is running, where available.
  • Use industrial firewalls or protocol-aware gateways that allow only specific function codes, for example read-only Modbus functions from the historian, and permit programming and write commands only from engineering workstations.
  • Monitor OT networks with passive tools that understand industrial protocols, and alert on writes, logic downloads and stop commands from unexpected sources.

As an interim measure, block the industrial protocol ports at the boundary between corporate and OT networks. Confirm the fix by repeating read-only discovery from the corporate network and other untrusted networks and checking that the services can no longer be reached.

entries.title: OT Devices Reachable From the Corporate Network
entries.summary: Operational technology such as PLCs, HMIs and engineering workstations can be reached directly from the corporate network, without a controlled boundary between the two.
entries.description:
Operational technology (OT) networks contain the systems that monitor and control physical processes: programmable logic controllers, human-machine interfaces, engineering workstations, historians, safety systems and building management controllers. Recognised reference models, such as the Purdue model and the zones and conduits of IEC 62443, place a controlled boundary between the corporate (IT) network and OT, usually a demilitarised zone that holds shared systems such as historian replicas and remote access gateways, so that no traffic passes directly between the two.

The weakness is present where systems on the corporate network can connect directly to OT devices, because the networks are routed together without filtering, firewall rules permit broad access, dual-homed computers connect both networks, or remote access tools on OT systems bypass the boundary. It is identified by scanning OT address ranges from user and server networks, with care and the agreement of the asset owner, and finding industrial protocols, remote desktop, VNC, web interfaces or file shares on OT systems that respond.
entries.impact: An attacker who compromises a corporate system, for example through phishing, can reach industrial systems directly and attack them with the techniques used against IT systems, or through industrial protocols that often have no authentication. Ransomware and other malware can spread into OT, where systems are often older, harder to patch and slower to recover. The consequences can include loss of view and control of the process, production stoppages, equipment damage and safety incidents. The likelihood depends on the weaknesses of the OT systems that become reachable, which are frequently significant.
entries.remediation:
• Separate OT from the corporate network with a firewall-enforced boundary and an industrial demilitarised zone, so that corporate systems communicate only with systems in the DMZ and nothing routes directly between IT and OT.
  • Allow only documented, necessary flows across the boundary, each with a business reason, preferring connections initiated from the OT side, such as a historian sending data outwards.
  • Provide remote and vendor access through a dedicated, monitored gateway in the DMZ with multi-factor authentication and approval for each session, and remove remote access tools and dual network connections that bypass it.
  • Segment the OT network itself into zones according to function and criticality, as IEC 62443 describes.
  • Monitor traffic crossing the boundary and within OT with tools that understand industrial protocols.
  • Plan for the case where the corporate network is compromised, with the ability to isolate OT quickly while keeping the process running.

As an interim measure, block all traffic from corporate networks to OT ranges except specific, documented flows. Confirm the fix by repeating the scan from corporate networks and checking that no OT systems respond.
